Rain in Book 1 and just rule in Book 2 hold the same position: neither is itself virtue, but virtue does not continue without it.
links.reason: The sceptre stands as 'ஆதி' of 'நூற்கும் அறத்திற்கும்' and 'தானம் தவம்இரண்டும் தங்கா ... வானம் வழங்காதெனின்': each is a non-moral precondition without which virtue does not continue.

links.note: 543 speaks of 'அந்தணர் நூல்', which Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take as the Veda belonging to Brahmins. 30 defines அந்தணர் as the virtuous (அறவோர்), so called because they live in kindness to every living being. Read with 30, the phrase in 543 can mean the books of the virtuous, which is how Kalaignar takes it; the choice changes what the sceptre is said to uphold.
links.reason: The shared word அந்தணர் is defined in 30 as அறவோர் (செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுகலான்), which bears directly on அந்தணர் நூல் in 543; the commentators split as the note says (Parimelazhagar/Manakkudavar வேதம், Kalaignar அறவோர் நூல்).

links.note: 543 says the king's sceptre stands as the first ground (ஆதியாய் நின்றது) of the books of the அந்தணர் and of virtue. 560 gives the failing case: if the guardian does not guard, the yield of cows shrinks and those of the six occupations forget their books (அறுதொழிலோர் நூல் மறப்பர்). The claim that learning depends on rule is made once as a principle and once as a consequence.
links.reason: 'அந்தணர் நூற்கும் … ஆதியாய் நின்றது மன்னவன் கோல்' and 'அறுதொழிலோர் நூல்மறப்பர் காவலன் காவான் எனின்' state the dependence of learning on rule as principle and as failure case.

links.note: 544 says the world holds to the king who embraces his people. Parimelazhagar explains the embrace as speaking pleasantly and giving what is needed in hardship, which is what 387 names: to one able to give with pleasant words and protect (இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க), this world answers. 387 says how the embrace is done; 544 adds that it goes together with the sceptre.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does explain 'குடிதழீஇ' as 'இன்சொல் சொல்லுதலும், தளர்ந்துழி வேண்டுவன கொடுத்தலும்', which is 387's 'இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க', and both end with the world's adherence ('அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும் உலகு'). The identification rests on the commentator, as the note says.

links.note: 544: the world stands embracing the feet (அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும்) of the king who embraces his people (குடிதழீஇ) while wielding the sceptre. 1025: the world gathers round as kin (சுற்றமாச் சுற்றும் உலகு) the man who raises his family and lives without fault. In both the world's attachment is the return for care of one's own குடி, the word meaning the king's subjects in 544 and a man's family in 1025.
links.reason: 'குடிதழீஇ ... அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும் உலகு' and 'குடிசெய்து வாழ்வானைச் சுற்றமாச் சுற்றும் உலகு' both make the world's attachment the return for care of one's குடி, subjects in one and family in the other.

links.note: 545 ties rain to the king's right rule. 55 ties it to a wife's fidelity: she who rises worshipping her husband says 'rain' and it rains (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). In the household and in the kingdom the book makes rain answer to a person keeping to their proper role.
links.reason: 'கோலோச்சும் மன்னவன் நாட்ட பெயலும்' and 'பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை' both make rain answer to a person keeping their role, in kingdom and in household.

links.note: 545 says harvest (விளையுள்) comes with just rule. 239 says land that bears a body without renown declines in its blameless rich yield (வண்பயன் குன்றும்). Both let the moral state of people show in the fertility of the land; 239 does it for any person, 545 for the king.
links.reason: 'பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு' under a just king and 'வண்பயன் குன்றும் இசையிலா யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்' both let human moral standing show in the land's yield.

links.note: 545: rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who wields the sceptre as it should be (இயல்புளிக் கோலோச்சும்). 559: if the king acts bending justice (முறைகோடி), the sky bends its showers and does not rain (உறைகோடி). The two verses state one causal claim in both directions, and 559 echoes the bent sceptre in the bent rain.
links.reason: 'இயல்புளிக் கோலோச்சும் ... பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு' and 'முறைகோடி ... உறைகோடி ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்' state the same rule-and-rain causality in both directions.

links.note: 546's condition is that the கோல் does not bend (கோடாது). 118 praises not leaning to one side (ஒருபால் கோடாமை), like the கோல், here the balance beam, that first levels itself and then weighs. The same word and the same verb serve for the king's sceptre and the scales, so the straightness asked of the ruler is the impartiality asked of the worthy in Book 1.
links.reason: கோல் ... கோடாது of the sceptre and கோல்போல் ... ஒருபால் கோடாமை of the balance: same noun and verb for royal justice and personal impartiality.

links.note: 546 sets spear against sceptre: it is not the வேல் that gives victory but the king's கோல், if it does not bend. 552 uses the same pair to opposite effect: the demand of one who stands with a கோல் is like one standing with a வேல் and saying 'hand it over'. The sceptre is better than the spear only while straight; bent toward extortion, 552 says it is the spear.
links.reason: வேல் and கோல் are paired in both: வேலன்று வென்றி தருவது ... கோல் when கோடாது, and கோலொடு நின்றான் இரவு likened to வேலொடு நின்றான் இடுவென்றது. A distinctive shared pair used to opposite effect.

links.note: 547: the king guards the earth, and justice guards the king (இறை காக்கும் ... முறை காக்கும்). 57: what can the guard of confinement do? The guard that women keep by their own steadfastness is the chief guard (சிறை காக்கும் காப்பு ... நிறை காக்கும் காப்பே தலை). Both verses, in the same rhyming pattern, say that real protection comes from the guarded person's own conduct and not from outside force.
links.reason: இறைகாக்கும் ... முறைகாக்கும் and சிறைகாக்கும் ... நிறைகாக்கும் match in rhyme and in logic: what truly guards is the person's own முறை or நிறை. 'Not from outside force' is explicit only in 57, a small overstatement for 547.

links.note: 547 says justice protects the king if he does it without fail. 448 calls the king who has no one to rebuke him 'ஏமரா மன்னன்', a king without a guard, and says he perishes even with no one to ruin him. Together they name what guards a ruler: his own just practice and the people who correct him.
links.reason: 'அவனை முறைகாக்கும்' and 'இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத ஏமரா மன்னன்' (ஏமம் = guard) both name what protects the protector; pairing just practice with rebuking counsellors is instructive.

links.note: 548: a king who is not easy of access (எண்பதத்தான் in the negative, as Parimelazhagar construes it) and does not examine and do justice sinks and perishes. 386: a king easy to see (காட்சிக்கு எளியன்) and not harsh in speech has his land praised. Accessibility is stated as a virtue in chapter 39 and its lack as a cause of ruin in chapter 55.
links.reason: 'எண்பதத்தான்' (taken in the negative, as Parimelazhagar explains) and 'காட்சிக்கு எளியன்' state accessibility as a cause of ruin when absent and of praise when present.

links.note: 548 says the unjust, unapproachable king perishes of himself (தானே கெடும்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even without enemies'. 448 says the king with no one to rebuke him perishes though no one sets out to ruin him (கெடுப்பார் இலானும் கெடும்). Both describe a ruler's fall with no outside agent, caused by shutting out complaint in one case and criticism in the other.
links.reason: தானே கெடும் and கெடுப்பாரிலானும் கெடும்: a ruler ruined with no outside agent, by refusing access/justice in one and rebuke (இடிப்பார்) in the other.

links.note: 548 and 553 share most of a line: a king who does not examine and do justice (ஓரா / நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்). In 548 the king himself perishes; in 553 he loses his land day by day (நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்). The pairing shows the same neglect ruining the ruler and the country.
links.reason: 'ஓரா முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்' and 'நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்' are the same subject, with 'தானே கெடும்' in one and 'நாடு கெடும்' in the other; ruler and country ruined by the same neglect.

links.note: 314 tells a person how to punish those who hurt him: shame them by doing them good and let it go (அவர் நாண நன்னயம் செய்து விடல்). 549 says that for a king, guarding the people and removing offences (குற்றம் கடிதல்) is no stain but his work (வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்). The words 'no stain' answer the doubt that punishing goes against virtue, which Parimelazhagar spells out; 549 limits 314's rule to one's own injuries and exempts the office.
links.reason: 314's ஒறுத்தல் by 'நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்' against 549's 'குற்றம் கடிதல் வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்'; Parimelazhagar does raise and answer the doubt that punishing is a stain, as the note says.

links.note: 549 makes removing offences the king's work. 436 sets an order for it: if he first removes his own fault and then looks at others' (தன்குற்றம் நீக்கிப் பிறர்குற்றம் காண்கிற்பின்), what fault can attach to a ruler? The right to punish in 549 is, by 436, clear of blame only for a king who has corrected himself first.
links.reason: 549's 'குற்றம் கடிதல் வடுவன்று' is conditioned by 436's order 'தன்குற்றம் நீக்கிப் பிறர்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின் என்குற்றமாகும் இறைக்கு'.

links.note: 549 clears the punishing king of blame. 567 says harsh words and punishment that goes beyond bounds (கையிகந்த தண்டம்) are a file that wears down a king's strength to defeat enemies. Punishment is the king's work only within measure; past it, the same act damages him.
links.reason: 549: குற்றம் கடிதல் வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்; 567: கையிகந்த தண்டம் is the அரம் that wears down his அடுமுரண். A clean limit of measure on the first.

links.note: 550 justifies the king's use of death against the cruel (கொடியார்). 551 turns the same words on the king: one who takes up harassing his people and does wrong is crueller than those who have taken up murder (கொலைமேற்கொண்டாரிற் கொடிதே). Placed on either side of the chapter break, the two verses make the king both the one who removes the cruel and the one who can be the worst of them.
links.reason: கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல் and கொலைமேற்கொண்டாரிற் கொடிதே ... வேந்து reuse கொலை/கொடி/வேந்து across the chapter boundary, turning the measure onto the king himself.

links.note: 550 compares the king's execution of the cruel to weeding the green crop (பைங்கூழ் களைகட்டதனொடு நேர்). 1038, on farming itself, says that after weeding (கட்டபின்) guarding the crop is better than watering it. In the farmer's own chapter weeding is one step and guarding counts for more, which fits 549's order of guarding the people first and punishing second.
links.reason: The weeding figure is shared ('பைங்கூழ் களைகட்டதனொடு' / 'கட்டபின்'), but 1038 ranks காப்பு above நீர், not above weeding, so the note's claim that guarding outranks weeding and mirrors 549's order is not in the verse.

links.note: 483 asks whether anything called அருவினை exists for one who acts with கருவி and knowing காலம். 631 uses the same three words but keeps அருவினை as a separate item the minister must be good at. The pair shows where the minister's list comes from: tools and timing are what make a hard task doable.
links.reason: கருவி, காலம் and அருவினை appear in both; 483's rhetorical 'அருவினை யென்ப உளவோ' explains why the minister's list in 631 holds these items together.

links.note: 631 defines the minister as one excellent in கருவி, காலம், செய்கை and the அருவினை itself. 675 turns nearly the same list into a rule for anyone acting: பொருள், கருவி, காலம், வினை, இடன், 'ஐந்தும் இருள்தீர எண்ணிச் செயல்'. Read together, the minister's defining competence is the checklist of 675, with resources and place added there.
links.reason: கருவி, காலம், செய்கை/வினை appear in both lists; 675 adds பொருள் and இடன் and turns the list into a rule (இருள்தீர எண்ணிச் செயல்). The note describes both correctly.

links.note: 632 lists the minister's qualities: வன்கண், குடிகாத்தல், கற்றறிதல், ஆள்வினை. 382 lists the king's: அஞ்சாமை, ஈகை, அறிவு, ஊக்கம் (383 adds கல்வி and துணிவுடைமை). Firmness, knowledge and drive appear on both lists, so the minister is described on the king's pattern; Manakkudavar even glosses வன்கண் as அஞ்சாமை. Giving is on the king's list only.
links.reason: 'வன்கண் ... கற்றறிதல் ஆள்வினை' line up with 'அஞ்சாமை ... அறிவு ஊக்கம்', and Manakkudavar does gloss வன்கண் as அஞ்சாமை; the note also correctly marks ஈகை as the king's alone.

links.note: 187 says those who cannot make friends with pleasant talk 'கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர்', split even their own kin, by divisive speech. 633 uses the same verb, பிரித்தல், for a minister's skill, which Parimelazhagar restricts to detaching an enemy's allies. The same act is a fault at home and a craft in statecraft, and what differs is whose bond is being broken.
links.reason: கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர் in 187 and பிரித்தல் in 633 are the same act, a fault among one's own and a skill against an enemy's allies (Parimelazhagar's restriction is correctly reported). The contrast teaches something.

links.note: 633 names rejoining those who parted as a minister's skill. 530 says how the king should handle such a return: one who left (உழைப்பிரிந்து) and came back for a reason is to be taken in after thought, 'எண்ணிக் கொளல்'. The pair shows that பொருத்தல் is not unconditional welcome; 530 supplies the caution.
links.reason: 'பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்' as a skill meets 'உழைப்பிரிந்து காரணத்தின் வந்தானை … எண்ணிக் கொளல்', which adds deliberation before taking the returner in.

links.note: 633 says a minister must be able to divide (பிரித்தல்), keep his own side (பேணிக் கொளல்) and rejoin those who broke away (பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்). 679 ranks one such act: 'ஒட்டாரை ஒட்டிக் கொளல்', bringing the unattached over, is more urgent than doing good to friends. 679 gives a priority among the alliance skills that 633 only lists.
links.reason: 679 does rank alliance-making above 'நட்டார்க்கு நல்ல செயல்', but 'ஒட்டாரை ஒட்டிக் கொளல்' is about foes (or the foe's foes, per Parimelazhagar), not 633's 'பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்'; the note's 'unattached' and 'one such act' blur that.

links.note: 462 tells the one acting that nothing is out of reach if he examines with a chosen circle and thinks it over himself: 'தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணிச் செய்வார்க்கு'. 634 describes the minister with the same two verbs, தெரிதல் and தேர்ந்து செயல். The pairing shows the two sides of one arrangement: 462 is the ruler's need for such company, 634 is what that company must be able to do.
links.reason: Both verses use the roots தெரி and தேர் (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி / தெரிதலும் தேர்ந்து செயலும்); 462's 'chosen company' is plausibly the ministerial circle whose abilities 634 lists. In 462 தெரிந்த means 'chosen', a small looseness in 'same two verbs'.

links.note: 634 asks of a minister தெரிதல், தேர்ந்து செயல் and 'ஒருதலையாச் சொல்லல்', speaking so that the matter is settled. 671 says 'சூழ்ச்சி முடிவு துணிவெய்தல்': deliberation ends in reaching a resolve, and letting that resolve linger is a fault. Parimelazhagar glosses ஒருதலையாச் சொல்லல் as speaking so that துணிவு arises, which makes the minister's decisive word the point where 671's deliberation closes.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does gloss 'ஒருதலையாச் சொல்லல்' as speaking so that 'துணிவு பிறக்கும் வகை', which matches 671's 'சூழ்ச்சி முடிவு துணிவெய்தல்'. His gloss is narrower (about dividing or uniting others) than the note suggests, but ஒருதலை itself supports the link.

links.note: 441 tells the king to choose the friendship of those who are 'அறனறிந்து மூத்த அறிவுடையார்', 'திறனறிந்து தேர்ந்து'. 635 describes the counsel-companion in the same words: 'அறனறிந்து ... திறனறிந்தான் தேர்ச்சித் துணை'. 441 is the instruction to seek such a person and 635 is the portrait of him, with settled speech (ஆன்றமைந்த சொல்) added.
links.reason: The shared 'அறனறிந்து … திறனறிந்து … தேர்' vocabulary links the instruction to choose such men (441) with the portrait of the 'தேர்ச்சித் துணை' (635).

links.note: 635 asks for one who knows அறன், has full and settled speech, and knows திறன். 644 joins the same three terms in one rule: 'திறனறிந்து சொல்லுக சொல்லை', since no அறன் or பொருள் is beyond that. The next chapter thus takes the speech item of 635 and makes fitted speech itself the place where knowing virtue and knowing method show.
links.reason: அறன், சொல், திறனறிந்து do recur, but திறன் in 635 is the minister's knowledge of how to act and in 644 it is fitting speech to the hearer, and 644 says only that no அறன் or பொருள் exceeds such speech. The claim that fitted speech is 'where knowing virtue and method show' goes beyond the Tamil.

links.note: 636 asks what subtle scheme can stand before those who have மதிநுட்பம் together with நூல். 373 says that however many subtle books one studies (நுண்ணிய நூல்பல கற்பினும்), one's own உண்மை அறிவு still prevails. 373 explains why 636 puts native subtlety first and adds books 'ஓடு': study does not replace the native intelligence, so the combination is not open to everyone who reads. Parimelazhagar ties 373's native understanding to ஊழ்.
links.reason: மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு in 636 and நுண்ணிய நூல்பல கற்பினும் ... உண்மையறிவே மிகும் in 373 both rank native understanding against book learning, and 373 does limit what நூல் alone can supply. Note's commentary citation is accurate.

links.note: 636 implies that nothing withstands the person who has native subtlety and learning. 503 says that even in those who have studied hard texts and are free of fault (அரியகற்று ஆசற்றார்), close examination rarely finds no blankness: 'இன்மை அரிதே வெளிறு'. The praise in 636 concerns outwitting opposing schemes; 503 limits it, since the learned still have gaps.
links.reason: 636's rhetorical 'யாவுள முன்நிற்பவை' praises wit plus learning against opposing schemes, while 503's 'இன்மை அரிதே வெளிறு' is about residual ignorance found when vetting; they touch the limits of learning but 503 does not really condition 636's claim.

links.note: 637 says that even when one knows the செயற்கை, which Parimelazhagar takes as the method taught in treatises, one should act knowing the உலகத்து இயற்கை. 140, in the chapter on conduct, says those who have not learned 'உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்' are without understanding though they have learned much (பலகற்றும்). The same ranking of learning below fit with the world appears once for personal conduct and once for a minister's action.
links.reason: உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல் even after knowing செயற்கை; உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல் கல்லார் are அறிவிலாதார் though பலகற்றும். Same ranking in a minister's action and in personal conduct.

links.note: 426 defines அறிவு as living with the world in the way the world lives: 'உலகத்தோடு அவ்வது உறைவது'. 637 gives the working form of this for one who already knows the method: 'உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்'. Together they treat attention to how the world actually goes as part of knowledge and not a concession against it.
links.reason: 'உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்' and 'உலகத்தோடு அவ்வது உறைவது அறிவு' both make conformity to how the world goes part of knowing, for the minister and as a definition of அறிவு.

links.note: 638 makes it the duty (கடன்) of the one at the king's side to say what is sound (உறுதி) even if the king rejects knowledge and knows nothing himself. 448 gives the stake: a king without those who rebuke, 'இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத ஏமரா மன்னன்', perishes even with no one to ruin him. 448 shows why 638 does not release the minister when the king will not listen.
links.reason: 'உறுதி உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்' even to an 'அறிகொன்று அறியான்' is explained by the stake in 'இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத … கெடும்'.

links.note: 638 obliges the minister to speak sound counsel regardless of the king's reception. 696 governs the manner: knowing the king's mood and considering the time, say what is needed without what is disliked, so that it is wanted ('வெறுப்பில வேண்டுப வேட்பச் சொலல்'). The duty of 638 stands, and 696 conditions how and when it is discharged.
links.reason: 638 makes 'உறுதி கூறல்' a 'கடன்' whatever the king's reception; 696 conditions the delivery with 'குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி ... வேட்பச் சொலல்'. A genuine qualification of manner, not of the duty.

links.note: 849 says 'காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான்': one who tries to show something to a person who does not see ends up not seeing himself, while the other keeps to what he saw. 638 requires exactly this of a minister when the king 'அறிகொன்று அறியான்'. The conflict holds if 849 is read as general advice not to instruct the conceited; Parimelazhagar reads it as a report that the instructor is reviled, which would leave 638 as a duty carried at that cost.
links.reason: 'அறிகொன்று அறியான் எனினும் … கூறல் கடன்' requires what 'காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான்' says rebounds on the instructor; the note states which reading makes it a conflict and gives Parimelazhagar's 'பழிக்கப்பட்டு' reading correctly.

links.note: 639 and 817 use the same construction and the same kind of figure: 'மந்திரியின் ... எழுபது கோடி உறும்' and 'நட்பின் பகைவரால் பத்தடுத்த கோடி உறும்'. In both an inflated count of open enemies is set against one false intimate, a plotting minister in 639 and a friend good only for laughter in 817. Parimelazhagar reads உறும் in 639 as 'that many enemies will come', and notes others read it as 'that many times better', which is how 817 is read.
links.reason: Both end '…இன் … கோடி உறும்', setting crores on the open-enemy side against one false intimate (பழுதெண்ணும் மந்திரி / நகைவகையர் நட்பு). Small imprecision: in 817 the crores count times-better, not enemies, and Parimelazhagar's 'உறுவர்' in 639 is closer to 'are equal to' than 'will come'.
links.text_issue: 639 prints பக்கததுள் for பக்கத்துள்.

links.note: 639 says seventy crore enemies are better than a minister at one's side who plots harm ('பழுதெண்ணும் மந்திரி'). 882 gives the general rule: do not fear enemies like swords, fear the bond of enemies who are like kin ('கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு'). Parimelazhagar explains 639 on the same ground, that open enemies can be guarded against and the one inside cannot.
links.reason: 'பழுதெண்ணும் மந்திரி' at one's side being worse than 'தெவ்வோர் எழுபது கோடி' is a case of 882's 'கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு' being feared over 'வாள்போல பகைவர்'; Parimelazhagar explains 639 by உட்பகை as the note says.
links.text_issue: 639 is printed 'பக்கததுள்' for 'பக்கத்துள்'.

links.note: 640 says those without திறப்பாடு leave things unfinished even after planning them in proper order ('முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே செய்வர்'). 664 says saying is easy for anyone and doing as said is hard ('சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்'). Both locate failure in the gap between a correct plan and its execution; Parimelazhagar glosses the 'saying' of 664 as stating in order how the task will be done.
links.reason: 'முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே செய்வர்' and 'அரியவாம் சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்' both put failure between plan and execution; Parimelazhagar's 'நிரல்படச் சொல்லுதல்' on 664 is as cited.

links.note: 640 says sound planning comes to nothing in those who lack the capacity to carry it through. 728 says those who have learned many things are of no use ('பயமிலரே') if they cannot speak well and tellingly in a good assembly. The same pattern appears in two domains: knowledge or planning is counted worthless without the ability that delivers it.
links.reason: முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே ... திறப்பாடு இலாதவர் and பல்லவை கற்றும் பயமிலரே ... செலச்சொல்லாதார் share the 'though X, useless without the delivering skill' pattern in action and in speech.

links.note: 595 says a person's height matches their inner drive, as a water-flower's stem matches the water: 'உள்ளத்து அனையது உயர்வு'. 971 opens the chapter on greatness by calling that same inner abundance (உள்ள வெறுக்கை) one's light. Both make standing a function of spirit and not of circumstance.
links.reason: உள்ள வெறுக்கை is ஒளி in 971; உள்ளத்தனையது உயர்வு in 595. Both tie standing to ஊக்கம், across the chapters on energy and greatness.

links.note: 971 says 'ஒளி ஒருவற்கு உள்ள வெறுக்கை' and 600 says 'உரம் ஒருவற்கு உள்ள வெறுக்கை': the same phrase, abundance of spirit, is called a person's light in one and a person's strength in the other. Each then states the lack: living without it is disgrace (இளி) in 971, and those without it are trees in 600. The repetition shows the chapter on greatness resting on the earlier chapter on ஊக்கம்.
links.reason: The identical phrase 'ஒருவற்கு உள்ள வெறுக்கை' is predicated of ஒளி in 971 and உரம் in 600, each followed by the verdict on those lacking it (இளி / மரம்).

links.note: 133 says having conduct is what good family is ('ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை') and a lapse becomes low birth. 972 says birth is equal and distinction follows from deeds. Both move rank from descent to what a person does, though 133 keeps the vocabulary of birth and Parimelazhagar reads it within varna.
links.reason: ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை / இழுக்கம் இழிந்த பிறப்பு and சிறப்பொவ்வா செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான் both tie rank to conduct; the note rightly flags that 133 keeps birth vocabulary and Parimelazhagar reads it within வருணம்.

links.note: 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction differs 'செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான்', by the difference in what they do. 505 gives the test: for greatness and for smallness, one's own deeds are the touchstone ('தத்தம் கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்'). 505 is the practical form of 972, used when choosing whom to trust; Parimelazhagar uses the word கட்டளைக் கல் in his note on 972.
links.reason: 972's 'சிறப்பொவ்வா செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான்' and 505's 'தத்தம் கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்' both measure greatness and smallness by deeds, and Parimelazhagar does call the differences of work 'பெருமை சிறுமைகட்குக் கட்டளைக் கல்' on 972.

links.note: 972 says 'பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும்'. 951 says uprightness and shame are found together naturally only in those born in a good house: 'இற்பிறந்தார்கண் அல்லது இல்லை இயல்பாக'. The conflict holds when பிறப்பு in 972 is read as social birth, as Manakkudavar does (greatness is not known by குலம்); Parimelazhagar avoids it by reading 972 as the common fact of embodied birth, with differences of work still falling by varna.
links.reason: பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் against இற்பிறந்தார்கண் அல்லது இல்லை இயல்பாக. Conflict holds on Manakkudavar's reading (பெருமை குலத்தினால் அறியப்படாது); the note correctly reports how Parimelazhagar avoids it.

links.note: 973 says those who are not high are not high even when seated high, and those who are not low are not low when seated low ('மேலிருந்தும் ... கீழிருந்தும்'). 409 uses the same frame for learning: the unlearned, though 'மேற்பிறந்தார்', do not have the standing of the learned who are 'கீழ்ப்பிறந்தும்'. In both, an outward high or low position fails to settle worth; 409 names learning as what does.
links.reason: மேலிருந்தும் / கீழிருந்தும் and மேற்பிறந்தாராயினும் / கீழ்ப்பிறந்தும் use the same high-low frame to deny that position or birth settles worth; 409 names கல்வி as the measure. Accurate.

links.note: 751 says nothing but wealth makes people of no account into people of account ('பொருளல்லவரைப் பொருளாகச் செய்யும்'). 973 says the not-high do not become high by being placed high, which Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read as a seat given by wealth. On that reading 973 limits 751: wealth gets a person regarded, and it does not make them great.
links.reason: பொருளல்லவரைப் பொருளாகச் செய்யும் is limited by மேலிருந்தும் மேலல்லார் மேலல்லர்; both commentators do take the high seat as one given by wealth (செல்வ நல்குரவுகளும்; செல்வத்தினால் இருக்குமிடம்), and the note says the link rests on that reading.

links.note: 57 says confinement does little and the guard a woman keeps by her own steadfastness is the chief guard ('நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பே தலை'). 974 takes this as its comparison: like single-minded women, greatness exists only 'தன்னைத்தான் கொண்டொழுகின்', if one keeps hold of oneself. 974 carries 57's claim about self-guarding into the Porul chapter on greatness, so that greatness, like கற்பு, cannot be kept for someone from outside.
links.reason: 974's own simile 'ஒருமை மகளிரே போல … தன்னைத்தான் கொண்டொழுகின்' points straight at 57's 'நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பே தலை'; the self-guarding idea is carried over explicitly.

links.note: 974 says greatness exists only as long as one keeps oneself. 965 shows the loss: even those like a hill sink if they do a lowering thing the size of a குன்றி seed. Together they present greatness as a condition that continues only through conduct and can be forfeited by a small act.
links.reason: 974: பெருமை exists only if தன்னைத்தான் கொண்டொழுகின்; 965: even குன்றின் அனையார் sink for a குன்றி-sized lowering act. Together: standing is kept by conduct and lost by small lapses.

links.note: 26 says those who do what is hard to do are great and those who cannot are small ('செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர்'). 975 says those who have greatness accomplish 'அருமை உடைய செயல்' and do so 'ஆற்றின்', by the proper way. The claim made of renouncers in Book 1 returns in the Porul chapter on greatness with the added condition of right method; Parimelazhagar cites 26 in this chapter.
links.reason: 'செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர்' returns as 'பெருமை யுடையவர் ஆற்றுவார் ... அருமை உடைய செயல்' with 'ஆற்றின்' added; Parimelazhagar does cite Kural 26 in chapter 98 (under 971) and glosses ஆற்றின் as 'செய்யும் நெறியால்'.

links.note: 975 says the great carry out hard deeds 'ஆற்றின்', in the right way. 468 states the other side with the same word: effort not made in the right way ('ஆற்றின் வருந்தா வருத்தம்') collapses even if many stand guard over it. The pair shows that ஆற்றின் in 975 carries weight: hard deeds done by the wrong route fail.
links.reason: ஆற்றின் in both: the great accomplish hard deeds ஆற்றின்; ஆற்றின் வருந்தா வருத்தம் fails (பொத்துப்படும்) however many guard it. The pairing gives weight to the adverb in 975.

links.note: 443 calls it the rarest of rare things to cherish the great and make them one's own: 'பெரியாரைப் பேணித் தமராக் கொளல்'. 976 uses the same words and says the aim 'பெரியாரைப் பேணிக் கொள்வேம்' does not even occur in the minds of the small. 976 gives one reason the thing is rare: the difficulty starts with not wanting it.
links.reason: Same phrase பெரியாரைப் பேணிக் கொள்: 443 calls it அரியவற்றுள் எல்லாம் அரிது, 976 says the very நோக்கு is absent from சிறியார் உணர்ச்சி. A fair account of why it is rare.

links.note: 451 says greatness fears small company while smallness takes it as kin ('சுற்றமாச் சூழ்ந்து விடும்'). 976 says the small have no thought of attaching themselves to the great. Both describe the same sorting from two ends: the small seek their own kind and do not look upward.
links.reason: 451's 'சிறுமைதான் சுற்றமாச் சூழ்ந்து விடும்' and 976's 'பெரியாரைப் பேணிக் கொள்வேம் என்னும் நோக்கு ... இல்லை' are the two halves of one sorting: the small take the small as kin and have no aim of attaching to the great.

links.note: 977 says even distinction (சிறப்பு), if it falls to the unworthy, results in acts of excess ('இறப்பே புரிந்த தொழிற்று'). 838 says a fool getting something in hand is like a man already deranged getting drunk. Both say a good thing makes its holder worse when the holder is unfit; 838 says it of possessions and a fool, 977 of distinction and the small. Manakkudavar reads the சிறப்பு of 977 as wealth, which brings the two closer.
links.reason: 977's 'சிறப்புந்தான் சீரல்லவர்கண் படின்' and 838's 'பேதை தன் கையொன்று உடைமை பெறின்' share the pattern of a good thing worsening an unfit holder; Manakkudavar does gloss சிறப்பு as செல்வம்.

links.note: 1000 says great wealth obtained by one without பண்பு is like good milk turned by the fault of its vessel. 977 says distinction landing on the unworthy produces excess. The logic is the same, that the recipient's quality decides what a gift becomes, but 1000 has the wealth spoiled and useless while 977 has the distinction turn into overbearing action.
links.reason: Both turn on a good thing landing with an unfit holder: சிறப்பு 'சீரல்லவர்கண் படின்' becomes இறப்பே புரிந்த தொழில், and பெருஞ்செல்வம் of the பண்பிலான் spoils like நன்பால் through கலந்தீமை. The note states the difference in outcome correctly.

links.note: 125 says bowing is good for everyone and for the wealthy it is a further wealth. 978 says greatness bows and smallness decks itself out in self-admiration. Both attach humility to those who have most reason for pride; Parimelazhagar glosses the பணிதல் of 125 as being without பெருமிதம், the word 979 uses.
links.reason: 'பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை' and 'பணிதல் ... செல்வர்க்கே செல்வம் தகைத்து' both put bowing where pride would be expected; Parimelazhagar does gloss பணிதல் in 125 as 'பெருமிதம் இன்றி அடங்குதல்'.

links.note: 439 commands 'வியவற்க எஞ்ஞான்றும் தன்னை', never admire yourself, among faults a ruler must avoid. 978 uses the same verb to define smallness: 'அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து'. What 439 forbids as a fault, 978 treats as the mark by which the small are known.
links.reason: 'வியவற்க எஞ்ஞான்றும் தன்னை' and 'அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து' use the same verb and object; the forbidden fault of 439 becomes the defining mark of சிறுமை in 978.

links.note: 978 says greatness bows always ('பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை'). 963 says bowing is needed in abundance and standing tall is needed in reduced circumstances ('சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு'). Taken plainly, 963 limits the என்றும் of 978; Parimelazhagar reads என்றும் in 978 as 'even when distinction has come', which makes the two verses say the same thing about prosperity.
links.reason: 963 splits what 978 states with 'என்றும்': 'பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல் ... சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு'. Parimelazhagar does read என்றும் as 'அச்சிறப்பு உண்டாய ஞான்றும்', and the note gives both the plain and the harmonised reading.

links.note: 979 defines greatness as the absence of பெருமிதம் and smallness as riding it to the end. 431 uses the same word with approval: the prosperity of those free of செருக்கு, anger and சிறுமை is 'பெருமித நீர்த்து', which Parimelazhagar glosses as having the quality of eminence. The word means conceit in 979 and dignity in 431, and both verses agree that the person without pride is the one who has real stature.
links.reason: பெருமிதம் is conceit in 979 (பெருமிதம் இன்மை) and eminence in 431 (பெருமித நீர்த்து), yet 431 gives it only to those செருக்கு ... இல்லார், so the two converge as the note says.

links.note: 844 defines வெண்மை, poor understanding, as the pride that says 'we have brightness' ('ஒண்மை உடையம் யாம் என்னும் செருக்கு'). 979 defines smallness as being carried away by பெருமிதம். In both a defect is identified with the claim to its opposite: the foolish are those sure of their intelligence, and the small are those sure of their greatness.
links.reason: 979 defines சிறுமை as 'பெருமிதம் ஊர்ந்து விடல்' and 844 defines வெண்மை as 'ஒண்மை உடையம்யாம் என்னும் செருக்கு': in both the defect is the proud claim to its opposite, across two domains.

links.note: 846 and 980 share the words அற்றம், மறை and குற்றம். In 846 covering one's own nakedness is itself poor understanding while one's faults stay uncovered, which Parimelazhagar takes as faults not removed. In 980 greatness covers the அற்றம் of others. The image of covering what is exposed is used for self-deception in one verse and for consideration toward others in the other.
links.reason: The shared அற்றம் / மறை / குற்றம் is used for covering others' exposure in 980 and for covering only one's own body in 846; Parimelazhagar's 'குற்றம் மறைத்தலாவது அவற்றை இலவாக்குதல்' is as cited.

links.note: 984 says fullness of character lies in the goodness of not telling others' evil ('பிறர் தீமை சொல்லா நலத்தது சால்பு'). 980 says greatness covers another's weakness (அற்றம் மறைக்கும்) and smallness only tells faults. The next chapter repeats the claim for சால்பு, and 980 goes a step further than 984 by speaking of covering and not only of keeping silent.
links.reason: 'அற்றம் மறைக்கும் பெருமை' and 'பிறர்தீமை சொல்லா நலத்தது சால்பு' make the same claim in adjacent chapters, and the note rightly sees that மறைக்கும் goes beyond சொல்லா.

links.note: 1079 says the base, on merely seeing others clothed and fed, are able to find a blemish in them ('வடுக்காண வற்றாகும் கீழ்'). 980 says smallness tells only faults ('குற்றமே கூறி விடும்'). 1079 adds a cause the Tamil of 980 leaves out: Parimelazhagar reads the fault-finding of the base as coming from being unable to bear others' prosperity.
links.reason: சிறுமை குற்றமே கூறி விடும் and கீழ் ... வடுக்காண வற்றாகும் make the same claim about the low; 1079 adds the trigger (seeing others உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம்), which Parimelazhagar glosses with பொறாது.

links.note: 1091 says the same eyes hold the look that makes him ill and the look that cures it. 15 says rain is both what ruins ('கெடுப்பதூஉம்') and what, as support to the ruined, lifts them again ('எடுப்பதூஉம்'). In both, one source is credited with the harm and with its remedy, once in love and once in the world's subsistence.
links.reason: 'நோய்நோக்கு … அந்நோய் மருந்து' in one pair of eyes matches 'கெடுப்பதூஉம் … எடுப்பதூஉம் எல்லாம் மழை': one source of harm and remedy, in love and in subsistence.

links.note: 1091 finds two looks in her kohl-lined eyes, one a 'நோய்நோக்கு' and the other 'அந்நோய் மருந்து'. 1102 states the general rule that a disease's medicine is something else ('பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிற') and then the exception: she is herself the medicine for the disease she causes ('தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து'). 1102 turns the glance-level observation of 1091 into an explicit paradox about cause and cure being one.
links.reason: 'நோய்நோக்கொன் றந்நோய் மருந்து' in her two glances becomes the explicit paradox 'தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து' set against 'பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிற'.

links.note: 1090 says brewed liquor gladdens only those who drink it and does not, like love, gladden those who merely see ('கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல்'). 1092 puts a measure on that: the small look her eyes steal ('கண்களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம்') is not an even half of love but more ('செம்பாகம் அன்று பெரிது'). Together they make sight alone a large share of love's pleasure; Parimelazhagar takes the 'half' in 1092 to be half of physical union.
links.reason: கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல் in 1090 makes sight a source of love's pleasure, and 1092 measures it: சிறுநோக்கம் is காமத்தில் செம்பாகம் அன்று பெரிது. Adjacent chapters, a real step from one to the other.

links.note: 1092 ranks a brief stolen look as more than half of love. 1326 ranks sulking above union ('புணர்தலின் ஊடல் இனிது'), as digesting is sweeter than eating. Both verses place the greater part of love's pleasure in something beside the embrace, one before it and one around it.
links.reason: சிறுநோக்கம் ... செம்பாகம் அன்று பெரிது and புணர்தலின் ஊடல் இனிது do both place love's larger share outside union, but both are in the same domain (காமம்), so this is two verses making a similar claim, not a pattern carried into another domain.

links.note: In 1093 her look followed by a lowered head is 'water she poured' ('அட்டிய நீர்') into the 'யாப்பு', which Parimelazhagar reads as the crop of love binding the two. 718 says speaking before those able to understand is like pouring water into the bed of something already growing ('வளர்வதன் பாத்தியுள் நீர்சொரிந்தற்று'). Both use watering for a sign or word given to someone already receptive: the gesture or speech does not start the growth, it feeds it.
links.reason: 'யாப்பினுள் அட்டிய நீர்' and 'வளர்வதன் பாத்தியுள் நீர்சொரிந்தற்று' both pour water on something already growing, for a sign and for speech to the receptive.

links.note: 1093 makes her shy look the water that feeds their bond. In 1147 the woman says her sickness grows long with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water ('அன்னைசொல் நீராக நீளும் இந்நோய்'). The same cultivation figure serves first for what encourages love and later for what, meant to check it, only makes its pain grow.
links.reason: 'யாப்பினுள் அட்டிய நீர்' and 'அன்னைசொல் நீராக நீளும் இந்நோய்' both water a growing love as a crop; the contrast of encouragement and failed restraint is accurate.

links.note: In 1094 she looks at the ground when he looks at her ('நிலன்நோக்கும்') and looks at him and smiles when he does not. In 1114 the blue lilies, if they could see, would bend and look at the ground ('கவிழ்ந்து நிலன்நோக்கும்') because they cannot match her eyes. The identical phrase marks shyness in the first verse and conceded defeat in the second; Parimelazhagar glosses both as bowing from நாண்.
links.reason: The identical 'நிலன்நோக்கும்' is the girl's shyness in 1094 and the lilies' bowed defeat in 1114; Parimelazhagar attributes both to நாண் (1094 heading, 'அந்நாணினால்' in 1114).

links.note: 1096: though they speak like those unattached ('உறாஅதவர்போல் சொலினும்'), the words of those without anger are quickly understood ('செறாஅர்சொல் ஒல்லை உணரப்படும்'). 826 has the same frame reversed: though they say good things like friends ('நட்டார்போல் நல்லவை சொல்லினும்'), the words of the unreconciled are quickly understood ('ஒட்டார்சொல் ஒல்லை உணரப்படும்'). The shared wording shows one claim applied in love and in statecraft: a spoken mask, harsh or kind, does not long hide the disposition behind it.
links.reason: The frames are nearly identical: '...போல் சொலினும் செறாஅர்சொல் ஒல்லை உணரப்படும்' and 'நட்டார்போல் ... சொல்லினும் ஒட்டார்சொல் ஒல்லை உணரப்படும்', reversed between love and false friendship.

links.note: 709 says the eye itself tells enmity and friendship, if one has people who understand the eye's kinds ('கண்ணின் வகைமை உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்'). 1097 is a case that needs that skill: here a look like an enemy's is a mark of closeness, not of enmity. The pairing shows why 709 adds its condition; a hostile look cannot be taken at face value.
links.reason: 709 conditions the eye's testimony on கண்ணின் வகைமை உணர்வார்; 1097's செற்றார்போல் நோக்கும் as உற்றார் குறிப்பு is exactly a look that misleads without that skill. Both sit in chapters titled குறிப்பறிதல்.

links.note: 1097 lists small harsh words spoken without anger and looks like an enemy's ('செற்றார்போல் நோக்கும்') as the signs of those who are close while seeming distant. 824 warns of the opposite pairing: a sweet smile on the face with bitterness inside ('முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா'). In both the surface is the reverse of the heart; the lover reads the mismatch with relief, the Book of Wealth reads it with fear.
links.reason: 'செற்றார்போல் நோக்கும் ... உறாஅர்போன்று உற்றார்' and 'முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா' are mirror cases of surface reversing heart, read with relief in one book and fear in the other.

links.note: In 1098, when he looks she softens and smiles gently ('பசையினள் பைய நகும்'), and he says there is a certain grace in her then ('உண்டு ஆண்டு ஓர் ஏஎர்'). 1274 says there is something inside the bud of her smile, like scent inside a closed bud ('நகைமொக்குள் உள்ளதொன்று உண்டு'). Both treat her slight smile as holding an unspoken meaning, and both leave that meaning as an unnamed 'something'.
links.reason: Both find an unnamed 'something' in her slight smile, each with உண்டு: 'உண்டாண்டோர் ஏஎர் ... பைய நகும்' and 'நகைமொக்குள் உள்ளதொன் றுண்டு'.

links.note: 1099 says looking at each other with the common look, like strangers ('ஏதிலார் போலப் பொதுநோக்கு நோக்குதல்'), is found in lovers. 528 uses the same word for a king: he should not look on all in common ('பொதுநோக்கான்') but by rank, and many will live looking to that. In 528 the undifferentiated look is a failure to distinguish; in 1099 it is put on deliberately by the two people who distinguish each other most.
links.reason: பொதுநோக்கு is a rare shared term: lovers put it on (ஏதிலார் போலப் பொதுநோக்கு நோக்குதல்) and a king should not look that way (பொதுநோக்கான் ... வரிசையா நோக்கின்). The note reads both correctly and the contrast is meaningful.

links.note: 1100: when eyes agree with eyes in their look, spoken words are of no use at all ('வாய்ச்சொற்கள் என்ன பயனும் இல'). 705, in the Book of Wealth's chapter of the same name, asks what use eyes are among the limbs if they cannot read a sign by a sign ('என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்'). Both hold that the eye is the organ for knowing another's mind; 705 says so for court service and 1100 for lovers, where it makes speech redundant.
links.reason: Both verses of same-named chapters turn on 'என்ன பயன்': eyes useless if they cannot read 'குறிப்பிற் குறிப்பு', words useless once 'நோக்கொக்கின்'. The eye as the organ of knowing another's mind appears in court and in love.

links.note: 1100 says that once the eyes agree, words from the mouth serve no purpose. 1280 says that telling love's sickness with the eyes and pleading ('கண்ணினால் காமநோய் சொல்லி இரவு') adds womanhood to womanhood. 1280 moves from the fact that eyes can replace speech to praise of the woman who chooses to speak that way.
links.reason: 1100's eyes that make 'வாய்ச்சொற்கள்' useless become in 1280 a chosen mode of speech, 'கண்ணினால் காமநோய் சொல்லி இரவு', praised as 'பெண்ணினால் பெண்மை'.

links.note: 1151 tells him to announce his quick return to those who will be alive then ('வாழ்வார்க்கு உரை'), implying she will not be. 1160 says many consent to the hard thing, endure the parting and live on afterwards ('பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்'); Parimelazhagar reads this as her ironic reply to the friend, meaning she is not one of them. The chapter opens and closes on the same word, 'வாழ்வார்', for the survivors she sets herself apart from.
links.reason: 'வாழ்வார்க் குரை' and 'பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்' frame the chapter with the same word for survivors; Parimelazhagar does give 1160 as her reply to the friend, and 1151 as implying she will not live.

links.note: In 1151 the speaker (the friend for Parimelazhagar, the woman for Manakkudavar) says a promise of quick return is only for those who will survive. In 1263 the woman, after he has gone, says she is still alive through wanting his return ('வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்'). The later speech shows the claim of 1151 as said in the moment: the hope of return that was dismissed there is what keeps her alive here.
links.reason: 1151 dismisses 'வல்வரவு' as news only for 'வாழ்வார்'; in 1263 she says 'வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்', alive by exactly that hope (Parimelazhagar: without it she would die). The later verse limits the earlier claim, as the note says.

links.note: 1152 says union now carries the fear of separation. 1276 gives the reason in a concrete case: his very soothing and eager lovemaking ('பெரிதாற்றிப் பெட்பக் கலத்தல்') contains something that makes her think of his lack of love and of having to endure again; Parimelazhagar and Kalaignar take it as her reading his intention to leave. 1276 shows how the union itself becomes the sign she fears in 1152.
links.reason: பிரிவஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு in 1152 is made concrete in 1276, where பெரிதாற்றிப் பெட்பக் கலத்தல் itself அன்பின்மை சூழ்வது உடைத்து. The note reports the commentators correctly.

links.note: 1152: once even his look was pleasant, but now union itself holds the pain of fearing separation ('பிரிவஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு'). 1295: her heart fears not having him and, having him, fears parting ('பெறின் பிரிவு அஞ்சும்'), so its misery never ends. Both say that the prospect of parting takes away the pleasure of being together; 1295 states it as the heart's standing condition.
links.reason: 'பிரிவஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு' and 'பெறின் பிரிவு அஞ்சும்' say the same thing: having him is spoiled by fear of parting.

links.note: 1153: trust is hard ('அரிதரோ தேற்றம்'), because parting occurs at some point even with those who understand ('அறிவுடையார் கண்ணும்'). 514: even when people have been trusted after every kind of test ('எனைவகையான் தேறியக் கண்ணும்'), many turn different through the nature of the work. Both say that knowing a person's qualities does not secure their future conduct, one about a lover and one about a king's appointee.
links.reason: 'அரிதரோ தேற்றம் அறிவுடையார் கண்ணும்' and 'எனைவகையான் தேறியக் கண்ணும் ... வேறாகும்' share the தேறு root and the 'even with ... கண்ணும்' concession: known quality does not guarantee later conduct, in love and in appointments.

links.note: 1154 asks whether any fault lies with those who believed the assuring words, if the one who was gracious and said 'fear not' ('அஞ்சல் என்றவர்') leaves. 1149 asks how she can be ashamed of gossip when the one who said 'fear not' ('அஞ்சலோம்பு என்றார்') has left in a way that shames many. Both quote the same promise back and place the blame or shame on the one who broke it, not on her.
links.reason: அஞ்சல் என்றவர் நீப்பின் and அஞ்சலோம்பு என்றார் ... நீத்தக்கடை quote the same promise against the man who left, and both clear her (உண்டோ தவறு / அலர்நாண ஒல்வதோ). Accurate note; pairing across two chapters is useful.

links.note: 1154 holds up his words 'fear not' and says the fault, if he leaves, is not the believer's. 1209 holds up another of his sayings, 'we are not separate' ('வேறல்லம் என்பார்'), and says her life is ending from thinking on his lack of grace. 1154 is the argument made before the parting; 1209 is the same contrast of word and conduct felt after it.
links.reason: 'அஞ்சல் என்றவர் நீப்பின்' and 'வேறல்லம் என்பார் அளியின்மை' both set his quoted assurance against his conduct, before and after the parting.

links.note: 1151 asks him to say he is not going, and leaves talk of return to those who will survive. 1155 turns to the friend: if you would protect, prevent his parting ('பிரிவோம்பல்'), since once he goes union is hard ('நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு'). Both reject return as a remedy and allow only not-leaving; Parimelazhagar supplies that what is to be protected in 1155 is her life.
links.reason: 1151 accepts only 'செல்லாமை' and 1155 asks to 'பிரிவோம்பல்' because 'நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு'; both refuse return as a remedy, and Parimelazhagar does supply her life as the object of ஓம்பின்.

links.note: 1156 calls him hard-eyed if he can speak of parting ('பிரிவுரைக்கும் வன்கண்ணர்'), and says hope of his later grace is then hard to hold. 1198 uses the same word for the other side: none are harder ('வன்கணார் இல்') than those who live on without a kind word from the one they love. The hardness she charges him with before parting she later charges to herself, or to women like her, for surviving it.
links.reason: 'வன்கண்ணர்' is charged to him for 'பிரிவுரைக்கும்' and 'வன்கணார் இல்' to those who 'வாழ்வார்' without his 'இன்சொல்'; the same word turned from the leaver to the survivor is a meaningful reuse.

links.note: 1156 names him 'வன்கண்ணர்' for announcing his departure. In 1222 she asks the evening, which looks as wretched as she is, whether its partner too is hard like hers ('எம்கேள்போல் வன்கண்ணதோ'). The epithet given conditionally in 1156 has become her settled description of him once he is gone.
links.reason: 'வன்கண்ணர் ஆயின்' is conditional in 1156 and has become her comparison term in 'எம்கேள்போல் வன்கண்ணதோ நின் துணை'; same epithet for the same man, meaningfully reused.

links.note: In 1157 the slipping bangles broadcast ('தூற்றா') his leaving. In 1235 the shoulders that have lost bangles and their old beauty tell of the cruel one's cruelty ('கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும்'). Both make her thinning body a speaker that reports on him without her consent; 1235 adds a judgment of him to the bare news of 1157.
links.reason: இறை இறவா நின்ற வளை ... தூற்றா and தொடியொடு ... வாடிய தோள் ... கொடுமை உரைக்கும்: in both the bangles and wasting limbs speak about him.

links.note: 1157 asks whether the bangles slipping past her wrist do not proclaim that the man of the shore has left her ('துறைவன் துறந்தமை தூற்றாகொல்'). 1277 says the bangles understood before she did that the man of the cool shore had parted ('தணந்தமை நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை'). Same man, same ornament: in 1157 the bangles tell others, in 1277 they know ahead of her, which Parimelazhagar takes as his parting in mind while still present.
links.reason: The same 'துறைவன்' and the same 'வளை': in 1157 the bangles 'தூற்றாகொல்' his leaving to others, in 1277 they 'நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த' it. Distinctive shared image, accurately described.

links.note: 1158: living in a town without one's own people is painful, and parting from one who is dear is more painful still ('அதனினும் இன்னாது இனியார்ப் பிரிவு'). 839 says, with irony, that the friendship of fools is very sweet because parting brings no pain at all ('பிரிவின்கண் பீழை தருவதொன்று இல்'). Read together, both verses use the pain of parting as the measure of what a bond was worth: none for a fool's friendship, more than exile among strangers for a lover.
links.reason: 'அதனினும் இன்னாது இனியார்ப் பிரிவு' and the ironic 'பிரிவின்கண் பீழை தருவதொன்றில்' both measure a bond by what parting costs; the note marks the irony and that this is a joint reading.

links.note: 1159 asks whether fire, which burns when touched, can burn when one lets go as love's sickness does ('விடிற்சுடல் ஆற்றுமோ தீ'). 1104 has the man ask where she got a fire that burns when he moves away and is cool when he comes near ('நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும்'). The same reversed fire is a marvel in the man's mouth at union and a complaint in the woman's (for Parimelazhagar) at parting.
links.reason: The same reversed fire: 'விடிற்சுடல் ஆற்றுமோ தீ' and 'நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும் தீ', a wonder at union and a complaint at parting.

links.note: 1160 says many agree to the hard thing, put away their pain, endure the parting and live on ('பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்'); Parimelazhagar reads it as irony against the friend's advice. 1198 says outright that none in the world are harder than those who live on ('வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்') without a kind word from the beloved. Both treat surviving separation as something that needs explaining, not as the expected course.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does read 'பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்' as implying that no one does so ('குறிப்பால் தோன்ற'), and 1198 says 'வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்'; both treat living on after separation as the abnormal case. The agreement depends on the ironic reading of 1160, which the note flags.

links.note: Verse 11 gives rain the name அமிழ்தம் because the world's life continues through it. In 1106 the lover says her shoulders must be made of amrita (அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன தோள்) because his life puts out new shoots at each touch (உயிர் தளிர்ப்ப). Both verses award the word for the same reason, that the thing keeps life going, once for the whole world and once in a lover's speech about himself.

links.note: Verse 13 says that if the sky proves false (விண் பொய்ப்பின்), hunger stays and torments the world (உள்நின்று உடற்றும் பசி), sea-girt though it is. Verse 734 defines a land as one that severe hunger (உறுபசி), unending disease and destructive enemies do not reach. Read together, the first mark of a proper country in the Book of Wealth rests on something no ruler supplies, the rain of chapter 2.

Verse 14 names one cause that would fold those hands, so the failure of rain reaches as far as the renouncer.

In 1102 the lover says that for other diseases the medicine is something else, but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து). The pattern of one thing being both the harm and the only remedy appears for rain and the world and, in a lover's speech, for the beloved.

Verse 16 supplies the picture that 557's comparison assumes: without the king's அளி, the people are the bare ground.

links.note: Verse 211 asks what the world does for the rain-cloud in return (மாரிமாட்டு என் ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ உலகு) and makes it the model of duty that wants no repayment. On that reading the cloud is not a pure giver: it returns what it drew from the sea, and the sea suffers if it withholds. Both use the withholding cloud; 1010 turns it into a figure for a giver's temporary incapacity, with the suggestion that it is as general a loss and as passing.

links.note: Verse 18 says that if the sky dries up (வானம் வறக்குமேல்), festival and worship for the gods will not go on here (சிறப்பொடு பூசனை செல்லாது). Verse 560 says that if the guardian does not guard (காவலன் காவான் எனின்), the cows' yield shrinks and those of the six duties forget their book (நூல் மறப்பர்). Both say religious practice has a material precondition that can fail; chapter 2 names the rain and chapter 56 names the king.

Verse 559 says that if the king acts with justice bent (முறைகோடி), the sky will not pour in season (ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்). Chapter 2 makes virtue depend on rain; 559 makes the rain depend in turn on a human virtue, the ruler's justice, so the dependence runs both ways.

Verse 1036 gives the step in between: if the ploughmen's hands fold, those who say they have left desire have no standing (விட்டேம் என்பார்க்கும் நிலை இல்லை). The renouncer's practice rests on the farmer's food, and the farmer's on the sky.

links.note: Verse 20 ends the chapter by saying nothing in the world, for anyone, holds without the sky. Verse 55 says that for the wife who rises worshipping her husband, it rains when she says 'rain' (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). Three chapters after rain is made the condition of everything, the rain is said to answer to one person's steadfastness.

Parimelazhagar takes ஒழுக்கு as the water's unbroken flow; Pope's verse rendering and Kalaignar take it as ordered conduct. Verse 542 states the first half as a given (வானோக்கி வாழும் உலகெல்லாம்) and sets the people's dependence on the sceptre beside it. On either reading of ஒழுக்கு, 542 treats the dependence 20 argues for as the standard case of something one cannot live without.

links.note: Verse 21 says the settled view of the texts (பனுவல் துணிவு) sets the greatness of those who have renounced within their discipline (ஒழுக்கத்து நீத்தார் பெருமை) highest among excellent things. Verse 48 says the household life that keeps others on their path and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). If 48 is read as ranking the householder above the ascetic, as its plain wording allows, the two chapters give the first place to different lives; if 48 is read as praising only the householder's endurance, they do not collide.

links.note: Verse 21 rests its claim on பனுவல் துணிவு, the settled conclusion of the texts. Verse 533 uses the same appeal: that the heedless have no fame is the conclusion of authors of every school (எப்பால் நூலோர்க்கும் துணிவு). These are two places where the Kural, which usually argues from observation, cites the agreement of the books as its ground.

links.note: Verse 22 says that to state the measure of the greatness of renouncers (துறந்தார்) is like counting the dead of the world (இறந்தாரை எண்ணிக்கொண்டற்று). Verse 310 rhymes the same two words: those who exceed in anger (இறந்தார்) are like the dead, and those who have renounced anger are equal to renouncers (துறந்தார் துணை). In 22 the dead supply only a number too large to count; in 310 the same pairing sets renouncers and the dead as opposite ends, and extends the renouncer's standing to anyone who gives up anger.

links.note: Verse 23 says the greatness of those who have discerned the two (இருமை வகைதெரிந்து) and taken on அறம் here stands highest in the world; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read the two as birth and release and the அறம் as renunciation. Verse 49 says that what is called அறம் is household life (அறன் எனப்பட்டதே இல்வாழ்க்கை). On the commentators' reading of 23 the two verses attach the word அறம், and the highest standing, to different lives. Kalaignar reads 23 as choosing good over bad in general, and on that reading there is no conflict.

links.note: Verse 24 calls the one who guards the five senses a seed (வித்து) for the ground called வரன், which Parimelazhagar takes as release. Verse 361 calls craving the seed (வித்து) that bears unceasing birth for all beings. The book uses the seed for both outcomes: restraint of the senses is sown toward release, and craving is what sprouts as rebirth.

links.note: Verse 26 divides people by whether they can do what is hard to do. Verse 664 says saying is easy for anyone and doing as one has said is hard (அரியவாம் சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்). The chapter on firmness in action applies the renouncer's standard to statecraft and names what is hard in a deed: carrying it out as announced.

links.note: Verse 27 says the world lies within the one who discerns the kinds of the five (ஐந்தின் வகைதெரிவான் கட்டே உலகு): taste, light, touch, sound and smell. Verse 354 says that even having gained the fivefold awareness (ஐயுணர்வு எய்தியக் கண்ணும்) is of no benefit to those without perception of the real (மெய்யுணர்வு). Verse 354 sets a limit on 27: command of the five is not the end, and without true perception it yields nothing.

In 1101 the lover lists the same five as acts, seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching (கண்டுகேட்டு உண்டுயிர்த்து உற்றறியும் ஐம்புலனும்), and says they are all found in this one woman (ஒண்தொடி கண்ணே உள). The same inventory serves the renouncer as a field to be understood and the lover as a field of enjoyment; the second is a speech in the moment and not a counter-teaching.

links.note: Verse 28 says the greatness of people whose word is full (நிறைமொழி மாந்தர்) is shown on earth by their மறைமொழி; Parimelazhagar explains நிறைமொழி as speech that produces its result whether spoken in grace or in anger. Verse 55 says that when the wife who worships her husband says 'rain', it rains (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). Both give a person's word power over the world as the proof of their standing, for the renouncer through austerity and for the wife through steadfastness at home.

links.note: Verse 29 speaks of the anger (வெகுளி) of those who stand on the hill of good qualities; on Parimelazhagar's reading they are sages whose anger, though it lasts a moment, cannot be warded off by its target. Verse 310 says those who have renounced anger are the equals of renouncers (சினத்தைத் துறந்தார் துறந்தார் துணை), which makes freedom from anger the renouncer's mark. On Parimelazhagar's reading the book's model renouncer still gets angry, and dangerously. Kalaignar reads 29 as saying their anger does not stay even a moment, and on that reading the two verses agree.
links.reason: குன்றேறி நின்றார் வெகுளி read with Parimelazhagar (முனிவரது வெகுளி ... காத்தல் அரிது) conflicts with சினத்தைத் துறந்தார் துறந்தார் துணை; the note names the reading and Kalaignar's dissolving alternative correctly.

links.note: 41 makes the householder the support of the three, read by Parimelazhagar as the other orders, ascetics included. 263 asks, with கொல், whether 'the others' (மற்றையவர்கள்) have forgotten தவம் because they want to provide for the renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி); Parimelazhagar glosses 'the others' as householders. The Thavam chapter thus looks at the same arrangement from the ascetic side: the householder's support of renouncers is given as the reason he does no austerity himself.
links.reason: இயல்புடைய மூவர்க்கும் ... துணை and துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி மறந்தார்கொல் மற்றையவர்கள் தவம் view the same householder-supports-renouncer arrangement from two sides; glosses cited are accurate.

links.note: 41 calls the householder the துணை who stands on the good path (நல்லாற்றின் நின்ற) for 'the three' (இயல்புடைய மூவர்), whom Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take as the other three orders of life (Kalaignar instead reads parents, spouse and children). 1036 says that if the ploughmen's hands fold (கைம்மடங்கின்), even those who say 'we have let go of desire' (விட்டேம் என்பார்) have no standing (நிலை). On the older commentators' reading both verses make the renouncer's state depend on someone who stays in the world and produces: the householder in Book 1, the farmer in Book 2.
