links.note: 41 names the householder the support of 'the three of proper nature' (இயல்புடைய மூவர்); 42 repeats the frame இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் துணை and adds three more: துறந்தார், துவ்வாதவர், இறந்தார். Parimelazhagar takes these as the abandoned, the poor and those who died with no one of their own, so the pair moves from the recognised orders to people with no claim on anyone. Pope and Kalaignar read துறந்தார் as ascetics, which would make 42 overlap 41 rather than extend it.
links.reason: இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் ... துணை is repeated and 42 adds துறந்தார், துவ்வாதவர், இறந்தார்; the note correctly reports Parimelazhagar's reading (களைகண் ஆனவரால் துறக்கப்பட்டார்) and that the extension weakens if துறந்தார் means ascetics.

links.note: 42 lists துவ்வாதவர், those who have nothing to eat or enjoy, among the people the householder supports. 226 says that ending the destroying hunger of those without means (அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல்) is the place where a person who has gained wealth stores it (பொருள் வைப்புழி). 226 turns the duty stated in 42 into a claim about what wealth is for.
links.reason: துவ்வாதவர் in 42 and அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல் in 226 are the same people and duty; 226 adds the claim that this is பொருள் வைப்புழி, which is a real extension.

links.note: 43 lists five quarters to be tended (ஐம்புலத்தாறு ஓம்பல்): ancestors, gods, guests (விருந்து), kin and oneself, and calls this the chief thing (தலை). 81 says that all of staying, guarding one's goods and living at home (இருந்தோம்பி இல்வாழ்வதெல்லாம்) is for the sake of tending guests and doing them good (விருந்தோம்பி வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு). One of the five items of 43 is taken up, with the same verb ஓம்பு, and made the purpose of the whole household.
links.reason: விருந்து is one of the five in ஐம்புலத்தாறு ஓம்பல் (43), and 81 makes விருந்தோம்பி வேளாண்மை செய்தல் the purpose of இல்வாழ்வதெல்லாம், with ஓம்பு in both.

links.note: 43 puts kin (ஒக்கல்) among the five the householder must tend. 524, in the chapters on kingship, says that living so as to be surrounded by one's kin (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்பட ஒழுகல்) is the fruit of having gained wealth. The household duty of Book 1 reappears in Book 2 as the point of a ruler's prosperity.
links.reason: 43 lists 'ஒக்கல்' among the five to be tended; 524 'சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப் படஒழுகல் செல்வந்தான் பெற்றத்தால் பெற்ற பயன்' makes the same care the point of wealth in Book 2.

links.note: 44 promises an unfailing line (வழி) to the life that fears blame (பழியஞ்சி) and shares its food; Parimelazhagar reads the fear of blame as applying to how the wealth is earned. 112 says the prosperity of the person of rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security to those who come after (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). In both, wealth held without wrong is what lasts into the next generation.
links.reason: பழியஞ்சி ... வழியெஞ்சல் எஞ்ஞான்றும் இல் and செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம் ... எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு both tie blameless wealth to what lasts for descendants.

links.note: 44 says a life that fears blame and has பாத்தூண், food shared out, never sees its line fail (வழியெஞ்சல் எஞ்ஞான்றும் இல்). 227 uses the same compound: the one habituated to shared food (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை) is hardly touched by the disease called hunger. Both attach a protective result to the same practice, one for the descendants and one for the sharer himself.
links.reason: Both attach protection to the same compound பாத்தூண்: வழியெஞ்சல் எஞ்ஞான்றும் இல் for the line, பசியென்னும் தீப்பிணி தீண்டல் அரிது for the sharer.

links.note: 44 names பாத்தூண், shared food, as the mark of the householder's life. In 1107 the lover says the embrace of the woman is like staying in one's own home and eating one's own after sharing it (தம்மில் இருந்து தமது பாத்து உண்டற்று). The Book of Love takes the householder's sharing meal as a standard of pleasure, where 44 gives it as a duty with a reward; the comparison is the speaker's, not a teaching.
links.reason: பாத்தூண் in 44 and தமது பாத்து உண்டற்று in 1107 are the same sharing meal, as duty in one and as measure of pleasure in the other. The note's caution that 1107 is the speaker's comparison is right.

links.note: 45 says that if household life has love and virtue (அன்பும் அறனும்), that is its character and its fruit (பண்பும் பயனும்). 75 says the distinction reached by those who have had joy in this world is, 'they say', the result of a way of life settled in love (அன்புற்று அமர்ந்த வழக்கு); Parimelazhagar takes this as household life lived with love, rewarded with heaven. 75 spells out the பயன் that 45 only names.
links.reason: அன்பும் அறனும் ... பண்பும் பயனும் அது (45) and அன்புற்று அமர்ந்த வழக்கு as the cause of the சிறப்பு reached by இன்புற்றார் (75); the reliance on Parimelazhagar for household life and heaven is stated.

links.note: 46 asks what one who conducts household life in the way of virtue would gain by going to the outside way (புறத்தாற்றில் போஒய்ப் பெறுவது எவன்); Parimelazhagar and Pope take the outside way as renunciation. 348 says those who have renounced completely (தீரத் துறந்தார்) have reached the head, and the rest (மற்றையவர்) are confused and caught in the net. If புறத்தாறு is renunciation and the question in 46 is rhetorical, 46 denies the gain that 348 reserves for renouncers alone; if புறத்தாறு means only ways outside virtue, the conflict disappears.
links.reason: புறத்தாற்றில் போஒய்ப் பெறுவது எவன் against தலைப்பட்டார் தீரத் துறந்தார் ... வலைப்பட்டார் மற்றையவர் is a real conflict if புறத்தாறு is renunciation, and the note names that dependence.

links.note: 47 says the one who lives household life according to its nature is first among all who strive (முயல்வாருள் எல்லாம் தலை). 266 says those who do தவம் are doing their own work and the rest (மற்றல்லார்), caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார்). On Parimelazhagar's reading of 47, where the strivers are those working to leave the senses, the householder is ranked above ascetics, while 266 counts everyone but the ascetic as wasting effort. Manakkudavar reads முயல்வார் as those who strive for wealth, and on that reading the two do not collide.
links.reason: முயல்வாருள் எல்லாம் தலை, with Parimelazhagar's புலன்களை விட முயல்வார், ranks the householder above strivers after release, while தவஞ்செய்வார் தங்கருமஞ் செய்வார் மற்றல்லார் அவஞ்செய்வார் leaves only ascetics doing their proper work; the note names the reading and Manakkudavar's way out (பொருட்கு முயறல்).

links.note: 48 says a household life that keeps others on their path (ஆற்றின் ஒழுக்கி) and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). 225 says the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, and that comes behind the strength of those who remove that hunger (மாற்றுவார் ஆற்றலின் பின்). Both rank the one who provides above the one who abstains, and both do it by granting the ascetic's own virtue, endurance, and awarding more of it to the provider.
links.reason: 48 நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து and 225 மாற்றுவார் ஆற்றலின் பின் both rank the provider above the abstainer in the ascetic's own virtue.

links.note: 44 opens with பழியஞ்சி: the household life that fears blame and shares its food keeps its line. 49 calls household life virtue itself, then adds that it is good if there is nothing others blame (பிறன் பழிப்பது இல்லாயின்). On Manakkudavar's reading, where அஃதும் still refers to household life, 49 makes absence of blame the condition on the chapter's whole praise of the householder, which 44 had already built into its description.
links.reason: பழியஞ்சி (44) and பிறன் பழிப்பது இல்லாயின் (49, with அஃதும் as household life in Manakkudavar) state the same blamelessness condition, as the note itself admits; 49 does not limit 44, so the type is wrong, and the two பழி are different in the commentaries.

links.note: 49 says what is called virtue is household life, and 'that too' (அஃதும்) is good if it is not something others blame (பிறன் பழிப்பது இல்லாயின்). Parimelazhagar takes அஃதும் as renunciation and the blame as false conduct in ascetics (Manakkudavar keeps it on household life). 280 says neither shaving nor growing the hair is needed if one drops what the world has blamed (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின்). On Parimelazhagar's reading the chapter on false ascetics works out the condition 49 states in passing: the renouncer's standing rests on being free of blame.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does take 49's அஃதும் as துறவறம் and பிறன் பழிப்பது as கூடாவொழுக்கம், which 280 உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின் works out; the note states the dependence on that reading and Manakkudavar's dissent.

links.note: 50 places the person who lives rightly on earth (வையத்துள்) among the gods of the sky. 413 says those who have listening as food for the ear are, though on earth (நிலத்து), equal to the gods who are fed by oblations. Both verses set 'on earth' against the gods and say a human excellence closes the gap, right living in one case and learning by listening in the other.
links.reason: Both set earth against the gods: 50 வையத்துள் ... தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப்படும், 413 ஆன்றாரோடு ஒப்பர் நிலத்து, with right living and கேள்வி as the equalisers.
links.text_issue: 50: 'வான்உநற்யும்' is corrupted; the standard text is வானுறையும்.

links.note: 52 says that if excellence of the home (மனைமாட்சி) is not in the wife, the life is nothing, whatever excellence it has (எனைமாட்சித் தாயினும் இல்). 750 says that whatever excellence a fort has (எனைமாட்சித் தாகியக் கண்ணும்), it is as nothing in those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). The two share the phrase and the argument: the outward assets of a home or a fortress count for nothing without the quality of the person inside who runs it.
links.reason: எனைமாட்சித்தாயினும் இல் and எனைமாட்சித்தாகியக் கண்ணும் ... இல்லது share the phrase and the argument, with மனைமாட்சி / வினைமாட்சி as the deciding quality in the person (இல்லாள்கண் / இல்லார்கண்).

links.note: 53 asks what is lacking if the wife has worth (இல்லதென் இல்லவள் மாண்பானால்) and what is there if she does not (உள்ளதென் ... மாணாக் கடை). 430 says those with understanding have everything, and those without it have nothing whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்). The same two-sided formula, one possession that makes all others count or not count, is applied to a wife's character in the home and to understanding in a ruler.
links.reason: இல்லதென் ... உள்ளதென் and எல்லாமுடையார் ... என்னுடையரேனும் இலர் use the same two-sided formula of one possession that decides the value of all others.

links.note: 54 asks what is greater than a woman, if she has the firmness called கற்பு (கற்பென்னும் திண்மை உண்டாகப் பெறின்). 988 says poverty is no disgrace to a person, if he has the firmness called சால்பு (சால்பென்னும் திண்மை உண்டாகப் பெறின்). The second line is the same but for one word, so the book describes a woman's fidelity and a worthy person's character with the same term, திண்மை, a firmness that outweighs outward circumstances.
links.reason: The second lines கற்பென்னும் திண்மை உண்டாகப் பெறின் and சால்பென்னும் திண்மை உண்டாகப் பெறின் differ by one word, giving fidelity and worth the same term திண்மை.

links.note: 55 praises a wife who does not worship a god (தெய்வம் தொழாஅள்) and worships her husband, and credits her with power over the rain. 2 asks what use learning is if the learned do not worship the feet of the one of pure knowledge (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்), with the same verb in the same negative form. Read literally, 55 commends for the wife the not-worshipping that the first chapter treats as making a person's attainments useless. Parimelazhagar removes the conflict by reading 'other gods' (பிற தெய்வம்) and making the husband her god; the tension depends on taking தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் at face value.
links.reason: தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் read at face value commends the not-worshipping that நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின் condemns, with the same verb; the note says the conflict depends on that reading and that Parimelazhagar removes it.

links.note: 56 defines the woman as one who guards herself (தற்காத்து), cares for her husband and guards the good name (சொற்காத்து) without flagging. 57 asks what guarding by confinement (சிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு) can do, and says the guard women keep by their own நிறை is the chief one. 57 explains why 56 makes her the subject of the verb 'guard': the guarding that counts cannot be done by anyone else.
links.reason: தற்காத்து in 56 and நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பே தலை against சிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு in 57 are the same verb of guarding, and 57 explains why the guarding is hers to do.

links.note: 56 includes guarding the well-founded word, the couple's good name (தகைசான்ற சொற்காத்து), in its definition of the wife. 59 says those whose home does not seek renown (புகழ்புரிந்த இல் இலோர்க்கு) cannot walk with a proud gait before those who deride them. Parimelazhagar connects them directly, saying 59 states the fault that follows when that good name is not kept: the husband's standing in public depends on it.
links.reason: 56 has தகைசான்ற சொற்காத்து and 59 புகழ்புரிந்த இல்லிலோர்க்கு இல்லை ... பீடு நடை; Parimelazhagar's closing remark on 59 does say it gives the fault that follows when தகைசான்ற சொல் is not kept.

links.note: 58 says women who 'obtain the one who obtained them' (பெற்றாற் பெறின்) gain great distinction in the world where the gods live (புத்தேளிர் வாழும் உலகு); Parimelazhagar supplies 'honour' and reads it as wives who revere their husbands. 50 says the man who lives on earth as he should is placed among the gods of the sky. The two adjacent chapters end on the same reward, one for the householder and one for the wife, each for fulfilling the household role.
links.reason: 58 பெருஞ்சிறப்புப் புத்தேளிர் வாழும் உலகு and 50 தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப் படும் give wife and householder a matching divine reward; minor slips only (58 is not the last verse of its chapter, and Parimelazhagar supplies வழிபடுதல், not 'honour').
links.text_issue: 50: வான்உநற்யும் is a typo for வானுறையும்.

links.note: 59 says those whose home does not seek renown (புகழ்புரிந்த இல்) have no proud gait before those who deride them (இகழ்வார்முன்). 237 asks why those who cannot live with renown (புகழ்பட வாழாதார்) resent those who deride them (இகழ்வாரை நோவது எவன்) and not themselves. Both set புகழ் against இகழ்வார்: 59 says that without renown one has no answer to scorners, and 237 adds that the scorn is then one's own doing.
links.reason: புகழ்/இகழ்வார் do pair in both, but புகழ்புரிந்த இல் இல்லோர் means those without a wife who cherishes renown (இல் = இல்லாள் in both commentaries), which the note flattens to a 'home' and then to lacking renown oneself; 237 is about one's own புகழ்.

links.note: 59 says that without a home that seeks renown there is no walking with a bull's (Parimelazhagar: lion's) proud gait, ஏறுபோல் பீடு நடை. 1014 says shame is an ornament to the worthy, and without it their பீடு நடை is a disease. The proud walk appears twice as something that must be earned by an inner or domestic quality, the household's good name in one verse and a sense of shame in the other.
links.reason: பீடு நடை stands in both: denied without புகழ்புரிந்த இல் (59) and called பிணி without நாணுடைமை (1014). The shared phrase is distinctive and used in the same conditional way.

links.note: 60 says the excellence of the home is called its blessing (மங்கலம்) and the gaining of good children (நன்மக்கட் பேறு) its fine ornament. 61, opening the next chapter, says that of all things to be gained we know none like the gaining of children who know what should be known (அறிவறிந்த மக்கட்பேறு). 61 picks up the word மக்கட்பேறு from 60 and specifies what makes the children 'good': their understanding.
links.reason: 60 closes on நன்மக்கட் பேறு and 61 opens the next chapter on அறிவறிந்த மக்கட்பேறு, picking up the word and saying what makes the children good.

links.note: Verse 61 says that among all things gained (பெறுமவற்றுள்) 'we' know of nothing to set beside knowing children. Verse 162 says that among excellent gains (விழுப்பேற்றின்) nothing equals (அஃதொப்பது இல்லை) being free of envy. The two top rankings conflict only if each superlative is read literally as a ranking across all gains; read as each chapter's idiom of praise they do not.
links.reason: பெறுமவற்றுள் ... இல்லை and விழுப்பேற்றின் அஃதொப்பது இல்லை share a superlative of praise over பேறு, but the note itself says they conflict only if read as literal rankings, which is not a defensible reading.

links.note: Both verses rank their subject first by the author's own witness in the first person plural: 61 has யாமறிவது இல்லை ('we know of none') for knowing children, 300 has யாமெய்யாக் கண்டவற்றுள் இல்லை ('among what we have seen as true there is none') for truthfulness. The pairing shows the same rare device, the poet's 'we', used to vouch for a household good and for a virtue of speech.
links.reason: யாமறிவது இல்லை and யாமெய்யாக் கண்டவற்றுள் இல்லை are both the poet's first-person plural vouching for a superlative, a distinctive and uncommon device in the text.

links.note: Verse 44 says that if a household life fears blame (பழியஞ்சி) and shares its food, its line (வழி) never fails. Verse 62 says that if one gets children in whom blame does not grow (பழிபிறங்கா), no evil touches one for seven births. In 44 the parent's freedom from blame secures the descendants; in 62 the descendants' freedom from blame secures the parent.
links.reason: பழியஞ்சி ... வழியெஞ்சல் இல் (44) and பழிபிறங்கா ... மக்கட் பெறின் தீயவை தீண்டா (62) are correctly read, and the reciprocal blame-free parent/child protection is a real extension.

links.note: Verse 62 says evils will not touch a person in all seven births (எழுபிறப்பும் தீயவை தீண்டா) if they get children of character who bring no blame. Verse 398 says the learning gained in one birth is a protection in seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). Both name a good of this life whose protection outlasts it by seven births: in one case one's children, in the other one's own learning.
links.reason: எழுபிறப்பும் தீயவை தீண்டா and எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து both give a good gained in this life a protective reach of seven births, for children and for learning.

links.note: Verse 62 has blameless children keep evil away through seven births (எழுபிறப்பும்). Verse 835 has the fool, in one birth's doing (ஒருமைச் செயல்), make the mire (அளறு) he sinks in for seven (எழுமையும்). The same seven-birth reckoning is applied in the opposite direction, once to a safeguard and once to a ruin made by oneself.

links.note: Verse 63 says people call their children their wealth (தம்பொருள் என்ப தம் மக்கள்), and ties that wealth to deeds (வினையான் வரும்). Verse 114 says whether people are worthy or not is seen from their எச்சம், what they leave behind, which Parimelazhagar takes as their offspring and Kalaignar as the name they leave. On Parimelazhagar's reading the pair makes children both a person's property and the evidence by which that person is judged.
links.reason: The link is only that children figure in both, and only on Parimelazhagar's reading of எச்சம் (as the note says). 63's அவர்பொருள் தம்தம் வினையான் வரும் is not extended by 114, which is about நடுவுநிலைமை.

links.note: Verse 63 reports the saying that one's children are one's wealth (தம்பொருள்). Verse 400 says learning is the imperishable wealth (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம்) and that other things are not wealth (மாடல்ல). Both move the word for property from goods to something else, but 400 denies the title to everything other than learning, while 63 only reports what people say.
links.reason: தம்பொருள் என்ப தம் மக்கள் and கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் கல்வி both relocate 'wealth', but with different words (பொருள் vs செல்வம்/மாடு) and different points; the note itself concedes the mismatch, so the shared pattern is thin.

links.note: Verse 64 sets a child's messy gruel above amrita. In 1103 the lover asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one (தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு) can be sweeter (இனிதுகொல்) than sleeping on the soft arms of the one he loves; Parimelazhagar has him say this to a companion who reproved him. The same move, a heavenly standard of sweetness outdone by an intimate bodily one, appears in the parent's voice in Book 1 and in a lover's speech in Book 3.
links.reason: அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிதே (64) and இனிதுகொல் தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு (1103) both set a heavenly standard of sweetness below an intimate bodily one, child's gruel and the beloved's மென்றோள். Parimelazhagar's setting for 1103 is as stated.

links.note: Verse 65 names two sense pleasures a child gives: touching the child's body is joy to the body (உடற்கின்பம்) and hearing its words is joy to the ear (இன்பம் செவிக்கு). In 1101 the lover says the five senses, seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching (கண்டுகேட்டு உண்டுயிர்த்து உற்றறியும்), all have their objects in one woman. Both list pleasures sense by sense and locate them in a single loved person, a child in one and a lover in the other.

links.note: Verse 66 says only those who have not heard their own children's prattle call the flute (குழல்) and the lute sweet. In 1228 the woman left alone says the herdsman's flute (ஆயன் குழல்) is now a messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills; Parimelazhagar notes that it had been sweet to her before. In both the flute stands for accepted sweetness, and in both that sweetness is made to depend on the hearer's situation.
links.reason: குழல் இனிது in 66 and ஆயன் குழல் as கொல்லும் படை in 1228 both make the flute's sweetness depend on the hearer; Parimelazhagar's முன்னெல்லாம் இனிதாய்ப் போந்த supports the note.

links.note: Verse 67 makes it the father's gift that the son sits ahead in the assembly (அவையத்து முந்தி இருப்ப). Verse 715 says the best of good things is the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு). The shared root முந்து shows the limit: standing first in the assembly is the goal, but being first to speak before one's seniors is what the book warns against.

links.note: Verse 67 says a father's good to his son is to make him sit foremost in the assembly; Parimelazhagar takes this as making him learned beyond the learned there. Verse 722 says those called learned among the learned (கற்றாருள் கற்றார்) are those who can make what they learned go home before the learned. 722 supplies what the front seat of 67 requires in practice: learning that can be delivered in front of that assembly.
links.reason: 67 அவையத்து முந்தி இருப்பச் செயல் and 722 கற்றாருள் கற்றார் ... கற்றார்முன் கற்ற செலச்சொல்லுவார் both concern standing first among the learned, and 722 states what that takes.

links.note: Verse 68 says one's children's understanding (அறிவுடைமை) is sweet to all beings on the great earth (மன்னுயிர்க்கெல்லாம் இனிது); Parimelazhagar reads தம்மின் as 'more than to oneself', while Kalaignar and Subramuniyaswami take it as children who surpass their parents. Verse 399 says the learned love learning more on seeing that what delights them delights the world (தாமின்புறுவது உலகின்புறக் கண்டு). Both treat knowledge as a pleasure that is not private: the parent's pride in 68 and the scholar's delight in 399 are each measured against the world's share in it.

links.note: Verse 69 has the mother's joy grow when she hears others call her son worthy (சான்றோன் எனக் கேட்ட தாய்). Verse 1047 says one in poverty unconnected with virtue (அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு) is looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல நோக்கப்படும்). In both the mother's regard follows the son's standing, rising with his name in 69 and withdrawn in 1047.

links.note: Verse 70 has onlookers explain a good son by asking what the father did as penance (என்நோற்றான்). Verse 265 says தவம் is striven for here because whatever is wanted is obtained as wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்). The onlookers' question in 70 assumes the doctrine 265 states, and it applies that doctrine to a son.

links.note: Verse 71 says tears raise a public noise (பூசல் தரும்) about the love inside. In 1180 the woman says it is not hard for the town to get at the secret (மறை) of those like her whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). In both the eyes make public what the heart holds, and both describe this as sound: a clamour in 71, a drum in 1180.

links.note: Verse 72 says those who have love belong to others even in their bones (என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு). Verse 220 says that if ruin comes through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin is worth buying even by selling oneself (விற்றுக்கோள் தக்கது). Both carry giving past one's goods to one's own person, 72 as a description of love and 220 as the price of duty to the community.

links.note: Verse 72 says the loveless belong to themselves in everything (எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர்) while the loving belong to others (பிறர்க்கு) even in their bones. Verse 1009 says wealth piled up by putting love aside (அன்பொரீஇ), denying oneself and ignoring virtue will be taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). 1009 gives the outcome of the stance in 72: what the loveless keep for themselves ends with பிறர் anyway.

links.note: Verse 73 says the life's connection with the bone (என்போடு) goes with love. Verse 80 says the seat of life (உயிர்நிலை) follows love, and that for those without it the body is bone wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). The chapter's last verse gives the negative of 73: take away the love and what remains of the union is the bone alone.

Verse 338 says the friendship between body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு) is like a bird flying off and leaving its குடம்பை alone. The pairing sets a limit on 73: the bond that exists for love's sake is, in the chapter on impermanence, one the life will abandon.

links.note: Verse 73 says the tie of the life with the body (ஆருயிர்க்கு என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) is, they say, a matter of being joined with love (அன்போடு இயைந்த வழக்கு); Parimelazhagar takes embodiment as the result of a course meant for joining with love. links.note: Verse 74 says love gives birth (ஈனும்) to eagerness, and that gives birth to friendship, an unsought distinction (நாடாச் சிறப்பு). Verse 757 calls அருள் the child born of love (அன்பீன் குழவி), raised by the foster-mother wealth. Both use the figure of birth for what comes out of அன்பு, and together they give love two offspring, friendship in the home and grace toward all.

The friendship chapter of Book 2 keeps the account given in Book 1: friendship comes from an inner disposition and not from arrangement or contact.
links.reason: உணர்ச்சிதான் நட்பாங் கிழமை தரும் and அன்பு→ஆர்வம்→நண்பு both ground friendship inwardly, but 74 says nothing against புணர்ச்சி/பழகுதல், and its நண்பு is general goodwill in Parimelazhagar, so 'keeps the account' overstates.

Set side by side, 75 adds love to the source that 39 confines to அறம், which agrees with verse 45's coupling of the two.

Verse 862 asks how a man without love (அன்பிலன்), without allies and without strength of his own can wear down an enemy's might. On Kalaignar's reading 862 is the case in point: in Book 2 love is listed first among the things a fighter needs.

Verse 80 says the body of those without love is bones wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). The chapter uses bone twice for the loveless in opposite ways, once as what they lack and once as all they are.

Verse 204 says that if one plots another's ruin, அறம் plots the plotter's ruin (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). The verb தளிர் carries both: life sprouts where love is, and 78 uses the same sprouting to mark what a loveless life cannot do.

Verse 407 says the fine looks (எழில்நலம்) of one without subtle, penetrating understanding are like those of a well-made clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). Both set a complete exterior against a missing interior, love in Book 1 and understanding in Book 2.

links.reason: உயிர்நிலை occurs in both (அன்பின் வழியது உயிர்நிலை; உண்ணாமை உள்ளது உயிர்நிலை), each time making a virtue the condition of life; the note's account of 255 follows Parimelazhagar.

links.note: Verse 80 says that for those without love the body is only bones wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). Verse 1020 says the movements of those with no shame within (நாண் அகத்தில்லார்) are like a wooden puppet feigning life by its string (மரப்பாவை ... உயிர்மருட்டியற்று). Both describe a moving body that lacks an inward quality as something without life in it, a frame of bone in one and a puppet in the other.
links.reason: என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு and மரப்பாவை ... உயிர்மருட்டி அற்று both picture a body moving without the inward quality (அன்பு, நாண்) as lifeless.

links.note: 82 says eating alone while the guest is outside (விருந்து புறத்ததாத் தானுண்டல்) is not to be desired even if the food were the medicine against death. 229 says eating by oneself alone (தாமே தமியர் உணல்) to fill up one's store is more bitter than begging. Both judge the solitary meal itself, one by setting it against the best imaginable food and the other against the worst condition.
links.reason: 82 விருந்து புறத்ததாத் தானுண்டல் and 229 தாமே தமியர் உணல் both condemn the unshared meal, measured against சாவா மருந்து in one and இரத்தல் in the other.

links.note: 83 says the life of one who tends the arriving guest every day (வைகலும் ஓம்புவான்) does not suffer and go to ruin (பருவந்து பாழ்படுதல் இன்று). 227 says the disease called hunger rarely touches one accustomed to sharing his food (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை). Both promise that habitual sharing of food protects the sharer from want, once for the host of guests and once for the giver to the poor.
links.reason: வைகலும் ஓம்புவான் வாழ்க்கை பருவந்து பாழ்படுதல் இன்று and பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனைப் பசி ... தீண்டல் அரிது both promise the habitual sharer protection from want.

links.note: 83 says daily hospitality never brings a household to ruin (பாழ்படுதல் இன்று), which Parimelazhagar takes to mean the host's goods are not used up. 480 says helpfulness that does not weigh the extent of what one has (உளவரை தூக்காத ஒப்புரவாண்மை) quickly ends one's wealth (வல்லைக் கெடும்). The Book of Wealth thus attaches a condition of measure to the kind of promise 83 makes without one.
links.reason: பருவந்து பாழ்படுதல் இன்று is an unconditional promise that உளவரை தூக்காத ஒப்புரவாண்மை ... வல்லைக் கெடும் limits by measure.

links.note: 84 has the goddess of fortune (செய்யாள்) living in the home of the glad-faced host. 617 says she of the lotus (தாமரையினாள்) lives in the effort of the unslothful (மடியிலான் தாளுளாள்), and her dark sister in sloth. The same figure is given two different dwellings, generosity in the Book of Virtue and exertion in the Book of Wealth.
links.reason: செய்யாள் உறையும் ... இல் and தாளுளாள் தாமரையினாள் place the same goddess in the host's house and in the worker's effort. The contrast between the two books holds.
links.text_issue: 617 reads தாளுளான் for தாளுளாள்.

links.note: 85 implies that the field of the host who feeds guests first yields without sowing. 545 says rain and harvest gather together (பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு) in the land of the king who wields the sceptre as he should. In both, right conduct is said to make the land fruitful, at the scale of one household's field and at the scale of a kingdom.
links.reason: 85 வித்தும் இடல்வேண்டும் கொல்லோ and 545 பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு both make right conduct yield fertility, for one host's புலம் and for a king's நாடு.

links.note: 85 asks whether one who feeds guests and eats what is left (விருந்தோம்பி மிச்சில் மிசைவான்) need even sow his field (வித்தும் இடல்வேண்டும் கொல்லோ); Parimelazhagar supplies that it will bear by itself. 1039 says that if the owner stays away and does not go to it (செல்லான் கிழவன் இருப்பின்), the land sulks like a wife. The conflict holds only if 85 is taken literally, as Parimelazhagar does, and not as a figure of praise; Kalaignar reads 85 quite differently, as asking whether such a host would hold back even his seed-grain.
links.reason: On the literal reading of வித்தும் இடல்வேண்டும் கொல்லோ (Parimelazhagar's தானே விளையும்) the field yields unworked, against செல்லான் கிழவன் இருப்பின் நிலம் ... ஊடி விடும்; the note names the reading and reports Kalaignar correctly.

links.note: 86 says one who tends the departing guest and watches for the next (வருவிருந்து பார்த்திருப்பான்) will be a good guest to those in the sky (வானத்தவர்க்கு). 50 says one who lives on earth as one should (வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன்) will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (வான்உறையும் தெய்வத்துள்). 86 names one specific practice that earns what 50 promises the householder in general, and turns it into a reciprocity: the host becomes the guest. (This edition prints நல்வருந்து in 86 and உநற்யும் in 50; both are typos.)
links.reason: வானத்தவர்க்கு நல்விருந்து and வான்உறையும் தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப் படும் promise the same reward, with 86 naming one householder practice (வருவிருந்து பார்த்திருப்பான்) and turning host into guest.
links.text_issue: 86 prints நல்வருந்து for நல்விருந்து; 50 prints வான்உநற்யும் for வான்உறையும்.

links.note: On Parimelazhagar's reading, 87 scales the fruit of hospitality to the guest's worth (விருந்தின் துணைத்துணை). 221 says giving to those who have nothing (வறியார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈவதே ஈகை) is the only real giving, and all the rest is like a loan expecting return. One verse values the gift by the receiver's merit and the other by the receiver's need; the conflict depends on reading துணை in 87 as merit and on treating feeding a guest and giving as the same kind of act.
links.reason: 87 விருந்தின் துணைத்துணை measures the fruit of hospitality while 221 வறியார்க்கொன்று ஈவதே ஈகை defines giving; they are about different acts, as the note itself concedes, so the conflict is thin rather than incompatible claims about one thing.

links.note: 87 calls hospitality a வேள்வி (sacrifice) whose fruit has no fixed measure; Parimelazhagar notes it is one of the five great sacrifices. 259 says not taking a life and eating it is better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices (அவிசொரிந்து ஆயிரம் வேட்டலின்). In both verses the ritual word is used to rank an ethical practice: one is named a sacrifice, the other is set above a thousand of them.
links.reason: Both use the sacrifice word (வேள்விப் பயன்; ஆயிரம் வேட்டலின்) to rank an ethical practice, hospitality as a வேள்வி and non-killing above a thousand.

links.note: 88 says those who do not take up the sacrifice of tending guests guard their goods painfully (பரிந்தோம்பி) and end by saying 'we have no support' (பற்றற்றேம்). 228 asks whether the hard-eyed who store what they have and lose it (வைத்திழக்கும்) do not know the joy of giving. Both describe the same sequence of hoarding and then loss, and both set it against a use of wealth the hoarder never tried.
links.reason: 88 'பரிந்தோம்பிப் பற்றற்றேம் என்பர்' and 228 'தாமுடைமை வைத்திழக்கும் வன்கணவர்' both describe hoarding followed by loss, set against hospitality (வேள்வி) and the joy of giving (ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம்).

links.note: 88 pictures people guarding their goods with pain (பரிந்தோம்பி) and still losing them. 376 says what is not allotted to one will not stay even if guarded with pain (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல), and what is one's own will not leave even if poured away (சொரியினும் போகா தம). The fate chapter gives a general ground for 88's observation: anxious guarding does not decide whether wealth stays, so spending it on guests risks nothing that guarding would have saved.
links.reason: பரிந்தோம்பிப் பற்றற்றேம் என்பர் and பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல share the verb for anxious guarding, and 376 gives the general ground for 88's observation.

links.note: 89 says poverty in the midst of wealth is the folly (மடமை) of not caring for guests. 841 says lack of understanding is the poverty of poverties (அறிவின்மை இன்மையுள் இன்மை) and that the world does not count other lack as lack. 841 states as a general principle what 89 shows in one case: the real want is a failure of understanding, whatever one owns.
links.reason: 89 உடைமையுள் இன்மை ... மடமை and 841 அறிவின்மை இன்மையுள் இன்மை both relocate real poverty in a failure of understanding, 841 as the general statement.

links.note: 90 gives the negative case: a face that turns (முகந்திரிந்து) and looks makes the guest wilt. 93 gives the positive rule in nearly the same terms: with a glad face, looking sweetly (முகத்தான் அமர்ந்து இனிது நோக்கி), then sweet words from the heart. The last verse of the hospitality chapter and the third of the next share the face-and-look sequence; Parimelazhagar on 90 also lists the glad face, the sweet word and the good deed as successive stages of welcome.
links.reason: முகந்திரிந்து நோக்க (90) and முகத்தான் அமர்ந்து இனிது நோக்கி (93) are the negative and positive of the same face-and-look sequence, and 93 adds the இன்சொல்.
links.text_issue: Verse 90's second line reads 'குநழ்யும்' in this edition, a typo for 'குழையும்'.

links.note: 90 says a guest wilts when looked at with an altered face (முகந்திரிந்து நோக்க). 707 says nothing is as knowing as the face, since whether one is pleased or angry it gets there first (உவப்பினும் காயினும் தான்முந்துறும்). 707 explains why 90's guest is hurt before a word is spoken: the face has already reported the host's mind.
links.reason: முகந்திரிந்து நோக்கக் குழையும் விருந்து is explained by உவப்பினும் காயினும் தான் முந்துறும்: the face reports the mind before speech.
links.text_issue: Verse 90's second line reads 'குநழ்யும்' in this edition, a typo for 'குழையும்'.

links.note: 91 says sweet words are the speech of those who have seen the செம்பொருள் (செம்பொருள் கண்டார் வாய்ச்சொல்), which Parimelazhagar glosses here as those who know virtue. 358 defines understanding as seeing the செம்பொருள் so that the folly of birth departs (செம்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு). The same phrase links ordinary kind speech to the insight the renunciation chapters describe, though the commentator gives the word a more modest sense in 91.
links.reason: செம்பொருள் கண்டார் (91) and செம்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு (358) share the phrase, and the note is candid that Parimelazhagar glosses it as அறம் in 91.

links.note: 92 says being sweet-spoken with a glad face is better than giving with a glad heart (அகன்அமர்ந்து ஈதலின் நன்றே). 295 says one who speaks truth in accord with his heart (மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின்) is above those who do austerity together with giving (தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை). Twice the book ranks a quality of speech above material giving, once for kindness and once for truthfulness.
links.reason: ஈதலின் நன்றே ... இன்சொலன் and தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை both rank a quality of speech above giving.

links.note: 93 says virtue lies in sweet words that come from within (அகத்தானாம் இன்சொலினதே அறம்), after a glad face and a kind look. 34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர பிற); Parimelazhagar counts speech and outward guise among that rest. 93's word அகத்தானாம் is what keeps sweet speech on the right side of 34's line: it counts as virtue because it issues from the mind.
links.reason: அகத்தானாம் இன்சொல் ties speech to the mind, which is what 34's மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் requires; Parimelazhagar does list சொல்லும் வேடமும் under the பிற that are ஆகுல நீர.

links.note: 93 requires the glad face and the sweet word to come from within (முகத்தான் அமர்ந்து ... அகத்தானாம்). 786 says friendship that makes only the face smile is not friendship; friendship that makes the heart within smile is (முகநக ... நெஞ்சத்து அகநக). The same முகம்/அகம் pairing sets the test of genuineness for kind speech and for friendship.
links.reason: 93 'முகத்தான் அமர்ந்து... அகத்தானாம் இன்சொல்' and 786 'முகநக... நெஞ்சத்து அகநக' use the same முகம்/அகம் pair to test genuineness, in speech and in friendship.

links.note: 93 places virtue in a glad face followed by sweet words from within (அகத்தானாம்). 824 warns that deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சரை) are to be feared. 824 describes the counterfeit of 93's first half, so the outward signs 93 begins with cannot by themselves be taken as proof of the inner part.
links.reason: முகத்தான் அமர்ந்து ... அகத்தானாம் இன்சொல் (93) against முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சர் (824): the same முகம்/அகம் pair, with 824 showing the face without the inside. A real limit on 93's outward signs.

links.note: 94 asserts that sweet speakers do not fall into want, without saying how. 525 says one who can give and speak sweetly (கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின்) will be surrounded by layer on layer of kin (அடுக்கிய சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). 525 supplies a worldly mechanism for 94's promise: sweet speech gathers people around one, and a person so surrounded is not left destitute.
links.reason: 94 says துவ்வாமை இல்லாகும் for the இன்சொலவர்; 525 needs கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் together and speaks of சுற்றம், not of freedom from want. The 'mechanism' is the note's inference, not something 525 says.

links.note: 94 says want that brings suffering (துன்புறூஉம் துவ்வாமை) does not come to those whose sweet speech gives joy to everyone. 566 says that if a ruler is harsh of speech and without kindly regard (கடுஞ்சொல்லன் கண்ணிலன்), his long-standing wealth perishes on the spot. The two verses state the same link between speech and prosperity from opposite sides, for anyone in the Book of Virtue and for a king in the Book of Wealth.
links.reason: இன்சொலவர்க்கு துவ்வாமை இல்லாகும் (94) and கடுஞ்சொல்லன் கண்ணிலன் ஆயின் நெடுஞ்செல்வம் ... கெடும் (566) tie speech to prosperity from opposite sides in two books; 566 adds கண்ணிலன், which the note includes.

links.note: 95 makes humility (பணிவு) the true ornament (அணி). 978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம்) while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration (அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). The same two roots are set against each other in 978: the small person's self-adornment is the false ornament, and the bowing 95 praises is what the great actually wear.
links.reason: பணிவுடையன் ... அணி in 95 and பணியுமாம் ... பெருமை / அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து in 978 set the same two roots together, with true and false ornament.

links.note: 95 says humility and sweet speech are a person's ornament and other things are not (அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற). 1014 asks whether shame is not the ornament of the worthy (அணிஅன்றோ நாணுடைமை சான்றோர்க்கு), and 575 names kindly regard as the eye's ornament. The exclusive wording of 95 is therefore the chapter's emphasis: other chapters award the same title to other inner qualities, while agreeing with 95 (as Parimelazhagar reads it) that bodily ornaments are not meant.
links.reason: 95's அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற is exclusive, yet 1014 calls நாணுடைமை an அணி of the சான்றோர்; Parimelazhagar does limit பிற to bodily ornaments, so the qualification is accurately described.

links.note: 35 defines virtue as what proceeds without slipping into four things, the last being painful speech (இன்னாச்சொல்). 96 says virtue grows and its opposite wears away when one speaks good things sweetly (அல்லவை தேய அறம்பெருகும்). 35 only requires avoiding harsh words; 96 adds that the positive practice of sweet, well-chosen speech actively increases virtue.
links.reason: 35 only excludes இன்னாச்சொல்; 96 adds that நல்லவை நாடி இனிய சொலின் makes அறம் பெருகும், a positive extension of the same theme.

links.note: 96 says that if one seeks out good things and says them sweetly (நல்லவை நாடி இனிய சொலின்), what is not virtue wears away and virtue grows. 128 says that if even one harmful word has its effect (ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல் பொருட்பயன் உண்டாயின்), what was good turns out not good. Together they give speech power over one's stock of virtue in both directions: good words build it and a single bad word undoes it.
links.reason: 96 has அல்லவை தேய அறம்பெருகும் from இனிய சொல்; 128 has நன்றாகாதாகி விடும் from ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல்: the same claim that speech governs one's virtue, stated from both sides.

links.note: 97 says speech that yields benefit and does not part from pleasantness (பயன்ஈன்று பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியாச் சொல்) produces நயன் and brings forth good (நன்றி). 194 says speech with no benefit and no pleasantness (பயன்சாராப் பண்பில்சொல்) is without நயன் and removes one from good (நன்மையின் நீக்கும்). The four terms பயன், பண்பு, நயன் and நன்மை recur in the negative, so 194 is 97 inverted; Parimelazhagar glosses பண்பு as sweetness and நயன் as justice in both.
links.reason: 97 நயன் ஈன்று நன்றி பயக்கும் பயன்ஈன்று பண்பின் and 194 நயன்சாரா நன்மையின் நீக்கும் பயன்சாராப் பண்பில்சொல் do repeat the four terms in the negative; Parimelazhagar's நீதி gloss is in both.

links.note: 97 asks for speech that has both benefit (பயன்) and pleasantness (பண்பு), and credits it with producing நயன். 197 says the worthy may say what lacks நயன் if they must, but should not say what lacks பயன் (நயனில சொல்லினும் சொல்லுக ... பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று). 197 thus ranks the qualities 97 holds together: use is the one that cannot be given up. Parimelazhagar takes நயன் in 197 as justice; Subramuniyaswami takes it as pleasantness, which makes the limit on chapter 10 more direct.
links.reason: 97 joins பயன் and பண்பு and says such speech yields நயன்; 197 lets நயனில pass but not பயனில. The ranking is in the Tamil and the note states the two readings of நயன் correctly.

links.note: 98 says sweet speech that is clear of smallness (சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய இன்சொல்) gives joy in the next life and this one; Parimelazhagar explains சிறுமை as causing pain to others by what the words mean. 291 defines truth as speech containing no harm at all (யாதொன்றும் தீமை இலாத சொலல்). Sweetness and truthfulness are both defined by the same test, the absence of harm to others, and not by sound or by literal accuracy. (This edition prints சிறுமையுவு in 98, a typo for சிறுமையுள்.)
links.reason: சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய இன்சொல் and யாதொன்றும் தீமை இலாத சொலல் both define a virtue of speech by absence of harm; the note also flags the typo correctly.
links.text_issue: 98 prints சிறுமையுவு for சிறுமையுள்.

links.note: 98 says sweet speech free of smallness gives joy (இன்சொல் ... இன்பம் தரும்) here and hereafter. 911 says the sweet speech of women who desire wealth and not the man brings harm (இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). The two predicates answer each other, and the condition in 98 (சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய) marks the difference: what 98 promises holds only for sweet words that are not serving a mean purpose.
links.reason: இன்சொல் ... இன்பம் தரும் and இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும் are answering predicates, and சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய is the condition that separates them.
links.text_issue: 98 reads சிறுமையுவு, a typo for சிறுமையுள்.

links.note: 99 asks why one who sees how sweetly sweet words yield (இன்சொல் இனிதீன்றல் காண்பான்) would use harsh words (எவன்கொலோ வன்சொல் வழங்குவது); Parimelazhagar takes it as one who has felt the pleasure of others' kind words to himself. 318 asks why one who knows what is painful to his own life does painful things to other lives (என்கொலோ மன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னா செயல்). The two rhetorical questions have the same form and the same argument from one's own experience to the treatment of others, applied to words in 99 and to harm in general in 318. (The first line of 318 is misprinted in this edition, but the verse is recoverable.)
links.reason: எவன்கொலோ வன்சொல் வழங்குவது (99) and என்கொலோ மன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னா செயல் (318) have the same rhetorical form and the same argument from one's own experience (காண்பான் / தானறிவான்).
links.text_issue: 318 line 1 is misprinted (தன்னுயிர்ககு ஏன்னாமை for தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை), as the note says; the Parimelazhagar text printed under 318 is the commentary for 319.

links.note: 99 asks what could lead someone who knows the good that sweet words do to use harsh ones (வன்சொல்). 784 says friendship is not for laughing together but for going ahead to rebuke when a friend oversteps (மிகுதிக்கண் மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு). The friendship chapter supplies a case where sharp words have a purpose, so 99's question is best read as aimed at needless harshness and not at every hard word.
links.reason: எவன்கொலோ வன்சொல் வழங்குவது meets மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு; Parimelazhagar on 784 says rebuke is used because sweet words do not turn the friend back, so the limit on 99 is real.

links.note: 100 pictures someone who has ripe fruit at hand and takes the unripe: unpleasant words chosen while pleasant ones exist (இனிய உளவாக இன்னாத கூறல்). 831 defines folly as taking hold of harm and letting gain go (ஏதங்கொண்டு ஊதியம் போக விடல்). Harsh speech in 100 is an instance of exactly the choice 831 names as folly, which fits the chapter's closing argument that harsh words are a bad bargain for the speaker as well as wrong.
links.reason: இனிய உளவாக இன்னாத கூறல் / கனிஇருப்பக் காய்கவர்ந்தற்று has the same shape as ஏதங்கொண்டு ஊதியம் போக விடல்: taking the worse when the better is at hand.

links.note: 100 says speaking unpleasant things when pleasant ones are available is like taking the unripe fruit when the ripe is there (கனிஇருப்பக் காய்கவர்ந்தற்று). 1306, a speech in the Book of Love, says that love without serious and light quarrels is like over-ripe fruit and unripe fruit (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று). The ripe/unripe pair is used differently: in 100 the ripe fruit is simply the right choice, while the lover treats fruit that is too ripe and fruit that is too raw as two ways of missing the right point.
links.reason: கனிஇருப்பக் காய்கவர்ந்தற்று (100) and கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று (1306) share the ripe/unripe fruit pair, used differently as the note says; Parimelazhagar does read 1306's கனி as over-ripe.

links.note: 101 says that for help given without any prior help (செய்யாமல் செய்த உதவி) even earth and heaven are hardly a match (ஆற்றல் அரிது). 211 says obligation wants no return (கைம்மாறு வேண்டா) and asks what the world does for the rain in exchange (என் ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ). The same verb ஆற்று marks both: one verse looks from the receiver who cannot repay, the other from the giver who does not ask to be repaid.
links.reason: ஆற்றல் அரிது and என் ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ share the verb and the theme of unrepayable help, but 101 is about the receiver's debt and 211 says கைம்மாறு வேண்டா கடப்பாடு; these are complementary, not the same claim.

links.note: Both open with செய்யாமல், 'without (the other) having done anything first'. 101 applies it to help: unprompted help is beyond repayment. 313 applies it to hatred: even toward those who hate you though you did nothing (செய்யாமல் செற்றார்க்கும்), doing hurt brings sorrow with no escape. Read together, the unprovoked good creates a boundless debt while the unprovoked wrong still gives no licence to retaliate.
links.reason: செய்யாமல் செய்த உதவி and செய்யாமல் செற்றார்க்கும் open with the same word in the same sense of 'without anything having been done first', applied to unprompted help and unprovoked hatred.

links.note: 102 says help done at the time of need (காலத்தினால் செய்த நன்றி), though small, is greater than the earth. 788 makes that timeliness the definition of friendship: it removes distress there and then (ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது), like the hand going to a slipping garment. 102 values the help by its moment; 788 says what kind of helper acts in that moment.
links.reason: காலத்தினாற் செய்த நன்றி is given its agent in 788, where friendship removes distress ஆங்கே like the hand at a slipping garment.

links.note: 103 praises help from those who do not weigh the return (பயன்தூக்கார்), calling its good greater than the sea. 813 uses the same weighing verb for the opposite case: friends who weigh what they will get (உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பு) are put level with thieves. The pair shows the book judging help and friendship by one test, whether the giver was calculating.
links.reason: பயன்தூக்கார் செய்த உதவி in 103 and உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பு in 813 use the same weighing verb for uncalculating help and calculating friendship, praised and condemned respectively.

links.note: 104 says a millet of good is taken as a palmyra by those who know its worth. 109 says even harm like killing (கொன்றன்ன இன்னா) vanishes when one thinks of a single good the person did (ஒன்று நன்று உள்ளக் கெடும்). Parimelazhagar connects them in his note on 109: because the small good is held as large, that one good can cancel the later harm.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar on 109 explicitly ties 'ஒன்றுநன்று உள்ளக் கெடும்' to 104's 'தினைத்துணை ... பனைத்துணையாக் கொள்வர்', as the note says.

links.note: Both verses use the phrase மாசற்றார் கேண்மை, the bond of the stainless: 106 says do not forget it (மறவற்க), 800 says keep close to it (மருவுக). Each then adds a second command about a kind of friend, 106 never to abandon those who were a support in distress, 800 to drop the unsuitable (ஒப்பிலார்) even at a cost. The chapter on choosing friends repeats the gratitude chapter's rule and supplies its other half, whom to leave.
links.reason: மாசற்றார் கேண்மை stands in both with a paired command: மறவற்க/துறவற்க in 106 and மருவுக/ஒருவுக in 800. 800 supplies whom to leave.

links.note: 106 commands: do not abandon (துறவற்க) the friendship of those who were a support in distress. 806 states it as a description: those who keep within the bounds will not abandon (துறவார்) the tie of long-standing friends even in ruin (தொலைவிடத்தும்). The same verb is used in both, with the direction reversed: 106 is loyalty owed for help received in one's own trouble, 806 loyalty kept when trouble comes.
links.reason: துறவற்க ... துன்பத்துள் துப்பாயார் நட்பு and துறவார் தொலைவிடத்தும் ... தொடர்பு share the verb and the claim of not abandoning a friend, from the two sides of trouble.

links.note: 107 says the friendship of one who removed one's distress is remembered through seven births (எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும்). 398 says learning gained in one birth (ஒருமைக்கண்) is a protection through seven (எழுமையும்). The seven-birth span is the book's figure for what outlasts a single life, used here for a debt of gratitude and there for learning.
links.reason: எழுமை in 107 (எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும்) and 398 (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து) is a stock formula used in several other verses; the note is accurate but the pairing teaches little beyond the shared number.

links.note: 107 says people will remember (உள்ளுவர்) through seven births the friendship of those who wiped away their distress. 799 says the bond with those who abandoned one in ruin (கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார்) burns the heart even when thought of (உள்ளினும்) at the hour of death. Both are about how conduct in another's hard time is remembered: the helper for lives to come, the deserter up to the last moment.
links.reason: விழுமந் துடைத்தவர் நட்பு ... உள்ளுவர் and கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார் கேண்மை ... உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும் pair helper and deserter in hardship through the same verb of remembering.

links.note: 108 says a wrong done to you should be forgotten that very day (அன்றே மறப்பது). 113 says gain that comes from leaving fairness should be let go that very day (அன்றே ஒழிய விடல்). The shared அன்றே gives both the same urgency: neither a grievance nor an unfair gain is to be kept overnight.
links.reason: அன்றே மறப்பது and அன்றே ஒழிய விடல் share only the common adverb அன்றே for promptness; the acts and reasoning are unrelated, so the image is thin.

links.note: 109 says that even harm like killing disappears when one recalls a single good the person once did (அவர் செய்த ஒன்று நன்று உள்ள). 807 says those whose bond has come by the way of love do not cut off love even when the friend does ruinous things (அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார்). Both have the same 'even if they do grave harm' (செயினும்) clause; what outweighs the harm is a remembered favour in one and long affection in the other.
links.reason: கொன்றன்ன இன்னா செயினும் and அழிவந்த செய்யினும் share the concessive form, with a remembered நன்று in one and அன்பின் வழிவந்த கேண்மை in the other outweighing the harm.

links.note: 110 says those who kill any good may have an escape (உய்வுண்டாம்), but there is none for one who kills a good done to him (செய்ந்நன்றி கொன்ற மகற்கு). 207 has the same shape: those who incur any enmity (எனைப்பகை உற்றாரும்) escape (உய்வர்), but the enmity of one's deeds follows and kills. Both use 'everything else can be survived' to single out one thing, ingratitude in 110 and evil deeds in general in 207.
links.reason: Same construction in both: 'எந்நன்றி கொன்றார்க்கும் உய்வுண்டாம் உய்வில்லை ...' and 'எனைப்பகை யுற்றாரும் உய்வர் ... அடும்', with 'உய்' marking the one inescapable case.

links.note: 110 says there is escape (உய்வுண்டாம்) for other wrongs but none (உய்வில்லை) for killing gratitude. 896 says one burned by fire may survive (உய்வுண்டாம்), but those who go on offending the great will not (உய்யார்). The same உய்வு formula marks what each chapter treats as its unforgivable offence, so a reader should take 'only this has no escape' as the book's way of stressing gravity and not as a strict ranking.
links.reason: The same உய்வுண்டாம் / உய்வில்லை (உய்யார்) formula frames each chapter's gravest offence; the note's caution about not reading it as a strict ranking is fair.

links.note: 111 asks that fairness be kept alike across the divisions of people, on Parimelazhagar's reading toward enemy, stranger and friend. 528 says a king should not look on all in common (பொதுநோக்கான்) but according to rank or merit (வரிசையா நோக்கின்), and many will then stay by him. Together they show that impartiality in 111 does not mean identical treatment: one may not favour by relationship, but one should distinguish by desert.
links.reason: 111's தகுதி kept பகுதியால் (Parimelazhagar: foe, stranger, friend) is not the பொதுநோக்கு that 528 rejects in favour of வரிசையா நோக்கின்; impartiality is limited to not favouring by relationship.

links.note: 111 says the virtue called தகுதி is good if one keeps to what is due in each case (பகுதியால் பாற்பட்டு ஒழுக); Parimelazhagar takes பகுதி as enemy, stranger and friend. 541 defines a king's justice (முறை) as inquiring, showing favour to no one (யார்மாட்டும் கண்ணோடாது) and acting after consideration. The householder's impartiality of 111 reappears as the procedure of the ruler's court.
links.reason: 111 'பகுதியால் பாற்பட்டு ஒழுக' (Parimelazhagar: foe, stranger, friend) and 541 'கண்ணோடாது ... யார்மாட்டும் தேர்ந்து செய்வஃதே முறை' are impartiality as household virtue and as royal procedure; Parimelazhagar glosses 541's 'இறைபுரிந்து' as நடுவு நிலைமை.

links.note: 112 says the wealth of a person of rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security to his descendants. 169 admits the opposite case occurs: the prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright (செவ்வியான் கேடு) are things to be pondered (நினைக்கப்படும்). 169 thus limits 112 to the usual course of things; Parimelazhagar explains the exceptions by deeds of earlier births.
links.reason: 112 promises செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம் is சிதைவின்றி; 169 concedes செவ்வியான் கேடு and the crooked man's ஆக்கம் occur and are நினைக்கப்படும், which limits 112 to the normal course.

links.note: 112 says a fair person's wealth is a support to his posterity (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). 171 states the reverse: if one covets others' goods without fairness (நடுவின்றி), the family perishes (குடிபொன்றி) and guilt comes at once. Both tie நடுவு to what happens to one's line, 112 as promise and 171 as warning.
links.reason: செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம் ... எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு and நடுவின்றி ... வெஃகின் குடிபொன்றி state the same link between fairness and one's line, positively and negatively.

links.note: 113 says to give up at once gain that comes from leaving fairness (நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம்), even if it yields only good (நன்றே தரினும்). 328 says that, however great the gain that brings good (நன்றாகும் ஆக்கம் பெரிதெனினும்), gain that comes by killing (கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கம்) is lowest to the worthy. The same concession, 'even if it is good and large', is refused in both; only the forbidden means differs.
links.reason: நன்றே தரினும் நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கத்தை (113) and நன்றாகும் ஆக்கம் பெரிதெனினும் ... கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கம் கடை (328) refuse the same concession about ஆக்கம் got by a forbidden means.

links.note: 115 and 118 end with the same line, கோடாமை சான்றோர்க்கு அணி, 'not bending is the ornament of the worthy'. In 115 the bending is of the heart under loss and gain (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை); in 118 it is leaning to one side (ஒருபால் கோடாமை), like a balance. The repetition joins two sides of நடுவு: steadiness under one's own fortunes and impartiality between others.
links.reason: The identical close கோடாமை சான்றோர்க்கு அணி is applied to நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை under கேடும் பெருக்கமும் in 115 and to ஒருபால் கோடாமை like the கோல் in 118.

links.note: 115 says loss and increase both occur, and the worthy keep the heart from bending because of them. 169 gives the hard case: the crooked-hearted prosper and the upright are ruined (செவ்வியான் கேடு), which calls for reflection. 169 shows the situation in which 115's advice is tested, when fortune seems to reward bending.
links.reason: 115's கேடும் பெருக்கமும் ... நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை meets its hard case in 169's அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கமும் செவ்வியான் கேடும்; the vocabulary overlaps and Parimelazhagar explains both by பழவினை.

links.note: 116 says that if one's heart leaves fairness and does wrong (நடுவொரீஇ அல்ல செயின்), one should know 'I will perish' (கெடுவல்யான்). 204 says do not plot another's ruin even by a lapse, for அறம் will plot the plotter's ruin (சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). Both say that harm intended for others returns as one's own ruin; 116 makes it the wrongdoer's own knowledge, 204 gives the agent as அறம்.
links.reason: Both end in the wrongdoer's own கேடு (கெடுவல்யான் / சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு), but 116 is about leaving நடுவு and doing அல்ல, not about harm intended for another, so the note's common formula fits 204 only; what remains is the book's general point that wrong ruins the doer.

links.note: 117 says the world (உலகம்) will not count as ruin the low state (தாழ்வு) of one who stays in virtue by standing fair. 752 says everyone scorns those who have nothing (இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even if they have every good quality'. They conflict if உலகம் in 117 means people in general; Parimelazhagar avoids this by reading உலகம் there as the high-minded (உயர்ந்தோர்).
links.reason: கெடுவாக வையாது உலகம் ... தாழ்வு against இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர் conflict if உலகம் is people at large; the note names that reading and Parimelazhagar's உயர்ந்தோர் gloss that avoids it.

links.note: 117 says the low state of a person who stands fair is not held to be ruin (கெடுவாக வையாது). 988 says poverty is no disgrace (இன்மை இளிவன்று) for one who has the firmness called சால்பு. Both deny that poverty lowers a person of character; 117 says it for fairness in particular, 988 for worth as a whole.
links.reason: கெடுவாக வையாது ... நன்றிக்கண் தங்கியான் தாழ்வு and இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று சால்பென்னும் திண்மை both deny that a low or poor state degrades a person of character.

links.note: 118 describes a balance that first makes itself level (சமன்செய்து) and then weighs (சீர்தூக்கும்). 561 says a king is one who examines a case fittingly (தக்காங்கு நாடி) and punishes in proportion (ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது); Parimelazhagar glosses the examining as done 'standing in the middle' (நடுவாக நின்று). The two steps of the scale, being level and then measuring, match the two steps of just punishment.
links.reason: சமன்செய்து சீர்தூக்குங் கோல் (level, then weigh) matches தக்காங்கு நாடி ... ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது (examine impartially, then punish in proportion); Parimelazhagar's நடுவாக நின்று is quoted correctly.

links.note: 119 says rectitude is the absence of crookedness in speech (சொற்கோட்டம்), provided there is none within (உட்கோட்டம்). 279 says the straight arrow is cruel and the bent lute (யாழ்கோடு) is good, so judge people by what their deeds do. Both use straight and bent to separate appearance from substance: 119 will not take straight words as proof without a straight mind, and 279 will not take outward shape as proof at all.
links.reason: 119 சொற்கோட்டம் / உட்கோட்டம் with செப்பம், and 279 யாழ்கோடு செவ்விது, both work the straight/bent figure to separate show from substance.

links.note: 119 makes unbent speech count as rectitude only if the mind too is unbent (உட்கோட்டம் இன்மை பெறின்). 295 praises one who speaks truth together with the mind (மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின்) above those who do austerity and give. Both attach the same condition to good speech, agreement between word and mind, in the fields of fairness and of truthfulness.
links.reason: உட்கோட்டம் இன்மை பெறின் and மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின் both make good speech conditional on the mind matching it.

links.note: 120 says true trade for traders is to look after others' things as their own (பிறவும் தமபோல்). 315 asks what use understanding is if one does not guard against another's pain as one's own (பிறிதின்நோய் தந்நோய்போல்). The same 'as one's own' (தம்போல்) test is applied to goods in the market and to suffering in the chapter on not hurting.
links.reason: பிறவும் தமபோல் and பிறிதின்நோய் தந்நோய்போல் apply the same as-one's-own test to goods and to pain.
links.text_issue: Parimelazhagar's entry for 315 is the commentary on a different verse (இன்னா எனத் தான் உணர்ந்தவை..., i.e. 316).

links.note: 120 asks traders to care for what belongs to others as for what is theirs (பிறவும் தமபோல் பேணி). 1015 says the world calls those who feel shame at others' blame and their own (பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும் நாணுவார்) the dwelling of shame; Parimelazhagar reads this as weighing the two alike. Both define a virtue, fairness in one and shame in the other, by removing the difference between oneself and others.
links.reason: 120 பிறவும் தமபோல் பேணி and 1015 பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும் நாணுவார் both define a virtue by treating others' and one's own alike.

links.note: 121 says restraint brings one among the immortals (அமரருள் உய்க்கும்); 50 says one who lives on earth as one should will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப்படும்). Both promise a place among the gods to a person living an ordinary household life well, without renunciation, and 121 names restraint as the quality that does it.
links.reason: அமரருள் உய்க்கும் and தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப்படும் make the same promise within the householder section; note that Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take 50 as being esteemed as a god while on earth, which the note's 'promise a place' slightly flattens.
links.text_issue: 50: வான்உநற்யும் is a typo for வானுறையும்.

links.note: 121 ends அடங்காமை ஆரிருள் உய்த்து விடும், and 168 ends with envy, called a பாவி, which destroys fortune and தீயுழி உய்த்து விடும். The same closing verb phrase, 'drives and leaves one there', is used for lack of restraint and for envy, so the two vices are given the same power to deliver a person to a bad place.
links.reason: Both close on உய்த்து விடும் with a bad destination (ஆரிருள், தீயுழி), a distinctive shared figure for a vice delivering its owner.

links.note: 31 asks what gain is greater for a living being than virtue (அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கம் எவனோ உயிர்க்கு); 122 says there is no gain for a living being beyond restraint (ஆக்கம் அதனினூஉங்கு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு) and tells one to guard it as wealth. 122 reuses chapter 4's formula almost word for word and applies it to one particular virtue, so restraint is given the rank the earlier verse gave to virtue as a whole.
links.reason: அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கம் எவனோ உயிர்க்கு and ஆக்கம் அதனினூஉங் கில்லை உயிர்க்கு are the same formula. 122 gives அடக்கம் the rank 31 gives அறம்.

links.note: 122 tells one to guard restraint as பொருள், wealth, since nothing is a greater gain; 363 says there is no fine wealth (விழுச்செல்வம்) here like not wanting, and nothing equal to it there either. Both verses count an inner holding-back as the real wealth and both use the 'nothing equals it' form, once for the householder's restraint and once for the renouncer's freedom from craving.
links.reason: காக்க பொருளா அடக்கத்தை and வேண்டாமை அன்ன விழுச்செல்வம் both call an inner restraint the true wealth, each with a 'nothing exceeds it' clause.

links.note: 123 calls restraint செறிவு and says that, recognised, it yields distinction; 715 calls not speaking first among elders a செறிவு and ranks it the best of good things (முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு). The shared word shows the general restraint of chapter 13 turning up in the assembly as a concrete act, holding back one's speech before those who know more.
links.reason: செறிவு in 123 is general restraint that yields சீர்மை; 715's முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு is the same word applied to holding speech among முதுவர்.

links.note: 123 says that if one knows and then restrains oneself in the proper way (அறிவறிந்து ஆற்றின் அடங்கப் பெறின்), that restraint is recognised and yields distinction; Parimelazhagar takes அறிவறிந்து as knowing that restraint is itself what knowledge is. 834 gives the negative: no fool is greater than one who has studied, understood and taught others but is not himself restrained (தானடங்காப் பேதை). Together they say knowledge is finished only when it turns into restraint.
links.reason: 123 அறிவறிந்து ஆற்றின் அடங்கப் பெறின் (Parimelazhagar: அடங்குதலே அறிவாவது) and 834 ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் ... தானடங்காப் பேதை state positively and negatively that knowledge must end in restraint.

links.note: 29 speaks of those who have climbed and stand on the hill called good qualities (குணமென்னும் குன்றேறி நின்றார்), whom Parimelazhagar takes to be ascetics; 124 says the restrained person's stature is greater than a mountain (மலையினும் மாணப் பெரிது), and Parimelazhagar reads நிலை there as the householder's state. On his readings the renouncer stands on a hill while the householder who stays restrained in his own station is said to overtop one.
links.reason: குன்றேறி நின்றார் and மலையினும் மாணப் பெரிது use different words and different figures (standing on a hill of virtues; stature exceeding a mountain); the contrast of renouncer below householder is built by the note from Parimelazhagar's glosses, not by the verses.

links.note: 124 says the stature of one who is restrained without shifting from his station (நிலையின் திரியாது அடங்கியான்) is far greater than a mountain's. 965 says even those like a hill will sink if they do a lowering thing as small as a kundri seed (குன்றின் அனையாரும் குன்றுவர்). The mountain stature of 124 holds only while the 'not shifting' holds; 965 states how little it takes to lose it.
links.reason: மலையினும் மாணப் பெரிது is conditioned on நிலையின் திரியாது; 965's குன்றின் அனையாரும் குன்றுவர் ... குன்றி அனைய செயின் states how small a lapse undoes hill-like stature. Note is accurate, though Parimelazhagar takes 965's height as birth, not restraint.

links.note: 124 praises one who is restrained and does not shift from his station (நிலையின் திரியாது); 989 says those called the ஆழி of worth do not shift even when the age shifts (ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம் பெயரார்). Both measure a person by immovability, 124 against a mountain and 989 against the turning of an age.
links.reason: நிலையின் திரியாது and ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம் பெயரார் both measure a person by not moving, against a mountain and against the turn of an age.

links.note: 125 treats bowing (பணிதல்) as an excellence, a second wealth for the rich; 985 says bowing is the strength of those who get things done and the weapon by which the worthy turn opponents around (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பணிதல்). The same act is valued as character in the Book of Virtue and as effective power in the Book of Wealth.
links.reason: பணிதல் is நன்று and a further செல்வம் in 125, and ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் and மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை in 985; the same act valued as character and as power.

links.note: 126 says that drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is a protection through seven (ஒருமையுள் ... எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து); 398 says the learning one gains in one birth is a protection through seven (ஒருமைக்கண் ... எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). The closing formula is identical, so sense-restraint and learning are set side by side as the two acquisitions that carry across births.
links.reason: The frame ஒருமை... எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து is word-for-word shared, setting ஐந்தடக்கல் beside கல்வி as what carries across births.

links.note: 126 says restraint of the five in one birth protects through seven; 835 says a fool can, by what he does in one birth (ஒருமைச் செயல்), make the mire he will sink in through seven (எழுமையும் தான்புக்கு அழுந்தும் அளறு). The one-birth and seven-births arithmetic runs in both directions: one life is enough to secure the next seven or to ruin them.
links.reason: The ஒருமை / எழுமை pairing runs both ways: 126 ஒருமையுள் ... எழுமையும் ஏமாப்பு, 835 ஒருமைச் செயலாற்றும் பேதை எழுமையும் ... அளறு.

links.note: 127 says whatever else they fail to guard, let them guard the tongue, or they will grieve through a fault of speech (நாகாக்க காவாக்கால் சோகாப்பர்); 305 says if you would guard yourself, guard against anger, or anger will kill you (சினங்காக்க காவாக்கால் தன்னையே கொல்லும்). The sentence frame காக்க / காவாக்கால் is the same, and in both the harm of the unguarded thing falls on the person who failed to guard it.
links.reason: நாகாக்க காவாக்கால் சோகாப்பர் and சினங்காக்க காவாக்கால் தன்னையே கொல்லும் share the காக்க / காவாக்கால் frame, with the harm falling on the one who fails to guard.

links.note: 128 says that if even one bad word has its effect, the good turns out not good (ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல் ... நன்றாகாதாகி விடும்); Parimelazhagar takes this as the person's other merit turning bad. 965 says even hill-like people sink if they do a lowering thing the size of a kundri seed. Both hold that a single small lapse is enough to cancel a large standing good, in speech in one verse and in honour in the other.
links.reason: ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல் ... நன்றாகா தாகி விடும் and குன்றி அனைய செயின் குன்றுவர் both let one small lapse cancel a large standing good.

links.note: 129 says the scar left by the tongue never heals; 159 says those who bear the harsh words from the mouths of people who exceed all bounds (இறந்தார்வாய் இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்கிற்பவர்) are as pure as renouncers. 129 gives the reason 159's praise is so high: what the forbearing person takes without retaliation is the one kind of wound the book says does not close.
links.reason: நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு ஆறாதே explains the weight of what இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்கிற்பவர் endure; the reason is the note's inference, but it fits both verses.

links.note: 129 sets a fire-burn, which heals, against the tongue's scar, which does not; 1049 says one can even sleep in the middle of fire but cannot close an eye in the middle of poverty (நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும்). The book repeatedly takes fire as the measure of bearable pain and places a non-physical hurt beyond it.
links.reason: தீயினாற் சுட்டபுண் உள்ளாறும் and நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும் both use fire as the bearable benchmark surpassed by a non-bodily hurt (the tongue's வடு, நிரப்பு); 'repeatedly' rests on just these two but the shared use is real.

links.note: 130 says அறம் itself watches for the right moment and enters the path of one who has guarded against anger, learned, and is restrained (அறம் பார்க்கும் ஆற்றின் நுழைந்து); 204 says that if you plot another's ruin, அறம் plots the ruin of the plotter (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). In both verses virtue is an agent that acts on a person, seeking out the restrained and planning against the malicious.
links.reason: அறம் பார்க்கும் ஆற்றின் நுழைந்து and அறஞ்சூழும் both make அறம் the grammatical agent of a deliberate act toward a person.
links.text_issue: 204 reads அறஞ்சூழம், a typo for அறஞ்சூழும்.

links.note: 130 has virtue looking for its chance and coming along the path to the restrained person; 594 has prosperity asking the way and going to the one of unwavering energy (ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும்). The same figure, a good that seeks out the person fit for it instead of being pursued, is used for virtue in the first book and for worldly gain in the second. The edition's text of 594 has lost its first letter (க்கம் for ஆக்கம்), but the reading is not in doubt.
links.reason: 130 அறம் பார்க்கும் ஆற்றின் நுழைந்து and 594 ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும் both personify a good that finds its own way to the fit person, once for virtue and once for prosperity.
links.text_issue: 594 is printed க்கம்; the first letter of ஆக்கம் is missing.

links.note: 131 says conduct is to be guarded more than life because it gives excellence (ஒழுக்கம் உயிரினும் ஓம்பப்படும்); 1017 says those ruled by shame will give up life for shame and will not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்). Both place a quality of character above life itself; 1017 states as what such people actually do what 131 states as a rule.
links.reason: ஒழுக்கம் உயிரினும் ஓம்பப்படும் and நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால் நாண்துறவார் both set a trait of character above life, as rule and as observed conduct.

links.note: 133 makes conduct the thing that constitutes good family (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை); 951 says integrity and shame are found together by nature only in those born in a good house (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்அல்லது இல்லை இயல்பாக). If குடிமை in 133 means that conduct alone makes one well-born, 951 runs the other way and makes birth the source of the conduct. The conflict disappears on Parimelazhagar's reading of 133, where conduct only preserves or forfeits a rank that birth has already given.
links.reason: ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை makes conduct the criterion while இற்பிறந்தார் கண்அல்லது இல்லை இயல்பாக makes birth the source, and the note names the reading it depends on. Its summary of Parimelazhagar is slightly too narrow, since he lets conduct raise a low clan within the varna.

links.note: 133 says a lapse from conduct turns into low birth; 1019 says a lapse in கொள்கை burns one's lineage (குலஞ்சுடும் கொள்கை பிழைப்பின்), and Parimelazhagar glosses கொள்கை there as ஒழுக்கம். Both say family standing is lost through the individual's failure in conduct, one calling the result a low birth and the other a burning.
links.reason: இழுக்கம் இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும் and குலஞ்சுடும் கொள்கை பிழைப்பின் make the same claim, and both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar gloss கொள்கை as ஒழுக்கம்.

links.note: 134 treats forgetting the Veda (மறப்பினும் ஓத்துக் கொளலாகும்) as a loss that can be made good; 560 lists among the effects of a king who does not protect that those of the six occupations forget their books (அறுதொழிலோர் நூல்மறப்பர்). The same forgetting appears as a private, repairable lapse in 134 and as a sign of public ruin in 560, while 134 keeps conduct as the loss that cannot be repaired.
links.reason: மறப்பினும் ஓத்துக் கொளலாகும் and அறுதொழிலோர் நூல்மறப்பர் share the motif of the learned forgetting their text, repairable in one and a mark of misrule in the other.
links.text_issue: 134 has a stray space in பார் ப்பான்.

links.note: 135 takes it as given that the envious have no gain (ஆக்கம்); 169 says the gain of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright are things to be pondered (அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கமும் ... நினைக்கப்படும்). 169 concedes that the case 135 calls non-existent can occur and needs explaining, which weakens the simile's premise; Parimelazhagar softens it by adding 'if they occur'.
links.reason: 135 assumes அழுக்காறுடையான்கண் ஆக்கம் இல்லை, while 169 speaks of அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கமும் as something நினைக்கப்படும்; Parimelazhagar's added உளவாயின் is as the note reports.

links.note: 135 argues by comparison: as there is no gain in the envious, there is no elevation in one without conduct (அழுக்காறுடையான்கண் ஆக்கம் போன்று இல்லை). 170 states the premise on its own: none have grown great through envy (அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை). 135 takes chapter 17's claim as already known and builds its point about conduct on it.
links.reason: 135 uses அழுக்காறுடையான்கண் ஆக்கம் இல்லை as the known term of a comparison, and 170 states that premise directly (அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை).
