links.note: 136 says the strong do not slacken in conduct, knowing the harm that comes of a lapse (இழுக்கத்தின் ஏதம் படுபாக்கறிந்து); 164 says people do no wrong out of envy, knowing the harm that comes of the wrong path (இழுக்காற்றின் ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து). The second lines are nearly the same words, and both verses ground good behaviour in foreseeing consequences, which 136 counts as strength (உரவோர்).
links.reason: 136 இழுக்கத்தின் ஏதம் படுபாக்கறிந்து and 164 இழுக்காற்றின் ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து share nearly the whole second line and the same grounding in foreseen harm.

links.note: 137 says that from conduct people reach high standing and from a lapse they reach எய்தாப் பழி, which Parimelazhagar takes as blame that is not properly theirs, laid on them because the lapse makes it believable. 117 says the world will not count as ruin the low state of one who stays in the right by being fair (கெடுவாக வையாது உலகம்). In both the world's verdict follows character more than facts: it discounts the upright person's fall and charges the lapsed person with more than he did.
links.reason: The link rests on Parimelazhagar's reading of எய்தாப் பழி as undeserved blame; 117's தாழ்வு is the upright man's low estate (poverty), not a 'fall', and neither verse extends the other, so the 'world's verdict follows character' synthesis is the note's own.

links.note: 138 calls good conduct the seed of good (நன்றிக்கு வித்தாகும் நல்லொழுக்கம்) and says bad conduct always gives suffering; 361 calls craving the seed that produces unending birth for all beings (தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து). The seed figure is used for a cause whose yield comes later and keeps coming, once for a good crop and once for a bad one.
links.reason: நன்றிக்கு வித்தாகும் நல்லொழுக்கம் and தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து use வித்து for a cause of opposite harvests; the note slightly overextends 'keeps coming' to 138, where என்றும் belongs to தீயொழுக்கம், but the shared figure is real and instructive.

links.note: 139 says speaking evil things even by a slip is not possible for those who have conduct (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல் ஒல்லாவே); 199 says those of stainless sight do not say meaningless things even in forgetfulness (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லார்). Both claim that a settled quality rules out even the accidental lapse of speech, and they trace that quality to conduct in one case and to clear understanding in the other.
links.reason: வழுக்கியும் ... சொலல் ஒல்லாவே and பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லார் both exclude even the accidental lapse of speech, tied to ஒழுக்கம் and to மாசறு காட்சி.

links.note: 139 makes the absence of evil speech a test of having conduct; 959 says that as a sprout shows the ground it lay in, the words from the mouth show the family of the one born in it (குலத்தில் பிறந்தார் வாய்ச்சொல்). Both treat what comes out of the mouth as the evidence of what a person is.
links.reason: தீய வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல் ஒல்லா and குலத்தில் பிறந்தார் வாய்ச்சொல் காட்டும் both make speech the outward evidence of character.

links.note: 139 says a person of conduct cannot speak evil even by a slip; 1044 says that even in the well-born, poverty brings the slackness from which degrading words are born (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும் இன்மை இளிவந்த சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு தரும்). 1044 names a condition, want, under which the slip of speech that 139 calls impossible does happen to good people.
links.reason: ஒல்லாவே தீய வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல் is limited by இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும் இன்மை இளிவந்த சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு தரும்: want produces the very slip 139 rules out.

links.note: 140 makes accord with the world the test that learning must pass; 280 says neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்துவிடின்). In both, the world's standard outranks a formal qualification, learning for the scholar and outward marks for the ascetic. Parimelazhagar takes உலகம் in both verses as the worthy and not people at large.
links.reason: உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல் over பலகற்றும், and உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்துவிடின் over மழித்தலும் நீட்டலும், both set the world's standard above a formal qualification; Parimelazhagar reads உலகம் as உயர்ந்தோர் in both.

links.note: 832 defines the folly of all follies (பேதைமையுள் எல்லாம் பேதைமை) as setting one's love on what is not proper to one (கையல்லதன்கண் காதன்மை). 141 names one case of exactly that: the பேதைமை of desiring (பெட்டு ஒழுகும்) a woman who is another's. Read together, 141 is an instance of the general definition that 832 gives much later.
links.reason: 832 காதன்மை கையல்லதன்கண் செயல் defines the worst பேதைமை as desire for what is improper to one, and 141 calls பிறன்பொருளாள் பெட்டொழுகும் exactly a பேதைமை; the instance fits the definition.

links.note: 141 says the folly (பேதைமை) of desiring a woman who is another's (பிறன்பொருளாள்) is not found (இல்) in those who have seen aram and porul; 910 says the folly that comes of attachment to a woman (பெண்சேர்ந்தாம் பேதைமை) is never found (இல்) in those with a deliberating mind. Both end on 'பேதைமை ... இல்' and treat the lapse as a failure of understanding that knowledge excludes, once about another's wife in the Book of Virtue and once about subservience to one's own in the Book of Wealth.
links.reason: Both end on பேதைமை ... இல் and exclude the lapse by understanding (அறம்பொருள் கண்டார் / எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சத்து), across the two books.

links.note: 142 says that among all who stand outside virtue (அறன்கடை நின்றாருள் எல்லாம்) none is a greater fool than the one who stands at another's door (பிறன்கடை); 150 says that even one who does not keep to virtue and does wrong (அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும்) does well not to desire another's woman. Both verses rank within the class of the non-virtuous, and both put this one offence at the bottom, 142 by naming the worst case and 150 by naming the one abstention still worth having.
links.reason: அறன்கடை நின்றாருள் எல்லாம் ... பேதையார் இல் and அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும் ... நயவாமை நன்று both rank this offence as worst among wrongdoers.

links.note: 143 counts the betrayer of a trusting household as no different from the dead (விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர்); 214 says only the one who knows what is fitting lives (உயிர்வாழ்வான்), and anyone else is placed among the dead (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). In both, being alive is measured by conduct and not by breath, once for a wrong committed and once for a duty to others left undone.
links.reason: விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர் and செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும் both count the living as dead on grounds of conduct; note reads both accurately.
links.text_issue: 143: 'விளிந்தா஡஢ன்' has stray characters; should be விளிந்தாரின்.

links.note: 143 says those who go on doing evil in the home of people who trust them (தெளிந்தாரில்) are 'no different from the dead' (விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர்); 926 uses the same construction for sleepers (துஞ்சினார் செத்தாரின் வேறல்லர்) and extends it to drinkers. Parimelazhagar explains 926 by the absence of awareness and 143 by the loss of aram, porul and inbam, so the same formula of living death is applied to a moral failure in one verse and to loss of consciousness in the other.
links.reason: விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர் and செத்தாரின் வேறல்லர் are the same formula; Parimelazhagar's grounds (அறம் பொருள் இன்பங்கள் ... எய்தாமை for 143, அறிவின்மை for 926) are reported correctly. Strictly 926 applies the formula to sleepers and gives drinkers the poison comparison.
links.text_issue: 143: 'விளிந்தா஡஢ன்' is an encoding corruption of விளிந்தாரின்.

links.note: Both verses use the millet's measure (தினைத்துணை). In 433 those who are ashamed of blame (பழிநாணுவார்) take a fault of a millet's size as large as a palmyra; in 144 the man entering another's home does not reflect even a millet's worth (தினைத்துணையும் தேரான்). The pair shows the same measure from opposite sides: the careful person enlarges the smallest fault, and the adulterer does not give the smallest thought.
links.reason: தினைத்துணை is the measure in both: the adulterer தினைத்துணையும் தேரான், while பழிநாணுவார் take a தினைத்துணை fault as பனைத்துணை.

links.note: 144 asks what greatness comes to, however great a person is (எனைத்துணையர் ஆயினும் என்னாம்), if he enters another's home without weighing it even a millet's worth (தினைத்துணையும் தேரான்). 965 says even those like a hill (குன்றின் அனையார்) sink if they do a lowering deed as small as a kunri seed. Both hold that standing does not outweigh a degrading act; 965 gives the general rule and 144 one named act.
links.reason: எனைத்துணையர் ஆயினும் என்னாம் ... தினைத்துணையும் (144) and குன்றின் அனையாரும் குன்றுவர் ... குன்றி அனைய செயின் (965): greatness set against a tiny measure in both, rule and instance.

links.note: 233 says that apart from high renown nothing in the world stands without perishing (புகழல்லால் பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன்று இல்). 145 says the blame of the man who violates another's home also stands forever without dying (எஞ்ஞான்றும் விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி). Taken literally 145 names a second undying thing, so the pair shows the book treating lasting blame as the counterpart of lasting fame.
links.reason: 233 'புகழல்லால் பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன்றில்' is literally limited by 145 'எஞ்ஞான்றும் விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி', a second thing that stands undying; the note states the literal reading it depends on.

links.note: 145 says one who crosses into another's home thinking it easy (எளிதென இல்லிறப்பான்) gets blame that stands forever without dying (விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி). 284 says a love grown strong in theft (களவின்கண் கன்றிய காதல்) yields at harvest a distress that does not die (வீயா விழுமம்). The same logic, a desire for what is another's that looks light at the start and has a permanent result, is applied to another's wife and to another's goods.
links.reason: எளிதென இல்லிறப்பான் ... விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி and களவின்கண் கன்றிய காதல் ... வீயா விழுமம் share the pattern of desire for what is another's ending in an undying result.

links.note: 146 lists four things that never leave the man who crosses into another's home: enmity, sin, fear and blame (பகை பாவம் அச்சம் பழி). 171 says that one who covets another's good property without fairness finds his family ruined and fault brought on at once (குடிபொன்றிக் குற்றமும் ஆங்கே தரும்). Coveting another's wife and coveting another's goods are both given immediate, compound consequences; Parimelazhagar reads the பழி of 146 as blame on the family (குடிப்பழி), which brings it closer to the குடி of 171.
links.reason: பகைபாவம் அச்சம் பழி (146) and குடிபொன்றிக் குற்றமும் (171) attach compound consequences to coveting wife and goods; only 171 says ஆங்கே (at once), 146 says இகவா (never leave), so 'immediate' fits one verse only.

links.note: Both verses use the formula 'the one called a householder' (இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான்). 41 defines him by what he supports: he is the steady help of the three on their good path. 147 defines him by what he refrains from: he lives the household life with aram (அறனியலான்) who does not desire the womanhood of one who belongs to another (பிறனியலாள் பெண்மை நயவாதவன்). Together they give a positive and a negative test for the same title.
links.reason: இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் opens the definition in 41 (மூவர்க்கும் ... துணை) and recurs in 147 with அறனியலான் and பிறனியலாள் பெண்மை நயவாதவன்; a positive and a negative test, as the note says.

links.note: 49 says that what is called aram is household life, and that it is good if there is nothing in it that another blames (பிறன்பழிப்பது இல்லாயின்). 147 says the householder living by aram is the one who does not desire another's woman. 147 can be read as naming a specific condition under which the household life of 49 stays free of others' blame; chapter 15 itself (145, 146) names பழி as the result of the offence.
links.reason: Both define the அறன் householder, but the bridge rests on taking 49's அஃதும் as household life (Manakkudavar); Parimelazhagar takes it as renunciation, which the note does not flag, and the பழி link comes from 145-146, not from 147's own words.

links.note: 148 praises not even looking at (நோக்காத) another's wife; Parimelazhagar glosses this as not taking her into the mind. 282 says that even thinking in the heart (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும்) of taking another's goods (பிறன்பொருளை) by stealth is wrong. In both chapters the prohibition is moved back from the act to the look or the thought, for another's wife and for another's property.
links.reason: பிறன்மனை நோக்காத (Parimelazhagar: உட்கொள்ளாத) and உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும் தீதே பிறன்பொருளை both push the prohibition back from act to look or thought, for another's wife and another's goods.

links.note: 150 says not desiring another's woman is good even in one who practises no aram and does wrong; 297 says that if one can keep to not lying, then not doing the other virtues (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை) is still good. Both isolate a single restraint and say it holds its value without the rest of virtue. Set side by side, the book makes this kind of claim for more than one virtue, so each is better read as emphasis than as a ranking.
links.reason: அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும் ... நயவாமை நன்று (150) and பொய்யாமை ஆற்றின் அறம்பிற செய்யாமை நன்று (297) isolate one restraint in the same way; the note's caution about ranking is sensible.

links.note: 151 says bearing with those who scorn us is the foremost thing (பொறுத்தல் தலை). 579, in the chapter on kindly regard in the Book of Wealth, says that showing regard and bearing (கண்ணோடிப் பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை) even with those whose nature is to hurt us is the foremost quality. The same ranking, with the same words பொறுத்தல் and தலை, is given for the householder and again for the ruler.
links.reason: இகழ்வார்ப் பொறுத்தல் தலை and ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும் ... பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை give the same ranking with the same words in two books.

links.note: Parimelazhagar reads 152 as telling one to bear a wrong even when one is able to punish it (தாம் ஒறுத்தற்கு இயன்ற காலத்தும்). 301 states that condition outright: only the one who holds back anger where it can take effect (செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான்) truly holds it back, and where it cannot, it makes no difference. 301 supplies the reason the commentator's condition matters: forbearance toward those one cannot hurt is not yet forbearance.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar's gloss on 152's என்றும் (தாம் ஒறுத்தற்கு இயன்ற காலத்தும்) is the condition 301 states as செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான் சினங்காப்பான்; the note attributes the reading correctly.

links.note: 152 says to bear transgression always (என்றும்) and better still to forget it. 488, advising a king on timing, says: on seeing enemies, bear them (சுமக்க); when their end is seen to have come, the head goes down (கிழக்காம் தலை). In 488 the bearing is temporary and is kept in mind until the moment to act, where 152 asks for a bearing with no end that passes into forgetting. The Book of Wealth thus limits to a tactic what the Book of Virtue states without condition.
links.reason: பொறுத்தல் இறப்பினை என்றும் is forbearance of a wrong even when one could punish (Parimelazhagar), while செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க is a king bowing to enemies until இறுவரை; different verbs, objects and situations, so 488 does not limit 152 so much as show endurance used as a tactic in another domain.

links.note: 153 says the strength within strength (வன்மையுள் வன்மை) is bearing with fools (மடவார்ப் பொறை); 444 says the chief of all strengths (வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை) is to live so that those greater than oneself become one's own. Neither verse puts strength in force. One finds it in enduring those below one in understanding and the other in attaching oneself to those above.
links.reason: Both redefine strength with the same phrase: வன்மையுள் வன்மை மடவார்ப் பொறை and வன்மையு ளெல்லாந் தலை for தம்மிற் பெரியார் தமரா ஒழுகுதல்; neither is force.
links.text_issue: 153: 'இன்நம்யுள்' is a typo for இன்மையுள்.

links.note: Both verses name a 'poverty within poverty' (இன்மையுள் இன்மை) and give different answers: in 153 it is turning away a guest, in 841 it is lack of understanding (அறிவின்மை), with other lack not counted as lack by the world. The same superlative formula serves hospitality in the Book of Virtue and intelligence in the Book of Wealth, which shows the formula working as emphasis within each chapter's topic.
links.reason: Both use the formula 'இன்மையுள் இன்மை', for 'விருந்தொரால்' in 153 and 'அறிவின்மை' in 841; the note is accurate about each.
links.text_issue: 153: the edition's 'இன்நம்யுள்' is a typo for 'இன்மையுள்'.

links.note: 154 ties நிறை to forbearance: to keep நிறையுடைமை, live guarding பொறையுடைமை. 864 pairs the same two things in the negative, describing the man who does not leave off anger and has no நிறை (நீங்கான் வெகுளி நிறையிலன்) as easy prey for anyone. The commentators gloss நிறை differently in the two places (Parimelazhagar: சால்பு in 154; Pope, following him, has keeping secrets in 864; Manakkudavar on 154 has a conduct of self-guarding), but in both verses its presence goes with restraint of anger and its absence with unchecked anger.
links.reason: நிறையுடைமை goes with பொறையுடைமை in 154 and நிறையிலன் with நீங்கான் வெகுளி in 864; the note is candid that the commentators gloss நிறை differently.
links.text_issue: 154 is printed 'பொநற்யுடைமை' for பொறையுடைமை.

links.note: 154 says that one who wants நிறையுடைமை never to leave should guard forbearance; Parimelazhagar glosses நிறை here as சால்பு. 987 asks what use சால்பு is if one does not do pleasing things even to those who have done one harm (இன்னாசெய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்). On Parimelazhagar's reading the two say the same thing from both ends: forbearance keeps சால்பு in place, and சால்பு that does not show in the treatment of offenders is worth nothing.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does gloss 154's நிறையுடைமை as சால்புடைமை, and 987 tests சால்பு by இன்னாசெய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்தல்; the note makes the link conditional on that gloss.
links.text_issue: 154 பொநற்யுடைமை is a misprint for பொறையுடைமை.

links.note: 155 says the wise do not count as anything those who punish in return (ஒறுத்தாரை ஒன்றாக வையார்) and keep those who forbear like stored gold. 314 keeps the word ஒறுத்தல் and gives it a new content: the way to punish those who have done harm is to shame them by doing them good (அவர்நாண நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்). 314 thus shows the only form of 'punishing' that 155's judgment leaves open. (The Parimelazhagar text displayed for 314 in this edition belongs to 315.)
links.reason: 155 dismisses ஒறுத்தாரை and 314 keeps the word (ஒறுத்தல்) but redefines it as அவர்நாண நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்; the note reads both correctly and rightly flags the misplaced commentary.
links.text_issue: The Parimelazhagar text shown under 314 (அறிவினான் ஆகுவது உண்டோ) belongs to 315.

links.note: 155 says those who punish (ஒறுத்தார்) are not counted as anything. 549 says that guarding the people and removing wrongdoing (குற்றம் கடிதல்) is no stain on a king but his work (வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்). Parimelazhagar restricts 155 to a harm done to oneself, and 549 concerns a ruler acting for his subjects, so 549 marks the limit of 155: the low regard for punishing applies to personal retaliation and not to the office of justice.
links.reason: 155 'ஒறுத்தாரை ஒன்றாக வையாரே' is limited by 549 'குற்றம் கடிதல் வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்'; Parimelazhagar restricts 155 to harm done to oneself ('பிறன் தமக்குத் தீங்கு செய்தவழி'), as the note says.

links.note: 156 says those who forbear have renown until the end (பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ்), against one day's pleasure for those who retaliate; 145 says the man who violates another's home thinking it easy gets blame that never dies (விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி). The adjacent chapters use the same accounting, a brief gratification weighed against a permanent reputation, with புகழ் on one side and பழி on the other. Manakkudavar takes பொன்றுந் துணையும் as until the person's own death, Parimelazhagar as until the world ends.
links.reason: பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ் and விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி do set lasting praise against lasting blame, but only 156 has the brief gratification (ஒருநாளை இன்பம்); 145 says எளிதென, 'thinking it easy', so 'the same accounting' holds for one verse only.

links.note: 156 sets the one day's joy of those who retaliate (ஒருநாளை இன்பம்) against the lasting renown of those who forbear. 173 says those who want the other joy (மற்றின்பம்) will not do what is not aram out of desire for a small joy (சிற்றின்பம்). Both argue against a wrong by the shortness of the pleasure it buys, for retaliation in one verse and for coveting in the other.
links.reason: ஒருநாளை இன்பம் against பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ், and சிற்றின்பம் against மற்றின்பம்: both argue from the smallness of the pleasure the wrong buys.

links.note: 156 grants the retaliator one day's pleasure and gives the forbearing renown to the end. 856 says that the life of one who says it is sweet (இனிது) to prevail in hostility is close to failure and ruin (தவலும் கெடலும் நணித்து). Both admit that getting the better of an opponent tastes sweet and both say the sweetness is brief; the verse in the Book of Wealth names ruin where the verse in the Book of Virtue names only the loss of lasting fame.
links.reason: ஒறுத்தார்க்கு ஒருநாளை இன்பம் and இகலின் மிகல் இனிது என்பவன் ... தவலும் கெடலும் நணித்து both grant the sweetness of prevailing and deny that it lasts.

links.note: 157 says that though others do what is improper to one (திறனல்ல தற்பிறர் செய்யினும்), it is good not to do what is not aram. 312 says that even when someone has done harm out of hatred, not doing harm in return (மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை) is the settled principle of the stainless. The same rule appears in the householder's chapter on forbearance and in the ascetic's chapter on not harming, which makes it common to both ways of life.
links.reason: 157 'திறனல்ல தற்பிறர் செய்யினும்... அறனல்ல செய்யாமை நன்று' and 312 'கறுத்துஇன்னா செய்தவக் கண்ணும் மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை' state the same non-retaliation rule in the householder and ascetic sections.

links.note: Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read நோநொந்து in 157 as grieving for the suffering that will come to the wrongdoers. 319 states the mechanism behind that expectation: if one does harm to others in the forenoon, harm comes to oneself in the afternoon of its own accord (தாமே வரும்). On the commentators' reading 157 presupposes 319: the injured person pities the offender because the offence will return on him, and for the same reason does not add a wrong of his own. Kalaignar instead takes the pain in 157 as the injured person's own.
links.reason: The link rests on Parimelazhagar's reading of நோநொந்து (grief for the suffering coming to the wrongdoer), which does fit 319's தாமே வரும்; but Manakkudavar is misreported, since he reads it as the pain the others would feel if one retaliated (தானுஞ் செய்தால் அவர்க்கு உளதாம் நோவு).

links.note: 157: though others do one wrong, not doing what is not aram is good (அறனல்ல செய்யாமை நன்று). 852: though someone does unbearable things intending division (பகல்கருதிப் பற்றா செயினும்), not doing harm with hostility in mind is the chief thing (இன்னாசெய்யாமை தலை). The 'even if they do ... not doing' structure and the refusal to answer in kind recur in the Book of Wealth's chapter on hostility, where the reason given is political prudence as well as virtue.
links.reason: செய்யினும் ... செய்யாமை நன்று/தலை is the same structure of non-retaliation in both; the note's remark about political prudence is context from the chapter, not from 852 itself.

links.note: 158 says to overcome those who do excessive wrong out of arrogance (மிகுதியான்) by one's own worthiness (தகுதியான் வென்றுவிடல்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as forbearance. 985 says the strength of the able is to bow (பணிதல்), and that this is the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Both describe yielding as the means of prevailing and use the vocabulary of contest, வெல்லல் and படை, for it.
links.reason: 158 தகுதியான் வென்றுவிடல் and 985 பணிதல் ... மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை both cast non-retaliation or bowing in contest terms; the note follows the Tamil of 985 even though Parimelazhagar takes பணிதல் in the first half as humbling oneself to helpers.

links.note: 158 calls forbearance toward the arrogant a victory (வென்றுவிடல்). 986 says the touchstone of சால்பு is to accept defeat (தோல்வி ... கொளல்) even from those who are not one's equals. The same conduct toward an overbearing lesser person is named winning in one verse and taking a loss in the other; 986 adds that it has to be felt and accepted as a defeat, which guards against reading 158 as a way of scoring over the offender. Manakkudavar on 158 says explicitly that forbearing is not defeat but is itself the victory.
links.reason: 158 calls forbearance toward the overbearing வென்றுவிடல் and 986 makes தோல்வி துலையல்லார் கண்ணும் கொளல் the touchstone; Manakkudavar on 158 does say பொறுத்தல் தோல்வியாகாது, அது தானே வெற்றி, so the verses check each other.

links.note: 158 says one defeats the overbearing by one's own forbearing worth. 1327, spoken by the man in the Book of Love, says that in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses has won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), as is seen in the union that follows. The paradox that giving way is the real victory appears in ethics and again, in a dramatised speech, in love; the second is a lover's remark and not a moral rule, but the shape of the thought is the same.
links.reason: தகுதியான் வென்று விடல் (158) and ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார் (1327) share the paradox of winning by yielding; the note marks the second as a lover's remark, not a rule.

links.note: 159 says those who endure (நோற்கிற்பவர்) the harsh words of transgressors are as pure as renouncers. 48 says a household life that keeps others on their path and does not slip from aram has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). Both apply the ascetic's verb நோல் to the householder and set him level with or above the ascetic; Parimelazhagar on 159 adds that these are people who remain in household life.
links.reason: நோற்கிற்பவர் set beside துறந்தார் in 159 and நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து in 48: the ascetic's verb given to the householder. Parimelazhagar's இல்வாழ்க்கைக்கண் நின்றேயும் on 159 is as cited.

links.note: Both verses play on இறந்தார் and துறந்தார். 310: those who go beyond bounds in anger (இறந்தார்) are like the dead, and those who have renounced anger are equal to renouncers (துறந்தார் துணை). 159: those who endure harsh words from the mouths of those who go beyond bounds (இறந்தார்வாய் இன்னாச்சொல்) have the purity of renouncers (துறந்தாரின் தூய்மை). In both, a householder's control over anger, his own or his response to another's, earns the standing of renunciation.
links.reason: Both verses pair இறந்தார் (those who exceed bounds) with துறந்தார் and grant the restrained person the renouncer's standing; only quibble is that 310 sits in the ascetic section, so 'householder' fits 159 better than 310.

links.note: 159 praises those who endure harsh words (இன்னாச்சொல்) from people who overstep. 389 says the world rests under the parasol of the king who has the character to bear words bitter to the ear (செவிகைப்பச் சொற்பொறுக்கும்). The same capacity is a private virtue in one verse and a quality of rule in the other. Parimelazhagar takes the bitter words of 389 to be the rebukes of advisers, so there the speaker means well, unlike the transgressors of 159.
links.reason: இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்கிற்பவர் and செவிகைப்பச் சொற்பொறுக்கும் பண்புடை வேந்தன் show the same endurance of bitter words in a householder and a king, and the note flags the difference in who speaks.

links.note: 261 defines the form of tavam as two things: bearing the pain that comes to one (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்) and doing no harm to living beings. 160 uses the same verb for both the faster and the one who endures harsh words (நோற்பார்). By 261's definition the person in 160 who bears abuse and does not retaliate already meets both parts of tavam, which explains how 160 can rank him ahead of those who fast.
links.reason: 160 uses நோற்பார் for both the faster and the one who bears இன்னாச்சொல், and 261 defines தவம் by உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்; reading 160 through that definition is apt, though 'does not retaliate' is the note's inference and not in 160's words.

links.note: 160 ranks those who fast behind those who bear harsh words; 295 says one who speaks truth in accord with his heart is above those who practise austerity together with giving (தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை). In both a virtue of everyday speech, enduring it in one case and keeping it truthful in the other, is placed above formal religious practice.
links.reason: 160 puts உண்ணாது நோற்பார் 'பின்' those who bear இன்னாச்சொல்; 295 puts மனத்தொடு வாய்மை above தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வார் ('தலை'). Both rank a virtue of speech over austerity, in different chapters.

links.note: 135 pairs the same two words: as the envious have no ஆக்கம், so one without ஒழுக்கம் has no உயர்வு. 161 fuses them, asking that freedom from அழுக்காறு be taken as ஒழுக்காறு. The rhyme ஒழுக்கு/அழுக்காறு is used in both to set envy and conduct side by side.
links.reason: ஒழுக்காறாக் கொள்க ... அழுக்காறு இலாத இயல்பு (161) and அழுக்காறுடையான் ... ஒழுக்கமிலான் (135) both place envy beside conduct by the same sound-pair, each in the other's chapter.

links.note: 162 says that among excellent gains (விழுப்பேற்றின்) nothing equals being free of envy toward anyone (அஃதொப்பது இல்லை). 363 says there is no excellent wealth (விழுச்செல்வம்) like வேண்டாமை, here or there (அஃதொப்பது இல்). The same formula ranks an absence, of envy in the householder book and of wanting in the ascetic book, above every positive possession.
links.reason: விழுப்பேற்றின் அஃதொப்பது இல்லை and விழுச்செல்வம் ... அஃதொப்பது இல் use the same ranking formula for an absence: of அழுக்காறு in one, வேண்டாமை in the other.

links.note: 141 says the folly of desiring a woman who is another's (பிறன்பொருளாள்) is not found in those who have seen அறம் and பொருள். 163 says the envier of பிறனாக்கம் is one who wants neither அறன் nor ஆக்கம். In adjacent chapters a wrong attitude to what is another's is measured against the same pair, virtue and wealth.
links.reason: பிறன்பொருளாள் ... அறம்பொருள் கண்டார்கண் இல் and அறன் ஆக்கம் வேண்டாதான் ... பிறனாக்கம்: the same pair as the measure of a wrong attitude to what is another's. The chapters (15 and 17) are near, not adjacent as the note says.

links.note: 163 says the one who does not cherish another's prosperity (பிறனாக்கம் பேணாது) and envies it is called one who wants neither அறன் nor ஆக்கம். 1079 shows the same reaction in the கீழ்: on seeing others clothed and fed (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் காணின்) he is quick to find a fault in them. The later verse gives the behaviour that the earlier one judges.
links.reason: பிறனாக்கம் பேணாது அழுக்கறுப்பான் is the disposition, and உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் காணின் பிறர்மேல் வடுக்காண வற்றாகும் is its behaviour; Manakkudavar explicitly labels 1079 as envy.

links.note: 304 asks whether there is any other enemy than anger (சினத்தின் பகையும் உளவோ பிற), which kills smile and joy. 165 says the envious need no enemy since envy itself brings ruin. Two of the four things 35 excludes from virtue, anger and envy, are each described as the person's own enemy.
links.reason: அதுசாலும் ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது and சினத்தின் பகையும் உளவோ பிற both make an inner vice the person's own sufficient enemy.

links.note: 434 says fault itself is the enemy that brings one's end (குற்றமே அற்றம் தரூஉம் பகை). 165 says the same of one fault: envy suffices to ruin its holder without any ஒன்னார். The king's general rule in Book 2 has a specific case already stated in Book 1.
links.reason: குற்றமே அற்றம் தரூஉம் பகை states generally what 165 says of envy, that it suffices for ruin even where ஒன்னார் fail (கேடீன்பது).
links.text_issue: 165 prints வழுக்காயும் for வழுக்கியும்; 434 prints த்ரூஉம் for தரூஉம்.

links.note: 165 says envy is enough for the envious: it brings ruin even when enemies fail (ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது). 448 says a king without people who rebuke him perishes even with no one to ruin him (கெடுப்பார் இலானும் கெடும்). Both describe ruin that needs no outside enemy, once in a private vice and once in a ruler's unguarded state.
links.reason: ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது and கெடுப்பார் இலானும் கெடும் both describe ruin without an outside enemy, in a private vice and in kingship.
links.text_issue: 165 is printed வழுக்காயும்; the accepted reading, which the note and Parimelazhagar use, is வழுக்கியும்.

links.note: 527 says crows do not hide food but call the others and eat, and that ஆக்கம் belongs only to those of that nature (அன்ன நீரார்க்கே). 166 gives the opposite disposition and result: one who grudges giving leaves his சுற்றம் without food or clothing. Both tie a household's kin and its prosperity to the attitude taken toward sharing.
links.reason: கொடுப்பது அழுக்கறுப்பான் is one who envies what another gives to others (both commentators), not one who grudges sharing his own, so the note's 'attitude toward sharing' blurs envy into stinginess; the சுற்றம்/food contrast with 527 is real but looser than stated.

links.note: Both verses use the phrase உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம். In 1079 the base man sees others' clothing and food and finds fault with them; in 166 the kin of one who envies what is given (கொடுப்பது அழுக்கறுப்பான்) perish without clothing or food. The pairing shows what is envied returning as what is lost.
links.reason: The distinctive phrase உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் occurs in both, as what the envier's kin lose in 166 and what the base begrudge in others in 1079.

links.note: 167 says the fair goddess (செய்யவள்) grudges the envious man and shows him to her elder sister (தவ்வை). 617 names both sisters by residence: மாமுகடி lives in sloth, and தாமரையினாள் in the effort of the unslothful. The same pair of goddesses marks envy in Book 1 and sloth in Book 2 as conditions that hand a person over from fortune to misfortune.
links.reason: The sister pair is in both: 167 செய்யவள் ... தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும், 617 மாமுகடி in மடி and தாமரையினாள் in தாள்; the shared figure is distinctive and used the same way.

links.note: 117 says the world will not set down as ruin (கெடுவாக வையாது) the low state of one who stays in what is right through fairness. 169 lists the ruin of the upright (செவ்வியான் கேடு) as something to be pondered. 117 limits how that கேடு should be counted: the upright person's decline is not regarded as real ruin.
links.reason: செவ்வியான் கேடு (169) and கெடுவாக வையாது ... தாழ்வு (117) speak of the same case, the upright person's decline, and 117 does limit how that கேடு is to be counted.

links.note: 171 says that coveting another's goods without fairness makes the family perish and brings faults at once (குடிபொன்றிக் குற்றமும் ஆங்கே தரும்). 604 says of the slothful that the family dies down and faults multiply (குடிமடிந்து குற்றம் பெருகும்). The same double penalty, on the குடி and in குற்றம், is attached to greed in Book 1 and to sloth in Book 2.
links.reason: 'குடிபொன்றிக் குற்றமும் ஆங்கே தரும்' and 'குடிமடிந்து குற்றம் பெருகும்' attach the same twin penalty on குடி and குற்றம் to coveting and to sloth.

links.note: 172 says those ashamed of unfairness (நடுவன்மை நாணுபவர்) will not do blameworthy things out of desire for the gain to be had (படுபயன் வெஃகி). 113 gives the instruction that goes with it: gain that comes from leaving fairness (நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம்) is to be dropped that very day, even if it brings only good. 172 describes the character and 113 the rule it follows.
links.reason: நடுவன்மை நாணுபவர் who will not act from படுபயன் வெஃகி (172) are the people who follow 113's rule to drop நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம் even if it நன்றே தரினும்.

links.note: 164 says people do no wrong out of envy because they know the harm that comes of the wrong path (ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து). 172 says people do nothing blameworthy out of coveting because they are ashamed of unfairness (நாணுபவர்). The neighbouring chapters use the same sentence shape, ending in செய்யார், with knowledge of consequences as the check in one and shame in the other.
links.reason: Both end in செய்யார் with a named check: நடுவன்மை நாணுபவர் in 172 and ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து in 164; the note describes shape and difference accurately.

links.note: 754 says wealth that comes without wrong and with knowledge of the means (தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்) yields both அறன் and இன்பம். 173 says the small joy got by coveting is refused by those who want the other joy. Together they show the choice in 173 is not between wealth and joy: wealth rightly got delivers the joy that coveting forfeits.
links.reason: On Parimelazhagar's reading மற்றின்பம் is the lasting joy that comes by virtue, which is what தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள் ... இன்பமும் ஈனும் promises; Manakkudavar's reading (release) would loosen it, but the note's wording holds on the Tamil.

links.note: 174 says those of faultless sight who have conquered the senses will not covet on the thought 'we have nothing' (இலமென்று வெஃகுதல் செய்யார்). 205 forbids doing evil on the same plea (இலன் என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க) and adds that doing so makes one poor again. Both name poverty as the excuse and reject it; 205 gives the consequence that 174 leaves unstated.
links.reason: இலமென்று வெஃகுதல் செய்யார் and இலன் என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க reject the same plea of poverty, and 205 adds இலனாகும் மற்றும் பெயர்த்து.

links.note: 656 says that even if one must see the mother who bore one go hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்), one should not do what the worthy condemn. 174 says the thought of being without does not make the self-controlled covet. 656 pushes the same refusal to its hardest case, where the want is another's and not one's own.
links.reason: இலமென்று வெஃகுதல் செய்யார் refuses wrong under one's own want, and ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும் செய்யற்க pushes the refusal to a mother's hunger.

links.note: 1040 says the good woman called Land laughs on seeing those who sit idle saying 'we have nothing' (இலமென்று அசைஇ இருப்பாரை). 174 has the same words, இலமென்று, as the thought that does not move the self-controlled to covet. The plea of having nothing is refused twice: it excuses neither taking from others nor sitting idle.
links.reason: Both open with இலமென்று: 174 இலமென்று வெஃகுதல் செய்யார் and 1040 இலமென்று அசைஇ இருப்பாரை; the plea of want is refused as an excuse for coveting and for idleness.

links.note: 175 asks what fine and wide understanding comes to (அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவு என்னாம்) if one covets and acts senselessly toward everyone. 315 asks whether anything comes of understanding (அறிவினான் ஆகுவதுண்டோ) if one does not guard against another's pain as one's own. Both test அறிவு by how its owner treats other people, in coveting and in causing hurt.
links.reason: Two rhetorical questions on the worth of அறிவு, 'அறிவென்னாம்... வெஃகி வெறிய செயின்' and 'அறிவினான் ஆகுவதுண்டோ... போற்றாக் கடை', both judging understanding by conduct toward others.

links.note: 834 says no one is a greater fool than the person who has studied, understood and taught others and yet does not restrain himself (தானடங்கா). 175 says subtle and wide understanding is worth nothing if its owner covets and does வெறிய things. Both hold that learning which does not govern conduct does not count.
links.reason: அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவென்னாம் ... வெறிய செயின் (175) and ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் ... தானடங்காப் பேதை (834) both say learning that does not govern conduct is worthless.

links.note: 204 says not to plot another's ruin even by a lapse (சூழற்க), because அறம் will plot the ruin of the plotter (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). 176 says that one who plots wrongs for wealth (பொல்லாத சூழ) will perish (கெடும்). The shared verb சூழ் places the ruin at the stage of planning, before any act; 204 names the agent of that ruin.
links.reason: பொல்லாத சூழக் கெடும் and சூழற்க ... அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு both attach ruin to the plotting (சூழ்), and 204 names அறம் as agent.
links.text_issue: 204 reads அறஞ்சூழம், a typo for அறஞ்சூழும்.

links.note: 285 says a loving nature with அருள் in view (அருள்கருதி) is not found in those who, with goods in view (பொருள்கருதி), watch for another's lapse. 176 says one who stands on the path desiring அருள் (அருள்வெஃகி) perishes if he desires பொருள் (பொருள்வெஃகி) and plots wrongs. Both verses set அருள் and பொருள் as rival objects of one desire and say the second drives out the first.
links.reason: அருள்வெஃகி ... பொருள்வெஃகி (176) and அருள்கருதி ... பொருள்கருதி (285) set the same two objects against each other with the same parallel construction, in adjacent topics of coveting and stealing.

links.note: 177 argues from the outcome: gain got by coveting does not turn out well when enjoyed. 113 says gain that comes from leaving fairness is to be given up that very day even if it brings only good (நன்றே தரினும்). 113 removes the dependence on outcome, so the prohibition would stand even where 177's prediction failed.
links.reason: 177 argues from outcome (விளைவயின் மாண்டற் கரிதாம் பயன்), and 113 forbids such gain நன்றே தரினும். 113 does remove the dependence on outcome.

links.note: 177 says not to want gain that comes by coveting, since at its ripening (விளைவயின்) the fruit is hard to make good. 284 says the love grown strong in stealth yields, at its ripening (விளைவின்கண்), a sorrow that does not die. Coveting in the householder book and theft in the ascetic book are both judged by the harvest image, where the gain looks sound until it ripens.
links.reason: விளைவயின் மாண்டற்கரிதாம் பயன் and விளைவின்கண் வீயா விழுமம் தரும் both judge ill-got gain by its ripening; the shared harvest term is meaningful.

links.note: 931 opens with the same prohibition, வேண்டற்க: do not want gambling even if you win, because the winnings are like the hook a fish has swallowed. 177 says வேண்டற்க of the gain got by coveting, whose fruit turns out badly. Both warn against a gain that is real at the moment of taking and harmful afterwards.
links.reason: Both open வேண்டற்க and warn of a gain that turns bad later (விளைவயின் மாண்டற்கரிதாம் பயன்; தூண்டிற்பொன் மீன்விழுங்கி அற்று).

links.note: 283 says gain made by stealth perishes beyond measure even as it seems to grow (ஆவது போலக் கெடும்). 178 says the way to keep wealth from shrinking is not to covet another's goods. 283 gives the negative side of the same claim: what is added by taking another's property is not a lasting addition.
links.reason: அஃகாமை செல்வத்திற்கு ... வெஃகாமை and களவினால் ஆகிய ஆக்கம் ... ஆவது போலக் கெடும் are the positive and negative sides of one claim about taking another's goods.

links.note: 167 says the fair goddess grudges the envious man and shows him to her elder sister. 179 says திரு goes to those who know virtue and do not covet. The two neighbouring chapters use the goddess in opposite directions: she leaves the one who resents others' goods and comes to the one who does not want them.
links.reason: 167 'செய்யவள் தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும்' for the envious and 179 'வெஃகா அறிவுடையார்ச் சேரும்... திரு' use the goddess in converse directions in adjacent chapters, as the note says.

links.note: 179 says திரு, knowing the way (திறன் அறிந்து), goes to those who know virtue and do not covet. 594 says ஆக்கம் asks the way (அதர்வினாய்) and goes to the one of unwavering drive. In both, fortune is a traveller that seeks the person out; Book 1 gives non-coveting as what draws it and Book 2 gives energy.
links.reason: திறன்அறிந் தாங்கே திரு சேரும் and ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும் both make fortune a traveller that seeks the person out, for non-coveting and for energy.
links.text_issue: 594's first word is truncated ('க்கம்' for ஆக்கம்).

links.note: 692 says that not desiring what kings desire (மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை) brings lasting prosperity through those kings. 180 says not wanting others' goods yields victory, while coveting without thought yields destruction. The courtier's rule in Book 2 follows the same logic as 180: refraining from what belongs to another is what secures gain.
links.reason: வேண்டாமை ... விறல் ஈனும் and மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை ... மன்னிய ஆக்கந் தரும் share the logic that not desiring what is another's yields gain, moved to the court.

links.note: 181 holds that not backbiting is still good in a man who otherwise does wrong (அல்ல செயினும் ... இனிது). 297 says that if one keeps to not lying, not doing the other virtues is good (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை செய்யாமை நன்று). Both single out one restraint of speech and weigh it against the whole of the rest of conduct, though 297 goes further and treats it as sufficient.
links.reason: அல்ல செயினும் ... புறங்கூறான் என்றல் இனிது and பொய்யாமை ஆற்றின் அறம்பிற செய்யாமை நன்று each weigh one restraint of speech against the rest of conduct; the note marks that 297 goes further.

links.note: 182 calls it worse than denying virtue to slander someone when absent and smile at him when present. 820 tells one not to come near those who are friendly in the house and blame you in the assembly (மனைக்கெழீஇ மன்றில் பழிப்பார்). 820 turns the moral verdict of 182 into practical advice about which friendships to refuse.
links.reason: 182 'புறனழீஇப் பொய்த்து நகை' is the two-faced conduct that 820 'மனைக்கெழீஇ மன்றில் பழிப்பார் தொடர்பு' tells one to keep away from; Manakkudavar calls 820 a verse on the friendship of backbiters.

links.note: 183 ranks death above a life kept up by backbiting and pretence. 230 says nothing is more bitter than death (சாதலின் இன்னாத தில்லை), yet even it is sweet when one cannot give. Each verse measures a fault or lack by setting death beside it and finding death the better; the pairing shows how the book uses that comparison for both a wrong done and a good left undone.
links.reason: புறங்கூறி ... வாழ்தலின் சாதல் and சாதலின் இன்னாத தில்லை இனிததூஉம் ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை both rank death above a life with a fault or a lack; the note describes both accurately.

links.note: 183 says that dying yields more of the gain the books of virtue speak of than living by backbiting and falsehood (பொய்த்துயிர் வாழ்தலின் சாதல்). 967 says that rather than live by following those who scorn you (வாழ்தலின்), it is better to be called ruined as you are. Both use the comparative 'than living thus' to say that a kind of life can cost more than its end, once for the slanderer's two faces and once for lost honour.
links.reason: Both turn on வாழ்தலின்: 183 பொய்த்துயிர் வாழ்தலின் சாதல் and 967 ஒட்டார்பின் சென்று வாழ்தலின் அந்நிலையே கெட்டான் எனப்படுதல் நன்று, each ranking an end above a degraded way of living.

links.note: 184: though you speak harshly to his face (சொல்லினும்), do not speak (சொல்லற்க) the heedless word behind his back. 197: let the worthy say what lacks நயன் if they must (சொல்லினுஞ் சொல்லுக), it is good that they not say what lacks use. The two neighbouring chapters use the same concessive move, granting a lesser fault of speech in order to isolate the one the chapter is about.
links.reason: 'கண்ணறச் சொல்லினும் சொல்லற்க...' and 'நயனில சொல்லினுஞ் சொல்லுக... பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று' share the same concessive சொல்லினும் construction, granting a lesser speech-fault to isolate the chapter's own.

links.note: 184 concedes speaking without kindly regard to a person's face (கண்ணின்று கண்ணறச் சொல்லினும்) and forbids only the word said in his absence that does not look to what follows (முன்னின்று பின்நோக்காச் சொல்). 795 goes further and tells one to seek out friends able to speak so that one weeps and to rebuke (அழச்சொல்லி ... இடித்து). What 184 merely tolerates, hard speech face to face, 795 treats as a mark of the friend worth choosing.
links.reason: 184's concessive கண்ணின்று கண்ணறச் சொல்லினும் only tolerates blunt speech to the face, while 795's அழச்சொல்லி ... இடித்து makes it a criterion for choosing friends; the note states both accurately.

links.note: 185 says that a man's heart does not really speak virtue is seen from the meanness of his backbiting (புறஞ்சொல்லும் புன்மையாற் காணப்படும்). 193 says that expansive talk of useless things itself declares the speaker to be without நயன் (நயனிலன் என்பது சொல்லும்). In both a kind of speech is treated as evidence about the speaker, whatever he professes.
links.reason: புறஞ்சொல்லும் புன்மையாற் காணப்படும் and நயனிலன் என்பது சொல்லும் ... உரை both make a man's speech the evidence of his character, as the note says.

links.note: 185 reads a man's inner lack of virtue from his backbiting. 959 says that as the sprout shows what lies in the soil, the words of the mouth show the family one is born in (காட்டும் குலத்தில் பிறந்தார் வாய்ச்சொல்). Both treat speech as the visible sign of something hidden, the heart in one case and lineage in the other.
links.reason: புறஞ்சொல்லும் புன்மையாற் காணப்படும் and காட்டும் ... வாய்ச்சொல் both treat speech as the visible evidence of something hidden, the heart in one and lineage in the other.

links.note: 186 says the one who tells another's blame (பிறன்பழி கூறுவான்) will have his own faults sorted through and told (தன்பழியுள்ளும் திறன்தெரிந்து கூறப்படும்). 319 says that hurt done to others in the forenoon comes back on oneself in the afternoon (பிற்பகல் தாமே வரும்). The same return of the deed appears for speech and for injury; in 186 the return is carried out by other people's tongues.
links.reason: 186 பிறன்பழி கூறுவான் தன்பழி ... கூறப்படும் and 319 பிறர்க்கின்னா ... தமக்கு இன்னா பிற்பகல் தாமே வரும் show the same return of the deed for speech and for injury.

links.note: 186 warns the teller of others' faults that his own will be told. 980 says greatness covers another's weakness while smallness only tells faults (சிறுமைதான் குற்றமே கூறிவிடும்). 186 gives the consequence of the habit and 980 gives its diagnosis: fault-telling is what smallness does.
links.reason: பிறன்பழி கூறுவான் தன்பழி ... கூறப்படும் gives the consequence, and சிறுமைதான் குற்றமே கூறிவிடும் gives the character behind the habit.

links.note: 187 says those who do not know how to make friends by words that bring laughter (நகச்சொல்லி நட்பாடல் தேற்றாதவர்) will part even their own kin by words that divide (பகச்சொல்லிக் கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர்). 525 says one who can give and speak pleasantly will be surrounded by kin in layers (இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின் ... சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). The two state the same link between speech and keeping one's people, from its negative and positive sides, in the Book of Virtue and the Book of Wealth.
links.reason: பகச்சொல்லிக் கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர் ... நகச்சொல்லி நட்பாடல் தேற்றாதவர் (187) and இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின் ... சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும் (525): speech loses or keeps one's people, negative and positive.

links.note: 187 treats speaking so that others laugh (நகச்சொல்லி) as the way friendship is made. 784 says friendship is not for laughing (நகுதற் பொருட்டன்று நட்டல்) but for going ahead to rebuke when the friend oversteps. 784 limits 187: pleasant talk may begin a friendship, but it is not what the friendship is for.
links.reason: நகச்சொல்லி நட்பாடல் and நகுதற் பொருட்டன்று நட்டல் use the same verb for friendship's means and its purpose. 784 does limit what 187 assumes.

links.note: 188 describes people whose habit is to broadcast (தூற்றும்) the faults of those near them. 1076 likens the base to a beaten drum because they carry any secret they have heard to others (கேட்ட மறை பிறர்க்கு உய்த்துரைக்கலான்). 1076 places the habit of 188 in the Kural's portrait of the base person.
links.reason: 188 is about தூற்றும் the குற்றம் of துன்னியார்; 1076 is about carrying கேட்ட மறை to others. Slander of faults and leaking secrets are related indiscretions, but 1076 does not place 188's habit among the base.

links.note: 188 asks what those whose way is to spread even the faults of people close to them (துன்னியார் குற்றமும் தூற்றும்) would do to strangers (என்னைகொல் ஏதிலார் மாட்டு). In 1165 the woman asks what those who can bring grief within friendship (நட்பினுள்) would become in enmity. Both argue from conduct toward intimates to what must follow toward others; in 1165 it is a lover's complaint, not a general teaching.
links.reason: துன்னியார் குற்றமும் தூற்றும் ... என்னைகொல் ஏதிலார் மாட்டு and துயர்வரவு நட்பினுள் ஆற்றுபவர் ... துப்பின் எவனாவர் are the same a fortiori argument from intimates to others.

links.note: 189 speaks of the backbiter as a weight the earth bears (வையம் ... பொறை). 572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a burden to the earth (நிலக்குப் பொறை). The figure of a person as dead weight on the ground is used in both for someone who fails others in ordinary dealings, by malicious speech in one and by lack of regard in the other.
links.reason: வையம் ... பொறை ஆற்றுங்கொல் and உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை: the person as a load the earth bears, used for two failures toward others.

links.note: 189 wonders that the earth bears the backbiter's weight at all. 990 says that if the worthy decline in worth, the great earth will not bear its load (இருநிலந்தான் தாங்காது மன்னோ பொறை). Together they show the image used at both ends: the earth strains under the bad man, and is able to carry its load only while the worthy stay worthy.
links.reason: Both use the earth bearing a பொறை: 189 ஆற்றுங்கொல் வையம் ... பொறை for the backbiter, 990 இருநிலந்தான் தாங்காது மன்னோ பொறை if the சான்றவர் decline.

links.note: 190 wishes that people would see their own faults as they see a stranger's. 930 asks whether a drinker, when sober and seeing another man drunk, does not think of his own lapse when he drinks (உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு). 930 is a concrete instance of the failure 190 names: the other man's fault is seen clearly and one's own identical fault is not.
links.reason: 190 ஏதிலார் குற்றம்போல் தங்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின் is instanced by 930, where the sober drinker sees களித்தானை and yet உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு.

links.note: 193 says that a man's spreading out useless matter in speech itself announces that he is without நயன் (நயனிலன் என்பது சொல்லும்). 959 says the words of the mouth show the family one comes from, as a sprout shows the soil. In both the speech testifies about the speaker; 193 makes the talk itself the subject of the verb 'says', which Parimelazhagar notes.
links.reason: நயனிலன் என்பது சொல்லும் ... உரை (193) and காட்டும் குலத்தில் பிறந்தார் வாய்ச்சொல் (959) both make speech testify about the speaker, his character in one and his family in the other.

links.note: 195 says useless talk costs people of fine nature their distinction (சீர்மை சிறப்பொடு நீங்கும்). 957 says a fault in the well-born shows up high, like the spot on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து). 957 supplies a reason for 195: a fault that would pass unnoticed in others is conspicuous in those held high.
links.reason: 195 சீர்மை சிறப்பொடு நீங்கும் for நீர்மையுடையார் and 957 குற்றம் ... மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் are akin, but 195 does not say the loss is because they stand high; 'supplies a reason' is the note's inference.

links.note: 195 says that if people of fine nature (நீர்மையுடையார்) speak useless things, their distinction and the regard it earned leave them. 965 says even those like a hill will sink if they do a lowering thing the size of a kunri seed. Both hold that standing does not protect the eminent from a small lapse; 195 applies this to idle speech.
links.reason: 195 சீர்மை சிறப்பொடு நீங்கும் ... நீர்மை யுடையார் சொலின் and 965 குன்றின் அனையாரும் குன்றுவர் ... குன்றி அனைய செயின் both say eminence is lost by a small lapse, in speech and in conduct.

links.note: 196 calls the habitual idle talker chaff, a husk with nothing in it. 406 says the unlearned can only be said to exist and are like barren saline land that yields nothing (பயவாக் களரனையர்). Both take a farming image of something that looks like the useful thing and gives no yield, and both turn on பயன், what a person produces.
links.reason: மக்கட் பதடி (chaff) and பயவாக் களரனையர் (barren saline land) are both farming figures for a person without yield, tied to பயன்.

links.note: 193 says that useless talk at length shows the speaker to be without நயன், so the two faults go together. 197 separates them and ranks them: speech without நயன் may be let pass in the worthy, speech without use may not. Read together, 197 makes uselessness the graver of the two; Parimelazhagar draws the same ranking from சொல்லினும்.
links.reason: 193 makes பயனில talk the proof that one is நயனிலன்; 197 நயனில சொல்லினுஞ் சொல்லுக ... பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று ranks the two, and Parimelazhagar does say நயன் இலவற்றினும் பயன் இல தீய.

links.note: 197 lets the worthy say even what lacks நயன் but holds that they should not say what lacks use (பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று). 697 tells one who serves a king to say what is wanted and never to say what is without use even if asked (வினையில எஞ்ஞான்றும் கேட்பினும் சொல்லாவிடல்); Parimelazhagar glosses வினையில as matters without benefit. The rule against useless speech is kept as firmly at court as in private ethics, and neither verse lets circumstances excuse it.
links.reason: பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று and வினையில எஞ்ஞான்றும் கேட்பினும் சொல்லாவிடல்: the same rule in private ethics and at court; Parimelazhagar does gloss வினையில as பயனிலவாயவற்றை.

links.note: 199 says what those of stainless sight will not say. 258 says those whose sight has parted from fault (செயிரின் தலைப்பிரிந்த காட்சியார்) will not eat flesh that has parted from life. The book repeatedly states a restraint as what people of clear காட்சி simply do not do; here the same form covers speech and diet.
links.reason: Both use the form 'people of clear காட்சி do not ...' (மாசறு காட்சியவர் சொல்லார் / செயிரின் தலைப்பிரிந்த காட்சியார் உண்ணார்), applied to speech and to diet.

links.note: Both end on the phrase 'என்னும் செருக்கு'. In 201 it is 'தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு', which Parimelazhagar glosses as a delusion (மயக்கம்) and Manakkudavar as an exhilaration (களிப்பு) that the good fear; in 180 it is 'வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு', the pride of not wanting, which yields victory (விறல்). The same word names a heady state to be dreaded in one verse and a state worth having in the other, depending on what it rests on.
links.reason: Both close on என்னும் செருக்கு (தீவினை; வேண்டாமை), feared in one and victorious (விறல்ஈனும்) in the other; the glosses மயக்கம், களிப்பு and பெருமிதம் are reported correctly.

links.note: 201 makes fear of evil deeds the mark of the excellent. 244 says that for one who sustains living beings and practises அருள் there are no deeds his own life need fear ('தன்னுயிர் அஞ்சும் வினை இல்'). The fear 201 commends is aimed at one's own possible deeds, and 244 names the condition under which nothing of that kind remains to be feared.
links.reason: The link through அஞ்சுவர் தீவினை and தன்னுயிர் அஞ்சும் வினை இல் is real, but 244 does not limit 201: it says such deeds do not arise for the compassionate, which extends the idea, not conditions it.

links.note: 201 says those practised in evil do not fear 'தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு' while the excellent (விழுமியார்) do. 428 gives the general rule in the chapter on understanding: not fearing what is to be feared (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சாமை) is folly, and fearing it is 'அறிவார் தொழில்'. Read together, the fear in 201 is a working of knowledge and not timidity; Parimelazhagar on 428 lists sin, blame and ruin among the things to be feared.
links.reason: விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர் is an instance of அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில், and தீவினையார் அஞ்சார் of அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சாமை பேதைமை; Parimelazhagar's list on 428 (பாவமும் பழியும் கேடும்) is reported correctly.

links.note: 202 says evil deeds are to be feared more than fire ('தீயினும் அஞ்சப்படும்') because they yield evil. 129 sets fire against the tongue: a wound burned by fire heals, the scar burned by the tongue does not ('ஆறாதே நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு'). In both, fire is the harm that ends, used to measure a harm that lasts; Parimelazhagar on 202 makes this explicit, saying fire cannot follow one into another time, place or body.
links.reason: தீயினும் அஞ்சப்படும் (202) and தீயினாற் சுட்டபுண் உள்ளாறும் (129) both use fire as the lesser, passing harm against which a lasting one is measured; Parimelazhagar's gloss on 202 supports it.

links.note: 202 ranks evil deeds above fire as a thing to fear. 896, in the Book of Wealth, says one burned by fire may still survive ('எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம்') but those who keep wronging the great will not. The same comparison, fire as the survivable danger, is applied once to one's own deeds and once to the anger of the powerful.
links.reason: தீயினும் அஞ்சப்படும் and எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம்: fire as the lesser, survivable danger in two domains.

links.note: 203 calls it the chief of all understanding to refrain from doing evil even to those who hate one ('செறுவார்க்கும் செய்யா விடல்'). 312 says that not hurting in return even one who has hurt you out of hatred ('கறுத்து இன்னா செய்த அக்கண்ணும்') is the settled stand of the stainless. The same rule is called knowledge (அறிவு) in the householder's chapter and purity (மாசற்றார் கோள்) in the ascetic's.
links.reason: தீய செறுவார்க்கும் செய்யா விடல் and கறுத்து இன்னா செய்தவக் கண்ணும் மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை state the same rule, called அறிவினுள் தலை in one and மாசற்றார் கோள் in the other.

links.note: 203 asks only for restraint: do no evil even to enemies. 987 asks what worth (சால்பு) is good for if it does not do pleasant things even to those who did one harm ('இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்'). The Book of Wealth's ideal of the சான்றோர் goes one step beyond the householder's rule, from not returning harm to returning good.
links.reason: தீய செறுவார்க்கும் செய்யா விடல் is abstention; இன்னாசெய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால் asks for positive good to the same people, a clear step further.

links.note: 204 says that if one plots another's ruin, virtue plots one's own. 319 states the return in terms of time: harm done to others in the forenoon brings harm to oneself in the afternoon, of itself ('பிற்பகல் தாமே வரும்'). 319's 'தாமே' leaves the return impersonal where 204 gives it an agent, and Parimelazhagar on 204 adds the same point about speed: virtue begins plotting at the very moment the plotter does.
links.reason: 204 gives the return an agent (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு); 319 times it and makes it impersonal (பிற்பகல் தாமே வரும்). Parimelazhagar's remark on 204 about virtue plotting at the same moment is reported accurately.
links.text_issue: 204 reads 'அறஞ்சூழம்', a typo for அறஞ்சூழும்.

links.note: 205 rules out poverty as a ground for evil deeds. 656 takes the hardest case: even if one must see the mother who bore one go hungry ('ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்'), one should not do what the worthy condemn. Parimelazhagar notes that 656 sets aside a general rule of the dharma texts allowing wrong to feed one's dependants, which shows how far 205's principle is taken.
links.reason: 205 இலன் என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க is taken to its extreme in 656 ஈன்றாள் பசிகாண்பான் ஆயினுஞ் செய்யற்க; Parimelazhagar does cite the dharma-text rule that 656 declines to apply.

links.note: 205 quotes the plea 'இலன் என்று' as an excuse for wrongdoing. 1040 quotes the same plea, 'இலமென்று', as an excuse for sitting idle, and says the good woman called Land laughs at those who make it. The book hears 'I have nothing' twice as a pretext, once for evil and once for sloth, and rejects it both times.
links.reason: இலன் என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க and இலமென்று அசைஇ இருப்பாரை quote the same plea of poverty as a pretext, for wrongdoing and for idleness, and both verses reject it.

links.note: 206: one who does not want afflicting things to overpower him ('நோய்ப்பால தன்னை அடல் வேண்டாதான்') should not do evil to others. 320: all pains rest on those who caused pain, so those who want freedom from pain cause none ('நோய் செய்யார் நோயின்மை வேண்டுபவர்'). The claim and its form (நோய், வேண்டு-) are nearly the same, stated once for the householder in the chapter on fearing evil deeds and once among the ascetic virtues.
links.reason: நோய்ப்பால தன்னை அடல் வேண்டாதான் and நோய்செய்யார் நோயின்மை வேண்டுபவர் make the same claim in near-identical form across two chapters.

links.note: 207 says the enmity of deeds does not leave and follows behind to kill ('வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும்'). 208 gives the image for it: the ruin of evildoers is like a person's shadow that does not leave and stays at the foot ('வீயாது அடி உறைந்தற்று'). The repeated 'வீயாது' ties them, and both Manakkudavar and Parimelazhagar say 208 illustrates what 207 asserted.
links.reason: வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும் is pictured by நிழல் தன்னை வீயாது அடியுறைந்தற்று, with வீயாது repeated; Manakkudavar says outright that 208 shows how the வினைப்பகை of 207 kills.
links.text_issue: 208 prints அஇஉறைந் for அடியுறைந்.

links.note: 207 treats one's evil deeds as an enemy ('வினைப்பகை') worse than any outward one. 434, advising the king, says fault itself is the enemy that brings ruin ('குற்றமே அற்றம் தரூஉம் பகை') and so guarding against fault should be one's aim. The two verses, one in the Book of Virtue and one in the Book of Wealth, both move the real enemy from outside to one's own conduct.
links.reason: வினைப்பகை (207) and குற்றமே அற்றந் தரூஉம் பகை (434) both name one's own conduct as the real enemy, in two books.
links.text_issue: 434 reads த்ரூஉம், a typo for தரூஉம்.

links.note: 208: the ruin of those who did evil is like a shadow that never leaves a person. 36: virtue done now is, at the time one perishes, a companion that does not perish ('பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை'). Both say a person's deeds stay with him; the good deed stays as a companion and the evil deed's ruin as a shadow at his heel.
links.reason: Evil's ruin follows like நிழல் ... அடியுறைந்தற்று and virtue is பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை: the same idea of deeds staying with the doer, for bad and good.
links.text_issue: 208 is printed அஇஉறைந் தற்று, a corruption of அடியுறைந் தற்று.

links.note: 208 uses a simile of something that cannot fail to happen: ruin stays with the evildoer as his shadow stays at his foot. 307 does the same for anger: the ruin of one who treats anger as a thing of worth is like the hand of one who strikes the ground, which cannot miss ('கை பிழையாதற்று'). Both verses take 'கேடு' as their subject and end on a simile of certainty, one for evil deeds and one for anger.
links.reason: Both have கெடுதல்/கேடு as subject and close on a simile of what cannot fail: நிழல் ... வீயாது அடிஉறைந்தற்று and நிலத்தறைந்தான் கைபிழையாதற்று.
links.text_issue: 208: 'அஇஉறைந் தற்று' is a typo for அடிஉறைந்தற்று.

links.note: 209 assumes that doing evil is acting against oneself: one who loves himself stays away from it. 843 says the suffering that those without understanding inflict on themselves is hard even for their enemies ('செறுவார்க்கும்') to inflict. 843 describes the person who fails 209's test, and Parimelazhagar's comment there names poverty, blame and sin as what such people bring on themselves.
links.reason: தன்னைத்தான் காதலனாயின் ... துன்னற்க தீவினைப்பால் (209) treats evil as self-harm; தாந்தம்மைப் பீழிக்கும் பீழை (843) describes that self-harm. Parimelazhagar on 843 does list வறுமை, பழி, பாவம்.

links.note: 210: know ('அறிக') that one who does not turn aside to do evil has no ruin. 116: if one's heart leaves what is fair and does wrong, let one know ('அறிக') 'I shall perish' ('கெடுவல் யான்'). They state the same law from its two sides with the same imperative, 210 for the one who keeps straight and 116 for the one who leaves the middle.
links.reason: அருங்கேடன் என்பது அறிக (210) and கெடுவல்யான் என்பது அறிக (116) state the same law of ruin from the side of the one who keeps straight and the one who நடுவொரீஇ.

links.note: 210 promises that the one who does no evil will not come to ruin. 117 says the world will not count as ruin ('கெடுவாக வையாது') the low state (தாழ்வு) of one who stays in virtue by standing fair. 117 allows that the upright may be brought low and changes what counts as 'கேடு', which limits how literally 210's promise can be taken.
links.reason: அருங்கேடன் (210) is limited by 117's கெடுவாக வையாது ... தாழ்வு, which admits the upright may fall low and redefines கேடு.

links.note: 211 says duty-giving seeks no return (கைம்மாறு). 221, opening the next chapter, defines giving as giving to those who have nothing, and says everything else has the nature of 'குறியெதிர்ப்பை', a measured loan to be returned. 221 turns 211's point into a test: a gift that looks to a return is not giving.
links.reason: கைம்மாறு வேண்டா கடப்பாடு (211) is sharpened in 221, where giving other than வறியார்க்கு is குறியெதிர்ப்பை நீரது, a gift that looks to return.

links.note: 212 says all the wealth produced by exertion ('தாளாற்றித் தந்த பொருள்') is for doing 'வேளாண்மை', benefaction. 613 says the proud distinction called benefaction ('வேளாண்மை என்னும் செருக்கு') rests in the quality called exertion ('தாளாண்மை'). The same two words are paired from opposite ends: in the Book of Virtue helping others is the purpose of earning, and in the Book of Wealth effort is the basis that makes helping possible.
links.reason: தாள்/வேளாண்மை are paired in both: தாளாற்றித் தந்த பொருள் ... வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு, and தாளாண்மை ... தங்கிற்றே வேளாண்மை. The two directions, purpose and basis, are described correctly.

links.note: 212 says wealth is for benefaction, with 'தக்கார்க்கு' read by Manakkudavar and Kalaignar as the worthy who receive it and by Parimelazhagar as the worthy who own it. 1006 describes the failure of this purpose: one who neither enjoys his great wealth nor gives anything to the worthy ('தக்கார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈதல் இயல்பிலாதான்') is an affliction (ஏதம்) to it. 1006 uses 'தக்கார்க்கு' plainly of recipients, which supports the Manakkudavar reading of 212.
links.reason: 1006's 'தக்கார்க்கொன்று ஈதல் இயல்பிலாதான்' is the failure of 212's 'பொருளெல்லாம் தக்கார்க்கு வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு'; the note's account of the split over தக்கார்க்கு (Parimelazhagar 'தகுதி உடையார்க்கு ஆயின்' vs Manakkudavar's recipients) is accurate.

links.note: 213 ranks ஒப்புரவு above anything to be had in the gods' world or this one. 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world ('மேலுலகம் இல்லெனினும் ஈதலே நன்று'). Both detach the worth of helping others from heaven as a reward: in 213 heaven holds nothing better, and in 222 the good stands even without heaven.
links.reason: 222 does detach giving from reward (மேலுலகம் இல்லெனினும் ஈதலே நன்று), but 213 is a superlative: nothing as good as ஒப்புரவு is to be had புத்தேளுலகத்தும் ஈண்டும். It does not make the point about heaven as a reward that the note assigns to both.

links.note: 213: neither in the world of the gods nor here ('புத்தேள் உலகத்தும் ஈண்டும்') is it easy to find another good like ஒப்புரவு. 363: there is no excellent wealth here like not wanting, and nothing there equals it either ('ஈண்டில்லை ஆண்டும் அஃதொப்பது இல்'). The same two-world formula crowns benevolence in the householder's section and desirelessness in the renouncer's; taken literally the two superlatives compete, and the pairing shows each section naming its own highest good.
links.reason: புத்தேளுலகத்தும் ஈண்டும் பெறலரிதே and ஈண்டில்லை ஆண்டும் அஃதொப்பது இல் apply the same two-world superlative to ஒப்புரவு and வேண்டாமை.

links.note: Parimelazhagar reads 'ஒத்தது' in 214 as the way of the world (உலகநடை): one who knows and follows it lives. 140 says those who have not learned to conduct themselves in accord with the world ('உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்') lack understanding however much they have studied. On that reading both make accord with the world the test of a person, of being alive in 214 and of having understanding in 140; Manakkudavar instead takes ஒத்தது as ஒப்புரவு itself.
links.reason: On Parimelazhagar's reading of ஒத்தது as உலகநடை, 214 matches 140's உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்; the note marks the dependence and Manakkudavar's alternative.

links.note: 217 makes a tree the figure of a generous man's wealth: a tree that is medicine and does not fail ('மருந்தாகித் தப்பா மரம்'). 576 makes a tree the figure of people who have eyes but no kindly regard: they are like trees joined to the soil ('மண்ணோடு இயைந்த மரத்தனையர்'). The book uses the tree in two ways, for what gives to all who come to it and for what stands unmoved, so the image alone carries no fixed value.
links.reason: மரம் is a common figure put to unrelated uses here (மருந்தாகித் தப்பா மரம் versus மண்ணோடியைந்த மரம்); the note itself concedes the image carries no fixed value, so the shared use is not meaningful.

links.note: 218: even at a time without means ('இடனில் பருவத்தும்'), those who see what is due do not slacken in ஒப்புரவு. 955: even when what they have to give has shrunk ('வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும்'), an old family does not part from its character. The Book of Virtue credits this constancy to insight into duty ('கடனறி காட்சி'), and the Book of Wealth credits it to lineage ('பழங்குடி').
links.reason: இடனில் பருவத்தும் ஒப்புரவிற்கு ஒல்கார் (218) and வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும் ... பண்பில் தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று (955) make the same claim of constancy in reduced means, credited to கடனறி காட்சி in one and பழங்குடி in the other.

links.note: 219 redefines poverty for the benevolent man: it is not lacking goods but being unable to do good with them. 89 redefines it from the other side: poverty in the midst of having ('உடைமையுள் இன்மை') is the folly of not tending guests. In both verses poverty is measured by what one does for others and not by what one holds.
links.reason: நல்கூர்ந்தா னாதல் செயும்நீர செய்யாது அமைகலா வாறு and உடைமையுள் இன்மை விருந்தோம்பல் ஓம்பா மடமை both redefine poverty by what one fails to do for others.

links.note: 220: if ruin comes through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin is worth getting even by selling oneself ('விற்றுக்கோள் தக்கது உடைத்து'). 780: a death at which the eyes of one's lord fill with tears is worth getting even by begging ('இரந்துகோள் தக்கது உடைத்து'). The same closing formula takes something normally shunned, ruin or death, and declares it worth a degrading price, once for the benefactor and once for the soldier.
links.reason: விற்றுக்கோள் தக்கது உடைத்து and இரந்துகோள் தக்கது உடைத்து: the same closing formula sets a degrading price on கேடு and சாக்காடு.

links.note: 220 speaks of a man selling himself ('ஒருவன் விற்றுக்கோள்') as a price worth paying for the ruin that benevolence brings. 1080 says the base are fit for one thing: when something befalls them, to sell themselves quickly ('விற்றற்கு உரியர் விரைந்து'). Self-sale is honourable in the first as the cost of giving and contemptible in the second as an escape from one's own trouble.
links.reason: Self-sale appears in both, 220 ஒருவன் விற்றுக்கோள் தக்கது and 1080 விற்றற்கு உரியர் விரைந்து, with opposite valuation as the note says.

links.note: 222 says taking is bad even if it were called a good path (நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல் தீது). 1054 says that asking from those who do not know concealment even in a dream is itself like giving (இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும்). They conflict if கொளல் is read, with Parimelazhagar, as accepting alms without exception; on Kalaignar's reading of கொளல் as taking goods from others by whatever fair means, the two address different acts.
links.reason: On Parimelazhagar's reading of கொளல் as accepting alms, நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல் தீது does conflict with இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும்; the note names the reading the conflict depends on.

links.note: 222 holds receiving to be bad whatever is said in its favour. 1061 says that not asking is worth a crore even from those dear as one's eyes who give gladly without hiding (கரவாது உவந்தீயும் கண்ணன்னார் கண்ணும் இரவாமை). Both refuse the best case that could be made for receiving: 222 the claim that it is a good path, 1061 the excellence of the giver.
links.reason: நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல் தீது and கரவாது உவந்தீயும் கண்ணன்னார் கண்ணும் இரவாமை both reject receiving even in its best case.

links.note: Both verses turn on the quoted plea 'I have nothing': 223 has இலன் என்னும் எவ்வம், 205 has இலன் என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க. In 205 the plea is an excuse for doing evil and is answered with the warning that one will have nothing all over again; in 223 it is a plea the well-born do not voice. In both the book refuses to let want serve as a reason.
links.reason: இலனென்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை and இலன் என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க both quote the plea of having nothing and refuse it as a reason, for withholding and for wrongdoing.

links.note: On Parimelazhagar's first reading, 223 says the well-born do not speak to others the beggar's degrading word 'I am poor'. 1044 says that even in the well-born (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும்) poverty produces the lapse from which degrading words are born (இளிவந்த சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு). The conflict depends on that reading of 223; if 'இலன்' is the giver's refusal to an asker, as Pope takes it, the two speak of different utterances.
links.reason: On the reading of இலனென்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை as the well-born not voicing their own want, 1044's இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும் ... இளிவந்த சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு says the opposite; the note names the reading the conflict rests on.

links.note: In 224 the giver watches the asker's face and is uneasy until it turns glad. In 90 the guest watches the host's face and wilts, like the anicham flower when smelled, if that face changes (முகந்திரிந்து நோக்க). The face is the measure of the exchange in both, read in opposite directions.
links.reason: Both hinge on the face: இரந்தவர் இன்முகங் காணும் அளவு in 224, முகந்திரிந்து நோக்கக் குழையும் விருந்து in 90; the note describes both accurately and the reversed direction of watching is a real observation.

links.note: 224 says the unease of being asked lasts until the asker's face is glad. 228 names what follows as a pleasure in its own right, ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம், which Parimelazhagar explains as the joy the giver has from the receiver's rejoicing. 228 then uses that pleasure as a charge against those who hoard and lose.
links.reason: 224 இன்முகம் காணும் அளவு ends the giver's unease at the receiver's glad face, and 228 ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம் names that joy; Parimelazhagar's அவர் உவத்தலான் ... எய்தும் இன்பம் is quoted fairly.

links.note: 224 gives the giver's side: being asked is painful (இன்னாது இரக்கப்படுதல்) until one sees the asker's glad face (இன்முகம்). 1057 gives the asker's side: on seeing those who give without scorn or contempt, the heart rejoices deep within (உள்ளுள் உவப்பது உடைத்து). The two describe one moment from both ends, and the asker's gladness in 1057 is what ends the giver's discomfort in 224.
links.reason: இரந்தவர் இன்முகம் காணும் அளவு (giver) and ஈவாரைக் காணின் ... உள்ளுள் உவப்பது (asker) describe the same exchange from the two ends, in the chapters on giving and on asking.

links.note: Both verses use the act of putting wealth away (வை). In 226 feeding the destitute is the வைப்புழி, the place of deposit; in 228 the hard-eyed 'keep and lose' what they own (வைத்திழக்கும்). The chapter sets a store that holds beside a store that is lost.
links.reason: 226 பொருள்வைப் புழி and 228 வைத்திழக்கும் both turn on வை, a deposit that holds against one that is lost, within the same chapter.

links.note: 227 promises that the one who shares his food will not meet hunger. 85 asks whether the field of one who feeds guests and eats what is left even needs sowing (வித்தும் இடல் வேண்டும் கொல்லோ). Both state as a rule that feeding others first secures one's own food.
links.reason: பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனைப் பசி ... தீண்டல் அரிது and விருந்தோம்பி மிச்சில் மிசைவான் புலம் both promise that the one who feeds others first will not lack food.

links.note: 227 praises habitual shared eating (பாத்தூண்). In 1107 the man compares his beloved's embrace to living in one's own home and eating one's own food after sharing it (தமது பாத்து உண்டற்று). The lover's simile takes the householder's sharing of 227 as its standard of pleasure.
links.reason: பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவன் and தமது பாத்து உண்டற்று share the distinctive பாத்து + உண், and 1107 does use the householder's shared meal as its measure of pleasure.
