links.note: 228 speaks of a pleasure the hoarder never learns, ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம். 598, which Parimelazhagar applies to kings, says those without inner drive never reach the proud joy of saying 'we have been generous' (வள்ளியம் என்னும் செருக்கு). The pleasure of giving is missed through hardness in the one verse and through lack of energy in the other.
links.reason: 228 ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம் அறியார் and 598 வள்ளியம் என்னும் செருக்கு எய்தார்: the giver's joy missed by the hard-eyed and by the spiritless; Parimelazhagar's அரசர் gloss reported correctly.

links.note: 228 says only that the hoarder keeps his goods and loses them. 1009 says how: bright wealth gathered by giving up love, denying oneself and ignoring virtue is taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). The later verse fills in the 'losing' of 228.
links.reason: 228's வைத்திழக்கும் leaves the losing unexplained and 1009's ஈட்டிய ஒண்பொருள் கொள்வார் பிறர் says who ends up with the hoard.

links.note: 229 condemns those who eat alone to build up their own wealth. 527 says crows do not hide their food but call and eat (காக்கை கரவா கரைந்துண்ணும்), and that gain belongs only to those of that nature. The rule against eating alone appears in the ethics of giving in 229 and as advice on keeping kin and prosperity in 527.
links.reason: 229 condemns தாமே தமியர் உணல்; 527's காக்கை கரவா கரைந்துண்ணும் gives the opposite conduct as the condition of ஆக்கம் among kin.

links.note: 230 holds death sweet for one who can no longer give. 968 asks whether a life of tending the flesh is any medicine once greatness has lost its dignity (பீடழிய வந்த இடத்து). In both a life is not worth keeping once the thing that gave it worth is gone: giving in 230, honour in 968.
links.reason: இனிததூஉம் ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை and மருந்தோமற்று ஊன்ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை ... பீடழிய வந்த இடத்து apply the same reasoning, that life loses its worth with the thing that gave it worth, to giving and to honour.

links.note: 1041 says that the only thing as painful as poverty is poverty itself (இன்மையின் இன்மையே இன்னாதது). 230 opens by saying nothing is more painful than death (சாதலின் இன்னாதது இல்லை), then reverses it for the person who cannot give. Taken together, 230's second half brings it into line with 1041: the want that stops giving is placed above death in bitterness.
links.reason: The convergence is real, but neither verse limits the other, and ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை is inability to give, which the note equates a little too readily with the இன்மை of 1041.

links.note: 231 ends 'ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு' and 31 ends 'ஆக்கம் எவனோ உயிர்க்கு': both use the figure of profit to a living being. 31 gives the place to virtue in general, which yields distinction and wealth; 231 gives it to renown that comes from giving. The shared formula shows 231 naming one particular form of the gain that 31 states broadly.
links.reason: 231 ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு and 31 ஆக்கம் எவனோ உயிர்க்கு share the profit-to-a-life formula, with giving and renown as one form of what 31 claims for virtue.

links.note: 231 says that apart from living with renown through giving there is no profit for a living being (அது அல்லது ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு). 122 says no gain for a living being is greater than restraint (ஆக்கம் அதனினூஉங்கு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு). Read literally the two exclusive claims cannot both hold; the conflict disappears if each is taken as the emphasis its own chapter gives its subject.
links.reason: அதுவல்லது ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு and ஆக்கம் அதனினூஉங்கு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு clash only as chapter superlatives, as the note itself concedes; a generic rhetorical clash, not a real disagreement.

links.note: 232 makes giving the subject of all praise. 296 says there is no renown like not lying (பொய்யாமை அன்ன புகழில்லை). They conflict if both are read as naming the single greatest source of renown; Parimelazhagar's gloss on 296, that truthfulness is the cause of renown in this life, keeps the claim just as strong.
links.reason: 232 உரைப்பவை எல்லாம் ... ஈவார்மேல் நிற்கும் புகழ் and 296 பொய்யாமை அன்ன புகழில்லை are rival superlatives about புகழ்; the note names the reading and Parimelazhagar's புகழ்க் காரணம் gloss correctly.

links.note: 232 says the world's speech settles as praise on the giver. 387 says that for one able to give and protect with sweet words (இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க வல்லார்க்கு), this world is as his own word would have it. In the chapter on kingship the same giving that earns the world's words in 232 earns its compliance.
links.reason: 232 puts all that speakers say as praise on ஈவார், and 387 gives the one able to இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க a world that follows தன்சொல்; giving wins the world's speech in one and its compliance in the other.

links.note: 233 says only renown stands undying. 156 says those who punish have a day's pleasure, while those who forbear have renown பொன்றுந் துணையும், which Pope and Parimelazhagar take as until the world ends. 156 measures a virtue's reward by the lasting quality that 233 attributes to renown, and gives it a source other than giving.
links.reason: பொன்றாது நிற்பது (233) and பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ் (156) both rest on renown's lastingness with the same root பொன்று; the note is right that Pope and Parimelazhagar take the latter as the world's end, and that 156 ties it to forbearance.

links.note: 234 joins earthly renown (புகழ்) to honour in the gods' world (புத்தேள் உலகு). 966 names the same pair as the two things lost by following those who scorn you: it brings no renown and does not carry one to the gods' land (புகழ் இன்றால் புத்தேள் நாட்டு உய்யாதால்). In both verses renown here and the gods' world there are counted together, as gained in 234 and forfeited in 966.
links.reason: Both pair புகழ் with the gods' world: 234 நீள்புகழ் ... புத்தேள் உலகு, 966 புகழ் இன்றால் புத்தேள்நாட்டு உய்யாதால; the gained/forfeited contrast is accurate.

links.note: 235 says a loss can be an increase. 117 says the world will not set down as ruin (கெடுவாக வையாது உலகம்) the low state of one who stays in virtue by standing fair. Both deny that the decline of a good person's fortunes is a real loss, 235 from the side of renown and 117 from the world's judgement.
links.reason: நத்தம்போல் கேடு (a ruin that is like growth) and கெடுவாக வையாது உலகம் ... தாழ்வு both deny that a good person's decline is real ruin; the note describes each fairly.

links.note: 235 calls rare a death that is really a coming into existence. 780 says that if one can die so that the eyes of those who sustained one fill with tears, that death (சாக்காடு) is worth getting even by begging. The soldier's death in 780 is an instance, in the domain of war, of the death 235 says only the skilled achieve.
links.reason: 235 உளதாகும் சாக்காடு ... வித்தகர்க் கல்லால் அரிது and 780 சாக்காடு இரந்துகோள் தக்கது both value a death that is itself a gain, with 780 as the soldier's case.

links.note: On Parimelazhagar's reading of தோன்றுதல் as birth, 236 treats being born with renown as good and not being born as only the better alternative for those without it. 362 says that if one wants anything it should be not to be born (வேண்டுங்கால் வேண்டும் பிறவாமை), with no exception. The conflict depends on the birth reading; on Kalaignar's reading, where 236 is about entering a field of activity, the two do not meet.
links.reason: On the birth reading of தோன்றுதல், 236 endorses birth with புகழ் while 362 says வேண்டும் பிறவாமை outright; the note states the reading the conflict depends on. One imprecision: Parimelazhagar takes தோன்றாமை as birth as an animal, not as non-birth (that is Manakkudavar).

links.note: Parimelazhagar reads 236 as: if born human, be born with the qualities that lead to renown. 972 says birth is alike for all living beings (பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும்) and distinction differs through the difference in what they do. On the birth reading, 972 limits 236: no one is born with renown, so the 'appearing with renown' has to be made by deeds.
links.reason: The link needs Parimelazhagar's 'be born with qualities' for தோன்றின் புகழொடு தோன்றுக and then takes 972's பிறப்பொக்கும், which is about birth-rank versus செய்தொழில், as denying innate qualities; a real but indirect qualification that leans on one gloss and on தோன்று meaning birth.

links.note: 236 says: if you appear, appear with renown, and for those without it not appearing is better than appearing (தோன்றலின் தோன்றாமை நன்று). 1003 says the appearance (தோற்றம்) of men who cling to accumulation and do not want renown (இசை வேண்டா) is a burden to the land. Both judge a person's coming into the world by renown, and 1003 names the misers as a case of those who 'appear' without it.
links.reason: தோன்றலின் தோன்றாமை நன்று (236) and இசைவேண்டா ஆடவர் தோற்றம் நிலக்குப் பொறை (1003) both judge தோற்றம் by புகழ்/இசை; Parimelazhagar glosses தோற்றம் as பிறப்பு and Manakkudavar on 1003 echoes 236 outright.

links.note: 237 tells those without renown to blame themselves and not their scorners. 1060 tells the asker not to be angry at a refusal, since the affliction of his own want is witness enough (நிரப்பிடும்பை தானேயும் சாலும் கரி). In both the grievance against another person is turned back to one's own condition.
links.reason: 237 turns blame from இகழ்வாரை to தம்மை (தந்நோவார்); 1060 tells the இரப்பான் not to be angry because நிரப்பிடும்பை தானேயும் சாலும் கரி. In both the grievance is redirected to one's own condition, in different chapters.

links.note: 238 says it is a disgrace to leave no legacy of renown. 1004 asks what the man whom no one wants (நச்சப்படாதவன்) supposes will remain as his எச்சம்; Parimelazhagar explains that he is unwanted because he has never given. 1004 applies 238's standard to the miser and finds nothing left.
links.reason: Both turn on எச்சம்: 238 calls it a disgrace not to gain இசையென்னும் எச்சம், and 1004 asks what எச்சம் the நச்சப்படாதவன் expects; Parimelazhagar does gloss him as one who never gave (ஈந்தறியாமையின்).

links.note: In 239 the land bears (பொறுத்த) a body without renown and yields less. 189 asks whether it is out of regard for virtue that the earth carries the weight (பொறை) of one who speaks ill of a person behind his back. Both picture the earth as bearing a moral load, and they differ in that 189's earth endures while 239's earth declines.
links.reason: யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம் and வையம் ... பொறை both picture the earth bearing a morally worthless person; the contrast is accurate.

links.note: 239 says the land's rich yield shrinks (வண்பயன் குன்றும்) under a person without renown. 560 says the yield of cows shrinks (ஆபயன் குன்றும்) if the guardian does not guard. The same phrase ties natural yield to human conduct, a private person's in 239 and the king's in 560.
links.reason: The same phrase பயன் குன்றும் ties yield to conduct: வண்பயன் குன்றும் under இசையிலா யாக்கை, ஆபயன் குன்றும் if காவலன் காவான்.

links.note: 239 says land that has borne a body without renown (இசையிலா யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்) will decline in its yield. 1003 says the appearance of men who cling to accumulation and do not want renown is a burden to the land (நிலக்குப் பொறை). Both make the person without renown a weight the earth carries; 239 adds the cost to the earth.
links.reason: 239 இசையிலா யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம் and 1003 இசைவேண்டா ஆடவர் தோற்றம் நிலக்குப் பொறை both make the man without renown a burden the land bears.

links.note: 240 says that to live without renown is not to live. 970 says the world worships and praises the radiance of those with honour who will not live when disgrace comes (இளிவரின் வாழாத மானம் உடையார்). 970 shows a person acting on 240's equation, and the result is the renown 240 demands.
links.reason: 240 equates living with வசையொழிய வாழ்தல் and not living with இசையொழிய வாழ்தல்; 970's இளிவரின் வாழாத மானம் உடையார் act on that and receive the world's praise of their ஒளி.

links.note: 240 uses the formula வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார் for those who live without blame. 1033 uses the same formula for those who live by eating what they plough (உழுதுண்டு வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார்), with all others following and bowing for their food. The phrase 'they alone live' is awarded on two different grounds, a good name in 240 and self-reliance in 1033.
links.reason: வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார் occurs in both, awarded for வசையொழிய living in 240 and உழுதுண்டு living in 1033.

links.note: 72 says the loveless keep everything for themselves, while the loving belong to others even in their bones (என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு). 251 describes the reverse movement: another's body (பிறிது ஊன்) taken to build one's own. Read together, the body is the measure in both: love gives it over, and the eater of flesh takes another's.
links.reason: The contrast between என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு and பிறிது ஊனுண்பான் is suggestive, but the words differ (என்பு, ஊன்) and neither verse uses a distinctive shared figure, so same_image does not fit well.

links.note: 315 asks what understanding has achieved if one does not guard another's pain as one's own (பிறிதின்நோய் தந்நோய்போல்). 251 sets the same pair, self and other (தன் ஊன் / பிறிது ஊன்), the wrong way round: the other's flesh serves one's own. 315 gives the general test that 251's rhetorical question about அருள் applies to eating.
links.reason: பிறிது ஊன் / தன் ஊன் in 251 and பிறிதின் நோய் / தந்நோய் in 315 set the same self-other pair, and 315's general test of treating another's pain as one's own is what 251's question about அருள் applies to eating flesh.

links.note: 251 asks how one who eats another's flesh to enlarge his own (தன்னூன் பெருக்கற்கு) can exercise அருள்; 968 asks whether a life that nurses the flesh (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) is any medicine once dignity is lost. Both use ஊன், one's own flesh, for a body tended at the cost of something higher: அருள் in one verse, honour in the other.
links.reason: ஊன் as one's own body fed at a cost appears in both, தன்னூன் பெருக்கற்கு against அருள் and ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை against பெருந்தகைமை/பீடு.

links.note: Both verses explain அருள் by putting it beside பொருள்: 247 says that world is not for those without அருள் just as this world is not for those without wealth, and 252 says holding அருள் (அருளாட்சி) is not for flesh-eaters just as holding wealth (பொருளாட்சி) is not for those who do not guard it. 252 takes the comparison one step on: அருள், like wealth, is something that can be lost through carelessness.
links.reason: Both verses explain அருள் by an analogy with பொருள் (பொருளில்லார்க்கு இவ்வுலகம் / பொருளாட்சி போற்றாதார்க்கு இல்லை), and the note reports each side correctly.

links.note: 252 takes it as given that holding wealth is not for those who do not look after it (பொருளாட்சி போற்றாதார்க்கு இல்லை). 376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however anxiously it is guarded, and what is one's own will not leave even if carried out and poured away (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் ... சொரியினும் போகா தம). The conflict holds if ஆட்சி is read as possession, as Manakkudavar and Pope read it; Parimelazhagar reads it as getting the benefit of wealth, which softens it.
links.reason: பொருளாட்சி போற்றாதார்க்கு இல்லை makes keeping wealth depend on guarding it, while பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல ... சொரியினும் போகா தம denies that guarding or squandering decides it; the note names the reading of ஆட்சி on which they conflict.

links.note: 253 says the mind of one who has eaten a creature's body with relish does not turn to good (நன்னூக்காது), like the heart of one holding a weapon. 285 says a loving nature with அருள் in view (அருள்கருதி) is not found in those who, with goods in view (பொருள்கருதி), watch for another's lapse. In both, what the mind is fixed on, flesh or another's property, leaves no room for அருள்; Parimelazhagar glosses 253 the same way, as a mind that looks only to the meat.
links.reason: 253 நன்னூக்காது ... உடல்சுவை உண்டார் மனம் and 285 அருள்கருதி ... பொருள்கருதிப் பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார்கண் இல் both say a mind fixed on its object has no room for அருள்; Parimelazhagar's gloss on 253 is as reported.

links.note: Both verses use பொருள் in an unusual, moral sense alongside அருள். 246 says those who leave அருள் and do what should not be done have left பொருள் and forgotten (பொருள்நீங்கிப் பொச்சாந்தார்); 254 calls eating flesh பொருளல்லது. Parimelazhagar takes பொருள் in 254 as virtue (so that பொருளல்லது is sin) and in 246 as the lasting good one should have done.
links.reason: பொருள் is set against அருள் in both (பொருளல்லது அவ்வூன் தினல் / பொருள்நீங்கிப் பொச்சாந்தார்), and Parimelazhagar does take it as அறம் in both places; Manakkudavar reads 246 as wealth, which the note leaves out but does not contradict.
links.text_issue: 254 opens with ருளல்லது; the initial அ of அருளல்லது is missing.

links.note: 326 says Death, the eater of life (உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று), does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing. 255 gives hell a mouth (அண்ணாத்தல்), which on Parimelazhagar's reading has swallowed the eater of flesh and will not open again. In both the language of eating is turned on the human: the one who spares life is not eaten, and the one who eats is.
links.reason: உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று and அளறு ... அண்ணாத்தல் both give the punisher a mouth; Parimelazhagar's 'hell that swallowed him will not open to release him' is reported correctly.

links.note: 255 says that if one eats flesh, அளறு (the mire, hell) will not open its mouth (அண்ணாத்தல் செய்யாது), which Parimelazhagar explains as not opening to let him out again. 835 says a fool can in one birth make the அளறு he will enter and sink in for seven (எழுமையும் தான் புக்கழுந்தும் அளறு). Both use the same rare word for a hell one makes for oneself and does not get out of.
links.reason: Both verses use அளறு for a hell of one's own making: 255 அண்ணாத்தல் செய்யாது அளறு, 835 தான் புக்கழுந்தும் அளறு; the note reports Parimelazhagar's gloss on 255 correctly.

links.note: 1059 asks what distinction givers could have if there were none who wished to ask and receive (இரந்துகோள் மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை). 256 says none would bring flesh to sell if the world did not kill for eating. Both reason from a counterfactual about one party to the existence of the other: askers make givers possible, and eaters make sellers of flesh possible.
links.reason: Both are counterfactuals ('கொல்லாது உலகெனின் ... ஊன்றருவா ரில்'; 'இரந்துகோள் மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை') but the likeness is only one of argument form: 256 blames the eater for the killing, 1059 credits the asker for the giver's 'தோற்றம்'. Accurate note, thin link.

links.note: 575 says that without kindly regard the eye is perceived as a wound (புண்ணென்று உணரப்படும்); 257 says flesh would not be eaten if people perceived it as another creature's wound (புண்ணது உணர்வார்). Both use புண் with உணர் to strip something of its usual standing, and both are about compassion: the eye without it is a sore, and food seen with it is a sore.
links.reason: புண்ணது உணர்வார் and புண்ணென்று உணரப்படும் use the same noun and verb to re-see flesh and the unkind eye; distinctive and meaningful.

links.note: 174 says those of faultless vision who have conquered the senses (புலம்வென்ற புன்மையில் காட்சியவர்) will not covet, even thinking 'we have nothing'. 258 says those whose vision is free of fault do not eat flesh. Both attach an abstention that costs something, from another's goods or from meat, to காட்சி, and 174 adds the mastery of the senses that 258 leaves unstated.
links.reason: செயிரின் தலைப்பிரிந்த காட்சியார் உண்ணார் and புன்மையில் காட்சியவர் ... வெஃகுதல் செய்யார் both derive an abstention from faultless காட்சி.

links.note: 295 says one who speaks truth in accord with his heart is above those who practise austerity together with giving (தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை). 259 says not killing one creature and eating it is better than a thousand sacrifices. Both rank a plain restraint, not lying and not killing, above the religious practices that carry the most prestige.
links.reason: ஆயிரம் வேட்டலின் ... உண்ணாமை நன்று and தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை both rank a plain restraint above prestigious religious practice.

links.note: 326 says Death, the eater of life, does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing; 260 says all living beings fold their hands (கைகூப்பி) and worship the one who does not kill and refuses flesh. Both state what the non-killer receives in return, and both put it as a response of life itself: living beings honour him, and the taker of life leaves him alone.
links.reason: Both name the return for கொல்லாமை: எல்லா உயிருந் தொழும் in 260 and வாழ்நாள்மேல் செல்லாது உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று in 326.

links.note: 157 says that though others do you wrong, it is good to feel the pain and not do what is contrary to virtue (நோநொந்து அறனல்ல செய்யாமை). 261 defines தவம் by the same two parts: bearing pain, and causing none to living beings. The chapter on forbearance asks of the householder, in dealings with those who wrong him, what 261 gives as the whole form of austerity.
links.reason: உற்றநோய் நோன்றல் with உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை in 261 matches நோநொந்து with அறனல்ல செய்யாமை in 157 on the reading the note follows; Parimelazhagar takes நோநொந்து differently, but the two-part match holds either way.

links.note: 262 says தவம் comes to those who already have தவம், and that for those without it taking it up is futile; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read this as merit from earlier births. 273 pictures a person without strength (வலியில் நிலைமையான்) who takes on the form of the strong: a cow grazing in a tiger's skin. 273 shows what the futile undertaking of 262 looks like in practice. (The edition's text of 262 lacks the word அவம் at the start of the second line.)
links.reason: 262's futility concerns those lacking prior தவம் who take it up; 273's வலியில் நிலைமையான் வல்லுருவம் is in the hypocrisy chapter and Parimelazhagar reads the grazing cow as covert indulgence under a disguise, not a sincere attempt that fails. The note merges failure with fraud.
links.text_issue: 262 as printed lacks அவம் at the head of line 2 (commentaries read மேற்கொள்வது அவம்).

links.note: 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, the understanding that is truly one's own still prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்). 262 says austerity too succeeds only for those who already have it. Both hold that a discipline taken up now, study or austerity, yields only according to what the person brings to it; Parimelazhagar refers both to what earlier births have fixed.
links.reason: 262 தவமும் தவமுடையார்க்கு ஆகும் and 373 தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும் share the logic that a discipline yields by what one already has; Parimelazhagar's முன்தவம் and ஊழ் glosses are as the note reports.

links.note: 262 says that for those without தவம், undertaking it is futile. 620 says those who toil on without flagging or delay will see the back even of fate (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்). If the தவம் one must already have is merit from former births, as Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read it, then 262 makes present effort useless without a prior endowment, which is what 620 denies. On Kalaignar's reading, where it means present firmness and self-control, the conflict disappears.
links.reason: On the prior-merit reading of 'தவமுடையார்க்கு ஆகும்' (Parimelazhagar's 'முன்தவம்', Manakkudavar's 'முன்பு நல்வினை') effort without endowment is futile, against 620 'ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர் ... உஞற்றுபவர்'; the note names the reading the conflict depends on.
links.text_issue: 262 as printed lacks 'அவம்' (standard: 'ஆகும் அவம்அதனை'); the second line 'அதனை அஃதிலார் மேற்கொள்வது' has no predicate, though both commentaries gloss the missing word.

links.note: 42 names the householder as the support of those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்கும் ... இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் துணை), along with the destitute and the dead. 263 asks, with a wry கொல், whether the rest have forgotten தவம் out of a wish to provide for renouncers (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). It turns the duty stated in 42 into an explanation, or an excuse, for why householders do no austerity themselves.
links.reason: 42 துறந்தார்க்கும் ... இல்வாழ்வான் துணை and 263 துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி மறந்தார்கொல் share the opening word and the duty; note does not mention that Parimelazhagar reads 42's துறந்தார் as the forsaken, but the plain sense and Manakkudavar support it.

links.note: 263 speaks of the others, householders on Parimelazhagar's reading, as having forgotten தவம் while they provide for renouncers. 48 says a household life that keeps others on their way and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து); Parimelazhagar reads 'keeps on their way' as supporting ascetics. On 48's account the provider has not forgotten austerity: his life already contains more of it.
links.reason: 263's மற்றையவர்கள் தவம் மறந்தார்கொல் is answered by 48's இல்வாழ்க்கை நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து; the note correctly marks both householder readings as Parimelazhagar's.
links.text_issue: 48 is printed with stray spaces ('ஒழுக் கி', 'இல்வாழ் க்கை').

links.note: 1036 says that if ploughmen fold their hands, even those who say 'we have given up desire' (விட்டேம் என்பார்) cannot keep their state. 263 assumes the same dependence: renouncers need others to supply their needs (துப்புரவு). Both verses note that renunciation rests on people who have not renounced.
links.reason: 263 துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு and 1036 விட்டேம் என்பார்க்கும் நிலை இல்லை both rest renunciation on those who have not renounced.

links.note: 29 says the anger of those who stand on the hill of good qualities cannot be withstood even for a moment (கணமேயும் காத்தல் அரிது), on Parimelazhagar's and Pope's reading; Kalaignar takes it to mean their anger does not last a moment. On the first reading it agrees with 264 that renouncers hold a power to ruin those who oppose them, though 264 makes it a matter of intention (எண்ணின்) and 29 of anger.
links.reason: 264 ஒன்னார்த் தெறலும் ... எண்ணின் தவத்தான் வரும் and 29 வெகுளி கணமேயும் காத்தல் அரிது (as Parimelazhagar reads it) both give the ascetic power to ruin; the note correctly flags Kalaignar's different reading and the எண்ணின் / வெகுளி difference.

links.note: 261 says the form of தவம் is just this: bearing one's own pain and doing no harm to living beings (உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை அற்றே). 264 says crushing foes (ஒன்னார்த் தெறல்) and raising friends come through தவம், if one so intends. Read plainly, austerity defined by harmlessness is credited three verses later with the power to destroy. Parimelazhagar eases this by taking the foes as enemies of virtue and by reading எண்ணின் as implying that ascetics do not normally think of such things.
links.reason: உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை as the form of தவம் does sit against ஒன்னார்த் தெறல் ... தவத்தான் வரும்; Parimelazhagar's easing (foes of அறம்; எண்ணின் implying they do not normally think so) is reported accurately.

links.note: 899 says that if those of exalted resolve flare up (ஏந்திய கொள்கையார் சீறின்), even the king breaks midway and loses his rule. Parimelazhagar reads them as people of high vows, and Pope likewise. This is the power of 264, ஒன்னார்த் தெறல் through austerity, seen from the side of the king who must not provoke it.
links.reason: ஒன்னார்த் தெறல் ... தவத்தான் வரும் and ஏந்திய கொள்கையார் சீறின் ... வேந்தனும் வேந்து கெடும் state the same destructive power of the vowed, with Parimelazhagar glossing கொள்கை as உயர்ந்த விரதங்கள்.

links.note: 265 says austerity is practised because through it whatever is wanted is obtained as wanted. 362 says that if one must want, one should want not to be born, and that this comes by wanting not to want (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்). 362 narrows what the வேண்டிய of 265 should be; Parimelazhagar reads 265 itself as referring to results in the next life and release, while Manakkudavar takes it to include enjoyments.
links.reason: வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால் is narrowed by வேண்டுங்கால் வேண்டும் பிறவாமை ... வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும். The commentators' readings (மறுமை/வீடு; போக நுகர்ச்சி) are reported correctly.

links.note: The two verses share a formula: வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால் (265), what is wanted is obtained as it is wanted, and எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப (666), what is thought of is obtained as it was thought. 265 gives this as the reason austerity is striven for; 666 makes it depend on the planner's firmness (திண்ணியர் ஆகப் பெறின்). The promise made for austerity in the book of virtue is made for resolute action in the book of statecraft.
links.reason: வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால் and எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப are one formula, promised to தவம் in one book and to திண்ணியர் in the other.
links.text_issue: 666 reads எய்து எண்ணியார், dropping the ப of எய்துப.

links.note: 348 divides people the same way: those who have thoroughly renounced have reached the head, and the rest, confused, are caught in the net (மயங்கி வலைப்பட்டார் மற்றையவர்). 266 says those who do தவம் do their own work and the rest act in vain, caught in desire (ஆசையுட் பட்டு). Both use பட்டு / பட்டார், being caught, for everyone outside the ascetic's path; Parimelazhagar supplies 'the net of desire' in his gloss on 266.
links.reason: Both divide people into ascetics and மற்றல்லார் / மற்றையவர் who are caught (ஆசையுட் பட்டு / வலைப்பட்டார்); Parimelazhagar does gloss 266 as ஆசையாகிய வலையுள்பட்டு.

links.note: 308 says that even if harm is done to you like the touch of massed flames (இணர்எரி தோய்வன்ன), not being angry is good if one can manage it. 267 says pain that burns (துன்பஞ் சுடச்சுட) makes those who can endure it shine like gold in fire. Both picture suffering as fire applied to a person; 308 asks only that it be borne without anger, and 267 says what the bearing produces.
links.reason: Fire is in both (சுடச்சுட; இணர்எரி தோய்வன்ன) but it does different work: self-undertaken austerity that refines like gold versus harm done by another that one should not resent. A generic fire figure, not a distinctive shared image.

links.note: 267 says that for those able to endure, pain burning them makes them shine (ஒளிவிடும்), as gold shines the more it is heated. 630 says that if one takes what hurts as pleasure (இன்னாமை இன்பம் எனக்கொளின்), there comes a distinction even one's enemies admire. The ascetic's gain from pain in the first book has a worldly counterpart in the second: in both, pain borne in the right way adds to the person.
links.reason: துன்பஞ் சுடச்சுட ... ஒளிவிடும் and இன்னாமை இன்பம் எனக்கொளின் ... சிறப்பு both say pain rightly borne raises the person, in ascetic and worldly settings.

links.note: 620 says those who toil on without flagging will see the back even of fate (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்); 269 says even getting past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும்) is within reach of those with the power of austerity. Each uses the particle உம், 'even', to name the one thing thought unbeatable and then says sustained effort beats it: labour in the book of statecraft, austerity in the book of virtue. (The edition's text of 269 ends with a stray letter, தலைப்பட்டவர்க்குல்.)
links.reason: கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் and ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர் both use உம் to put the seemingly unbeatable within reach of sustained effort (நோற்றலின் ஆற்றல்; தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்), in two different books.
links.text_issue: 269 ends தலைப்பட் டவர்க்குல், with a stray final ல்.

links.note: 616 says effort creates prosperity and the absence of effort brings in want (முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்). 270 says the have-nots (இலர்) are many because few practise austerity (நோற்பார் சிலர்). Both trace poverty to something people fail to do, but they name different things: present exertion in the chapter on labour, and austerity here, which the commentators take to bear fruit across births.
links.reason: இலர்பலராகிய காரணம் நோற்பார் சிலர் and முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்திவிடும் both trace want to something left undone; the note is careful to keep தவம் and முயற்சி distinct.

links.note: 842 says that when a person without understanding gives gladly, the cause is nothing other than the receiver's தவம் (பெறுவான் தவம்). 270 says the have-nots are many because those who practise austerity are few. Both explain who gets and who lacks by austerity, and 842 shows the idea used in passing in the second book, as an accepted explanation.
links.reason: 270 இலர்பலராகிய காரணம் நோற்பார் சிலர் and 842 பிறிதியாதும் இல்லை பெறுவான் தவம் both explain who receives by தவம்; the note is accurate that 842 uses it in passing.

links.note: 271 says the five elements laugh within (பூதங்கள் ஐந்தும் அகத்தே நகும்) at the concealed conduct of a deceitful mind; 293 says that after a lie about what one's own heart knows, that heart itself burns one (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). Both place the witness to a hidden fault inside the person; 293 moves it from the body's elements, which only laugh, to the heart, which punishes.
links.reason: பூதங்கள் ஐந்தும் அகத்தே நகும் and தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும் both put the witness to a hidden fault inside the person, and 293 moves from mockery to punishment.

links.note: In 271 the five elements laugh within at a hypocrite's hidden conduct; in 1040 the good woman called Land laughs (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்) at those who sit idle saying 'we have nothing'. In both a part of the material world is the one that laughs at a human pretence, and Parimelazhagar glosses the laugh in 1040 too as inward (தன்னுள்ளே).
links.reason: 'பூதங்கள் ஐந்தும் அகத்தே நகும்' and 'நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்' both personify the material world laughing at a person; Parimelazhagar does gloss 1040 as 'தன்னுள்ளே நகா நிற்கும்'.

links.note: 34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர பிற); 272 says a sky-high appearance (வானுயர் தோற்றம்) does nothing when the heart is in known fault. 272 applies the general rule of 34 to the specific case of the ascetic's appearance.
links.reason: வானுயர் தோற்றம் எவன்செய்யும் with தன்னெஞ்சம் ... குற்றப்படின் is 34's மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் / ஆகுல நீர பிற applied to the ascetic's outward guise.

links.note: 24 praises the one who guards the five senses with the goad called firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான்); 273 likens one of strengthless nature (வலியில் நிலைமையான்) who takes the form of the strong to a cow grazing in a tiger's skin. Parimelazhagar reads the missing strength in 273 as the power to bring the mind under control, which is what 24 names as the mark of the real renouncer, so 273 shows the outward form of 24 without its substance.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does gloss வலியில் நிலைமையான் as lacking the strength to bring the mind under control, which is what உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான் names. 273 is the outward வல்லுருவம் without that உரன்.

links.note: 261 gives the form of தவம் as bearing one's own pain and doing no harm to living beings (உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை); 274 speaks of doing 'what is not it' (அல்லவை) under cover of தவம் and compares this to a hunter snaring birds. Read together, the hunter simile shows the hypocrite doing the very thing, harm to creatures, whose absence 261 makes the definition of austerity.
links.reason: 274's தவமறைந்து அல்லவை does connect to 261's definition of தவம், but the note takes the simile's vehicle (வேட்டுவன் புள்சிமிழ்த்தற்று) as the hypocrite's actual deed, harm to creatures; the Tamil only compares the concealment, and Parimelazhagar takes அல்லவை as seducing others' women.

links.note: 274 has the hunter hidden in the bush as the image of evil done under cover of austerity; 828 says a weapon hides even in an enemy's hands folded in worship (தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்), and likewise in his tears. In both a gesture of piety is the cover for harm, once in ascetic life and once in false friendship.
links.reason: 274 தவமறைந்து அல்லவை செய்தல் and 828 தொழுதகையுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும் both show harm hidden inside a gesture of piety, in ascetic life and in false friendship.

links.note: 275 says the concealed conduct of those who say 'we are free of attachment' brings many harms with the cry எற்றெற்று; 655 says do not do what will make you grieve saying எற்று ('what is this I have done'). The same exclamation of regret marks the test in both, in the renouncer's conduct and in the minister's action; Manakkudavar, however, takes the cry in 275 as other people's, not the doer's.
links.reason: The cry எற்று is in both (எற்றெற்றென்று, எற்றென்று இரங்குவ), and the note correctly records that Manakkudavar assigns the cry in 275 differently.

links.note: 42 makes the householder the support of those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்கும் ... துணை); 276 says none are more hard-eyed than those who, unrenounced at heart, live by deceiving as if they had renounced (துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து வாழ்வார்). Parimelazhagar takes the deceived to be the givers, so the pairing shows what the false renouncer exploits: the duty of support that 42 lays on the householder.
links.reason: 42 makes the இல்வாழ்வான் the துணை of துறந்தார்; 276's துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து வாழ்வார் is glossed by Parimelazhagar as deceiving தானம் செய்வாரை, so the false renouncer exploits exactly that support.

links.note: 276 ends 'வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்': none are harder than those who live by posing as renouncers. 1198, spoken by the woman in separation, ends with the same words: none in the world are harder than those who go on living without a kind word from the one they love. The shared formula uses வன்கண் in two senses, the cruelty of the deceiver in 276 and the grim endurance of the one left behind in 1198.
links.reason: Both end வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல், with வன்கண் meaning the fraud's cruelty in 276 and the forsaken woman's hard endurance in 1198; the note is accurate.
links.text_issue: 276's Parimelazhagar text prints வண்கணார் once for வன்கணார்.

links.note: 706 says the face shows what is strongest in the heart, as crystal shows what is next to it (நெஞ்சம் கடுத்தது காட்டும் முகம்); 277 says there are people red outside and black inside. 277 limits 706: the face may betray a passing feeling to a skilled reader, but a settled outward appearance can be the opposite of the inside.
links.reason: 706 நெஞ்சம் கடுத்தது காட்டும் முகம் against 277 புறங்குன்றி கண்டனையரேனும் அகம் ... கரியார்: the outside can hide the inside, which limits the rule that the face shows the heart.
links.text_issue: 277: 'முக்கிற்' is a typo for மூக்கிற்.

links.note: 277 says the world has people who look outwardly like the red kunri seed but are inwardly black like its tip (புறம் ... அகம்); 824 says to fear deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய ... அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சர்). The same outside/inside split is described for the false ascetic and for the false friend.
links.reason: புறம் ... அகம் in 277 and முகத்தின் இனிய ... அகத்தின்னா in 824 draw the same fair-outside, foul-inside split for the false ascetic and the false friend.

links.note: 277 uses the kunri seed for its two colours, red body and black tip; 965 uses it for its size, saying even those like a hill sink if they do a lowering thing as small as a kunri (குன்றி அனைய). The same seed serves both verses as a figure for a small dark flaw in something that otherwise looks fine, by colour in one and by measure in the other.
links.reason: The kunri seed appears in both (புறங்குன்றி ... குன்றி மூக்கிற் கரியார்; குன்றி அனைய செயின்), by colour in one and by size in the other as the note says; 'dark flaw' fits only 277, a small overreach.
links.text_issue: 277 prints முக்கிற் for மூக்கிற்.

links.note: 279 says the straight arrow is cruel and the bent lute is upright, so take people by the nature of their deeds (வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்); 505 says one's own deeds are the touchstone of greatness and smallness (கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்). The same rule appears as a test for ascetics in the book of virtue and as a test for choosing officers in the book of statecraft.
links.reason: 279 வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல் and 505 தத்தம் கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல் give the same judge-by-deeds rule for ascetics and for officers.

links.note: 279 warns against reading uprightness from shape, with the arrow and lute as examples; 667 says do not scorn on seeing someone's form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை), because the great chariot has its small linchpin. One verse guards against being impressed by form and the other against despising it, and both replace form with function.
links.reason: வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல் and உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை ... அச்சாணி both put function above form, from opposite directions.

links.note: 281 tells one who wants not to be scorned to guard his heart from stealing anything at all (கள்ளாமை காக்க தன் நெஞ்சு); 178 says that what keeps one's wealth from shrinking is not coveting the goods in another's hand (வெஃகாமை ... பிறன்கைப் பொருள்). Each gives restraint toward others' property as the means to something one wants for oneself, standing in 281 and one's own wealth in 178; Parimelazhagar reads 281 differently, as about one esteemed for not despising release.
links.reason: எள்ளாமை வேண்டுவான் ... கள்ளாமை காக்க and அஃகாமை செல்வத்திற்கு ... வெஃகாமை both offer restraint toward others' goods as the way to a good of one's own; the note also flags Parimelazhagar's different reading of 281.

links.note: 282 says even thinking in the mind (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும்) of taking another's goods by stealth is wrong; 317 says the highest thing is not to do, with the mind (மனத்தானாம்), anything ill to anyone at any time in any degree. Both place the fault at the level of intention before any act, for theft in one and for harm in general in the other.
links.reason: உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும் தீதே and மனத்தானாம் மாணா செய்யாமை both locate fault in the mind, on Manakkudavar's and Kalaignar's reading of மனத்தானாம்; Parimelazhagar's 'knowingly' sense is not flagged but does not undo the pairing.
links.text_issue: The Parimelazhagar text printed under 317 in the packet is the commentary on 318 (தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை), not 317.

links.note: 283 says gain made by stealth perishes beyond measure while seeming to grow (ஆவது போலக் கெடும்); 660 says making wealth by deceit (சலத்தால் பொருள்செய்து) and feeling secure in it is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot. The same claim, that wrongly got wealth looks held and is being lost, is made to the renouncer in one book and to the minister in the other.
links.reason: 283 'ஆவது போலக் கெடும்' and 660 'சலத்தால் பொருள்செய்து ஏமார்த்தல் பசுமண் கலத்துள் நீர்' both say ill-got wealth only seems held while it is being lost.

links.note: 368 says those without craving have no sorrow, and where craving exists sorrow comes on and on without fail (தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும்); 284 says desire hardened in stealing (கன்றிய காதல்) yields sorrow that does not die (வீயா விழுமம்). 284 is the general law of 368 applied to one desire, with the same stress on sorrow that does not end.
links.reason: கன்றிய காதல் ... வீயா விழுமம் (284) is one craving yielding undying sorrow; அஃதுண்டேல் தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும் (368) is the general law. The application holds.

links.note: 284 speaks of காதல் grown in களவு and means desire for stealing, which ends in undying sorrow; in 1092 the man says the small look her eyes steal (கண் களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம்) is more than half of love's pleasure. The same word களவு is condemned as theft of goods in the book of virtue and prized as the stolen glance in the book of love, where it is a lover's speech and not a teaching about theft.
links.reason: களவு is an ordinary word: literal theft in 284 (களவின்கண் கன்றிய காதல்) and 'by stealth' in 1092 (கண் களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம்). The note is accurate but the shared word is not a distinctive image.

links.note: 285 says அருள் with love is not found in one who watches to take another's goods; 251 asks how one who eats another creature's flesh to swell his own can hold to அருள் (எங்ஙனம் ஆளும் அருள்). Both test a claim to அருள் against a practice of taking from another for oneself, property in one case and the body in the other.
links.reason: Both deny அருள் to one who takes from another for himself: பொருள்கருதிப் பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார்கண் இல், and பிறிது ஊனுண்பான் எங்ஙனம் ஆளும் அருள். The note is accurate on both.

links.note: 285 opposes having அருள் in view to having பொருள் in view; 757 says the child அருள், born of அன்பு, is reared by the wealthy foster-mother பொருள். 757 limits how far 285 can be taken: the opposition holds for goods taken from others by watching for their lapses, not for wealth as such, which 757 makes the support of the same அருள் and அன்பு that 285 names.
links.reason: 285 opposes அருள் to பொருள்கருதிப் பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார், i.e. to theft, not to wealth as such, so 757 limits a claim 285 does not make; the shared அருள்/அன்பு/பொருள் vocabulary is real but the qualification is manufactured.

links.note: 286 says those with hardened desire for stealing cannot stand and walk within அளவு (அளவின்கண் நின்றொழுகல் ஆற்றார்); 474 says the one who does not live in accord, does not know his measure (அளவறியான்) and admires himself perishes quickly. On Kalaignar's reading of அளவு in 286 as a limit one lives within, the two apply one idea, conduct kept inside a known measure, to the renouncer and to the king; Parimelazhagar instead takes அளவு in 286 as the reasoned measuring of the soul and its ends, on which reading the link is only verbal.
links.reason: அளவு is shared, but 474's அளவறியான் is not knowing one's own strength and 286's அளவின்கண் நின்றொழுகல் is keeping within bounds; on Parimelazhagar's reading of 286 (அளவை, reasoned measuring) the link is verbal, as the note concedes. The common idea holds only on one modern reading and is generic.

links.note: 287 calls stealing a dark knowledge (களவென்னும் காரறி வாண்மை) that is not found in those set on the strength called அளவு; 175 asks what a fine and wide understanding (அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவு) comes to if, coveting, one acts senselessly toward everyone. Both deny that cleverness in the service of taking others' goods counts as real understanding.
links.reason: 287 denies காரறிவாண்மை to those of அளவு, but 175 grants the அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவு and asks what use it is if one covets; neither is about cleverness used for taking, so 'same claim' overstates it.
links.text_issue: 287 is printed புரிந்தார்கண்ட இல் (for புரிந்தார்கண் இல்).

links.note: 422 defines understanding as what does not let the mind go wherever it has gone, but turns it from evil toward good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது அறிவு); 287 grants stealing the name அறிவு only with the qualifier கார், dark. By 422's definition the thief's skill fails as அறிவு, which explains why 287 marks it as darkened.
links.reason: 422 defines அறிவு as what தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது; 287 names theft காரறிவாண்மை. The definition explains why the thief's cleverness is qualified as கார்.

links.note: 34 locates virtue in the mind being without stain; 288 says virtue stands in the heart of those who know அளவு just as concealment stands in the heart of those who know stealing (நெஞ்சத்து அறம் ... நெஞ்சில் கரவு). 288 adds to 34 that the heart is occupied either way: what one practises, measure or theft, decides whether virtue or deceit takes up residence there.
links.reason: 288's நெஞ்சத்து அறம் / நெஞ்சில் கரவு extends 34's மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் by showing what occupies the heart of the measured and of the thief.
links.text_issue: 288 reads அளவறாந்தார், a typo for அளவறிந்தார்.

links.note: 289 says those who know nothing but stealing do what is beyond measure and perish right there (அளவல்ல செய்தாங்கே வீவர்); 479 says the life of one who does not live knowing the measure seems to exist, then is not, and perishes without trace. Both make ignoring அளவு the cause of ruin, in the renouncer's conduct and in the management of means; Parimelazhagar reads அளவல்ல in 289 as wrong thoughts and not as excess of spending, so the likeness is of pattern, not of subject.
links.reason: அளவல்ல செய்து ஆங்கே வீவர் and அளவறிந்து வாழாதான் வாழ்க்கை ... கெடும்: ignoring அளவு leads to ruin in both, and the note properly marks that அளவு differs in sense between them.
links.text_issue: 479: 'அளவற஧ந்து' is an encoding corruption of அளவறிந்து.

links.note: 290 gives the two outcomes of stealing and not stealing: loss of உயிர்நிலை, and the world of the gods (புத்தேள் உலகு) not failing; 121 gives the two outcomes of restraint and its lack: a place among the immortals (அமரருள்) and thick darkness. Each closes or opens its chapter with the same two-sided reward and penalty attached to a single virtue.
links.reason: Both attach a paired outcome with the gods' world to one virtue and its lack (தள்ளும் உயிர்நிலை / தள்ளாது புத்தேளுலகு; அமரருள் உய்க்கும் / ஆரிருள் உய்த்துவிடும்), and the chapter positions are as stated.
links.text_issue: 290 reads ளுளகு, a typo for ளுலகு.

links.note: 290 says that for those who steal the உயிர்நிலை fails, while for those who do not steal the world of the gods does not fail; 255 says உயிர்நிலை rests in not eating flesh, and that hell will not open its mouth for one who eats it. Both verses hang உயிர்நிலை, the standing of life in the body on Parimelazhagar's gloss, on one abstention and pair it with a fate after death; Manakkudavar reads the word in 290 as release itself.
links.reason: உயிர்நிலை is the hinge word of both verses, each tying it to an abstention and to an afterlife (புத்தேளுலகு / அளறு); the differing glosses of Parimelazhagar (உடம்பு) and Manakkudavar (வீடு) are reported accurately.
links.text_issue: 290 line 1 ends 'கள்வார்க்குத்' where the sense and both commentaries require கள்ளார்க்குத்; 'புத்தே ளுளகு' is a typo for புத்தேளுலகு.

links.note: 291 defines truth (வாய்மை) not as reporting what happened but as speech with no harm in it at all (யாதொன்றும் தீமை இலாத சொலல்). 292 draws the consequence: even a falsehood stands in truth's place (பொய்மையும் வாய்மை யிடத்த) if it yields faultless good. Read together, the second verse is the first's definition applied to its hardest case.
links.reason: யாதொன்றும் தீமை இலாத சொலல் defines வாய்மை by harmlessness; பொய்மையும் வாய்மை யிடத்த புரைதீர்ந்த நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின் follows from that definition, as the note says.

links.note: 292 makes good results decisive: a falsehood that yields faultless good (நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின்) counts as truth. 113 says gain got by leaving fairness is to be dropped that very day even if it yields nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும்). The conflict holds only if both are read as answers to whether a good outcome can license a breach of a norm; 113 is about gain and 292 about speech, and 292's புரைதீர்ந்த (free of fault) may already exclude what 113 forbids.
links.reason: நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின் against நன்றே தரினும் ... ஒழிய விடல் conflict on whether a good outcome licenses a breach; the note names the reading and the limits (புரைதீர்ந்த, gain vs speech).

links.note: In 129 a burn from fire heals inside but the scar burned by the tongue (நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு) does not; in 293 the liar's own heart burns him (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). Both use burning for the lasting damage of speech: the harsh word burns the hearer, the false word burns the speaker.
links.reason: சுட்ட வடு (129) and தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும் (293) both make speech a thing that burns, the hearer in one and the speaker in the other; the note describes both accurately.

links.note: 294 says one who lives without falsehood in the heart (உள்ளத்தாற் பொய்யாது) is present in the hearts of all the world. 119 says rectitude is speech without bend, provided there is surely no bend within (உட்கோட்டம் இன்மை). In truthfulness and in impartiality alike, straight speech is counted only when the inside matches it.
links.reason: 294 உள்ளத்தாற் பொய்யாது and 119 உட்கோட்டம் இன்மை பெறின் both make the inner state the condition for straight speech to count.

links.note: 295 sets the truthful speaker above those who practise austerity and giving. 48 says a household life that keeps others on their way and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). In both, the ascetic is the standard of comparison and an ordinary life rightly lived is placed above it.
links.reason: தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை and நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து both rank a non-ascetic practice above the ascetic standard.

links.note: 296 says not lying gives all the virtues (எல்லா அறமுந் தரும்); Parimelazhagar takes எய்யாமை as 'without wearying the body'. 297 then concludes that one who keeps steadily to not lying does well even without doing the other virtues (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை நன்று). The second verse depends on the first: the others can be left undone because this one already supplies them.
links.reason: 296's எல்லா அறமுந் தரும் is the ground for 297's அறம்பிற செய்யாமை நன்று; the gloss of எய்யாமை as மெய் வருந்தாமல் is Parimelazhagar's and correctly reported.

links.note: 299 names not lying the one true lamp for the worthy (பொய்யா விளக்கே விளக்கு). 601 calls lineage an undimming lamp (குடியென்னும் குன்றா விளக்கம்) that nevertheless goes out when the grime of sloth covers it. The lamp figure marks what a person's standing depends on, and 601 adds that such a lamp can be put out by neglect.
links.reason: Both use விளக்கு/விளக்கம், but 299's 'பொய்யா விளக்கு' is truthfulness as the lamp that dispels inner darkness and 601's 'குடியென்னும் குன்றா விளக்கம்' is family lustre; the lamp is a common figure and 'what a person's standing depends on' fits 299 only on a minority reading.

links.note: 301 counts restraint of anger only where the anger could have its way. 153 says the strength of strengths is bearing with fools (வன்மையுள் வன்மை மடவார்ப் பொறை). Both locate the real test of forbearance where one has the upper hand and nothing outside compels it.
links.reason: 301 does restrict real restraint to செல்லிடத்து, but 153 only says மடவார்ப் பொறை is வன்மையுள் வன்மை and says nothing about having the upper hand; the note reads that condition into it.
links.text_issue: 153 reads இன்நம்யுள், a typo for இன்மையுள்.

links.note: 302 says anger is bad where it cannot take effect, and where it can, nothing is worse (செல்லிடத்தும் இல்அதனின் தீய பிற); Parimelazhagar reads the two places as the stronger and the weaker. 861 advises avoiding opposition to the strong and pressing enmity against the weak (மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). They conflict if 302 is taken as a rule for everyone; if the anger chapter is addressed to ascetics, as Parimelazhagar holds, and 861 to a king, they are advice for different people.
links.reason: செல்லிடத்தும் இல் அதனின் தீய பிற (anger at the weaker is the worst, per Parimelazhagar) against மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை is a real conflict on the general reading, and the note names the reading that dissolves it.

links.note: 302's first half says anger where it cannot take effect is bad, which Parimelazhagar explains as harm coming back from the stronger party. 895 states that harm at its extreme: those a king of fierce might is angry with (வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர்) will not survive wherever they go. The chapter on not offending the great fills in what 302 leaves as a bare 'bad'.
links.reason: 302 is about one's own anger toward the stronger (செல்லா இடத்துச் சினந்தீது); 895 வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர் is about being the object of a king's anger, whatever the offence. Related by the theme of the stronger party, but 895 is not the consequence 302 leaves unstated.

links.note: 152 says always bear with an excess done to you, and that forgetting it is better still (அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). 303 uses the same verb for the anger itself: forget anger toward anyone (மறத்தல் வெகுளியை யார்மாட்டும்), since evils are born from it. One forgets the offence and the other the anger at it; 303 adds the reason.
links.reason: Both turn on மறத்தல்: 152 அதனை மறத்தல் (the இறப்பு done to one) and 303 மறத்தல் வெகுளியை, with 303 adding the reason தீய பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும்.

links.note: 303 says evils are born from anger (தீய பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும்). 360 names anger (வெகுளி) with desire and confusion as the three whose very names must perish for pain to perish. What 303 says of anger as a source of evils, 360 places in a full account of the roots of suffering.
links.reason: 303 says தீய பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும் of வெகுளி, and 360 lists வெகுளி with காமம் and மயக்கம் as what must perish for நோய் to perish; a modest, accurate develops.
links.text_issue: 360 prints இநவ்முன்றன் for இவைமூன்றன்.

links.note: 304 counts the death of laughter and joy (நகையும் உவகையும்) as the harm that makes anger the worst enemy. 999 says that for those not capable of laughing (நகல்வல்லர் அல்லார்க்கு) the great world lies in darkness even by day. 999 describes the state that 304 says anger produces.
links.reason: Shared நகை/நகல், but 999's நகல்வல்லர் அல்லார் are those lacking பண்பு who cannot mix and rejoice with others; nothing in it says anger produced the state, so 'describes the state 304 says anger produces' overstates.

links.note: 306 says anger, the fire that kills what it adjoins (சேர்ந்தாரைக் கொல்லி), burns even the safe raft of one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணை). 526 says no one on earth has more people around him than one who gives greatly and does not cherish anger (பேணான் வெகுளி). The two give the loss and the gain of the same fact: kin stay with the one who is free of anger.
links.reason: 306 has anger burning இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணை and 526 gives the largest மருங்கு to one who பேணான் வெகுளி; the note's reading of இனம் as one's own people matches Manakkudavar (நட்டோர்), though Parimelazhagar takes it more narrowly.

links.note: 306 calls one's people a safe raft (ஏமப் புணை) that anger burns. In 1164 the woman says the sea of love certainly exists and the safe raft to swim it (ஏமப் புணை) does not. The same phrase names what keeps a person afloat; in one verse a passion destroys it and in the other a passion leaves the speaker without one.
links.reason: ஏமப் புணை occurs in both: burned by சினம் in 306 and absent for the காமக் கடல் in 1164.

links.note: 308 says that even if someone does harm like the touch of massed flames (இணர்எரி தோய்வன்ன இன்னா செயினும்), not being angry is good, if one can manage it (புணரின்). 312 says that even when someone has done hurt in hatred, not doing hurt in return is the settled stand of the stainless (மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை). 308 governs the feeling and 312 the act that would follow from it; 308 alone concedes that it may not be possible.
links.reason: 308 வெகுளாமை நன்று with the concession புணரின், and 312 மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை மாசற்றார் கோள்: feeling then act, as the note says.

links.note: 308 asks for no anger even under harm like fire. 852, in the chapter on hostility in the Book of Wealth, says that even if someone does what cannot be borne, meaning division, not doing harm in return is best (இன்னா செய்யாமை தலை). The same advice, with the same 'even if ... செயினும்' form, is given as virtue in one book and as policy in the other.
links.reason: இன்னா செயினும் ... வெகுளாமை நன்று and பற்றா செயினும் ... இன்னாசெய்யாமை தலை give the same non-retaliation in the same concessive form in two books.

links.note: 309 praises one who does not think of anger in the heart at all (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளான் வெகுளி). 487 says the bright do not flare up outwardly on the spot but, watching for the time, burn within (காலம்பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர்). They conflict if both describe how a wise person treats anger inwardly, one removing it and the other keeping it for later; the conflict lessens if 309 is for the ascetic, as Parimelazhagar reads it, and 487 for a ruler facing enemies.
links.reason: உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளான் வெகுளி and காலம்பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர் do conflict on inward anger if both describe the wise in general; the note names the reading the conflict depends on and what removes it.

links.note: 309 says all one has thought of is gained at once (உள்ளியதெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்) if one never thinks of anger in the heart. 540 says gaining what one has thought of is easy (உள்ளியது எய்தல் எளிது) if one can keep thinking of it. Both promise the same result in nearly the same words and set a condition on the mind: one removes a thought, the other holds one.
links.reason: உள்ளியதெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும் (309) and உள்ளியது எய்தல் எளிது (540) promise the same result on a mental condition, உள்ளான் வெகுளி versus உள்ளியது உள்ளப் பெறின்.

links.note: 113 tells one to let go, that very day, of gain that comes from leaving fairness even if it brings only good (நன்றே தரினும் நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கத்தை). 311 refuses wealth that would require hurting others (பிறர்க்கு இன்னா செய்யாமை). Both grant that the gain is real and still rule out the means, one in the householder's ethics and one in the renouncer's.
links.reason: சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும் and நன்றே தரினும் both concede the gain and still rule out the means; the householder/renouncer placement is correct.

links.note: 755, in the chapter on making wealth, says wealth that does not come with grace and love (அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாராப் பொருளாக்கம்) should be let go and not embraced. 311 makes not hurting others the settled stand of the stainless even at the cost of wealth. The condition that 311 states for the pure is repeated in the Book of Wealth as a rule for acquisition itself.
links.reason: செல்வம் பெறினும் பிறர்க்கு இன்னா செய்யாமை (311) and அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாராப் பொருளாக்கம் ... விடல் (755) apply the same limit on gain in two books. Parimelazhagar narrows 311's செல்வம் to yogic powers, which the note leaves out.

links.note: 852, on hostility, says that even if someone does unbearable things intending division, not doing hurt in return out of hostility is the highest course (இகல்கருதி இன்னாசெய்யாமை தலை). 312 says not hurting in return (மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை) is the stand of the stainless. The same rule, in nearly the same words, is carried from personal purity into the politics of faction.
links.reason: 312 மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை and 852 இகல்கருதி இன்னாசெய்யாமை தலை state the same non-retaliation rule in near-identical words in two domains.

links.note: 313 says that doing hurt, even to those who hated you though you did nothing to them (செய்யாமல் செற்றார்க்கும்), brings sorrow with no escape (உய்யா விழுமம்). 207 says people escape any enmity (உய்வர்) but the enmity of their own deeds follows and kills (வினைப்பகை வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும்). The shared root உய் shows the reasoning: an enemy can be survived, one's own retaliation cannot.
links.reason: உய்யா விழுமம் in 313 and உய்வர் ... வினைப்பகை வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும் in 207 use the same root to the same end: enmity can be survived, the consequence of one's own harmful act cannot.

links.note: 152 says bearing an excess done to you is good and forgetting it is better still (அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). 314 ends on விடல்: do good and let it go. Parimelazhagar takes this விடல் as forgetting both the hurt and the good done in return, which would make 314 the fuller form of 152's advice; the Tamil itself says only 'do and leave'.
links.reason: 152's மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று and 314's செய்து விடல் do connect as the note says, and it correctly marks that 'forgetting both' is Parimelazhagar's gloss on விடல், not the Tamil.
links.text_issue: Packet's Parimelazhagar entry under 314 is the commentary on 315 (அறிவினான் ஆகுவது உண்டோ), not 314.

links.note: 158 says to defeat those who did wrong out of arrogance by one's own worthiness (தம் தகுதியான் வென்று விடல்), which Parimelazhagar reads as forbearance. 314 goes a step further: do them a kindness so that they feel shame. Both keep the vocabulary of contest (winning, punishing) while replacing retaliation, and 314 adds the active good that 158 leaves unstated.
links.reason: தகுதியான் வென்று விடல் and அவர்நாண நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல் share the contest vocabulary (வென்று / ஒறுத்தல்) and 314 adds active kindness.
links.text_issue: Packet's Parimelazhagar entry for 314 is the commentary of a different verse (பிறிதின் நோய் தந்நோய்போல்...); the note does not rely on it.

links.note: 34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்து அறன்). 317 makes the highest thing the absence of any mind-born ill toward anyone (மனத்தானாம் மாணா செய்யாமை தலை), in a chapter whose first two verses speak of the மாசற்றார். 317 gives 34's general claim a specific content: the unstained mind is one that harbours no hurt.
links.reason: மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் (34) is given content by மனத்தானாம் மாணா செய்யாமை தலை (317); the மாசற்றார் reference to 311-312 is correct.

links.note: 209 says that if a person loves himself (தன்னைத்தான் காதலனாயின்) he should not come near evil deeds, however small. 318 asks why one who knows what hurts his own life does hurt to other lives. Both reason from self-regard, by different routes: 209 from the doer's own interest, 318 from the doer's own knowledge of pain.
links.reason: 209 argues from தன்னைத்தான் காதலன், 318 from தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை தானறிவான்: both make the self the ground for not harming, by different routes as the note says.
links.text_issue: 318's Tamil is misprinted (தன்னுயிர்ககு ஏன்னாமை for தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை), and the Parimelazhagar entry shown under 318 is the commentary on 319.

links.note: 316 gives the rule: what one has perceived as painful, do not do to another (துன்னாமை வேண்டும் பிறன்கண் செயல்). 318 turns it into a question: one who knows what hurts his own life (தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை தானறிவான்), why (என்கொலோ) does he hurt other lives? The second verse treats breaking the rule as something needing explanation; Parimelazhagar suggests delusion as the implied answer. (The edition's text of 318 has typos in its first line.)
links.reason: 316's rule (இன்னா எனத்தான் உணர்ந்தவை துன்னாமை) becomes the question தானறிவான் என்கொலோ in 318. The development is in the Tamil itself.
links.text_issue: 318 reads தன்னுயிர்ககு ஏன்னாமை for தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை. The Parimelazhagar entry printed under 318 is actually the commentary on 319 (பிறர்க்கு இன்னா முற்பகல்), so the note's claim about his 'delusion' gloss cannot be checked from this edition.

links.note: 208 says the ruin of those who do evil is like a shadow that never leaves and rests at the foot (நிழல் ... அடி உறைந்தற்று). 319 puts the same inevitability in time: forenoon and afternoon (முற்பகல், பிற்பகல்). One verse uses space and the other the day's two halves to say that consequence is attached to the deed; the day figure also fits a shadow lengthening after noon, though the text does not say so.
links.reason: 208 has the shadow (நிழல் ... அடியுறைந்தற்று) and 319 has முற்பகல் / பிற்பகல்; there is no shared image, and the note admits the shadow connection is not in 319. The shared claim of inescapable consequence would be an agrees link.
links.text_issue: 208 prints அஇஉறைந் for அடியுறைந்.

links.note: 320 says all pains fall on those who caused pain (நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம்). 169 admits that the crooked-hearted prosper and the upright meet ruin, and says only that this is to be pondered (நினைக்கப் படும்). 169 concedes cases that 320's rule does not show on its face; Manakkudavar's reading of 320, that present pain comes from hurt done earlier, and Parimelazhagar's of 169, that such cases are to be examined for causes, are the way the commentators reconcile them.
links.reason: நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம் (320) states a rule that அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கமும் செவ்வியான் கேடும் (169) concedes exceptions to; Manakkudavar on 320 and Parimelazhagar's ஆராயப்படும் on 169 are reported correctly.

links.note: 349 says the moment attachment ends births are cut off, and otherwise impermanence is what is seen (மற்று நிலையாமை காணப்படும்). 331 faults the understanding that takes the unlasting for lasting. 349 explains why the error in 331 matters: for one still attached, impermanence is the standing condition, and Parimelazhagar on 331 likewise ties the error to attachment and rebirth.
links.reason: நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும் is the error and பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும் மற்று நிலையாமை காணப்படும் gives its stakes; Parimelazhagar on 331 does link it to பற்று and பிறவித்துன்பம்.

links.note: 331 calls lowest the paltry understanding that takes what does not last for lasting (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்). 351 says a joyless birth comes from the confusion that takes what is not real for real (பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும் மருள்). The two verses are built on the same sentence frame; 331 applies the misperception to duration and 351 to reality, and 351 adds the consequence, rebirth.
links.reason: நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும் (331) and பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும் (351) share the frame of misperception, applied to permanence and to reality.

links.note: 332 says great wealth (பெருஞ்செல்வம்) arrives and leaves like a theatre crowd, with no exception stated. 112 says the wealth of a person of rectitude does not decay and is a support to his descendants (சிதைவின்றி எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு உடைத்து). If 332 is read as a claim about all wealth, 112's durable wealth contradicts it; the conflict eases if 332 is taken, with Parimelazhagar, as wealth that stays only while its cause in good deeds lasts.
links.reason: பெருஞ்செல்வம் ... போக்கும் அதுவிளிந்தற்று stated without exception conflicts with ஆக்கஞ் சிதைவின்றி in 112 (Parimelazhagar: பிறர் செல்வம் போல அழிவு இன்றி); the note names the reading the conflict depends on.

links.note: 376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however it is guarded, and what is one's own will not go even if thrown out (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல ... சொரியினும் போகா தம). 332 says wealth comes and goes like a crowd at a show. 376 puts a cause behind 332's picture: coming and going follow one's allotted portion; Parimelazhagar reads 332 the same way, the crowd coming for the dance and leaving when it ends.
links.reason: 376 supplies a cause (பால்) rather than a limit, and its சொரியினும் போகா தம pulls against 332's wealth that leaves like a crowd; Parimelazhagar's gloss of 332 is only the dance-hall simile, not a reading by allotted portion as the note implies.

links.note: 332 likens the coming of great wealth to a crowd gathering at a dance hall and its going to that crowd dispersing. 592 says possession of goods does not stay and slips away (பொருளுடைமை நில்லாது நீங்கிவிடும்), while possession of inner drive is real possession. The impermanence of wealth taught to the renouncer is restated in the Book of Wealth, where it becomes a reason to value energy and not a reason to withdraw.
links.reason: பொருளுடைமை நில்லாது நீங்கிவிடும் restates 332's impermanence of பெருஞ்செல்வம், turned in Book 2 toward உள்ளம் உடைமை; cross-book pairing is instructive.

links.note: 437 says the wealth of the miser who does not do with it what should be done (செயற்பால செய்யாது) perishes without anything surviving. 333 says wealth does not stay and should be turned at once into what does. The Book of Wealth gives the same instruction negatively: unused wealth is simply lost.
links.reason: அற்கா இயல்பிற்றுச் செல்வம் ... அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல் and செயற்பால செய்யாது இவறியான் செல்வம் ... கெடும் give the same instruction positively and negatively.

links.note: 334 presents each day as a blade cutting life, with no one exempted. 326 says Death, the eater of life, does not advance on the days (வாழ்நாள்மேல் செல்லாது) of one who lives by not killing. Read literally, 326 exempts the non-killer from the daily loss of life that 334 treats as universal; the conflict depends on taking 326 as a promise about lifespan and not as praise of the vow.
links.reason: நாள் ... உயிர் ஈரும் வாள் states the loss as general, and வாழ்நாள்மேல் செல்லாது உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று read literally (as Parimelazhagar's long-life reading does) exempts the non-killer; the note names the reading.

links.note: 342 says if you want what renunciation brings, renounce while there is still something (உண்டாகத் துறக்க), which Parimelazhagar takes as 'while there is time'. 335 says to hurry to good deeds before the death rattle. On that reading the next chapter applies the same urgency to renouncing that 335 applies to good deeds.
links.reason: 335's விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன் ... மேற்சென்று செய்யப்படும் and 342's உண்டாகத் துறக்க share urgency on Parimelazhagar's காலம் பெறத் துறக்க; the note marks the dependence on that reading, which Manakkudavar does not share.

links.note: 336 says this world has the 'greatness' that one who was here yesterday is not here today (நெருநல் உளனொருவன் இன்றில்லை). 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except high renown (புகழல்லால் பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன்றில்). 233 agrees with 336 about everything else and names one exception; the renouncer's chapter offers none.
links.reason: நெருநல் உளனொருவன் இன்றில்லை states impermanence without exception, and புகழல்லால் பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன்றில் grants it but excepts fame.

links.note: 336 says a person who was yesterday is not today (இன்றில்லை). 235 speaks of a death that is really existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு), possible only for the skilled, which Parimelazhagar explains as the body of fame surviving. The two verses use the same pair, உள and இல், in opposite directions: 336 for the plain fact of death and 235 for the rare death that leaves something that is.
links.reason: 336 has the pair உளன்/இல்லை, but 235 has only உளதாகும் சாக்காடு (with அரிது), not இல், so 'the same pair in opposite directions' overstates. The thought link, plain ceasing versus a death in which fame remains, is real but rests on Parimelazhagar's புகழுடம்பு gloss.

links.note: 338 pictures the body as a குடம்பை, shell or nest, that the bird leaves empty; 340 pictures it as a lodging (துச்சில்) where life stays as a tenant without a home of its own (புக்கில்). Both make the body a dwelling and life its occupant. 338 shows the departure, and 340 asks why there has to be one; Manakkudavar takes the permanent home to be liberation.
links.reason: குடம்பை தனித்து ஒழியப் புள் பறந்தற்று and புக்கில் ... துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு both make the body a dwelling and life its occupant, in the same chapter; the note reads both correctly.

links.note: 339 presents death and birth as alternating like sleep and waking, which both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read as a cycle that keeps turning. 356 says those who have learned here and seen the true thing reach the path of not coming back here (மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி). 356 limits 339: the waking that follows each death is the rule only for those who have not seen the real.
links.reason: 339 உறங்கி விழிப்பது போலும் பிறப்பு gives rebirth as the recurring rule; 356 மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி names those exempt from it, a true limiting condition.

links.note: 341's doubled யாதனின் யாதனின் ... அதனின் அதனின் allows release thing by thing: each thing left stops hurting. 343 demands that everything wanted be let go together (வேண்டிய வெல்லாம் ஒருங்கு). Parimelazhagar notices the difference under 341, calling giving up everything at once the chief way while granting that giving things up one by one still removes the pain each brings.
links.reason: யாதனின் யாதனின் ... அதனின் அதனின் allows piecemeal release where வேண்டிய வெல்லாம் ஒருங்கு demands all at once; Parimelazhagar states exactly this under 341 (ஒருங்கே விடுதல் தலைமை ... ஒரோ ஒன்றாக விடினும்).

links.note: 341 says that whatever one has left (யாதனின் நீங்கியான்), from that one has no pain (நோதல் இலன்). 626, in the chapter on not being undone by trouble, asks whether those who never guarded wealth saying 'we have got it' (பெற்றேமென்று ஓம்புதல் தேற்றாதவர்) would grieve saying 'we have lost it' (அற்றேமென்று). The renouncer's rule reappears in the book of wealth as a habit of mind for someone who still owns things.
links.reason: யாதனின் நீங்கியான் நோதல் அதனின் இலன் and பெற்றேமென்று ஓம்புதல் தேற்றாதவர் ... அற்றேமென்று அல்லற்படுபவோ share the logic that non-attachment removes the pain of loss, once as renunciation and once as an owner's attitude.

links.note: 341 ties freedom from pain to having left the thing itself (நீங்கியான்). 629 says one who does not crave the pleasure in pleasure (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்) does not suffer the pain in pain; Parimelazhagar reads this as someone who goes on experiencing the pleasure without wanting it. The pairing shows the same result claimed for an inward letting go, without the outward leaving.
links.reason: 341 நீங்கியான் நோதல் ... இலன் and 629 இன்பம் விழையாதான் துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன் claim the same freedom from pain; Parimelazhagar's அனுபவியாநின்றே மனத்தான் விரும்பாதான் supports the inward reading the note gives.

links.note: 36 tells one to do virtue without saying 'we will see to it then' (அன்றறிவாம் என்னாது). 342's உண்டாகத் துறக்க is read by Parimelazhagar as 'renounce while there is time', i.e. in youth, so the joys last long; Manakkudavar instead reads it as 'if you want gain for your life'. On Parimelazhagar's reading the chapter on renunciation repeats, for renouncing, the earlier rule against postponing virtue.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does gloss உண்டாகத் துறக்க as காலம் பெறத் துறக்க (இளமைக்கண்), matching 36's அன்றறிவாம் என்னாது; the note flags Manakkudavar's different reading.

links.note: 46 asks what a person who runs household life by the way of virtue would gain by going to the outside way (புறத்தாற்றில் போஒய்ப் பெறுவது எவன்). 342 says that after renouncing there are many things to be had here, and urges renouncing if one wants them (வேண்டின் ... துறக்க). The conflict depends on reading புறத்தாறு as the ascetic path, as Pope does: on that reading 46's rhetorical 'what is gained?' gets the answer 'much' in 342.
links.reason: On the reading of புறத்தாறு as the ascetic way (Pope, and Parimelazhagar too), 46's போஒய்ப் பெறுவது எவன் is answered by 342's துறந்தபின் ஈண்டு இயற்பால பல; the note names the reading the conflict depends on.

links.note: 342 says that after renouncing, many things come about here (ஈண்டு இயற்பால பல), which Parimelazhagar takes as joys in this life. 369 says joy is unbroken even here (இன்பம் இடையறாது ஈண்டும்) once craving, the sorrow of sorrows, is gone. Both place the reward of letting go in this world (ஈண்டு), not only after death.
links.reason: 342 துறந்தபின் ஈண்டு இயற்பால பல and 369 இன்பம் இடையறாது ஈண்டும் both place the reward in this life with ஈண்டு; Parimelazhagar's 'joys in this life' gloss on 342 is as reported.

links.note: 6 describes God as the one who quenched the five whose gates are the senses (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்) and promises long life to those who keep to his path. 343 lays the same thing on the renouncer as a duty (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை). The renouncer is asked to do what the invocation names as the mark of the Lord.
links.reason: பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான் and அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை name the same conquest of the five, as mark of the Lord and as duty of the renouncer.

links.note: 126, in the householder's chapter on restraint, speaks of drawing in the five like a tortoise (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்), which protects through seven births. 343 uses a harder verb for the renouncer: the field of the five must be killed or crushed (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை), and every wanted thing dropped at once. Read together they show two degrees of the same discipline, withdrawal that can be reversed and destruction that cannot.
links.reason: ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல் and அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை treat the same five, with அடக்கல் in the householder's chapter and the harsher அடல் in the renouncer's.

links.note: 344 makes possessionlessness the nature of austerity. 263 asks whether the others have forgotten austerity out of a wish to provide for those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). The pairing shows that the ascetic's having nothing is sustained by householders who keep possessions in order to give.
links.reason: ஒன்று இன்மை as the nature of நோன்பு (344) is conditioned by 263's துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி, where others stay out of தவம் to supply renouncers.

links.note: 344 says having nothing at all is natural to the vow (இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கு ஒன்றின்மை) and that owning anything brings back confusion. 1036 says that if ploughmen fold their hands, even those who say 'we have given up what is desired' have no standing (விட்டேம் என்பார்க்கும் நிலை இல்லை). The renouncer's owning nothing rests on others who produce food.
