links.reason: 1036 விட்டேம் என்பார்க்கும் நிலை இல்லை if உழவினார் கைம்மடங்கின் does place a condition on the renouncer's ஒன்றின்மை of 344.

links.note: 344 treats having nothing (ஒன்றின்மை) as the proper state of the vow. 1050 speaks of those who have nothing to enjoy (துப்புரவில்லார்) and yet do not fully renounce (துவரத் துறவாமை), calling them death to salt and gruel. Lacking things is therefore not the same as renouncing: poverty without the inner giving up is counted as a burden, not as austerity.
links.reason: 1050's துவரத் துறவாமை of துப்புரவில்லார் does show that lacking things is not renunciation, but it does not limit 344's ஒன்று இன்மை, which concerns ascetics; the note's 'inner giving up' is Manakkudavar's reading only, as Parimelazhagar takes முற்றத் துறத்தல் as giving up the body too.

links.note: 73 says the bond of the precious life with the body (ஆருயிர்க்கு என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) is the way that came to be joined with love, so embodiment is given a purpose. 345 says that for those undertaking to cut off births (பிறப்பறுக்கல் உற்றார்க்கு) the body itself is excess and other ties (தொடர்ப்பாடு) pointless. The value 73 gives the body-bond holds within the life of love; 345 marks where, for the renouncer, it stops holding.
links.reason: என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு is given a purpose in அன்பு in 73, while 345 calls உடம்பும் மிகை and other தொடர்ப்பாடு pointless for பிறப்பறுக்கல் உற்றார்; the note limits 73's valuation correctly.

links.note: 345 says even the body is too much for one seeking to end birth. 627, in the book of wealth, says the great do not take trouble as trouble, knowing the body is a target for suffering (இலக்கம் உடம்பு இடும்பைக்கு). Both start from the body as a liability, but 627 uses that view to keep steady in worldly trouble while 345 uses it to argue for giving up every tie.
links.reason: உடம்பும் மிகை (345) and இலக்கம் உடம்பு இடும்பைக்கு (627) both treat the body as liability, put to ascetic and to worldly use respectively.

links.note: 50 says one who lives on earth as life should be lived will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (வானுறையும் தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப்படும்). 346 promises the one who ends 'I' and 'mine' a world higher than the gods' (வானோர்க்கு உயர்ந்த உலகம்). Set side by side the two verses give a scale: the good householder reaches the gods, the renouncer goes beyond them.
links.reason: வான்உறையும் தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப் படும் and வானோர்க்கு உயர்ந்த உலகம் புகும் set the householder among the gods and the renouncer above them, a real scale between the two chapters.
links.text_issue: 50 prints வான்உநற்யும் for வான்உறையும்.

links.note: 346 says one who cuts off the pride of saying 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods. 72 says the loveless keep everything for themselves (எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர்) while the loving belong to others even to their bones (என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு). The householder's love already loosens 'mine', and even the body as 'I', by giving it to others; renunciation does it by cutting the notion itself.
links.reason: 346 யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு அறுப்பான் and 72 தமக்குரியர் / என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு both concern giving up self-ownership, by renunciation and by love; the bridge is interpretive but stays within the Tamil.

links.note: 347 uses பற்று for attachment in general and says its holders are held by griefs. 438, on a ruler's faults, names miserliness as 'the clinging heart' (பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை) and says it is not to be counted with any other fault. The same word and the same refusal to let go appear in the domain of wealth, where Parimelazhagar glosses it as not releasing goods when they ought to be released.
links.reason: பற்றினைப் பற்றி விடாஅதவர் in 347 and பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை in 438 use the same word for not letting go, and Parimelazhagar does gloss 438 as பொருளை விடத்தகும் இடத்து விடாது பற்றுதல்.
links.text_issue: 347 has a stray space in தவர் க்கு.

links.note: 347 says griefs hold and do not let go of those who hold attachment and do not let go (பற்றினைப் பற்றி விடாஅதவர்க்கு). 940 says that as a gambler loves the game more with each loss, the life grows more fond with each suffering it undergoes (துன்பம் உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்); Parimelazhagar and Pope take the object of that fondness to be the body. 940 supplies what 347 leaves unexplained: suffering does not loosen the grip but tightens it.
links.reason: 347's பற்றி விடாஅ இடும்பைகள் for those who do not let go, and 940's துன்பம் உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர், fit as claim and mechanism: suffering tightens the clinging; the note correctly attributes 'body' to the commentators.

links.note: 348 sets those who have fully renounced above everyone else. 276 says none are harder-hearted than those who have not renounced in the heart (நெஞ்சின் துறவார்) and live by deceiving as though they had (துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து). The praise in 348 therefore applies to renunciation of the heart; the outward form without it is placed among the worst.
links.reason: 276's நெஞ்சின் துறவார் துறந்தார்போல் does contrast with 348's தீரத் துறந்தார், but 348 already carries its own condition in தீர, so little is qualified; and தலைப்பட்டார் means 'have attained (release)', not 'set above everyone else'.

links.note: 348 gives the prize only to those who renounce thoroughly (தீரத் துறந்தார்). 365 says those called 'freed' are those freed of craving, and the others are not freed in that way (மற்றையார் அற்றாக அற்றது இலர்), whatever else they have given up. 365 specifies what 348's 'thoroughly' requires: the giving up must reach craving, not only things.
links.reason: தீரத் துறந்தார் is specified by அற்றவர் என்பார் அவாஅற்றார் மற்றையார் அற்றாக அற்றது இலர்: thorough renunciation means being cut off from craving.

links.note: 361 says craving is the seed that yields unceasing birth for all beings (தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து). 349 says the moment attachment is cut off, that cuts off birth (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும்). One verse names the cause and the other states what follows when the cause is removed; Parimelazhagar makes the same cause-and-effect point under 349.
links.reason: தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து names the cause and பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும் its removal; Parimelazhagar on 349 does state the cause-and-effect rule.

links.note: 350 says to hold to the hold of the one who has none. 359 says that if one knows the support and lives so that supports perish (சார்புணர்ந்து சார்புகெட ஒழுகின்), the pains due to come will not come. The two are built alike on a repeated word, பற்று and சார்பு, and Parimelazhagar reads the சார்பு that is known as the true reality on which all rests, so 359 states the result of the practice 350 prescribes.
links.reason: பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை ... பற்று விடற்கு (350) and சார்புணர்ந்து சார்பு கெட ஒழுகின் ... சார்தரா சார்தரு நோய் (359) have the same shape of holding one thing so that holds fall away; Parimelazhagar's reading of சார்பு as the செம்பொருள் is correctly reported.

links.note: 351 says an inglorious birth comes from the delusion that takes what is not real for real (மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு). 1002 ends with the same words: the delusion of thinking everything comes by wealth, and so hoarding without giving, produces an inglorious birth. The book of wealth applies the metaphysical formula to one concrete error, treating money as the thing that matters.
links.reason: Both end மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு, and பொருளானாம் எல்லாமென்று in 1002 is a concrete case of பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும்.

links.note: 352 has darkness leave and joy arise for those who see truly. 243 says those whose hearts are joined with compassion do not enter the painful world joined with darkness (இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம்). 243's wording supports Parimelazhagar's reading of இருள் in 352 as a dark world of suffering, and shows the book promising escape from it by compassion as well as by knowledge.
links.reason: இருள் is escaped in both: 352 இருள்நீங்கி for மாசறு காட்சியவர், 243 இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம் புகல் இல்லை for அருள்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சினார்; knowledge and compassion as two routes is a fair reading.

links.note: 50 says one who lives on earth (வையத்துள்) as one should is placed among the gods who dwell in the sky. 353 uses the same pair, earth and sky (வையத்தின் வானம்), and says the sky is the nearer of the two for one who is clear of doubt. The householder gets there by right living and the knower by certainty, and in both the sky is brought within reach of someone still on earth.
links.reason: Both pair வையம் and வான்: 50 வையத்துள் வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன் வான்உறையும் தெய்வத்துள், 353 வையத்தின் வானம் நணியது; the sky is reached from earth by right living in one and by certainty in the other.
links.text_issue: 50: 'வான்உநற்யும்' is a typo for வான்உறையும்.

links.note: 353 says that for those who have left doubt and become clear (ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு) the sky is nearer than the earth. 702 says one who knows without doubt what is within another (ஐயப்படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானை) should be held equal to a god. In both, knowing free of doubt lifts a person toward the divine, once in the knowledge of reality and once in a courtier's reading of minds.
links.reason: ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு ... வானம் நணியது and ஐயப்படாஅது ... உணர்வானைத் தெய்வத்தோடொப்ப both tie doubt-free knowing to the divine, in different domains.

links.note: 2 asks what learning has achieved (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல்) if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge. 354 says command of the five senses has no benefit (பயமின்றே) for those without perception of the real. Both verses grant an attainment and then deny its fruit when the final step is missing, learning without worship in one and discipline without insight in the other.
links.reason: கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல் (2) and ஐயுணர்வு எய்தியக் கண்ணும் பயமின்றே (354) both grant an attainment and deny its பயன் when the last step is missing.

links.note: 126 says that drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is a protection for seven. 354 says the attained fivefold awareness yields no fruit without true perception; Parimelazhagar reads ஐயுணர்வு as the mind withdrawn from the senses and held under control, and the missing fruit as release, while Manakkudavar reads it as knowing all that the five senses can know. On Parimelazhagar's reading sense-restraint earns protection across births, as 126 says, but not the end of birth.
links.reason: On Parimelazhagar's reading of 'ஐயுணர்வு எய்தியக் கண்ணும் பயமின்றே' (senses withdrawn and mastered), 354 limits what 126 'ஐந்தடக்கல் ... எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து' can deliver; the note states that dependence and gives Manakkudavar's different reading.

links.note: 355 makes seeing the true thing the definition of understanding. 857 says those of bitter understanding who hold to hostility do not see the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காணார்); Parimelazhagar takes it there as the substance of the texts on right policy that bring success. The same phrase marks, in the book of wealth, what a mind bent on quarrel cannot perceive.
links.reason: The phrase 'மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு' (355) recurs negatively in 'மெய்ப்பொருள் காணார்... இன்னா அறிவினவர்' (857); Parimelazhagar's 'வெற்றி பொருந்துதலையுடைய நீதி நூற்பொருள்' is cited correctly.

links.note: 398 says the learning acquired in one birth protects through seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). 356 says those who have learned here and seen the true thing (கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார்) reach the path of not coming back here (மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி). Learning in the book of wealth is an asset carried across births; learning that ends in seeing the real is said to end the births themselves.
links.reason: கற்ற கல்வி ... எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து carries learning across births, and கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார் ... மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி has learning end them.

links.note: 356 speaks of those who learn and see the true thing; 357 adds the mind's own work: if the mind examines and knows with certainty what is (ஓர்த்து ... உள்ளது உணரின் ஒருதலையா), one need not think of birth again. Parimelazhagar reads the two as successive means, hearing instruction in 356 and reasoned examination in 357. The printed text here has உணரான், but Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's glosses read உணரின், which the sense requires.
links.reason: 356's கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார் is followed by 357's ஓர்த்து ... உள்ளது உணரின்; Parimelazhagar labels them கேள்வி and விமரிசம் in sequence, as the note says.
links.text_issue: 357 prints உணரான்; both commentaries gloss உணரின், which the sense needs.

links.note: 351 says a joyless birth comes from the delusion (மருள்) that takes the unreal for real. 358 goes a step further and calls birth itself a folly (பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை); Parimelazhagar explains this as naming the effect in place of its cause. The chapter moves from delusion as the cause of birth to birth and delusion spoken of as one thing, removed together by seeing the real.
links.reason: 351 'மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு' gives delusion as cause of birth; 358 'பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை' fuses the two, which Parimelazhagar explains as effect named for cause.

links.note: 358 speaks of 'the folly called birth' departing when the real is seen. 835, in the chapter on folly in the book of wealth, says a fool can in one birth's doing make the mire he will sink into for seven (எழுமையும் தான்புக் கழுந்தும் அளறு). Both tie பேதைமை to the chain of births, 358 as its root and 835 through the fool's deeds.
links.reason: Both verses have பேதைமை/பேதை and mention births, but 358's பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை is metaphysical ignorance as the cause of birth while 835's பேதை is an ordinary fool earning hell by deeds; the link is a shared word plus a shared backdrop.

links.note: 5 says the two kinds of deed do not attach (சேரா) to those devoted to the Lord's praise. 359 says the pains due to attach will not attach (சார்தரா சார்தரு நோய்) to one who knows the support and lives so that supports perish; Parimelazhagar takes these as the fruits of stored deeds still awaiting experience, and Manakkudavar takes சார்பு itself as the hold of deeds. Devotion in 5 and knowledge with practice in 359 are credited with the same effect on karma.
links.reason: சேரா (5) and சார்தரா சார்தரு நோய் (359) both deny that karmic consequence attaches; Manakkudavar's 'சார்பு - வினைச் சார்பு' supports the karma reading, and the devotion/knowledge contrast is real.

links.note: 347 says griefs hold and do not let go of those who hold on to attachment. 359 gives the other case: for one who knows the support and lives so that supports fall away (சார்புகெட ஒழுகின்), the pains that were due do not come to cling. 347 states the bondage and 359 the way out, in the same language of things that cling.
links.reason: 347's பற்றி விடாஅ இடும்பைகள் states the bondage and 359's சார்பு கெட ஒழுகின் ... சார்தரா சார்தரு நோய் the release, both in terms of clinging.

links.note: 360 says pain perishes when desire, anger and confusion perish down to their names (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் ... நாமம் கெட); Parimelazhagar glosses the three as wanting, aversion and ignorance. 4 describes God as the one without wanting or not-wanting (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்) and says those who reach his feet have no suffering. The state 360 sets as the goal is the nature 4 gives to the Lord, with the same result, the end of suffering.
links.reason: காமம் வெகுளி answer வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை, and both end in the loss of suffering (கெடும் நோய், இடும்பை இல). The state sought in 360 matches the nature 4 gives the Lord.
links.text_issue: 360 reads இநவ்முன்றன் for இவைமூன்றன்.

links.note: 360 lists desire, anger and confusion as what must perish for pain to end. 431 lists three faults whose absence gives a ruler's prosperity its dignity: arrogance, anger and smallness (செருக்கும் சினமும் சிறுமையும்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as pride, anger and lust. A similar triad, sharing anger and, on that gloss, desire, is the obstacle to release in one book and to good rule in the other.
links.reason: காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் and செருக்குஞ் சினமும் சிறுமையும் are both triads with anger; Parimelazhagar's gloss of சிறுமை as காமம் is cited correctly, and the note limits the overlap to that gloss.
links.text_issue: 360: இநவ்முன்றன் is a typo for இவைமூன்றன்.

links.note: 34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்து அறன்). 364 defines purity as the absence of craving (அவாவின்மை). Taken together, 364 names the stain that 34 leaves unnamed.
links.reason: மாசிலன் (34) and தூஉய்மை என்பது அவாவின்மை (364) do connect, but 34's stain is not 'left unnamed': the next verse lists அழுக்காறு அவா வெகுளி இன்னாச்சொல், and Parimelazhagar reads 364's தூஉய்மை as வீடு, not purity of mind.

links.note: 275 warns that the hidden conduct of those who say 'we are free of attachment' (பற்றற்றேம் என்பார்) brings many harms. 365 says who may rightly be called freed (அற்றவர் என்பார்): only those freed of craving. 275 shows the claim made falsely; 365 gives the inner criterion that the claim has to meet.
links.reason: பற்றற்றேம் என்பார் (275, the false claim) and அற்றவர் என்பார் அவாஅற்றார் (365, the criterion) fit as claim and test.

links.note: 35 defines virtue as what proceeds without slipping into four things, one of which is craving (அழுக்காறு அவா வெகுளி இன்னாச்சொல்). 366 says craving is what deceives a person (வஞ்சிப்பது அவா), and that fearing it is itself virtue (அஞ்சுவதோரும் அறனே). 366 takes one item from the list in 35 and gives the reason for singling it out: it works by deceit, so it needs constant watch.
links.reason: 35 lists அவா among the four that virtue avoids; 366 singles it out with வஞ்சிப்பதோரும் அவா and அஞ்சுவதோரும் அறனே, giving a reason for the watch.

links.note: 428 says fearing what should be feared is the work of the knowing (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில்) and leaves the object open. 366 names an object, craving, and calls the fear of it virtue (அஞ்சுவதோரும் அறனே). The general rule about right fear in the book of statecraft gets a specific content in the renouncer's chapter.
links.reason: 428 'அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில்' leaves the object open; 366 'அஞ்சுவதோரும் அறனே ... அவா' fills it with craving.

links.note: Fear and craving appear together in both verses with opposite roles. In 1075 fear is the whole conduct of the base (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம்), with a little more if there is something they crave (அவாவுண்டேல்); Parimelazhagar takes the fear as fear of punishment. In 366 fear is directed at craving itself and is called virtue. The pairing separates fear that serves craving from fear that guards against it.
links.reason: அச்சம் and அவா do occur together in both, but in 1075 they are two separate motives for whatever ஆசாரம் the base show (அச்சமே ... எச்சம் அவாவுண்டேல்), not 'fear that serves craving', and a co-occurrence of two common ideas is thin as a shared image.

links.note: 266 says those who do austerity do their own work, and the others, caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு). 367 says that if craving is cut off thoroughly, the deed that does not fail (தவாவினை) comes in the way one wishes. They state the same link from opposite sides: desire makes action futile, and its removal makes action unfailing.
links.reason: ஆசையுட் பட்டு அவஞ்செய்வார் and அவாவினை அறுப்பின் தவாவினை வரும் are converse statements linking desire to futile or unfailing action; Manakkudavar's கேடில்லாத வினை supports the reading of தவாவினை, though Parimelazhagar takes it more narrowly as the deeds that prevent perishing.

links.note: 309 says all that one has thought of is reached at once if one does not think of anger in the heart (உள்ளியதெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்). 367 says the unfailing deed comes as one wishes (தான் வேண்டுமாற்றான் வரும்) once craving is cut. Each verse removes one passion, anger or craving, and promises that what one intends then arrives.
links.reason: உள்ளான் வெகுளி எனின் உள்ளியதெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும் and அவாவினை ஆற்ற அறுப்பின் ... தான்வேண்டு மாற்றான் வரும் share the same conditional promise for removing a passion.

links.note: 341 says a person has no pain from each thing he has left (யாதனின் யாதனின் நீங்கியான் நோதல் அதனின் அதனின் இலன்), taking objects one by one. 368 says those without craving have no sorrow at all (அவாஇல்லார்க்கு இல்லாகுந் துன்பம்). 368 moves from the objects given up to the craving behind them, so the relief is complete instead of item by item.
links.reason: 341's யாதனின் யாதனின் நீங்கியான் ... அதனின் அதனின் இலன் is item-by-item relief; 368's அவாஇல்லார்க்கு இல்லாகுந் துன்பம் removes the root craving, so the step from objects to அவா is real.

links.note: 347 says sorrows hold and do not let go of those who hold attachment and do not let go (பற்றி விடாஅ இடும்பைகள்). 368 says that where craving exists sorrow keeps coming without fail, one after another (தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும்). Both describe suffering as continuing for as long as its cause is kept.
links.reason: பற்றி விடாஅ இடும்பைகள் for those who do not let go of பற்று, and துன்பம் தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும் while அவா exists: the same claim in adjoining renunciation chapters.

links.note: 628, in the chapter on not being undone by trouble, says one who does not desire pleasure (இன்பம் விழையான்) and calls hardship natural does not come to sorrow (துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்). 368 says those without craving have no sorrow. The renouncer's doctrine reappears as practical advice for a person at work in the world, where Parimelazhagar relates it to the pains of effort.
links.reason: அவாஇல்லார்க்கு இல்லாகுந் துன்பம் and இன்பம் விழையான் ... துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன் share the logic in two settings; Parimelazhagar does gloss 628 with வினையால் இடும்பை and தன் முயற்சியால் துன்பமுறான்.

links.note: The two verses share one sentence frame. 369: joy is unbroken if the sorrow of sorrows called craving perishes (அவாவென்னும் துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்). 854: it yields the joy of joys if the sorrow of sorrows called hostility perishes (இகலென்னும் துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்). The same title, sorrow of sorrows, is given to craving in the book of virtue and to hostility in the book of statecraft, each as the worst thing in its own field.
links.reason: The frame X என்னும் துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின் is identical, with அவா in one and இகல் in the other, each yielding இன்பம்.

links.note: 370 says that giving up craving gives, in that very state (அந்நிலையே), a nature that does not shift (பேரா இயற்கை). 349 says the moment attachment ends (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே) it cuts off birth. Both make the result immediate on the cause ending, with no further step between.
links.reason: அந்நிலையே பேரா இயற்கை தரும் and பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும் both stress immediacy with the emphatic ஏ; same claim in adjacent renunciation chapters.

links.note: 370 says craving has a nature that is never filled (ஆரா இயற்கை அவா). 940 gives a picture of that: as the gambler loves the game more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும்), a living being's love grows with each suffering (துன்பம் உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்); Parimelazhagar takes this as love of the body. 940 shows why satisfying craving cannot end it, which is why 370 says it has to be given up.
links.reason: 940 இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் / துன்பம் உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று says attachment grows with loss and suffering; it says nothing about satisfying craving, so it does not show why ஆரா இயற்கை அவா cannot be filled. The likeness is a self-feeding attachment.

links.note: 617 says the dark goddess of misfortune lives in sloth (மடியுளாள் மாமுகடி) and the lotus goddess lives in the effort of the one without sloth. 371 says sloth (மடி) and its opposite are themselves produced by the fate of loss and the fate of gain. In 617 fortune depends on whether one is slothful; 371 adds that whether one is slothful depends on fate.
links.reason: 617 lodges fortune in மடி versus தாள்; 371 says மடி and அசைவின்மை themselves arise from போகூழ் and ஆகூழ், a real condition on 617.

links.note: 371 says tireless effort arises from a fate of gain and sloth arises from a fate of loss (போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). 618 says lacking good fortune (பொறியின்மை) is no one's disgrace, but lacking effort after learning what should be known is a disgrace (ஆள்வினை இன்மை பழி). If sloth itself is produced by fate, as 371 says on a plain reading, the line 618 draws between blameless fortune and blameworthy idleness is hard to hold.
links.reason: 371 போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி makes sloth a product of fate, while 618 calls பொறியின்மை blameless and ஆள்வினை இன்மை பழி; on the plain reading of 371 the two cannot both hold, and the note names that reading.

links.note: 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) meet no affliction that shakes them. 372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish (பேதைப் படுக்கும் இழவூழ்); Parimelazhagar adds that this happens even to one who has understanding. The protection 429 promises rests on understanding, and 372 says understanding itself can be taken away by fate.
links.reason: 429 rests safety on எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவு, while 372's பேதைப் படுக்கும் இழவூழ் (Parimelazhagar: எல்லா அறிவும் உளவாயினும்) lets fate remove that very understanding; a genuine limit.

links.note: 372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish and a fate of gain, when it arrives, widens understanding (அறிவகற்றும் ஆகலூழ் உற்றக் கடை). 859 says that when gain is coming a person does not look at hostility (இகல்காணான் ஆக்கம் வருங்கால்), and to bring ruin on himself he looks to excel at it. In both, approaching gain or ruin shows first as a change in the person's own judgement.
links.reason: பேதைப் படுக்கும் இழவூழ் / அறிவகற்றும் ஆகலூழ் and இகல்காணான் ஆக்கம் வருங்கால் / மிகல்காணும் கேடு தரற்கு both show coming gain or ruin as a change in the person's own judgement.

links.note: 823 says that even after learning many good things it is hard for the unworthy to become good in heart (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்தும் மனநல்லர் ஆகுதல் மாணார்க்கு அரிது); Parimelazhagar applies this to enemies. 373 says that after much study a person's own understanding still prevails. The same limit on what books can change is stated once for understanding and once for the heart.
links.reason: 373 நூல்பல கற்பினும் ... உண்மை யறிவே மிகும் and 823 பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்தும் மனநல்லர் ஆகுதல் ... அரிது state the same limit on learning for understanding and for the heart; Parimelazhagar does apply 823 to பகைவர்.

links.note: 169 says the prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright are things to be pondered (நினைக்கப்படும்), and gives no answer; Parimelazhagar says the wise look for the earlier deed behind it. 374 notes a like mismatch between wealth and understanding and gives it as the two-fold nature of the world. One verse separates wealth from goodness and the other separates it from wisdom.
links.reason: 169 'அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கமும் செவ்வியான் கேடும்' and 374 'திருவேறு தெள்ளியராதலும் வேறு' both register fortune parting from desert, one against goodness and one against understanding.

links.note: 374 states as a general fact that wealth and clear understanding are separate lots. 408 judges one result of that: wealth lodged with the unlearned is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு). 408 takes for granted the mismatch that 374 explains.
links.reason: 374's திருவேறு தெள்ளியராதலும் வேறு explains the mismatch that 408 judges in கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு against நல்லார்கண் பட்ட வறுமை.

links.note: 483 asks whether anything is hard for one who acts with the right means and knowing the time (கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து செயின்). 375 says that in making wealth all that is good turns bad and bad turns good (நல்லவை எல்லாஅந் தீயவாம்); Parimelazhagar takes the good and bad things to be time, place, means and action, reversed by fate. On that reading the favourable conditions 483 relies on do not secure the result, and the two conflict. Kalaignar reads 375 differently, as good and bad deeds turning out contrary to intent.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does take 375's நல்லவை / தீயவை as காலம், இடன், கருவி, தொழில் reversed by ஊழ், which undercuts 483's கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து செயின்; the note states the reading and Kalaignar's alternative.

links.note: 376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however carefully it is guarded (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல), and what is one's own will not leave even if thrown out. 659 says all that is taken with others' tears leaves with tears, and what is of the good kind (நற்பாலவை) pays later even if lost. Both say some goods stay and some go whatever one does; 659 gives a test the person controls, the way the wealth was gained, where 376 gives only fate's allotment.
links.reason: பாலல்ல ... ஆகா / போகா தம and அழக்கொண்ட எல்லாம் அழப்போம் ... நற்பாலவை both say which goods stay and which go; 659 ties it to how they were gained, 376 to allotment. The shared பால் adds to the link.

links.note: 1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with crores piled up (அடுக்கிய கோடியுண்டாயினும் இல்), and treats this as the miser's own failing. 377 says even those who have gathered crores can enjoy them only as the apportioner has apportioned (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகையல்லால் ... துய்த்தல் அரிது). Both separate owning from enjoying; 377 places part of enjoyment outside the owner's choice, which limits the blame in 1005.
links.reason: Both have கோடி and துய்த்தல்: 1005 blames the one with கொடுப்பதூஉம் துய்ப்பதூஉம் இல்லார், while 377 வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகையல்லால் ... துய்த்தல் அரிது puts enjoyment partly beyond choice.

links.note: 344 says having nothing is natural to austerity (இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கொன்று இன்மை). 378 looks at those who already have nothing through poverty and says they would renounce, but for what fate makes them undergo. Parimelazhagar makes the connection: they have already lost what a renouncer gives up, and still suffer because their intent differs. Having nothing is the condition of austerity in 344, and 378 shows it is not enough by itself.
links.reason: 344 நோன்பிற்கு ஒன்று இன்மை இயல்பு makes having nothing the condition of austerity; 378 துறப்பார்மன் துப்புரவில்லார் shows the destitute still fail to renounce, and Parimelazhagar's கருத்து வேறுபாட்டால் is reported correctly.

links.note: 379 asks why those who see things as good when good comes should grieve (அல்லற்படுவது எவன்) when it does not. 626 asks whether those who never clutched at wealth saying 'we have got it' would grieve (அல்லற்படுபவோ) saying 'we have lost it'. Both are rhetorical questions with the same verb and the same symmetry between gain and loss. 626 adds the practical point that grief at loss depends on how one held the gain.
links.reason: அல்லற் படுவது எவன் and அல்லற் படுபவோ are rhetorical questions with the same verb and the same symmetry of gain and loss (நன்றாங்கால் / அன்றாங்கால்; பெற்றேம் / அற்றேம்).

links.note: 380 says fate is the strongest thing and gets ahead of any plan. 619 grants that a thing may not come about because of fate (தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும்), and adds that effort still pays the wage of the body's labour (மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி தரும்). 619 accepts the limit that 380 states and marks out what remains for effort within it.
links.reason: தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும் concedes the limit of ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள, and மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி தரும் marks what effort still earns within it.

links.note: 391 treats right conduct as what should follow flawless learning. 823, on false friends, says that even after studying many good things (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்தும்) it is hard for the unworthy (மாணார்) to become good at heart. It limits 391: study does not by itself produce the standing-by-it, which is why 391 has to command it separately.
links.reason: 391 commands கற்றபின் நிற்க அதற்குத் தக, and 823 says பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்தும் மனநல்லர் ஆகுதல் மாணார்க்கு அரிது, so learning does not by itself yield the conduct; the note's 'unworthy' follows Manakkudavar, Parimelazhagar taking மாணார் as enemies.

links.note: 391 asks for two things in order: learn without flaw (கசடறக் கற்க), then stand in keeping with it (நிற்க அதற்குத் தக). 834 names the person who does the first and skips the second: one who has studied, understood and even taught others but is not himself restrained (தானடங்கா) is the greatest of fools. The pair shows that the second half of 391 is not an afterthought: learning without it is classed as folly.
links.reason: நிற்க அதற்குத் தக is what ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் பிறர்க்குரைத்தும் தானடங்காப் பேதை fails to do; 834 shows the second half of 391 is essential.

links.note: 392 makes numbers and letters the eyes of the living. 445 says a king goes about with his counsellors as his eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக) and so must choose them with care. Both treat sight as something acquired from outside oneself, through learning in one case and through chosen advisers in the other.
links.reason: கண்ணென்ப in 392 and சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக in 445 both make the eye something supplied from outside the person; the shared figure is meaningful.

links.note: 393 denies real eyes to the unlearned. 418 says ears not pierced by listening (கேள்வியால் தோட்கப்படாத செவி) are of a deaf kind even though they hear. The next chapter repeats the pattern for the other sense: an organ counts only when it has been trained by learning or listening.
links.reason: முகத்திரண்டு புண்ணுடையர் கல்லாதவர் (393) and கேட்பினுங் கேளாத் தகையவே ... தோட்கப்படாத செவி (418): the same pattern, an untrained organ does not count, for eye and ear.

links.note: 394 describes the learned as people whose company others want again after it ends. 643 defines speech as what binds those who heard it and makes even those who did not hear want it (கேளாரும் வேட்ப). 643 gives the means, speech, for the effect 394 describes.
links.reason: உவப்பத் தலைக்கூடி உள்ளப் பிரிதல் and கேளாரும் வேட்ப மொழிவது both describe leaving others wanting more, but 394 does not mention speech and 643 is not about the learned; calling 643 the 'means' for 394 is the note's inference.

links.note: 394 says the work of the learned is to meet so that others are glad and to part so that others think of them (உள்ளப் பிரிதல்). 839 says, ironically, that friendship with fools is very sweet because parting from them (பிரிவின்கண்) brings no pain at all. Both judge a person by what the parting leaves behind; the fool is the case where it leaves nothing.
links.reason: உள்ளப் பிரிதல் (394) and பிரிவின்கண் பீழை தருவதொன்றில் (839) both measure a person by what parting leaves, with 839 as the ironic null case.

links.note: 395 praises learning in the stance of one who lacks before one who has. 724 tells even the learned to state what they have learned before the learned and take more from those who know more (மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்). The asking stance of 395 is thus not only for beginners; it continues among the learned.
links.reason: 395's ஏக்கற்றுங் கற்றார் and 724's மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல் both have the learner taking from those who have more, and 724 carries it into the assembly of the already learned.

links.note: 395 uses the poor standing before the rich (உடையார்முன் இல்லார்போல்) as its figure for the learner, and on Parimelazhagar's reading those who learned standing so are foremost while those who would not are lowest. 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking (இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்), even asking water for a cow. Read together, the posture the book calls degrading when the object is goods is the one it honours when the object is learning.
links.reason: 395 honours standing உடையார்முன் இல்லார்போல் to learn, while 1066 says இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்; the note is accurate that the same posture is valued differently by its object.

links.note: 397 says that for the learned any land is one's land and any town one's town (யாதானும் நாடாம் ஊராம்). 753 says the unfailing lamp called wealth goes to whatever country one has in mind (எண்ணிய தேயத்துச் சென்று) and cuts away the darkness there. Learning and wealth are each credited with making foreign places open to a person.
links.reason: யாதானும் நாடாமால் ஊராமால் and எண்ணிய தேயத்துச் சென்று both give a human good reach across lands. In 753 it is the wealth that travels and cuts இருள் (enmity, per Parimelazhagar), so 'open to a person' is a little loose.

links.note: 399 assumes the learned person's learning gives the world joy. 650 says those who cannot unfold what they have learned so that others grasp it (கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்) are like a cluster of flowers in bloom without scent. It adds the condition 399 leaves unstated: the world's delight depends on being able to convey the learning.
links.reason: உலகு இன்புறக் கண்டு in 399 assumes learning reaches the world, and 650 makes that depend on கற்றது உணர விரித்துரைத்தல்; a fair condition added from another chapter.
links.text_issue: 650's first word is printed இண்ருழ்த்தும், a typo for இணரூழ்த்தும்.

links.note: 400 gives the title of real wealth to learning. 241 gives it to grace (அருட்செல்வம் செல்வத்துள் செல்வம்), with the reason that wealth of goods is found even among the base. The same move appears in the Book of Virtue with a different winner, and 241's reason, who can hold it, differs from 400's, whether it can be lost.
links.reason: 400 கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் கல்வி and 241 அருட்செல்வம் செல்வத்துள் செல்வம் make the same 'true wealth' move with different winners and different reasons (பூரியார் கண்ணும் உள vs கேடில்).

links.note: 400 says learning is the imperishable, excellent wealth and other things are not wealth (மாடல்ல மற்றையவை). 411 says the wealth of the ear is the wealth among wealths and the head of them all (செல்வத்துளெல்லாம் தலை). Adjacent chapters use the same 'true wealth' figure for study and then for listening, without ranking the two against each other.
links.reason: கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் கல்வி and செல்வத்துட் செல்வம் செவிச்செல்வம் apply the same true-wealth figure to study and listening in adjacent chapters.

links.note: 401 says holding forth in an assembly without full book-learning (நிரம்பிய நூலின்றிக் கோட்டி கொளல்) is like playing dice without a marked board. 728 says those who have learned many things are still of no use if they cannot speak well and tellingly in a good assembly. Together they give both halves: speech without learning has nothing to stand on, and learning without speech yields nothing.
links.reason: The complement is real (401 நிரம்பிய நூலின்றிக் கோட்டி கொளல்; 728 பல்லவை கற்றும் ... செலச்சொல்லாதார்), but both are in the one domain of speaking in the assembly and they give converse halves, not one pattern carried to a new domain.

links.note: 402 compares the unlearned man's desire to speak (சொற்காமுறுதல், as Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read it) to a woman without breasts desiring womanhood. 727 compares the learning of one who fears the assembly to a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி among enemies. Both use a figure of lacking what one's role requires, and they cover the two opposite failures: wanting to speak without learning, and having learning without the nerve to speak. Kalaignar reads 402 differently, as desiring to hear the unlearned man's words.
links.reason: முலையிரண்டும் இல்லாதாள் and பேடிகை ஒள்வாள் are both figures of lacking what the role needs, for speech without learning and learning without nerve; the note flags the divergent reading of சொற்காமுறுதல்.

links.note: 403 says even the unlearned are very good if they can keep from speaking before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 715 says the best of all good things is the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு). 715 turns the rule 403 gives the unlearned into a general virtue of the assembly that binds capable speakers too.
links.reason: கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின் for the unlearned becomes முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு as the best of good qualities for anyone in an assembly.

links.note: 403 counts silence before the learned as the unlearned person's merit. 729 says those who have studied and understood yet fear an assembly of the good are lower than the unlearned (கல்லாதவரின் கடை). Silence is therefore not good in itself: it is right for the one with nothing to say and a failing in the one who has something.
links.reason: கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின் makes silence the unlearned person's merit, while கற்றறிந்தும் நல்லாரவை அஞ்சுவார் are கல்லாதவரின் கடை, so the value of silence depends on who is silent.

links.note: 404 says that however good an unlearned person's brightness (ஒட்பம்) may be, those with understanding do not accept it. 423 says understanding is seeing the true substance of a thing from whoever's mouth it is heard (யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும்). If 404 means the wise set aside what the unlearned say even when it is good, it conflicts with 423's rule to judge the matter and not the speaker; on Parimelazhagar's reading, that they only decline to credit him with real brightness because an occasional hit is accidental, the conflict is smaller.
links.reason: கல்லாதான் ஒட்பம் ... கொள்ளார் அறிவுடையார் conflicts with யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும் ... மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது if கொள்ளார் means rejecting the content; the note names that reading and Parimelazhagar's softer one (ஒண்மையாகக் கொள்ளார்).

links.note: 404 says native brightness without learning is not accepted by the wise. 636 says nothing over-subtle can stand before those who have keen native intelligence together with book-learning (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்). 636 states positively what 404 implies: natural intelligence gains its force when joined to study.
links.reason: கல்லாதான் ஒட்பம் ... கொள்ளார் அறிவுடையார் (404) is completed by மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்க்கு (636): native sharpness counts when joined to learning.

links.note: 405 says an unlearned person's standing collapses once he converses. 717 says the learning of those who have studied and understood shines out (விளங்கும்) among those able to examine words without fault. Conversation with the competent is the test in both, with opposite results for the unlearned and the learned.
links.reason: தலைப்பெய்து சொல்லாட (405) and சொல்தெரிதல் வல்லார் அகத்து (717) are the same domain, learning tested in speech before the competent, so this is a complementary pair and not a pattern carried to a different domain.

links.note: 405 says the unlearned person's self-regard gives way when he engages and speaks (சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்); Parimelazhagar supplies that the talk is with a learned person. 1046 says that even when the poor speak of good matters well understood, their words go slack (சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்). The same closing phrase marks two ways speech fails: in 405 for want of learning in the speaker, in 1046 for want of standing with the hearers, though the content is sound.
links.reason: Both close on சோர்வு படும் for speech that fails, சொல்லாட in 405 and சொற்பொருள் in 1046. Parimelazhagar does supply கற்றவன் in 405, and the contrast of causes is accurate.

links.note: 406 grants the unlearned existence only and compares them to land that yields nothing (பயவாக் களர்). 572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a burden to the earth (உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை). Both reduce a person lacking a quality to mere existence and express it through land, as barren soil in one and as weight on the ground in the other.
links.reason: உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர் and அஃதிலார் உண்மை both reduce the person to bare existence, and each puts it through land (பயவாக் களர், நிலக்குப் பொறை). Parimelazhagar glosses both by uselessness to self and others.

links.note: 406 says the unlearned are no more than 'they exist' (உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர்) and are like barren saline ground that yields nothing. 730 says those who, fearing the arena, cannot convey what they have learned are, though they exist, equal to those who do not (உளரெனினும் இல்லாரொடு ஒப்பர்). The same bare-existence wording puts the learned who cannot speak in nearly the place of the unlearned.
links.reason: உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர் and உளரெனினும் இல்லாரொடு ஒப்பர்: the same bare-existence formula for the unlearned and for the learned who cannot speak.

links.note: 407 says good looks without understanding are worth what a clay doll's are. 667 says not to scorn anyone on seeing their form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை), since the great chariot has its small linchpin. Both deny that appearance measures a person, 407 for the handsome and empty, 667 for the slight and capable.
links.reason: எழில்நலம் of one without நுழைபுலம் is a மண்மாண் புனைபாவை (407); உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை வேண்டும் (667). Appearance fails as a measure in both directions.

links.note: 407 compares the good looks of one without fine, penetrating understanding to a well-decorated clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). 1020 compares the movements of those with no shame within to a wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை) made to seem alive by its string. Both use a doll for a human form missing its inner part, understanding in one and shame in the other.
links.reason: புனைபாவை and மரப்பாவை both picture a human form lacking an inner faculty (நுழைபுலம் இல்லான் / நாண் அகத்தில்லார்); the shared doll figure is meaningful.

links.note: 408 says wealth is worse than poverty when it sits with the unlearned (வறுமையின் இன்னாதே). 558 says having is more painful than not having (இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை) under a ruler who does no justice. Both invert the usual ranking of wealth over poverty under a stated condition: the holder's lack of learning in one, the king's injustice in the other.

links.text_issue: 408 has a stray space in 'பட் ட'; meaning is unaffected.

links.note: 408 says wealth lodged with the unlearned (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு) is more painful than poverty lodged with the good. 837 shows what happens when a fool gets great wealth: strangers feast and his own people go hungry. 837 gives one concrete form of the harm; Manakkudavar likewise reads 408 as harm done to others.
links.reason: கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு as worse than the good man's poverty is made concrete by ஏதிலார் ஆரத் தமர் பசிப்பர் பேதை பெருஞ்செல்வம் உற்றக்கடை. Manakkudavar's பிறர்க்கு இன்னாமை reading is as cited.

links.note: 409 says the unlearned, though born high, do not have the worth (பாடு) of the learned born low. 133 says having conduct is good family, and lapse from it becomes low birth (இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்). Both make birth give way to something acquired, learning in 409 and conduct in 133.
links.reason: மேற்பிறந்தாராயினும் கல்லாதார் ... பாடு இலர் and இழுக்கம் இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும் both subordinate birth to something acquired.

links.note: 410 says others stand to those who have studied the shining books as beasts stand to people (விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர்). 420 calls those who know taste by the mouth and not by the ear மாக்கள், and asks what it matters whether they die or live. The next chapter carries the comparison on, from those who have not studied to those who do not even listen.

links.note: 410 makes book-learning the difference between people and beasts. 1012 says food, clothing and the rest are no different for any living being, and that the distinction of human beings is having shame (நாணுடைமை மாந்தர் சிறப்பு). The two verses give different answers, learning and shame, to what sets humans apart.
links.reason: விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர் ... கற்றாரோடு ஏனையவர் and உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல / நாணுடைமை மாந்தர் சிறப்பு both mark off the human from other creatures, by learning in one and shame in the other.

Both deny full human standing to some who have the human shape, for lack of learning in one and for baseness in the other.
links.reason: விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர் and மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர் both withhold full human standing from people of human kind; 'though human in form' is not in 410's Tamil but is a harmless gloss.

links.note: 412 treats listening as food for the ear (செவிக்குணவு) and lets the stomach have a little (சிறிது) only when that food is absent. 420 turns the same ear-and-mouth pairing into a judgment: for those who know taste by the mouth and not by the ear (செவியிற் சுவையுணரா வாயுணர்வின் மாக்கள்), living and dying come to the same. The chapter's ranking of the two appetites starts as a rule for mealtimes and ends as a measure of a life.

links.note: 412 allows the stomach only a little (சிறிது), and Parimelazhagar explains the word by saying heavy eating multiplies disease and desire. 946, in the chapter on medicine, says well-being stays with the one who eats knowing to stop short (இழிவறிந்து உண்பான்) and disease with the heavy eater (கழிபேர் இரையான்). The same restraint at the table is asked for in the name of listening in one verse and in the name of health in the other.

links.note: 413 makes listeners equal to the oblation-fed (ஆன்றாரோடொப்பர்). 702 says one who knows without doubt what is inside another (அகத்தது உணர்வான்) should be taken as equal to a god (தெய்வத்தோடொப்பக் கொளல்). In both, a human being is ranked with the gods for a faculty of taking in what others carry: their teaching in one, their unspoken thought in the other.
links.reason: ஆன்றாரோடு ஒப்பர் and தெய்வத்தோடு ஒப்பக் கொளல் both rank a person with the gods for a receptive faculty, listening and reading minds.

links.note: 403 says even the unlearned are very good if they can keep from speaking before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 414 addresses the same person (கற்றிலனாயினும்) and tells him to listen (கேட்க). The silence that 403 only recommends as damage control becomes in 414 the means of gaining what he lacks.
links.reason: Both address the unlearned (கல்லாதவரும் / கற்றிலனாயினும்); 403 asks only for silence before the learned (சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்) and 414 turns that into listening (கேட்க) as ஊற்றாந் துணை.

links.note: 415 says the words from the mouth of those with conduct (ஒழுக்கமுடையார் வாய்ச்சொல்) are like a staff where the ground is slippery (இழுக்கல் உடையுழி). 139 says of the same people (ஒழுக்கமுடையவர்க்கு) that speaking evil with the mouth, even by a slip (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்), is not possible. 139 gives the reason 415 needs: those who do not slip in what they say are the ones whose words can steady someone who is slipping.
links.reason: ஒழுக்கமுடையார் வாய்ச்சொல் as ஊற்றுக்கோல் where there is இழுக்கல் (415), and ஒழுக்கமுடையவர்க்கு ஒல்லாவே ... வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல் (139): same people, mouth and slipping in both, and the reason the note draws is well grounded.

links.note: 415 presents the words of people of conduct as the staff that keeps a person upright on slippery ground. 447 asks who can ruin a ruler who keeps as his own those who will rebuke him (இடிக்குந் துணையார்). Both verses locate safety in another person's speech; 447 applies it to a king and makes the helpful words explicitly unwelcome ones.
links.reason: ஒழுக்கமுடையார் வாய்ச்சொல் as ஊற்றுக்கோல் and இடிக்குந் துணையார் whom none can கெடுக்கும் both place one's safety in another's speech, with 447 applying it to rulers and to rebuke.

links.note: 417 says well-grounded listeners do not speak folly even when they have misunderstood (பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும்). 139 says that for those who have conduct, speaking evil even by a slip (வழுக்கியும்) is not possible. The same guarantee, speech that holds even under error, is attached to listening in the Book of Wealth and to conduct in the Book of Virtue.
links.reason: பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும் பேதைமை சொல்லார் and வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல் ஒல்லாவே both promise speech that stays sound even in error, credited to கேள்வி and to ஒழுக்கம்.

links.note: 417 says those whose wide listening rests on their own close inquiry (இழைத்துணர்ந்து ஈண்டிய கேள்வியவர்) do not speak folly even when they have misunderstood (பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும் பேதைமை சொல்லார்). 199 says those of stainless vision, free of delusion (மருள்தீர்ந்த மாசறு காட்சியவர்), do not say empty things even in forgetfulness (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லார்). The two verses have the same shape, a kind of person whose speech stays sound even when the mind lapses, and they credit it to different sources: listening in one, clear vision in the other.
links.reason: பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும் பேதைமை சொல்லார் and பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லார் have the same shape, speech that stays sound through a lapse, credited to கேள்வி in one and மாசறு காட்சி in the other.

links.note: 418 denies real hearing to ears that listening has not opened. 577 says those without kindly regard have no eyes (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர்), and those who have eyes do not lack it. The form of argument is the same, an organ is counted as present only when it is used for its higher purpose, applied to instruction in 418 and to kindness in 577.
links.reason: கேட்பினுங் கேளாத் தகையவே ... செவி and கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர் use the same argument, that an organ not put to its higher use does not count as present, for ear and eye.

links.note: 95 says being humble and sweet-spoken (பணிவுடையன் இன்சொலன் ஆதல்) is a person's ornament, and nothing else is. 419 says a mouth that bows (வணங்கிய வாய்) is hard to come by without fine listening. 95 holds humble speech up for everyone, and 419 adds a condition: it has to be prepared for by listening.
links.reason: 95 பணிவுடையன் இன்சொலன் ஆதல் is held up for everyone; 419 வணங்கிய வாயினராதல் அரிது without நுணங்கிய கேள்வி adds a precondition.

links.note: 419 says humble speech is hardly to be had without fine listening. 844 defines வெண்மை, shallowness of understanding, as the conceit that says 'we have brightness' (ஒண்மை உடையம் யாம் என்னும் செருக்கு). The pair links lack of instruction and self-praise from both ends: 419 says the uninstructed will not speak humbly, and 844 says boasting of one's understanding is itself the mark of lacking it.
links.reason: வணங்கிய வாயினர் ஆதல் அரிது and ஒண்மை உடையம் யாம் என்னும் செருக்கு join lack of learning and self-praise from two sides; Parimelazhagar on 419 draws the same inference (தம்மை வியந்து கூறுவர்).

links.note: 420 treats those without the ear's taste as people whose death and life are the same. 214 says only one who knows what is fitting truly lives (உயிர்வாழ்வான்), and anyone else is counted among the dead (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). The book repeatedly denies real life to those who lack one defining quality; here the quality is listening, and in 214 it is knowing one's duty to others.
links.reason: அவியினும் வாழினும் என் (420) and செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும் (214) both treat a person lacking one quality, செவிச்சுவை or knowing ஒத்தது, as no different from the dead.
links.text_issue: 214 prints ஒத்த தறவோன்; the commentaries read ஒத்தது அறிவான், so தறவோன் looks like a typo for தறிவான்.

links.note: 406 says the unlearned can only be said to exist (உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர்) and are otherwise like saline ground that yields nothing (பயவாக் களர்). 420 says of those who have no taste for what the ear takes in that their dying or living makes no difference (அவியினும் வாழினும் என்). The chapters on not learning and on listening reach the same verdict, a life that merely exists; Manakkudavar reads 420, as Parimelazhagar reads 406, as about being of no use to others.
links.reason: உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர் ... பயவாக் களர் (406) and அவியினும் வாழினும் என் (420) reach the same verdict in adjacent chapters; Manakkudavar on 420 says பிறர்க்குப் பயன்படார், and Parimelazhagar on 406 says of use neither to self nor others.

links.note: 420 asks what it matters whether they die or live, those மாக்கள் who know taste by the mouth and not by the ear. 1012 says food, clothing and the rest are no different for all living beings (ஊணுடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல), and the distinction of மாந்தர் is having shame. Both verses treat eating as what humans share with every creature and put human worth elsewhere, in the ear's taste for one and in shame for the other.
links.reason: 420's வாயுணர்வின் மாக்கள் against செவியிற் சுவை and 1012's ஊணுடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல against மாந்தர் சிறப்பு both place human distinction above eating; 420 only implies the 'shared with creatures' point through மாக்கள், but that is a fair reading.

links.note: 421 names understanding as the tool that guards against ruin (அற்றங் காக்குங் கருவி). 781 asks what guard is as hard for hostile action to get past as friendship (வினைக்கரிய யாவுள காப்பு). The Book of Wealth offers two protections that are not walls or weapons, one within the person and one between persons, and praises each in the vocabulary of defence.
links.reason: அற்றங் காக்குங் கருவி / உள்ளழிக்கலாகா அரண் and வினைக்கரிய யாவுள காப்பு both describe a non-military good in defensive vocabulary.

links.note: 24 says one who guards the five with the goad called firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்) is a seed for the highest ground; the goad makes the senses elephants, as Parimelazhagar spells out. 422 gives understanding a similar job, not letting one go where one has gone (சென்ற இடத்தால் செலவிடா), which Parimelazhagar explains with a rider directing a horse. 422 goes a step past 24's holding back: it also sorts good from evil and steers toward the good.
links.reason: உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான் and சென்ற இடத்தால் செலவிடா ... நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது both picture a driver curbing a mount; Parimelazhagar's யானை and குதிரை ... வாதுவன் glosses are as the note says, and 422 adds the steering toward good.

links.note: 422 says understanding does not let one go wherever the mind has gone, but draws away from evil and directs toward good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது). 787 says friendship removes one from what ruins and sets one on the path (அழிவினவை நீக்கி ஆறுய்த்து). The two verses use the same pair of actions and the same verb of steering (உய்); what understanding does for a person from inside, the friend does from outside.
links.reason: தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது and அழிவினவை நீக்கி ஆறுய்த்து share the remove-then-steer pair and the verb உய்; inner faculty vs outer friend is apt.

links.note: 424 makes it part of understanding to put things so that hearers take them in easily. 650 says those who cannot lay out what they have learned so that others understand (கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்) are like a cluster of flowers in bloom with no scent. 650 gives the failure case of 424's first half: learning that cannot be conveyed is counted as lacking something essential. The first word of 650 is misprinted in this edition, though the image is clear from the commentary.
links.reason: எண்பொருளவாகச் செலச்சொல்லி as part of அறிவு, and கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார் as scentless blossom: 650 is the failure case of 424's first half, as stated.
links.text_issue: 650's first word இண்ருழ்த்தும் is a misprint for இணரூழ்த்தும்.

links.note: 424 says understanding sees the fine meaning in what others say (பிறர்வாய் நுண்பொருள்); Manakkudavar takes this as seeing what they mean without their spelling it out. 701 praises one who knows what is intended by looking, without its being said (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்). 701 carries the second half of 424 one step further, from reading what lies within words to reading what is never put into words.
links.reason: 424 பிறர்வாய் நுண்பொருள் காண்பது, which Manakkudavar glosses as அவர் சொல்லாமல் தானே காண்பது, leads on to 701 கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்.

links.note: 115 says loss and increase are not absent from life, and that not bending in the heart (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை) is the ornament of the worthy. Parimelazhagar records a second reading of 425, in which the opening and closing are expanding in wealth and shrinking in want. On that reading the two verses say the same thing, that a person should stay the same through gain and loss, one under the heading of fairness and the other of understanding.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does record the reading செல்வத்தில் மலர்தலும் நல்குரவில் கூம்பலும் இல்லது for 425, and on it the verse matches 115's கோடாமை through கேடும் பெருக்கமும். The note marks the dependence.

links.note: 425 says embracing the world is brightness (உலகம் தழீஇயது ஒட்பம்). 544 uses the same verb twice: the world stands embracing the feet (அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும் உலகு) of the king who rules embracing his people (குடிதழீஇ). In 544 the embrace is returned, which gives a concrete reason why 425 counts drawing the world close as intelligence. Parimelazhagar narrows 'the world' in 425 to the high-minded.
links.reason: தழீஇயது (425) and குடிதழீஇ / அடிதழீஇ (544) share the embrace verb with the world as a party to it; the note also flags Parimelazhagar's narrowing of உலகம்.

links.note: 425 says understanding is what has neither opening nor closing (மலர்தலும் கூம்பலும் இல்லது), which Parimelazhagar reads as steadiness in friendship with the high-minded, unlike a pond flower that opens and shuts. 782 says the friendship of the wise fills like the crescent moon and that of fools shrinks like the moon after full. Both verses judge attachment by a natural cycle; 782 praises the bond that grows, while 425 asks for one that does not swing in either direction.
links.reason: மலர்தலும் கூம்பலும் இல்லது (steady, on Parimelazhagar's friendship reading) against பிறை நிறை நீர / மதிப் பின்னீர: both measure a bond by a natural cycle, and the note states the difference between them correctly.

links.note: 426 makes accord with the world part of what understanding is. 850 says one who says 'it is not' of what the world says is (உலகத்தார் உண்டென்பது இல்லென்பான்) will be set down as a demon on earth. 850, in the chapter on shallow understanding, extends 426 from conduct to belief and states the cost of breaking with the world's view.
links.reason: உலகத்தோடு அவ்வது உறைவது அறிவு is extended by உலகத்தார் உண்டென்பது இல்லென்பான் ... அலகையா வைக்கப்படும், from living with the world to assenting to it, with the cost stated.
links.text_issue: 426's Pope gloss is printed 'T o'; the Tamil is sound.

links.note: 427 makes knowing what is to come the mark of having understanding, as if it were a trait of the person. 372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish (பேதைப்படுக்கும் இழவூழ்) and a fate of gain, when it arrives, widens understanding (அறிவகற்றும் ஆகலூழ்). Read with 372, the division in 427 is not fixed: the same person may see ahead or fail to, depending on what fate is at work.
links.reason: ஆவது அறிவார் makes foresight the mark of the wise, and 372 says இழவூழ் makes even the knowing foolish (பேதைப் படுக்கும்), so the division in 427 is not fixed.

links.note: 427 defines those with understanding as those who know what is going to be (ஆவதறிவார்). 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is ahead (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that comes to shake them. 429 gives the use of the foresight that 427 only defines: knowing beforehand matters because it lets one guard beforehand.
links.reason: ஆவதறிவார் defines foresight and எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்க்கு இல்லை அதிர வருவதோர் நோய் gives its use, in the same chapter.

links.note: 427 separates the wise from the unwise by whether they know what will be (ஆவது). 461 tells one to act after weighing what will be lost, what will come of it (ஆவதூஉம்), and the gain that follows later. 461 turns the foresight of 427 into a procedure, a reckoning of outcomes made before acting.
links.reason: ஆவது அறிவார் in 427 is the capacity that 461 turns into a step before acting: அழிவதூஉம் ஆவதூஉம் ... ஊதியமும் சூழ்ந்து செயல்.

links.note: 428 makes fear of the right things the work of the knowing (அறிவார் தொழில்). 1075 says fear is the whole basis of proper behaviour among the base (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம்), which Parimelazhagar takes as fear of harm from the king. Together they show that fear in itself does not separate the wise from the low; what separates them is that the wise fear what deserves it and the base behave only for fear of being punished.
links.reason: 428 அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில் against 1075 அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம்: fear alone does not mark the wise, and Parimelazhagar's king's-punishment gloss is reported correctly.

links.note: 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is ahead have no affliction that comes to shake them (அதிர வருவதோர் நோய்). 435 says the life of one who does not guard before it comes (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்) perishes like a straw-heap before fire. They are the positive and negative statements of one rule; 435 stands in the chapter on faults, where Parimelazhagar supplies 'fault' as what comes, while 429 speaks of harm in general.
links.reason: 429 எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்க்கு இல்லை ... நோய் and 435 வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான் வாழ்க்கை ... கெடும் are positive and negative of guarding beforehand; the note rightly flags that 'fault' in 435 is supplied.

links.note: 429 credits freedom from shock to an understanding that guards against what is coming. 442 tells a ruler to cherish and keep those who can remove the trouble that has come and guard beforehand against what has not (உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும் பெற்றியார்). 442 shows that the foresight of 429 need not be the ruler's own: it can be secured by choosing the right people.
links.reason: 429 'எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்' is the foresight that 442 'உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும் பெற்றியார்ப் பேணிக் கொளல்' tells the ruler to secure in others.

links.note: 430 defines having by understanding: the wise have all, and the unwise have nothing whatever they own. 591 uses the same turn for energy of mind: it is what makes someone 'one who has' (உடையர் எனப்படுவது ஊக்கம்), and those without it do not really have what they have (உடையது உடையரோ). The book redefines possession in the same words for two different inner qualities.
links.reason: அறிவிலார் என்னுடையரேனும் இலர் and அஃதில்லார் உடையது உடையரோ redefine உடைமை by an inner quality in the same turn of phrase, for understanding and for energy.

links.note: 430 says those with understanding have everything, and those without it have nothing whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்). 841 says lack of understanding is the lack among lacks (அறிவின்மை இன்மையுள் இன்மை), and the world does not count other lack as lack. 841, opening the chapter on shallow understanding, restates 430 from the side of poverty.
links.reason: 430 'அறிவிலார் என்னுடைய ரேனும் இலர்' and 841 'அறிவின்மை இன்மையுள் இன்மை' are the same claim, restated in the later chapter in terms of want.

links.note: 431 lists செருக்கு first among the faults whose absence gives prosperity its dignity. 180 names a செருக்கு it approves of, 'வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு', the pride of not wanting, which yields victory (விறல் ஈனும்); Parimelazhagar there glosses the word as wealth. Read together they separate arrogance from a pride that consists in refusing to covet.
links.reason: செருக்கு is a fault to be absent in 431 and an approved quality in வேண்டாமை என்னுஞ் செருக்கு (180); Parimelazhagar's gloss செல்வம் there is cited correctly and the contrast is instructive.

links.note: 432 lists 'மாணா உவகை' among a ruler's faults; Parimelazhagar takes it as joy beyond measure. 531 says why such joy is dangerous: the slackness that comes from the elation of great joy (சிறந்த உவகை மகிழ்ச்சியிற் சோர்வு) is worse than excessive anger. 531 supplies the mechanism for the fault 432 only names.
links.reason: மாணா உவகை (Parimelazhagar: அளவிறந்த உவகை) is named as a fault in 432, and சிறந்த உவகை மகிழ்ச்சியிற் சோர்வு in 531 says how it harms.

links.note: 432 calls honour that has passed beyond the fine a fault in a ruler. 1028 says that for one raising his family, idling and minding his மானம் brings ruin (மடிசெய்து மானங் கருதக் கெடும்). Both treat a misplaced sense of honour as a fault, one in the king and one in the head of a house.
links.reason: மாண்பிறந்த மானம் is a fault in the king and மடிசெய்து மானங் கருதக் கெடும் ruins the house; both fault a misplaced sense of honour. Manakkudavar construes 1028 differently, but the Tamil supports the note.

links.note: 433 describes how those ashamed of blame weigh a small fault of their own. 957 says a fault in the well-born shows up raised high, like the spot on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து). 957 adds the public side: in a person of standing a small fault is seen large by others too.
links.reason: 433 has the blame-fearing magnify their own fault ('தினைத்துணை... பனைத்துணையாக் கொள்வர்'); 957 has others see a well-born person's fault raised high ('மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து'): inward and public sides of the same magnification.

links.note: 433 says the blame-fearing treat a millet-sized fault as palmyra-sized. 965 says even people like a hill are diminished if they do a lowering thing the size of a குன்றி seed. 965 gives the outward fact, that a tiny act does lower the great, which makes the inward magnifying in 433 an accurate estimate and not an exaggeration.
links.reason: தினைத்துணை ... பனைத்துணையாக் கொள்வர் and குன்றின் அனையாரும் குன்றுவர் ... குன்றி அனைய செயின்: the same small-seed-to-great scale, inward estimate and outward fact.

links.note: 434 says fault itself is the enemy that brings ruin. 304 asks whether there is any other enemy (பகையும் உளவோ பிற) than anger, which kills laughter and joy. 304 applies to one named fault the claim 434 makes of fault in general: the real enemy is inside.
links.reason: குற்றமே அற்றந் தரூஉம் பகை and சினத்தின் பகையும் உளவோ பிற both name an inner fault as the enemy. 304 is the particular case of 434's general claim.
links.text_issue: 434 reads த்ரூஉம் for தரூஉம்.

links.note: 435: the life of one who doesn't guard before it comes (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்) perishes like straw before fire. 535: one who slipped by not guarding beforehand (முன்னுறக் காவாது இழுக்கியான்) will later grieve over his own error. The same failure is given two outcomes, sudden destruction in 435 and late regret in 535.
links.reason: வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான் and முன்னுறக் காவாது இழுக்கியான் name the same failure, with கெடும் and பின்னூறு இரங்கிவிடும் as its two outcomes.

links.note: 437: the wealth of one who clings to it without doing what should be done with it (செயற்பால செய்யாது இவறியான்) perishes without lasting. 228 asks whether the hard-eyed who keep what they have and lose it (வைத்திழக்கும்) don't know the joy of giving. Both assume hoarded wealth is lost anyway; 228 adds what the hoarder missed in the meantime.
links.reason: இவறியான் செல்வம் ... கெடும் and வைத்திழக்கும் வன்கணவர் both say hoarded wealth is lost; 228 adds ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம்.

links.note: 437 says wealth perishes when its owner does not do the things that ought to be done (செயற்பால செய்யாது ... கெடும்). 466 says one perishes by doing what is unfit and also by not doing what is fit (செய்தக்க செய்யாமை யானுங் கெடும்). The miser of 437 is a case of 466's second half: ruin by omission.
links.reason: செயற்பால செய்யாது ... கெடும் is a wealth-specific instance of செய்தக்க செய்யாமை யானுங் கெடும்; develops would fit equally well.

links.note: 437 says the miser's wealth perishes because he does not do what should be done with it; Parimelazhagar lists these as virtue, increase of wealth and enjoyment. 1006 says one who neither uses his wealth himself nor gives to the deserving (தான்துவ்வான் ... ஈதல் இயல்பிலாதான்) is an ஏதம், a harm, to great wealth. 1006 spells out the two uses left undone and turns the miser himself into the wealth's affliction.
links.reason: 437's செயற்பால செய்யாது இவறியான் is unpacked by 1006's தான்துவ்வான் ... ஈதல் இயல்பிலாதான், who is himself the ஏதம் to பெருஞ்செல்வம்; Parimelazhagar's list under 437 is cited correctly.

links.note: 432 lists இவறல் as one of three faults in a ruler, beside excessive honour and excessive joy. 438, on Parimelazhagar's reading, takes it out of any such list as greater than the rest (எற்றுள்ளும் எண்ணப்படுவதொன்று அன்று). Manakkudavar reads 438 differently, as saying miserliness is not to be valued as anything, and on that reading the two verses simply agree.
links.reason: 432 counts இவறல் among three ஏதம்; 438's எற்றுள்ளும் எண்ணப்படுவதொன்று அன்று, on Parimelazhagar's 'மிக்கது', sets it beyond the list. The note correctly states the dependence on that reading and Manakkudavar's alternative.

links.note: 438 says the miserliness called the clinging heart (பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை) is not to be counted among any others; Parimelazhagar takes this to mean it exceeds all other faults. 1002 names what lies behind it, the delusion (மருள்) that everything comes by wealth, so that one clings without giving (ஈயாது இவறும்), and gives its result as an inglorious birth. 1002 supplies a cause and a consequence for the fault 438 ranks.
links.reason: 438 ranks பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை above other faults; 1002 gives its root (பொருளானாம் எல்லாமென்று ... மருள்) and its result (மாணாப் பிறப்பு) using the same இவறு- word.

links.note: 439 commands: never admire yourself (வியவற்க எஞ்ஞான்றும் தன்னை). 474 gives the outcome for one who doesn't live in accord with others, doesn't know his measure and admires himself (தன்னை வியந்தான்): he perishes quickly. Parimelazhagar connects them in his note on 439, saying that self-admiration keeps one from knowing place, time and strength.
links.reason: 439 வியவற்க எஞ்ஞான்றும் தன்னை is given its consequence in 474 தன்னை வியந்தான் விரைந்து கெடும்; the citation of Parimelazhagar's note on 439 matches the commentary.

links.note: 439 ends 'நயவற்க நன்றி பயவா வினை', do not desire a deed that yields no good. 652 ends with the same phrase and extends it: one must always avoid a deed that yields neither renown nor good (புகழொடு நன்றி பயவா வினை). The rule is given in 439 as part of a ruler's guarding against faults and in 652, on Parimelazhagar's reading, as a rule for ministers.
links.reason: Both end on நன்றி பயவா வினை (நயவற்க / என்றும் ஒருவுதல் வேண்டும்), 652 adding புகழொடு; Parimelazhagar does address 652 to ministers.

links.note: 440: if a ruler can enjoy what he loves without the love being known (காதல் அறியாமை உய்க்கிற்பின்), his enemies' designs come to nothing. 866, from the enemy's side, says one of blinding anger and excessive desire (கழிபெருங் காமத்தான்) is an opponent whose enmity is worth having. Together they show the reasoning: a visible passion is an opening for an enemy, which Parimelazhagar states in his note on 440.
links.reason: காதல் அறியாமை உய்க்கிற்பின் ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல் and கழிபெருங் காமத்தான் பேணாமை பேணப்படும் are the two sides of exposed passion as an opening; Parimelazhagar on 440 (அறிந்தவழி அவை வாயிலாகப் புகுந்து) says so.

links.note: 441 tells a ruler to choose, after weighing, the friendship of those who know virtue and are mature in understanding (கேண்மை ... தேர்ந்து கொளல்). 795 tells anyone to examine and take the friendship (நட்பு ஆய்ந்து கொளல்) of those able to make one weep, to rebuke, and to teach the right way. The same instruction, to select friends for their capacity to guide, is given for the king's advisers and for ordinary friendship.
links.reason: Both end in the same instruction, கேண்மை ... தேர்ந்து கொளல் and நட்பு ஆய்ந்து கொளல், and both pick the friend for capacity to guide (அறனறிந்து மூத்த அறிவுடையார்; இடித்து வழக்கறிய வல்லார்), once for a king and once for anyone.
links.text_issue: 795 prints வல்லார்நடபு for வல்லார்நட்பு.

links.note: 435 says the life of one who does not guard before it comes will burn like straw. 442 tells the ruler to cherish and take as his own those whose nature is to remove the affliction that has come and to guard beforehand against what has not (உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும் பெற்றியார்). The foresight 435 demands of the ruler is, in 442, something he obtains through the people he keeps.
links.reason: வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான் is answered by உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும் பெற்றியார்ப் பேணிக் கொளல். The foresight 435 demands is obtained in 442 through the people one keeps.

links.note: 442 describes the people a ruler should keep: they remove the trouble that has come and guard in advance against more. 787 describes friendship in similar terms: it removes what leads to ruin (அழிவினவை நீக்கி), sets one on the path, and shares the suffering when ruin comes. The great adviser and the friend are given the same protective work, though 787 adds a sharing of suffering that 442 does not ask of the adviser.
links.reason: உற்றநோய் நீக்கி உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும் and அழிவினவை நீக்கி ஆறுய்த்து give adviser and friend the same protective work; the note correctly marks அல்லல் உழப்பது as extra in 787.

links.note: 443 calls winning the great as one's own the rarest of rare things (அரியவற்றுள் எல்லாம் அரிது). 781 asks what is as hard to make as friendship (செயற்கரிய யாவுள நட்பின்), and what guard is as hard for an enemy's work to get past. Both rank a bond with others as the hardest thing to obtain, and 781 adds that it is also the strongest protection, which is what chapter 45 goes on to claim for the great.
links.reason: அரியவற்றுள் எல்லாம் அரிது of winning the great and செயற்கரிய யாவுள நட்பின் both rank a bond as the hardest thing to get, and 781 adds காப்பு.

links.note: 444: to conduct oneself so that those greater than oneself are one's own is the chief of all strengths (வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை). 891: not slighting the power of the able is the chief of all the safeguards of those who guard themselves (போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை). The two verses use the same ranking formula for the two sides of dealing with the great, winning them as the highest strength and not offending them as the highest protection.
links.reason: வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை and போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை apply the same ranking formula to winning the பெரியார் and to not slighting ஆற்றுவார், in the paired chapters on the great.

links.note: 444 places the chief strength in attaching oneself to those greater than oneself; Parimelazhagar adds that this means following their lead. 985 says the strength of those who accomplish things is to bow (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பணிதல்). Both locate strength in deference and not in standing alone.
links.reason: 444 'தம்மிற் பெரியார் தமரா ஒழுகுதல் வன்மையுள் எல்லாந் தலை' and 985 'ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பணிதல்' both place strength in deferring to others; the 'following their lead' is credited to Parimelazhagar ('அவர் வழிநின்று').

links.note: 445 tells the ruler to choose his counsellors after deliberation (சூழ்வாரைச் சூழ்ந்து கொளல்), since they serve as his eyes. 462 says nothing is out of reach for those who act after considering a matter with chosen company (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி). Both put the selection of the people one deliberates with before the deliberation itself.
links.reason: சூழ்வாரைச் சூழ்ந்து கொளல் and தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி both make a chosen circle the precondition of deliberation.

links.note: 445 says a ruler proceeds with his counsellors as his eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக) and so must choose them with thought. 581 says a ruler should hold spies and the respected treatise as his eyes (மன்னவன் கண்). The king's 'eyes' are advisers in one verse and intelligence plus learning in the other, and in both he sees through something other than himself. This follows Parimelazhagar's reading of 445; Manakkudavar takes its second line differently.
links.reason: சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக and மன்னவன் கண் both make the king's eyes something outside himself; the note's caveat about Manakkudavar's different second line is correct.

links.note: 445 says counsellors must be chosen with care because the ruler sees by them. 639 states the cost of choosing badly: a minister at one's side who plots harm (பழுதெண்ணும் மந்திரி) is worse than seventy crore enemies. 639 shows what the care in 445 protects against.
links.reason: சூழ்வாரைச் சூழ்ந்து கொளல் because they are the king's eyes; பழுதெண்ணும் மந்திரி at one's side is worse than எழுபது கோடி foes. 639 gives the cost of failing 445.
links.text_issue: 639 prints பக்கததுள் for பக்கத்துள்; 445 prints சூழ்வாரைக் சூழ்ந்து.

links.note: 446 says enemies can do nothing against one who keeps the company of the worthy. 460 says there is no support greater than good company (நல்லினத்தின் ஊங்கும் துணையில்லை) and nothing that brings more affliction than bad company. 460 states as a general rule what 446 applies to a ruler facing enemies.
links.reason: 446 தக்காரினத்தனாய் ... செற்றார் செயக்கிடந்தது இல் is the particular case of 460 நல்லினத்தின் ஊங்கும் துணையில்லை.
