links.note: 446: against one who can conduct himself as having the worthy for his company (தக்கார் இனத்தனாய்), enemies have nothing left to do. 868 gives the reverse case: one with no good qualities and many faults is without company (இனன் இலன்), and that is a protection to his opponents. Both verses use the word இனம் and both make a ruler's exposure to enemies depend on who stands with him.
links.reason: தக்கார் இனத்தனாய் leaves enemies nothing to do, and இனனிலனாம் is மாற்றார்க்கு ஏமாப்பு: the same dependence on இனம், stated both ways.

links.note: 447 speaks of the ruler who keeps rebukers. 638 gives the matching duty of the one beside him: even if the king rejects knowledge and knows nothing himself, the one at his side is bound to tell him what is sound (உறுதி உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்). 638 extends the idea to the case where the king is not the willing listener 447 assumes.
links.reason: 447 'இடிக்குந் துணையாரை யாள்வாரை' is the ruler's side; 638 'அறிகொன்று அறியான் எனினும் உறுதி உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்' is the adviser's duty even to an unwilling king.

links.note: 447 values supporters for their rebuking (இடிக்கும்) and says a ruler who has them cannot be ruined. 784 defines friendship by the same act: it is not for laughing but for going ahead to rebuke when one oversteps (மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு). Rebuke is treated as the purpose of the bond in both statecraft and friendship.
links.reason: இடிக்குந் துணையார் and மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு use the same verb for what the ruler's support and the friend are valued for.
links.text_issue: 784 reads மேற்செனறு, a typo for மேற்சென்று.

links.note: 449 says there is no standing (நிலை) for those without the support of a prop (மதலையாம் சார்பு). 1030 says a family with no good person to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its base. The image of a structure that needs a prop is applied to a king in one verse and to a household in the other.
links.reason: மதலையாஞ் சார்பிலார்க் கில்லை நிலை and அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி வீழும் both use the prop that keeps a thing standing, for the king and for the family.
links.text_issue: 449 prints முதலிலார்க for முதலிலார்க்கு.

links.note: 450 says abandoning one's tie with the good (நல்லார் தொடர் கைவிடல்) is ten times worse than the enmity of many. 800 says to hold close the friendship of the stainless (மருவுக மாசற்றார் கேண்மை) and to be rid of the friendship of the unfit even at a price. 800 gives the same instruction for friendship and adds its other half, which bonds to drop.
links.reason: நல்லார் தொடர் கைவிடல் as tenfold harm and மருவுக மாசற்றார் கேண்மை give the same instruction to hold on to the good, with 800 adding ஒருவுக ஒப்பிலார் நட்பு.

links.note: 450 weighs losing the good against the enmity of many and finds it ten times worse. 816 weighs close friendship with a fool against being a stranger to the wise and finds the second ten million times better (கோடி உறும்). Both rank relationships by a multiplied comparison, and in both the quality of the person outweighs whether the relation is friendly or hostile.
links.reason: பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்து (450) and கோடி உறும் (816) both rank ties by a multiplied comparison in which who the person is counts more than whether the tie is friendly; ஏதின்மை as estrangement is a fair reading.

links.note: 873 says one who, being alone, takes on the enmity of many (பல்லார் பகை கொள்பவன்) is more wretched than the mad. 450 uses the same phrase as its measure: letting go the tie with the good is ten times worse than that (பல்லார் பகை கொளலிற் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்து). Read together, what 873 treats as an extreme of folly becomes the smaller of two harms in 450.
links.reason: The phrase பல்லார் பகை கொளல் / கொள்பவன் is shared; 873 makes it worse than madness and 450 makes it only a tenth (பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்து) of losing நல்லார் தொடர்.

links.note: 451 says greatness fears small company (சிற்றினம் அஞ்சும் பெருமை) while smallness takes it for kin. 201 says those given to evil deeds do not fear them but the excellent do (தீவினையார் அஞ்சார் விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்). In both, what marks the better person is fear of the thing the worse person is at ease with, once about company and once about deeds.
links.reason: 451 சிற்றினம் அஞ்சும் பெருமை and 201 விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர் both mark the better person by fear of what the worse (சிறுமை / தீவினையார்) is at ease with.

links.note: 452 says water takes the nature of the land, and understanding the nature of one's company (இனத்தியல்பு). 959 says the sprout shows what lay in the ground (நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால் காட்டும்) and speech shows the family one was born in. Both treat a person as carrying the mark of the ground they stand in, 452 for the company kept and 959 for birth.
links.reason: நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர் திரிந்து and நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால்காட்டும் both use the ground to figure what marks a person, இனம் in one and குலம் in the other; same_image would fit as well.

links.note: 452 uses water changing with the nature of the land it meets (நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர் திரிந்து) for understanding taking on the nature of one's company. In 1323 a lover calls the pair those joined as water with earth (நிலத்தொடு நீர் இயைந்தன்னார்), and Parimelazhagar explains that image by water taking on the land's nature. The same picture of water absorbed into soil is a caution about company in one place and a figure of union in the other.
links.reason: நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர் திரிந்து and நிலத்தொடு நீர் இயைந்தன்னார் share water joined to earth. Parimelazhagar explains 1323 by நீர் தான் நின்ற நிலத்தியல்பிற்றாமாறு, which is 452's figure.

links.note: 453 says perception comes from the mind, but the word that one is 'such a person' comes from one's company (இன்னான் எனப்படும் சொல் இனத்தான் ஆம்). 505 says the touchstone of greatness and smallness is each person's own deeds (தத்தம் கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as that and nothing else. If 453 is read as saying what a person really is, and not only what people call them, the two name different tests of character: company or deeds.
links.reason: 453 says explicitly இன்னான் எனப்படும் சொல், the name one is given, so the conflict needs a reading against that word; even then company shaping a person and கருமமே கட்டளைக்கல் as the test are compatible. A contrast of standards, not an incompatibility.

links.note: 298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truthfulness (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). 455 says purity of mind comes resting on purity of company. The book thus gives inner purity two supports, one's own truthfulness and the people one keeps.
links.reason: அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும் and மனந்தூய்மை ... இனந்தூய்மை தூவா வரும் give inner purity two distinct supports, as the note says.
links.text_issue: 298 prints புறள்தூய்மை for புறந்தூய்மை.

links.note: 456 says no deed fails to turn out well for those whose company is pure (இனந்தூயார்க்கு இல்லை நன்றாகா வினை), and Parimelazhagar gives the reason: their deeds are thought through with good company. 462 states that mechanism directly: nothing is hard to attain for those who act after examining the matter with chosen company (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி).
links.reason: 456: இனந்தூயார்க்கு இல்லை நன்றாகா வினை, and Parimelazhagar's reason (நல்லினத்தோடு எண்ணிச் செய்யப்படுதலின்) is reported accurately; 462 states that mechanism outright with தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணிச் செய்வார்க்கு.

links.note: 457 says goodness of mind gives gain (ஆக்கம்) and goodness of company gives all praise as well (இனநலம் எல்லாப் புகழும் தரும்). 651 has the same two-step form but says goodness of companions gives gain and goodness of action gives all that is wanted (துணைநலம் ஆக்கம் தரூஉம் வினைநலம் வேண்டிய எல்லாம் தரும்); Parimelazhagar there reads companions as giving wealth only. Company holds the higher place in 457 and the lower in 651, where one's own action outranks it.
links.reason: Both have the form X ... ஆக்கம், Y ... எல்லாம் தரும்; இனநலம் takes the higher slot in 457 and துணைநலம் the lower in 651 beneath வினைநலம். The reversal is real, granting that இனம் and துணை are near, not identical, terms.
links.text_issue: 651 reads த்ருஉம்; should be தரூஉம்.

links.note: 458 says that even for the worthy who have goodness of mind in full, goodness of company is a safeguard (ஏமாப்பு உடைத்து). 448 says a king without the guard of people who rebuke him (இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத ஏமரா மன்னன்) perishes even with no one to ruin him. Both use the same word for protection (ஏமம்), and 448 shows what the company protects against: one's own unchecked faults.
links.reason: இனநலம் ஏமாப்புடைத்து and ஏமரா மன்னன் use the same ஏமம் for the protection good company gives, and 448's கெடுப்பார் இலானும் கெடும் shows the danger is internal.

links.note: 243 says those whose hearts are joined to அருள் do not enter the dark world of pain (அருள் சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சினார்க்கு இல்லை இருள் சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம் புகல்). 459 agrees that the next world comes from goodness of mind (மனநலத்தின் ஆகும் மறுமை) and adds that even this is made secure by goodness of company. The afterlife that 243 rests on the heart alone is given a second support in 459.
links.reason: 243 rests escape from இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம் on the heart joined to அருள்; 459 grants மனநலத்தின் ஆகும் மறுமை and adds அஃதும் இனநலத்தின் ஏமாப்புடைத்து.

links.note: 460 is built on the form 'nothing beyond X as support, nothing beyond Y as affliction' (நல்லினத்தின் ஊங்கும் துணையில்லை). 32 uses the same form and the same word ஊங்கு for virtue: no gain beyond virtue, no ruin beyond forgetting it (அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கமும் இல்லை). The pairing shows good company being given, in the book on statecraft, the kind of unqualified ranking the opening chapters give to virtue.
links.reason: நல்லினத்தின் ஊங்கும் துணையில்லை ... அல்லற் படுப்பதூஉம் இல் follows the frame of அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கமும் இல்லை ... மறத்தலின் ஊங்கில்லை கேடு; same superlative-pair form with ஊங்கு.

links.note: 460 says there is no support greater than good company and nothing that afflicts more than bad company (தீயினத்தின் அல்லற் படுப்பதூஉம் இல்). 450 says letting go the tie with the good is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many (பல்லார் பகை கொளலிற் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்து). 460 names keeping bad company as the worst harm and 450 names losing good company; both rank these above open enemies, and Parimelazhagar glosses 460's second half as enmity.
links.reason: 460's தீயினத்தின் அல்லற் படுப்பதூஉம் இல் (Parimelazhagar: no greater பகை) and 450's பல்லார் பகை கொளலிற் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்து ... நல்லார் தொடர்கை விடல் give the two halves of one ranking, with the commentator's part marked as his.

links.note: 461 lists the outcomes to be weighed before acting: loss, gain and later yield. 471, opening the next chapter with the same imperative, lists the strengths to be weighed: of the deed, oneself, the opponent and the allies (வினைவலியும் தன்வலியும் மாற்றான் வலியும் துணைவலியும் தூக்கிச் செயல்). The second supplies what the first's calculation of gain and loss depends on.
links.reason: சூழ்ந்து செயல் (461) and தூக்கிச் செயல் (471) close on the same imperative at the head of adjacent chapters, outcomes in one and the four வலி in the other.

links.note: 461 tells one to weigh what will be lost, what will be gained and the later yield, and then act (அழிவதூஉம் ஆவதூஉம் ... ஊதியமும் சூழ்ந்து செயல்). 676 has the same closing command and also three items, but different ones: what it takes to finish, the obstacles, and the great yield at completion (முடிவும் இடையூறும் ... படுபயனும் பார்த்துச் செயல்). 461 is an account of cost and return; 676 keeps the return and adds the course of the work itself.
links.reason: Both are three-item checklists closing on செயல் (அழிவதூஉம் ஆவதூஉம் ... ஊதியமும் சூழ்ந்து / முடிவும் இடையூறும் ... படுபயனும் பார்த்து), and the note's account of the overlap and difference is exact.

links.note: 462 says nothing is hard to attain for those who act after examining a matter with chosen company and thinking it through themselves (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி). 568 gives the negative case: the fortune of a king who does not think matters through with his circle (இனத்தாற்றி எண்ணாத வேந்தன்) and then rages will shrink. Both make deliberation with one's இனம் the condition of success, stated once as promise and once as warning.
links.reason: 462 தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி and 568 இனத்தாற்றி எண்ணாத வேந்தன் state deliberation with one's இனம் as promise and warning; the note's reading of 568 matches Manakkudavar and is compatible with Parimelazhagar.

links.note: 463 says the wise do not undertake what loses the principal in hope of gain. 932 asks whether gamblers, who get one and lose a hundred (ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும் சூதர்), have any way of living well. The gambler is the plain case of the venture 463 rules out, a small gain pursued at the cost of what one already had.
links.reason: 463's ஆக்கம் கருதி முதலிழக்கும் செய்வினை is exactly what 932's ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும் சூதர் do; the gambler instantiates the rule.

links.note: 464 says those who fear the harm called disgrace do not begin what is not clear to them (தெளிவிலதனைத் தொடங்கார் ... அஞ்சுபவர்). 172 has the same form: those ashamed of unfairness do not do blameworthy things out of desire for the gain (பழிப்படுவ செய்யார் நடுவன்மை நாணுபவர்). In both a fear or shame is what holds a person back, in 172 from a wrong act and in 464 from an unexamined one.
links.reason: தொடங்கார் ... அஞ்சுபவர் (464) and செய்யார் ... நாணுபவர் (172) share a sentence shape found all over the Kural; fear or shame holding one back is too generic a pattern, and the acts restrained (unexamined, covetous) are unrelated.

links.note: 428 says not fearing what should be feared is folly and fearing it is the work of the knowing (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில்). 464 gives one such fear and what it does: fear of disgrace (இளிவென்னும் ஏதப்பாடு) keeps people from beginning what they have not made clear. The general rule of 428 is applied in 464 to the start of an undertaking.
links.reason: அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில் (428) is applied in 464 to இளிவென்னும் ஏதப்பாடு அஞ்சுபவர், who do not begin தெளிவிலதனை; a clear general-to-specific step.

links.note: 465 says rising without full deliberation (வகையறச் சூழாது எழுதல்) benefits the enemy. 473 says many who did not know their own strength pressed on in enthusiasm and broke midway (ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் பலர்). 473 names one of the things left unconsidered, one's own strength, and shows the cost to oneself where 465 shows the gain to the enemy.
links.reason: வகையறச் சூழாது எழுதல் is given a specific case in வலியறியார் ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார்.

links.note: 465 says setting out without thinking through every aspect is a way of setting one's enemies in a planting bed (பகைவரைப் பாத்திப் படுப்பது); Parimelazhagar reads this as establishing them in ground where they grow. 718 says speaking before those who understand is like pouring water into the bed of a growing plant (வளர்வதன் பாத்தியுள் நீர் சொரிந்தற்று). The same garden bed stands for fostering growth in both, wanted in 718 and brought on oneself in 465.
links.reason: பாத்திப் படுப்பது and பாத்தியுள் நீர் சொரிந்தற்று share the planting bed as the place of growth, unwanted in 465 and wanted in 718.

links.note: 465 pictures a rash attack as planting the enemy in a bed where he will grow. 879, in a chapter on enemies, says to cut a thorn tree while it is young, since when hardened it wounds the hand that cuts it (இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க). Both treat the enemy as a plant whose growth is the danger: 879 says to stop it early, 465 warns against tending it by one's own haste.
links.reason: பகைவரைப் பாத்திப் படுப்பது and இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க both figure the enemy as a plant whose growth is the danger; note describes both accurately.

links.note: 466 says one is ruined by doing what is not fit to do, and also by not doing what is fit (செய்தக்க செய்யாமை யானும் கெடும்). 510 says trusting someone unexamined and doubting someone already examined and trusted both bring unending trouble (தேரான் தெளிவும் தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்). Each verse sets an error of excess beside an error of defect and gives them the same result, once for action and once for trust.
links.reason: Each verse pairs two opposite errors with one result: செய்தக்க அல்ல செய / செய்தக்க செய்யாமை ... கெடும், and தேரான் தெளிவும் / தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும் ... இடும்பை. 'Excess and defect' is loose for commission and omission, but the pattern is the same.

links.note: 466 says both doing the unfit and leaving the fit undone bring ruin. 672 gives the same two-sided rule for timing: delay what should be done slowly, and do not delay what must be done without delay (தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால தூங்கற்க தூங்காது செய்யும் வினை). 672 carries 466's point, that holding back is no safer than acting, into the question of when to act.
links.reason: 466's two-sided செய்தக்க அல்ல செய / செய்தக்க செய்யாமை is matched by 672's தூங்குக / தூங்கற்க, where wrongly delaying is as much an error as wrongly hurrying; the note describes both accurately.

links.note: 467 fixes the order for action: think first, then resolve, and no thinking postponed until after. 509 fixes the same order for trusting people: trust no one without examining, and after examining, trust what is to be trusted (தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக). In both the examination belongs wholly before the commitment, and the commitment is then not to be reopened.
links.reason: எண்ணித் துணிக ... துணிந்தபின் எண்ணுவம் என்பது இழுக்கு and தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக have the same two-step shape, scrutiny before commitment and none after, for action and for trust.
links.text_issue: 509 prints தே றற்க with a stray space.

links.note: 616 says effort produces fortune and lack of effort brings want (முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும்). 468 says exertion that is not made by the right way (ஆற்றின் வருந்தா வருத்தம்) will give way even if many stand guarding it. 468 puts a condition on 616's praise of effort: it has to follow the proper method, and neither strain nor helpers make up for that.
links.reason: 616's முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும் is conditioned by 468's ஆற்றின் வருந்தா வருத்தம் ... பொத்துப் படும்: effort outside the right method fails even with helpers.

links.note: 468 says effort without the right method fails whatever support it has (பலர் நின்று போற்றினும் பொத்துப்படும்). 640 says those without practical capacity leave things unfinished even after planning them in proper order (முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே செய்வர் திறப்பாடு இலாதவர்). The two are complementary failures: effort without method in 468, and method on paper without the ability to carry it out in 640.
links.reason: Both are accurately read (ஆற்றின் வருந்தா வருத்தம் ... பொத்துப்படும்; முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே செய்வர் திறப்பாடு இலாதவர்), but both sit in the same domain of statecraft and action; 640 shows right method is not sufficient, which is a qualification, not a cross-domain parallel.

links.note: 469 says doing good can itself be a mistake if the character of the person is not taken into account. 987 asks what worth has achieved if it does not do what is sweet even to those who have done one harm (இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்), which makes the recipient's conduct irrelevant. The conflict holds if 469's நன்றாற்றல் is read as doing good in general, as Pope and Kalaignar take it; Parimelazhagar narrows it to a king's use of gifts and soft words toward other kings, and on that reading the two do not meet.
links.reason: On the general reading of நன்றாற்றல், அவரவர் பண்பறிந்து ஆற்றாக்கடை conflicts with இன்னாசெய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்தல்; the note states the reading and Parimelazhagar's narrowing.

links.note: 469 says there is error even in doing good when it is done without knowing each person's character (அவரவர் பண்பறிந்து ஆற்றாக்கடை). 1078 says the worthy are of use at a word, while the base, like sugar-cane, are of use only when crushed (சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர் சான்றோர் கரும்புபோல் கொல்லப் பயன்படும் கீழ்). 1078 is an instance of the difference in character 469 says must be known first: the approach that works on one kind of person does nothing with another.
links.reason: 469 is about doing good to people without knowing their பண்பு; 1078 is about what it takes to get anything out of the கீழ். That characters differ is common ground, but 1078 is not an application of 469's rule about benefaction.

links.note: 470 says to think and do what will not be scorned, because the world does not accept what does not accord with oneself (கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது உலகு). 140 says those who have not learned to conduct themselves in accord with the world lack understanding, however much they have studied (உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்). Both make the world's acceptance a test that sound judgement has to meet, 470 for a ruler's choice of action and 140 for conduct in general.
links.reason: கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது உலகு and உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல் both make fit with the world a test of judgement, for deliberate action and for conduct.

links.note: 470 tells the one who acts to avoid what the world will scorn and not accept. 280 tells the ascetic that neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if he gives up what the world has condemned (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின்); Parimelazhagar takes 'the world' there as the high-minded. The same measure, what the world rejects, governs a king's policy in one verse and a renouncer's conduct in the other.
links.reason: 470's கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது உலகு and 280's உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின் use the world's rejection as the measure for a king's method and an ascetic's conduct.

links.note: 471 makes comparing strengths the test of whether to act. 250, in the chapter on compassion, uses the same comparison as a brake: when going against those weaker than oneself (தன்னின் மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து), one should think of oneself before the stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). Being the stronger party permits action in 471, while 250 asks the stronger party to remember what that position feels like from below.
links.reason: 250's வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க ... மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து is advice on compassion, while 471's வலி ... தூக்கிச் செயல் is strategic weighing and grants the stronger no licence; the link rests mostly on the shared வலி and the note overstates what 471 permits.

links.note: 471 tells one to weigh four strengths before acting: of the deed, oneself, the opponent and the allies (வினைவலி, தன்வலி, மாற்றான் வலி, துணைவலி ... தூக்கிச் செயல்). 675 gives a second checklist with the same closing command, five things to think through until the darkness clears: resources, means, time, the deed and the place (பொருள் கருவி காலம் வினை இடன் ... எண்ணிச் செயல்). Read together, 471 measures the parties to a contest and 675 adds the circumstances of the act, and only the deed (வினை) is on both lists.
links.reason: Two checklists ending in the same command (தூக்கிச் செயல்; எண்ணிச் செயல்), with only வினை on both; the note's description of each list matches the Tamil.

links.note: 471 says to weigh one's own strength against the opponent's before acting (தன்வலியும் மாற்றான் வலியும் தூக்கிச் செயல்). 861 states what follows from that weighing when choosing an enemy: avoid opposing the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக) and pursue enmity with the weaker (மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). 861 is 471's comparison turned into a rule.
links.reason: தன்வலியும் மாற்றான் வலியும் தூக்கிச் செயல் yields 861's rule வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக ... மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை.

links.note: 472 says nothing fails for those who know what they can do and what must be known and proceed resting in that (ஒல்வது அறிவது அறிந்து ... செல்லாதது இல்). 462 says nothing is out of reach for those who act after examining the matter with chosen company and thinking it over themselves (தேர்ந்தெண்ணிச் செய்வார்க்கு அரும்பொருள் யாதொன்றும் இல்). The promise is the same in both and the condition differs: knowledge of one's own capacity in 472, counsel and deliberation in 462.
links.reason: What is shared is the closing formula (செல்லாதது இல்; அரும்பொருள் யாதொன்றும் இல்), while the conditions differ, as the note says. A common 'nothing is impossible' promise with different grounds is a thin, generic agreement.

links.note: 472 promises that nothing fails for one who knows his capacity (ஒல்வது அறிந்து ... செல்லாதது இல்). 483 asks whether anything is hard for one who acts with the means and knows the time (அருவினை என்ப உளவோ கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து செயின்). The chapters on knowing strength and knowing time each make the same claim for their own subject, which suggests each is meant as one necessary condition, not a sufficient one.
links.reason: செல்லாதது இல் for one who knows ஒல்வது (472) and அருவினை என்ப உளவோ for one who knows காலம் (483) make the same unlimited promise for strength and for time.

links.note: 594 says gain asks the way and goes to one whose ஊக்கம் does not waver (அசைவிலா ஊக்கமுடையான் உழை). 473 says many who did not know their own strength set out on ஊக்கம் and broke midway (வலியறியார் ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் பலர்). The same word names the quality praised in chapter 60 and the cause of failure here, so 473 limits 594: drive pays only when it is matched to a measured strength.
links.reason: ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் makes ஊக்கம் without வலியறிதல் the cause of breaking, limiting 594's அசைவிலா ஊக்கமுடையான்.
links.text_issue: 594 prints 'க்கம்' for ஆக்கம் (initial ஆ dropped).

links.note: 612 warns against letting a task perish in the middle of doing it (வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல்), because the world gives up on those who leave work unfinished. 473 describes how that happens: people start on enthusiasm without knowing their strength and break midway (இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார்). 612 demands finishing; 473 puts the remedy before the start, in measuring one's strength.
links.reason: 473's இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் are broken by a stronger opponent after misjudging their வலி, while 612's வினைகெடல் is slackening in a task (ஆள்வினை); 'unfinished work' is shared, but 473 does not describe how 612's failure happens.

links.note: 473 says many who did not know their strength broke midway (இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார்). 899 uses the same figure for a king: if those of exalted resolve are angered, even the king breaks midway and loses his kingship (இடைமுரிந்து வேந்தனும் வேந்து கெடும்). Parimelazhagar reads 473 as starting something against those stronger than oneself, and 899 gives one such case, a ruler who misjudges the power of the great.
links.reason: இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் (473) and இடைமுரிந்து வேந்தனும் வேந்து கெடும் (899) share the phrase of breaking midway, and 899 is a case of misjudging a stronger party. Parimelazhagar takes வேந்தன் in 899 as Indra, which the note does not mention but which does not affect the link.

links.note: 474 lists three failings that bring quick ruin: not living in accord (அமைந்தாங்கு ஒழுகான்), not knowing one's measure (அளவறியான்) and admiring oneself. 863 lists the traits of one who is easy for an enemy, and two of them match: he does not know (அறியான்) and does not fit in with others (அமைவிலன்). The chapter on what makes a good enemy to have describes, from the other side, the man 474 says will perish.
links.reason: 474 அமைந்தாங்கு ஒழுகான், அளவறியான் and 863 அமைவிலன், அறியான் overlap in wording and sense; the easy enemy of 863 is close to the man 474 says விரைந்து கெடும், though அறியான் is broader than அளவறியான்.

links.note: 474 says the one who admires himself (தன்னை வியந்தான்) perishes quickly. 978 uses the same phrase to define smallness: greatness always bows, and smallness adorns itself in self-admiration (சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). In 978 self-admiration is a mark of character, and in 474 it is a miscalculation of strength with a practical result.
links.reason: தன்னை வியந்தான் in 474 and தன்னை வியந்து in 978 are the same phrase, with a practical ruin (விரைந்து கெடும்) in one and a mark of சிறுமை in the other.

links.note: 475 says even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle if too many are piled on (பீலிபெய் சாகாடும் அச்சிறும்). 667 says not to scorn people for their appearance, since there are those who are like the linchpin of a great rolling chariot (உருள்பெருந்தேர்க்கு அச்சாணி அன்னார்). Both use the axle of a vehicle to say that size misleads: the light thing can break it and the small thing holds it.
links.reason: The shared item is அச்சு / அச்சாணி, but 475's point is cumulative overload (சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்), not that size or appearance misleads as in 667's உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை; the common lesson in the note is stretched.

links.note: 475 says a light load breaks the axle when there is too much of it (அப்பண்டம் சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்). Parimelazhagar takes the verse as an indirect statement that a strong king who makes enemies of many because each is weak loses his strength when they combine. 873 says this outright: one who, alone, takes on the enmity of many (தமியனாய்ப் பல்லார் பகைகொள்பவன்) is more foolish than the mad.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does read 475 as பிறிது மொழிதல் for one who makes enemies of many எளியர், and 873 தமியனாய்ப் பல்லார் பகைகொள்பவன் states that directly.

links.note: 475 says that feathers, light as they are, break an axle when piled too high. 889 says that enmity within, though as small as a split sesame seed (எட்பகவன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும்), has ruin in it. Both warn against judging a danger by the smallness of its unit, 475 because small things add up and 889 because of where the small thing sits.
links.reason: பீலிபெய் சாகாடும் அச்சிறும் (475) and எட்பகவன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும் ... கேடு (889) both warn that smallness of the unit is no measure of the danger; the note marks the difference in mechanism.

links.note: 596 says that whatever one thinks of, one should think of rising (உள்ளுவதெல்லாம் உயர்வுள்ளல்), and that even if this is thwarted it is as if it were not. 476 says that those who have climbed to the tip of a branch and push beyond it (அஃதிறந்து ஊக்கின்) end their lives. 596 sets no ceiling on aspiration, while 476 sets one on action: there is a point past which striving higher is fatal.
links.reason: உள்ளுவதெல்லாம் உயர்வுள்ளல் sets no ceiling on aim, while நுனிக்கொம்பர் ஏறினார் அஃதிறந்து ஊக்கின் உயிர்க்கிறுதி sets one on action; the note draws the limit accurately.

links.note: 476 says pushing on past the tip of the branch (இறந்து ஊக்கின்) ends one's life. 858 uses the same verb of hostility: leaning away from it is gain, and if one pushes on to excel in it (மிகல் ஊக்கின்), ruin pushes on in turn (ஊக்குமாம் கேடு). In both, the drive that the book elsewhere praises becomes the cause of ruin when it is carried past a limit.
links.reason: அஃதிறந்து ஊக்கின் and மிகலூக்கின் ஊக்குமாம் கேடு use the same verb for pushing past a limit into ruin.
links.text_issue: 858 reads மிக்லூக்கின், a typo for மிகலூக்கின்.

links.note: 477 says to give knowing the measure, for that is the way of guarding wealth while bestowing it (அளவறிந்து ஈக அது பொருள் போற்றி வழங்கு நெறி). 943 says to eat knowing the measure once the last meal is digested, for that is the way to carry the body far (அளவறிந்து உண்க அஃது உடம்பு பெற்றான் நெடிதுய்க்கும் ஆறு). The two verses have the same build, a command to know the measure followed by 'that is the way', applied to wealth in one and the body in the other. Both verses are printed with அறவறிந்து in this edition; the reading அளவு is from Parimelazhagar's gloss.
links.reason: Read with அளவறிந்து as the commentaries do, 'அளவறிந்து ஈக அது ... நெறி' and 'அளவறிந்து உண்க அஃது ... ஆறு' have the same build applied to wealth and to the body; the note flags the printed அறவறிந்து itself.
links.text_issue: Both 477 and 943 print அறவறிந்து where Parimelazhagar's gloss reads அளவு அறிந்து; likely a base-text typo in both.

links.note: 478 says a small income does no harm if spending does not exceed it. 463 says those with understanding do not undertake a deed that loses the capital for the sake of gain (ஆக்கம் கருதி முதலிழக்கும் செய்வினை ஊக்கார்). Both put keeping what one has ahead of getting more: 478 for the regular flow of income and spending, 463 for a single venture.
links.reason: 463 முதலிழக்கும் செய்வினை ஊக்கார் is about not risking capital; 478 போகாறு அகலாக் கடை is about outgo not exceeding income and says nothing of preferring keeping to gaining. Related prudence, not the same claim.

links.note: 512 says the work should go to one who widens the sources of income (வாரி பெருக்கி) and increases the yield. 478 says that even if the channel of income is narrow (ஆகாறு அளவிட்டிதாயினும்) there is no ruin, as long as the channel of outgo is not wider (போகாறு அகலாக்கடை). 512 values enlarging income, and 478 adds that safety depends on the relation between the two channels and not on the size of the first.
links.reason: 512 prizes வாரி பெருக்கி; 478 ஆகாறு அளவிட்டிதாயினுங் கேடில்லை போகாறு அகலாக் கடை adds that safety lies in the ratio of the two channels, a fair qualification.

links.note: 479 says the life of one who lives without knowing the measure (அளவறிந்து வாழாதான்) perishes. 947 says that one who eats a great deal without regard to the measure of his digestive fire (தீயளவன்றித் தெரியான் பெரிதுண்ணின்) gets disease without measure (நோய் அளவின்றிப் படும்). Ignoring a measure brings ruin of wealth in one verse and of health in the other. 479 is printed with a corrupted character in அளவறிந்து in this edition.
links.reason: அளவறிந்து வாழாதான் ... கெடும் and தீயளவன்றி ... நோய் அளவின்றிப் படும் apply the same ignored-measure logic to wealth and to eating.
links.text_issue: 479 is printed 'அளவற஧ந்து' for அளவறிந்து, as the note itself says.

links.note: 218 says those who see what is due do not slacken in ஒப்புரவு even in a time without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும் ஒப்புரவிற்கு ஒல்கார்). 480 says ஒப்புரவு that does not weigh the limit of one's means (உளவரை தூக்காத) quickly destroys those means. The Book of Virtue praises not letting scarcity stop one's helpfulness, and the Book of Wealth, speaking of a ruler's resources, makes the weighing of means a condition of it.
links.reason: Same word, opposite emphasis: இடனில் பருவத்தும் ஒப்புரவிற்கு ஒல்கார் (218) against உளவரை தூக்காத ஒப்புரவாண்மை வளவரை வல்லைக் கெடும் (480); 480 puts a condition on what 218 praises.

links.note: 481 says the crow beats the owl by day (பகல்வெல்லும் கூகையைக் காக்கை), and Parimelazhagar notes that the owl is the stronger bird. 500 says a jackal kills a fearless war elephant in mud where its feet sink (காலாழ் களரில் நரியடும்). In both a weaker animal defeats a stronger one through a circumstance, time in 481 and ground in 500, which is how the two adjacent chapters make their cases.
links.reason: காக்கை beats கூகை by பகல் (481), நரி kills களிறு in காலாழ் களர் (500): the weaker animal wins by time in one and by ground in the other.

links.note: 482 pictures fortune (திரு) as something that leaves unless tied, and names timely action as the rope (தீராமை ஆர்க்கும் கயிறு). 617 pictures her as living in the effort of the one without sloth (மடியிலான் தாளுளாள் தாமரையினாள்), with her dark elder sister living in sloth. Both treat fortune as a visitor kept by conduct, and they name different conduct: timing in 482, steady effort in 617.
links.reason: 482 ties திரு with a rope so she does not leave (தீராமை ஆர்க்குங் கயிறு); 617 has தாமரையினாள் dwell in the தாள் of the unslothful. Both personify fortune as kept by conduct, naming different conduct.
links.text_issue: 617 reads 'தாளுளான்', a typo for தாளுளாள்.

links.note: 482 says that acting in accord with the season (பருவத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்) is the rope that keeps fortune from leaving. 1028 says those who raise their family have no season (குடிசெய்வார்க்கு இல்லை பருவம்), and that idling and thinking of one's dignity ruins it. The two conflict if பருவம் in 1028 means the right moment for action; Parimelazhagar instead takes it there as seasons of heat, rain and cold used as an excuse to put work off, which removes the conflict.
links.reason: The shared word பருவம் is real, but 482 concerns a king timing action and 1028 says family-raisers must not wait on a season (மடிசெய்து ... கெடும்); that is different advice for different cases, and the note itself concedes Parimelazhagar's reading dissolves the conflict.

links.note: 483 names two conditions that make a hard deed possible, means and time (கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து). 675 lists five things to think through before acting: resources, means, time, the deed and the place (பொருள் கருவி காலம் வினை இடன்). 675 keeps 483's pair and sets it inside a fuller list.
links.reason: 483's pair 'கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து' reappears inside 675's five, 'பொருள் கருவி காலம் வினை இடனொடு ஐந்தும்'; the fuller list extends the earlier pair.

links.note: 484 says that even if one has the world in mind, it comes to hand when one considers the time and acts by the place (ஞாலம் கருதினும் கைகூடும் காலம் கருதி இடத்தாற் செயின்). 485 reverses the same words: those who have the world in mind wait, unshaken, considering the time (காலம் கருதி இருப்பர் கலங்காது ஞாலம் கருதுபவர்). 484 states the condition for acting and 485 its other side, that until the time comes the ambitious do not move.
links.reason: The words ஞாலம் கருது and காலம் கருதி are reversed between the two verses, one on acting at the time and one on waiting கலங்காது until it comes.

links.note: 484 says the world comes to hand if one considers the time and acts by the place (இடத்தாற் செயின்). 497, in the next chapter, uses the same phrase: one needs no support but fearlessness if one thinks everything through and acts by the place (எண்ணி இடத்தால் செயின்). 484 names place as a second condition beside time, and the following chapter, with 497, takes it up as its own subject.
links.reason: காலம் கருதி இடத்தாற் செயின் and எண்ணி இடத்தால் செயின் share the closing phrase, and the next chapter takes place up as its own subject.

links.note: 484 says a king who considers time and place can gain even the world (ஞாலம் கருதினும் கைகூடும்). 610 says a king without sloth gains at once all the expanse crossed by the one who measured with his foot (மடியிலா மன்னவன் எய்தும் அடியளந்தான் தாஅயதெல்லாம்). Both promise the whole earth, one to timing and the other to unremitting effort, so the two chapters make the same claim for different qualities.
links.reason: ஞாலம் கருதினும் கைகூடும் and எய்தும் அடியளந்தான் தாஅயதெல்லாம் both promise the whole earth, to காலம்/இடம் and to மடியின்மை.

links.note: 485 praises waiting for the right time. 671 says deliberation ends in reaching a resolve, and it is bad for that resolve to rest in delay (அத்துணிவு தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). 671 marks the limit of 485: waiting that is fixed on the time (காலம் கருதி) is part of the plan, and holding back after the decision, for no such reason, is a fault.
links.reason: 485 praises waiting காலம் கருதி; 671 faults a resolve that தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் after துணிவு is reached. 671 marks where purposeful waiting ends and delay begins.

links.note: 485 says those who aim at the world wait, unshaken, with their mind on the time (காலம் கருதி இருப்பர் கலங்காது). 672 says to take one's time over what should be done slowly (தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால) and not to delay what should be done without delay. Both treat waiting as a decision that fits some tasks, and 672 adds the second half that 485 leaves out.
links.reason: காலம் கருதி இருப்பர் கலங்காது and தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால both make deliberate waiting the right act for some undertakings; 672's தூங்கற்க half is noted as the addition.

links.note: 486 says the holding back of a person of energy is like a fighting ram stepping back in order to charge (பொருதகர் தாக்கற்குப் பேருந் தகைத்து). 827 says not to trust humble words from an enemy, because the bending of a bow means harm (வில்வணக்கம் தீங்கு குறித்தமையான்). Both use a drawing back that comes before a blow: 486 recommends it to oneself, and 827 teaches one to see it in an opponent.
links.reason: பொருதகர் தாக்கற்குப் பேருந் தகைத்து and வில்வணக்கம் தீங்கு குறித்தமையான் both use a drawing back that precedes a blow, from the actor's side and from the observer's.

links.note: 152 says always to bear with an excess done to one, and that forgetting it is better still (பொறுத்தல் இறப்பினை என்றும் அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). 487 says the bright do not flare up outwardly at once but, watching for the time, burn within (காலம் பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர்). Both hold back the outward response, and they differ on what happens inside: 152 wants the wrong forgotten, 487 wants the anger kept. The conflict holds if both are read as general advice; 152 belongs to the householder's virtues and Parimelazhagar takes 487 as addressed to kings facing enemies.
links.reason: 152 அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று against 487 காலம்பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர்: forget the wrong versus keep the anger within until the time comes. The note states the reading the conflict depends on and the differing addressees.

links.note: 301 says that the one who truly guards against anger guards it where it can take effect (செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான் சினங்காப்பான்); where it cannot, guarding or not makes no difference. 487 has the bright hold back anger now, when showing it would not serve, and keep it inside for the right time. On the reading that 487's anger is to be released when it can succeed, it describes the restraint that 301 says does not count, and withholds the one that does.
links.reason: 301 counts only restraint செல்லிடத்து; 487's ஒள்ளியவர் hold anger in (உள்வேர்ப்பர்) only until காலம், i.e. while it cannot succeed; the note names the reading the conflict depends on.

links.note: 151 says that bearing with those who scorn one, as the earth holds up those who dig into it (அகழ்வாரைத் தாங்கும் நிலம்போல), is the highest thing. 488 uses a verb of carrying for the same act, bearing with those who would harm one (சுமக்க), and makes it a means: one bears them until their end comes and their head goes down. The two conflict if both are read as answers to how one should treat those who wrong one, since forbearance is the goal in 151 and a way to the enemy's fall in 488. 151 is addressed to the householder and 488 to a king, which is the other way to read them.
links.reason: சுமக்க (till இறுவரை) and தாங்கும்/பொறுத்தல் are a real contrast of forbearance as tactic versus forbearance as தலை, but 488 advises a king awaiting his moment and 151 a person scorned, so this is different advice for different situations, as the note itself half-concedes.

links.note: 488 says to bear with enemies until their end comes (இறுவரை காணின்). 879 says to cut down a thorn tree while it is young, because once it has hardened it destroys the hand that cuts it (இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க ... காழ்த்த இடத்து). 879 limits 488's patience: waiting serves when time works against the enemy, and not when the enemy is growing stronger.
links.reason: செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க இறுவரை counsels waiting, and இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க ... காழ்த்த இடத்து limits it to cases where delay does not strengthen the enemy.

links.note: 26 says the great are those who do what is hard to do, and the small are those who cannot (செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர்). 489 uses the same phrase and adds a condition of time: hard deeds are to be done at the moment a rare opportunity arrives (செய்தற்கரிய செயல்). 26 places the ability in the person; 489 says it also depends on a moment that is itself hard to come by (எய்தற்கரியது).
links.reason: The link is the near-identical phrase செயற்கரிய / செய்தற்கரிய; 26 is about the greatness of renouncers and 489 about seizing a moment, so 489 does not extend 26's idea or add a condition to it.

links.note: 489 says that when what is hard to get has come, one should at that very point do what is hard to do (இயைந்தக்கால் அந்நிலையே செய்தற்கரிய செயல்). 333 says wealth has the nature of not staying, and that on getting it one should at once do what stays (அதுபெற்றால் அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்). Both reason from something that will not last, an opportunity in 489 and wealth in 333, to acting at once, and 333 turns the king's rule of timing toward lasting good.
links.reason: அந்நிலையே செய்தற்கரிய செயல் (489) and அதுபெற்றால் அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல் (333) share the same structure: a passing thing obtained, so act at once. Statecraft timing in one, impermanence and lasting good in the other.

links.note: 490 says to be like the heron in the season for folding up (கூம்பும் பருவத்து), and like its strike when the moment is right. 126 says that one who can draw in the five senses like a tortoise (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்) in one birth has protection for seven. Both teach restraint through an animal that draws itself in. The tortoise's withdrawal is the discipline itself, and the heron's is half of a pair that ends in a strike (குத்து).
links.reason: 'கொக்கொக்க கூம்பும் பருவத்து' and 'ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்' both teach restraint through an animal drawing itself in, and the note rightly marks that the heron's is tactical, ending in 'குத்து'.

links.note: 490 holds up the heron, which stays still until the moment and then strikes, as a model for acting on enemies. 274 says that doing wrong under cover of austerity is like a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds (புதல்மறைந்து வேட்டுவன் புள்சிமிழ்த்தற்று). The pattern of stillness that hides a coming strike is the same in both. It is recommended to the king waiting for his time, and it is the figure of fraud in one who wears the ascetic's appearance.
links.reason: 490 'கொக்கொக்க கூம்பும் பருவத்து ... குத்தொக்க' is restraint until the moment; 274 'புதல்மறைந்து வேட்டுவன் புள்சிமிழ்த்தற்று' is concealment behind a disguise ('தவமறைந்து'), not stillness. A lying-in-wait likeness exists, but 'the same pattern of stillness' overstates 274.

links.note: 464 says those who fear disgrace do not begin what is not clear to them (தெளிவு இலதனைத் தொடங்கார்). 491 gives the same ban on beginning (தொடங்கற்க எவ்வினையும்) a concrete test: until the place has been seen (இடங்கண்ட பின் அல்லது). Read together, knowing the ground is one specific form of the clarity 464 demands before any start.
links.reason: தெளிவிலதனைத் தொடங்கார் (464) and தொடங்கற்க ... இடங்கண்ட பின் அல்லது (491) share the ban on beginning; knowing the ground is a specific case of clarity (Parimelazhagar restricts 491 to a siege position, which does not undo this).

links.note: Parimelazhagar reads 491's முற்றும் இடம் as a place from which the enemy can be encircled, and tells the king neither to act nor to scorn the foe before finding one. 747 defines a fort from the other side as what cannot be taken even by encircling (முற்றியும் ... பற்றற்கு அரியது). The shared siege verb shows attacker and defender reasoning about the same ground; Manakkudavar instead reads 491 as 'the place where the task can be completed', which would loosen this link.
links.reason: On Parimelazhagar's reading முற்றும் இடம் in 491 is the siege verb of முற்றியும் in 747; the note states that Manakkudavar's 'complete' reading would loosen the link.

links.note: 492 says that even for those with fighting strength (முரண்சேர்ந்த மொய்ம்பினவர்க்கும்) the advantage of joining a fort (அரண்சேர்ந்தாம் ஆக்கம்) yields many gains. 741 says a fort is of value to those able to go on the offensive (ஆற்றுபவர்க்கும்) as well as to those who guard themselves in fear. Both deny that a fort is only for the weak: the chapter on place and the chapter on forts make the same point about the strong.
links.reason: The உம் in மொய்ம்பினவர்க்கும் (492) and ஆற்றுபவர்க்கும் (741) both extend the fort's value to the strong; the note reads both accurately.

links.note: 861 advises avoiding opposition to the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக) and pursuing enmity against the weaker. 493 says the weaker side can still become strong and win when it knows the ground and protects itself. 493 therefore sets a condition under which 861's rule about relative strength does not settle the outcome.
links.reason: 861's வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக is a rule from relative strength; 493's ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி அடுப ... இடனறிந்து gives the condition under which the weaker still win. Note matches both verses.

links.note: 493 says even those without strength win (ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி அடுப) if they know the place and act against foes while guarding themselves (போற்றிச் செயின்). 878 says the enemy's pride dies when one knows the way, builds oneself up and guards oneself (வகையறிந்து தற்செய்து தற்காப்ப). Self-guarding plus knowledge is the common recipe; 878 generalises 493's 'place' to knowing the way of acting.
links.reason: 493's இடனறிந்து ... போற்றிச் செயின் and 878's வகையறிந்து தற்செய்து தற்காப்ப share knowledge plus self-guarding as the means against foes; 'generalises' is a little loose but the common recipe is in the Tamil.

links.note: 494 says those who had planned (against you) lose their plan (எண்ணியார் எண்ணம் இழப்பர்) when you advance knowing the place and hold close to it. 440 says the enemies' scheme becomes void (ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல்) when a ruler enjoys what he loves without letting the love be known. In both, the opponent's design is defeated before any fight by removing what it relied on: bad ground in one case, a known weakness in the other.
links.reason: 494 எண்ணியார் எண்ணம் இழப்பர் and 440 ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல் both void the enemy's design in advance, by holding the right இடன் and by keeping one's காதல் unknown.

links.note: 495 shows a strong animal losing outside its own element: the crocodile out of water is killed by others. 500 gives the sharper case, where a jackal kills a fearless war elephant in mud where its feet sink (காலாழ் களரில் நரியடும்). Together they state both halves: one's own ground makes one win, and the wrong ground lets even a much weaker creature win.
links.reason: 495 புனலின் நீங்கின் அதனைப் பிற அடும் and 500 காலாழ் களரில் நரியடும் ... களிறு give the two halves of the same lesson on ground.

links.note: 496 says chariots with strong wheels do not run on the sea and sea-going ships do not run on land (கடலோடா ... நாவாயும் ஓடா நிலத்து); Manakkudavar takes it to mean that instruments must be made to suit the place. 675 lists means and place together (கருவி ... இடனொடு ஐந்தும்) among the five things to think through before acting. 496 shows why the two items in 675's list cannot be weighed separately: a tool is only a tool in its own medium.
links.reason: 496 'கடலோடா ... நெடுந்தேர் ... நாவாயும் ஓடா நிலத்து' illustrates why 'கருவி' and 'இடன்' in 675 go together; Manakkudavar's 'இடத்திற்கான கருவி' is reported accurately.

links.note: 497 says that one who thinks everything through and acts by the place needs no support but fearlessness (அஞ்சாமை அல்லால் துணைவேண்டா). 534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை): Parimelazhagar explains that forest or hill forts are of no use to a frightened mind. The pair shows the two sides of one claim: place is enough given courage, and place is worthless without it.
links.reason: அஞ்சாமை அல்லால் துணைவேண்டா ... இடத்தால் செயின் and அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை are converse statements about place and courage; Parimelazhagar's forest-and-hill gloss is reported correctly, though in 534 the fort is the simile and not the main claim.

links.note: 497 says no ally is needed (துணைவேண்டா) beyond fearlessness when the plan is complete and the ground right. 875 advises one who has no ally and two enemies (தன்துணை இன்றால் பகையிரண்டால்) to make one of the enemies a pleasing ally. 875 shows that the book does not treat being without allies as generally safe; 497's claim holds only under its stated condition of complete planning and the right place.
links.reason: 497's துணைவேண்டா is about needing no aid for an act done எஞ்சாமை எண்ணி இடத்தால், and already carries its own condition; 875's தன்துணை இன்றால் concerns a political ally against two foes, so the link rests mostly on the shared word துணை.

links.note: 473 says many who did not know their own strength pressed on out of zeal and broke midway (ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார்). 498 says the large army's zeal (ஊக்கம்) is destroyed when it enters the small army's ground. In both, drive that outruns a sober measure, of one's strength in one chapter and of the ground in the other, is what gets broken.
links.reason: Both use ஊக்கம் for drive that fails when it ignores a limit: ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் (strength) and ஊக்கம் அழிந்து விடும் (ground).

links.note: 498 says the drive of a commander with a large army is destroyed (உறுபடையான் ஊக்கம் அழிந்து விடும்) if he enters ground suited to a small army. 744 defines a fort as having little to guard and much room, and as destroying the drive of the foe who comes against it (உறுபகை ஊக்கம் அழிப்பது அரண்). The shared phrase shows that a fort is the built form of 498's principle: ground chosen so that numbers stop counting.
links.reason: உறுபடையான் ஊக்கம் அழிந்து விடும் and உறுபகை ஊக்கம் அழிப்பது அரண் share the phrase, and சிறுகாப்பிற் பேரிடத்தது is the built version of the சிறுபடையான் செல்லிடம்.

links.note: 495 gives the image: the crocodile wins in its own deep water. 499 states the human case without an image: even people with no fortress and no great standing (சிறைநலனும் சீரும் இலரெனினும்) are hard to engage on the land where they live (உறைநிலத்தோடு ஒட்டல் அரிது). 499 applies the crocodile's lesson to an invader's estimate of a weak-looking people.
links.reason: 495's crocodile wins in நெடும்புனல் and is killed out of it; 499 says even those without சிறைநலனும் சீரும் are hard to attack on their உறைநிலம். The plain statement applies the image's lesson within the same chapter.

links.note: 501 names four tests, virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life (அறம்பொருள் இன்பம் உயிரச்சம்), by which a person is examined before being trusted (தேறப்படும்). 513 names four qualities, love, understanding, clarity and freedom from desire, in whoever has which trust lies (நன்குடையான் கட்டே தெளிவு). The first four are trials applied from outside (Parimelazhagar describes staged temptations); the second four are the traits such trials are meant to find.
links.reason: நான்கின் திறந்தெரிந்து தேறப்படும் gives four tests and இந்நான்கும் நன்குடையான் கட்டே தெளிவு four traits in the next chapter; the mapping of traits to tests is the note's inference, but a reasonable one (அவாவின்மை to the பொருள் test).

links.note: 501's fourth test is fear for one's life (உயிரச்சம்). 690 defines the envoy as one who, even if it brings his end (இறுதி பயப்பினும்), does not fall short in securing his lord's good. The envoy chapter shows what passing that fourth test looks like in service.
links.reason: 501's fourth test is உயிரச்சம்; 690's envoy does his lord's உறுதி எஞ்சாது even இறுதி பயப்பினும், which is that test passed in service.

links.note: 502 makes birth in a good family (குடிப்பிறந்து) a ground for trust alongside freedom from fault. 133 says having good conduct is itself good birth, and a lapse in conduct becomes low birth (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை இழுக்கம் இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்). On 133's definition, 502's first criterion cannot be checked apart from its second: family does not vouch for a person whose conduct fails.
links.reason: 502 lists குடிப்பிறந்து beside குற்றத்தின் நீங்கி, while 133 makes ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை itself குடிமை and இழுக்கம் an இழிந்த பிறப்பு, so birth cannot vouch apart from conduct.

links.note: 502 places trust in one born of good family, free of faults, with a shame that recoils from blemish (குடிப்பிறந்து ... வடுப்பரியும் நாணுடையான்). 794 says the friendship of one born of good family who is ashamed of blame on himself (குடிப்பிறந்து தன்கண் பழிநாணுவானை) should be had even at a price. The same two criteria, birth and shame, are used to choose a king's officer and to choose a friend.
links.reason: குடிப்பிறந்து ... வடுப்பரியும் நாணுடையான் (502) and குடிப்பிறந்து தன்கண் பழிநாணுவானை (794) apply the same two criteria, birth and shame of blame, to choosing an officer and a friend.

links.note: 502 lists good family first and shame last among the grounds for trust. 951 says integrity and shame are found together by nature (இயல்பாகச் செப்பமும் நாணும் ஒருங்கு) only in those born to a good house. 951 supplies the reasoning 502 leaves unstated: family is asked for because it is taken to be where shame comes naturally.
links.reason: 502 asks for குடிப்பிறந்து ... நாணுடையான்; 951 says செப்பமும் நாணும் are இயல்பாக found only in இற்பிறந்தார், which is the unstated ground for 502's family criterion.

links.note: 503 says hard learning and freedom from fault still leave some ignorance when one looks closely. 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own inherent understanding still prevails (தன் உண்மை அறிவே மிகும்). Both set a limit on what study can change in a person, one in the chapter on choosing officers and one in the chapter on fate.
links.reason: அரியகற்று ஆசற்றார் கண்ணும் ... வெளிறு and நூல்பல கற்பினும் ... உண்மை யறிவே மிகும் both limit what study achieves, in different chapters.

links.note: 503 observes that even in those who have learned hard things and are free of fault, it is rare on examination to find no blankness (இன்மை அரிதே வெளிறு). 504 gives the rule that follows: examine the qualities and the faults and judge by what predominates (மிகைநாடி மிக்க கொளல்). Parimelazhagar on 504 makes the bridge explicit, saying no one in the world has only qualities or only faults.
links.reason: 503 'இன்மை அரிதே வெளிறு' (no one wholly without a blank spot) leads to 504 'குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி... மிக்க கொளல்'; Parimelazhagar's 'குணம் குற்றங்களுள் ஒன்றேயுடையார் உலகத்து இன்மையின்' is cited correctly.

links.note: 504 tells the king to examine a person's qualities and faults (குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி) and take whichever predominates. 793 tells one to know a person's qualities, family, faults and kin (குணமும் குடிமையும் குற்றமும் ... இனனும்) before forming a friendship. The same inventory is used in both domains, but only 504 says how to decide when the inventory is mixed.
links.reason: குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி and குணமும் குடிமையும் குற்றமும் ... இனனும் அறிந்து use the same list for appointing and for befriending, and only 504 adds the rule மிகைநாடி மிக்க கொளல்.

links.note: 504 lets the predominant side decide what a person is. 965 says even those like a hill are diminished if they do a lowering thing the size of a kundri seed (குன்றி அனைய செயின்). 965 names a kind of fault, the degrading act, that is not outweighed by the mass of a person's merits, which limits the simple weighing of 504.
links.reason: மிகைநாடி மிக்க கொளல் weighs the predominant side, but குன்றின் அனையாரும் குன்றுவர் ... குன்றி அனைய செயின் lets one small degrading act outweigh a great standing; a real limit, though the contexts (selection, honour) differ.

links.note: 505 says a person's own deeds are the touchstone (கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்) of greatness and smallness. 986 asks what the touchstone of worth is (சால்பிற்குக் கட்டளை யாதெனின்) and answers: accepting defeat even from those not one's equal. Both use the assayer's stone for testing people; 505 names the general test, deeds, and 986 picks one particular deed as the decisive one.
links.reason: கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல் and சால்பிற்குக் கட்டளை use the same touchstone figure for testing persons, general test and one decisive deed.

links.note: 506 treats having no attachment (பற்றிலர்) as a reason not to trust a person, since such a one does not fear blame. 350 tells the renouncer to hold to the one without attachment (பற்றற்றான்) in order to let attachment go. The same word is a disqualification in the chapter on choosing officers and the goal in the chapter on renunciation; the contexts differ, so this is a contrast of valuation across the books and not a contradiction.
links.reason: பற்றிலர் disqualifies in 506 and பற்றற்றான் is the object to hold to in 350; the note presents it as a contrast in the word's value, not a contradiction.

links.note: 502 puts trust in one who has a shame that recoils from blemish (நாணுடையான்). 506 warns against trusting those who are cut off (அற்றார்), because they have no attachment and are not ashamed of blame (பற்றிலர் நாணார் பழி); Parimelazhagar takes அற்றார் as those without kin, Manakkudavar as those without conduct. The two verses are the positive and negative of one criterion, and 506 adds a cause: shame depends on having ties.
links.reason: 502's வடுப்பரியும் நாணுடையான் and 506's பற்றிலர் நாணார் பழி are the two faces of one test; the note reports both commentators' readings of அற்றார் correctly.

links.note: 507 says trusting the ignorant with affection as the ground (காதன்மை கந்தா அறிவறியார்த் தேறுதல்) yields every kind of folly. 515 says work is not to be assigned to someone because he is dear (சிறந்தானென்று ஏவற்பாற்றன்று), only to one who knows, endures and can do it. Both exclude affection as a ground of appointment, one at the stage of trust and the other at the stage of assigning work.
links.reason: காதன்மை கந்தா ... தேறுதல் and சிறந்தானென்று ஏவற்பாற்றன்று both rule out affection as the ground, at the stages of trust and of assignment.

links.note: 507 warns that trusting those without understanding out of fondness brings all folly on the one who trusts. 836 describes the result from the other side: when a fool who does not know how takes up a task (கையறியாப் பேதை வினைமேற் கொளின்), it fails and he ends in fetters. 836 shows the outcome that 507's warning anticipates.
links.reason: 507 'அறிவறியார்த் தேறுதல் பேதைமை எல்லாந் தரும்' is met by 836 'கையறியாப் பேதை வினைமேற் கொளின்' with its failure and 'புனைபூணும்'; Parimelazhagar on 507 already speaks of work placed on the ignorant failing.

links.note: 508 and 510 share their closing line (தீரா இடும்பை தரும்) and their first fault, trusting without examining. 510 adds a second fault of equal weight: doubting one who has been trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்). Read after 508, 510 shows that the chapter's warning is not simply 'trust less': misplaced doubt is punished in the same words as misplaced trust.
links.reason: Both end 'தீரா இடும்பை தரும்' and begin from 'தேரான்... தெளி-'; 510 adds 'தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்', so misplaced doubt is penalised in the same words as unexamined trust.

links.note: 508: one who trusts an outsider without examining (தேரான் பிறனைத் தெளிந்தான்) gets trouble that does not end, extending to his descendants (வழிமுறை தீரா இடும்பை). 792: the friendship of one who does not inquire again and again ends in a grief that kills him (கடைமுறை தான்சாம் துயரம்). The same structure, unexamined acceptance followed by lasting harm, is stated for a king's officer and for a friend.
links.reason: தேரான் தெளிந்தான் ... வழிமுறை தீரா இடும்பை and ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான் ... கடைமுறை தான்சாம் துயரம் have the same build, down to the paired வழிமுறை/கடைமுறை, for an appointee and a friend.
links.text_issue: 508's Parimelazhagar gloss as printed reads ஆராய்ந்து தெளிந்த where the sense of தேரான் requires 'without examining'; likely an edition typo.

links.note: 509 says trust no one without examining, and after examining, trust what is to be trusted (தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக தேறும் பொருள்). 518 says that after examining a person's fitness for the work (வினைக்குரிமை நாடிய பின்றை), make him fully entitled to it (அதற்குரியனாகச் செயல்). 518 turns 509's second half into an act: the trust that follows examination is shown by handing over real authority.
links.reason: 509's தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக and 518's வினைக்குரிமை நாடிய பின்றை அவனை அதற்குரியனாகச் செயல் have the same examine-then-commit sequence; 518 applies it as delegation of the work.

links.note: 509 says that once a person has been examined, what is to be trusted should be trusted. 588 says even what a spy has found and brought back should be checked through another spy (மற்றுமோர் ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றிக் கொளல்). For intelligence reports the book keeps verifying after the agent is chosen, which bears on 509's phrase தேறும் பொருள்: Manakkudavar reads it as the matters in which the person is reliable, not everything.
links.reason: 509 concerns trusting persons after examination (தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக), 588 concerns cross-checking a report (மற்றுமோர் ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றிக் கொளல்), so the limit is indirect; and Manakkudavar's closing line as printed (ஒரு பொருளிற் றேற்றமுடையாரை எல்லாப் பொருளினுந் தெளிக) says the opposite of the note's 'not everything'.

links.note: 509 orders examination first and commitment after. 791 says nothing ruins like befriending without inquiry, because for those who keep friendship there is no letting go once it is made (நட்டபின் வீடில்லை). Friendship follows the same sequence as appointment, and 791 states the reason the order matters: the commitment is hard to reverse.
links.reason: 509 தேராது தேறற்க ... தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக and 791 நாடாது நட்டலின் கேடில்லை ... நட்டபின் வீடில்லை give the same inquire-then-commit order for appointment and friendship.

links.note: 510 says doubting one who has been trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு) brings endless trouble. 519 says fortune leaves the one who thinks otherwise of the closeness of a man devoted to his work (கேண்மை வேறாக நினைப்பானை நீங்கும் திரு). Both make the ruler's unfounded suspicion of a proven servant a cause of his own loss.
links.reason: 510's தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு and 519's கேண்மை வேறாக நினைப்பானை நீங்கும் திரு both make suspicion of a proven man the ruler's own loss.

links.note: 510 speaks to the ruler: doubt of one already trusted brings trouble that does not end. 693 speaks to the courtier: guard against grave faults, because once suspicion has arisen it is hard for anyone to clear it (கடுத்தபின் தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது). The two verses describe the same event, a ruler's suspicion, as lasting damage from each side of the relationship.
links.reason: தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும் தீரா இடும்பை தரும் and கடுத்தபின் தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது describe the ruler's suspicion as lasting damage from the ruler's and the courtier's side.

links.note: 511 says the man to employ is one whose nature, having looked into good and bad (நன்மையும் தீமையும் நாடி), has taken to the good (நலம்புரிந்த தன்மையான்). 422 defines understanding as not letting the mind go wherever it goes but turning it from bad to good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது). The test for a king's officer is the book's general definition of அறிவு applied to a person at work.
links.reason: நன்மையும் தீமையும் நாடி நலம்புரிந்த தன்மையான் tracks தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது அறிவு closely; 'the definition applied' is slightly strong since Parimelazhagar ties 511 to the acts within an assigned task.

links.note: 504 tells the king to examine a man's qualities and faults and judge by what predominates (குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி ... மிகைநாடி). 511 uses the same verb நாடி, but now it is the candidate who examines good and bad and settles on the good. The king's weighing of the man in chapter 51 becomes, in chapter 52, a check on how the man himself weighs.
links.reason: குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி (the king weighing the man) and நன்மையும் தீமையும் நாடி நலம்புரிந்த தன்மையான் (the man's own weighing): same verb, shifted subject.

links.note: 513 places trust in one who has love, understanding, clarity and freedom from desire (அன்பறிவு தேற்றம் அவாவின்மை). 682 opens with the same pair, அன்பறிவு, and adds considered eloquence as the three things an envoy cannot lack. The two lists share a core of loyalty and knowledge and then differ by office: the officer handling affairs needs steadiness and no greed, the envoy needs speech.
links.reason: Both lists open with அன்பறிவு, but they are different lists for different offices, as the note itself says, so 'agrees' (the same claim) does not fit; the shared core is real.

links.note: 505 makes each person's own deeds the touchstone of greatness and smallness (தத்தம் கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்). 514 says tests of every kind before the appointment still leave many who change once in the work. Both put the decisive evidence in action, and 514 adds that the action that counts is the work itself, after trust has been given.
links.reason: 505's கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல் locates the test in deeds; 514's தேறியக் கண்ணும் வினைவகையான் வேறாகும் adds that the decisive deeds come after appointment.

links.note: 510 says that doubting a man one has examined and trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு) brings endless trouble. 514 says that even when tested in every way (எனைவகையான் தேறியக் கண்ணும்), many people turn different through the nature of the work (வினைவகையான் வேறாகும்). Read together, 514 limits 510: testing does not settle the matter, so the ban on doubt cannot mean a ban on watching how the man changes in office.
links.reason: தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு is limited by எனைவகையான் தேறியக் கண்ணும் வினைவகையான் வேறாகும்; Manakkudavar's remark on 514 (do not grow careless because you have tested) supports the note.

links.note: 514 observes that many who passed every test turn different through the work (வினைவகையான் வேறாகும் மாந்தர் பலர்). 520 tells the king to look into the one doing the work every day (நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன்). The chapter's closing instruction answers the problem 514 raises: since office changes people, examination has to continue after appointment.
links.reason: வினைவகையான் வேறாகும் மாந்தர் பலர் (514) is answered by நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன் வினைசெய்வான் (520) in the same chapter.

links.note: 515 requires for a task one who knows and endures and can carry it through (அறிந்தாற்றிச் செய்கிற்பாற்கு). 640 says that those without practical ability (திறப்பாடு இலாதவர்), though they plan in proper order, do things that never reach completion. 640 shows what 515's last requirement guards against: knowing is not enough without the capacity to finish.
links.reason: 515 demands one who அறிந்தாற்றிச் செய்கிற்பான்; 640 shows the failure case, முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே செய்வர் திறப்பாடு இலாதவர்.

links.note: 516 asks the king to examine the doer, examine the deed, and act seeing how they fit the time (செய்வானை நாடி வினைநாடிக் காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல்). 675 lists five things to think through before acting: resources, means, time, the deed and the place (பொருள்கருவி காலம் வினையிடனொடு ஐந்தும்). Deed and time are in both lists; 516 adds the one item 675 lacks, the person who will do it, which is the concern of a chapter on employing people.
links.reason: வினை and காலம் appear in both lists, and செய்வானை நாடி in 516 is the one item absent from 675's பொருள் கருவி காலம் வினை இடன்.

links.note: 516: examine the doer, the deed and the fit with the time, then act (காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல்). 949: the trained physician acts after considering the measure of the patient, the measure of the illness and the time (உற்றான் அளவும் பிணியளவும் காலமும் ... கருதிச் செயல்). Both end in செயல் after a three-part assessment of person, matter and time, the same procedure in statecraft and in medicine.
links.reason: செய்வானை நாடி வினைநாடிக் காலத்தோடு ... செயல் and உற்றான் அளவும் பிணியளவும் காலமும் ... கருதிச் செயல் are the same three-part assessment (person, matter, time) ending in செயல், in statecraft and in medicine.

links.note: 517 says that once the king has reasoned 'this man will finish this by this means', he should leave it with him (அதனை அவன்கண் விடல்). 510 says that doubting one who has been examined and trusted brings endless trouble. Leaving the task with the man is the practical form of 510's rule: examination comes first and is then followed by a real handing over.
links.reason: 517 'ஆய்ந்து அதனை அவன்கண் விடல்' is the acting-out of 510 'தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும் தீரா இடும்பை தரும்': examine, then really hand over.

links.note: 517 tells the king to leave the task to the chosen man (அவன்கண் விடல்). 520, in the same chapter, tells the king to look into the one doing the work daily (நாடோறும் நாடுக), because the world stays straight only if he does. The delegation in 517 is therefore not a withdrawal of attention; Parimelazhagar's note on 520 says the checking should be done privately so that the man's standing is not damaged.
links.reason: அதனை அவன்கண் விடல் is bounded by நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன் in the same chapter; Parimelazhagar's அவன் உரிமை அழியாமல் தன்னுள்ளே ஆராய்ந்து supports the note's point about discreet checking.

links.note: 519 warns the king against taking amiss the familiarity of a hard-working officer (வினைக்கண் வினையுடையான் கேண்மை). 700, addressed to the courtier, says that familiarity which does improper things on the thought 'we are old associates' (பழையம் எனக்கருதிப் பண்பல்ல செய்யும் கெழுதகைமை) brings ruin. The king must tolerate the liberty and the servant must not presume on it; each verse limits the other.
links.reason: 519 warns the king against taking வினையுடையான் கேண்மை amiss, and 700 warns the courtier that பழையம் எனக்கருதிப் பண்பல்ல செய்யும் கெழுதகைமை கேடு தரும். Each limits the other from its own side.

links.note: 519 says fortune leaves the one who thinks otherwise of the closeness of a man devoted to the work (கேண்மை வேறாக நினைப்பானை நீங்கும் திரு). 808 praises those with the strength of intimacy not to listen to talk of a friend's lapse (கேளிழுக்கம் கேளாக் கெழுதகைமை). The duty not to reinterpret a close person's conduct appears in kingship and in friendship; Parimelazhagar reads 519 as the king being turned by the words of those who resent the officer, which is the situation 808 names.
links.reason: 519's கேண்மை வேறாக நினைப்பானை and 808's கேளிழுக்கம் கேளாக் கெழுதகைமை both bar turning against a close person on report; Parimelazhagar does read 519 as the king hearing those who resent the officer (பொறாதார் சொற் கேட்டு).

links.note: 520 says that if the one doing the work does not bend, the world will not bend (கோடாமை கோடாது உலகு). 546 says victory comes from the king's sceptre, provided it does not bend (கோலதூஉங் கோடாதெனின்). கோடாமை, not bending, is the mark of the just sceptre, and 520 applies the same word to the officer, on whose straightness the world's straightness is made to depend.
links.reason: கோடாமை கோடாது உலகு and கோல் ... கோடாதெனின் use the same not-bending figure for the officer and for the sceptre.

links.note: 520: let the king look daily into the one doing his work (நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன்). 553: the king who does not look daily and do justice loses his land daily (நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன் நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்). The same phrase of daily examination is used for officers and for justice, and both tie the state of the land to that routine.
links.reason: நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன் and நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன் share the phrase and both tie the land's condition (கோடாது உலகு / நாடு கெடும்) to daily scrutiny.

links.note: 520 requires the king to examine the worker daily. 584 defines the spy as one who examines everyone, beginning with those who do the king's work (வினைசெய்வார்), then his kin and his enemies. 584 supplies the means by which the daily examination of 520 is carried out.
links.reason: நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன் வினைசெய்வான் and வினைசெய்வார் ... அனைவரையும் ஆராய்வது ஒற்று: the spy is the instrument for the scrutiny of the king's workers.

links.note: 521: kin keep honouring old ties (பழைமை) even when all is lost. 806: those who keep within the bounds do not give up, even in ruin (தொலைவிடத்தும்), the bond of those who have stood with them from of old (தொல்லைக்கண் நின்றார் தொடர்பு). Loyalty to a long tie when fortune is gone is claimed as the mark of kin in one chapter and of true old friends in the other.
links.reason: Both praise keeping an old tie, but in 806 both commentators take தொலைவிடத்தும் as ruin the old friend himself causes (அவரால் தொலைவு வந்தவிடத்தும்), the chapter's theme of bearing a friend's liberties, not loyalty to someone whose fortune is gone as in 521's பற்றற்ற கண்ணும்; the note flattens this.

links.note: 521 says that honouring the old tie even when a man's means are gone (பற்றற்ற கண்ணும் பழைமை பாராட்டுதல்) is found among kin. 1047 says that one in poverty will be looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல நோக்கப்படும்). The conflict holds if 1047 is read as Pope reads it, of poverty in general; the verse's own qualifier அறஞ்சாரா, poverty unconnected with virtue, which Parimelazhagar and Subramuniyaswami keep, narrows it and reduces the conflict.
links.reason: பற்றற்ற கண்ணும் பழைமை பாராட்டுதல் சுற்றத்தார் கண்ணே against ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல நோக்கப்படும்; the note correctly makes the conflict depend on dropping அறஞ்சாரா.

links.note: 522 says that if a man gets kin whose love does not lapse (விருப்பறாச் சுற்றம் இயையின்), they give many gains (ஆக்கம் பலவும் தரும்). 884 says that if hidden enmity of unreformed mind appears, it gives many ills that turn his circle bad (இனமாணா ஏதம் பலவும் தரும்). The two verses have the same shape with opposite content, and Parimelazhagar notes that 'whose love does not lapse' in 522 is said to exclude the inner enmity of chapter 89: kin are an asset only on that condition.
links.reason: The two are built alike (…இயையின் … ஆக்கம் பலவும் தரும் / …தோன்றின் … ஏதம் பலவும் தரும்), and Parimelazhagar on 522 does say விருப்பறாச் சுற்றம் is specified 'உட்பகையின் நீக்குதற்கு', so the condition is real.

links.note: 524 says the fruit of having gained wealth is to live surrounded by one's kin (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்பட ஒழுகல்). 837 says that when a fool gets great wealth, strangers eat their fill and his own people go hungry (ஏதிலார் ஆரத் தமர்பசிப்பர்). 837 shows the failure of exactly the use 524 names: wealth that does not reach one's own people has missed its purpose.
links.reason: 524 names சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்பட ஒழுகல் as செல்வம் பெற்ற பயன்; 837's ஏதிலார் ஆரத் தமர் பசிப்பர் shows the fool's wealth failing exactly that use.

links.note: 525 names giving and pleasant speech as what surrounds a man with kin. 526 keeps giving, now great giving (பெருங்கொடை), and replaces pleasant speech with not cherishing anger (பேணான் வெகுளி), and raises the result to a following unmatched on earth. The pair is not a repetition: the second verse moves from a positive manner to the removal of what drives people away.
links.reason: Adjacent verses: கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் (525) becomes பெருங்கொடையான் பேணான் வெகுளி (526), with the result raised from சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும் to மருங்குடையார் மாநிலத்து இல்; the note is accurate.

links.note: 527 ties gain (ஆக்கம்) to those who, like the crow, call others before eating. 227 says the disease of hunger does not touch one who is habituated to sharing his food (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை). Both hold that sharing food protects the sharer's own fortune, stated in the Book of Virtue as freedom from hunger and here as prosperity.
links.reason: காக்கை கரவா கரைந்துண்ணும் ஆக்கமும் அன்னநீரார்க்கே உள and பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனைப் பசியென்னும் தீப்பிணி தீண்டல் அரிது both say that sharing one's food secures the sharer's own welfare.

links.note: 527 praises the crow for not hiding (கரவா) its food and for calling others to eat. 1035 says those who live by eating what their own hands produce do not beg and give to those who ask without hiding (கரவாது). Not concealing what one has, கரவு being the book's word for the withholder's fault in chapters 106 and 107, is the shared mark of the crow and of the farmer.
links.reason: கரவா in 527 and கரவாது in 1035 both mark open sharing of one's food with others (கரைந்துண்ணும்; இரப்பார்க்கொன்று ஈவர்), so the shared word carries the same point and is not incidental.

links.note: 528 ends: many will live looking to that (அதுநோக்கி வாழ்வார் பலர்). 542 says the world lives looking to the sky and the people live looking to the king's sceptre (கோல்நோக்கி வாழுங் குடி). The phrase 'live looking to' makes the king's conduct something people depend on as they depend on rain; 528 uses it for his recognition of each person's worth.
links.reason: அதுநோக்கி வாழ்வார் பலர் and வானோக்கி வாழும் ... கோல்நோக்கி வாழுங் குடி share the phrase நோக்கி வாழ் for dependence on the king; quoted correctly.
