links.note: 528 says that if the king looks at people not in common but according to rank (பொதுநோக்கான் வேந்தன் வரிசையா நோக்கின்), many will live looking to that. 972 says birth is alike for all, but distinction is not alike, because of the difference in what people do (சிறப்பொவ்வா செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான்). 972 gives a basis for the differential regard of 528: Parimelazhagar reads வரிசை there as each person's merit, and 972 locates such difference in conduct, not birth.
links.reason: வரிசையா நோக்கின் in 528 is advice on holding kin, and 972's சிறப்பொவ்வா செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான் is a general claim on worth; linking them through 'merit' is a thematic bridge that neither verse makes, and Manakkudavar reads 528 as singling out one man.

links.note: 529 says estranged kin return of themselves once the cause of discord is gone. 530 turns to one who left and has come back for a reason (காரணத்தின் வந்தானை) and tells the king to attend to it and accept him only after reflection (இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல்). The pair separates two kinds of return, one that follows from the king's own correction and one prompted by the returner's interest, and prescribes welcome for the first and caution for the second.
links.reason: 529's அமராமைக் காரணம் இன்றி வரும் (return when the cause of disaffection is gone) is limited by 530's காரணத்தின் வந்தானை ... இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல், which prescribes caution for an interested return.
links.text_issue: 529 reads தமராகிக் தற்றுறந்தார்; should be தமராகித் தற்றுறந்தார்.

links.note: 529 says those who were one's own and left will return to kinship when the cause of the discord is absent (அமராமைக் காரணம் இன்றி வரும்). 633 lists among a minister's abilities reuniting those who have parted (பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்). 529 says how that reunion comes about: the ground of the estrangement has to be removed, which Parimelazhagar takes as a fault on the king's own side.
links.reason: 529 அமராமைக் காரணம் இன்றி வரும் (Parimelazhagar: தன் மாட்டு இல்லையாக) gives the how of 633 பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்.

links.note: 509 gives the rule: trust no one without examining, then trust (தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது). 530 applies examination to a man who was already one's own, left, and came back for a reason: he is to be received after reflection (எண்ணிக் கொளல்). Leaving resets the earlier trust, so the test of chapter 51 has to be done again.
links.reason: தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது (509) is applied in 530 to the one who உழைப்பிரிந்து காரணத்தின் வந்தான்: இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல். 'Leaving resets the trust' is an inference but a fair one.

links.note: 530 says the king should attend to the reason for which a man who left has come back, wait, and accept him after thinking it over (இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல்). 830 says that when an enemy turns friend, one should be friendly in face and withhold the heart (முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்). Both deal with someone who comes over after having been apart and both withhold immediate trust, but 530 ends in acceptance of the kinsman while 830 ends in letting the former enemy go.
links.reason: இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல் and முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல் both withhold immediate trust from one who comes over, ending in கொளல் versus விடல்; the note describes both correctly.

links.note: 531 states the danger: slackness from the elation of great joy is worse than excessive anger. 539 gives the practice against it: when one grows strong in one's own joy (மகிழ்ச்சியின் மைந்துறும் போழ்து), call to mind those ruined by negligence (இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக).
links.reason: 531 names the danger, உவகை மகிழ்ச்சியிற் சோர்வு, and 539 gives the remedy at that moment, மகிழ்ச்சியின் மைந்துறும் போழ்து இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக.

links.note: 532 says heedlessness kills fame (பொச்சாப்புக் கொல்லும் புகழை). 601 says the undimmed lamp called family goes out when the grime called sloth creeps over it (மடியென்னும் மாசூர மாய்ந்து கெடும்). In both, an inner lapse, not an outside enemy, destroys a standing built up over time.
links.reason: பொச்சாப்புக் கொல்லும் புகழை and மடியென்னும் மாசூர மாய்ந்து கெடும் do share 'a lapse destroys standing', but that is a generic pattern, and the contrast with an outside enemy that the note leans on is in neither verse.

links.note: 532 uses as its comparison that constant poverty kills understanding (அறிவினை நிச்ச நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு). 1046 describes one form of it: even when the poor speak good matter well understood, their words and meaning go slack (சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்); Parimelazhagar says nobody listens, so their learning yields nothing. Read together, the 'killing' of understanding in 532 includes its losing all effect in the world.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar reads 532's simile as poverty destroying the wise man's standing (நன்கு மதிப்பினை அழிக்கும்), which is what 1046's சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும் describes; the note's reading follows the commentary.

links.note: 430 says those without understanding have nothing, whatever they possess (என்னுடைய ரேனும் இலர்). 534 says the heedless have no good (பொச்சாப் புடையார்க்கு நன்கு இல்லை), which Parimelazhagar reads as: even with every kind of wealth, they get no benefit from it. The same logic of having without having is applied to lack of understanding in one verse and to lack of vigilance in the other.
links.reason: 430 என்னுடையரேனும் இலர் and 534 பொச்சாப்புடையார்க்கு நன்கு இல்லை, which Parimelazhagar glosses as செல்வமெல்லாம் உடையராயினும் பயன் இல்லை, share the logic of possessing without benefit.

links.note: 534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்ச முடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை). 741 says a fort is of value both to those who march out and to those who, in fear, protect themselves (அஞ்சித் தற்போற்றுபவர்க்கும் பொருள்). The conflict holds if 534's first half is taken as a plain claim about forts and the fearful; Parimelazhagar's readings ease it, since he takes 534 as fear in the mind making a fort useless and 741 as the weaker side prudently taking refuge.
links.reason: Taken plainly, அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை conflicts with அஞ்சித் தற்போற்றுபவர்க்கும் பொருள்; the note states the reading the conflict needs and how Parimelazhagar eases it.

links.note: 750 says a fort, whatever its excellences, is as nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்). 534 says the fearful have no fort and the heedless have no good (நன்கு). Both hold that an outward advantage counts for nothing without the inner quality needed to use it, and both use the fort to say so.
links.reason: அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை and வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண் both make the fort worthless without an inner quality in its holders.

links.note: 429 gives the positive case: those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) meet no affliction that shakes them. 535 gives the negative: one who did not guard beforehand later grieves over his own fault (தன்பிழை பின்னூறு இரங்கி விடும்). Together they show foresight treated as part of understanding and its absence as heedlessness.
links.reason: முன்னுறக் காவாது இழுக்கியான் ... இரங்கி விடும் is the negative of எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்க்கு இல்லை ... நோய்.

links.note: 655 tells one not to do deeds over which one will grieve, saying 'what have I done' (எற்றென்று இரங்குவ செய்யற்க). 535 uses the same verb, இரங்கு, for the grief of one who failed to guard in advance. The pairing shows regret following from omission in 535 as it follows from commission in 655.
links.reason: இரங்கி விடும் after முன்னுறக் காவாது and எற்றென்று இரங்குவ செய்யற்க share the verb and set regret from omission beside regret from commission; parallel_domain would fit as well.

links.note: 536 says nothing equals unfailing vigilance toward everyone at all times (யார்மாட்டும் என்றும்). 582 says it is the king's work to know quickly everything that happens to everyone at all times (எல்லார்க்கும் எல்லாம் நிகழ்பவை எஞ்ஞான்றும்). The same universal scope appears in both, and 582 gives the general vigilance of 536 a concrete form in intelligence gathering.
links.reason: The universal-scope wording matches (யார்மாட்டும் என்றும் / எல்லார்க்கும் ... எஞ்ஞான்றும்), but 536's இழுக்காமை is non-forgetfulness in one's own conduct, not knowing what happens to others, so calling 582 its concrete form overstates.

links.note: 611 says one must not lose heart on the thought that a thing is hard (அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை வேண்டும்), since effort gives the greatness needed. 537 says nothing is beyond doing as 'hard' (அரிய என்று ஆகாத இல்லை) when done with unforgetting care. Each denies that difficulty is a reason to give up, and each names its own remedy: effort in 611, sustained attention in 537.
links.reason: 537 அரியஎன்று ஆகாத இல்லை and 611 அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை வேண்டும் both refuse difficulty as a reason to give up, with பொச்சாவாக் கருவி and முயற்சி as the respective remedies.
links.text_issue: 611: the Parimelazhagar entry is missing the start of its gloss.

links.note: 466 says one is ruined by not doing what is fit to do (செய்தக்க செய்யாமை யானுங் கெடும்). 538 says what has been praised must be carefully done, and those who slight it and do not do it (செய்யாது இகழ்ந்தார்க்கு) have nothing through seven births. 538 takes the omission half of 466 and extends its cost beyond this life.
links.reason: செய்தக்க செய்யாமையானுங் கெடும் (466) is taken up by 538's செய்யாது இகழ்ந்தார்க்கு எழுமையும் இல், which extends the cost of omission to seven births.

links.note: 835 says a fool can make, in one birth, the mire he will sink into for seven (எழுமையும் தான்புக் கழுந்தும் அளறு). 538 says those who neglect what is praised have no good through seven births (எழுமையும் இல்). Both attach a seven-birth consequence to conduct in this life, folly in one and neglect of duty in the other.
links.reason: இகழ்ந்தார்க்கு எழுமையும் இல் and எழுமையும் தான்புக்கழுந்தும் அளறு both attach a seven-birth penalty to this-life conduct, negligence and folly.

links.note: 250 says: when you move against those weaker than you, think of yourself before those stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). 539 says: when you grow strong in your own joy, think of those ruined by negligence (இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக). Both prescribe a deliberate act of recollection at the moment of feeling powerful, for the sake of compassion in 250 and of vigilance in 539.
links.reason: உள்ளுக at மகிழ்ச்சியின் மைந்துறும் போழ்து and நினைக்க at மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து both order a recollection at the moment of power.

links.note: 930 asks whether a drinker, when sober and seeing another man drunk (களித்தானைக் காணுங்கால்), does not reflect on the slackness of his own drinking (உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு). 539 tells one elated with joy to reflect (உள்ளுக) on those whom negligence ruined. Both correct an intoxicated state by looking at its effect in other people, and 930's word சோர்வு is the one 531 uses for the slackness of joy.
links.reason: இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக ... மகிழ்ச்சியின் மைந்துறும் போழ்து and களித்தானைக் காணுங்கால் உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு both sober an intoxicated state by looking at others; சோர்வு is indeed 531's word.

links.note: 551 compares the oppressive king to murderers and finds him worse. 552 compares the king who demands wealth to a man standing with a spear saying 'hand it over' (வேலொடு நின்றான் இடுவென்றது). Together the two opening verses of the chapter set the unjust ruler beside common criminals, first the killer and then the robber.
links.reason: கொலைமேற்கொண்டாரிற் கொடிதே and வேலொடு நின்றான் இடுவென்றது போலும் set the unjust king beside the killer and then the robber in the chapter's first two verses.

links.note: 756 names what is the king's wealth: what comes unowned, customs duty, and tribute from enemies (உறுபொருளும் உல்கு பொருளும் தன் ஒன்னார்த் தெறுபொருளும்). 552 treats a sceptre-holder's 'asking' (இரவு) of his people as highway robbery; Parimelazhagar notes that the word இரவு marks it as something other than the due tax. 756 shows the lawful sources against which 552's demand is measured.
links.reason: 756 lists the வேந்தன் பொருள் (உறுபொருள், உல்கு பொருள், தெறுபொருள்); 552 condemns கோலொடு நின்றான் இரவு, and Parimelazhagar does say 'இரவு' என்றதனால் இறைப்பொருள் அன்மை. The lawful sources bound what 552 condemns.

links.note: 381 lists the six things a king must have, among them people and resources (படைகுடி கூழ்...). 554 says a king who bends the sceptre and acts without reflection loses resources and people together (கூழுங் குடியும் ஒருங்கிழக்கும்). The two things injustice costs him in 554 are two of the six that make a king in 381.
links.reason: 554's கூழுங் குடியும் ஒருங்கிழக்கும் names two of the six possessions listed in 381 (படைகுடி கூழ்...), so the unjust king loses what makes him a king.

links.note: 568 says the fortune of a king who does not think things through with his circle and then rages in anger will shrink (எண்ணாத வேந்தன் ... சிறுகும் திரு). 554 says a king who acts without reflection (சூழாது) and bends the sceptre loses wealth and people. In both, the king's loss is traced to acting without deliberation, shown in anger in 568 and in injustice in 554.
links.reason: சூழாது செய்யும் அரசு and எண்ணாத வேந்தன் both trace the king's loss (கூழுங் குடியும் இழக்கும்; சிறுகும் திரு) to acting without deliberation.

links.note: 567 says harsh words and punishment beyond bounds are a file that wears down a king's conquering strength (அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்). 555 says the tears of the afflicted are a tool that wears down wealth (செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை). Both describe the effect of a king's cruelty as slow abrasion by a tool, using the same verb தேய்க்கும்.
links.reason: 555 செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை and 567 அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம் both make a king's cruelty a tool that wears him away, with the same verb தேய்க்கும்.

links.note: 828 says a weapon hides within an enemy's folded hands, and his shed tears are the same (படையொடுங்கும் ... அழுத கண்ணீரும் அனைத்து). 555 calls the tears shed by the afflicted the weapon that wears away wealth (அழுத கண்ணீர் ... படை). Both join the same two words, tears and weapon: in 828 the tears conceal a weapon, and in 555 the tears are the weapon.
links.reason: அழுத கண்ணீர் with படை occurs in both (செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை / படையொடுங்கும் ... அழுத கண்ணீரும் அனைத்து), and the note states the difference correctly.

links.note: 563 says a king of cruel sceptre who goes on doing what terrifies will certainly and quickly perish (ஒருவந்தம் ஒல்லைக் கெடும்). 556 says kings endure through just rule (மன்னர்க்கு மன்னுதல் செங்கோன்மை) and without it their lustre does not endure. Both tie how long a king lasts to how he rules; Parimelazhagar takes what endures in 556 to be the king's fame.
links.reason: மன்னுதல் செங்கோன்மை ... இன்றேல் மன்னாவாம் and வெங்கோலனாயின் ... ஒல்லைக் கெடும் both tie a king's lasting to his rule; the note rightly says Parimelazhagar takes 556 of fame.

links.note: In 1192 a woman says that the tender care a lover gives the one who loves him (வீழ்வார் அளிக்கும் அளி) is like the sky giving rain to those who live by it (வாழ்வார்க்கு வானம் பயந்தற்று). 557 says a king's lack of அளி is to living beings what lack of rain is to the earth. The same word அளி and the same rain comparison describe dependence on a ruler in one book and on a beloved in the other.
links.reason: Both pair அளி with rain (துளியின்மை / வானம் பயந்தற்று) and with those who live by it (வாழும் உயிர்க்கு / வாழ்வார்க்கு), for a king in one and a lover in the other.

links.note: 55 says that when a wife who worships her husband says 'rain', it rains (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). 559 says that when a king bends justice, the sky will not rain (ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்). In both, rain responds to a person's keeping or failing the duty of their station, the wife's in the household and the king's in the realm.
links.reason: பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை and ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல் both make rain answer to a person's conduct in their station, wife and king.

links.note: 239 says land that bears a body without renown declines in its blameless rich yield (வண்பயன் குன்றும்). 559 says the sky holds back rain when the king bends justice, and the next verse, 560, uses the same verb for cows' yield (ஆபயன் குன்றும்). In each, nature's yield falls in response to a human moral failing, an individual's in 239 and a ruler's in 559.
links.reason: 239 'வண்பயன் குன்றும்... இசையிலா யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்' and 559 'முறைகோடி... ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்' both have nature's yield fall for a human moral failure; the 560 'ஆபயன் குன்றும்' citation is correct.

links.note: 19 says that if the sky does not give, giving and austerity will not remain in the wide world (தானம் தவம்இரண்டும் தங்கா). 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, cows' yield declines and the six-occupation men forget their book. In both, religious and learned life depends on a provider, the rain in 19 and the king in 560, and fails when the provider fails.
links.reason: 19's தானம் தவம் இரண்டும் தங்கா ... வானம் வழங்காதெனின் and 560's அறுதொழிலோர் நூல்மறப்பர் காவலன் காவான் எனின் have the same conditional form making religious and learned life depend on a provider.

links.note: 561 makes the king the one who punishes in proportion (ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது வேந்து), while 579 calls it the highest quality to show kindly regard and bear with even those whose way is to hurt (ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும் ... பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை). The same root ஒறு sits on opposite sides. Parimelazhagar separates the cases: 561 concerns wrongs done to weaker subjects, 579 wrongs done to the ruler himself, so forbearance is limited to injuries that are the ruler's own to forgive.
links.reason: ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது வேந்து against ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும் ... பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை. Parimelazhagar does read 561 as தன்னின் மெலியார்மேல் and 579 as தம்மை ஒறுக்கும், which sets the limit the note describes.

links.note: 562 asks for a light stroke after a stern show (மெல்ல எறிக); Manakkudavar takes this to mean the penalty should fall short of what the offence deserves. 550 says a king's punishing the cruel with death (கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல்) is like weeding the young crop. The pairing marks where gentleness stops: for those 550 calls கொடியார், the book accepts the severest penalty.
links.reason: 562 கடிதோச்சி மெல்ல எறிக against 550 கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல் does mark where leniency stops; Manakkudavar's gloss on 562 (penalty below what the offence deserves) is reported correctly.

links.note: 562 tells those who want lasting prosperity to raise the rod sharply but strike gently (கடிதோச்சி மெல்ல எறிக). 567 names what happens when the stroke is not gentle: punishment past the bound (கையிகந்த தண்டம்), with harsh words, is a file that wears down the king's strength. 562 gives the practice and 567 the cost of abandoning it; the 'long prosperity' (நெடிதாக்கம்) of one is the 'conquering strength' (அடுமுரண்) eroded in the other.
links.reason: கடிதோச்சி மெல்ல எறிக gives the practice and கையிகந்த தண்டம் ... அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம் the cost of abandoning it, in the same chapter.

links.note: 563 says a cruel-sceptred king who keeps doing what terrifies (வெருவந்த செய்தொழுகும் வெங்கோலன்) will certainly and quickly perish (ஒருவந்தம் ஒல்லைக் கெடும்). 548 says a king who is not easy of access and does not inquire and do justice will sink and perish of himself (தானே கெடும்). Neither verse needs an enemy to bring the king down: in both the misrule is itself the cause of the fall.
links.reason: ஒருவந்தம் ஒல்லைக் கெடும் and தானே கெடும் both make misrule its own cause of ruin, with தானே stating outright what 563 leaves implicit; the pairing joins active cruelty and neglect of justice.

links.note: 386 says that if a king is easy to see and not harsh of speech, his land is spoken of above others (மீக்கூறும் மன்னன் நிலம்). 564 gives the reverse case: where people say 'our lord is harsh' (இறைகடியன்), the king quickly perishes. Both verses measure a reign by what is said about it.
links.reason: கடுஞ்சொல்லன் அல்லனேல் மீக்கூறும் and இறைகடியன் என்றுரைக்கும் இன்னாச்சொல் ... ஒல்லைக் கெடும் are converse cases tied to what people say of the king.

links.note: 564 says the king of whom the painful words 'our lord is harsh' (இறைகடியன் என்றுரைக்கும் இன்னாச்சொல்) are spoken will quickly perish. 555 says the tears of those who cannot bear their affliction are the weapon that wears away wealth (செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை). In both, what destroys the ruler comes from the subjects' suffering, as speech in one verse and as tears in the other.
links.reason: இறைகடியன் என்றுரைக்கும் இன்னாச்சொல் and அல்லற்பட்டு ... அழுத கண்ணீர் both make the subjects' distress the agent of the ruler's ruin.

links.note: 565 says the great wealth (பெருஞ்செல்வம்) of an inaccessible, grim-faced man is as if seen by a demon; Parimelazhagar explains that no one approaches him, so the wealth is of use neither to him nor to others. 1000 says the great wealth (பெருஞ்செல்வம்) gained by one without courtesy (பண்பிலான்) is like good milk spoiled by its vessel. Outside the court the same judgment holds: the holder's manner ruins wealth that is sound in itself.
links.reason: Both verses take பெருஞ்செல்வம் and say the holder's manner (இன்னா முகத்தான் / பண்பிலான்) spoils it; Parimelazhagar's 'of use to neither himself nor others' on 565 is quoted accurately.

links.note: 566 says that if the ruler is harsh of speech and 'eyeless' (கண்ணிலன்), his long-standing wealth perishes at once; Parimelazhagar takes கண் here to stand for கண்ணோட்டம். 577, in the next chapter, states the equation directly: those without kindly regard have no eyes (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர்). The single word in 566 is the idea the following chapter spells out.
links.reason: 566 'கண்ணிலன்' is glossed by Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar as lacking கண்ணோட்டம்; 577 'கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர்' states that equation outright.

links.note: 567 calls harsh words and excessive punishment a file (அரம்) that wears down (தேய்க்கும்) the king's conquering strength. 888 says a family with enmity inside it wears away (தேயும்) like metal rubbed by a file (அரம்பொருத பொன்போல), its strength ground down. In both the file stands for slow loss of strength from within, by the king's own conduct in one and by a house's own members in the other.
links.reason: Both have அரம் with தேய்: 567 'அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்', 888 'அரம்பொருத பொன்போலத் தேயும்'; the file as slow self-inflicted loss of strength is the shared figure, and the note describes both accurately.

links.note: 306 says anger, the fire that kills what it touches, burns even the safe raft called one's people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணையைச் சுடும்). 568 shows this at court: the king who neglects his circle (இனம்) and then turns his anger on them (சினத்தாற்றிச் சீறின்) loses his fortune; Parimelazhagar adds that the frightened ministers leave him. The general warning in the book of virtue becomes a specific danger for a ruler.
links.reason: 306 இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணையைச் சுடும் and 568 இனத்தாற்றி ... சினத்தாற்றிச் சீறின் சிறுகும் திரு pair சினம் against இனம்; Parimelazhagar does say அவர் வெரீஇ நீங்குவர்.

links.note: 435 says the life of one who does not guard before a fault arrives (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்) perishes like straw before fire. 569 applies the same logic to war: the king who has not prepared his defence beforehand is overtaken when the battle arrives (செருவந்த போழ்தில்) and perishes. Both place the failure in the time before the danger, not in the moment of it.
links.reason: வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான் ... கெடும் and சிறைசெய்யா வேந்தன் ... செருவந்த போழ்தில் ... கெடும் both put the failure before the danger arrives; 'beforehand' in 569 is Parimelazhagar's supply but is the natural sense.

links.note: 569 says a king who has made no defence (சிறைசெய்யா வேந்தன்) will be seized by fear when war comes and quickly perish. 534 says that for the fearful there is no fort (அச்ச முடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை); Parimelazhagar explains that defences are no use to a frightened mind. One verse says lack of a fort produces fear, the other that fear cancels a fort, so the fort is necessary but not sufficient.
links.reason: 569 has the fortless king வெருவந்து கெடும்; 534 has அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை, so fear and fort condition each other as the note says.

links.note: 447 asks who can ruin a ruler who keeps as his own those who will rebuke him (இடிக்குந் துணையாரை யாள்வாரை). 570 shows the opposite court: the harsh sceptre gathers the unlearned around it (கல்லார்ப் பிணிக்கும்), because, as Parimelazhagar says, such a ruler admits only those who will go along with him. The two verses together make a ruler's choice of companions a sign of the kind of rule he runs.
links.reason: இடிக்குந் துணையாரை ஆள்வாரை against கல்லார்ப் பிணிக்கும் கடுங்கோல்; Parimelazhagar's gloss that the harsh ruler admits only those who go along with him is quoted accurately.

links.note: 557 says that a king's lack of tender care (அளியின்மை) is to those who live under him what lack of rain is to the earth. 571 states the positive side: the world exists because kindly regard exists; Parimelazhagar reads this of kings. In both verses the ruler's kindness is treated as a condition of life for the people, not as an ornament only.
links.reason: 557 வேந்தன் அளியின்மை is like துளியின்மை to the earth; 571 கண்ணோட்டம் ... உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு. Both make kindness a condition of the people's life, 571 of kings by chapter and commentary.

links.note: 571 says this world exists because the great beauty called kindly regard exists (கண்ணோட்டம் ... உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு). 996 says the world exists by resting on people of courtesy, and would otherwise sink into the earth and perish (பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டுண்டு உலகம்). Both use the same construction, உண்டு உலகு, to say that a human quality and not power keeps the world going; 571 says it in a chapter on kings and 996 of people in general.
links.reason: கண்ணோட்டம் ... உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு and பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டுண்டு உலகம் make the same claim in the same உண்டு-உலகு construction, in a kingship chapter and a general one.

links.note: 983 lists kindly regard (கண்ணோட்டம்) with love, shame, obligingness and truth as the five pillars that hold up worth (சால்பு). 572 gives it a wider load: the conduct of the world rests in it (கண்ணோட்டத் துள்ளது உலகியல்). The quality that is one support of personal character in 983 is the support of social life in 572.
links.reason: கண்ணோட்டம் is one of five தூண் of சால்பு in 983 and in 572 the thing in which உலகியல் rests; the widening from personal to social is accurate.

links.note: 572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a burden to the earth (அஃதிலார் உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை). 1003 says the very appearance of men who cling to accumulation and do not want renown is a burden to the earth (தோற்றம் நிலக்குப் பொறை). The phrase is identical, and in both the people called a burden are those who are of no use to others.
links.reason: The identical 'நிலக்குப் பொறை' is said of 'அஃதிலார் உண்மை' and of 'இசைவேண்டா ஆடவர் தோற்றம்'; both are people of no use to others.

links.note: 79 asks what all the outer limbs can do for those who lack love, the inner limb (புறத்துறுப் பெல்லாம் எவன்செய்யும் ... அன்பிலவர்க்கு). 573 asks the same kind of question of the eye that lacks kindly regard. In both a visible organ is counted useless without the inner quality it should serve.
links.reason: கண் என்னாம் கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண் and புறத்துறுப் பெல்லாம் எவன்செய்யும் ... அன்பிலவர்க்கு are the same rhetorical question about an outer organ without its inner quality.
links.text_issue: 79 line 1 reads 'எவன்செய்பு ம்', a typo for எவன்செய்யும்.

links.note: 573 asks what use an eye is without kindly regard (கண்என்னாம் கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்), as a melody is no use that does not fit the song. 705 asks what use eyes are among the limbs if they cannot read another's sign (என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்). Both judge the eye by what it does for another person, kindness in one verse and understanding in the other, and not by sight.
links.reason: 573 கண்என்னாம் கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண் and 705 என்ன பயத்தவோ கண் both ask what an eye is for and answer by what it does toward another.

links.note: 406 says the unlearned can only be said to exist (உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர்) and are otherwise like barren saline land. 574 says eyes without kindly regard only seem to be there in the face (உளபோல் முகத்து) and do nothing more. Both verses grant bare existence and deny any use, of unlearned persons in one case and of unkind eyes in the other.
links.reason: உளபோல் முகத்து and உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர் both concede bare existence and deny use (எவன் செய்யும்; பயவாக் களர்).

links.note: 574 says eyes without kindly regard in due measure (அளவினால் கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்) do nothing but seem to be in the face; Parimelazhagar takes அளவினால் as excluding excessive indulgence. 578 says what the measure is: kindly regard shown without ruining the task (கருமம் சிதையாமல் கண்ணோட வல்லார்). The one word of limit in 574 becomes the whole subject of 578.
links.reason: அளவினால் கண்ணோட்டம் in 574 is glossed by Parimelazhagar as excluding கழிகண்ணோட்டம், and 578's கருமம் சிதையாமல் கண்ணோட states that limit concretely.

links.note: 1014 asks whether shame is not an ornament (அணி) to the worthy, and whether without it their proud walk is not a disease (அஃதின்றேல் பிணி). 575 has the same shape: kindly regard is the eye's ornament (அணிகலம்), and without it (அஃதின்றேல்) the eye is a sore (புண்). In both the missing virtue does not leave the thing plain but turns it into an affliction.
links.reason: Identical construction: அணிகலம் ... அஃதின்றேல் புண் in 575 and அணி ... அஃதின்றேல் பிணி in 1014, in different domains.

links.note: 393 says those who are called 'people with eyes' are the learned (கண்ணுடையர் என்பவர் கற்றோர்). 577 says those without kindly regard are eyeless and those who have eyes do not lack it (கண்ணுடையார் கண்ணோட்டம் இன்மையும் இல்). The same title, கண்ணுடையார், is awarded on two different tests, learning and kindly regard; the verses do not conflict, but a reader should see that the book defines 'having eyes' twice.
links.reason: கண்ணுடையார்/கண்ணுடையர் is awarded for கண்ணோட்டம் in 577 and to கற்றோர் in 393, with the eyeless counterpart in each (கண்ணிலர் / புண்ணுடையர்); the note rightly says they do not conflict.

links.note: 152 says always bear with excess against you (பொறுத்தல் இறப்பினை என்றும்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even when you are able to punish'. 579 is that case in the ruler, who has the power to punish and is asked to bear with those who harm him. 152 goes a step further than 579 by preferring forgetting the wrong to bearing it.
links.reason: 579 பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை toward ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் is 152's பொறுத்தல் இறப்பினை என்றும் in the ruler's case; the note correctly marks 'able to punish' as Parimelazhagar's addition and 152's மறத்தல் as the further step.

links.note: 805 advises that when friends do something painful, one should take it as either folly or great intimacy (பேதைமை ஒன்றோ பெருங்கிழமை என்றுணர்க). 580 describes people who drink poison they have seen poured. 805 supplies a way of construing a friend's injury that makes the conduct in 580 intelligible, though 580's own stated motive is the wish for நாகரிகம் and not a charitable reading of the giver.
links.reason: Both concern bearing harm from an intimate (பெயக்கண்டும் நஞ்சுண்டமைவர்; நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின்), but 580's motive is நாகரிகம்/கண்ணோட்டம், not construing the act as பேதைமை or பெருங்கிழமை. The note concedes this, so the 'develops' claim is thin.

links.note: 520 tells the king to look daily (நாடோறும் நாடுக) into the one doing his work, since the world stays straight if he does; 582 makes constant, quick knowledge of everyone's affairs the king's own occupation (வேந்தன் தொழில்). Both treat continuous inquiry, not occasional inspection, as the core of rule; 582 widens the object from the king's officers to everyone.
links.reason: நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன் (520) and எஞ்ஞான்றும் வல்லறிதல் வேந்தன் தொழில் (582) both make daily, continuing inquiry the king's work, with 582 widening the object to எல்லார்க்கும் எல்லாம்.

links.note: 582 makes it the king's work to know quickly, at all times (எஞ்ஞான்றும் வல்லறிதல்), all that happens to everyone; 553 says a ruler who does not inquire daily and do justice (நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா) loses his land day by day. 553 gives the purpose and the cost: the daily knowing of 582 exists to feed daily justice, and its absence is paid for in the kingdom itself.
links.reason: எஞ்ஞான்றும் வல்லறிதல் வேந்தன் தொழில் and நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா share the king's daily inquiry, and 553 adds the cost (நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்); that 582's knowing exists for justice is the note's inference but a fair one.

links.note: 583 denies victory to a ruler who has things spied out but does not discern their meaning (ஒற்றிப் பொருள்தெரியா); 423 defines understanding as seeing the true substance of whatever is heard from anyone (அப்பொருள் மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது). The pairing shows the spy chapter applying the general rule about hearsay to intelligence: collecting reports is not yet knowing.
links.reason: ஒற்றிப் பொருள்தெரியா (gathering without sifting the பொருள்) is the intelligence-side application of 423's அப்பொருள் மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது; both commentators gloss தெரியா as not examining what was gathered.

links.note: 510 says that doubting a person one has examined and trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்) brings unending trouble; 584 has spies examine everyone (அனைவரையும் ஆராய்வது), including the king's own officers. The conflict holds if standing surveillance of appointed officers counts as the ஐயுறவு that 510 forbids; if spying is read as routine inquiry and not suspicion of a particular person, the two can stand together.
links.reason: தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும் தீரா இடும்பை தரும் does pull against வினைசெய்வார் ... அனைவரையும் ஆராய்வது ஒற்று, since the officers watched are the ones already trusted; the note states the reading on which the clash holds and the one on which it dissolves.

links.note: 584 defines the spy as one who examines everyone, beginning with those who do the king's work (வினைசெய்வார்); 514 observes that even people trusted after every test often turn different through the nature of the work (வினைவகையான் வேறாகும்). 514 supplies the reason for watching one's own appointed officers: the testing done before appointment does not settle how they behave afterwards.
links.reason: 584 lists வினைசெய்வார் first among those the spy examines; 514 எனைவகையான் தேறியக் கண்ணும் வினைவகையான் வேறாகும் supplies the reason tested officers still need watching.

links.note: 584 puts the king's own kin (தம் சுற்றம்) among those a spy examines, alongside his enemies (வேண்டாதார்); 882 says not to fear enemies who are like a sword but to fear the tie with enemies who are like kin (கேள்போல் பகைவர்). The chapter on internal enmity explains why 584 does not exempt relatives from scrutiny.
links.reason: தம்சுற்றம் is among those the spy examines in 584, and கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு in 882 gives a reason; கேள்போல் means posing as kin or friends, so the fit is good though not exact.

links.note: 585 requires of a spy an unsuspected appearance, not flinching before eyes (கண்ணஞ்சாது) and never letting anything out; 686 requires of an envoy that he not fear the eye (கண் அஞ்சான்), which Parimelazhagar glosses in both verses as the angry look of the other side. The open agent and the covert one are given the same nerve; what differs is that the envoy must speak so it goes home, and the spy must give nothing away.
links.reason: கண்ணஞ்சாது (585) and கண் அஞ்சான் (686) are the same phrase, and Parimelazhagar glosses both as not fearing the other's angry look (செயிர்த்து நோக்கிய).

links.note: 585 ends with the spy's ability never to let anything spill (யாண்டும் உகாஅமை); 689 wants the bearer of a king's message to be a hard man whose mouth does not let slip a damaging word (the edition prints வாய்சேரா; Parimelazhagar reads வாய் சோரா). Both make control of what leaves the mouth under pressure the test of the king's agents abroad.
links.reason: 585 யாண்டும் உகாஅமை (Parimelazhagar: not spilling what is in the mind even under all four means) and 689 வடுமாற்றம் வாய்சோரா வன்கணவன் both test the king's agent by what he does not let out of his mouth.
links.text_issue: 689 prints வாய்சேரா where the commentary reads வாய்சோரா.

links.note: 276 says none are more hard-hearted than those who, unrenounced at heart, live by deceiving in the likeness of renouncers (துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து வாழ்வார்); 586 has the spy take the guise of renouncers (துறந்தார் படிவத்தராகி) to get into places and investigate. The conflict holds if 276 condemns the false ascetic guise as such; Parimelazhagar narrows 276 to cheating donors, and on that reading the spy's disguise in the king's service falls outside it.
links.reason: துறந்தார் படிவத்தராகி (586) against துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து வாழ்வார் (276) is a real conflict if 276 condemns the false guise as such, and the note states that condition and the narrowing reading that removes it.

links.note: 695 tells those who serve a king not to listen in on or press after anything when a secret (மறை) is in progress, and to hear it only when he releases it; 587 makes the ability to hear concealed things (மறைந்தவை கேட்க வற்றாகி) the definition of a spy. The pairing marks a boundary: prying into secrets is a skill the king directs at others, and a fault when his own attendants turn it on him.
links.reason: மறைந்தவை கேட்கவற்றாகி defines the spy, while 695 எப்பொருளும் ஓரார் ... விட்டக்கால் கேட்க மறை forbids the attendant the same prying toward the king; the boundary the note draws is in the Tamil.

links.note: 587 defines the spy as able to learn what was concealed and to hold what he has learned without doubt (ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே); 702 ranks with a god the one who knows without doubt what is within another (ஐயப்படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானை). Both prize certain knowledge of what others hide, one gained by inquiry among informants and the other by reading a person's mind from signs.
links.reason: 'அறிந்தவை ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே ஒற்று' and 'ஐயப்படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானை' set the same standard of doubt-free knowledge of what is hidden (மறைந்தவை / அகத்தது) in spying and in reading minds.

links.note: 587 requires the spy to be free of doubt about what he has learned (அறிந்தவை ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே); 588 tells the king to check even such a report (தந்த பொருளையும்) through another spy. The spy's certainty is a quality of the source and not a warrant for the king, who is to keep doubting until reports agree.
links.reason: அறிந்தவை ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே ஒற்று is limited by தந்த பொருளையும் மற்றுமோர் ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றிக் கொளல்: the spy's certainty does not settle it for the king.

links.note: 588 says that even what one spy found and brought should be confirmed through another spy (மற்றுமோர் ஒற்றினால்); 589 adds that spies should be run so that one does not know of another, and that what three say in agreement is to be accepted (மூவர் சொற்றொக்க தேறப்படும்). 589 turns the second opinion of 588 into a procedure: sources kept independent, and a threshold of agreement.
links.reason: 588 மற்றுமோர் ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றிக் கொளல் is cross-checking; 589 ஒற்றொற்றுணராமை ஆள்க and மூவர் சொற்றொக்க தேறப்படும் add independence and a threshold. Accurate.

links.note: 509 says to trust no one without examining and, after examining, to trust what is to be trusted (தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக); 589 says to run spies unknown to one another and to accept what three say in agreement (தேறப்படும்). Both give the same two-step rule, test first and then commit, 509 for persons and 589 for reports.
links.reason: தேராது தேறற்க ... தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக (509) and மூவர் சொற்றொக்க தேறப்படும் (589) share தேறு and the rule of testing before accepting, for persons and for reports.

links.note: 440 says that if a ruler can enjoy what he loves without others knowing of his love (காதல் அறியாமை), his enemies' schemes come to nothing; 590 forbids showing favour to a spy where others can know of it. Both treat a ruler's visible attachments and rewards as information that others can use against him.
links.reason: சிறப்பறிய ஒற்றின்கண் செய்யற்க and காதல காதல் அறியாமை உய்க்கிற்பின் both treat a ruler's visible favour or liking as intelligence for others.

links.note: 590 warns that a king who honours a spy so that others know of it (சிறப்பறிய) has himself let the secret out (புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை); 663 says a deed should be done so that it shows only at the end, since showing midway brings lasting trouble (இடைக்கொட்கின்). In both the actor's own conduct, not an enemy's skill, is what exposes the undertaking.
links.reason: புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை and இடைக்கொட்கின் எற்றா விழுமந் தரும் both concern the actor's own exposure of his business, on Parimelazhagar's reading of கொட்க as 'be revealed'; Manakkudavar reads 663 as turning back midway, which the note does not mention.

links.note: 1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with crores piled up (கோடியுண்டாயினும் இல்); 591 asks whether those without energy really have what they have. Both separate holding goods from having them, 1005 by the test of use and 591 by the test of the holder's drive.
links.reason: உடையது உடையரோ and கோடியுண்டாயினும் இல் both deny that holding goods is having them, by ஊக்கம் and by கொடுப்பது/துய்ப்பது.

links.note: 333 says wealth has the nature of not staying (அற்கா இயல்பிற்று) and concludes that on getting it one should at once do what stays; 592 also says goods do not stay (நில்லாது நீங்கிவிடும்) and concludes that the lasting possession is the inner drive (உள்ளம் உடைமை). Starting from the same fact, the Book of Virtue points to enduring deeds and the Book of Wealth to an inner resource that can make wealth again.
links.reason: Both start from wealth not staying (நில்லாது நீங்கிவிடும் / அற்கா இயல்பிற்று) and draw different lasting things from it: உள்ளம் உடைமை in 592, அற்குப செயல் in 333.

links.note: 617 says the lotus goddess lives in the effort of the unslothful (மடியிலான் தாளுளாள்); 594 says prosperity finds its own way to the person of unwavering energy. Both personify fortune as choosing where it lives by the person's exertion, and neither leaves it to chance.
links.reason: ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும் and மடியிலான் தாளுளாள் தாமரையினாள் both personify fortune as locating itself by a person's exertion.
links.text_issue: 594's first word is truncated ('க்கம்' for ஆக்கம்); 617 prints 'தாளுளான்' where தாளுளாள் is expected.

links.note: 396 says a sand-well yields water as far as it is dug, and understanding as far as one has learned (தொட்டனைத்து... கற்றனைத்து); 595 says a water-flower's stem is as long as the water is deep, and a person's height as great as their inner drive (வெள்ளத்தனைய... உள்ளத்தனையது). Both use a water image and the same 'as much as' construction to state a strict proportion, one for learning and knowledge, the other for drive and stature.
links.reason: 396 தொட்டனைத்து / கற்றனைத்து and 595 வெள்ளத்தனைய / உள்ளத்தனையது share the அனைத்து proportion and a water figure, applied to learning and to drive.

links.note: 619 says that even if a thing cannot come about because of fate (தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும்), effort pays the wage of the body's strain; 596 says a high aim keeps its worth even when it is thrust aside, which Parimelazhagar takes as being denied by fate. Both hold that what fate withholds in outcome does not cancel the value of the striving or the aim.
links.reason: 596's தள்ளினுந் தள்ளாமை நீர்த்து (Parimelazhagar: பால்வகையாற் கூடிற்றில்லையாயினும்) and 619's தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும் ... கூலி தரும் both keep the worth of aim and effort when fate denies the result.

links.note: 774 shows a warrior who has thrown his spear at an elephant pulling out the spear lodged in his own body and laughing; 597 shows the elephant itself holding firm when struck by arrows, as the image of those who do not give way in ruin. In both, a wound taken is the occasion that shows firmness, and the Book of Wealth draws the general rule in 597 that the war chapter acts out in 774.
links.reason: 597's களிறு that பாடூன்றும் under புதையம்பு and 774's warrior who மெய்வேல் பறியா நகும் both show firmness at the moment of being wounded; the simile-versus-scene description is fair.

links.note: 598 says the person without drive does not attain the pride of generosity; 614 says the beneficence of one without effort comes to nothing, like a sword in the hand of a பேடி. 614 adds what happens when such a person tries anyway: the means are present but the capacity to use them is not.
links.reason: 598's உள்ளம் இலாதவர் never reach வள்ளியம்; 614 says the வேளாண்மை of one without தாளாண்மை கெடும் like பேடிகை வாள், extending the same link between drive and generosity.

links.note: 599 says an elephant, though huge and sharp-tusked, fears when a tiger attacks; 763 says a sea of roaring rats perishes when the cobra merely breathes. Both animal pairs teach that bulk or numbers do not decide a contest against an opponent with spirit, 599 of a person's drive and 763 of an army.
links.reason: பரியது கூர்ங்கோட்டது ஆயினும் ... வெரூஉம் and ஒலித்தக்கால் என்னாம் ... நாகம் உயிர்ப்பக் கெடும் both make size or numbers yield to a spirited opponent; Manakkudavar draws the same morals.
links.text_issue: 599 line 2 opens with a corrupted glyph ('஦வ்ருஉம்') where வெரூஉம் is meant.

links.note: 997 says those without human courtesy are like trees even if sharp as a file (மரம்போல்வர்); 600 says those without abundance of drive are trees, differing only in having human form (மரம் மக்களாதலே வேறு). The tree marks the person who lacks what makes one human, but the two verses name different lacks: fellow-feeling in 997, inner drive in 600.
links.reason: மரம் is the figure for the person lacking what makes one human in both (மரம் மக்களாதலே வேறு / மரம்போல்வர்), and the note correctly separates the lack named in each.

links.note: 601 calls the family a lamp that does not dwindle (குடியென்னும் குன்றா விளக்கம்) which dies when the grime of sloth spreads over it (மடியென்னும் மாசூர). 753 calls wealth a lamp that does not fail (பொருளென்னும் பொய்யா விளக்கம்) which goes where its owner intends and cuts the darkness. The same 'X என்னும் ... விளக்கம்' figure is used twice in the Book of Wealth, and Parimelazhagar glosses both as a நந்தா விளக்கு; one lamp is shown dispelling darkness abroad, the other being put out from within.
links.reason: குடியென்னும் குன்றா விளக்கம் and பொருளென்னும் பொய்யா விளக்கம் are the same figure, and Parimelazhagar glosses both as நந்தா விளக்கு as the note says.

links.note: 602 states the negative condition for a family's standing: remove sloth. 1022 states the positive one: the family lengthens (நீளும் குடி) through long work in two things, effort and mature knowledge (ஆள்வினையும் ஆன்ற அறிவும்). Read together, absence of sloth is necessary but 1022 adds knowledge beside effort.
links.reason: மடியை மடியா ஒழுகல் for those who want குடியைக் குடியாக (602) and ஆள்வினையும் ஆன்ற அறிவும் ... நீளும் குடி (1022): negative and positive conditions for the same குடி, with அறிவு added.

links.note: 602 tells those who want their family to be a family (குடியைக் குடியாக வேண்டுபவர்) to live treating sloth as sloth, or killing it (மடியை மடியா ஒழுகல்). 1028 says those who build the family have no season to wait for, and that if they idle and think of their dignity it is ruined (மடிசெய்து மானங் கருதக் கெடும்). 1028 gives 602's rule its practical form: for the family-builder sloth shows up as waiting for the right time and standing on dignity.
links.reason: 602's மடியை மடியா ஒழுகல் for those who want குடியைக் குடியாக is made concrete in 1028's குடிசெய்வார்க்கு இல்லை பருவம், மடிசெய்து மானங் கருதக் கெடும்; Parimelazhagar reads the sloth as waiting on the season.

links.note: 605 treats sloth and its companions as something the ruin-bound choose and desire (காமக் கலன்). 371 says sloth itself arises from a fate of loss (போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). 371 puts a cause behind what 605 describes as a preference, which matches 605's own word கெடுநீரார், people whose nature is already to perish.
links.reason: 605 calls மடி and its companions the காமக் கலன் of கெடுநீரார்; 371 says போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி. 371 places a cause behind what 605 presents as something desired, which fits கெடுநீரார்.

links.note: 605 lists delay, forgetting, sloth and sleep as the craft that those of a ruin-bound nature desire (கெடுநீரார் காமக் கலன்). 920 lists double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those Fortune has cast off (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு). Both verses give a short catalogue and tie it to people already marked for ruin, leaving open whether the listed things cause the ruin or are its sign.
links.reason: Both are short catalogues tied to the already doomed (கெடுநீரார் காமக் கலன் / திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு), and both leave cause and sign undecided, as the note says.

links.note: 605 makes four habits a boat (கலன்) that the ruin-bound love to board; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read it as a vessel that drops its passengers mid-sea, though Parimelazhagar notes others read கலன் as an ornament. 1068 makes begging an unsafe boat (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that splits on the rock of refusal. In both a way of living is a vessel trusted by the person in it and bound to fail him.
links.reason: காமக் கலன் as a boat (Parimelazhagar: விரும்பி ஏறும் மரக்கலம்; Manakkudavar: நடுக்கடலுள் தள்ளும் மரக்கலம்) and ஏமாப்பில் தோணி: a way of life as a failing vessel. The alternative ஆபரணம் reading is reported accurately.

links.note: 606: even when the holdings of those who own the earth come to them (படியுடையார் பற்றமைந்தக் கண்ணும்), the slothful rarely reach an excellent fruit. 591: what makes one 'a possessor' is energy; do those without it possess even what they possess (உடையது உடையரோ)? Both deny that having things amounts to benefiting from them when the inner quality is missing. Parimelazhagar notes another reading of 606 in which the earth-owners' support, not their wealth, is what comes.
links.reason: படியுடையார் பற்றமைந்தக் கண்ணும் மடியுடையார் மாண்பயன் எய்தல் அரிது and உடையது உடையரோ both deny that holding amounts to benefiting without the inner quality; Parimelazhagar's alternative (வேந்தர் துணையாதல்) is reported correctly.

links.note: 606 says the greatest possessions yield the slothful no excellent fruit (மாண்பயன் எய்தல் அரிது). 750 says a fort, whatever excellences it has, is as nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்). The two share the 'ஆகியக் கண்ணும் / அமைந்தக் கண்ணும்' concession: resources do not work without the action of those who hold them.
links.reason: பற்றமைந்தக் கண்ணும் மடியுடையார் மாண்பயன் எய்தல் அரிது and எனைமாட்சித்தாகியக் கண்ணும் வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது share the concessive frame and the point that resources need action.

links.note: 607: the slothful end up hearing words of scorn (எள்ளுஞ் சொல்). 1040: seeing those who sit idle saying 'we have nothing', the good woman called Land laughs (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்). Both give idleness the same penalty, being laughed at, once from people and once from the personified earth.
links.reason: 607 'எள்ளுஞ் சொல் கேட்பர்' and 1040 'நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்' give the idle the same penalty of derision, from people and from the personified land.

links.note: 608: if sloth lodges in one of family standing it puts him into slavery to his enemies (அடிமை புகுத்தி விடும்). 616: absence of effort puts one into want (இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்). The identical closing phrase makes sloth an agent that ushers a person into a condition; the neighbouring chapters thus name two destinations, poverty and subjection, and Parimelazhagar links them in his note on 616, where want leads to destruction by enemies.
links.reason: The identical close புகுத்தி விடும் (அடிமை; இன்மை) makes sloth and lack of effort agents that deliver a person into a state; Parimelazhagar on 616 does add பகைவரான் அழிவர், as the note says.

links.note: 604 says that for the slothful the family dies and faults multiply (குற்றம் பெருகும்). 609 says the fault is destroyed (குற்றம் ... கெடும்) once a man changes his sloth. 609 makes 604's decline reversible; Parimelazhagar goes further and takes 609's faults to include ones that arose from other causes.
links.reason: குற்றம் பெருகும் for the slothful (604) is reversed by மடியாண்மை மாற்றக் கெடும் (609). Parimelazhagar's extension to faults from பிற காரணங்கள் is as cited.

links.note: 609: when a man ends the rule of sloth over him (மடியாண்மை மாற்ற), the fault that came into his குடியாண்மை is gone; Parimelazhagar splits the word into family and manhood, Manakkudavar reads it as the management of the family. 1026 says good manhood is making the management of the house one was born in one's own (நல்லாண்மை ... இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்). 1026 supports reading the two terms of 609 together: manhood is measured in the household, and sloth is what unseats it.
links.reason: குடியாண்மை (609) and நல்லாண்மை ... இல்லாண்மை (1026) connect manhood with managing the family; the note reports the Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar readings of குடியாண்மை correctly.

links.note: 610 gives the unslothful king the whole measured world. 606, in the same chapter, says that even when the wealth of earth-owners arrives the slothful get no excellent fruit from it. Together they separate two things: sloth does not only block gaining the world, it also empties the world of value when it is handed over.
links.reason: The two are complementary, not limiting: மடியிலா மன்னவன் எய்தும் and மடியுடையார் மாண்பயன் எய்தல் அரிது state the positive and negative of one claim, and 606 puts no condition on 610.

links.note: 611: do not flag saying 'it is hard' (அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை), for effort will give the greatness (பெருமை முயற்சி தரும்). 26: those who do what is hard to do are great, those who cannot are small (செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர்). 26 defines greatness by hard deeds as if it were a fixed difference between people; 611 says the greatness needed is itself produced by trying.
links.reason: 26 செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர் and 611 அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை ... பெருமை முயற்சி தரும் share அருமை/பெருமை; Parimelazhagar on 611 (விடாது முயலத் தாம் பெரியராவர்) supports reading effort as the source of the greatness 26 defines.

links.note: 612: guard against the work failing in the doing, because the world has left those who left the work's need undone (வினைக்குறை தீர்ந்தாரின் தீர்ந்தன்று உலகு), on Parimelazhagar's reading; Manakkudavar takes the second line the other way, that the world does not leave those who finish. 670: whatever other firmness they have, the world does not want those who do not want firmness in action (வேண்டாரை வேண்டாது உலகு). Both make the world's regard answer in kind to how a person treats the task.
links.reason: தீர்ந்தாரின் தீர்ந்தன்று உலகு and வேண்டாரை வேண்டாது உலகு share the mirrored-verb figure of the world answering in kind, and the note flags Manakkudavar's opposite construal of 612 honestly.

links.note: 612 warns against abandoning a task midway (வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல்). 674 says the remainder of a task, like the remainder of an enmity, burns like the remainder of a fire (தீயெச்சம் போலத் தெறும்). 674 supplies a reason 612 does not give: the unfinished part is not inert but goes on doing damage.
links.reason: 612 வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல் warns against the half-done task and 674 வினை ... எச்சம் தீயெச்சம் போலத் தெறும் gives the harm the remainder does.

links.note: 613 says the standing of a benefactor rests on labour. 1035 says those whose way is to eat what their hands produce do not beg and give to those who beg without hiding anything (கைசெய்தூண் மாலையவர்). The farming chapter shows 613's general claim in one occupation: the person who works with his hands is the one in a position to give.
links.reason: 613 rests வேளாண்மை என்னும் செருக்கு on தாளாண்மை; 1035 shows கைசெய்தூண் மாலையவர் who இரவார் and ஈவர் கரவாது, the same dependence of giving on one's own labour in the farmer's case.

links.note: 614 says the generosity of a man without effort comes to nothing. 219 says that for a man of good feeling, being poor just is not being able to do the helpful things he would do (செயும்நீர செய்யாது அமைகலா வாறு). 219 shows the same blocked intention from the inside and without blame, so 614's scorn falls only on the case where the lack of means comes from not working.
links.reason: Both concern blocked generosity (வேளாண்மை ... கெடும் / செயும்நீர செய்யாது அமைகலாவாறு), but 219 says nothing about the cause of poverty, so the claimed limit on 614 is the proposer's inference, not a qualification in the text.

links.note: 615 praises the one who wants the work (வினைவிழைவான்) and not pleasure. 901 says those who desire the wife do not reach the excellent fruit, and that this is the very thing those who desire action do not want (வினைவிழையார் வேண்டாப் பொருளும் அது). Both set the desire for action against a desire for enjoyment and use nearly the same word for the man of action.
links.reason: வினைவிழைவான் set against இன்பம் விழையான் (615) matches வினைவிழையார் set against மனைவிழைவார் (901).

links.note: 615 makes the work-loving man a pillar that props his kin (துடைத்தூன்றும் தூண்). 1030 says a family with no good person to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. 1030 states the cost of the absence of the figure 615 praises, with the same verb ஊன்று.
links.reason: 615's துன்பம் துடைத்தூன்றும் தூண் and 1030's அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி ... வீழும் share the verb ஊன்று and the prop figure; 1030 states what happens when the figure 615 praises is absent.

links.note: 616: effort makes fortune (முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும்) and lack of effort brings one into want. 371: unflagging effort arises from a fate of gain, and sloth from a fate of loss (ஆகூழால் தோன்றும் அசைவின்மை ... போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). 616 makes effort the cause of wealth; 371 makes fate the cause of effort, so on 371's account the causal chain in 616 starts one step earlier and is not in the person's hands.
links.reason: முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும் is placed under ஆகூழால் தோன்றும் அசைவின்மை ... போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி, which makes effort itself fate's product.

links.note: 616 says effort produces fortune. 594 says increase asks the way and goes to the one of unwavering drive (அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும் அசைவிலா ஊக்கமுடையானுழை). Both place the source of prosperity in the person's exertion, and 594 pictures it as prosperity doing the seeking. The first word of 594 is truncated in this edition (க்கம் for ஆக்கம்).
links.reason: 616 முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும் and 594 ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும் ... ஊக்கமுடையானுழை both source prosperity in exertion; the note rightly flags the truncated first word.
links.text_issue: 594 opens with க்கம் in this edition; it should read ஆக்கம்.

links.note: 618 separates what is no disgrace (having no luck) from what is (not working). 988 says want is no disgrace to a person who has the firmness called worth (இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று). Both refuse to count an outward lack as shame and move the test to something in the person, effort in one and character in the other.
links.reason: பொறியின்மை யார்க்கும் பழியன்று and இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று both deny that an outward lack is a disgrace and move the test to ஆள்வினை and சால்பு.

links.note: 620 ends 'தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்', those who labour without delay, and says they see fate's back. 1024 ends with the same phrase, 'தம்குடியைத் தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்க்கு', and says that for them the outcome arrives by itself without deliberation (சூழாமல் தானே முடிவெய்தும்). The same people are described twice, once as defeating an opposing power and once as finding the result come unsought.
links.reason: Both end தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்(க்கு), with ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர் and சூழாமல் தானே முடிவெய்தும் as the two results; Manakkudavar construes தாழாது in 1024 differently, which the note does not mention.

links.note: 621 says to laugh when trouble comes (இடுக்கண் வருங்கால் நகுக), since nothing presses it back as well. 774 shows a warrior who, having thrown his spear at an elephant, pulls out the one lodged in his own body and laughs (மெய்வேல் பறியா நகும்). The battlefield verse acts out the advice of 621: the laugh comes at the moment of injury, and the injury is turned to use.
links.reason: இடுக்கண் வருங்கால் நகுக is enacted by மெய்வேல் பறியா நகும்; the commentators have him glad because the spear in his body gives him a weapon.

links.note: Both verses turn on the same play of உள்ளம் (mind) and உள்ளுதல் (to think): in 622 a flood of suffering perishes when the wise person thinks with the mind (உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளக் கெடும்), and in 309 all one has thought of is gained if one does not think anger in the mind (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளான் வெகுளி எனின்). Read together they make a single act of thought decide the outcome, once by what is thought and once by what is left unthought.
links.reason: உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளக் கெடும் (622) and உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளான் வெகுளி எனின் (309) share the distinctive உள்ளம்/உள்ளுதல் play, with thinking and not-thinking deciding the result in each.

links.note: 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that arrives to shake them; 622 says that for the person of understanding (அறிவுடையான்) even a flood of suffering already present is ended by thinking. The pair gives understanding two jobs, forestalling trouble and dissolving the trouble that came anyway, which Parimelazhagar takes in 622 to be trouble from fate.
links.reason: 429 எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார் forestalls trouble, 622 அறிவுடையான் உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளக் கெடும் dissolves trouble already present; Parimelazhagar does say 622 concerns ஊழினான் ஆய இடுக்கண்.

links.note: 623 says those who do not suffer at suffering (இடும்பைக்கு இடும்பை படாஅதவர்) make suffering itself suffer; Parimelazhagar places this in the middle of an undertaking. 261 makes bearing the pain that comes (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்) half of the form of தவம். The same endurance is a means to finishing work in one book and the definition of austerity in the other.
links.reason: இடும்பைக்கு இடும்பை படாஅதவர் and உற்றநோய் நோன்றல் describe the same endurance, as a means in the Book of Wealth and as the form of தவம் in the Book of Virtue.

links.note: 624 likens the person who pulls through every obstruction to a draught ox (மடுத்தவாயெல்லாம் பகடன்னான்) and says the trouble he meets is itself troubled. 597 says the strong do not give way where things break down (சிதைவிடத்து ஒல்கார்), like an elephant standing firm under arrows. Both make the same claim through a working or fighting animal; the ox adds forward motion to the elephant's holding of ground.
links.reason: பகடன்னான் pulling through மடுத்தவாயெல்லாம் and the களிறு that பாடூன்றும் under arrows both picture not yielding to adversity (சிதைவிடத்து ஒல்கார்) through a working or war animal.

links.note: 624 says trouble is troubled by one who hauls on like an ox through every blocked place. 620 carries the claim to its limit: those who labour on without flagging (தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்) see the back even of fate (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்). What 624 says of obstacles in the road, 620 says of the power behind them.
links.reason: 624's பகடன்னான் makes இடுக்கண் itself suffer; 620's தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர் see ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம், the same claim raised to fate.

links.note: 625 says that though troubles come stacked (அடுக்கி வரினும்), those of one who is not undone (அழிவிலான்) are themselves in trouble. 989 says those called the shore of worth do not shift even if the age shifts (ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம் பெயரார்). Both define a person by not moving under pressure, one in the chapter on a king's undertakings and one in the chapter on character.
links.reason: Both praise steadfastness (அழிவிலான்; ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம்பெயரார்), but 625 is about not being broken by piled-up இடுக்கண் and 989 about constancy in சான்றாண்மை. The common ground is a generic 'unmoved' theme, and 625's chapter is on not being undone by trouble, not on a king's undertakings.

links.note: 1045 states as plain fact that within the one suffering called poverty many sufferings arrive and settle (பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும்), and offers no remedy. 625 addresses exactly such piling up (அடுக்கி வரினும்) and says it fails against one who is not undone. Set side by side, 625's confidence is conditional on the person, while 1045 describes what the stacking is like for those in want.
links.reason: அடுக்கி வரினும் and பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும் both describe troubles in number, but 625 does not speak of poverty and neither verse limits the other. The note's 'conditional on the person' is already 625's own condition (அழிவிலான்), so the qualification is thin.

links.note: 629 makes freedom from pain depend on not desiring pleasure when it is present (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்). 4 describes the Lord as one without wanting or not-wanting (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்) and says those who reach his feet never have இடும்பை. The same link between having no pull toward or away from things and having no suffering appears as a divine attribute in Book 1 and as a human discipline here.
links.reason: இன்பம் விழையாதான் ... துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன் and வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான் ... இடும்பை இல both tie absence of wanting to absence of suffering; in 4 the freedom comes by reaching his feet, which the note states correctly.

links.note: 629 says one who does not crave pleasure in the midst of pleasure does not suffer in the midst of pain. 115 says loss and increase are both part of life and that not letting the heart bend (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை) is the ornament of the worthy. Both ask for the same evenness across good and bad turns; 115 treats it as fairness of mind, 629 as protection against pain.
links.reason: இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான் ... துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன் and கேடும் பெருக்கமும் ... நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை both ask for steadiness through good and bad turns, under different headings.

links.note: 669 says to do with resolve the deed that yields joy even though pain comes thick at first (துன்பம் உறவரினும் ... இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை): pain now, joy later. 630 goes a step further and has the person take the pain itself as joy (இன்னாமை இன்பம் எனக்கொளின்). Parimelazhagar reads the pain in both as the strain of effort.
links.reason: 669's துன்பம் உறவரினும் செய்க ... இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை is pain now for joy later; 630's இன்னாமை இன்பம் எனக்கொளின் takes the pain itself as joy. Parimelazhagar reads both as முயற்சித் துன்பம், as stated.

links.note: 630 measures the reward by the enemy: a distinction one's foes desire or esteem (ஒன்னார் விழையும் சிறப்பு). 810 uses the same measure with the same verb: those who do not depart from their nature toward old friends are wanted even by those who do not want them (விழையார் விழையப்படுப). Each verse marks an unusual constancy, under pain or toward friends who have erred, by saying that even the hostile regard it.
links.reason: ஒன்னார் விழையும் சிறப்பு (630) and விழையார் விழையப்படுப (810) both measure a constancy by the regard of the hostile, with the same verb விழை.

links.note: 641 sets the good of the tongue above every other good. 411 calls the wealth of the ear the wealth among wealths and the head of them all (செல்வத்துள் எல்லாம் தலை). The book gives the top place once to listening and once to speaking, in chapters addressed to the learner and to the minister.
links.reason: 641 நாநலம் ... யாநலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று and 411 செவிச்செல்வம் ... செல்வத்துள் எல்லாம் தலை make the same superlative move for tongue and ear.

links.note: The two verses end with the same formula, 'அந்நலம்/பிறநலம் யா/எந்நலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று', used in opposite directions. In 641 the goodness of the tongue (நாநலம்) is not contained in any other goodness, which Parimelazhagar takes to mean it exceeds them all; in 982 every goodness other than the goodness of character (குணநலம்) is not counted among goodnesses at all. One chapter ranks eloquence highest for a minister, the other ranks character alone for the worthy.
links.reason: The closing formula யாநலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று / எந்நலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று is near-identical and applied to நாநலம் vs பிறநலம் in opposite directions, as the note says.

links.note: 642 says ruin as well as gain comes from speech and asks for vigilance against slips. 128 gives the scale of the risk: if even one harmful word has its effect (ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல்), the good turns to no good (நன்றாகாதாகி விடும்). 128 supplies the reason why 642 treats a lapse (சோர்வு), and not only deliberate bad speech, as the danger.
links.reason: 642 காத்தோம்பல் சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு and 128 ஒன்றானுந் தீச்சொல் ... நன்றாகா தாகி விடும் fit as rule and scale of risk; the note slightly overstates in saying 128 'supplies the reason', since 642 gives its own (ஆக்கமுங் கேடும்).

links.note: Parimelazhagar reads 643 as speech that binds those who have accepted one as a friend (கேட்டார்ப் பிணிக்கும்) and makes even those who have not want friendship. 187 gives the failure of this skill: those who do not know how to make friends with pleasing talk (நகச்சொல்லி நட்பாடல் தேற்றாதவர்) part even their own kin with divisive talk. On that reading the two verses are the positive and negative of one ability, speech as what holds or breaks alliances.
links.reason: On Parimelazhagar's friend/foe reading of கேட்டார்ப் பிணிக்கும் ... கேளாரும் வேட்ப, 187's நகச்சொல்லி நட்பாடல் தேற்றாதவர் ... கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர் is the same ability failing; the note marks the dependence on that reading.

links.note: 644 says to speak after knowing the திறன் of those concerned. 469 says that even in doing good there is error when it is done without knowing each person's character (அவரவர் பண்பறிந்து ஆற்றாக்கடை). Both make a good thing, a word or a deed, depend on fitting it to the particular person receiving it.
links.reason: 644 திறனறிந்து சொல்லுக and 469 அவரவர் பண்பறிந்து ஆற்றாக்கடை both make a good word or deed depend on knowing the particular person.

links.note: 644 asks for speech fitted to its hearers and says no virtue or gain exceeds it. 696 applies this to a single hearer, the king: know his mood, consider the time, and say what is needed in a way he will want (குறிப்பறிந்து காலம் கருதி ... வேட்பச் சொலல்). The general rule for a minister's speech becomes a specific rule for speech to power.
links.reason: திறனறிந்து சொல்லுக is the general rule and குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி ... வேட்பச் சொலல் applies it to speech before a king.

links.note: 644 says to speak knowing the திறன், which Parimelazhagar takes as the relative standing of speaker and hearers. 711 gives the method: those who know the stock of words should speak after knowing the assembly and examining (அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து சொல்லுக). Chapter 72 works out as a practice what 644 states as a principle.
links.reason: 644 திறனறிந்து சொல்லுக is worked out as அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து சொல்லுக in 711; Manakkudavar even glosses தொகையறிதல் as திறனறிதல்.
links.text_issue: 711: 'அவையறிநது' is a typo for அவையறிந்து.

links.note: 645 says to speak a word only after knowing that no other word can defeat it (வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து). 467 says to think and then commit to a task, and that saying 'we will think after committing' is a fault (எண்ணித் துணிக). Both put the testing before the irreversible step; 645 applies to an utterance the rule 467 gives for action.
links.reason: Both say to test first (அறிந்து சொல்லுக / எண்ணித் துணிக), but that is a generic think-before-you-act likeness; 645 is specifically about a word no other word can beat, and 'irreversible step' is the note's addition.

links.note: 646 pairs speaking well with drawing the benefit from others' words. 724 sets that pair in the assembly of the learned: make what you have learned go home to them (கற்ற செலச்சொல்லி) and take what is more from those who know more (மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்). 724 adds what 646 leaves open, that listening is how the speaker's own knowledge grows.
links.reason: 646's சொல்லிப் பிறர்சொல் பயன்கோடல் is restated for the learned assembly in 724's செலச்சொல்லி ... மிக்க கொளல், with the gain specified as further learning.

links.note: 647 lists three things that make a person hard to beat in a contest: able to speak, free of lapses, unafraid (சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான்). 686 defines the envoy with nearly the same set: learned, not afraid of hostile eyes (கண் அஞ்சான்), speaking so it goes home, and knowing what fits the time. The envoy chapter puts the general portrait of 647 into the one post where it is tested before an enemy.
links.reason: 647's 'சொலல்வல்லன்... அஞ்சான்' matches 686's 'கண் அஞ்சான் செலச்சொல்லி'; the envoy portrait repeats the fearless, effective speaker (சோர்விலன் has no exact twin, and 'develops' would fit as well, but the claim holds).

links.note: 647 says no one can easily defeat a fearless, unfaltering speaker in a contest (இகல் வெல்லல் யார்க்கும் அரிது). 872 gives the advice that follows for the other side: take on the enmity of those whose plough is the bow if you must, but not of those whose plough is the word (சொல்லேர் உழவர் பகை). Parimelazhagar takes the latter to be ministers, the people 647 describes.
links.reason: அவனை இகல்வெல்லல் யார்க்கும் அரிது gives the reason for கொள்ளற்க சொல்லேர் உழவர் பகை; Parimelazhagar (சொல் = நீதிநூல், சூழ்ச்சி) and Manakkudavar (அமைச்சர்) take them as ministers.

links.note: 648 says the world listens readily to skilled, pleasing speakers. 1046 says the words of the poor go slack even when they speak good matter that they have understood well (நற்பொருள் நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லினும் ... சோர்வு படும்). 1046 limits 648: how the world receives speech depends on the speaker's means as well as his skill.
links.reason: 648 says ஞாலம் விரைந்து தொழில்கேட்கும் for skilled speakers, and 1046 says நல்கூர்ந்தார் சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும் even when the speech is நன்குணர்ந்து. 1046 adds the speaker's means as a condition.

links.note: 649 treats wanting to say many things as the sign of someone unable to say a few well. 193 says spread-out talk on useless matters (பயனில பாரித்துரைக்கும் உரை) itself announces that the speaker lacks நயன். In both, length of speech is evidence against the speaker; 193 judges his character, 649 his skill.
links.reason: பலசொல்லக் காமுறுவர் ... சிலசொல்லல் தேற்றாதவர் and பயனில பாரித்துரைக்கும் உரை both take lengthy speech as evidence against the speaker, of skill in one and of நயன் in the other.

links.note: 649 faults many words and praises a few faultless ones; the next verse faults those who cannot expound what they have learned so that others understand (உணர விரித்துரையாதார்). Manakkudavar reads the pair together: speak briefly, but also expand where it is needed. 650 keeps 649 from being taken as a rule of brevity alone.
links.reason: சில சொல்லல் தேற்றாதவர் is balanced by கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்; Manakkudavar on 650 does say சுருங்கச் சொல்லுதலே யன்றி வேண்டுமிடத்து விரித்துச் சொல்லல் வேண்டும்.
links.text_issue: 650 prints இண்ருழ்த்தும் for இணரூழ்த்தும்.

links.note: 649 says those who cannot say a few faultless words (மாசற்ற சில சொல்லல் தேற்றாதவர்) long to say many. 685 makes brevity the envoy's first mark: he speaks compactly (தொகச் சொல்லி), drops what is harsh, and speaks so as to please. 685 shows the positive skill whose absence 649 describes.
links.reason: 649 faults those who cannot say மாசற்ற சில சொல்லல் and so want பலசொல்ல; 685's தொகச் சொல்லி is that skill named as the envoy's first mark.

links.note: Both verses use a flower's scent (நாற்றம்) for what is inside a person. In 650 the flower is fully open and gives no scent, like the learned person who cannot convey what he knows; in 1274 the scent is held inside a closed bud, like the unspoken meaning inside the girl's budding smile. The two uses mirror each other: an open display with nothing reaching others, and a closed one whose content the lover already perceives.
links.reason: இணரூழ்த்தும் நாறா மலர் and முகைமொக்குள் உள்ளது நாற்றம் use a flower's scent for inner content, in mirrored ways as the note says.
links.text_issue: 650 base text reads இண்ருழ்த்தும், a typo for இணரூழ்த்தும்.

links.note: 651 sets வினைநலம் above துணைநலம்: support gives only ஆக்கம், good action gives all that is wanted. 455 says purity of mind and purity of action (செய்வினை தூய்மை) both come leaning on purity of company (இனந்தூய்மை தூவா வரும்). Read together, the action that 651 ranks above one's support is itself said to depend on the people one keeps.
links.reason: 651 ranks வினைநலம் over துணைநலம், while 455 makes செய்வினை தூய்மை come only with இனந்தூய்மை as its prop (தூவா வரும்); the second does condition the first, allowing that துணை (allies) and இனம் (company) are near, not identical, terms.

links.note: 653 tells those who say 'ஆஅதும்' (we shall rise) to stop doing what dims their ஒளி. 962 says those who want சீர் together with பேராண்மை will not do 'சீரல்ல' even for the sake of சீர். 962 takes the harder case 653 leaves open: the dimming deed may itself be a route to fame, and it is still refused.
links.reason: 653 bars ஒளிமாழ்கும் செய்வினை for those who say ஆஅதும், and 962's சீரினும் சீரல்ல செய்யாரே extends the bar to cases where the deed would itself bring சீர்.

links.note: 653 treats ஒளி as something the ambitious ('ஆஅதும் என்னுமவர்') must protect by refraining from certain deeds. 971 defines ஒளி as 'உள்ள வெறுக்கை', abundance of spirit, and இளி as saying one will live without it. Together they give ஒளி two sides: it is lost by what one does (653) and it consists in what one aspires to (971).
links.reason: 653's ஒளிமாழ்கும் செய்வினை and 971's ஒளி ஒருவற்கு உள்ள வெறுக்கை share ஒளி, and 653's ஆஅதும் என்னுமவர் connects with 971's aspiration; the two-sided account is a fair synthesis.
links.text_issue: 971's Parimelazhagar text prints இனி for இளி.

links.note: 654 says those of unshaken sight do nothing degrading even in distress (இடுக்கண் படினும்). 174 says those of 'புன்மையில் காட்சி' who have conquered the senses will not covet on the plea 'இலம்' (we have nothing). Both verses name a clear-sighted person (காட்சியவர்) and deny that need is an excuse; 174 applies it to coveting, 654 to action generally.
links.reason: Both close on காட்சியவர் and refuse need as an excuse: இடுக்கண் படினும் இளிவந்த செய்யார் and இலமென்று வெஃகுதல் செய்யார்.

links.note: 654: clear-sighted people do not do what is degrading even when trouble comes. 218: those of 'கடனறி காட்சி' do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும் ... ஒல்கார்). One verse says hardship does not make them do wrong, the other that it does not make them stop doing good; the two are the negative and positive halves of the same steadiness.
links.reason: Parallel closings நடுக்கற்ற காட்சியவர் / கடனறி காட்சியவர், with இடுக்கண் படினும் இளிவந்த செய்யார் and இடனில் பருவத்தும் ... ஒல்கார் as the negative and positive of steadiness in hardship.

links.note: 655 asks that one not do what will be regretted afterwards. 467 says to think and then resolve (எண்ணித் துணிக), and calls it a lapse to say 'we will think after resolving'. Both put the reflection before the act: 467 as a rule of planning, 655 as a rule about the purity of the deed.
links.reason: எண்ணித் துணிக is about deliberating before deciding, while எற்றென்று இரங்குவ செய்யற்க forbids regrettable deeds and does not mention prior reflection; the link is a generic 'think before acting'.

links.note: 656 forbids the blameworthy deed even when the need is a mother's hunger. 961 says to give up things that would diminish one (குன்ற வருப விடல்) even if they are indispensable (இன்றி அமையாச் சிறப்பின ஆயினும்). Both deny that necessity licenses a degrading act; 961 states the principle abstractly under honour, 656 gives it a concrete and painful instance.
links.reason: ஈன்றாள் பசிகாண்பான் ஆயினும் செய்யற்க and இன்றி அமையாச் சிறப்பின ஆயினும் குன்ற வருப விடல் both deny that necessity licenses a degrading act.
