links.note: 656 uses the mother who bore one (ஈன்றாள்) as the strongest pull toward wrongdoing for the sake of relief. 1047 says that one in poverty not joined with virtue (அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு) is looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும்). The mother marks the limit case in both: 656 holds conduct firm against her need, while 1047 says poverty without virtue loses even her regard.
links.reason: ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பானாயினும் and ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல நோக்கப்படும் both use the birth-mother as the limiting case, with an accurate contrast.

links.note: 657: the extreme poverty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு) is better than wealth got by taking on blame (பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கம்). 408: wealth lodged with the unlearned (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு) is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (நல்லார்கண் பட்ட வறுமை). The same comparison of good people's poverty with bad people's wealth is made from each side, once about how wealth was got and once about who holds it.
links.reason: சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு above பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கம், and கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு worse than நல்லார்கண் பட்ட வறுமை: the same ranking of good people's poverty over bad wealth, by manner of gain and by holder.

links.note: 657 ranks the utter poverty of the worthy above blame-laden wealth. 988 says poverty (இன்மை) is no disgrace (இளிவன்று) to one who has the firmness called சால்பு. 988 supplies the ground for 657's ranking: for the சான்றோர் poverty carries no இளிவு, whereas the wealth in 657 carries பழி.
links.reason: 657's சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவே தலை and 988's இன்மை ... இளிவன்று சால்பென்னும் திண்மை make the same ranking; பழி vs இளிவு contrast is accurate.

links.note: 658: forbidden deeds done without shunning them bring anguish even if they succeed (முடிந்தாலும் பீழை தரும்). 113: give up at once gain that comes from leaving fairness, even if it brings nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும்). Both concede success in advance and still reject the act, so the objection is not that such means fail.
links.reason: முடிந்தாலும் பீழை தரும் and நன்றே தரினும் ... ஒழிய விடல் both grant success first and still reject the act.

links.note: 658 warns that the gain of a forbidden deed turns to பீழை later. 177 says not to want gain that comes by coveting (வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம்), because at the time of enjoying it the fruit is hard to make good (விளைவயின் மாண்டற்கு அரிதாம் பயன்). Both place the harm at the stage of the result and not at the stage of getting.
links.reason: முடிந்தாலும் பீழை தரும் and விளைவயின் மாண்டற்கு அரிதாம் பயன் both put the harm of wrongful gain at the stage of its fruit.

links.note: 658 says forbidden actions bring anguish even when they are accomplished. 931 says not to want gambling even if one wins (வென்றிடினும்), since the winnings are like the hook a fish has swallowed. The gambling verse gives an image for 658's claim: the success itself is what carries the harm.
links.reason: 658 'முடிந்தாலும் பீழை தரும்' and 931 'வென்றிடினும்... தூண்டிற்பொன் மீன்விழுங்கி அற்று' both say success itself carries the harm, in forbidden deeds and in gambling.

links.note: The second half of 659 says what comes from good ways (நற்பாலவை) yields later even if it is lost (இழப்பினும் பிற்பயக்கும்). 112 says the wealth of a person of rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security for those who come after (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). Both give rightly got wealth a benefit that outlasts the moment, 659 for the person later and 112 for descendants.
links.reason: இழப்பினும் பிற்பயக்கும் நற்பாலவை and செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம் சிதைவின்றி எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு both give uprightly held wealth a lasting return, though 112's செப்பம் is impartiality rather than strictly 'rightly got'.

links.note: 660: wealth made by deceit is water kept in an unfired clay vessel. 1000: great wealth obtained by one without character is good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). Both use a faulty கலம் for wealth that cannot be kept, but the fault differs: in 660 it is how the wealth was made, in 1000 it is the holder's character.
links.reason: பசுமண் கலத்துள் நீர் and நன்பால் கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று both use a faulty கலம் for wealth that fails, and the note marks the difference in where the fault lies.

links.note: 661: firmness in action is a person's firmness of mind (மனத்திட்பம்); everything else is something other (மற்றைய எல்லாம் பிற). 34: being spotless in mind (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல்) is all of virtue; the rest is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர பிற). The two verses have the same shape, reducing a whole domain to a state of mind and dismissing the remainder as 'பிற', once for virtue and once for effective action.
links.reason: Same construction: மனத்திட்பம் / மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் as the whole of the thing, and the remainder dismissed with பிற (மற்றைய எல்லாம் பிற; ஆகுல நீர பிற).

links.note: 661 locates firmness in action in the mind and sets other things aside. 600 says a person's real strength (உரம்) is abundance of spirit (உள்ள வெறுக்கை), and those without it are trees. Both place strength within the person; Parimelazhagar's note on 661 lists the outer things meant by 'மற்றைய' as the firmness of army, fort and allies.
links.reason: வினைத்திட்பம் ... மனத்திட்பம் and உரம் ... உள்ள வெறுக்கை both place strength within, and Parimelazhagar's gloss of மற்றைய as படை, அரண், நட்பு is as the note cites.

links.note: 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that comes to shake them. 662 keeps that first rule (ஊறொரால்) but adds a second for when harm arrives anyway (உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை). 662 thus allows that foresight is not always enough; Parimelazhagar reads the second case as a task spoiled by fate.
links.reason: 429 says எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்க்கு இல்லை ... நோய்; 662 keeps ஊறொரால் but adds உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை, which presupposes that harm can still arrive. A genuine limit on 429.

links.note: 662 gives two rules as the way of those who have studied the matter: avoid harm (ஊறொரால்) and do not give way once it has come (உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை). 442 tells a king to cherish those who remove the trouble that has come (உற்றநோய் நீக்கி) and guard beforehand against what has not (உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும்). The same before-and-after pair appears as the doer's own discipline in 662 and as the quality to look for in advisers in 442.
links.reason: ஊறொரால் / உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை and உற்றநோய் நீக்கி / உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும் are the same before-and-after pair built on உறு, for the doer in one and for his advisers in the other, on Parimelazhagar's reading of 662.

links.note: 664: saying is easy for anyone; doing as one has said (சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்) is hard. 819: the bond with those whose deed is one thing and word another (வினைவேறு சொல்வேறு பட்டார்) is bitter even in a dream. 664 states the gap between word and deed as a difficulty of execution; 819 judges the same gap in a friend as a fault of character.
links.reason: 664's சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல் அரிய is about the difficulty of carrying out a stated plan, while 819's வினைவேறு சொல்வேறு பட்டார் is about duplicity in a friend; they share the word/deed topic but one does not extend the other, and 'the same gap' overstates it.

links.note: 666: what one has thought of is obtained as thought, if one is firm. 309: all one has thought of is obtained at once (உள்ளிய தெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்), if one does not think of anger in the heart. The same promise is attached to two different inner conditions, one positive (firmness) and one negative (absence of anger).
links.reason: எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப ... திண்ணியர் ஆகப்பெறின் and உள்ளியதெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும் ... உள்ளான் வெகுளி எனின் attach the same promise to firmness and to freedom from anger.
links.text_issue: 666 எய்து lacks its final ப (எய்துப).

links.note: 667: do not scorn anyone on seeing their form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை), for there are people like the linchpin (அச்சாணி) of a great rolling chariot. 1032: those who plough are the ஆணி of the world's people, because they bear all who cannot plough and take up other work. Both use the pin that holds the wheel for someone small in appearance on whom everything turns; 667 leaves the person unnamed and 1032 names the farmer. Parimelazhagar supplies the smallness in 667 from the simile.
links.reason: 'அச்சாணி அன்னார்' in 667 and 'உழுவார் உலகத்தார்க்கு ஆணி' in 1032 share the linchpin figure for those on whom all else turns; smallness is explicit only in 667 ('உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை'), a minor overreach for 1032, and Parimelazhagar is cited correctly.

links.note: 467 says to think and then resolve on a task, and that saying 'we will think after resolving' is a lapse. 668 takes up from that point: once the task has been seen without confusion (கலங்காது கண்ட), act without wavering (துளங்காது). Together they give a sequence in which doubt belongs before the decision and not after it.
links.reason: எண்ணித் துணிக and கலங்காது கண்ட வினைக்கண் துளங்காது form a sequence: deliberate before resolving, then act without wavering. 668 presupposes what 467 demands.

links.note: 668: in a task one has seen clearly and decided on (கலங்காது கண்ட வினை), act without wavering and without delay (தூக்கங் கடிந்து). 671, opening the next chapter, says deliberation ends in reaching resolve (துணிவு) and it is bad for that resolve to rest in delay (தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). The same rule closes the chapter on firmness and opens the chapter on method: once the thinking is done, delay is the fault.
links.reason: தூக்கங் கடிந்து செயல் after கலங்காது கண்ட வினை matches துணிவு ... தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது: the same rule against delay after decision in adjacent chapters.

links.note: 669 says to carry through the worthwhile deed despite the pain it brings at first. 611 says one must not slacken on the thought that a thing is hard (அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை), since effort gives the greatness needed. Both refuse the difficulty of a task as a reason to hold back; 611 speaks of effort and 669 of resolve (துணிவு).
links.reason: துன்பம் உறவரினும் செய்க and அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை both refuse hardship as a reason to hold back; the note reads both accurately.

links.note: 669: do with resolve the deed that yields joy (இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை), even though pain comes close at first (துன்பம் உறவரினும்). 615: one who does not want pleasure but wants the work (இன்பம் விழையான் வினை விழைவான்) is a pillar who wipes away his kin's துன்பம். Both set இன்பம், துன்பம் and வினை against each other; 669 justifies bearing pain by the joy the deed yields, while 615 describes a doer who is not after pleasure at all and whose work removes others' pain.
links.reason: Both set இன்பம், துன்பம் and வினை together: 669 bears துன்பம் for இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை, while 615's doer is இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான் and wipes away others' துன்பம்; the note states the difference correctly.

links.note: 670: whatever other firmness they have attained (எனைத்திட்பம் எய்தியக் கண்ணும்), the world does not want those who do not want firmness in action. 750: whatever excellences it has (எனைமாட்சித்து ஆகியக் கண்ணும்), a fort is nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண்). The two chapter-closing verses are built alike and make the same point, that other strengths count for nothing without the capacity to act, once of a minister and once of a fort's defenders.
links.reason: எனைத்திட்பம் எய்தியக் கண்ணும் வினைத்திட்பம் and எனைமாட்சித் தாகியக் கண்ணும் வினைமாட்சி are built identically and both close their chapters with the point that nothing counts without capacity in action.

links.note: 490 says to be like the heron in the season for folding up (கூம்பும் பருவத்து) and like its strike when the moment is right (சீர்த்த இடத்து). 672 gives the same double instruction without the image: take time over what is to be done slowly, and do not delay what must not be delayed. Both hold that waiting and speed are each correct in their place.
links.reason: கூம்பும் பருவத்து / சீர்த்த இடத்து (490) and தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால / தூங்கற்க (672) give the same two-sided rule on waiting and speed in different chapters.

links.note: 671 calls it a fault when a resolved deed lingers in delay (தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). 672 immediately limits this: there are deeds to be done slowly, and over those one should take time (தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால); only the deed that must be done without delay must not be slept on. Delay is therefore wrong by the nature of the task, not in itself.
links.reason: தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது is limited at once by தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால; adjacent verses, read correctly.

links.note: 485 says those who have the world in mind wait, unshaken, with their mind on the time (காலம் கருதி இருப்பர்). Manakkudavar reads the second half of 673 in that sense: when the deed is not possible, keep it in mind and act on seeing the place where it becomes possible. Parimelazhagar reads 673 differently, as open force where one is stronger and one of the other three expedients where one is not, so the link holds on Manakkudavar's reading.
links.reason: The verse itself only says ஒல்லாக்கால் செல்லும்வாய் நோக்கிச் செயல், but Manakkudavar does gloss it as waiting and watching for the time, which matches காலம் கருதி இருப்பர்; the note states that dependence honestly.
links.text_issue: 673 prints ஙல்லும்வா யெல்லாம்; it should read ஒல்லும்வா யெல்லாம்.

links.note: 462 says nothing is hard to attain for those who act after examining a matter with chosen company (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு) and thinking it over themselves. 677 narrows whose counsel counts for a particular task: the one who knows that deed from inside (அவ்வினை உள்ளறிவான்), whom Parimelazhagar takes to be someone who has done it before. General consultation in 462 becomes, in 677, learning the mind of the person with experience of the task.
links.reason: 462 'தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி' is general consultation; 677 'அவ்வினை உள்ளறிவான் உள்ளம் கொளல்' narrows it to the one who knows the task from inside.

links.note: 678 says to get one deed done by means of another, as one binds an elephant with a rutting elephant (யானையால் யானையாத் தற்று). Manakkudavar takes this as setting an enemy's own enemy against him. On that reading 875 is the case worked out: one who is alone with two enemies should take one of them as an ally (இன்துணையாக் கொள்க அவற்றின் ஒன்று). Parimelazhagar reads 678 more generally, as making a task in hand the means to another like it.
links.reason: Manakkudavar does read யானையால் யானையாத்தற்று as using an enemy's enemy, which 875's பகையிரண்டால் ... இன்துணையாக் கொள்கவற்றின் ஒன்று works out; note correctly flags Parimelazhagar's more general reading.

links.note: 875 says that one without allies and facing two enemies should take one of them as a pleasing ally. 679 says that winning over ஒட்டார் is more urgent than favours to friends; Manakkudavar takes ஒட்டார் as one's enemies, Parimelazhagar as those not allied with one's enemy. On either reading both verses treat alliance as something to be made out of the hostile or uncommitted when one is pressed.
links.reason: ஒட்டாரை ஒட்டிக் கொளல் and பகையிரண்டால் ... இன்துணையாக் கொள்கவற்றின் ஒன்று both make allies out of the non-aligned or hostile, and the note reports both commentators' senses of ஒட்டார் correctly.

links.note: 488 says to bear with enemies on meeting them (செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க), for when their end comes their head will go down; Parimelazhagar glosses சுமக்க as bowing. 680 has the small bow to the great to obtain terms. 488 adds what 680 does not say: that such bowing can be a way of waiting for the stronger side's fall.
links.reason: 488 செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க (Parimelazhagar: பணிக) until இறுவரை adds the waiting motive to 680 பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து கொள்வர்.

links.note: 861 says to avoid standing against the strong (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக). 680 describes what that means for a weak party: those of small domain, fearing the trembling of their own side (உள்நடுங்கல் அஞ்சி), bow to the greater and accept terms if they can get them (குறைபெறின் கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து). 861 gives the rule and 680 the settlement that follows from it.
links.reason: 861 வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக and 680 உறைசிறியார் ... கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து both say the weaker side should not resist the stronger; the note reads both accurately.

links.note: 967, on honour, says it is better to be called ruined as one stands than to live by going behind those who are hostile to one (ஒட்டார்பின் சென்று வாழ்தலின்). 680 says the small will bow to the great and take what terms they can. The conflict depends on reading 967's ஒட்டார் as covering a stronger enemy; Parimelazhagar limits it to following scorners for a living, but he also remarks on 680 that bowing is not the wish of those with honour, which is why the verse says 'they will accept' as a report of worldly practice.
links.reason: பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து கொள்வர் against ஒட்டார்பின் சென்று வாழ்தலின் ... கெட்டான் எனப்படுதல் நன்று; the note states the reading the conflict needs, and Parimelazhagar on 680 does say பணிதல் மானமுடையார்க்குக் கருத்து அன்மையின்.

links.note: 502 places trust in one born in a good family (குடிப்பிறந்து), free of faults and with a shame that recoils from blemish. 681 makes birth in a fit family (ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல்) one of the envoy's three marks. Family is used in both as evidence about a person before he is given a charge, for trust in general in 502 and for the embassy in 681.
links.reason: குடிப்பிறந்து (502) and ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல் (681) both make family a criterion for entrusting a person, general trust and embassy respectively.

links.note: 681 asks of the envoy 'qualities that kings desire' (வேந்தவாம் பண்புடைமை) without saying what they are. Manakkudavar glosses the phrase as not desiring what the king desires, which is the content of 692 (மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை), and Parimelazhagar says this quality is obtained from the following chapter on conduct around kings. 692 therefore supplies, on the commentators' reading, what 681 leaves unstated.
links.reason: வேந்தவாம் பண்புடைமை (681) is unspecified; Manakkudavar glosses it as அவன் விரும்புவனவற்றைத் தான் விரும்பாமை, which is மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை (692), and Parimelazhagar points to மன்னரைச் சேர்ந்தொழுகல். Both claims verified.

links.note: The first line of 681 and of 992 is the same: அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல். 992 says these two are what is called courtesy (பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு); 681 lists them and adds a third, the qualities kings desire (வேந்தவாம் பண்புடைமை), as the nature of one who carries a message. The envoy's qualification is thus the book's general definition of courtesy with a courtly requirement added.
links.reason: 681 and 992 open with the identical line அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல்; 992 calls the two பண்புடைமை and 681 adds வேந்தவாம் பண்புடைமை for the envoy.

links.note: 722 says those who can make what they have learned go home before the learned are called learned among the learned (கற்றாருள் கற்றார்). 683 uses the same construction for the envoy: he must be strong in the treatises among those who know treatises (நூலாருள் நூல்வல்லன்). Both measure learning by standing among the learned, not against the unlearned.
links.reason: நூலாருள் நூல்வல்லன் and கற்றாருள் கற்றார் use the same X-among-X construction to measure learning against the learned.

links.note: 684 counts presence (உரு) among the three things an envoy needs. 407 says the fine looks of one without fine, penetrating understanding are those of a well-made clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). 407 supplies the limit on 684's உரு: appearance counts only in the union (செறிவு) with understanding and learning that 684 itself demands.
links.reason: 684 requires உரு only in செறிவு with அறிவு and கல்வி, and 407 says எழில்நலம் without நுண்மாண் நுழைபுலம் is a மண்மாண் புனைபாவை.

links.note: 636 asks what subtle scheme can stand before those who have keen intelligence together with the treatises (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்க்கு). 684 requires of the envoy understanding and well-examined learning (அறிவு ... ஆராய்ந்த கல்வி) held together. Parimelazhagar glosses the first term in each verse as natural intelligence and the second as acquired learning, so both verses ask for the two in combination, for the minister and for the envoy.
links.reason: மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு and அறிவு ... ஆராய்ந்த கல்வி both pair native intelligence with learning, and Parimelazhagar glosses them as இயற்கை and செயற்கை as the note says.

links.note: 696 tells one who serves a king to say what is needed and not disliked, in a way that is wanted (வெறுப்பில வேண்டுப வேட்பச் சொலல்). 685 has the envoy remove what offends and speak so as to please (தூவாத நீக்கி நகச்சொல்லி) while securing good for his own side. The same manner of speech is prescribed toward one's own king in 696 and toward a foreign king in 685; in both the pleasing manner serves what has to be said.
links.reason: தூவாத நீக்கி நகச்சொல்லி for the envoy and வெறுப்பில வேண்டுப வேட்பச் சொலல் for the courtier prescribe the same pleasing manner in service of the message, to a foreign king and to one's own.

links.note: 724 says to make what one has learned go home before the learned (கற்றார்முன் கற்ற செலச்சொல்லி). 686 uses the same two terms for the envoy: having learned (கற்று), he speaks so that it goes home (செலச்சொல்லி). In both, learning is complete only when it can be delivered to a demanding audience, the assembly in 724 and a hostile court in 686.
links.reason: The phrase செலச்சொல்லி with கற்று / கற்ற occurs in both, for the envoy and before கற்றார்; 'hostile court' is a fair reading of கண் அஞ்சான். 'Learning is complete only when' slightly overstates but the shared claim is real.

links.note: 675 says to act after thinking through resources, means, time, deed and place (காலம் ... இடனொடு ... எண்ணிச் செயல்). 687 uses the same terms for speech: consider the time, know the place, think it through and then speak (காலங் கருதி இடனறிந்து எண்ணி உரைப்பான்). The envoy's speech is planned by the same checklist the book gives for any deed.
links.reason: காலங் கருதி இடனறிந்து எண்ணி உரைப்பான் repeats the காலம் ... இடனொடு ... எண்ணிச் செயல் checklist for speech.

links.note: 696 tells the courtier to read the king's mood and consider the time (குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி) before speaking. 687 has the best envoy know what is due, consider the time (காலங் கருதி) and know the place before he speaks. The phrase காலங் கருதி is common to both, so the discipline for speaking to one's own king is the same as for speaking to another's.
links.reason: காலங் கருதி stands in both, between கடனறிந்து/இடனறிந்து for the envoy and after குறிப்பறிந்து for the courtier; the same discipline of speech in two offices.

links.note: 712 says those who know how words work should discern the opening (இடைதெரிந்து), understand well and then speak; Parimelazhagar takes இடை as the receptive moment of the assembly. 687 asks the envoy to consider the time, which Parimelazhagar likewise glosses as the listener's receptive state (செவ்வி). Both make the listener's readiness a condition of speaking.
links.reason: காலங் கருதி (Parimelazhagar: அவர் செவ்வி பார்த்து) and இடைதெரிந்து (அதன் செவ்வியை ஆராய்ந்து) both make the hearer's readiness a condition of speaking.

links.note: 298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truth (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). 688 names தூய்மை first among the envoy's marks and then requires வாய்மை along with all three. 298 gives the reason the two words belong together: truthfulness is how inner purity shows.
links.reason: 688 lists தூய்மை and வாய்மை as separate qualities of the envoy (Parimelazhagar takes தூய்மை as purity regarding wealth and desire); 298's அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் is a different point, so the note's 'reason the two words belong together' is read into 688.

links.note: 383 names three things that never leave a ruler: promptness, learning and resolve (தூங்காமை கல்வி துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றும்). 688 has the same frame for the envoy who repeats the king's message: purity, support and resolve, these three (தூய்மை துணைமை துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றின்). துணிவுடைமை is the term common to king and envoy; the other two differ with the office.
links.reason: Both are triads closing on துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்று (தூங்காமை கல்வி / தூய்மை துணைமை), for king and for envoy; the note describes both accurately.

links.note: 501 says a man is to be trusted after being tested by virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life. 688 lists the faithful envoy's marks as purity, support, resolve and truthfulness (தூய்மை துணைமை துணிவுடைமை ... வாய்மை). Parimelazhagar explains தூய்மை as being clean in respect of wealth and pleasure and துணிவு as not holding back for fear of harm, which makes 688's qualities the passes of 501's tests.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar glosses 688's தூய்மை as purity regarding பொருள் and காமம் and துணிவுடைமை as not holding back for fear of harm, which line up with 501's பொருள், இன்பம், உயிரச்சம் tests; 'passes of the tests' is a small stretch but grounded.

links.note: 139 says that for people of good conduct it is not possible to speak evil with the mouth even by a slip (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்). 689 asks the same of the envoy in his own field: a firmness whose mouth does not let slip a word that brings blemish (வடுமாற்றம் வாய்சோரா). What Book 1 treats as a result of character, 689 makes a condition for carrying the king's word. (This edition prints வாய்சேரா; the commentaries read வாய்சோரா.)
links.reason: வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல் ஒல்லாவே and வடுமாற்றம் வாய்சோரா வன்கணவன் share the not-even-by-a-slip standard, moved from character to the envoy's office; the note flags the misprint.
links.text_issue: 689 prints வாய்சேரா; commentaries read வாய்சோரா.

links.note: 642 says to guard against a lapse in speech (சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு) because both gain and ruin come from it. 689 is that rule at the point where the stakes are the king's: the envoy must not let a word that discredits slip from his mouth (வாய்சோரா); Parimelazhagar adds that the slip in question would come from fear for himself. The verb சோர் is shared, and 689 names the hardness (வன்கண்) that prevents the lapse 642 warns of.
links.reason: 642's காத்தோம்பல் சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு is applied to the envoy who is வாய்சோரா வன்கணவன்; Parimelazhagar does add fear for himself as the cause of the slip.
links.text_issue: 689 reads வாய்சேரா in this edition; the commentary and sense require வாய்சோரா, which the note silently uses.

links.note: 638 says that even if the king destroys good counsel and knows nothing himself, the one at his side owes it to him to say what is good for him (உறுதி ... கூறல் கடன்). 690 says the envoy secures the lord's good (உறுதி) even at the cost of his own life. Both use உறுதி for the king's real interest and hold the servant to it under threat, from his own king in 638 and from a foreign one in 690.
links.reason: உறுதி as the king's real interest is in both and each binds the servant to it at cost, but 638's அறிகொன்று அறியான் describes a king who rejects counsel and is ignorant, not one who threatens the minister; only 690 (இறுதி பயப்பினும்) has the threat.
links.text_issue: 690 has a stray space in இறைவற் கு.

links.note: 723 says those who will die among enemies are easy to find and those who do not fear in an assembly are rare (பகையகத்துச் சாவார் எளியர் அரியர் அவையகத்து அஞ்சாதவர்). 690 asks the envoy to face death (இறுதி) while speaking in a hostile court. 723 separates the two kinds of courage and rates the second as rarer; the envoy of 690 needs both together, which indicates how much the verse asks.
links.reason: 723 பகையகத்துச் சாவார் எளியர் அரியர் அவையகத்து அஞ்சாதவர் separates two courages and 690 இறுதி பயப்பினும் எஞ்சாது asks the envoy for both; that is an application, not a limit or condition, so 'qualifies' does not fit.

links.note: 778 says warriors who do not fear for their life when battle comes (உறின் உயிர் அஞ்சா மறவர்) do not lose their distinction even if their lord is angry. 690 says the envoy is one who, even if it brings his end (இறுதி பயப்பினும்), does not fall short and secures what is good for his lord (இறைவற்கு உறுதி). The envoy's office is given the soldier's standard, with both verses naming the lord (இறைவன்) as the one served.
links.reason: 690 இறுதி பயப்பினும் எஞ்சாது and 778 உறின் உயிர் அஞ்சா மறவர் apply disregard of death to envoy and soldier; note that in 778 the இறைவன் is the one who restrains them, not the one whose good is sought.

links.note: 691 compares the king to a fire one warms at from a measured distance. 896 says one burned by fire may still survive, but those who go on offending the great will not (எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம் உய்யார் பெரியார்ப் பிழைத்தொழுகுவார்). Read together, the fire in 691 understates the danger: 896 ranks the offended great above fire, though Parimelazhagar takes its பெரியார் as those great in austerity, not kings.
links.reason: The fire figure is shared (தீக்காய்வார் / எரியால் சுடப்படினும்), but 896's பெரியார் are not 691's kings on Parimelazhagar's reading, as the note admits, so 'the fire in 691 understates the danger' is the note's inference and not a development one verse makes of the other.

links.note: 691 tells those who serve quarrelsome kings (இகல்வேந்தர்) to be like people warming at a fire, neither moving off nor closing in (அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க). In 1104 a lover asks where she got a fire that burns when he withdraws and is cool when he comes near (நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும் தீ). The king's fire burns at close range and the lover's reverses that rule, so the court calls for a kept middle distance and the love speech for none.
links.reason: அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் and நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும் தீ both use fire and distance, with the love verse reversing the ordinary rule that the court verse relies on.

links.note: 692 says that not desiring what kings desire (மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை) brings lasting prosperity through those same kings; Parimelazhagar takes விழைப as the enjoyments, adornment and precedence proper to a king. 179 says Fortune herself comes to the wise who, knowing virtue, do not covet (அறனறிந்து வெஃகா அறிவுடையார்ச் சேரும் ... திரு). Both make not-wanting the route by which wealth arrives, once as court prudence and once as virtue.
links.reason: விழையாமை ... மன்னிய ஆக்கந் தரும் and வெஃகா அறிவுடையார்ச் சேரும் ... திரு both make not-wanting the way wealth arrives, as court prudence and as virtue.

links.note: 693 says those who would guard themselves should guard against the gravest things (போற்றின் அரியவை போற்றல்), which Parimelazhagar reads as faults a king cannot forgive. 891 says not slighting the power of those able to act is the chief of all the guarding done by those who guard themselves (போற்றுவார் போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை). Both use போற்றல் for self-protection and locate its first object in one's dealings with the powerful.
links.reason: போற்றின் அரியவை போற்றல் and போற்றுவார் போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை both rank what self-guarding must attend to first, and both are set in dealings with those who hold power; the reading of அரியவை as grave faults is Parimelazhagar's, as the note says.

links.note: 694 says that in the presence of the great one should suppress whispering and shared smiles (செவிச்சொல்லும் சேர்ந்த நகையும் அவித்தொழுகல்). 715 calls the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு) the best of good things. Court and assembly get the same rule of holding speech back before superiors; 694 extends it to private asides and laughter, which Parimelazhagar says the king would take as aimed at himself.
links.reason: செவிச்சொல்லும் சேர்ந்த நகையும் அவித்தொழுகல் ஆன்ற பெரியாரகத்து and முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு give the same rule of restraint before superiors in court and assembly.

links.note: 695 treats the king's secret (மறை) as something to be heard only when he lets it go. 1076 says the base are like a beaten drum because they carry to others the secrets they have heard (தாம் கேட்ட மறை பிறர்க்கு உய்த்துரைக்கலான்). The two give the two ends of handling a secret: restraint in acquiring it in 695, and the failure to hold it in 1076.
links.reason: மறை appears in both: விட்டக்கால் கேட்க மறை (restraint in learning it) and கேட்ட மறை பிறர்க்கு உய்த்துரைக்கலான் (failure to keep it).

links.note: 696 opens with குறிப்பறிந்து, knowing the king's mood, as the first condition of speaking to him. 701 praises the one who looks and knows what is meant without its being said (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்) as an ornament to the earth. The skill 696 names in passing is taken up as the subject of the next chapter, beginning with 701.
links.reason: 696's opening குறிப்பறிந்து is the skill that 701 (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்) makes the topic of the following chapter.

links.note: 697 says to speak what is wanted and never to say what has no use, even if asked (வினையில எஞ்ஞான்றும் கேட்பினும் சொல்லாவிடல்). 200 gives the general rule: say words that have use, do not say words that have none (சொல்லிற் பயனிலாச் சொல்). The court verse applies the household rule and tightens it, since here even the king's own request does not license useless talk.
links.reason: 697 'வினையில எஞ்ஞான்றும் கேட்பினும் சொல்லாவிடல்' applies 200 'சொல்லற்க சொல்லிற் பயனிலாச் சொல்' at court and tightens it with கேட்பினும்; 'develops' would fit equally, but the agreement is real.

links.note: 698 forbids belittling a king on the grounds of youth or kinship (இளையர் இனமுறையர் என்றிகழார்). 667 says one must not scorn by outward form, since the great rolling chariot depends on its linchpin (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை வேண்டும்). Both reject judging a person by a surface measure, whether age, family relation or size, and point instead to the function he carries.
links.reason: இளையர் இனமுறையர் என்றிகழார் and உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை both forbid contempt based on a surface trait and point to what the person carries (நின்ற ஒளி, அச்சாணி).

links.note: 700 says the familiarity (கெழுதகைமை) that does improper things on the thought 'we are old associates' (பழையம் எனக்கருதி) brings ruin. 801 defines old friendship (பழைமை) as friendship that in no way cuts down the liberties of intimacy (கிழமையைக் கீழ்ந்திடா நட்பு). The liberty that defines friendship between equals is thus withdrawn where the other party is a king, as Parimelazhagar reads 700.
links.reason: 801 defines பழைமை as கிழமையைக் கீழ்ந்திடா நட்பு, and 700 withdraws exactly that licence (பழையம் எனக்கருதி ... கெழுதகைமை கேடு தரும்) before a king.

links.note: 700 says intimacy that does what is improper brings ruin (பண்பல்ல செய்யும் கெழுதகைமை கேடு தரும்). 805 says that when friends do something hurtful one should understand it as folly or as great intimacy (பேதைமை ஒன்றோ பெருங்கிழமை என்றுணர்க நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின்). The conflict holds on Manakkudavar's gloss of 700, which speaks of the nature of friendship in general; on Parimelazhagar's, 700 concerns a king and the two verses address different relationships.
links.reason: 700 warns the one who presumes on age-old ties (பழையம் எனக்கருதிப் பண்பல்ல செய்யும்) while 805 tells the one hurt how to take it (பெருங்கிழமை என்றுணர்க); they address opposite parties and so are complementary rather than incompatible, and Manakkudavar's நட்பின் தகைமை still sits in the chapter on serving kings.

links.note: 701 praises the one who knows what is meant by looking, without its being said (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்). 1100, in the love chapter that has the same title குறிப்பறிதல், says that when eyes agree with eyes in their look, spoken words have no use (வாய்ச்சொற்கள் என்ன பயனும் இல). Reading without speech is a minister's rare skill in 701 and the ordinary condition of two lovers in 1100.
links.reason: கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான் and கண்ணொடு கண்இணை நோக்கொக்கின் வாய்ச்சொற்கள் என்ன பயனும் இல both make the look do the work of speech, in court and in love, under the same chapter title.

links.note: 703 urges the king to pay any price for those who read signs. 445 says that since counsellors serve as the ruler's eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக ஒழுகலான்), he must choose them with care. 445 gives the reason behind 703: the king sees through his advisers, so an adviser who can read what is unsaid is worth what Parimelazhagar lists as wealth, land, elephants and horses.
links.reason: Both end in கொளல் of advisers; 445's சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக ஒழுகலான் supplies a reason for 703's யாது கொடுத்தும், and Parimelazhagar's list of உறுப்பு (பொருளும் நாடும் யானை குதிரைகளும்) is quoted correctly.

links.note: 703 says to give whatever it takes from one's resources and secure those who read a sign by a sign (யாது கொடுத்தும் கொளல்). 794 says the friendship of one of good family who is ashamed of blame should be had even by giving (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் நட்பு). The shared formula marks the two kinds of person the book thinks worth paying for, the perceptive adviser and the friend with a sense of shame.
links.reason: யாது கொடுத்தும் கொளல் and கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் நட்பு share the formula of acquiring a person even at a price, for the குறிப்புணர்வார் and the பழிநாணுவான்.

links.note: 704 stops at saying that those who cannot grasp the unspoken are 'different' (வேறு) from those who can. 410 says others stand to those who have studied the shining books as beasts stand to people (விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர்). Parimelazhagar glosses the வேறு of 704 with this very comparison, the idea being that they are animals, so 410 states outright what 704 leaves implied.
links.reason: 704 ends on வேறு after உறுப்போரனையர்; Parimelazhagar's note there says விலங்கு என்னும் கருத்தான் 'வேறு' என்றார், which is 410's விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர். The claim checks out.

links.note: 704 says those who grasp what is meant without being told and the rest are alike in limbs (உறுப்போ ரனையரால்) and yet different. 993 says likeness of limbs is not likeness among people (உறுப்பொத்தல் மக்களொப்பு அன்றால்), and true likeness is likeness of character. Both deny that the shared body makes people alike, with perception the dividing line in 704 and பண்பு in 993.
links.reason: Both set உறுப்பு-likeness against real likeness: 704 உறுப்போ ரனையரால் வேறு, 993 உறுப்பொத்தல் மக்களொப்பு அன்றால்; the dividing line is perception in one and பண்பு in the other, as the note says.

links.note: 704 says readers of the unspoken and others share the same limbs but are different (வேறு). 1071 says the base look just like people (மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர்), a resemblance the speaker has seen nowhere else. The same figure of outward human likeness hiding an inner difference serves a point about intelligence in 704 and about moral baseness in 1071.
links.reason: உறுப்போரனையரால் வேறு and மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர் both use bodily likeness that hides an inner difference, for discernment in one and baseness in the other.

links.note: 705 says eyes that cannot read another's meaning are of no use. 393 says only the learned have eyes, and the unlearned have two sores in the face (முகத்திரண்டு புண்ணுடையர் கல்லாதவர்). In both the physical eye is treated as worthless without a trained capacity behind it, learning in one and the reading of signs in the other.
links.reason: என்ன பயத்தவோ கண் and முகத்திரண்டு புண்ணுடையர் both deny the worth of the bodily eye without a trained faculty behind it.

links.note: 705 asks what use eyes are among the limbs if they cannot read a sign by a sign (என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்). 574 asks what eyes without measured kindly regard do, beyond seeming to be there in the face (உளபோல் முகத்தெவன் செய்யும் ... கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்). Each denies the eye its name unless it does more than see, perceiving another's mind in 705 and looking kindly in 574.
links.reason: Both are rhetorical questions about the eye's use (என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்; முகத்தெவன் செய்யும் ... கண்) that make the eye worth its place only if it does more than see.

links.note: 706 says the face shows what fills the heart, as crystal shows what is beside it. 959 says the sprout shows what lay in the ground, and the spoken word shows the lineage of the one born in it (நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால்காட்டும்). Both rest on காட்டும்: something visible discloses a hidden source, mood in the face and family in speech.
links.reason: Both run on காட்டும் with an analogy: பளிங்கு and முகம் show what is within, கால் and வாய்ச்சொல் show ground and lineage.

links.note: 707 says nothing is as knowing as the face, since whether one is pleased or angry it gets there first (உவப்பினும் காயினும் தான்முந்துறும்). 830 advises that when an enemy turns friend one should befriend with the face and let go in the heart (முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்). If the face always runs ahead of the mind, as 707 says, the control 830 recommends should not be possible; the two agree only if 707 describes the unguarded face.
links.reason: தான் முந்துறும் says the face shows pleasure or anger first, while முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ asks for a face that hides the heart. The note states the reading the conflict rests on and how it dissolves.

links.note: 707 says the face is ahead of the person in showing pleasure or anger (தான் முந்துறும்). In 1277 a woman says her bangles knew before she did that her lover had left (நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). Both give the body a knowledge that arrives before the mind's own, a general observation in 707 and a lover's remark on her thinning arms in 1277.
links.reason: முகம்... தான் முந்துறும் and நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை both credit the body with getting there before the person; the note's 'had left' follows Manakkudavar, while Parimelazhagar takes தணந்தமை as parting in mind only.

links.note: 708 says that if one has people who look within and understand what has happened, it is enough to stand looking them in the face (முகம்நோக்கி நிற்க அமையும்). 1100 says that once eyes agree with eyes, spoken words are of no use. Both make speech unnecessary between the right pair; Parimelazhagar adds for 708 that going on to speak would lessen both parties, a concern for dignity the love verse does not have.
links.reason: முகம்நோக்கி நிற்க அமையும் and வாய்ச்சொற்கள் என்ன பயனும் இல both make speech unnecessary where looks are read, in the two chapters both titled குறிப்பறிதல்; Parimelazhagar's remark that speaking further would lessen both is in his 708 commentary.

links.note: 710 says the measuring rod (அளக்குங்கோல்) of those who call themselves subtle is nothing but the eye. 796 says ruin has one benefit: it is a rod that measures one's people to full length (கிளைஞரை நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல்). The book uses the measuring rod twice for gauging other people, the eye taking a present reading of a mind in 710 and adversity testing loyalty over time in 796.
links.reason: அளக்குங்கோல் in 710 and நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல் in 796 are the same measuring-rod figure, both for gauging people.

links.note: Both verses end with the identical line சொல்லின் தொகையறிந்த தூய்மையவர். 711 commands such people to know the assembly before speaking; 721 says that, having known the kinds (வகையறிந்து), they do not let their speech slip before the capable (வல்லவை வாய்சோரார்). The repeated line makes 721 the outcome of 711's instruction: knowing the assembly is what removes the fear that causes slips.
links.reason: Both close with சொல்லின் தொகையறிந்த தூய்மையவர்; 711 commands அவையறிந்து சொல்லுக and 721 has the same people, வகையறிந்து, not slip before வல்லவை. The causal gloss about fear is interpretation but matches Parimelazhagar's அச்சத்தான்.
links.text_issue: 711 prints அவையறிநது for அவையறிந்து.

links.note: 712 asks the speaker in an assembly to discern the opening (இடைதெரிந்து), which Parimelazhagar glosses as the hearers' readiness to listen. 696 asks the same of one speaking to a king: know his mood and consider the time (குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி) and say it so that it is wanted. The timing rule is the same before an assembly and before a single ruler.
links.reason: 712's இடைதெரிந்து (Parimelazhagar: அவையின் செவ்வி) and 696's குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி give the same rule of reading the hearer's readiness, before an assembly and before a king.

links.note: 713 says those who take up speaking without knowing the assembly (அவையறியார்) do not know the kinds of speech and have no ability at all. 401 says holding forth in an assembly (கோட்டி கொளல்) without full learning is like playing dice with no marked board. Each names a different missing precondition for speaking in an assembly, knowledge of the hearers in 713 and knowledge of the books in 401, and each treats the speech that results as empty.
links.reason: The connection is real (அவையறியார் சொல்லல் / நூலின்றிக் கோட்டி கொளல்) but, as the note itself says, each names a different missing precondition, so they do not make the same claim.

links.note: 714 tells the speaker to change with the audience, bright before the bright and blank before the blank. 425 says understanding is what does not open and close (மலர்தலும் கூம்பலும் இல்லது அறிவு). If 425's second half is read generally, as steadiness of bearing, the two disagree about whether the wise adapt their display; on Parimelazhagar's reading, where 425 is about constancy in friendship with the world, the conflict disappears.
links.reason: 425 மலர்தலும் கூம்பலும் இல்லது அறிவு concerns constancy (of friendship, per Parimelazhagar), and even read generally a steady understanding is compatible with 714's adapting one's display to the audience; the note itself admits the conflict vanishes on the main reading.

links.note: 714 uses a colour pair for intelligence: be bright (ஒள்ளியர்) before the bright, and take the colour of white plaster (வான்சுதை வண்ணம்) before the blank (வெளியார்). 844 uses the same pair: whiteness (வெண்மை) is the conceit that says 'we have brightness' (ஒண்மை உடையம் யாம்). Read together, the learned person of 714 puts on whiteness knowingly before those who, by 844, are white because they think themselves bright.
links.reason: ஒளியார்/ஒள்ளியர் against வெளியார்/வான்சுதை வண்ணம் in 714 is the same bright/white pair as ஒண்மை/வெண்மை in 844, and the combined reading is apt.

links.note: 715 praises the restraint (செறிவு) of not speaking first among elders. 419 says a mouth that bows (வணங்கிய வாய்) is hard to have for those without fine listening. Both treat modest speech as a mark of what a person has learned, and 419 supplies the source 715 leaves unstated: the habit of listening.
links.reason: முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு and வணங்கிய வாயினர் both praise humble restraint in speech, and 419 ties it to நுணங்கிய கேள்வி as the note says.

links.note: 642 gives the general rule: since gain and ruin come from speech, guard against a lapse in it (சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு). 716 applies it to one setting, a slip before the widely learned, and measures the damage by comparing it to falling from the path (ஆற்றின் நிலைதளர்ந்தற்று), which Parimelazhagar reads as a renouncer's lapse from the good path.
links.reason: 642's general காத்தோம்பல் சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு is applied in 716 to இழுக்கு before வியன்புலம் ஏற்றுணர்வார்; Parimelazhagar's reading of ஆற்றின் நிலைதளர்ந்தற்று as a lapse from the path to release is cited correctly.

links.note: 716 says a slip (இழுக்கு) before those who have taken in wide learning is like faltering from one's footing on the path. 957 says a fault in the well-born shows up high, like the spot on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல்). In both, the weight of a fault depends on where it is seen, the standing of the witnesses in 716 and of the person in 957, and not only on its size.
links.reason: 716 makes a இழுக்கு grave because it is வியன்புலம் ஏற்றுணர்வார் முன்னர், and 957 makes a குற்றம் conspicuous because it is in குடிப்பிறந்தார், like மதிக்கண் மறு; both weigh a fault by where it shows.

links.note: 717 says the learning of those who have studied and understood shines among those able to examine words without fault (சொல்தெரிதல் வல்லார் அகத்து). 404 says the wise do not accept an unlearned person's brightness (ஒட்பம்), however good it is. The same expert hearers decide both cases: before them real learning becomes visible and untaught cleverness is not accepted.
links.reason: Both turn on a discerning audience (சொல்தெரிதல் வல்லார் / அறிவுடையார்), but neither verse limits the other; the two are complementary statements, so QUALIFIES does not fit.

links.note: 719 and 728 share the phrase நல்லவையுள் நன்கு செலச் சொல்லு-. 728 says those who cannot speak tellingly in a good assembly are of no use though they have learned much; 719 tells those who can do so not to speak in a mean assembly even by forgetting (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லற்க). Together they set the limits: silence in a good assembly is a failure, and silence in a mean one is required.
links.reason: The shared நல்லவையுள் நன்கு செலச் சொல்- is turned two ways: 728 பயமிலரே for those who cannot, 719 புல்லவையுள் பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லற்க for those who can.
links.text_issue: 719 is printed நன்குசலச்; it should read நன்கு செலச்.

links.note: 719 forbids speaking good things in a mean assembly. 849 gives a reason in another chapter: one who shows something to a person who does not see becomes himself unseeing (காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான்), while that person goes on seeing as he saw. Parimelazhagar makes the same point on 719, that both assemblies would then look down on the speaker.
links.reason: 719 'புல்லவையுள் பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லற்க' gets a reason from 849 'காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான்'; the note's report of Parimelazhagar on 719 matches his gloss.

links.note: 720 says holding forth before those not of one's kind is like nectar spilled in a dirty yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்து). 1000 says great wealth in the hands of one without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). Both describe a fine liquid ruined by where it lands, and so place the loss in the receiver and not in the thing given.
links.reason: அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்து and நன்பால் கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று are both a fine liquid ruined by its receptacle, placing the fault in the receiver.

links.note: 721 says those who know the body of words and the kinds of assembly do not let their speech slip before the capable (வாய்சோரார்), which Parimelazhagar reads as not slipping out of fear. 647 lists the same qualities, able to speak, without slips, without fear (சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான்), and says such a person is hard for anyone to defeat. 647 states the payoff of the fearlessness that 721 describes.
links.reason: 721 வாய்சோரார், which Parimelazhagar glosses அச்சத்தான் வழுப்படச் சொல்லார், matches 647's சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான், whose payoff is இகல்வெல்லல் யார்க்கும் அரிது.

links.note: 716 says a slip (இழுக்கு) before those of wide learning is like falling from the path. 721 answers from the next chapter: those who know words and know the assembly do not slip before the capable (வல்லவை வாய்சோரார்). One verse gives the cost of the slip and the other says what prevents it.
links.reason: 716's இழுக்கு before the learned is answered by 721's வல்லவை வாய்சோரார் for those who know சொல்லின் தொகை; cost and prevention in adjacent chapters.

links.note: 722 says those who make what they have learned go home before the learned (கற்ற செலச் சொல்லுவார்) are called learned among the learned. 424 defines understanding with the same verb: saying things so that they go in easily (எண்பொருளவாகச் செலச்சொல்லி) and seeing the subtle meaning in what others say. Both measure learning or understanding by whether it reaches the hearer, not by what the speaker holds.
links.reason: The verb செலச்சொல்லு is shared and in both the test is whether the matter reaches the hearer (கற்ற செலச்சொல்லுவார் / எண்பொருளவாகச் செலச்சொல்லி).

links.note: 722 gives the title 'learned among the learned' to those who can convey their learning to the learned. 650 gives the reverse case: those who cannot unfold what they have learned so that others understand (கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்) are like flowers that bloom in clusters without scent. Together they treat communication as part of learning itself.
links.reason: கற்ற செலச்சொல்லுவார் are the learned among the learned; கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார் are scentless flowers. Positive and negative of the same claim from two chapters.

links.note: 723 calls those who die amid enemies எளியர், easy to find. 762 says the hardness that does not fear wounds when the king falters is rare except in an old army (தொல்படைக்கல்லால் அரிது). If 723's first half is read as saying battle courage is common, the two disagree about how rare it is; if 762 is limited to courage in defeat and with reduced numbers, they do not.
links.reason: 723's பகையகத்துச் சாவார் எளியர் is the foil in a comparison with அவையகத்து அஞ்சாதவர், and 762 is conditioned by உலைவிடத்து and தொலைவிடத்து; the claims concern different situations and conflict only on a strained reading, as the note half admits.

links.note: 723 says those who will die amid enemies are easy to find, and those who do not fear within an assembly are hard to find (அவையகத்து அஞ்சாதவர்). 872 says one may take on the enmity of those who plough with the bow but not of those who plough with the word (சொல்லேர் உழவர்). Both rank the word above the weapon, 723 by how rare the courage is and 872 by how dangerous the opponent is.
links.reason: பகையகத்துச் சாவார் எளியர் / அவையகத்து அஞ்சாதவர் அரியர் and வில்லேர் / சொல்லேர் உழவர் both set the word above the weapon.

links.note: 724 joins two acts: convey your learning (செலச்சொல்லி) and take in what those more learned have. 424 joins the same two as its definition of understanding: say things so that they go in (செலச்சொல்லி) and see the subtle meaning in what others say (பிறர்வாய் நுண்பொருள் காண்பது). What 424 calls understanding, 724 presents as what a fearless speaker gains from an assembly.
links.reason: Both verses use செலச்சொல்லி and pair it with taking in from others (மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்; பிறர்வாய் நுண்பொருள் காண்பது); the note describes both accurately.

links.note: Both verses open with the command to learn. 391 says learn without flaw and then stand in keeping with it (கற்க கசடற ... நிற்க அதற்குத் தக); 725 says learn with measure so as to give a fearless reply (மாற்றங் கொடுத்தற் பொருட்டு). 391 gives learning its end in conduct, and 725 gives it a second end in public speech.
links.reason: கற்க is in both and 725 does add மாற்றங் கொடுத்தற் பொருட்டு as an aim, but 725 opens with ஆற்றின், not கற்க, and அளவறிந்து is read by Parimelazhagar as learning logic, not 'with measure'; the link is real but closer to develops, in a nearby domain.

links.note: 725 says to learn by the proper path and with measure (ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து கற்க) in order to reply in the assembly without fear; Parimelazhagar takes அளவு as the science of logic. 645 says to speak a word only after knowing no other word can defeat it (வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து). 725 names the training that makes 645's test possible.
links.reason: 725's ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து கற்க for அவையஞ்சா மாற்றங் கொடுத்தல் (அளவு as logic in Parimelazhagar) is the training behind 645's வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து.

links.note: 726 asks what a sword is to those who are not hard-eyed, and what books are to those who fear a subtle assembly (நுண்ணவை அஞ்சுபவர்க்கு). 534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை), which Parimelazhagar explains as a fortress being of no use to them. In each, fear cancels an instrument that is sound in itself: sword, books, fort.
links.reason: வாளொடென் / நூலொடென் for the fearful matches அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை, which Parimelazhagar explains as the fort being of no use; fear cancels the instrument in each.

links.note: 726 says books are nothing to one who fears a subtle assembly. 647 says the one who can speak, does not slip and does not fear (அஞ்சான்) is hard for anyone to defeat, and Parimelazhagar takes that fearlessness as fearlessness of the assembly. 647 states positively the condition whose absence 726 says makes learning useless.
links.reason: நுண்ணவை அஞ்சுபவர்க்கு நூலொடென் and அஞ்சான் ... வெல்லல் அரிது are the negative and positive sides of the same condition; Parimelazhagar does gloss அஞ்சான் as அவைக்கு அஞ்சான்.

links.note: 728 and 140 have the same form: 'though they have learned much'. In 140, those who have not learned to live in accord with the world are without understanding though they have learned much (பலகற்றும்). In 728, those who cannot speak well in a good assembly are without use though they have learned many things (பல்லவை கற்றும்). Each names a practical ability without which the amount learned does not count.
links.reason: பல்லவை கற்றும் பயமிலரே (728) and பலகற்றும் ... அறிவிலாதார் (140) share the concessive frame and each names a practical ability that learning needs.

links.note: 395 calls the unlearned the lowest (கடையரே கல்லாதவர்). 729 uses the same word to put someone beneath them: those who have studied and understood and still fear an assembly of the good are lower than the unlearned (கல்லாதவரின் கடை). 729 thus limits 395's ranking, since learning that is not voiced does not lift a person above the bottom rank and, as Parimelazhagar explains, leaves them with only the labour of having studied.
links.reason: 395 கடையரே கல்லாதவர் is directly undercut by 729 கல்லாதவரின் கடை for கற்றறிந்தும் நல்லாரவை அஞ்சுவார்; same word, real limitation.

links.note: 730 counts those who cannot voice their learning as equal to those who are not, though they exist. 214 says one who knows what is fitting truly lives and anyone else is placed among the dead (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). Both apply the figure of a living person counted as dead or absent to someone who gives nothing to others, wealth in 214 and learning in 730; Parimelazhagar reads 730's இல்லார் as the dead.
links.reason: உளரெனினும் இல்லாரொடு ஒப்பர் and செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும் both count a living person as dead; Parimelazhagar does gloss இல்லார் as இறந்தார், and Manakkudavar as செத்தார்.
links.text_issue: 214: 'ஒத்த தறவோன்' is a typo for ஒத்த தறிவான்.

links.note: 731 sets unfailing yield and worthy people (தக்கார்) side by side as marks of a land. 239 says land that bears a body without renown (இசையிலா யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்) declines in its blameless rich produce (வண்பயன் குன்றும்). 239 makes a causal claim where 731 only lists: the land's yield depends on the quality of the people it carries.
links.reason: 731 lists தள்ளா விளையுளும் தக்காரும் together, and 239 says வண்பயன் குன்றும் on land bearing இசையிலா யாக்கை; the causal step is in 239's Tamil.

links.note: 731 makes unfailing yield (தள்ளா விளையுள்) one of three things that must come together (சேர்வது) for a land. 545 says rain and yield (பெயலும் விளையுளும்) gather (தொக்கு) in the land of the king who wields the sceptre as it should be wielded. Read together, the yield that defines a land in 731 is traced in 545 to just rule.
links.reason: 731 'தள்ளா விளையுளும் ... சேர்வது நாடு' and 545 'பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு' share 'விளையுள்'; 545 traces it to 'இயல்புளிக் கோலோச்சும் மன்னவன்'.

links.note: Parimelazhagar takes விளையுள் in 731 to stand for the cultivators, since the verse lists it beside two kinds of people (தக்கார், செல்வர்). 1032 calls those who plough the linchpin (ஆணி) of the world because they carry all who go off to other work. 1032 gives the reason the cultivators come first in 731's list.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does take தள்ளா விளையுள் as the cultivators and 1032 does call உழுவார் the ஆணி, but the link rests wholly on that commentarial reading (Manakkudavar reads fertile land), and nothing in 731 makes the order of its list a ranking that 1032 could explain.

links.note: 732 says a land yields greatly because ruin is rare there (அருங்கேட்டால் ஆற்ற விளைவது). 15 says rain is what ruins (கெடுப்பதூஉம்) and also what raises up the ruined. Parimelazhagar's list of the கேடு meant in 732 begins with too much rain and no rain, so 15 names the chief source of the ruin that 732 wants to be rare.
links.reason: 732's அருங்கேட்டால் does not mention rain; the link comes only through Parimelazhagar's list (மிக்க பெயல், பெயலின்மை ...), and 15's கெடுப்பதூஉம் is mainly ruin by rain's failure. A real but thin connection, and not a development of one verse by the other.

links.note: 732 asks that ruin be rare (அருங்கேடு) so that the land yields abundantly. 736 goes a step further: the foremost land does not know ruin, and its richness does not shrink even where ruin has come (கெட்ட இடத்தும் வளங்குன்றா). 732 states the ordinary standard and 736 the highest one.
links.reason: 732 அருங்கேட்டால் ஆற்ற விளைவது நாடு is stepped up in 736 கேடறியாக் கெட்ட இடத்தும் வளங்குன்றா ... நாட்டின் தலை, the best land.

links.note: 733 defines a land as one that bears burdens arriving all at once and still agrees to give the king his whole due (இறையொருங்கு நேர்வது). 552 says that asking (இரவு) by one who stands with the sceptre is like a man standing with a spear saying 'hand it over'. The land's willingness to pay in 733 is not a licence for the king to demand: Manakkudavar reads 733's burdens as levies beyond the fixed due, which is the situation 552 condemns.
links.reason: Manakkudavar does read 733's பொறை as குடிமை, levies beyond the fixed கடமை, and under 552 calls demands above the fixed due highway robbery; so இறையொருங்கு நேர்வது does not license கோலொடு நின்றான் இரவு. Note accurate.

links.note: In 733 the land bears the load that comes upon it (பொறை ... தாங்கி). In 990 the great earth will not bear its load (தாங்காது ... பொறை) if the worthy decline in worth. The same words describe a land's capacity to carry weight, and 990 makes that capacity depend on the character of its best people.
links.reason: Both verses pair பொறை with தாங்கு (பொறை ... தாங்கி / தாங்காது ... பொறை) for a land carrying weight; the note describes both accurately and 990's dependence on சான்றாண்மை is in the Tamil.

links.note: 734 lists what must not reach a land from outside or by nature: hunger, disease and the enemy who destroys (செறுபகை). 735 lists what must not exist inside it: many factions (பல்குழு), the inner enemy that lays waste (உட்பகை) and murderous bands that harass the king. The two verses divide the threats into external and internal.
links.reason: 734 lists what must not reach the land (உறுபசி, ஓவாப் பிணி, செறுபகை சேராது) and 735 what must not exist in it (பல்குழு, உட்பகை, கொல்குறும்பு இல்லது); the outer/inner split is a fair reading of adjacent verses.
links.text_issue: Parimelazhagar's entry for 734 opens with the gloss of another verse (பொறை ஒருங்கு மேல் வருங்கால்...), so the commentary text is misaligned at the start.

links.note: 735 says a land has no murderous bands that harass the king (வேந்தலைக்கும் கொல்குறும்பு). 550 says a king's punishing the cruel with death (கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல்) is like weeding the young crop. 550 gives the ruler's means of producing the condition 735 describes; Parimelazhagar on 735 likewise says these three are to be removed by the king and the inhabitants.
links.reason: 735's வேந்தலைக்கும் கொல்குறும்பும் இல்லது is the state that 550's கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல் produces; Parimelazhagar on 735 does say the three are to be removed by king and inhabitants.

links.note: 735 requires a land to be without the inner enemy that lays waste (பாழ்செய்யும் உட்பகை). 889 says inner enmity, though as small as a split sesame seed (எட்பகவு), holds ruin within it (உள்ளதாங் கேடு). 889 explains why 735 demands its complete absence and not just its reduction.
links.reason: பாழ்செய்யும் உட்பகை ... இல்லது நாடு and எட்பகவன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும் உட்பகை உள்ளதாங் கேடு: the second explains why the first asks for total absence.

links.note: 736 calls foremost the land whose richness does not shrink even where ruin has come (கெட்ட இடத்தும் வளங்குன்றா). 955 says an old family does not part from its character even when what it has to give has fallen away (வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும் ... பண்பில் தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று). Both use the same 'even when' construction to test excellence by what remains after loss, one for a land and one for a family.
links.reason: 736 கெட்ட இடத்தும் வளங்குன்றா and 955 வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும் ... தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று both test excellence by what survives loss, for a land and a family.

links.note: 737 names a strong fort (வல்லரண்) among the limbs (உறுப்பு) of a land, with its waters and hill. 381 names the fort (அரண்) and the people or land (குடி) as two of the six things a king must have, which Parimelazhagar calls his six limbs (அங்கம்). 737 nests one of the king's limbs inside another, which fits the order of the chapters: land, then fort.
links.reason: 737 lists வல்லரண் as an உறுப்பு of நாடு, and 381 lists குடி and அரண் among the six a king has, which Parimelazhagar calls அங்கம் and reads குடி as நாடு; the nesting the note describes is in the texts.

links.note: 738 lists five ornaments (அணி) of a land: freedom from disease (பிணியின்மை), wealth, yield, happiness and protection (ஏமம்). 734 defines a land by three absences: severe hunger, unceasing disease (ஓவாப் பிணி) and destructive enemies. The two lists match as positive and negative: yield answers hunger, பிணியின்மை answers disease, and ஏமம் answers the enemy, while 738 adds wealth and happiness.
links.reason: பிணியின்மை / விளைவு / ஏமம் in 738 answer ஓவாப் பிணி / உறுபசி / செறுபகை in 734, with செல்வம் and இன்பம் added; the positive and negative lists do match as the note says.

links.note: 739 says lands are those whose riches come without being sought (நாடா வளத்தன). 594 says prosperity itself asks the way and goes (ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும்) to the person of unwavering drive. Both picture wealth arriving unsought, but 594 makes it the result of the person's energy, where 739 makes it a property of the land.
links.reason: நாடா வளத்தன and ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும் share only the conceit of wealth coming of itself; 594 praises the striver and 739 praises land needing no toil, so the common ground is a figure of speech. The note is accurate but the link is thin.
links.text_issue: 594 prints க்கம் for ஆக்கம்.

links.note: 739 praises land whose riches need no seeking. 1040 says the good woman called Land laughs (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்) at those who say 'we have nothing' and sit idle (அசைஇ இருப்பாரை). 1040 limits 739: the land has riches to give, but not to those who do nothing.
links.reason: நாடா வளத்தன praises riches that come unsought, while 1040 has நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் laugh at அசைஇ இருப்பார்; 1040 does limit what unsought abundance can mean.

links.note: 740 says a land's excellences bring no benefit (பயமின்று) without accord between it and its king. 558 says that under the sceptre of a king who does not do justice, having is more painful than not having (இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை). 558 shows one way the wealth praised in this chapter turns useless or worse under the wrong ruler.
links.reason: 740's பயமின்றே for a land without வேந்தமைவு is made specific by 558's இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை under a king who is முறைசெய்யா.

links.note: 740 says that a land with every excellence is of no use without accord with its king. 770 says that though an army has plenty of steadfast men (நிலைமக்கள் சால உடைத்தெனினும்), there is no army where there are no leaders (தலைமக்கள் இல்வழி இல்). In both, a body that is complete in its own parts is counted as nothing without its head.
links.reason: வேந்தமைவில்லாத நாடு is பயமின்று despite every excellence, and a தானை rich in நிலைமக்கள் is இல் where தலைமக்கள் are lacking: the same whole-without-head logic in land and army.

links.note: 741 says a fort matters to those who fear attack and look to their own safety. 569 says a king who has not made his defences (சிறைசெய்யா வேந்தன்) will, when war comes, be struck with fear and quickly perish (வெருவந்து வெய்து கெடும்). 569 states the cost of ignoring 741: without a fort prepared beforehand, fear has nowhere to turn.
links.reason: 741 makes அரண் a பொருள் for those who அஞ்சித் தற்போற்றுபவர்; 569's சிறைசெய்யா வேந்தன் (சிறை = defences per both commentators) வெருவந்து வெய்து கெடும் shows the cost of lacking it.

links.note: 742 says a fort has clear water (மணிநீர்), open ground, a hill (மலை) and a forest of fine shade. 737 lists as limbs of a land the two waters (இருபுனல்), a well-placed hill (வாய்ந்த மலை), the water that comes from it, and a strong fort. The same features of the terrain, water and hill, are counted first as a land's resources and then as a fort's defences, and 737 already names the fort as part of the land.
links.reason: Water and hill occur in both lists (மணிநீரும் ... மலையும்; இருபுனலும் வாய்ந்த மலையும்), and 737 names வல்லரண் as a limb of the land, so the chapters do connect. But these are literal inventories, not a distinctive shared image or figure.

links.note: 743 defines the fort as a wall complete in four measures: height, breadth, strength and difficulty of approach (உயர்வு அகலம் திண்மை அருமை). 421 calls understanding the tool that guards against ruin and an inner fort that enemies cannot destroy (செறுவார்க்கும் உள்ளழிக்கலாகா அரண்). 421 moves the fort inside the person: the quality 743 seeks in masonry, that it cannot be broken into, 421 claims for understanding.
links.reason: 421 calls அறிவு an உள்ளழிக்கலாகா அரண், moving inward the impregnability (திண்மை அருமை) that 743 requires of a built fort.

links.note: 745 says a fort is hard to take, holds stored food (கொண்ட கூழ்த்து) and is easy for those inside to hold their position in (அகத்தார் நிலைக்கு எளிது). 499 says that even people with no good defences or standing (சிறைநலனும் சீரும் இலரெனினும்) are hard to take on in the land where they live (உறைநிலத்தோடு ஒட்டல் அரிது). 499 shows that the insiders' advantage of position, which 745 asks the fort to give, already belongs to home ground without walls.
links.reason: அகத்தார் நிலைக்கு எளிதாம் (745) is the advantage 499 grants even to those with no சிறைநலன், on their உறைநிலம்; the note reads both accurately.

links.note: 746 wants in a fort good men who help at the place where it would otherwise fall; Parimelazhagar glosses இடத்து as the point of destruction by those outside. 762 says the hardness that does not fear a wound when things give way and the force is reduced (உலைவிடத்து ஊறஞ்சா வன்கண்) is rare except in an ancient army. Both measure fighting men by what they do at the moment of collapse, in the fort and in the field.
links.reason: 746 இடத்துதவும் நல்லாள், which Parimelazhagar glosses as the point of destruction by outsiders, and 762 உலைவிடத்து ஊறஞ்சா வன்கண் both judge fighters at the moment of collapse.

links.note: 746 says a fort has every needed thing and good men who help at the critical place (இடத்துதவும் நல்லாள்). 1030 says a family with no good man to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. The same word நல்லாள் names the person on whom a fort and a family each depend at the moment of danger; goods alone hold up neither.
links.reason: இடத்துதவும் நல்லாள் உடையது அரண் and அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி use the same word for the person a fort and a family depend on in danger.

links.note: 747 says a fort is hard to seize by encircling, by assault without encircling, or by subversion (அறைப்படுத்தும்), which Parimelazhagar explains as undermining those inside through people they trust. 764 defines an army as one that does not break and cannot be subverted (அறைபோகாதாகி). The same word அறை marks treachery from within as a danger that fort and army must both be proof against, beside open force.
links.reason: 'அறைப்படுத்தும் பற்றற்கரியது அரண்' and 'அறைபோகாதாகி... படை' use the same அறை for subversion from within as a test of fort and army alike.

links.note: 748 says a fort is where those who hold it keep their hold (பற்றாற்றி) and defeat even those strong enough to besiege them; Parimelazhagar notes that the smaller force does not just endure but wins. 493 says even those without strength become strong and win (ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி அடுப) if they know the place and act against foes while guarding themselves. 748 is 493's rule about place applied to the fort.
links.reason: 748 பற்றாற்றிப் பற்றியார் வெல்வது and 493 ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி அடுப இடனறிந்து both say the weaker side wins from the right position; Parimelazhagar's remark that the small force wins and his mention of அரண் under 493 are as reported.

links.note: 749 says a fort has its distinction from what is done in action (வினைமுகத்து வீறெய்தி) so that enemies fall at the front of battle. 750 says that whatever excellence a fort has, it is nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). 750 turns 749's praise into a condition; Parimelazhagar says the two verses together show that a fort cannot do without its defenders.
links.reason: வினைமுகத்து வீறெய்தி is turned into a condition by வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்; Parimelazhagar's closing remark that the two verses show defenders are indispensable is quoted accurately.

links.note: 749 places a fort's distinction in the actions by which enemies are brought down as soon as battle is joined (முனைமுகத்து); Parimelazhagar explains these as recognising the attack begun and choosing the acts that defeat it. 767 says an army is one that knows the way to bear the battle coming at it (தலைவந்த போர்தாங்கும் தன்மை அறிந்து) and advances. Both ask for trained response to the enemy's opening move, from the walls and in the field.
links.reason: முனைமுகத்து மாற்றலர் சாய வினை (fort) and தலைவந்த போர்தாங்கும் தன்மை அறிந்து (army) both locate excellence in the response to the enemy's onset; the 'trained response' wording for 749 leans on Parimelazhagar, as the note acknowledges.

links.note: 750 says a fort's excellences do not exist for those who lack excellence in action. 727 says the treatise learned by one who fears the assembly is like a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி amid enemies (பகையகத்துப் பேடிகை ஒள்வாள்). In both a good instrument, a fort or learning, is worth nothing in the hands of someone who cannot act when the test comes.
links.reason: வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண் and பேடிகை ஒள்வாள் = அஞ்சுமவன் கற்ற நூல்: a good instrument made worthless by its holder, in defence and in the assembly.

links.note: 751 treats wealth's power to give standing to persons of no account as its distinction. 241 notes the same fact, that material wealth is found even among the base (பொருட்செல்வம் பூரியார் கண்ணும் உள), and uses it to rank wealth below grace, the 'wealth among wealths'. What 751 counts in wealth's favour, 241 counts against it.
links.reason: 751 praises wealth for making பொருளல்லவர் count, while 241 uses wealth's presence பூரியார் கண்ணும் to rank it below அருட்செல்வம்; the two facts are close though not strictly identical as the note says.

links.note: 752 reports that all scorn the poor and all honour the rich. 988 says lack is no disgrace to one who has the firmness called worth (இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று சால்பென்னும் திண்மை). 752 describes how the world behaves; 988 denies that the scorn is deserved where character is present, which Parimelazhagar's gloss on 752 (scorned 'even if they have every good') makes pointed.
links.reason: இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர் (752) reports the world's scorn; இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று சால்பென்னும் திண்மை உண்டாகப் பெறின் (988) limits it where character exists, and Parimelazhagar's எல்லா நன்மையும் உடையராயினும் on 752 is as cited.

links.note: 752 says everyone scorns those who have nothing (இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்). 1046 gives a particular case: even when the poor understand a good matter well and say it, their words go slack (சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்). The general contempt of 752 is shown reaching what a poor person says.
links.reason: இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர் is given a specific case in 1046, where even well-understood good matter from நல்கூர்ந்தார் suffers சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு.

links.note: 752's 'everyone' (எல்லாரும்) scorns the have-nots. 1047 carries that to the limit case: one in poverty not joined to virtue is looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல). The pairing shows how far 'everyone' reaches, with 1047 adding the condition அறஞ்சாரா.
links.reason: இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர் is carried to its limit in ஈன்றதா யானும் பிறன்போல நோக்கப் படும், and the note correctly flags the added condition அறஞ்சாரா.

links.note: 753 says wealth cuts away darkness (இருளறுக்கும்), which Parimelazhagar takes to be enmity. 759 says no steel is sharper than wealth for cutting the pride of foes (செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும்). Both use the verb அறு for what wealth does, once as a lamp and once as a blade; on Parimelazhagar's reading of 753 they make the same claim.
links.reason: இருளறுக்கும் and செருக்கறுக்கும் share the verb, and both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar gloss 753's இருள் as பகை, which makes the claims coincide as the note says.

links.note: 754 says wealth that came by knowing the right means and without wrong yields virtue and also pleasure (அறன்ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும்). 39 says only what comes through virtue is pleasure (அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம்). 754 fits wealth into 39's rule: wealth produces real pleasure only when it was itself acquired without wrong.
links.reason: 39 அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம் sets the rule and 754 தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள் அறன் ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும் applies it to wealth.

links.note: 754 limits its promise to wealth that came without wrong (தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்). 659 says what was taken making others weep leaves with weeping, while what came by good ways pays later even if lost (பிற்பயக்கும் நற்பாலவை). Both make the manner of acquisition decide what wealth yields.
links.reason: 754 தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள் yields அறன் and இன்பம்; 659 அழக் கொண்ட எல்லாம் அழப்போம் versus நற்பாலவை பிற்பயக்கும். Both make the manner of getting decide the yield.

links.note: 755 says a gain of wealth that does not come with grace and love should be let go, not embraced (புல்லார் புரள விடல்). 113 says gain that comes from leaving fairness should be let go that very day even if it brings only good (அன்றே யொழிய விடல்). Both end on the same command, விடல், for gain acquired the wrong way, one naming love and grace as the test and the other fairness.
links.reason: Both end on விடல் for wrongly sourced ஆக்கம் (அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாரா; நடுவிகந்தாம்), with different tests.

links.note: 755 tells one to refuse wealth that comes without grace and love. 1009 says what becomes of such wealth: bright wealth amassed by setting love aside and not looking to virtue (அன்பொரீஇ ... அறநோக்காது ஈட்டிய) is taken by others. 1009 supplies a consequence for the wealth 755 rejects.
links.reason: அன்பொடும் வாராப் பொருளாக்கம் (755) and அன்பொரீஇ ... அறநோக்காது ஈட்டிய ஒண்பொருள் கொள்வார் பிறர் (1009) share the loveless-wealth condition, and 1009 supplies an outcome; 1009's miser (தற்செற்று) is a narrower case than 755's.

links.note: 757 says the child grace, born of love, is reared by the nurse called wealth (பொருளென்னும் செல்வச் செவிலி). 247 sets the two side by side: that world is not for those without grace, as this world is not for those without wealth. Both pair அருள் with பொருள்; 247 keeps them parallel, while 757 makes grace depend on wealth to grow.
links.reason: Both pair அருள் and பொருள், but they do not make the same claim: 247 only compares the two by analogy (இல்லாகி யாங்கு), while 757 makes grace depend on wealth (செல்வச் செவிலியால் உண்டு). The note says as much, which contradicts the 'agrees' type.

links.note: 757 says grace is raised by wealth. 755, in the same chapter, says wealth that does not come with grace and love (அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாரா) is to be let go. The dependence runs both ways: grace needs wealth, but only wealth that itself came with grace and love.
links.reason: 757 has அருள் reared by பொருள்; 755 rejects பொருளாக்கம் that is அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாரா, so the wealth that nurses grace must itself come with grace.

links.note: 758 says doing a task with something in one's own hand (தன்கைத்தொன்று உண்டாக) is like watching an elephant fight from a hilltop, which Parimelazhagar explains as acting without fear or strain. 449 says those without capital have no profit (முதலிலார்க்கு ஊதியம் இல்லை).
