Both make resources in hand the precondition of an undertaking; 758 adds the safety they give.
links.reason: தன்கைத்தொன்று உண்டாக is literal capital, but முதலிலார்க்கு ஊதியம் இல்லை is only the simile half of 449, whose claim is about மதலையாஞ் சார்பு (supporters of a king); the note treats the vehicle as the verse's point.
links.text_issue: 449 line 1 reads 'முதலிலார்க', missing the final கு of முதலிலார்க்கு.

links.note: 758 praises acting with wealth in hand (கைத்து உண்டாக). 593 says those who hold steady energy as what is in their hand (ஊக்கம் ஒருவந்தம் கைத்துடையார்) do not grieve that they have lost their gains. The same word கைத்து is used for money in 758 and for drive in 593, which treats energy as the holding that matters when the money is gone.
links.reason: தன்கைத்தொன்று உண்டாக uses கைத்து for money in hand and ஊக்கம் ஒருவந்தம் கைத்துடையார் uses it for steady drive as one's holding.
links.text_issue: 593 prints 'க்கம்' for ஆக்கம் (initial ஆ dropped).

links.note: 759 says wealth is sharper than any steel against foes. 546 says it is not the spear that gives victory but the king's sceptre, if it does not bend (வேலன்று வென்றி தருவது). In both the literal weapon is set below something else, wealth in one and just rule in the other.
links.reason: எஃகதனிற் கூரியது இல் and வேலன்று வென்றி தருவது ... கோல் both set the literal weapon below something else, wealth and just rule.

links.note: 759 says to make wealth, since no steel is sharper for cutting the pride of foes (செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும்). 878 says the pride found in enemies dies (மாயும் பகைவர்கண் பட்ட செருக்கு) when one knows the way, builds oneself up and guards oneself (தற்செய்து தற்காப்ப). Both aim at the enemy's செருக்கு; Parimelazhagar glosses 878's தற்செய்து as enlarging oneself, and 759 names wealth as the means.
links.reason: செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும் and பகைவர்கண் பட்ட செருக்கு மாயும் aim at the same thing, and Parimelazhagar glosses தற்செய்து as பொருள் படைகளாற் பெருகச் செய்தல், which ties it to 759's செய்க பொருளை.

links.note: 759 calls wealth the sharpest steel (எஃகு) against enemies' pride. 985 says bowing is the weapon (படை) by which the worthy turn their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Each names a non-military thing as the real weapon against foes: resources for the ruler, humility for the person of character.
links.reason: 759 calls wealth எஃகு that cuts செறுநர் செருக்கு and 985 calls பணிதல் the படை that turns மாற்றார்; each names a non-martial thing as the real weapon.

links.note: 760 makes wealth the route to the other two aims, virtue and pleasure. 31 makes virtue the source of distinction and wealth (சிறப்பு ஈனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும்). Each verse, speaking from within its own book, puts its own aim first as the one from which the others follow.
links.reason: The note is accurate (760 ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு from wealth, 31 செல்வமும் ஈனும் from virtue), but no image or wording is shared; it is the same primacy claim made from two books.

links.note: 760 says that for those who have made bright wealth in full, the other two, virtue and pleasure, are easy to have together (ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு). 754 says the wealth that yields virtue and pleasure is wealth that came without wrong (தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்). 754 supplies the condition; Parimelazhagar reads it into 760's ஒண்பொருள் as wealth that comes by the right way.
links.reason: 760 states the result of ஒண்பொருள் and 754 states the condition தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்; Parimelazhagar does gloss ஒண்பொருள் as நெறியான் வரும் பொருள்.

links.note: 760 says abundant wealth makes virtue and pleasure easy to get. 1002 calls it a delusion to hoard without giving on the thought that everything comes from wealth (பொருளானாம் எல்லாமென்று ஈயாது இவறும் மருள்), and says it leads to a low birth. 760's claim holds for wealth that is made and used; held back by a miser, the same belief is called delusion.
links.reason: 760 says for one with ஒண்பொருள் the other two are எண்பொருள்; 1002 calls பொருளானாம் எல்லாமென்று ஈயாது இவறும் a மருள், which limits 760 to wealth that is used.

links.note: 761 says a conquering army, complete in its parts and unafraid of wounds, is the chief of all a king's wealth (வெறுக்கையுள் எல்லாம் தலை). 381 lists the six things a king must have and puts the army first (படைகுடி கூழ் ...). The placing in 381's list and the ranking in 761 agree.
links.reason: 761 does call the army 'வெறுக்கையுள் எல்லாம் தலை', but first position in 381's list 'படைகுடி கூழ்...' is not a ranking: Parimelazhagar says the proper order is otherwise and it was displaced for the verse ('செய்யுள் நோக்கிப் பிறழ வைத்தார்'). The agreement the note claims rests on list order alone.

links.note: 761 counts the army as a form of the king's wealth (வெறுக்கை). 759 counts wealth as a weapon, the sharpest steel against foes (எஃகு). The two neighbouring chapters describe each thing in terms of the other: wealth is a weapon and the army is wealth.
links.reason: வெல்படை வேந்தன் வெறுக்கையுள் எல்லாம் தலை and செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும் எஃகதனிற் கூரிய தில் do describe each thing through the other, army as wealth and wealth as steel; the type is a loose fit since the image is crossed and not shared.

links.note: 762 says steadfastness in defeat is rare except in an old army (தொல்படை). 764 defines an army by courage that has come down to it (வழிவந்த வன்கண்), along with not collapsing and not being turned by subversion. 764 makes a requirement of what 762 observes, and both use வன்கண் for the quality.
links.reason: Both name the quality வன்கண்; 762's தொல்படை and 764's வழிவந்த வன்கண் are the same inherited hardness, observed in one verse and made a defining requirement in the other.

links.note: 762 says the hardness that does not fear harm in a time of decline (தொலைவிடத்து) is found only in an old army (தொல்படை). 806 says those who keep to the bounds do not give up, even in decline (தொலைவிடத்தும்), the bond of those who stood by them of old (தொல்லைக்கண் நின்றார்). Both use the same two words to tie loyalty in bad times to length of standing, in an army and in friendship.
links.reason: தொலைவிடத்துத் தொல்படைக்கு and தொலைவிடத்தும் தொல்லைக்கண் நின்றார் தொடர்பு use the same two words to tie steadfastness in decline to long standing, in army and in friendship.

links.note: 762 says only a long-established army stays firm when it is reduced and the king is faltering. 955 says an old family (பழங்குடி) does not part from its nature even when its means of giving have shrunk. In both, age of standing is what keeps character intact under loss.
links.reason: தொலைவிடத்து ... தொல்படைக்கல்லால் அரிது and வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும் பழங்குடி பண்பில் தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று: age of standing holds character under loss in both.

links.note: 763 says a crowd of weak enemies is nothing to one strong fighter. 873 says one who, being alone, takes on the enmity of many is more foolish than the mad (தமியனாய்ப் பல்லார் பகைகொள்பவன்). 763 holds only where the one is a cobra and the many are rats; 873 is the warning for a lone person who assumes that.
links.reason: 763 dismisses numbers (எலிப்பகை ... நாகம் உயிர்ப்பக் கெடும்) while 873 calls தமியனாய்ப் பல்லார் பகைகொள்பவன் more foolish than the mad; 873 marks the limit of 763's confidence.

links.note: 764 says an army has courage that has come down to it (வழிவந்த வன்கண்). 766 lists the four things that protect an army: valour, honour, walking the excellent path of those before (மாண்ட வழிச்செலவு) and தேற்றம். 766 spells out the inherited quality of 764 as following the path of earlier warriors, which is how Parimelazhagar reads வழிச்செலவு.
links.reason: 764 'வழிவந்த வன்கண்' and 766 'மாண்ட வழிச்செலவு' both rest on 'வழி'; Parimelazhagar reads the latter as following earlier warriors' path, as the note states.

links.note: 768 says an army gains stature through its array (படைத்தகையால் பாடு பெறும்) even if it lacks striking power and endurance; Parimelazhagar takes படைத்தகை as splendour of appearance. 750 says a fort, whatever excellences it has, is as nothing with people who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). They conflict if 768's பாடு is read as real military worth; if it means only repute, 768 is a concession and 750 still stands.
links.reason: 768 is about an army's பாடு from படைத்தகை and 750 about a fort being nothing without வினைமாட்சி in its men; different objects, and the note itself admits that if பாடு is repute there is no conflict, which is the ordinary reading.

links.note: 769 names a resentment that will not leave (செல்லாத் துனி) among the things an army must be free of to win; Parimelazhagar says it arises from degrading treatment. 567 says harsh words and punishment beyond bounds are a file that wears down a king's conquering strength (அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்). 567 gives a cause on the king's side for the condition 769 warns of.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar derives செல்லாத் துனி from இளிவரவாயின செய்தல் and says of 567 that கடுமொழி ruins the army (தானை), so 567 does supply the king-side cause.

links.note: 769 says an army wins if it is free of dwindling, of resentment that does not leave, and of poverty (வறுமை). 759 says to make wealth because it is the sharpest weapon against foes. Parimelazhagar links them from both sides: under 769 he says desertion and want arise when the king does not pay, and under 759 that making wealth brings a large army.
links.reason: 769's வறுமை and சிறுமை are tied by Parimelazhagar to the king not paying (அரசன் பொருள் கொடாமையான் வருவன), and under 759 he says making wealth yields a large army (பெரும்படையும் நட்பும்); the note reports both glosses accurately.

links.note: 770 says an army does not exist without leaders. 1030 says a family with no good person to prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. Both make a group's survival depend on a capable person at its head, in the army and in the household.
links.reason: தலைமக்கள் இல்வழி இல் and நல்லாள் இலாத குடி வீழும் apply the same dependence on a leading person to army and family.

links.note: 771 dismisses the enemy by pointing to the many (பலர்) who faced his lord and became stones. 763 asks what it matters if a host of rats roars like the sea, since they perish when the cobra merely breathes (நாகம் உயிர்ப்பக் கெடும்). Both say numbers on the other side count for nothing against one real fighter; Parimelazhagar reads 763 as the hero not fearing a crowd of non-heroes.
links.reason: 763 is about a noisy host (எலிப்பகை) dying at one cobra's breath, but 771's பலர் are those who each faced the lord and now stand as stones (கல்நின்றவர்); it boasts of his record and doesn't say numbers are irrelevant, so the note overstates the shared claim.

links.note: 771 has a warrior warn enemies not to stand before his lord (என்ஐமுன் நில்லன்மின்), since many who did now stand as memorial stones (கல்நின்றவர்). 894 states the rule behind the warning: for the unable to do harm to the able is like beckoning Death with the hand (கூற்றத்தைக் கையால் விளித்தற்று). The battlefield taunt and the political maxim give the same counsel, one from the strong side and one addressed to the weak.
links.reason: என்ஐமுன் நில்லன்மின் is a soldier's boast about his chief's kills and does not call the enemy ஆற்றாதார்; 894's rule is about wronging the mighty (பெரியார்). The shared logic of courting death by opposing the stronger is real, but 'the same counsel' overstates it.

links.note: 771 is a warrior's boast about a might that turns opponents into memorial stones. In 1088 a lover says his பீடு, which even enemies who had not met him feared in battle (ஞாட்பினுள் நண்ணாரும் உட்கும்), has broken before her bright forehead. The Book of Love borrows the same figure of the warrior whose name alone frightens foes, here as a speaker's way of measuring her effect on him.
links.reason: There is no shared image or word: 771 warns foes about the speaker's lord (என் ஐ) with the memorial stone (கல் நின்றவர்), 1088 speaks of the lover's own பீடு feared by நண்ணார்; the note blurs whose might 771 concerns and 'name alone frightens foes' is only in 1088. It is a martial boast reused in love, not a same image.

links.note: 772 prefers the failed throw at an elephant to the successful shot at a hare, and Manakkudavar takes it with 771 as saying the warrior should send the weak away and fight those who can oppose him. 861 advises the reverse: avoid meeting the strong (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக) and keep up enmity against the weak (மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). The conflict holds if 772 is read as a rule for choosing opponents and 861 as Parimelazhagar reads it; it is the warrior's pride against the king's policy. Kalaignar's gloss of 861 turns it into fighting the strong, which would remove the conflict.
links.reason: யானை பிழைத்த வேல் over முயல் எய்த அம்பு prizes facing the strong, while 861 says வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக and மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை; the note states the readings needed and reports Kalaignar's contrary gloss of 861 correctly.

links.note: 773 makes help to a foe in trouble the cutting edge of valour; Parimelazhagar illustrates it with the king of Ayodhya telling his disarmed enemy to go and come back tomorrow. 987 asks what use worth (சால்பு) is if one does not do what is sweet even to those who did one harm (இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே). The ideal of the worthy person in the chapter on சால்பு appears here as the height of a soldier's manhood.
links.reason: ஒன்றுற்றக்கால் ஊராண்மை (help to a foe in trouble) as the எஃகு of valour matches இன்னாசெய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே; the Ayodhya illustration is in Parimelazhagar.

links.note: 775 asks whether it is not a rout (ஒட்டு in this edition, which Parimelazhagar glosses as turning the back) for the fierce if the eye glaring at the enemy closes in a blink when a spear is thrown. 686 requires the envoy to be one who does not fear the eye (கண் அஞ்சான்), which Parimelazhagar explains as the hostile king's angry stare; 585 says the same of the spy. Holding one's gaze under threat is a test in the court as on the field.
links.reason: 775 is about one's own விழித்த கண் not blinking (இமைப்பின்) at a spear, while 686's கண் அஞ்சான் is not fearing another's angry look (Parimelazhagar: செயிர்த்து நோக்கின்); the shared courage is real but 'holding one's gaze' is the note's bridge, not what 686 says.
links.text_issue: 775 reads ஒட்டன்றோ (standard ஓட்டன்றோ) and வேல்கொண டெறிய (for கொண்டெறிய).

links.note: 775 treats a single blink (இமைப்பின்) before a flung spear as equal to flight. In 1129 the woman says she will not blink because her lover, who lives in her eyes, would be hidden (இமைப்பின் கரப்பாக்கு அறிவல்). Both make the refusal to blink a measure of devotion, to valour in one and, in the speaker's conceit, to the beloved in the other.
links.reason: Both turn on the conditional இமைப்பின்: a blink is ஒட்டு (defeat) for the warrior and hides the lover (கரப்பாக்கு) for the woman, so not blinking marks steadfastness in each.

links.note: 777 says that for those who want fame that circles the earth and do not want life (வேண்டா உயிரார்), tying on the war-anklet is an adornment. 235 says a ruin that is growth and a death that is existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு) are possible only for the skilled, which Parimelazhagar explains by the body of fame outliving the body of flesh. 235 gives the reasoning for the warrior's choice in 777.
links.reason: வேண்டா உயிரார் seeking இசை in 777 is the martial case of 235's உளதாகும் சாக்காடு; Parimelazhagar's புகழுடம்பு gloss is cited correctly.

links.note: 777 describes warriors who prefer fame (இசை) to life. 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame and will not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்). Both rank a value above staying alive; in one it is public renown won in battle, in the other an inner restraint.
links.reason: இசைவேண்டி வேண்டா உயிரார் and நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் ... நாண்துறவார் both rank a value above life, fame in battle and shame in conduct.

links.note: 779 asks who could fault for failure (பிழைத்தது ஒறுக்கிற்பவர்) those who die so as not to break what they vowed (இழைத்தது இகவாமை); Parimelazhagar explains that dying before the vow is accomplished still counts as keeping it. 772 says the spear that missed (பிழைத்த வேல்) the elephant is better to hold than the arrow that hit a hare. Both verses turn on பிழை, a miss, and deny that it is a disgrace when the attempt was great.
links.reason: பிழைத்தது ஒறுக்கிற்பவர் யார் and யானை பிழைத்த வேல் ஏந்தல் இனிது both refuse to count a miss as disgrace when the attempt was great; Parimelazhagar's point about dying before fulfilling the vow is correctly reported.

links.note: 781 praises friendship as the best protection. 815 says the poor friendship of small people, which gives no safety even after it is made (செய்து ஏமம் சாரா), is better not had than had. The protection claimed in 781 belongs only to friendship with the right people; made with the wrong ones it guards nothing.
links.reason: 781 calls நட்பு the காப்பு hardest to breach, and 815 says the புன்கேண்மை of சிறியவர் is செய்தேமஞ் சாரா, giving no protection; a clean limit on 781.

links.note: 782 contrasts friendships that grow and friendships that wane according to the kind of person. 811 says that with people without character, however ardent they look, it is better for the friendship to shrink than to grow (பெருகலிற் குன்றல் இனிது). The waning that 782 observes in bad friendships is in 811 what one should want for them.
links.reason: பின்னீர பேதையார் நட்பு (waning) is what 811 recommends for பண்பிலார் கேண்மை: பெருகலிற் குன்றல் இனிது; a real extension.

links.note: 783 says that with people of character (பண்புடையாளர்) the bond grows sweeter with practice. 811 says that with those who lack character (பண்பிலார்), friendship is better shrinking than growing, even if they seem to drink one up with affection. The reward of long practice in 783 depends on பண்பு; without it, more closeness is worse.
links.reason: பயில்தொறும் பண்புடையாளர் தொடர்பு against பண்பிலார் கேண்மை பெருகலிற் குன்றல் இனிது: the gain from growing closeness is conditioned on பண்பு.

links.note: 784 gives rebuke as friendship's purpose. 795 turns it into a test for choosing friends: examine and take the friendship of those able to speak so that one weeps, to rebuke (இடித்து) and to teach what is proper. What 784 says a friend is for, 795 tells the reader to look for beforehand.
links.reason: இடித்தற் பொருட்டு in 784 becomes a criterion in 795: அழச்சொல்லி ... இடித்து ... வல்லார் நட்பு ஆய்ந்து கொளல்.
links.text_issue: 784 reads மேற்செனறு and 795 reads வல்லார்நடபு (for மேற்சென்று, வல்லார்நட்பு).

links.note: Manakkudavar reads 785 as saying many days of acquaintance are not needed to judge a friendship, because for those of the same understanding (உணர்ச்சி) one meeting gives the claim. 792 says the friendship of one who does not examine again and again (ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான்) ends in grief that kills him. On Manakkudavar's reading the two differ on whether friendship can safely be formed quickly; on Parimelazhagar's, 785 only says that feeling, more than contact, is what makes the bond, and there is no conflict.
links.reason: புணர்ச்சி பழகுதல் வேண்டா on Manakkudavar's gloss (many days of acquaintance are not needed) conflicts with ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான் கேண்மை, and the note says the conflict depends on that reading.
links.text_issue: The packet's Parimelazhagar entry for 785 is actually the commentary on 784 (நட்டல் நகுதற்பொருட்டன்று), so the note's claim about his reading of 785 can't be checked from the packet.

links.note: 786 says friendship in which only the face smiles is not friendship (முகநக நட்பது நட்பன்று), and that friendship in which the heart within smiles is. 824 says to fear deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா). The face and heart contrast that defines true friendship in 786 becomes in 824 the mark of a false friend to be feared.
links.reason: முகநக / அகநக in 786 returns as முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா in 824, the same face-versus-inside test applied to the false friend.

links.note: 787 ends with the friend who suffers along in ruin (அழிவின்கண் அல்லல் உழப்பது). 799 says the friendship of those who abandon one in ruin (கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார்) burns the heart even when remembered at the hour of death. 799 shows the cost of the failure of the third duty that 787 lists.
links.reason: 787's third duty அழிவின்கண் அல்லல் உழப்பது is exactly what கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார் fail, and 799 gives the cost (உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும்).

links.note: In 788 the hand goes at once to the slipping garment (உடுக்கை). In 1023, for one who says he will raise his family, தெய்வம் tucks up its garment (மடிதற்று) and goes ahead of him. Both use a gesture with one's clothing for help that comes unasked and promptly, from a friend in one and from the divine in the other.
links.reason: உடுக்கை இழந்தவன் கை (a hand catching a slipping cloth) and மடிதற்று (girding up to work) are different gestures that share only the fact of clothing; the real common ground is prompt, unasked help (ஆங்கே / தான் முந்துறும்).

links.note: 789 defines the height of friendship as a firm state of propping the other up (ஊன்றும் நிலை). 449 says those without the support of a prop (மதலையாம் சார்பு) have no standing (நிலை), as those without capital have no profit. 789 describes the supporter and 449 the one who needs supporting, in the chapter on a king's reliance on the great.
links.reason: ஊன்றும் நிலை and மதலையாஞ் சார்பிலார்க்கு இல்லை நிலை share the prop figure, seen from the supporter in friendship and from the supported king.

links.note: 789 places friendship's throne in supporting the friend without wavering wherever it is possible (ஒல்லும்வாய் ஊன்றும் நிலை). 818 says to let slip without a word the friendship of those who make difficult a task they could do (ஒல்லும் கருமம் உடற்றுபவர்). The same word for what lies within one's power sets the standard in 789 and identifies the friend who fails it in 818.
links.reason: ஒல்லும்வாய் ஊன்றும் நிலை sets the standard of help within one's power and ஒல்லும் கருமம் உடற்றுபவர் names the friend who fails it, with the same word ஒல்லும்.

links.note: 790 says friendship looks shabby (புல்லென்னும்) even when friends dress it up in words (புனையினும்) such as 'they are this to us and we are that to them'. 978 says greatness always bows while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration (அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). In both, the verbal ornament is the sign of the lesser thing: real friendship, like real greatness, does not advertise itself.
links.reason: புனையினும் புல்லென்னும் and சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து both make self-adornment in words the mark of the lesser thing; the note describes both accurately.

links.note: 791: inquire first, since after befriending there is no leaving (நட்டபின் வீடில்லை). 467: think and then resolve on a task, and to say 'we will think after resolving' (துணிந்தபின் எண்ணுவம்) is a lapse. The same order of thought before an irreversible step is applied to friendship and to action.
links.reason: 791 நட்டபின் வீடில்லை and 467 துணிந்தபின் எண்ணுவம் என்பது இழுக்கு apply the same think-before-committing order to friendship and action.

links.note: 791 grounds the need for inquiry on the claim that for those who keep friendship there is no leaving once it is formed (நட்டபின் வீடில்லை). 800 tells one to leave the friendship of the ஒப்பிலார், even by giving something (ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக), and Parimelazhagar takes this as the remedy for a friendship taken up unknowingly. If வீடில்லை is read as a flat 'there is no release', the two conflict; if it describes only what a true friend will not do, 800 is the exception the chapter allows.
links.reason: 791 நட்டபின் வீடில்லை against 800 ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக ஒப்பிலார் நட்பு is a real conflict on the flat reading of வீடில்லை; Parimelazhagar does supply அறியாது கொண்டாராயின் in 800, and the note states both readings.

links.note: 793 includes a person's இனன், his circle, among the things to learn before befriending him (Parimelazhagar takes it as kin). 453 says that the word 'he is such a one' comes from a person's company (இனத்தானாம் இன்னான் எனப்படுஞ் சொல்). 453 gives the reason the circle belongs on 793's list: it is where a person's character is read from.
links.reason: குன்றா இனனும் அறிந்து and இனத்தானாம் இன்னான் எனப்படுஞ் சொல் share இனம் as what a person is known by; the note correctly records that the commentators take 793's இனன் as சுற்றம் (kin) rather than company.

links.note: 794 picks out as a friend the well-born person who is ashamed of blame (பழிநாணுவான்). 951 says that integrity and shame together are found by nature only in those born in a good house (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்அல்லது இல்லை ... செப்பமும் நாணும்). 951 gives the book's reason for 794 pairing birth with shame as the test.
links.reason: குடிப்பிறந்து தன்கண் பழிநாணுவான் pairs birth with shame, and இற்பிறந்தார் கண்அல்லது இல்லை ... செப்பமும் நாணும் states the premise behind that pairing.

links.note: 795 says to choose as friends those who can rebuke (இடித்து) and bring one to tears over a wrong. 448 says a king without those who rebuke him (இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத) perishes even with no one to ruin him. The rebuker counts as a safeguard both for the private person choosing friends and for the king choosing his support.
links.reason: 795 இடித்து ... வல்லார் நட்பு and 448 இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத ... மன்னன் கெடும் value the rebuker for the private person and the king alike.

links.note: 797 counts leaving the friendship of fools as gain (ஊதியம்). 450 says that letting go the tie with the good (நல்லார் தொடர் கைவிடல்) is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many. Whether breaking a tie is profit or harm depends on who is at the other end of it.
links.reason: பேதையார் கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல் is ஊதியம் while நல்லார் தொடர் கைவிடல் is பத்தடுத்த தீமை: the value of breaking a tie depends on who is at the other end, as the note says.

links.note: 797 says leaving a fool's friendship is gain. 816 says that being a stranger to the wise (அறிவுடையார் ஏதின்மை) is ten million times better than close friendship with a fool (பேதை பெருங்கெழீஇ நட்பு); Pope and Subramuniyaswami render ஏதின்மை as enmity. Both verses put a fool's friendship below having no tie at all.
links.reason: 797 பேதையார் கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல் and 816 பேதை பெருங்கெழீஇ நட்பின் ... ஏதின்மை கோடி உறும் agree that a fool's friendship is worse than none; the commentators here also read ஏதின்மை as பகைமை, which only strengthens the point.
links.text_issue: 816: the Parimelazhagar entry lacks its word-by-word gloss and starts at விளக்கம்.

links.note: 797 calls it gain to give up and leave the friendship of fools (பேதையார் கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்). 839 uses the same phrase, பேதையார் கேண்மை, and says it is very sweet because there is no pain in parting from it. Read together, 839 is the ironic version of 797: the one good thing about such a friendship is the leaving of it.
links.reason: Both have பேதையார் கேண்மை and both turn on leaving it (ஒரீஇ விடல்; பிரிவின்கண் பீழை ... இல்); the note reads 839 as friendship with fools where Parimelazhagar has friendship among fools, but the link survives either way.

links.note: 798 says not to take the friendship of those who cut away in distress (அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார்). 106 says not to give up the friendship of those who were one's strength in sorrow (துன்பத்துள் துப்பாயார் நட்பு துறவற்க). The two prohibitions, கொள்ளற்க and துறவற்க, are complementary: how a friend behaves in trouble decides both whom not to take and whom not to drop.
links.reason: கொள்ளற்க அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார் நட்பு and துறவற்க துன்பத்துள் துப்பாயார் நட்பு are genuinely complementary, as the note says, but neither limits the other, so QUALIFIES is the wrong type.

links.note: 798 begins: do not think of what makes the spirit shrink (உள்ளற்க உள்ளம் சிறுகுவ). 596 gives the positive form: in all one thinks, think of rising (உள்ளுவதெல்லாம் உயர்வுள்ளல்). Both treat the direction of one's thoughts as something to be chosen for the sake of the spirit; 798 then sets fair-weather friends beside the shrinking thoughts as things to refuse.
links.reason: 'உள்ளற்க உள்ளம் சிறுகுவ' and 'உள்ளுவதெல்லாம் உயர்வுள்ளல்' are the negative and positive forms of the same rule about what to think on.

links.note: 798 uses ஆற்றறுப்பார் for friends who fail one in distress. 814 uses the same expression of the untrained horse that fails its rider in battle (அமரகத்து ஆற்றறுக்கும் கல்லாமா) and says solitude is better than such people as one's own. 814 supplies the picture for 798's word: support that holds until the moment it is needed.
links.reason: அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார் and அமரகத்து ஆற்றறுக்கும் கல்லாமா use the same expression. 814's horse gives the picture for 798's word.

links.note: 799 says the thought of false friends burns the heart (உள்ளஞ் சுடும்). 293 says that after a lie one's own heart burns one (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). In 293 the heart burns for one's own fault, in 799 for another's desertion, so the same inner fire is given two different causes.
links.reason: உள்ளஞ் சுடும் and தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும் share the burning-heart figure, with the note's contrast of causes accurate.

links.note: 799 ends உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும்: even to think of the deserter's friendship burns the heart. 1207 ends with the same words in the mouth of the parted woman, for whom even remembering her lover burns. The phrase is used once for betrayal and once for separation in love; in both the pain comes from memory of a bond, not from a present injury.
links.reason: Both end உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும், once for the deserting friend's கேண்மை and once for the absent lover; the shared line and the memory-of-a-bond reading are accurate.

links.note: 794 says the friendship of the well-born man who fears blame is worth getting even by giving (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்). 800 says the friendship of the ஒப்பிலார் is worth leaving even by giving something (ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக). The chapter uses the figure of payment in both directions, for acquiring a good friend and for getting free of a bad one.
links.reason: 794 கொடுத்தும் கொளல் and 800 ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக use payment for gaining a good friend and shedding a bad one; Parimelazhagar uses விலை கொடுத்தும் for both.

links.note: 800 says to leave the friendship of the unfit even at a cost. 818 says how to leave one kind of bad friend, those who make hard work of what they could do: without speaking of it, let the friendship slip (சொல்லாடார் சோர விடல்). 818 adds a manner of leaving to 800's instruction to leave.
links.reason: ஒருவுக ஒப்பிலார் நட்பு gives the instruction to leave and சொல்லாடார் சோர விடல் gives a manner of leaving for one kind of bad friend.

links.note: 802 calls it the duty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கடன்) to take a friend's liberties well. 981 says that for those who take on worthiness knowing what is due, all good things are கடன். 802 is one instance of 981's general statement, with the same word கடன்.
links.reason: சான்றோர் கடன் in 802 is one case of 981's கடன்என்ப நல்லவை எல்லாம் for those who take on சான்றாண்மை; the shared word கடன் is read as duty or nature by the commentators in both.

links.note: 803 asks what use long friendship is if one does not accept a friend's liberty as though one had done it oneself (செய்தாங்கு அமையாக் கடை). 790 says friendship looks shabby even when friends describe each other as 'they are this to us, we are that to them'. Both deny a separation of 'mine' and 'theirs' between friends: 790 in how they speak of each other, 803 in whose act an act is counted to be.
links.reason: செய்தாங்கு அமையாக் கடை (accept the friend's act as one's own) and the rejection of இனையர் இவர் எமக்கு, இன்னம் யாம் both deny a you/me division between friends; Parimelazhagar on 790 says the same.

links.note: 804 says that when friends act without asking, out of intimacy (கெழுதகையாற் கேளாது), it is welcomed. 788 compares friendship to the hand of a man whose garment slips, removing the distress there and then (ஆங்கே). The hand in 788 does not ask leave before acting; 804 states the same thing from the receiving side, that such unasked action is to be wanted and not resented.
links.reason: 804 is about friends taking liberties unasked (கெழுதகையாற் கேளாது செயின்) and 788 about speed of help (ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது); 'the hand does not ask leave' is the note's inference from the simile, not something 788 says.

links.note: 805 says a hurtful act by a friend is to be understood as folly or as great intimacy (பெருங்கிழமை). 109 says that even an injury like killing is cancelled when one thinks of a single good the person did. Both teach a way of reading an injury so that the bond survives it; 109 does it by remembering a past benefit, 805 by a charitable account of the cause.
links.reason: 805 reads a friend's நோதக்க act as பேதைமை or பெருங்கிழமை; 109 lets one நன்று உள்ள cancel a கொன்றன்ன இன்னா: the same bond-preserving reinterpretation in friendship and gratitude.

links.note: 187 says that those who cannot make friends by pleasant speech will divide even their own people by divisive talk (பகச்சொல்லிக் கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர்). 808 describes the friend on whom that does not work, who does not listen to reports of a friend's lapse. 187 gives the talebearer's side and 808 the hearer's refusal.
links.reason: பகச்சொல்லிக் கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர் is the talebearer and கேளிழுக்கம் கேளாக் கெழுதகைமை is the hearer who refuses such reports; the two sides of one transaction.

links.note: 808 speaks of those with the strength of intimacy not to listen to talk of a friend's lapse (கேளிழுக்கம் கேளா); Parimelazhagar takes this as not accepting it even when others report it. 510 says that doubting one who has been trusted after examination (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு) brings endless trouble. Both rule out reopening a settled trust, in friendship and in a king's appointments. The second half of 808 is read in opposite ways by Parimelazhagar (the day of the lapse is a day well spent) and Kalaignar (the days are wasted), so the link rests only on the first half.
links.reason: கேளிழுக்கம் கேளா and தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு ... தீரா இடும்பை both refuse to reopen a settled trust, and the note rightly rests only on 808's first half.

links.note: 791 says that for those who keep friendship there is no leaving once it is formed (வீடில்லை). 809 says the world wants (விழையும் உலகு) those who do not leave (விடாஅர்) the friendship of friends of unbroken long standing. What 791 gives as a reason for caution before befriending, 809 presents as what earns a person general regard.
links.reason: நட்டபின் வீடில்லை and கேண்மை விடாஅர் விழையும் உலகு treat the same non-abandonment, once as a ground for caution and once as what the world esteems (Parimelazhagar's construal of 809).

links.note: In 1266 the waiting wife says that when her husband returns she will drink him in (பருகுவன்) so that her pain ends. 811 uses the same verb for friends who look as though they would drink one up (பருகுவார் போலினும்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as from excess of love. The pair shows 'drinking' as the book's figure for consuming affection, sincere in the wife's mouth and only an appearance in the bad friend.
links.reason: பருகுவார் போலினும் (811) and பருகுவன் (1266) use drinking for consuming affection, apparent in the bad friend and real in the wife.

links.note: 812 treats the friendship of those who leave when the gain ends (அறின் ஒரூஉம்) as a matter of indifference, gained or lost. 799 says that the friendship of those who abandon one in ruin (கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார்) burns the heart even when recalled at the hour of death (உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும்). Read together, losing such a friend is no loss, yet having trusted one is not painless.
links.reason: பெறினும் இழப்பினும் என் treats the fair-weather friend with indifference while 799's அடுங்காலை உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும் says such a friendship still burns; a real qualification.

links.note: Both verses name the ஒப்பிலார். 812 says it makes no difference whether their friendship is had or lost; 800 goes further and says to leave it even by giving something (ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக). Parimelazhagar explains the word differently in each place: here as those who fit with no one because they look only to their own gain, there as those who do not accord with the world.
links.reason: Both name ஒப்பிலார்: 812 பெறினும் இழப்பினும் என், and 800 ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக; Parimelazhagar does explain the word as பிறரோடு பொருத்தமிலர் in 812 and உலகோடு ஒத்தலில்லார் in 800.
links.text_issue: 812 prints அறின்ஙருஉம், a corruption of அறின் ஒரூஉம்.

links.note: 839 says, with irony, that the friendship of fools is very sweet because parting from them brings no pain (பிரிவின்கண் பீழை தருவதொன்றில்). 812 asks what it matters whether one gains or loses (பெறினும் இழப்பினும் என்) the friendship of those who befriend when there is profit and leave when there is none. Both measure a worthless friendship by the same test: its loss costs nothing.
links.reason: பெறினும் இழப்பினும் என் and பிரிவின்கண் பீழை தருவதொன்றில் apply the same test, that losing the friendship costs nothing.
links.text_issue: 812: 'அறின்ஙருஉம்' looks like a typo for 'அறின்ஒரூஉம்'.

links.note: 813 sets friends who weigh what will come to them (உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பு) beside 'those who take what they get' (பெறுவது கொள்வார்), whom Parimelazhagar identifies as courtesans, and thieves. 912 describes those women directly: they weigh the profit and then speak of character (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). The later chapter spells out the comparison 813 makes in a phrase, with the same verb தூக்கு for the calculating look.
links.reason: உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் and பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும் share தூக்கு, and Parimelazhagar glosses பெறுவது கொள்வார் as பொது மகளிர், so 912 does spell out 813's comparison.

links.note: 788 defines friendship by the moment of need: like the hand of a man whose garment slips, it removes distress there and then (ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது). 814 pictures the reverse, a horse that gives way in the battle itself (அமரகத்து). Both locate the test of a friend at the instant of crisis, one by the hand that acts unasked and one by the mount that fails.
links.reason: 788 ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது and 814 அமரகத்து ஆற்றறுக்கும் கல்லாமா both test friendship at the moment of crisis, by the hand that acts and the mount that fails.

links.note: 106 says not to give up the friendship of those who were one's strength in sorrow (துன்பத்துள் துப்பாயார் நட்பு). 815 says the friendship of the small, which gives no safety (ஏமம்), is better not obtained at all. The same measure, support in trouble, decides in one verse which friends must be kept and in the other which should never be acquired.
links.reason: 106's துன்பத்துள் துப்பாயார் நட்பு must not be abandoned; 815's செய்தேமஞ் சாராச் சிறியவர் புன்கேண்மை is better never had. Support in trouble (துப்பு / ஏமம்) is the test in both, applied to keeping and to acquiring.

links.note: 799 says the friendship of those who abandon one in ruin burns the heart even to think of at the time of death (அடுங்காலை உள்ளினும்). 819 says the bond with those whose words and deeds differ is painful even in a dream (கனவினும் இன்னாது). Each verse extends the harm of a false friend beyond ordinary waking life, to the deathbed in one and to sleep in the other.
links.reason: கனவினும் இன்னாது and அடுங்காலை உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும் are parallel 'even in X' intensifiers about bad friends; neither extends the other, so this is a parallel pair, not a development.

links.note: 188 asks what people whose habit is to broadcast even the faults of those close to them (துன்னியார் குற்றமும் தூற்றும்) would do to strangers. 820 warns against the bond with those who are friendly in private and blame one in public. Both take the public exposure of an intimate as the mark of a person no one should be near.
links.reason: மனைக்கெழீஇ மன்றில் பழிப்பார் and துன்னியார் குற்றமும் தூற்றும் மரபினார் both mark out the person who exposes an intimate in public as one to keep away from.

links.note: 487 says the bright do not flare up outwardly at once but watch for the time and burn within (காலம்பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர்). 821 warns that those who keep close without inner consent will strike when they see the right place. The patience the book recommends to a ruler in 487 is the same conduct it tells him to expect from a false friend in 821.
links.reason: 487 'காலம்பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர்' and 821 'சீரிடம் காணின் எறிதற்கு ... நேரா நிரந்தவர் நட்பு' show the same concealed waiting, advised to the king and feared in the false friend.

links.note: 883 says to fear the enemy within, because at the moment of weakness (உலைவிடத்து) it cuts like the tool that cuts the potter's clay (மட்பகை). 821 says the friendship of those who join without inner accord (நேரா நிரந்தவர்) is an anvil (பட்டடை) for striking once they find the right opening (சீரிடம் காணின்). Both verses use a craftsman's tool for the hidden enemy and both place the blow at the moment that suits him.
links.reason: 821 சீரிடம் காணின் எறிதற்குப் பட்டடை and 883 உலைவிடத்து மட்பகையின் மாணத் தெறும் both figure the hidden enemy as a craftsman's tool that acts at the opportune moment.

links.note: 882 says not to fear enemies who are like swords but to fear the bond with enemies who are like kin (கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு). 822 says the friendship of those who seem one's own and are not (இனம்போன்று இனமல்லார்) will turn. Both identify the enemy in the guise of kin as the dangerous one; 882 gives the instruction and 822 the reason, that such a bond does not stay what it looks like.
links.reason: இனம்போன்று இனமல்லார் கேண்மை and கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு name the same figure, the enemy who looks like one's own, and 822's வேறு படும் gives the reason for 882's அஞ்சுக.

links.note: 920 lists two-minded women (இருமனப் பெண்டிர்) with liquor and dice as the company of those fortune has left. 822 compares false friendship to women's minds that become other (வேறுபடும்). The divided or shifting female mind serves in both as the book's figure for a tie that cannot be relied on, and 920 suggests which women the figure has in view.
links.reason: மகளிர் மனம்போல வேறுபடும் and இருமனப் பெண்டிர் share the divided female mind as figure for an unreliable tie. The last clause goes a little far: Parimelazhagar takes 822's மகளிர் as women in general (பெண்பாலார்), not the women of chapter 92.

links.note: 822 uses women's minds as its example of something that changes (மகளிர் மனம்போல வேறுபடும்); Parimelazhagar takes this of women in general and supports it with a line from the Valaiyapathi. 974 takes single-minded women (ஒருமை மகளிர்) as its model of the constancy that greatness needs. On Parimelazhagar's general reading of 822 the two figures conflict; if 822's மகளிர் is limited to the courtesans of chapter 92, they do not.
links.reason: 822's மகளிர் மனம்போல வேறுபடும் and 974's ஒருமை மகளிரே போல use women as opposite similes, but 974's qualifier ஒருமை already picks out a subset, so even on Parimelazhagar's general reading of 822 the claims are not strictly incompatible; a contrast of figures more than a tension.

links.note: 509 says to trust no one without examining them and, having examined, to trust what is to be trusted (தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது). 825 says that those who are not at one with you in mind are not to be judged trustworthy by their words in any matter (சொல்லினால் தேறற்பாற்று அன்று). 825 adds to the rule of examination a statement of what cannot count as evidence.
links.reason: தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது is extended by சொல்லினால் தேறற்பாற்று அன்று, which rules out words as grounds for trust.

links.note: 890 says that life with those who are not in accord (உடம்பாடு இலாதவர்) is like living with a snake in a hut. 825 says those whose minds are not settled with yours (மனத்தின் அமையாதவர்) are not to be trusted on their words. Both make inner agreement, not outward closeness or speech, the thing that decides whether a person near you is safe.
links.reason: மனத்தின் அமையாதவர் and உடம்பாடு இலாதவர் both make inner accord, not words or proximity, the test of safety; Parimelazhagar glosses the second as மனப் பொருத்தம் இல்லாதார்.

links.note: 709 says the eye itself tells of enmity and friendship (பகைமையும் கேண்மையும் கண்ணுரைக்கும்) to those who know how to read it. 826 says an enemy's words are soon recognised even when they sound like a friend's. Both hold that hostility shows through the surface; 709 makes this depend on a skilled reader, a condition 826 leaves unstated.
links.reason: 709: பகைமையும் கேண்மையும் கண்ணுரைக்கும், for those who know கண்ணின் வகைமை; 826: ஒட்டார்சொல் ஒல்லை உணரப்படும். Both say hostility shows through a friendly surface, and the note correctly marks 709's added condition.

links.note: 826 says the words of the unreconciled are quickly seen through although they say good things as friends do. 828, in the same chapter, says a weapon can lie hidden in hands joined in worship (தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்) and in an enemy's tears. 828 limits the confidence of 826: the speech may give itself away, but gestures of submission and grief can still conceal the intent.
links.reason: 828 (தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும், அழுத கண்ணீரும் அனைத்து) extends the same warning from words to gestures and tears; it does not limit 826's ஒல்லை உணரப்படும், which is about speech. The link is real but it is a development, not a qualification.

links.note: 488 advises that on meeting an enemy one should bear him, which Parimelazhagar glosses as bowing, until his end is in sight (செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க இறுவரை). 827 says not to accept an enemy's bowing speech (சொல்வணக்கம்), because the bending of a bow signals harm. The humility 488 teaches as a tactic is the humility 827 teaches one to distrust in the other side.
links.reason: 488 'செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க இறுவரை' (Parimelazhagar: பணிக) is exactly the feigned bowing 827 warns against in 'சொல்வணக்கம் ஒன்னார்கண் கொள்ளற்க'.

links.note: 985 says that bowing (பணிதல்) is the strength of those who accomplish and the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). 827 says that an enemy's verbal bowing should not be accepted, since it points to harm as a bent bow does. Bowing is a means of working on an adversary in both; 985 praises it in the worthy, and 827 says that from an enemy it must not be taken as goodwill.
links.reason: 985 makes பணிதல் the worthy man's படை against மாற்றார்; 827 warns that an enemy's சொல்வணக்கம் is like வில்வணக்கம்: the note states the limit accurately.

links.note: 488 says to bear an enemy when you meet him until his final limit comes, and then his head goes down. 829 says to keep the false friend pleased and hold him in the appearance of friendship while it dies inwardly. Both advise outward accommodation of an enemy who cannot yet be opposed openly, in the chapter on timing and in the chapter on false friendship.
links.reason: செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க and நகச்செய்து நட்பினுள் சாப்புல்லல் both prescribe outward accommodation with inward hostility; 'cannot yet be opposed' is explicit only in 488 (இறுவரை) but the shared counsel holds.

links.note: 824 says to fear deceivers who smile sweetly with the face while bitter within. 829 says that those who make much of you outwardly and despise you (மிகச்செய்து தம்மெள்ளுவார்) should be made to smile and be embraced within the friendship so that it dies (நகச்செய்து நட்பினுள் சாப்புல்லல்). The response 829 prescribes has the same form as the conduct 824 warns against; Parimelazhagar notes that it is allowed as royal policy although such doubleness is otherwise unfitting.
links.reason: நகச்செய்து நட்பினுள் சாப்புல்லல் mirrors 824's முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா; Parimelazhagar's அரச நீதி remark is cited correctly.

links.note: 488 advises bearing with enemies when one meets them until their end is in view. 830 advises a friendly face toward enemies at a time when, as Parimelazhagar explains, they cannot be openly put aside. Both treat outward civility toward an enemy as a matter of timing and not of feeling.
links.reason: முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல் and செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க இறுவரை both make outward forbearance toward an enemy depend on timing (காலம் வருங்கால்; இறுவரை காணின்).

links.note: 831 defines folly as taking up what harms and letting gain go (ஏதங்கொண்டு ஊதியம் போக விடல்). 422 defines understanding as the reverse movement: turning away from evil and steering toward good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது). Read together, the two definitions are mirror images, so folly in 831 is not a lack of information but the wrong choice between two things in view.
links.reason: ஏதங்கொண்டு ஊதியம் போக விடல் and தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது are mirror definitions of பேதைமை and அறிவு. The pairing is instructive, though strictly it is a contrast and not one claim stated twice.

links.note: 831 says folly is to let gain go (ஊதியம் போக விடல்). 797 uses the same two words to say what gain is: giving up and leaving the friendship of fools (ஊதியம் என்பது ... பேதையார் கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்). The fool lets gain go, and for everyone else letting the fool go is the gain.
links.reason: ஊதியம் போக விடல் (the fool's mark) and ஊதியம் என்பது ... பேதையார் கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்: the same words with the direction inverted, both about the பேதை.

links.note: 831 says folly is accepting harm and letting gain go. 925 gives a concrete case in drinking: handing over wealth to receive ignorance of one's own body (பொருள்கொடுத்து மெய்யறியாமை கொளல்), which it traces to கையறியாமை, not knowing what to do. The drinker's purchase is 831's exchange carried out literally.
links.reason: ஏதங்கொண்டு ஊதியம் போக விடல் is enacted literally in பொருள்கொடுத்து மெய்யறியாமை கொளல், which the verse itself attributes to கையறியாமை.

links.note: 832 names as the worst folly a liking (காதன்மை) for what is not fit for one. 439 gives the matching instruction: do not set your desire on a deed that yields no good (நயவற்க நன்றி பயவா வினை). Both locate the error in the wanting, before any deed is done.
links.reason: 832 கையல்லதன்கண் காதன்மை செயல் and 439 நயவற்க நன்றி பயவா வினை both fault the desire for a wrong or fruitless course; Parimelazhagar glosses 832 as காதன்மை செய்தல்.

links.note: 833 lists four absences as the fool's work: no shame, no inquiry, no tenderness, no care for anything (நாணாமை நாடாமை நாரின்மை யாதொன்றும் பேணாமை பேதை தொழில்). 428 defines folly as not fearing what should be feared and calls fearing it the work of the knowing (அறிவார் தொழில்). Both define folly as a missing response where one is due, and both set it out as a characteristic தொழில்.
links.reason: 833 lists நாணாமை நாடாமை நாரின்மை ... பேணாமை as பேதை தொழில்; 428 calls அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சாமை பேதைமை and its opposite அறிவார் தொழில். Both define folly by an absent due response and frame it as a தொழில்.

links.note: 833 describes the fool by four negations. 865 describes the ideal enemy to have by a similar string: he does not look to the way, does not do what is fitting, does not look to blame, has no character (வழிநோக்கான் ... பழிநோக்கான் பண்பிலன்), and so is sweet to his foes. The same profile that 833 treats as a moral portrait is, in the chapter on enmity, a strategic weakness.
links.reason: 833 நாணாமை நாடாமை நாரின்மை பேணாமை and 865 வழிநோக்கான் ... பழிநோக்கான் பண்பிலன் are matching strings of negations, a moral portrait in one chapter and பற்றார்க்கு இனிது in the other.

links.note: 833 puts shamelessness (நாணாமை) first among the fool's traits. 1018 says what that trait costs: if one is not ashamed of what makes others ashamed, the fault is one that virtue itself would be ashamed of (அறம் நாணத் தக்கது உடைத்து); Parimelazhagar reads it as virtue leaving him. 1018 supplies the consequence that 833 leaves unstated.
links.reason: நாணாமை heads 833's list and 1018 gives a consequence of not feeling shame (Parimelazhagar: அறம் விட்டு நீங்கத் தக்க குற்றம்), but the tie is one shared word from a four-item list and any verse of the shame chapter would serve as well.

links.note: 130 praises the one who guards against anger and, having learned, is restrained (கற்றடங்கல் ஆற்றுவான்): virtue itself seeks him out. 834 names the one who has read, understood and taught but is not restrained (ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் ... தானடங்கா) the greatest of fools. Both treat learning and அடங்கல் as a pair in which the learning is judged by the restraint.
links.reason: கற்றடங்கல் ஆற்றுவான் (130) and ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் ... தானடங்கா (834) are the positive and negative of learning joined to அடங்கல்.

links.note: 834 presents a puzzle: a person who has studied, understood and taught, and still does not restrain himself. 373 offers the chapter on fate's account of such a person: however many subtle books one studies, one's own underlying understanding prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்), which Parimelazhagar takes as the folly given by fate. 373 explains how the fool of 834 is possible.
links.reason: 834 'ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் ... தானடங்காப் பேதை' is accounted for by 373 'நுண்ணிய நூல்பல கற்பினும் ... தன் உண்மை யறிவே மிகும்', which Parimelazhagar reads as fate-given folly prevailing.

links.note: 835 calls the fool's destination an அளறு, a mire or hell, into which he enters and sinks (புக்கழுந்தும்). 919 calls the shoulders of women who draw no line the அளறு in which base men sink (பூரியர்கள் ஆழும் அளறு). 919 uses for one present indulgence the image that 835 uses for the result of a whole life of folly.
links.reason: அளறு with sinking is in both (புக்கழுந்தும் அளறு / ஆழும் அளறு), for the fool's fate over seven births in 835 and for the வரைவிலார் மென்தோள் in 919.

links.note: 836 says that when a fool who does not know the way of doing (கையறியாப் பேதை) takes up a task, the task fails (பொய்படும்) and he himself ends in fetters. 468 says effort not made by the right means will collapse (பொத்துப் படும்) even with many standing by to protect it. Parimelazhagar glosses both verbs as புரைபடும்; 468 states the rule about method and 836 adds the cost to the doer.
links.reason: பொய்படும் (836) and பொத்துப்படும் (468) are both glossed புரைபடும் by Parimelazhagar, and both tie failure to not knowing the method (கையறியா / ஆற்றின் வருந்தா); 836 adds புனை பூணும்.

links.note: 836 describes the fool as கையறியா, not knowing how to act. 925 uses the same compound, கையறியாமை, as the cause of paying money to lose awareness of oneself in drink. In both verses the word names a practical ignorance that ends in the person binding or losing himself.
links.reason: கையறியாப் பேதை (836) and கையறியாமை (925) are the same compound for practical ignorance, ending in புனைபூணும் and மெய்யறியாமை respectively.

links.note: 837 speaks of great wealth that has come to a fool (பெருஞ்செல்வம் உற்றக்கடை) and benefits the wrong people. 1000 says great wealth obtained by one without character (பண்பிலான் பெற்ற பெருஞ்செல்வம்) is like good milk spoiled by its vessel. Parimelazhagar notes on both verses that the verb marks wealth received and not made; both hold that the holder's defect ruins what the wealth could do.
links.reason: பேதை பெருஞ்செல்வம் உற்றக்கடை and பண்பிலான் பெற்ற பெருஞ்செல்வம் both have the holder's defect spoil great wealth; Parimelazhagar does remark on both that the holder lacked the power to make it (படைக்கும் ஆற்றல் இல்லாமை).

links.note: 837 says a fool's great wealth feeds strangers (ஏதிலார்) while his own go hungry. 1009 says wealth amassed by giving up love, denying oneself and ignoring virtue will be taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). The miser and the fool arrive at the same result by opposite routes, one by holding wealth back and one by letting it go to the wrong people.
links.reason: 837 ஏதிலார் ஆரத் தமர்பசிப்பர் and 1009 ஒண்பொருள் கொள்வார் பிறர் both end with outsiders getting the wealth, from the fool's misdirection and the miser's hoarding; the note describes both correctly.

links.note: 838 likens a fool's possession to drunkenness added to derangement. 408 says fortune lodged with the unlearned is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு). Both deny that wealth is a good independent of its holder; 838 gives the image and 408 the comparative judgment.
links.reason: 838 மையல் ஒருவன் களித்தற்று ... பேதை ... உடைமை பெறின் and 408 கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு both make wealth's worth depend on its holder, across the chapters on folly and lack of learning.

links.note: 840 treats the fool's mere entry (புகல்) into the company of the worthy as a defilement; Parimelazhagar adds that the assembly itself is lowered by it. 403 allows that even the unlearned are very good if they can stay silent before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 403 leaves a condition under which presence is acceptable, though its subject is the unlearned and 840's is the fool.
links.reason: பேதை புகல் and கல்லாதவரும் ... சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின் concern different persons, as the note admits, and Parimelazhagar takes பெறின் as a condition that won't be met; the qualification is thin.

links.note: 840 likens a fool entering an assembly of the worthy to setting an unwashed foot on a bed (கழாஅக்கால் பள்ளியுள் வைத்தற்று). 720 likens speaking before those not of one's own kind to nectar spilled in an unclean yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்து). The two are mirror images of the same mismatch: the unclean thing brought into the clean place, and the precious thing let fall in the unclean place.
links.reason: கழாஅக்கால் பள்ளியுள் வைத்தற்றால் and அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்தற்றால் are built alike and invert the same clean/unclean mismatch for assembly and person. The images are mirrored, not identical, as the note says.

links.note: 842 says that when a person without understanding gives gladly, the cause is nothing but the receiver's தவம். 70 says a son's service to his father is to make people ask what the father did as penance (என்நோற்றான் கொல்) to have him. Both use the same figure, explaining a good by the stored merit of the one who benefits; 70 uses it as praise of the son and 842 to deny the giver any credit.
links.reason: பெறுவான் தவம் (842) and என்நோற்றான் கொல் (70) both explain a good by the beneficiary's earlier merit; the note's contrast of praise for the son and denial of credit to the giver is accurate.

links.note: 92 treats giving with a glad heart (அகனமர்ந்து ஈதல்) as a real good, surpassed only by a glad face and sweet speech. 842 takes the same act, giving with a glad heart (நெஞ்சுவந்து ஈதல்), and says that in a person without understanding it reflects only the receiver's merit. 842 limits 92's valuation: the glad gift counts for the giver only when understanding is behind it, which is how Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read it.
links.reason: நெஞ்சுவந்து ஈதல் (842) and அகன்அமர்ந்து ஈதல் (92) are the same act, but 92 only uses it as a foil for இன்சொல், and Manakkudavar's point in 842 (giving without knowing rank) is not the 'counts for the giver' reading the note attributes to both commentators.

links.note: 843 says the suffering those without understanding inflict on themselves is hard even for their enemies to inflict (செறுவார்க்கும் செய்தல் அரிது). 165 says that for the envious, envy is enough: it brings ruin even when enemies fail to (ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது). Both measure an inner defect against an outside enemy and find the defect the more effective.
links.reason: செறுவார்க்கும் செய்தல் அரிது and ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது both rank an inner defect above an outside enemy as a source of ruin.
links.text_issue: 165 is printed வழுக்காயும் in the packet; the standard reading, which the note and Parimelazhagar use, is வழுக்கியும்.

links.note: 843 says the fool harms himself beyond what an enemy could. 434 says one's own fault is the enemy that brings ruin (குற்றமே அற்றந் தரூஉம் பகை) and is therefore the thing to guard against. 434 gives the general principle of which 843 is the case of the person who cannot do the guarding.
links.reason: 843 தாந்தம்மைப் பீழிக்கும் பீழை செறுவார்க்கும் செய்தல் அரிது and 434 குற்றமே அற்றந் தரூஉம் பகை both locate the worst enemy inside the person; the note's general-rule/case framing is really a develops relation.
links.text_issue: 434: 'த்ரூஉம்' is a typo for தரூஉம்.

links.note: 843 states generally that those without understanding torment themselves (தாந்தம்மைப் பீழிக்கும் பீழை). 847, in the same chapter, names one way it happens: the person without understanding lets the precious மறை slip and so does great harm to himself by himself (பெருமிறை தானே தனக்கு). 847 is a specific instance of 843's claim, with the same stress on தானே.
links.reason: 843's general தாந்தம்மைப் பீழிக்கும் பீழை is instanced by 847's அருமறை சோரும் அறிவிலான் doing பெருமிறை தானே தனக்கு, with the same reflexive stress.

links.note: 844 says the claim to ஒண்மை is itself what வெண்மை is. 404 says that however good an unlearned person's ஒட்பம் may be, those with understanding do not accept it (கொள்ளார் அறிவுடையார்). 404 shows the other side of 844's self-assessment: the brightness one credits to oneself is not credited by those able to judge.
links.reason: ஒண்மை/ஒட்பம் link the verses, but 404 concedes the unlearned man's ஒட்பம் may be கழிய நன்று and says nothing of self-credit, so calling it the other side of 844's செருக்கு overstates.

links.note: 844 locates want of understanding in the pride (செருக்கு) of saying 'we are bright'. 978 says smallness adorns itself in admiration of itself (சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து) while greatness bows. Both make self-admiration the identifying mark of the deficient state, one for understanding and one for stature.
links.reason: 844 ஒண்மை உடையம் யாம் என்னும் செருக்கு and 978 சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து both identify the deficient state by self-admiration.

links.note: 845 says one false claim to learning casts doubt on what one has mastered without flaw. 128 says that if even one bad word has its effect, the good comes to nothing (நன்றாகாதாகி விடும்). Both describe a single lapse spreading backward over what was sound, in knowledge and in speech.
links.reason: கசடற வல்லதூஉம் ஐயம் தரும் and ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல் ... நன்றாகாதாகி விடும் both have one lapse spoiling what was sound.

links.note: 391 tells one to learn what is to be learned without flaw (கற்க கசடற) and then stand by it. 845 uses the same phrase for what a person has truly mastered (கசடற வல்லதூஉம்) and says that carrying on as if one knew what one has not learned (கல்லாத மேற்கொண்டொழுகல்) brings doubt even on that. Pretence undoes the standing of the very learning 391 asks for.
links.reason: The phrase கசடற recurs (கற்க கசடற; கசடற வல்லதூஉம்) with the same sense of flawless mastery, and 845 shows how pretence (கல்லாத மேற்கொண் டொழுகல்) casts doubt on it.

links.note: 405 says an unlearned person's standing gives way once he meets others and speaks (சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்). 845 describes a further loss for one who has some real learning: by taking on what he has not learned, he puts even his genuine mastery in doubt (ஐயம் தரும்). 405 is the exposure of a claim; 845 is the damage the exposure does to what was true.
links.reason: 405: தகைமை ... சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்; 845: கல்லாத மேற்கொண்டொழுகல் கசடற வல்லதூஉம் ஐயம் தரும். 845 adds the further cost to genuine mastery; the note reads both correctly.

links.note: 846 asks whether covering one's nakedness is not itself small-minded when one's faults are left uncovered (தம்வயின் குற்றம் மறையா வழி); Parimelazhagar takes covering faults to mean removing them. 278 speaks of many who, with stain in the mind, bathe and go about concealed (மனத்தது மாசாக ... நீராடி மறைந்தொழுகு). Both set a bodily propriety, clothing or bathing, against an inner fault it does nothing about.
links.reason: 846 sets அற்றம் மறைத்தல் against குற்றம் மறையா; 278 sets நீராடி against மனத்தது மாசு: outward propriety beside an untreated inner fault in both.

links.note: 846 treats clothing the body as trivial beside dealing with one's faults. 1012 says food, clothing and the rest are no different for any living being, and the distinction of humans is having shame (ஊணுடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல நாணுடைமை மாந்தர் சிறப்பு). 1012 gives the reason behind 846: dress is common to all, and what marks a person is shame at fault.
links.reason: 846 calls அற்றம் மறைத்தல் petty when குற்றம் is uncovered; 1012 says ஊணுடை are வேறல்ல and நாணுடைமை is the சிறப்பு. 'Gives the reason' is a little strong, but the clothing-versus-moral-covering link is real.

links.note: Parimelazhagar reads 847 as a person who receives rare instruction and lets it run out without taking it in, harming himself. 418 says ears not pierced by listening are deaf even though they hear (கேட்பினுங் கேளாத் தகையவே). On that reading both describe teaching that reaches a person and does not enter; 847 adds that the loss is self-inflicted.
links.reason: The link needs Parimelazhagar's reading of அருமறை சோரும் as letting instruction run out; and 418's கேள்வியால் தோட்கப்படாத செவி are ears never trained by listening, not teaching that arrived and failed to enter, so 'same claim' overstates.

links.note: 847 says a person without understanding lets the precious மறை slip (அருமறை சோரும்) and so harms himself. Manakkudavar takes மறை as a secret let out to others, a reading Parimelazhagar reports and rejects. On that reading the verse meets 1076, where the base are like a beaten drum because they carry every மறை they hear to others; 1076 notes the harm to others, 847 the harm to the leaker.
links.reason: On Manakkudavar's gloss (சோரவிடுதல் - பிறர்க்குச் சொல்லுதல்) அருமறை சோரும் is leaking a secret, matching 1076 கேட்ட மறை பிறர்க்கு உய்த்துரைக்கலான்; the note names the reading it depends on and Parimelazhagar himself says the others read it so.

links.note: 448 says a king without people who rebuke him will perish even with no one to ruin him (கெடுப்பாரிலானுங் கெடும்). 848 takes the case one step further: a person who has people to direct him and still does not act on it, and cannot work it out alone. 448 makes having correctors the safeguard; 848 shows the safeguard is useless to one who will not be corrected.
links.reason: 448 makes இடிப்பார் the safeguard (கெடுப்பாரிலானுங் கெடும்); 848's ஏவவும் செய்கலான் தான்தேறான் is the case where counsel is present and ignored, a real extension.

links.note: 848 calls the life of one who neither heeds nor understands a disease until it leaves (போஒம் அளவுமோர் நோய்); Parimelazhagar takes this as a burden hard for the earth to bear, while Kalaignar takes the disease as the person's own. 572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a weight on the earth (உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை). On Parimelazhagar's reading the two share the figure of a person whose mere being alive is an affliction to the world.
links.reason: 848's own figure is நோய் and 572's is நிலக்குப் பொறை; the earth-burden enters 848 only through Parimelazhagar's gloss நிலத்திற்குப் பொறுத்தற்கு அரியதொரு நோய், so the two share a claim on his reading but not an image in the text.

links.note: 848 describes one who does not act when told and does not see for himself (ஏவவும் செய்கலான் தான் தேறான்), and calls that life a disease until it departs. 638 describes a king in the same two terms, one who destroys what the knowing say and does not know himself (அறிகொன்று அறியான்), and says the minister must still tell him what is sound. The same double failing appears in both; 848 gives the verdict on the person and 638 the duty of those beside him.
links.reason: ஏவவும் செய்கலான் தான் தேறான் and அறிகொன்று அறியான் describe the same double failing, with a verdict in one and the minister's கடன் in the other.

links.note: 849 ends with the unseeing person continuing to see as he saw (தான்கண்டவாறு). 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own underlying understanding prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்). Both hold that what is brought from outside, a teacher in 849 and books in 373, does not displace the understanding a person already has.
links.reason: காணாதான் கண்டானாம் தான்கண்டவாறு and தன் உண்மை யறிவே மிகும் both say outside instruction does not displace what a person already has; Manakkudavar's 'கொண்டது விடாமை' fits.

links.note: 849 says one who tries to show something to a person who does not see ends up the unseeing one, while that person goes on having seen it his own way (கண்டானாம் தான்கண்டவாறு). 929 says giving reasons to a drunk man is like searching with a flame for someone sunk under water (கீழ்நீர்க் குளித்தானைத் தீத்துரீஇ அற்று). Both describe instruction that cannot reach its target, and in both the effort reflects on the one making it.
links.reason: காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான் and களித்தானைக் காரணம் காட்டுதல் ... தீத்துரீஇ அற்று both describe showing (காட்டு) that cannot reach its hearer; that the effort reflects on the teacher is explicit in 849 and only implied in 929.

links.note: 850 condemns the one who denies what the world affirms. 140 says those who have not learned to conduct themselves in accord with the world (உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்) lack understanding however much they have studied. Parimelazhagar takes 'the world' in both as the high-minded many, so both make their consensus a test that private cleverness does not override.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar glosses உலகத்தார் in 850 and உலகத்தோடு in 140 as உயர்ந்தோர் பலரும்; on that reading both make their consensus the test over one's own cleverness (பலகற்றும்).

links.note: 851 names the fault as பகல், splitting apart, and its chapter closes (860) by setting நகல் against இகல். 187 uses the same pair of roots: those who do not know how to make friends by நகச்சொல்லி will பகச்சொல்லி and separate even their kin. The chapter on backbiting already holds the contrast between dividing and laughing together that the chapter on hostility is built on.
links.reason: 851 பகலென்னும் பண்பின்மை and 187 பகச்சொல்லி ... நகச்சொல்லி share the பகு root, and 860 does set நகல் against இகல்; 'built on' is a little strong but the observation holds.

links.note: 851 defines இகல் as the disease (நோய்) that spreads பகல், the ill nature of division, among all living beings. 886 takes the same division to its end inside one's own circle: if ஒன்றாமை arises among ஒன்றியார், escaping death (பொன்றாமை) is hard at any time. The general diagnosis of 851 becomes a specific warning about a ruler's own people; Parimelazhagar reads 886 of a king.
links.reason: 851's பகல் என்னும் பண்பின்மை (not uniting) spread by இகல் is the same thing as 886's ஒன்றாமை arising among ஒன்றியார், taken to its fatal end (பொன்றாமை ஒன்றல் அரிது).

links.note: 852 ranks not harming a provoker as தலை, the best course. 203 uses the same ranking word: the head of all understanding (அறிவினுள் எல்லாம் தலை) is not to do evil even to those who hate you (செறுவார்க்கும்). Together they show the text treating non-retaliation as a matter of good sense as well as of virtue; Parimelazhagar on 852 explains that retaliating feeds the enmity while refraining lets it die out.
links.reason: இன்னாசெய்யாமை தலை and அறிவினுள் எல்லாந் தலை ... செறுவார்க்கும் செய்யா விடல் share the ranking word and the claim, and Parimelazhagar's note on 852 is as cited.

links.note: 853 says that removing the painful disease of hostility gives a brightness that neither fails nor is flawed (தவலில்லாத் தாவில் விளக்கம்), which Parimelazhagar takes as lasting fame. 156 says those who punish have one day's pleasure while those who forbear have praise until the end (பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ்). Both make enduring renown the result of declining the quarrel, one in the householder's ethics and one in public life.
links.reason: 853 இகல் ... நீக்கின் தவலில்லாத் தாவில் விளக்கம் and 156 பொறுத்தார்க்குப் பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ் both give lasting renown for declining the quarrel; விளக்கம் as fame is the commentator's reading, as the note says.

links.note: 854 offers இன்பத்துள் இன்பம், the joy of joys, as what follows when hostility goes. 629 uses the same two phrases differently: one who does not crave pleasure within pleasure (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்) does not feel pain within pain (துன்பத்துள் துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்). Read together, the joy 854 promises is a result of removing a cause of suffering, and 629 warns against making such joy an object of desire.
links.reason: The shared இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் / துன்பத்துள் துன்பம் is real, but in 854 it is a superlative ('joy of joys') and in 629 a locative ('in pleasure, pleasure'); 629's விழையாதான் concerns ordinary pleasure in good times, so it does not limit 854's promise.

links.note: 855 says no one sets out to defeat a person who can lean away from hostility. 874 goes a step further: the world rests in the greatness of the person of character who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship (பகை நட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும்). 855 describes safety gained by not answering hostility; 874 describes actively turning the enemy into a friend and gives it a public value.
links.reason: இகலெதிர் சாய்ந்தொழுக வல்லார் cannot be overcome; பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும் பண்புடையாளன் holds the world. 874 moves from declining hostility to converting it, as the note says.
links.text_issue: 855 prints மிக்லூக்கும் for மிகலூக்கும்.

links.note: 855 asks who would be inclined to overcome those able to lean away when hostility confronts them (இகலெதிர் சாய்ந்தொழுக வல்லாரை). 985 says the strength of the capable is to bow (பணிதல்), and that this is the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Both treat yielding as what disarms an opponent; 985 states it as a trait of the சான்றோர், 855 as a skill (வல்லார்), which Parimelazhagar says is hard for kings.
links.reason: 855 இகலெதிர் சாய்ந்தொழுக வல்லாரை யாரே மிகலூக்கும் and 985 பணிதல் ... மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை both make yielding what disarms an opponent.
links.text_issue: 855: 'மிக்லூக்கும்' is a typo for மிகலூக்கும்.

links.note: 855 holds that the one who gives way before hostility cannot be beaten. In 1327 the man says that in a lovers' sulk the one who loses has won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), as the reunion shows. The speaker in 1327 is a lover talking about play-quarrels, so this is the same pattern of winning by yielding in a different setting, not a doctrine shared with 855.
links.reason: இகலெதிர் சாய்ந்தொழுக வல்லாரை யாரே மிகலூக்கும் and ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார் show winning by yielding in two settings (Manakkudavar glosses 1327 with எதிராது சாய்ந்தவர்), and the note limits the claim properly.
links.text_issue: 855 base text reads மிக்லூக்கும் for மிகலூக்கும்.

links.note: 856 says the life of one who declares it sweet to excel in hostility (இகலின் மிகல் இனிது என்பவன்) is close to failure and ruin. 307 says the ruin of one who takes anger to be a thing of worth (சினத்தைப் பொருளென்று கொண்டவன்) is as sure as the hand of one who strikes the ground. In both the fault is the valuing of the passion, and both attach certain or imminent ruin to it.
links.reason: இகலின் மிகல் இனிது என்பவன் and சினத்தைப் பொருளென்று கொண்டவன் both fault prizing the passion and attach near or certain ruin (தவலும் கெடலும் நணித்து; கைபிழையாதற்று).

links.note: 423 defines understanding as seeing the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு) in whatever one hears from anyone. 857 says those of harmful understanding who are attached to hostility (இகல்மேவல் இன்னா அறிவினவர்) do not see the மெய்ப்பொருள் that carries victory. So 857 names hostility as one thing that turns அறிவு against its defining task; Parimelazhagar narrows மெய்ப்பொருள் here to the content of the treatises on statecraft and says hostility clouds the understanding.
links.reason: 857 reuses 423's exact phrase மெய்ப்பொருள் காண் and denies it to இகல்மேவல் இன்னா அறிவினவர், so hostility defeating அறிவு's defining task is a fair development; the note reports Parimelazhagar's narrowing correctly.

links.note: 860 says all ills come from hostility, and from friendly gladness (நகல்) comes 'the pride called good conduct' (நன்னயம் என்னும் செருக்கு). 180 has the same shape and the same closing phrase: coveting without thought yields destruction, and 'the pride called not-wanting' (வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு) yields victory. In both the verse sets a ruinous impulse against its absence and calls that absence a செருக்கு, which Parimelazhagar glosses in both places as wealth.
links.reason: Both verses close on X என்னும் செருக்கு after an opposed ruinous impulse (இகலான் / எண்ணாது வெஃகின்), and Parimelazhagar glosses செருக்கு as செல்வம் in both places, as the note says.

links.note: 860 says இகலான் ஆம் இன்னாத எல்லாம்: every painful thing arises from hostility. 303 says to forget anger toward anyone, because the birth of evils comes from it (தீய பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும்). The Book of Virtue makes anger the source of evils and the Book of Wealth makes hostility the source, with nearly the same construction.
links.reason: இகலானாம் இன்னாத எல்லாம் and தீய பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும் make hostility and anger the source of all ills in parallel constructions.

links.note: 860 credits நகல், glad friendliness, with producing good conduct and its dignity. 999 describes those without the capacity: for people not able to laugh with others (நகல் வல்லர் அல்லார்) the wide world lies in darkness even by day. 860 gives what நகல் yields and 999 what its absence costs; Parimelazhagar reads நகல் in both as rejoicing in company with others.
links.reason: நகலானாம் நன்னயம் and நகல்வல்லர் அல்லார்க்கு ... இருள் give the yield of நகல் and the cost of lacking it; Parimelazhagar glosses நகல் as மகிழ்தல் in 860 and கலந்து உள்மகிழ்தல் in 999, as the note says, though he takes செருக்கு as wealth rather than dignity.

links.note: 862 asks how a man with no love, no worthy allies (ஆன்ற துணையிலன்) and no strength of his own can wear down an enemy's might. 449 states the principle: those without capital have no profit, and those without the prop of supporters (மதலையாஞ் சார்பிலார்) have no standing. 862 applies to a contest with an enemy what 449 says of a ruler's position in general.
links.reason: 862 ஆன்ற துணையிலன் ... என்பரியும் ஏதிலான் துப்பு applies to facing an enemy what 449 says generally, மதலையாஞ் சார்பிலார்க்கு இல்லை நிலை.

links.note: 862 describes the man without love, allies or strength as unable to resist an enemy. 873 judges the man in that position who nevertheless provokes: one who, alone (தமியனாய்), takes on the enmity of many is more foolish than the mad. 862 gives the weak position seen by an attacker; 873 gives the advice that follows for the one who is in it.
links.reason: ஆன்ற துணையிலன் தான் துவ்வான் (862, the easy enemy) and தமியனாய்ப் பல்லார் பகை கொள்பவன் (873) describe the same friendless position from the attacker's and the holder's side; the link is modest but accurately stated.

links.note: 863 puts fear first among the traits that make a man easy for his enemy. 534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை); Parimelazhagar explains that defences are of no use to one with fear in his mind. Both say that fear cancels whatever other protection a person has.
links.reason: 863 opens with அஞ்சும் as what makes one தஞ்சம் எளியன் பகைக்கு; 534 அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை says the same of fear and protection.

links.note: 863 lists fear and ignorance among the weaknesses that make a man easy prey (அஞ்சும் அறியான்). 869 keeps just those two and states them from the other side: joy does not go far from those who fight if they get enemies who are without understanding and afraid (அறிவிலா அஞ்சும் பகைவர்ப் பெறின்). The chapter moves from describing the weak enemy to stating what the attacker gains from him.
links.reason: அஞ்சும் அறியான் in 863 returns as அறிவிலா அஞ்சும் பகைவர்ப் பெறின் in 869, now from the attacker's side.

links.note: 864 says one who does not leave off anger (நீங்கான் வெகுளி) and has no நிறை is easy for anyone, at any time, anywhere. 305 says that if you would guard yourself, guard against anger, because unguarded anger kills oneself (தன்னையே கொல்லுஞ் சினம்). 305 states the self-destruction as an ethical fact; 864 shows how it works in a contest, by making the angry man open to any opponent.
