links.reason: தன்னையே கொல்லுஞ் சினம் and நீங்கான் வெகுளி ... யார்க்கும் எளிது both make unrelinquished anger the cause of one's own undoing, in ethics and in the enemy chapter.

links.note: 864 says the man who cannot leave anger is easy for anyone to overcome. 526 gives the opposite case: no one on earth has more people at his side than one who gives greatly and does not cherish anger (பேணான் வெகுளி). Put together, anger decides whether a man stands with many around him or exposed to all.
links.reason: Anger appears in both (நீங்கான் வெகுளி; பேணான் வெகுளி), but each verse has a second condition the note's conclusion drops: நிறையிலன் in 864 and பெருங்கொடையான் in 526. 'Anger decides' overstates it, and neither verse extends the other.

links.note: 866 says the enmity of a man of blind anger and excessive lust (காணாச் சினத்தான் கழிபெருங் காமத்தான்) is to be welcomed. 360 names the same two, with delusion, as what must perish for suffering to perish (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம்). What the chapter on true knowledge treats as obstacles to release, the chapter on enemies treats as what makes an opponent beatable; Parimelazhagar says such men destroy themselves.
links.reason: சினம்/வெகுளி and காமம் occur in both, but 866 is about which enemy is easy to take on and 360 about ending suffering; the pairing rests on a common stock pair of vices rather than a shared pattern, though the note describes each verse accurately.
links.text_issue: 360 prints 'இநவ்முன்றன்' for இவைமூன்றன்.

links.note: 867 advises paying to have a certain man as an enemy rather than keep him near. 800 advises paying to be rid of a certain friend: give something (ஒன்று ஈத்தும்) and leave the friendship of those who are not a match. Both accept a cost to end a harmful closeness; the commentators differ on who the man in 867 is, Parimelazhagar taking him as one who begins a task and acts unsuitably, Kalaignar as one who stays beside you.
links.reason: கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் ... பகை and ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக ஒப்பிலார் நட்பு share the striking idea of paying to end a harmful closeness, and the note is open about the disputed sense of அடுத்திருந்து.

links.note: 504 tells the ruler to examine a man's qualities, then his faults, and judge by what predominates (மிகை நாடி மிக்க கொளல்). 868 describes the result when the tally is all on one side: with no qualities and many faults (குணனிலனாய்க் குற்றம் பலவாயின்) he is left without companions, and that is a support to his opponents. The test used for choosing servants in 504 is applied by 868 to the ruler himself, with his enemies as the ones who benefit.
links.reason: The குணம்/குற்றம் tally of 504 (மிகைநாடி மிக்க கொளல்) reappears in 868 as குணனிலனாய்க் குற்றம் பலவாயின், with மாற்றார்க்கு ஏமாப்பு as the result; the reading of இனனிலனாம் follows Parimelazhagar.

links.note: 868 says a man without qualities and with many faults comes to have no one with him (இனனிலனாம்). 525 gives the positive case: one who can give and speak pleasantly will be surrounded by kin in rows (அடுக்கிய சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). Both make a person's following a product of his character; 868 adds the military consequence of losing it.
links.reason: குணனிலனாய்க் குற்றம் பலவாயின் ... இனனிலனாம் and கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின் ... சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும் are the negative and positive cases of character deciding one's following.

links.note: 869 says joy does not go far from those who fight if they get enemies who are ignorant and afraid. 772 says holding the spear that missed an elephant is sweeter (இனிது) than holding the arrow that hit a forest hare. One locates the pleasure of fighting in the easy opponent and the other in the hard one; the conflict holds if both are read as claims about what a fighter should want, and eases if 869 is a king's reckoning of advantage and 772 an individual warrior's sense of honour.
links.reason: 869's இன்பம் for செறுவார் is the lasting gain from weak foes (Parimelazhagar: no enmity and wealth together), not the pleasure of fighting, while 772's இனிது is a warrior's pride; the note admits the conflict needs both read as claims about what a fighter should want, which stretches 869.
links.text_issue: Parimelazhagar's entry for 869 is missing its word-by-word gloss; only the விளக்கம் survives.

links.note: 871 says enmity, a thing without good in it (பண்பிலதனை), is not to be wanted even in jest (நகையேயும் வேண்டற்பாற்று அன்று). 867 says the enmity of one who stays close and does unfitting things must certainly be got, even by paying for it (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் மன்ற). The conflict holds if 871 is read as a rule about all enmity; Parimelazhagar narrows it to enmity that brings no benefit, which would leave room for 867.
links.reason: நகையேயும் வேண்டற்பாற்று அன்று against கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் ... பகை is a real conflict on the universal reading, and Parimelazhagar's 'மாணாத பகையை ஆக்கிக் கோடல்' does narrow 871 as the note says.

links.note: 872 says that even if you take on the enmity of those whose plough is the bow (வில்லேர் உழவர்), you should not take on that of those whose plough is the word (சொல்லேர் உழவர்). 129 says a wound burned by fire heals within, but the scar burned by the tongue (நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு) does not. Both rank harm done by words above harm done by a physical instrument, one in statecraft and one in personal conduct.
links.reason: 872 ranks சொல்லேர் உழவர் பகை above that of வில்லேர் உழவர், and 129 ranks நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு above தீயினாற் சுட்ட புண்: the word outdoes the physical weapon in both.

links.note: 873 states the folly of standing alone (தமியனாய்) against many enemies. 875 gives the working rule for the smallest such case: with no ally and two enemies (தன்துணை இன்றால் பகையிரண்டால்), make one of them a pleasing ally (இன்துணையாக் கொள்க). 875 turns 873's condemnation into a remedy.
links.reason: தமியனாய்ப் பல்லார் பகைகொள்பவன் (873) is answered by தன்துணை இன்றால் பகையிரண்டால் ... இன்துணையாக் கொள்க (875).

links.note: 874 praises the one who takes enmity as friendship (பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும்) without saying how it is done. 985 names a means: bowing (பணிதல்) is the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Parimelazhagar glosses this as ending the opponents' enmity, so 985 reads as the method behind 874.
links.reason: பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும் names the result and பணிதல் ... மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை a means; Parimelazhagar's பகைமையொழிக்கும் கருவி supports reading 985 as the method.

links.note: 874 says the world rests in the greatness of the person of character who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship (பண்புடையாளன் தகைமைக்கண் தங்கிற்று உலகு). 996 says the world exists by resting on those of character (பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டுண்டு உலகம்), and would otherwise sink into the earth. Both make பண்பு the thing the world stands on; 874, in the chapter on enmity, specifies it as the capacity to turn enemies into friends.
links.reason: 874 பண்புடையாளன் தகைமைக்கண் தங்கிற்று உலகு and 996 பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டுண்டு உலகம் make the same claim that the world rests on people of பண்பு, in two chapters.

links.note: 875 advises a ruler caught alone between two enemies to make one of them an ally. 633 lists among a minister's abilities dividing (பிரித்தல்), which Parimelazhagar explains as separating the enemy's supporters from him, and rejoining those who broke away (பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்). The advice to the king in 875 is the skill required of the minister in 633.
links.reason: 633's பிரித்தல் is detaching an enemy's allies and பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல் is winning back one's own defectors; neither is 875's turning one of two enemies into இன்துணை. Related alliance craft, but the note's identification overstates it.

links.note: 876 says that whether or not one has trusted the enemy before, in a time of ruin (அழிவின்கண்) one should neither join him nor break from him (தேறான் பகாஅன் விடல்); Parimelazhagar explains that joining lets him destroy from inside and breaking makes him add to the ruin. 691 tells those who serve quarrelsome kings to be like people warming at a fire, neither moving off nor coming close (அகலாது அணுகாது). Both prescribe a deliberate middle distance from a dangerous party, once toward an enemy and once toward one's own king.
links.reason: தேறான் பகாஅன் விடல் and அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க both prescribe a middle distance from a dangerous party; Parimelazhagar's two reasons on 876 are reported correctly.

links.note: 877 says not to let softness show before enemies (மேவற்க மென்மை பகைவர் அகத்து); Parimelazhagar takes மென்மை as lack of strength, which enemies watch for. 440 says that if a ruler can enjoy what he loves without that love being known (காதல் அறியாமை), his enemies' designs come to nothing (ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல்). In both, what an enemy can use is what he is allowed to learn about one's inner state, weakness in one verse and desire in the other.
links.reason: மேவற்க மென்மை பகைவர் அகத்து and காதல் அறியாமை உய்க்கிற்பின் ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல் share the logic of denying enemies knowledge of one's inner state.

links.note: 879 speaks of those who remove the thorn tree with the word களையுநர், weeders. 550 compares a king's putting the cruel to death to weeding the green crop (பைங்கூழ் களைகட்டதனொடு நேர்). Both picture the removal of dangerous people as a cultivator's weeding; 879 adds that timing matters, since the weed grown hard injures the weeder's hand.
links.reason: The shared root களை (களையுநர் / களைகட்டு) is real, but 879's image is felling a முள்மரம் that injures the cutter's hand, about an enemy's growth, not a cultivator weeding a crop; the note overstates by calling both 'weeding'.

links.note: 880 states the cost of not breaking the pride of one's enemies (செயிர்ப்பவர் செம்மல் சிதைக்கலாதார்): one cannot be counted as living. 759 names the instrument for that task: wealth, the sharpest steel for cutting the pride of foes (செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும் எஃகு). One verse gives the necessity and the other the means.
links.reason: 880 செயிர்ப்பவர் செம்மல் சிதைக்கலாதார் gives the necessity and 759 செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும் எஃகு the means; the same object, the enemy's pride, in both.

links.note: 881 says the nature of one's own people is bad if it does harm (தமர்நீரும் இன்னாவாம் இன்னா செயின்). 522 says kin whose affection does not lapse (விருப்பறாச் சுற்றம்) yield many gains that keep branching; Parimelazhagar notes that this wording is chosen to exclude inner enmity. The condition written into 522 is the case 881 describes, so each verse marks the limit of the other.
links.reason: தமர்நீரும் இன்னாவாம் இன்னா செயின் is the case excluded by விருப்பறாச் சுற்றம்; Parimelazhagar's comment on 522 does say the phrase is chosen to exclude உட்பகை.

links.note: 881 says even shade and water are bad when they do harm (நிழல்நீரும் இன்னாத இன்னா), and so is the nature of one's own people when it does harm. In 1309 the man says water is sweet in the shade (நீரும் நிழலது இனிதே), and sulking is sweet only with those who love. Both take shade and water as the standard of what is pleasant and then make the pleasantness depend on a condition, which in both cases is the real disposition of those closest to one.
links.reason: நிழல்நீரும் இன்னாத இன்னா and நீரும் நிழலது இனிதே both start from shade-and-water as the pleasant thing and condition its sweetness, tied in each case to how one's own people (தமர், வீழுநர்) stand toward one.

links.note: 882 uses the verb of fear for kin-like enemies (அஞ்சுக கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு). 824 uses it for deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சரை அஞ்சப்படும்). The chapter on false friendship and the chapter on inner enmity reach the same instruction: what is to be feared is hostility presented as closeness.
links.reason: Both command fear of concealed hostility: 882 அஞ்சுக கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு, 824 முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சரை அஞ்சப்படும்.

links.note: 882 contrasts the enemy who is like a drawn sword (வாள்போல் பகைவர்) with the one who looks like kin, and fears the second. 828 says a weapon hides even within an enemy's hands folded in worship (தொழுதகையுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்), and his tears are the same. In 882 the visible sword is the safer one; 828 shows where the other sword is kept.
links.reason: 882 வாள்போல் பகைவரை அஞ்சற்க ... கேள்போல் பகைவர் and 828 தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும் share the weapon figure for open and disguised enemies; the note is accurate.
links.text_issue: 882: வாள்போல is usually printed வாள்போல்; minor.

links.note: 883 says to fear the enemy within and guard oneself (உட்பகை அஞ்சித் தற்காக்க), or it will destroy one. 305 says that if you would guard yourself, guard against anger (தன்னைத்தான் காக்கின் சினங்காக்க); unguarded, anger kills oneself. The same formula of self-guarding against something lodged inside is applied in one verse to people within the household or court and in the other to a passion within the mind.
links.reason: தற்காக்க and தன்னைத்தான் காக்கின் ... சினங்காக்க are the same self-guarding formula, each with a destroyer lodged inside (தெறும் / கொல்லும்); the note describes both accurately.

links.note: 885 says an inner enmity that comes in the form of kinship (உறல்முறையான் உட்பகை) brings many ills of a deadly kind (இறல்முறையான் ஏதம்) to the ruler. 735 defines a land as one without many factions, without ruinous inner enmity (பாழ்செய்யும் உட்பகை) and without murderous marauders who harass the king. The danger 885 describes for the king's person and household is, in 735, something whose absence is part of what makes a country a country.
links.reason: உட்பகை is named in both, as இறல்முறையான் ஏதம் for the ruler in 885 and as பாழ்செய்யும் உட்பகை whose absence defines நாடு in 735.

links.note: 886 says that if disunity arises among those who are one with a ruler (ஒன்றாமை ஒன்றியார் கட்படின்), it is always hard for him to escape perishing. 764 defines an army as one that is not destroyed, cannot be undermined from within (அறைபோகாதாகி) and has inherited hardness. Both treat the loyalty of one's own side as a condition of survival, stated once as a warning and once as a requirement.
links.reason: 886 is about hostility arising among one's own (ஒன்றாமை ஒன்றியார் கட்படின்), while அறைபோகாது in 764 is one of three defining traits of an army and concerns subversion by the enemy; a related concern, not the same claim.

links.note: 887 uses the casket and its lid for a family that fits together outwardly while divided within. 277 uses the kunri seed for false ascetics, red on the outside (புறங்குன்றி கண்டனையர்) and black within like its tip. Each verse chooses an everyday object to show an outside that does not match the inside, one for kin and one for renouncers.
links.reason: செப்பின் புணர்ச்சிபோல் கூடினும் கூடாதே and புறங்குன்றி ... அகங்குன்றி மூக்கிற் கரியார் both use a homely object for an appearance that hides the reverse, for kin and for false ascetics; the casket shows a join that is not a union more than outside/inside, but the note's wording allows that.
links.text_issue: 277: 'முக்கிற்' should be மூக்கிற்.

links.note: 887 says a family with inner enmity is not joined, though it joins like a casket and its lid (செப்பின் புணர்ச்சிபோல் கூடினும் கூடாதே). 786 says friendship that makes only the face smile is not friendship; friendship is what makes the heart within smile (நெஞ்சத்து அகநக). Both deny the name of union to a joining that is only on the surface, in the family and in friendship.
links.reason: செப்பின் புணர்ச்சிபோல் கூடினும் கூடாதே and முகநக நட்பது நட்பன்று both deny the name of union to a surface joining, in family and in friendship.

links.note: 889 holds that inner enmity is ruinous even at the size of a split sesame seed. 433 says those who are ashamed of blame take a fault the size of a millet seed (தினைத்துணை) to be as large as a palmyra. 433 describes the attitude that 889 calls for: treating the small thing at its eventual size.
links.reason: எட்பகவன்ன சிறுமைத்தே (889) is about inner enmity, தினைத்துணையாங் குற்றம் ... பனைத்துணையாக் கொள்வர் (433) about one's own faults; they share a seed-size measure and logic, not the same claim, and 889 does not itself call for an attitude.

links.note: 889 says inner enmity carries ruin even when it is as small as a split sesame seed. 879 says to cut a thorn tree while it is young (இளைதாக), since grown hard it destroys the cutter's hand. The two neighbouring chapters, on open and on inner enmity, make the same point that hostility should be judged by what it will grow into; only 879 goes on to say what to do about it.
links.reason: எட்பகவன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும் ... உள்ளதாங் கேடு and இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க ... காழ்த்த இடத்து both refuse to judge hostility by its present smallness. 889 says ruin is already within rather than that it will grow, so 'what it will grow into' fits 879 better, but the shared point stands.

links.note: 889 says that inner enmity, though as small as a split sesame seed (எட்பகவன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும்), has ruin in it. 965 says even those like a hill will be lowered if they do a lowering thing the size of a kunri seed (குன்றி அனைய செயின்). Both use a tiny seed as the measure of something that brings down what is large, a family or kingdom in 889 and a person's standing in 965.
links.reason: எட்பகவன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும் and குன்றி அனைய செயின் both use a tiny seed as the measure of what brings down something great (குன்றின் அனையார்).

links.note: 891 makes not slighting the able the chief safeguard; 861 tells the ruler to avoid standing against the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக). The chapter on enmity gives as a tactical rule what 891 gives as a rule of self-protection.
links.reason: 891 ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் இகழாமை and 861 வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக give the same counsel, as self-protection in one and as a rule about whom to fight in the other.

links.note: 892 says disregard of the great brings unending trouble (பேரா இடும்பை); 450 says letting go the tie with the good (நல்லார் தொடர் கைவிடல்) is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many. Both chapters on the great rank a bad relation to them above ordinary dangers, 450 by a number and 892 by permanence.
links.reason: 450 is a comparison (பல்லார் பகை கொளலின் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்து) about losing the support of நல்லார்; 892 is about slighting the powerful (பேணாது ஒழுகின்) and the harm they then cause (பெரியாரால் பேரா இடும்பை). 892 ranks nothing against ordinary dangers, and the two relations to 'the great' differ, so the agreement is generic.

links.note: 892 warns that going on without cherishing the great (பெரியாரைப் பேணாது ஒழுகின்) brings, through them, ills that do not leave. 976 says the intent to cherish and win the great (பெரியாரைப் பேணிக் கொள்வேம் என்னும் நோக்கு) is simply absent from the minds of the small. The shared verb பேணு ties them: 976 names who it is that fails to cherish, 892 what the failure costs.
links.reason: பெரியாரைப் பேணாது ஒழுகின் and பெரியாரைப் பேணிக்கொள்வேம் என்னும் நோக்கு share the phrase; the note passes over that Parimelazhagar's பெரியார் in 892 are the powerful, but the Tamil supports the pairing.

links.note: 893 states as irony what 861 states as a plain command: offending those with the power to destroy (அடல்வேண்டின் ஆற்றுபவர்) is a way to seek one's own ruin, and 861 says to avoid opposing the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக).
links.reason: கெடல்வேண்டின் ... ஆற்றுபவர்கண் இழுக்கு is the ironic form of வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக; same claim in two chapters.

links.note: 893 says: if you want ruin (கெடல்வேண்டின்), go ahead without listening and wrong those able to destroy. 922 says: do not drink, but if anyone will, let it be those who do not want the regard of the worthy (எண்ணப்பட வேண்டாதார்). Both forbid by an ironic permission addressed to whoever wants the bad result, once about offending the powerful and once about liquor.
links.reason: Both forbid through an ironic permission: 893 கெடல்வேண்டின் கேளாது செய்க, 922 உணில் உண்க சான்றோரான் எண்ணப்பட வேண்டாதார்.

links.note: 894 says the unable doing harm to the able (ஆற்றுவார்க்கு ஆற்றாதார் இன்னா செயல்) is like beckoning Death with the hand. 250 asks one about to go against someone weaker (மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து) to think of oneself before the stronger (வலியார்முன்). Both reason from the weak facing the strong: 894 uses it as prudence in the Book of Wealth, 250 turns the same experience into a ground for compassion in the Book of Virtue.
links.reason: ஆற்றுவார்க்கு ஆற்றாதார் and வலியார்முன் / மெலியார்மேல் both reason from the weak-strong asymmetry, toward prudence in 894 and compassion in 250.

links.note: 895 says those who draw the anger of a king of fierce might (வெந்துப்பின் வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர்) cannot go on existing anywhere they go. 691 gives the working rule for those who serve such kings: like people warming at a fire, neither move off nor come close (அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க). 895 states the danger, and 691 the conduct that lives beside it.
links.reason: வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர் யாண்டும் உளராகார் gives the danger and அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க the conduct beside it; Parimelazhagar takes 895's victims as rival kings, which the note does not say but does not contradict.

links.note: 895 makes the king's anger inescapable for those under him; 899 says that if those of exalted resolve flare up (ஏந்திய கொள்கையார் சீறின்), the king himself (வேந்தனும்) breaks midway and loses his kingship. Within the chapter the pair sets up an order of power: the king who destroys others can himself be destroyed by the anger of the great. Parimelazhagar takes வேந்தன் in 899 as Indra.
links.reason: 895 வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர் யாண்டும் உளராகார் and 899 ஏந்திய கொள்கையார் சீறின் ... வேந்தனும் வேந்து கெடும் set up the order of power described; the note discloses that Parimelazhagar (and Manakkudavar) take வேந்தன் as Indra.

links.note: 207 says those who incur any enmity whatever survive it (எனைப்பகை உற்றாரும் உய்வர்), and only the enmity of one's own evil deeds follows and kills. 896 says those who keep offending the great do not survive (உய்யார்). If எனைப்பகை is taken literally as every human enmity, the two conflict; the conflict eases if 207's phrase is read as a rhetorical foil for the enmity of deeds, or if the harm in 896 is understood as itself the fruit of a wrong deed.
links.reason: எனைப்பகை யுற்றாரும் உய்வர் and உய்யார் பெரியார்ப் பிழைத்தொழுகுவார் use the same verb with opposite verdicts. The note states the literal reading the conflict needs and the readings that ease it.

links.note: 444 says living so that those greater than oneself become one's own is the head of all strengths (வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை). 897 gives the other side: a fully appointed life and great wealth count for nothing (என்னாம்) once the worthy great are angered. Together they make one's standing with the great, and not one's possessions, the deciding strength.
links.reason: 444 தமரா ஒழுகுதல் வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை and 897 என்னாம் ... தக்கார் செறின் are positive and negative statements of one claim; neither limits the other, so this is not a qualification.

links.note: 897 asks what a life excellent in every part and lofty wealth (வகைமாண்ட வாழ்க்கையும் வான்பொருளும்) come to if the worthy of great stature are angered (தக்கார் செறின்). 900 says even those with support beyond measure (இறந்தமைந்த சார்பு) do not survive if those of the highest distinction are angered (சீரார் செறின்). The two close on the same word செறின் and between them cancel a person's own assets and then his outside supports.
links.reason: Both verses end on செறின், with வகைமாண்ட வாழ்க்கையும் வான்பொருளும் என்னாம் (897) and இறந்தமைந்த சார்புடையர் ஆயினும் உய்யார் (900); own assets and outside support is an accurate division.

links.note: 898 plays on குன்று (hill) and குன்ற (to diminish): if the hill-like intend diminishment, the seemingly permanent vanish. 965 uses the same play: even the hill-like (குன்றின் அனையாரும்) will diminish (குன்றுவர்) if they do a lowering thing as small as a kunri seed. In 898 the hill-like bring others low; in 965 they themselves can be brought low by their own act, so height gives power over others but no protection from one's own lapse.
links.reason: Both pun on குன்று/குன்ற (குன்றன்னார் குன்ற மதிப்பின்; குன்றின் அனையாரும் குன்றுவர்), and the contrast the note draws is accurate.

links.note: 900 says that even those with support beyond measure will not survive (உய்யார்) if those of the highest distinction are angered (சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார் செறின்). 29 says the anger (வெகுளி) of those standing on the hill of good qualities is hard to ward off (காத்தல் அரிது) even for a moment. The Book of Wealth applies to kings and their resources what the opening chapters said in praise of renouncers.
links.reason: 900 உய்யார் சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார் செறின் and 29 வெகுளி கணமேயும் காத்தல் அரிது state the same irresistible anger of the great, in the king's setting and in praise of renouncers.

links.note: 303 says to forget anger toward anyone at all (யார்மாட்டும்), because every evil is born from it. 900 treats the anger of the most distinguished (சீரார் செறின்) as a force no support can save one from, and Parimelazhagar and Pope take these as people of great austerity. If they are ascetics, the chapter on not being angry would have them without anger; the conflict depends on that identification and on reading 900 as accepting such anger, where it may only be warning the offender of what follows.
links.reason: 303's மறத்தல் வெகுளியை யார்மாட்டும் is advice to the hearer; 900's சீரார் செறின் warns an offender what follows and does not approve the anger. As the note admits, the conflict needs both the identification with ascetics (Parimelazhagar's தவத்தினை உடையார்) and an endorsing reading, so it is thin.

links.note: 45 says that when household life has love and virtue (அன்பும் அறனும்), these are its character and its fruit (பண்பும் பயனும்); Parimelazhagar takes the love as that owed to one's wife. 901 says those who fix their desire on the wife (மனைவிழைவார்) miss the excellent fruit (மாண்பயன்). The pair marks a line between love within the household, which is its fruit, and விழைவு that lets the wife rule the man, which loses it; Parimelazhagar reads 901 as men who follow the wife's lead for pleasure's sake.
links.reason: அன்பும் அறனும் ... பயனும் அது against மனைவிழைவார் மாண்பயன் எய்தார்: the same பயன் is gained by due love and lost by விழைவு, and Parimelazhagar's glosses (துணைவிமேல் செய்யத்தகும் அன்பு; அவள் தன்மையராய் ஒழுகுவார்) are cited accurately.

links.note: 903 calls a man's stooping before his wife (இல்லாள்கண் தாழ்ந்த) இயல்பின்மை, something against the natural order, which shames him among the good. 55 praises the wife who rises worshipping her husband (கொழுநன் தொழுதெழுவாள்). The two show that the book fixes the direction of deference in marriage: it is a merit in the wife and a disgrace in the husband.
links.reason: இல்லாள்கண் தாழ்ந்த இயல்பின்மை and கொழுநன் தொழுதெழுவாள் do show one direction of deference, but neither verse limits the other, and Parimelazhagar takes இயல்பின்மை as fear, not 'against the natural order'.

links.note: 978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை), and elsewhere the book calls bowing good for everyone. 903 names one bowing that brings shame: lowering oneself before one's wife (தாழ்ந்த இயல்பின்மை), which Parimelazhagar explains as arising from fear. The pair separates humility that comes from the absence of pride from submission that comes from fear.
links.reason: பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை praises bowing, and இல்லாள்கண் தாழ்ந்த இயல்பின்மை ... நாணுத் தரும் names a lowering that shames; Parimelazhagar does gloss it as தாழ்தற்கு ஏதுவாய அச்சம்.

links.note: 904 denies வீறு (distinction) to the action of the wife-fearing man: வினையாண்மை வீறெய்தல் இன்று. 665 says the firmness in action (வினைத்திட்பம்) of those who have attained distinction (வீறெய்தி மாண்டார்) reaches the king and is held in regard. The same phrase வீறு எய்து names what capable action normally earns and what, in 904, fear of the wife withholds.
links.reason: 'வீறெய்தல்' with 'வினை' does recur, but in 665 'வீறெய்தி மாண்டார்' names a quality the ministers already have (Parimelazhagar: 'எண்ணத்தால் சிறப்பெய்தி'), whose 'வினைத்திட்பம்' is then esteemed; the note's 'what capable action normally earns' fits 904 but not 665.

links.note: 904 says the man who fears his wife gets no distinction from his command of action (வினையாண்மை வீறெய்தல் இன்று). 1026 defines good manliness (நல்லாண்மை) as making the mastery of one's house one's own (இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்), which Parimelazhagar takes as leading one's family. Both build on ஆண்மை as mastery: the man of 904 has given up mastery at home, and his mastery of work earns no honour.
links.reason: Both use -ஆண்மை (வினையாண்மை, நல்லாண்மை/இல்லாண்மை), but 1026's 'தான்பிறந்த இல்' is the family one is born into (Parimelazhagar: குடியினை ஆளும் தன்மை), not authority over a wife as in 904's 'மனையாளை அஞ்சும்'; linking them as mastery at home blurs two different things.

links.note: 905 says the man who fears his wife fears to do good to the good; 908 says those who act as she wishes (பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகுபவர்) neither meet their friends' needs nor do good (நன்றாற்றார்). Both state the cost to others: the wife-ruled man fails the good in 905 and his friends in 908.
links.reason: அஞ்சும் நல்லார்க்கு நல்ல செயல் and நட்டார் குறைமுடியார் நன்றாற்றார் both state the cost to others of the wife-ruled man; close neighbours in one chapter but the pairing is accurate.

links.note: 906 says that even if they live like the gods (இமையாரின் வாழினும்), men who fear their wife's bamboo-like shoulders (அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சுபவர்) have no dignity (பாடிலர்). In 1088 a lover exclaims that his might (பீடு), feared by enemies in battle, has broken before her bright forehead alone. Both show male standing giving way before a woman's bodily feature; the Book of Wealth counts it a disgrace, while in the Book of Love it is a lover's speech in the moment and carries no judgment.
links.reason: அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சுபவர் பாடிலர் and ஒண்ணுதற்கு ... உடைந்ததே ... என் பீடு both show a man's standing giving way before a woman's bodily feature, and the note keeps the difference in register.

links.note: 1011 ranks shame at one's deeds (கருமத்தால் நாணுதல்) as true shame and sets aside the shame of fair-browed women (திருநுதல் நல்லவர் நாண்) as another kind. 907 says a woman who has shame (நாணுடைப் பெண்) has more greatness than the manhood of one who lives doing a woman's bidding. So the woman's modesty that 1011 treats as the lesser kind still outranks, in 907, manhood that has given up command.
links.reason: Both use நாண், but 907's நாணுடைப் பெண்ணே பெருமை உடைத்து is a foil to shame the henpecked man, not a ranking of women's modesty, and 1011 only sets திருநுதல் நல்லவர் நாணு apart as 'பிற'. The 'still outranks' construction is built by the note, not by either verse.

links.note: 907 pairs நாண் and ஆண்மை: manhood that obeys a woman is worth less than womanhood with shame. In 1134 a lover says the fierce flood of desire carries off the raft made of shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை). Both treat shame and manliness as the two things a man loses together under a woman's hold; 907 states it as a judgment, 1134 as a lover's own complaint.
links.reason: நாண் and ஆண்மை do co-occur, but in 907 the நாண் is the woman's (நாணுடைப் பெண்) and the man's shamelessness is only Parimelazhagar's addition, while in 1134 the force is காமம், not a woman's command; 'the two things a man loses together under a woman's hold' overstates a shared word pair.

links.note: 907 gives greatness to the woman with shame over the submissive man's manhood (பெண்ணே பெருமை உடைத்து). 1137, a speech in the Book of Love, says nothing has more worth than womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and still does not mount the palmyra horse (மடலேறாப் பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்கது இல்). In both, a woman's restraint is measured against a man's lack of it and ranked higher.
links.reason: Both rank பெண் above a man by நாண்/restraint (நாணுடைப் பெண்ணே பெருமை உடைத்து; மடலேறாப் பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்கது இல்), but 907's point is to shame the பெண்ணேவல் செய்தொழுகும் man, not to praise women's restraint, so they do not make the same claim.

links.note: 908 describes men who live as the woman wishes, பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகுபவர்; 141 speaks of the folly of living in desire for another man's woman, பெட்டொழுகும் பேதைமை. The same pairing of பெட்டு (desire, wish) with ஒழுகு (to conduct oneself) describes a life steered by desire in both, in 141 the man's own desire for a forbidden woman and in 908 the wishes of his own wife.
links.reason: பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகுபவர் and பெட்டொழுகும் பேதைமை share the distinctive பெட்டு + ஒழுகு collocation for conduct steered by desire, and the note distinguishes whose desire correctly.

links.note: 788 defines friendship as removing a friend's distress on the spot (ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது), like the hand of a man whose garment slips. 908 says those who live as the woman of the fine brow wishes (நன்னுதலாள் பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகுபவர்) do not see their friends' needs through (நட்டார் குறைமுடியார்). 908 names a condition under which the duty of 788 goes unmet: the man's actions are no longer his own to direct.
links.reason: நட்டார் குறைமுடியார் does describe a failure of the help that ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது defines, but it places no condition on 788's definition, and 'his actions are no longer his own' is the note's inference, not in the Tamil.

links.note: 754 says wealth that comes by right means and without wrong yields virtue and also pleasure (அறன் ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும்). 909 lists the same three goods as missing in men who do a woman's bidding (பெண்ஏவல் செய்வார்கண் இல்). Where 754 treats the three as flowing from one sound source, 909 treats them as shut off by one fault.
links.reason: Real trivarga link, but 754 names only two fruits (அறன் ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும்) of wealth, so the note's 'same three goods ... flowing from one source' miscounts; 909's third term is the vague பிறவினை, read as pleasure only by the commentators.

links.note: 760 says that for those who have made abundant wealth the other two, virtue and pleasure, are easily had together (ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு). 909 says that deeds of virtue, ample wealth and the other pursuits (அறவினையும் ஆன்ற பொருளும் பிறவினையும்) are all absent in those who do a woman's bidding; Parimelazhagar and Pope take பிறவினை as pleasure. Both use the three aims as the measure of a life: 760 shows how they are gained together, 909 a way they are lost together.
links.reason: Both invoke the three aims (ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு; அறவினையும் ஆன்ற பொருளும் பிறவினையும் ... இல்) and the note is accurate, but 909 does not limit or condition 760's claim; the note itself describes a shared measure, not a qualification.

links.note: 910 says those with deliberation and firmness of heart never fall into the folly of attachment to a woman. 917, in the next chapter, says it is those without a firm heart (நிறைநெஞ்சம் இல்லவர்) who touch the shoulders of women who embrace with their minds on other things. Both locate the safeguard in the man's own நெஞ்சம், stated positively in 910 for the wife-ruled man and negatively in 917 for the client of courtesans.
links.reason: 910 puts the safeguard in நெஞ்சத்து (எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சம்), 917 in நிறைநெஞ்சம் இல்லவர்; the paired positive/negative statement holds. The note's 'firmness of heart' takes திடன், where Parimelazhagar reads இடன் as wealth, without flagging it.

links.note: 911 warns that the இன்சொல் of women who want a man's wealth brings him harm. In 1258 a woman calls the soft speech (பணிமொழி) of her lover, a 'thief of many deceptions' (பன்மாயக் கள்வன்), the weapon that breaks her womanly reserve (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை). Both treat gentle words as an instrument that undoes the hearer, though 1258 is a lover's complaint in the Book of Love, not a warning the book gives in its own voice.
links.reason: இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும் and பணிமொழி ... பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை both make gentle words the instrument of harm, and the note marks the difference of voice.

links.note: 103 says help given by those who do not weigh the return (பயன்தூக்கார்) proves, when its worth is weighed (நயன்தூக்கின்), greater than the sea. 912 uses the same pair of words in the same order: the women weigh the gain (பயன்தூக்கி), and the man is to weigh their conduct (நயன்தூக்கி) and not join them. Weighing the return is what spoils a relationship in both verses, and weighing worth is the observer's proper response.
links.reason: பயன்தூக்கி ... நயன்தூக்கி and பயன்தூக்கார் ... நயன்தூக்கின் use the same word pair in the same order, with weighing the return as the mark of the false and the true giver.

links.note: 80 says the seat of life follows love, and that for those without it the body is bone wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). 913 likens the false embrace (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) of women who want wealth to embracing an unknown corpse in a dark room (ஏதில் பிணம்). 913 applies 80's premise to a particular case: a body offered without love is, for the one who holds it, a dead one.
links.reason: The resonance between 80's என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு and 913's ஏதில் பிணந்தழீஇ அற்று is real, but 913 as Parimelazhagar reads it makes the women like corpse-bearers handling an unknown body, the reverse of the note's 'for the one who holds it', and 80 is about one's own lovelessness; 'applies 80's premise' overstates.

links.note: 285 says that a loving nature with grace in view (அருள்கருதி) is not found in those who, with goods in view (பொருள்கருதி), watch for another's unguarded moment. 914 opposes those who examine அருட்பொருள் to women for whom பொருள் is the only thing of value. In the chapter on theft and in this one, the same pair, aiming at grace or aiming at goods, sorts people into two kinds that do not mix.
links.reason: அருள்கருதி / பொருள்கருதி (285) and பொருட்பொருளார் / அருட்பொருள் ஆயும் (914) use the same அருள்–பொருள் opposition to sort people.

links.note: 636 asks what subtle scheme can stand before those who have native acuteness together with book-learning (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்). 915 says those whose knowledge is made excellent by goodness of intellect (மதிநலத்தின் மாண்ட அறிவினவர்) do not touch the favours of women common to all; Parimelazhagar reads this too as natural intellect perfecting acquired knowledge. The pairing shows the same compound of mind being credited in statecraft with seeing through stratagems and here with keeping a man from a private vice.
links.reason: 'மதிநலத்தின் மாண்ட அறிவினவர்' and 'மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்' do share the native-wit-plus-learning compound (Parimelazhagar on both), but the claims differ: avoiding 'பொதுநலத்தார்' versus no 'அதிநுட்பம்' standing before them. That is one faculty in two domains, not the same claim.

links.note: 915 calls the women பொதுநலத்தார், those whose favours are common to all, and says the wise will not touch them. In 1311 a wife tells her husband that all women feast on him in common with their eyes (கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்), calls him பரத்த, and refuses his chest. The reproach of being 'common' is turned on the man there, and it is a sulking wife's charge in the Book of Love, not a judgement the book makes itself.
links.reason: பொதுநலத்தார் in 915 and கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர் ... பரத்த in 1311 share பொது as the reproach of being common property, and the note correctly marks the reversal onto the man and the speaker's sulking voice.

links.note: 57 says confinement does little to guard women, and that the guard kept by their own நிறை, firmness, is the chief one. 917 says it is men without a heart of நிறை (நிறைநெஞ்சம் இல்லவர்) who touch the shoulders of women who embrace while their hearts tend other things. The same inner firmness that 57 names as a wife's real protection is here named as what a man lacks when he goes to such women.
links.reason: நிறை is the deciding word in both: மகளிர் நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பே தலை and நிறைநெஞ்சம் இல்லவர் தோய்வார், so the same inner firmness is asked of the wife and found lacking in the man.

links.note: 864 says the man who does not let go of anger and has no நிறை (நிறையிலன்) is easy prey for anyone, at any time and place. 917 says those without நிறைநெஞ்சம் are the ones who go to women whose hearts are set on something else. In both the lack of self-command is what exposes a man, to enemies in 864 and to women who want what he has in 917.
links.reason: The shared word நிறை is real, but Parimelazhagar reads நிறையிலன் in 864 as failing to keep secrets, not general self-command, and the note does not say its parallel depends on the other reading.

links.note: 910 says the folly that comes of attachment to a woman never exists in those whose hearts hold deliberation (எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சத்து இடனுடையார்). 918 says the embrace of deceiving women is an affliction to those who lack examining understanding (ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்க்கு). The neighbouring chapters, on subservience to a wife and on courtesans, give the same safeguard: a mind that thinks the matter through.
links.reason: 918 ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்க்கு அணங்கு and 910 எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சத்து ... பேதைமை இல் give a reflective mind as the safeguard in adjacent chapters.

links.note: 918 says that for those without discerning understanding the embrace of deceiving women is an அணங்கு, which Parimelazhagar glosses as the touch of a spirit-woman who takes life through desire. In 1082 a lover says that her returning his look is like an attacking அணங்கு (தாக்கணங்கு) arriving with an army. The same figure of the woman as an afflicting spirit is a lover's praise in the Book of Love and a warning in 918.
links.reason: அணங்கு in both (அணங்கென்ப மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு; தாக்கணங்கு தானைக் கொண்டன்ன); Parimelazhagar's gloss 'காமநெறியான் உயிர் கொள்ளும் தெய்வமகள்' is reported correctly, and the warning/praise contrast holds.

links.note: 920 says double-minded women, liquor and dice are the companions of those whom Fortune has removed from herself (திருநீக்கப்பட்டார்). 936 says those covered by the goddess of misfortune named gambling (சூதென்னும் முகடி) do not eat their fill and suffer. Both verses describe a vice through the two sister goddesses: in 920 the vices attend the man Tiru has already left, in 936 one of them is Mugadi herself.
links.reason: திருநீக்கப்பட்டார் and சூதென்னும் முகடியான் மூடப்பட்டார் set vice under the paired goddesses of fortune and misfortune, with கவறு/சூது in both.

links.note: 920 names women of two minds (இருமனப் பெண்டிர்), which Parimelazhagar explains as a mind that joins and does not join a man at once. 974 says greatness, like women of one mind (ஒருமை மகளிர்), exists only by guarding oneself. The two phrases are opposites, and where single-mindedness is 974's model for keeping greatness, doubleness in 920 goes with dice and drink as the company of the unfortunate.
links.reason: 'இருமனப் பெண்டிர்' and 'ஒருமை மகளிர்' are opposed figures; Parimelazhagar glosses them as 'கவர்த்த மனம்' and 'கவராத மனம்', so the contrast is his too.

links.note: 653 tells those who mean to rise to leave off any deed that dims their lustre (ஒளிமாழ்கும் செய்வினை). 921 says those who live in love of liquor (கட்காதல் கொண்டொழுகுவார்) are never held in awe and lose their lustre (ஒளியிழப்பர்). 921 gives a named instance of the kind of act 653 warns against in general.
links.reason: 653 'ஒளிமாழ்கும் செய்வினை' to be avoided and 921 'ஒளியிழப்பர்... கட்காதல் கொண்டொழுகுவார்' share ஒளி; drink is a named instance of the lustre-dimming act.

links.note: 939 says that clothing, wealth, food, lustre (ஒளி) and learning do not come near a man who takes to gaming. 921 says those devoted to liquor lose their ஒளி and are not feared. The adjoining chapters on drink and dice both count the loss of ஒளி, the standing that makes a man regarded, among the costs.
links.reason: ஒளியிழப்பர் (921) and ஒளி among the five that அடையாவாம் (939) share the loss of ஒளி across the adjacent vice chapters; modest but accurate.

links.note: 922 forbids drinking and adds that if anyone drinks, it should be those who do not want to be counted by the worthy (சான்றோரான் எண்ணப்பட வேண்டாதார்). 656 forbids any act the worthy condemn (சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை), even to relieve one's own mother's hunger. In both the judgement of the சான்றோர் is the measure of conduct; 922 states it as the price a drinker must be willing to pay.
links.reason: 'சான்றோரான் எண்ணப்பட வேண்டாதார்' and 'சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை' both make the regard of the சான்றோர் the test of conduct, in two different chapters.

links.note: 924 says shame turns away from the drinker. In 1288 the speaker tells her lover that his chest is to her as liquor is to those who have enjoyed it, wanted even though it does harm that brings disgrace (இளித்தக்க இன்னா செயினும்). The simile in the Book of Love takes for granted what 924 teaches, that drink disgraces, and uses it to describe a desire that persists in spite of shame.
links.reason: 1288's simile களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே with இளித்தக்க இன்னா செயினும் assumes the disgrace of drink that 924 states as நாண் ... புறங்கொடுக்கும்; shared figure used meaningfully across books.

links.note: 838 says a fool getting something into his hand is like a deranged man getting drunk (மையல் ஒருவன் களித்தற்று). 925 says paying out wealth to buy oblivion shows ignorance. 838 uses drunkenness as the image for what a fool does with property, and 925 describes drunkenness itself as a fool's use of property.
links.reason: 838 likens the fool with உடைமை in hand to மையல் ஒருவன் களித்தற்று, and 925 calls பொருள்கொடுத்து மெய்யறியாமை கொளல் a mark of அறியாமை; drunkenness and foolish use of property are joined in both, from opposite directions.

links.note: 271 says the five elements laugh inwardly (அகத்தே நகும்) at the hidden conduct of a man with a deceitful mind. 927 says those who drink and droop are seen through and always laughed at by their own town (உள்ளொற்றி உள்ளூர் நகப்படுவர்); Parimelazhagar takes கள்ளொற்றி as drinking in concealment. In both, concealed conduct has a witness that laughs, the elements within the body in 271 and the neighbours who infer what is going on in 927.
links.reason: 271 பூதங்கள் ஐந்தும் அகத்தே நகும் and 927 உள்ளொற்றி உள்ளூர் நகப்படுவர் both give concealed conduct a laughing witness; Parimelazhagar's 'drinking in concealment' for கள்ளொற்றி is as reported.

links.note: 293 says not to lie about what one's own heart knows, for the heart will burn the liar afterwards. 928 concerns one such lie, 'I have never been drunk' (களித்தறியேன்), about something the speaker's heart knows, and says that drink brings the hidden thing out. 293 gives the inner penalty for this kind of lie and 928 adds an outward one, exposure.
links.reason: களித்தறியேன் என்பது கைவிடுக is a lie about what நெஞ்சத்து ஒளித்தது knows, the case 293's தன்நெஞ்சறிவது பொய்யற்க forbids; 293 gives the inner burning and 928 the outward exposure (ஆங்கே மிகும்).

links.note: 928 tells the drinker to stop saying he has never been drunk, because what he hid in his heart shows all the more at that moment (ஒளித்ததூஉம் ஆங்கே மிகும்). In 1161 a woman says she would hide her pain, but like spring water for those who draw it, it increases (ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்). Both end on மிகும்: the attempt to conceal an inner state is answered by its overflowing, in drink and in love.
links.reason: நெஞ்சத்து ஒளித்ததூஉம் ஆங்கே மிகும் and மறைப்பேன்மன் ... ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும் both answer an attempt to hide an inner state with மிகும், in drink and in love.

links.note: 113 says to let go, that very day, of gain that comes from leaving fairness even if it yields only good (நன்றே தரினும்). 931 uses the same concession, 'even if you win' (வென்றிடினும்), and still refuses the gain, calling it a swallowed hook. In both the apparent success of a wrong source is conceded and set aside.
links.reason: வென்றிடினும் and நன்றே தரினும் are the same concessive move, followed by refusal of the gain (வேண்டற்க / அன்றே யொழிய விடல்).

links.note: 385 defines a king as one able to create sources of wealth, gather it, guard it and apportion it (இயற்றலும் ஈட்டலும் காத்தலும்). 933, which Parimelazhagar reads of a king, says both the gathered wealth and its sources (பொருள் ஆயம்) leave him if he keeps at the dice. One habit undoes the gathering and the guarding that 385 makes the mark of rule.
links.reason: பொருளாயம் போஒய்ப் புறமே படும் does undo the ஈட்டலும் காத்தலும் of 385, but that is a negative application of 385, not a limit or condition on it.

links.note: 933 says that if one keeps calling the rolling dice-throw (உருளாயம்), wealth and its income (பொருளாயம்) go and fall outside (புறமே படும்); Parimelazhagar takes 'outside' as into enemies' hands. 1009 says the wealth a miser gathered without love, self-regard or virtue is taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). The gambler and the hoarder, by opposite habits, both end with their wealth in strangers' hands.
links.reason: பொருளாயம் போஒய்ப் புறமே படும் and ஒண்பொருள் கொள்வார் பிறர் give the same end, wealth passing to outsiders, for opposite habits; Parimelazhagar's பகைவர் கண்ணே தங்கும் is cited correctly.

links.note: 934 says nothing gives poverty like gambling, which does many small harms and ruins standing (சிறுமை பலசெய்து சீரழிக்கும்). 1045 says that within the one affliction called poverty many sufferings arrive (பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும்). Read together they form a chain: gambling brings harms on the way to poverty, and poverty then brings its own.
links.reason: 934 names gambling as the surest giver of வறுமை after சிறுமை பலசெய்து; 1045 says நல்குரவு holds பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள். The causal chain is fair to both.

links.note: 935 says those who clung (இவறியார்) in pride to dice, gaming hall and skilled hand became people with nothing (இல்லாகியார்). 437 uses the same word of the miser: the wealth of one who clings (இவறியான்) without doing what should be done perishes. இவறுதல், holding on and not letting go, ends in loss in both verses, whether the thing held is money or the game.
links.reason: இவறியார் இல்லாகியார் (935) and இவறியான் செல்வம் ... கெடும் (437) use the same verb இவறு, clinging, and both end in loss; Parimelazhagar glosses it as not letting go in 935 and பற்றுள்ளம் in 437.

links.note: 539 advises thinking, when swollen with one's own joy, of those who were ruined by negligence (இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக). 935 supplies such a memory: those who took pride (தருக்கி) in the dice and came to nothing; Parimelazhagar reads them as kings of former times and names the Pandavas. 935 does for gambling what 539 asks a ruler to do in general.
links.reason: 539 asks one to recall இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டார், those ruined by heedlessness in elation; 935's இவறியார் இல்லாகியார் were ruined by clinging to dice, not by இகழ்ச்சி. The shared move is recalling the ruined of the past, so 935 is not an instance of what 539 asks.

links.note: 167 says the fair goddess, grudging the envious man, shows him to her elder sister (தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும்). 936 names that sister, முகடி, as gambling itself, covering those who play. Envy hands a person over to misfortune; gambling, in 936, is misfortune under another name.
links.reason: செய்யவள் தவ்வை in 167 is the முகடி of 936, where சூதென்னும் முகடியான் identifies her with gambling. Both use the same goddess-figure.

links.note: 937 says time spent in the gaming hall ruins long-held wealth and character (பழகிய செல்வமும் பண்பும் கெடுக்கும்). 1043 says poverty destroys together one's ancient descent and one's தோல் (தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும்), which Pope takes as dignity of speech. The two sentences have the same shape: an inherited standing and a personal quality lost at one stroke, with gambling as a cause and poverty as a cause.
links.reason: 937 பழகிய செல்வமும் பண்பும் கெடுக்கும் and 1043 தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும் have the same shape, an inherited standing and a personal quality ruined together.

links.note: 938 lists what gambling does: it destroys wealth (பொருள் கெடுத்து), makes one take up lying, destroys compassion (அருள் கெடுத்து) and drives one through misery. 248 ranks two of these losses: those without wealth may flower again one day (பூப்பர் ஒருகால்), but those without அருள் are finished. By 248's measure the third item in 938's list is graver than the first.
links.reason: 938 lists பொருள் கெடுத்து and அருள் கெடுத்து; 248 ranks exactly these, பொருளற்றார் பூப்பர் ஒருகால் against அருளற்றார் அற்றார். The inference is fair and instructive.

links.note: 757 calls அருள் a child born of love that is raised by the wealthy foster-mother called பொருள். 938 has gambling destroy both பொருள் and அருள். Parimelazhagar assigns the losses in 938 to separate causes (losing, winning, resentment), but 757 suggests a link between them: with the nurse gone, the child is harder to raise.
links.reason: 938 pairs பொருள் கெடுத்து with அருள் கெடுத்து and 757 makes பொருள் the செவிலி of அருள்; Parimelazhagar's தோல்வி, வெற்றி, செற்றம் is cited correctly and the note presents its own inference as a suggestion.

links.note: 166 says the kin of one who envies a gift perish without anything to wear or eat (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் இன்றி). 939 begins its list of what gaming keeps away with the same pair, clothing and food (உடை ... ஊண்). Envy and gambling are both measured by the loss of the plainest necessities.
links.reason: உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் and உடை ... ஊண் are the stock pair for bare necessities, and in 939 they are the first and third items of a five-item list (உடை செல்வம் ஊண் ஒளி கல்வி), not an opening pair as the note says.

links.note: 939 names five things, among them learning (கல்வி), that 'அடையா' the one who takes to gaming. Parimelazhagar glosses this as 'do not come to him', but Pope's verse rendering and Kalaignar take the five as departing from him. On that second reading 939 conflicts with 400, which calls learning the wealth that cannot perish (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம்); on Parimelazhagar's reading there is no conflict, since the gambler never acquires it.
links.reason: அடையா plainly means 'do not reach', as Parimelazhagar's சாராவாம் has it; the conflict with கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் rests on Kalaignar's loose 'அகன்று ஒதுங்கி விடும்', and the packet's Pope says 'prevents the attainment', not departure as the note claims.

links.note: In 1145 a lover says love grows sweeter each time it is exposed, as drinking is wanted more each time one is drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால்). 940 has the same 'each time ... the more' construction with another vice, the dice, as the comparison (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல்). The lover uses the figure to praise his state, while 940 uses it to describe an attachment fed by its own losses.
links.reason: Both build on a -தொறும் simile from a vice: 'இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல்' and 'களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால்', an attachment that grows with each repetition, in life and in love.

links.note: 941 says the three humours counted by the learned, beginning with wind, cause disease whether they exceed or fall short (மிகினும் குறையினும்); Parimelazhagar refers the excess and shortfall to food and activity. 466 says one is ruined by doing what is unfit and also by not doing what is fit (செயக் கெடும் ... செய்யாமையானும் கெடும்). Both verses locate harm on two sides of a right amount, in the body and in action.
links.reason: 941's 'மிகினும் குறையினும்' is excess and shortfall of one measure; 466's 'செய்தக்க அல்ல செய' and 'செய்தக்க செய்யாமை' are commission and omission of different acts, not two sides of a right amount. Only the generic two-sided shape is shared.

links.note: 943 says to eat knowing the measure once digestion is complete, as the way one who has a body can carry it long (நெடிதுய்க்கும் ஆறு). 479 says the life of one who does not live knowing the measure (அளவறிந்து வாழாதான்) seems to exist and then perishes; Parimelazhagar refers that measure to one's wealth. The same phrase governs both the stomach and the purse. (This edition prints 'அறவறிந்து' in 943; Parimelazhagar's gloss reads அளவு அறிந்து.)
links.reason: அளவறிந்து உண்க and அளவறிந்து வாழாதான் apply one phrase to eating and to living within means (Parimelazhagar: பொருளின் எல்லை); the note itself flags the misprint.
links.text_issue: 943 prints 'அறவறிந்து' for அளவறிந்து; 479 has a corrupted character in 'அளவற஧ந்து'.

links.note: 946 says disease stays with the one of very great feed (கழிபேர் இரையான்), as pleasure stays with the one who eats knowing to stop short (இழிவறிந்து உண்பான்). 420 asks what it matters whether those live or die who know taste only by the mouth and not by the ear, and calls them மாக்கள். Both verses use a word with an animal sense for the person ruled by the mouth: இரை, feed, and மாக்கள்.
links.reason: கழிபேர் இரையான் (946) is about overeating and disease, வாயுணர்வின் மாக்கள் (420) about lacking the ear's taste; the link rests on a lexical observation about இரை and மாக்கள் and Parimelazhagar glosses மாக்கள் simply as மாந்தர். A thin shared theme, not a shared pattern.

links.note: 289 says those who know nothing but stealth do what is beyond measure and perish right there (அளவல்ல செய்தாங்கே வீவர்). 947 says the one who eats beyond the measure of his fire gets disease beyond measure. Chapter 29 uses அளவு as a moral measure and chapter 95 as a bodily one, and in each case overstepping it brings its own penalty.
links.reason: அளவல்ல செய்து ... வீவர் and தீயளவன்றி ... நோயளவின்றிப் படும் both make overstepping அளவு self-punishing, in moral and bodily terms.

links.note: 947 says that if one eats greatly without discerning the measure of the fire within (தீயளவு), disease arises without measure (நோயளவின்றிப் படும்). 475 says even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle if they are piled too high (சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்). In both a fixed capacity, the digestive fire or the axle, is what excess breaks, whatever the quality of the load.
links.reason: தீயளவன்றி ... பெரிதுண்ணின் and சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின் both make excess beyond a fixed capacity the cause of breakdown, in the body and in the cart; 'whatever the quality of the load' fits only 475's பீலி.

links.note: 948 tells the healer to look for the root of the disease (நோய்முதல்) before the remedy. 360 does this for suffering in general: when desire, anger and confusion perish even in name, the நோய் perishes. The chapter on true perception treats pain as chapter 95 treats illness, by naming causes and removing them.
links.reason: நோய்முதல் நாடி and காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் ... கெடக்கெடும் நோய் apply the same cause-then-cure logic to illness and to suffering, sharing the word நோய்.
links.text_issue: 360 prints 'இநவ்முன்றன்' for இவைமூன்றன்.

links.note: 948 sets out an order of enquiry: look into the disease, then its root, then the means that subdue it, and act so that it works (நோய்நாடி நோய்முதல் நாடி ... வாய்நாடி). 504 has the same threefold நாடி for judging a person: examine the qualities, examine the faults, examine which predominates, and take that. Diagnosis of a patient and assessment of a candidate are given the same grammar of step-by-step examination before a decision.
links.reason: நோய்நாடி நோய்முதல் நாடி ... வாய்நாடி ... செயல் and குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி ... மிகைநாடி ... கொளல் have the same threefold நாடி ending in an act.

links.note: 637 says that even when one knows the method of doing a thing, one should act knowing how the world goes (செயற்கை அறிந்தக் கடைத்தும் உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்); Parimelazhagar glosses the method as what the treatises teach. 949 addresses the one who has learned (கற்றான்) and still requires him to consider this patient, this illness and this moment. Both hold that book learning has to be fitted to the particular case.
links.reason: கற்றான் கருதிச் செயல் (patient, illness, time) and செயற்கை அறிந்தக் கடைத்தும் உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல் make the same claim that learned method must be fitted to the case, in medicine and in ministry.

links.note: 952 says the well-born do not slip (இழுக்கார்) in conduct, truthfulness and shame. 133 says having conduct is itself குடிமை and that a lapse (இழுக்கம்) turns into low birth (இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்). Read together, 952's claim is close to a definition: whoever slips has by 133 already left the class of the well-born, a point Parimelazhagar makes on 133 while keeping it within varna.
links.reason: இழுக்கார் குடிப்பிறந்தார் reads close to a definition beside ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை இழுக்கம் இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்; the shared இழுக்கு root and the varna limit in Parimelazhagar are correctly reported.

links.note: 952 lists three things the well-born keep: ஒழுக்கம், வாய்மை, நாண். 983 lists five pillars that hold up சால்பு: love, shame (நாண்), obligingness, kindly regard and truthfulness (வாய்மை). Two of the three marks of lineage reappear as supports of personal worth, so the same core is described once as inherited and once as a structure a person stands on.
links.reason: வாய்மை and நாண் stand in both lists (இம் மூன்றும் இழுக்கார் குடிப்பிறந்தார்; ஐந்து சால்பு ஊன்றிய தூண்); the note counts the overlap correctly and the birth/personal-worth contrast holds.

links.note: 953 names a smile, giving, sweet words and not scorning (நகை ஈகை இன்சொல் இகழாமை) as the share of a true lineage. 92 takes three of these and ranks them: being sweet-spoken with a glad face (முகனமர்ந்து இன்சொலன்) is better than giving with a glad heart (அகனமர்ந்து ஈதல்). The list in 953 is flat; 92 shows the book elsewhere weighing its items against one another.
links.reason: நகை ஈகை இன்சொல் in 953 reappear in 92 as முகனமர்ந்து, ஈதல், இன்சொலன், where ஈதலின் நன்றே ranks them.

links.note: 953 puts giving and not scorning (ஈகை ... இகழாமை) side by side among the marks of a good family; Parimelazhagar takes all four as the way one meets the poor who come. 1057 gives the receiver's side: on seeing those who give without scorn or contempt (இகழ்ந்தெள்ளாது ஈவார்), the asker's heart rejoices within. The pairing shows why 'not scorning' sits next to 'giving' in the list.
links.reason: இகழாமை beside ஈகை in 953 and இகழ்ந்தெள்ளாது ஈவார் in 1057 are giver's and receiver's sides of the same point; Parimelazhagar does set all four in the context of the poor arriving (வறியார் சென்ற வழி).

links.note: 954 says the well-born will not do diminishing things (குன்றுவ) even if they get crores piled up (அடுக்கிய கோடி பெறினும்). 311 says the stainless hold to not hurting others even if it would bring wealth that gives distinction (சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும்). Both use the same 'even if they gained' (பெறினும்) form to set a fixed refusal against a large reward, once for family standing and once for non-harm.
links.reason: அடுக்கிய கோடி பெறினும் ... செய்தல் இலர் and சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும் ... செய்யாமை share the பெறினும் concession and a fixed refusal, for birth and for non-harm.

links.note: 954 says no amount of wealth makes the well-born do what lowers them. 657 says the extreme poverty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு) ranks above gain reached by taking on blame (பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கம்). Both rank standing above wealth; 657 states the comparison outright, in the context of a minister's clean action.
links.reason: அடுக்கிய கோடி பெறினும் ... குன்றுவ செய்தல் இலர் (954) and பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கத்தின் ... கழிநல்குரவே தலை (657) both rank blameless standing above wealth.

links.note: 954 says the well-born do not do things that diminish (குன்றுவ செய்தல் இலர்), whatever the gain. 965 uses the same word to say what follows if they do: even those like a hill sink (குன்றுவர்) if they do a diminishing thing (குன்றுவ) the size of a kundri seed. 954 gives the rule and 965 the cost of breaking it, at a scale far below crores.
links.reason: 954 குன்றுவ செய்தல் இலர் and 965 குன்றுவர் குன்றுவ குன்றி அனைய செயின் share குன்றுவ; rule and cost of breaking it, as the note says.

links.note: 955 says an ancient family (பழங்குடி) does not part from its character when its means shrink. 1043 says poverty destroys together one's ancient descent and one's speech (தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும்). They conflict if 1043 is read as plain poverty undoing lineage; the conflict eases on Parimelazhagar's reading, which stresses that 1043 calls poverty a craving (நசை), so it is the wanting, not the lack, that ruins.
links.reason: பழங்குடி பண்பில் தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று even when means shrink conflicts with நல்குரவு ... தொல்வரவும் கெடுக்கும் on the plain reading, and the note correctly says the clash eases if நசை carries the weight.

links.note: 956 says those who mean to keep to a spotless line do not do what lacks worth (சால்பில செய்யார்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even in poverty'. 656 says one should not do what the worthy condemn (சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை) even if one must see one's mother hungry. Both set a standard of worthy conduct above need, 656 naming the hardest case.
links.reason: 956 சால்பில செய்யார் (Parimelazhagar: வறுமையுற்றவழியும்) and 656 ஈன்றாள் பசிகாண்பான் ஆயினும் செய்யற்க சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை both put worthy conduct above need.

links.note: 956 says those resolved to live by their spotless lineage will not do unworthy things by taking to deceit (சலம் பற்றி). 660 uses the same word for wealth-making: securing wealth made by deceit (சலத்தால் பொருள் செய்து) is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot. 956 rules deceit out on grounds of family honour; 660 adds that its gains do not hold anyway.
links.reason: சலம் in both: 956 சலம்பற்றிச் சால்பில செய்யார் from family honour, 660 சலத்தால் பொருள்செய்து ஏமார்த்தல் is water in a பசுமண் கலம், adding that such gains do not hold.

links.note: 958 says that if lack of affection (நாரின்மை) shows in a man, people will doubt his lineage (குலத்தின்கண் ஐயப்படும்). 992 names having love and being born in a seasoned family (அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல்) as the two things that make up courtesy. 992 pairs love and birth as partners; 958 shows that when the first is missing the second is no longer believed.
links.reason: 992 pairs அன்புடைமை with ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல், and 958 says that when நாரின்மை shows, the குலம் itself is doubted (ஐயப்படும்).

links.note: 960 says one who wants lineage must want humility toward everyone (யார்க்கும் பணிவு). 125 says bowing is good for all (எல்லார்க்கும் நன்றாம் பணிதல்) and is a further wealth for the rich. Both make humility general, and each singles out the highly placed, by family or by wealth, as those it most becomes.
links.reason: The shared 'பணிவு/பணிதல்' is real, but 960's 'யார்க்கும்' is humility toward everyone as the condition of 'குலம்', not a claim that it most becomes the well-born, whereas 125 'செல்வர்க்கே செல்வம் தகைத்து' does single out the rich; the note overstates the symmetry.

links.note: 960 asks for humility toward all (யார்க்கும் பணிவு) from anyone who wants to keep a lineage. 963, in the next chapter, limits when bowing is called for: in abundance one must bow (பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல்), but in reduced circumstances one must stand high (சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு). The humility of 960 is thus not meant to cover bending under want.
links.reason: வேண்டுக யார்க்கும் பணிவு is limited by பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல் ... சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு.

links.note: 960 pairs நலம் with shame and குலம் with humility: want நலம், then want நாணுடைமை; want குலம், then want பணிவு toward all. 1019 uses the same pair in negative form: a lapse in principle burns one's குலம், and settled shamelessness burns one's நலம் (நலஞ்சுடும் நாணின்மை). The two verses share the குலம்/நலம் pairing and agree that நலம் depends on shame.
links.reason: நலம்/குலம் are paired in both: நலம்வேண்டின் நாணுடைமை in 960, and குலஞ்சுடும் ... நலஞ்சுடும் நாணின்மை in 1019. Both tie நலம் to நாண்.

links.note: Parimelazhagar reads 961's இன்றி அமையா as things without which one would not survive, so the verse puts standing above life. 131 says conduct is to be guarded more than life (உயிரினும் ஓம்பப்படும்) because it gives excellence. The same ranking, a value kept ahead of survival, is made for honour in one chapter and for conduct in the other.
links.reason: 961 இன்றி அமையாச் சிறப்பின ஆயினும் குன்ற வருப விடல், with Parimelazhagar's அமையாமை - இறத்தல், and 131 உயிரினும் ஓம்பப் படும் both rank a value above survival.

links.note: 962 refuses unworthy acts even when they would bring renown (சீரினும்). 113 says to let go at once of gain that departs from fairness even if it brings nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும் நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம்). Both have the form 'even if it yields the thing you want, not by this means', applied to fame in one and to profit in the other.
links.reason: 'சீரினும் சீரல்ல செய்யாரே' and 'நன்றே தரினும் நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கத்தை... ஒழிய விடல்' share the form 'even if it brings the desired thing, not by this means', for fame and for gain.

links.note: 652 says to avoid any action that yields neither renown nor good (புகழொடு நன்றி பயவா வினை), which makes renown one of the tests of an act. 962 says those who want renown together with great manliness will not do unworthy things even for renown (சீரினும் சீரல்ல செய்யார்). 962 therefore narrows 652's test: bringing fame does not by itself make an act fit to do.
links.reason: 652 makes புகழ் one test of an act (புகழொடு நன்றி பயவா வினை), and 962 says சீரினும் சீரல்ல செய்யார். Renown alone does not license the act.

links.note: 963 says that in small and shrunken circumstances one must hold oneself high (சிறிய சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு). 680 says those whose domain is small (உறைசிறியார்), fearing their own people's trembling, will bow to the greater and accept terms (கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து). They conflict if 963's 'reduced state' includes weakness of position before a stronger party; if 963 is only about poverty and personal bearing, 680 is separate advice on statecraft.
links.reason: சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு (with பணிதல் reserved for பெருக்கம்) against உறைசிறியார் ... கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து; the note names the reading on which they clash.

links.note: 963 asks for an upright bearing (உயர்வு) when one's means have shrunk. 988 says poverty is no disgrace (இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று) for one who has the firmness called worth (சால்பென்னும் திண்மை). 988 supplies the ground for 963's demand: want does not itself lower a person, so there is no reason to stoop in it.
links.reason: 963 asks for உயர்வு in சுருக்கம்; 988 இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று given சால்பென்னும் திண்மை gives the ground for that demand, as the note says.

links.note: 124 says the stature of one who is restrained without shifting from his position (நிலையின் திரியாது அடங்கியான்) is far greater than a mountain. 964 uses the same word for the opposite case: those who descend from their position (நிலையின் இழிந்த) are like hair off the head. Together they give the two ends of one scale, both measured by whether a person keeps to their நிலை.
links.reason: நிலையின் is shared and the height figures (மலையினும் பெரிது, தலையின் இழிந்த மயிர்) answer each other, but நிலை is not one scale: Parimelazhagar takes it as the household path in 124 and high standing by birth in 964. The link is a shared word and figure, not a development.

links.note: 964 says people who have come down from their position (நிலையின் இழிந்தக் கடை) are like hair fallen from the head. 973 says those who are not low are not low even when placed low (கீழிருந்தும் கீழல்லார் கீழல்லவர்). They conflict if 964's நிலை means outward rank or station; on Parimelazhagar's reading it means the high standard the well-born hold themselves to, so the fall is their own doing and the verses agree.
links.reason: நிலையின் இழிந்தக் கடை read as outward station conflicts with கீழிருந்தும் கீழல்லார் கீழல்லவர்; the note states this and that Parimelazhagar's reading dissolves it.

links.note: 966 asks what is gained by going and standing behind those who scorn you (இகழ்வார் பின் சென்று நிலை). 1033 says only those who eat by their own ploughing truly live, and all others bow to eat and go behind (தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல்பவர்). Both use 'going behind' another as the picture of a dependent life, and 1033 names the livelihood that avoids it.
links.reason: இகழ்வார்பின் சென்று நிலை and தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல்பவர் share the figure of going behind another as dependence.

links.note: 966 says standing in the train of those who scorn you brings neither renown nor the gods' land. 1053 says that even asking has a certain beauty (ஏஎர் உடைத்து) when one stands before those of unconcealing heart who know what is due (கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சின் கடனறிவார் முன்நின்று). What 966 rejects is therefore not dependence as such but dependence on people who despise the one who comes to them.
links.reason: 966 rejects இகழ்வார்பின் சென்று நிலை, while 1053 grants ஏஎர் to asking before கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சின் கடனறிவார்; the difference in whom one stands before is exactly the limit the note draws.

links.note: 967 prefers being called ruined to a life got by following those who reject you. 230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is out of reach (ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை). In both, a life that cannot be lived on one's own terms, without honour or without the power to give, is ranked below death.
links.reason: ஒட்டார்பின் சென்று வாழ்தலின் ... கெட்டான் எனப்படுதல் நன்று and சாதல் ... இனிததூஉம் ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை each rank death above a diminished life, for honour and for giving; the note's 'on one's own terms' is a little loose but the parallel holds.

links.note: 968 asks whether a life that tends the flesh is a medicine (மருந்தோ) once greatness has lost its dignity; Parimelazhagar takes this as a medicine against dying. 82 says that eating while the guest waits outside is not to be wanted even if the food were the medicine of deathlessness (சாவா மருந்தெனினும்). Both raise the idea of an immortality-medicine only to rank it below a duty, honour in one and hospitality in the other.
links.reason: மருந்தோ ... ஊன்ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை and சாவா மருந்தெனினும் both raise a medicine against death and rank it below a duty; Parimelazhagar does gloss 968 as இறவாமைக்கு மருந்தாமோ.

links.note: 968 questions the worth of a life that merely feeds the body (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) when dignity is gone. 1017 says those governed by shame give up life for shame and do not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் ... நாண் துறவார்). The chapters on honour and on shame reach the same ordering of life and self-respect.
links.reason: 968's ஊன்ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை ... பீடழிய வந்த இடத்து and 1017's நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் both put self-respect above life.

links.note: 969 says those like the கவரிமா give up life when their honour is at stake (உயிர் நீப்பர் மானம் வரின்). 779 asks who could reproach as failures those who die so that what they vowed is not broken (இழைத்தது இகவாமைச் சாவார்). Dying to avoid going back on what one stands for appears as a matter of civil honour in 969 and as a soldier's vow in 779.
links.reason: 969 உயிர்நீப்பர் மானம் வரின் and 779 இழைத்தது இகவாமைச் சாவார் both treat death as the way to keep what one stands for, in the chapter on honour and in the war chapter.

links.note: 970 says the world worships and praises the radiance of the honourable who do not live on in disgrace. 235 says that a ruin which is growth and a death which is existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு) are hard to reach except for the skilled. 235 gives the general idea that 970 applies: a death can leave a person present in fame.
links.reason: உளதாகும் சாக்காடு (a death that is existence, in fame) is the general idea behind இளிவரின் வாழாத மானம் உடையார் ஒளி தொழுது ஏத்தும் உலகு.

links.note: 970 sets disgrace against radiance: the world worships the ஒளி of those who will not live when இளி comes. 971 defines the same two words: one's ஒளி is abundance of aspiration, and one's இளி is saying 'we will live without it' (அஃதிறந்து வாழ்தும் எனல்). In both, disgrace is a way of going on living, and radiance belongs to those who refuse it.
links.reason: The ஒளி / இளி pair appears in both: 970 has இளிவரின் வாழாத ... ஒளி and 971 defines ஒளி and இளி, with இளி as வாழ்தும் எனல்.

links.note: 981 says that for those who know what is due (கடன் அறிந்து) and take on worth, every good thing is கடன்; Parimelazhagar glosses this as the good qualities being natural to them. 218 uses the same phrase, கடனறி காட்சியவர், for people who do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும்). 218 shows one concrete case of 981's general claim: a duty that is felt as one's own does not wait on circumstances.
links.reason: The shared phrase கடன்அறிந்து / கடனறி காட்சியவர் is distinctive, and 218's இடனில் பருவத்தும் ஒல்கார் is a fair concrete case of 981's நல்லவை எல்லாம் கடன்.

links.note: 982 says the worthy have only the goodness of character (குணநலம்), and that other goodness is not counted among goodnesses; Parimelazhagar takes பிறநலம் to be the goodness of the bodily limbs. 79 asks what all the outer limbs (புறத்துறுப்பு) can do for those who lack love, the inner limb (அகத்துறுப்பு). Both verses rank an inner quality over the body's outward parts, one for worth and one for love.
links.reason: 982 counts only குணநலம் and Parimelazhagar glosses பிறநலம் as உறுப்புக்களானாய நலம்; 79 asks what புறத்துறுப்பு can do without the அகத்துறுப்பு, அன்பு. Inner quality over outer parts in both, on the plain sense of 79.
links.text_issue: 79 reads 'எவன்செய்பு ம்', apparently corrupt for எவன்செய்யும்.

links.note: 982 denies that any goodness other than character counts for the worthy. 407 says the handsome looks (எழில்நலம்) of one without fine, penetrating understanding are those of a decorated clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). Both dismiss outward நலம் that has nothing inside it, though 407 measures by understanding and 982 by character.
links.reason: 982 denies that பிறநலம் counts beside குணநலம்; 407 likens the எழில்நலம் of one without நுண்மாண் நுழைபுலம் to a மண்மாண் புனைபாவை. Both dismiss outward நலம் lacking an inner quality, with the difference in measure noted.

links.note: 983 calls its five qualities the pillar planted to bear worth (சால்பு ஊன்றிய தூண்). 615 calls the man who wants the work and not pleasure a pillar that wipes away his kin's troubles and props them (துடைத்து ஊன்றும் தூண்). The same figure, with the same verb ஊன்று, is used once for qualities holding up a character and once for a person holding up a family.
links.reason: சால்பு ஊன்றிய தூண் and துடைத்தூன்றும் தூண் share the pillar with the same verb ஊன்று, for qualities bearing character and for a man bearing his kin.

links.note: 983 lists five pillars that bear worth: அன்பு, நாண், ஒப்புரவு, கண்ணோட்டம், வாய்மை. 1013 singles out one of them: as all lives are fixed on the body (ஊனைக் குறித்த), சால்பு is fixed on the good called shame (நாண் என்னும் நன்மை குறித்தது). Read together, shame is one support among five in 983 and the seat of worth itself in 1013.
links.reason: நாண் is one of five தூண் in 983 and the thing சால்பு is fixed on in 1013 (நாண்என்னும் நன்மை குறித்தது சால்பு); a real deepening.

links.note: 985 says the strength of those who accomplish is bowing (பணிதல்), and that this is the weapon by which the worthy turn foes. 978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை) while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration. Both attach bowing to the strong and not the weak; 985 adds that it has an effect on opponents.
links.reason: பணிதல் is the ஆற்றல் of ஆற்றுவார் in 985 and பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை in 978; both assign bowing to the strong, and 985 adds மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை.

links.note: 986 says the touchstone of worth is accepting defeat (தோல்வி கொளல்) even from those who are not one's equal. In 1327 the man says that in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses has won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), as the reunion shows. Both treat yielding as the better outcome; 1327 is a lover's remark about a sulk, while 986 states a test of character.
links.reason: தோல்வி துலையல்லார் கண்ணும் கொளல் (986) and ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார் (1327) both value accepting defeat, as a test of சால்பு and in a lovers' quarrel; the note keeps the difference of register in view.
