links.note: 987 says worth is useless unless it does good even to those who did harm. 998, in the next chapter, says failing in courtesy even toward those who act without friendship or kindness (நயமில செய்வார்க்கும்) is lowness (கடை). Both verses use the particle 'even to' (-க்கும்) to extend the virtue to hostile people, one for சால்பு and one for பண்பு.
links.reason: இன்னாசெய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே and நயமில செய்வார்க்கும் பண்பு both use the emphatic -க்கும் to extend the virtue to those who do harm, for சால்பு and பண்பு in adjacent chapters.

links.note: 988 calls சால்பு a firmness (திண்மை) that keeps poverty from being a disgrace. 1064 describes that firmness at work: the worth that will not consent to begging even when no means remain (இடமில்லாக் காலும் இரவொல்லாச் சால்பு) is too large for all space to hold. 1064 shows what the poor but worthy person of 988 does and does not do.
links.reason: 988's சால்பென்னும் திண்மை that keeps இன்மை from being இளிவு is shown in 1064's இடமில்லாக் காலும் இரவொல்லாச் சால்பு; the shared word சால்பு and the poverty setting make the development real.

links.note: 990 says the earth cannot carry its burden (பொறை) once the worthy lose their worth. 572 says those without kindly regard are, by merely existing, a burden to the earth (நிலக்குப் பொறை). The same figure is used from two sides: the worthy are what lets the earth carry its load, and people without கண்ணோட்டம் are dead weight on it.
links.reason: Both close on பொறை with the earth as bearer: இருநிலந்தான் தாங்காது பொறை and உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை. The note's two-sided reading matches the alternative gloss Parimelazhagar records for 990.

links.note: 991 and 548 share the word எண்பதம், easy access. In 548 a king who is not accessible (எண்பதத்தான் ஓரா) and does not examine and do justice falls and perishes by himself; in 991 being accessible to all makes courtesy easy to attain. The quality whose absence ruins a ruler is the one whose presence makes a person courteous.
links.reason: எண்பதத்தால் (991) and எண்பதத்தான் (548) are the same quality, easy access, as the route to பண்புடைமை in one and its lack as a king's ruin in the other; the note reads both correctly.

links.note: 994 says the world honours the character (பண்பு) of those whose usefulness (பயன்) comes from doing good with fairness (நயனொடு நன்றி புரிந்த). 97 uses the same four words of speech: words that yield benefit (பயன்) and do not part from பண்பு produce நயன் and bring forth நன்றி. Parimelazhagar glosses நயன் as justice in both, so the cluster describes good speech in 97 and a good life in 994.
links.reason: The four words நயன், நன்றி, பயன், பண்பு occur together in both verses, and Parimelazhagar glosses நயன் as நீதி in both, of speech in 97 and of conduct in 994.
links.text_issue: 994 opens with யனொடு; the initial ந of நயனொடு is missing.

links.note: 994 praises people of நயன் whose doing good makes them useful (பயனுடையார்). 216 says wealth falling to one who has நயன் (நயனுடையான்) is like a fruit-bearing tree (பயன்மரம்) ripening in the middle of the town. 216 supplies the picture for 994: the person of நயன் is of பயன் to everyone within reach.
links.reason: நயனொடு ... பயனுடையார் and நயனுடையான் ... பயன்மரம் share the நயன்/பயன் pair, and the fruit tree in the town pictures the usefulness 994 praises.
links.text_issue: 994's first word is truncated in this edition: 'யனொடு' for நயனொடு.

links.note: 995 says courtesy is present even in enmity (பகையுள்ளும் பண்புள) in those who understand others. 874 says the world rests in the greatness of the person of courtesy who treats enmity as friendship (பகை நட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும் பண்புடையாளன்). 874 takes the step beyond 995, from staying courteous toward an enemy to turning him into a friend; Parimelazhagar reads 874 as a matter of policy.
links.reason: பகையுள்ளும் பண்புள and பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும் பண்புடை யாளன் share பகை and பண்பு, and 874 goes further, from courtesy within enmity to treating enmity as friendship.

links.note: 995 warns that இகழ்ச்சி, scorn, wounds even as a joke. 953 lists not scorning (இகழாமை) with a smile, giving and sweet words as the four marks of a true family. 953 names the trait as a mark of good birth, and 995 gives the reason for it.
links.reason: 953 lists இகழாமை among the four marks of வாய்மைக் குடி and 995's நகையுள்ளும் இன்னாது இகழ்ச்சி gives the reason scorn is avoided; 'develops' would fit about as well as 'agrees'.

links.note: 998 calls it lowness (கடை) to fail in courtesy even toward those who act without friendship or kindness. 579 calls it the highest thing (தலை) to extend kindly regard and bear with even those whose nature is to hurt (ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும்). The verses mark the two ends of the same scale: good conduct toward the hostile is தலை, and its failure is கடை.
links.reason: கடை and தலை mark the two ends of one scale for conduct toward the hostile (நயமில செய்வார்க்கும் பண்பாற்றார் ஆதல் கடை / ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும் ... பண்பே தலை).

links.note: 998 requires courtesy even toward those who do unfriendly, unkind things. 852 says that even if someone does what one cannot bear, intending division (பகல் கருதிப் பற்றா செயினும்), it is best not to do harm in return out of hostility. 852 gives the minimum, no retaliation, and 998 asks for more, that courtesy itself not lapse.
links.reason: Both hold a standard toward those who act unkindly (நயமில செய்வார்க்கும்; பற்றா செயினும்): 852 forbids இன்னா in return and 998 asks that பண்பு not lapse.

links.note: 999 says that for those not able to laugh (நகல் வல்லர் அல்லார்) the great world lies in darkness even by day; Parimelazhagar takes நகல் as mixing with others and being glad at heart. 523 says the life of one who does not mingle freely (அளவளாவு இல்லாதான்) is like a tank filling without a bank. On Parimelazhagar's reading both describe the cost of not mixing with people, as lost wealth in 523 and a darkened world in 999.
links.reason: The connection exists only on Parimelazhagar's gloss of நகல் as mixing gladly with others (the word itself is 'laughing'); 523's அளவளாவு is specifically with kin by chapter context, and neither verse extends the other.

links.note: 1000 says great wealth obtained by one without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). 1008 says the wealth of a man nobody seeks out is a poison tree bearing fruit in the middle of the village (நச்சு மரம் பழுத்தற்று). Both say a good thing is made useless or harmful by the character of its holder; Parimelazhagar reads 1000 as wealth that benefits no one.
links.reason: நன்பால் கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று (1000) and நச்சு மரம் பழுத்தற்று (1008) both make wealth worthless or harmful through its holder; Parimelazhagar's ஒருவற்கும் பயன்படாது on 1000 is quoted correctly.

links.note: 229 says eating alone in order to fill up one's store (நிரப்பிய தாமே தமியர் உணல்) is more bitter than begging; 1001 takes the case one step further, the man who does not even eat it (அஃதுண்ணான்), and calls him dead. Read together they grade the misuse of wealth: unshared use is wretched, no use at all is not living.
links.reason: தாமே தமியர் உணல் (229) is unshared use, அஃதுண்ணான் செத்தான் (1001) is no use at all; the gradation holds, though நிரப்பிய as 'to fill one's store' is Pope's reading and Parimelazhagar takes it of the needy.

links.note: 751 says nothing but wealth makes people of no account into people of account (பொருளல்லது இல்லை பொருள்). 1002 names nearly the same thought, பொருளானாம் எல்லாம், as what the miser thinks, and says that when it leads to not giving (ஈயாது இவறும்) it is delusion. The chapter on making wealth is thus limited here: the claim holds only for wealth that is given and used.
links.reason: 1002 puts பொருளானாம் எல்லாம் in the mouth of one who ஈயாது இவறும் and calls it மருள்; that limits 751's பொருளல்லது இல்லை பொருள் to wealth that is given.

links.note: 114 says whether people were worthy or not is seen from their எச்சம்; 1004 asks what எச்சம் the unwanted man imagines for himself. Parimelazhagar takes the word as offspring in 114 and as what remains after death, i.e. renown, in 1004, so the pairing shows the same test of a life by what it leaves, applied with two senses of the word.
links.reason: எச்சம் is the test word in both; Parimelazhagar reads it as நன்மக்கள் in 114 and as what remains after death (புகழ்) in 1004, as the note says.
links.text_issue: 114 is printed காணப்ப படும் (for காணப் படும்).

links.note: 430 says those without understanding have nothing, whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்); 1005 says the same of those who neither give nor enjoy, even with crores. The same form of argument, that owning is not having unless some further quality is present, is used for understanding in one place and for use and giving in the other.
links.reason: அடுக்கிய கோடி உண்டாயினும் இல் and என்னுடையரேனும் இலர் use the same 'having is not having' form, conditioned on giving and enjoying in one and அறிவு in the other.

links.note: 1000 says great wealth got by a man without courtesy is like good milk turned by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று); 1006 says the man who neither uses nor gives is ஏதம் to பெருஞ்செல்வம். In both the wealth is good in itself and the holder is what spoils it, which is how Parimelazhagar reads 1006 (others take the wealth to be a misery to him).
links.reason: ஏதம் பெருஞ்செல்வம் is read by Parimelazhagar as the man being a நோய் to the wealth, with the other reading noted, as the link says; that matches கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று in 1000, where the holder spoils good wealth.

links.note: 226 says ending the ruinous hunger of the destitute (அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல்) is the place where one who has got wealth stores it. 1007 says the wealth of one who does nothing for the destitute (அற்றார்க்கொன்று ஆற்றாதான்) is like a very beautiful woman growing old alone. 226 says where wealth is kept safe; 1007 shows what happens to wealth kept anywhere else: it passes its time unused.
links.reason: 226 makes அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல் the பொருள்வைப்புழி; 1007 shows the wealth of அற்றார்க்கொன்று ஆற்றாதான் wasting like தமியள் மூத்தற்று.

links.note: 1039 says land whose owner stays away sulks like a wife (இல்லாளின் ஊடிவிடும்); 1007 likens ungiven wealth to a beautiful woman who ages alone (தமியள் மூத்தற்று). Both picture a good left unattended as a woman without her partner, for farmland in one verse and for money in the other; Parimelazhagar notes for 1007 that the wealth itself loses its fruit.
links.reason: மிகநலம் பெற்றாள் தமியள் மூத்தற்று for ungiven wealth and இல்லாளின் ஊடிவிடும் for unvisited land both figure a neglected good as a woman without her partner.

links.note: 760 says that for those who have made bright wealth in plenty (ஒண்பொருள் காழ்ப்ப இயற்றியார்க்கு) the other two, virtue and pleasure, come easily. 1009 uses the same word, ஒண்பொருள், for wealth amassed by dropping love, denying oneself and not looking to virtue, and says others will take it. So the promise of 760 fails when the two ends it names are given up in the earning; Parimelazhagar reads 760 as wealth that comes by the right way.
links.reason: Both use ஒண்பொருள்: 760 promises ஏனை இரண்டும் to those who amass it, 1009 says wealth gathered அறநோக்காது and தற்செற்று goes to பிறர்; Parimelazhagar's நெறியான் வரும் பொருள் on 760 is reported correctly.

links.note: On Parimelazhagar's reading, 1010 says the brief want (சிறுதுனி) of the rich who have renown is like the rain cloud running dry (மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தனையது). 219 says the poverty of a man of நயன் is just his not being able to do what he is used to doing. Both treat the giver's poverty as a loss to others, not to himself, and 1010 adds by its image that it passes.
links.reason: 219 defines the giver's poverty as செயும் நீர செய்யாது அமைகலா ஆறு and 1010 likens it to மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தது; both measure it by the giving lost, as Parimelazhagar reads them.

links.note: 201 says the excellent fear the intoxication called evil deed (விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்); 1011 defines shame proper as shame on account of deeds (கருமத்தால் நாணுதல்). Fear and shame are given the same object, one's own wrong action, in two chapters, and Parimelazhagar glosses நாணுதல் elsewhere (433, 172) as அஞ்சுதல்.
links.reason: கருமத்தால் நாணுதல் and விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர் தீவினை give shame and fear the same object, one's own bad action; Parimelazhagar's gloss of நாணுவார் as அஞ்சுவார் at 433 checks out.

links.note: 1011 mentions the other shame, that of women, without describing it. In 1251 a woman in the Book of Love describes it from inside: shame is the bolt (நாணுத்தாழ்) on the door of her restraint, which the axe of desire breaks. This is a speech in character, but it shows what the shame 1011 calls பிற is: a guard on conduct in love, not a recoil from a wrong deed.
links.reason: 1011 sets aside திருநுதல் நல்லவர் நாணு as பிற; 1251 நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு shows that shame at work as a bolt on நிறை, matching Parimelazhagar's gloss of restraint.

links.note: 993 says likeness of limbs is not likeness among people; the likeness that counts is of character (பண்பொத்தல்). 1012 says the bodily needs are shared by all and shame is what sets people apart. Both refuse to take what is physically common as the measure of a human being.
links.reason: ஊணுடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல and உறுப்பொத்தல் மக்களொப்பு அன்று both set aside the physically common and locate human distinction in நாண் and பண்பு.

links.note: 80 says the seat of life goes by way of love (அன்பின் வழியது உயிர்நிலை) and without it a body is bones wrapped in skin; 1013 says worth depends on shame as life depends on flesh. Both use the life-and-body relation to say a quality is what a thing lives by, love for the person in 80 and shame for சால்பு in 1013. Parimelazhagar notes a variant ஊணை ('food') in 1013, which Manakkudavar follows; the link rests on the reading ஊனை.
links.reason: Both speak of உயிர் and body, but in 1013 ஊனைக் குறித்த உயிர் the flesh is what life rests on, as a simile for நாண், while in 80 love is what life rests on and the body is the husk; the common pattern is loose.

links.note: 118 (with 115) calls not leaning to one side the ornament of the worthy (கோடாமை சான்றோர்க்கு அணி); 1014 calls shame the ornament of the worthy (அணியன்றோ நாணுடைமை சான்றோர்க்கு). The same phrase names two inner restraints, and neither is an outward decoration.
links.reason: The shared phrase சான்றோர்க்கு அணி is real (கோடாமை in 118, நாணுடைமை in 1014), but the verses make different claims about different virtues, so this is a shared figure, not agreement.

links.note: 980 says greatness covers others' exposure (அற்றம் மறைக்கும்) and smallness only speaks their faults. 1015 gives the feeling behind that conduct: being ashamed of another's disgrace as of one's own. One who feels the other's பழி in this way has no reason to tell it.
links.reason: பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும் நாணுவார் supplies a plausible inner ground for அற்றம் மறைக்கும் பெருமை; the note's inference is modest.

links.note: 1015 praises one who feels shame even for others' disgrace; 1018 describes one who does not feel shame at what makes others ashamed (பிறர் நாணத்தக்கது தான் நாணான்). The two set out the ends of a scale inside the chapter: shame that extends beyond oneself, and shame that fails even for one's own act.
links.reason: பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும் நாணுவார் and பிறர் நாணத்தக்கது தான் நாணான் use பிறர் as the measure in opposite directions, the fullest and the failed form of நாண் within one chapter.

links.note: 57 says confinement does little to guard women and the guard kept by their own firmness (நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு) is best; 1016 says the high have shame for their fence (நாண்வேலி). In both the effective guard is a quality inside the person and not an outer barrier, for a wife's fidelity in one and for the conduct of the high in the other.
links.reason: 'நாண்வேலி' and 'நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு' are both inner guards, but 1016 sets shame against gaining the 'வியன்ஞாலம்' (Parimelazhagar), not against an outer barrier; the inner-versus-outer contrast the note claims for both is only in 57 'சிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு'.

links.note: 311 says the spotless hold to not hurting others even if it would bring wealth that gives distinction. 1016, on Parimelazhagar's reading, says the high take shame as their fence and do not want the wide world (வியன்ஞாலம் பேணலர்) where the two conflict. Both state a refusal of great gain at the price of a restraint; the other reading he reports, that they will not want the world without first having the fence of shame, gives the same result.
links.reason: 311 சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும் ... செய்யாமை and 1016 நாண்வேலி கொள்ளாது வியன்ஞாலம் பேணலர் both refuse great gain bought by breaking a restraint; both of Parimelazhagar's readings are reported correctly.

links.note: 421 calls understanding an inner fortress enemies cannot destroy (உள்ளழிக்கலாகா அரண்); 1016 calls shame a fence (வேலி), which Parimelazhagar explains as keeping blame and sin from entering. Both give an inner quality the work of a defensive structure, one against ruin and one against disgrace.
links.reason: வேலி (a fence) and அரண் (a fort) are different images, and a quality as a defence is a common figure, so this is an analogous pattern and not a shared distinctive image.

links.note: 130 says virtue watches for the right moment and comes by the path to the one who guards against anger and has learned restraint (அறம் பார்க்கும் ஆற்றின் நுழைந்து). 1018, as the commentators read it, has virtue ashamed to come near the shameless. Together they give the two directions of the same figure: virtue seeks out the restrained and shrinks from those without shame.
links.reason: அறம் பார்க்கும் ஆற்றின் நுழைந்து (130) and அறம் நாணத்தக்கது உடைத்து (1018) both personify அறம் as approaching or shrinking from a person according to his restraint or shamelessness; the note marks the 1018 reading as the commentators'.

links.note: 204 says that if one plots another's ruin, அறம் plots the plotter's ruin; 1018 says that if one is not ashamed, அறம் is ashamed. In both, virtue is an agent that answers the person's act in the terms of that act, with a penalty in 204 and with withdrawal in 1018.
links.reason: சூழின் அறஞ்சூழும் and நாணானாயின் அறம் நாண both make அறம் answer the person with the person's own verb.

links.note: 952 says the well-born do not slip in three things: conduct, truthfulness and shame (ஒழுக்கமும் வாய்மையும் நாணும்). 1019 says what happens when two of those three fail: a lapse in conduct burns the family, and shamelessness that stays burns every good. The chapter on good family gives the mark and 1019 gives the cost of losing it.
links.reason: 952's ஒழுக்கமும் வாய்மையும் நாணும் reappear in 1019 as கொள்கை பிழைப்பின் குலஞ்சுடும் (கொள்கை glossed ஒழுக்கம் by both commentators) and நாணின்மை ... நலஞ்சுடும், the cost of losing two of the three marks.

links.note: 1021 says no greatness has more dignity (பீடு) than that of the one who says 'I will not stay my hand' (கைதூவேன்) from the work. 611 says not to slacken at a task's difficulty because effort itself gives greatness (பெருமை முயற்சி தரும்). Both locate பெருமை in persistence rather than in rank or result; 1021 applies it to the work of raising one's family.
links.reason: கைதூவேன் என்னும் பெருமையின் பீடுடையது இல் and பெருமை முயற்சி தரும் both place பெருமை in unremitting effort; the note reads both correctly.

links.note: 1021 praises the resolve never to stop work once begun (கைதூவேன்). 612 gives the other side: guard against the work dying in mid-course (வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல்), since, in Parimelazhagar's reading, the world gives up on those who give up their unfinished work. The pair shows the same refusal to stop as honour in one verse and as a condition of the world's regard in the other.
links.reason: கைதூவேன் in 1021 and வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல் in 612 both forbid stopping work midway, with the world's abandonment (தீர்ந்தன்று உலகு) as 612's reason on Parimelazhagar's reading.

links.note: 1022 says the family (குடி) lengthens through long-continued work that has both effort (ஆள்வினை) and mature knowledge. 604 states the reverse case: for those sunk in sloth, without worthy exertion (மாண்ட உஞற்றிலவர்), the family dies down and faults multiply (குடிமடிந்து குற்றம் பெருகும்). Together they make one claim from both sides: the fortunes of a குடி follow the exertion of its members.
links.reason: நீள்வினையால் நீளும் குடி and குடிமடிந்து ... மாண்ட உஞற்றிலவர்க்கு state the same dependence of the குடி on exertion from both sides.

links.note: 1022 pairs effort with full knowledge (ஆள்வினையும் ஆன்ற அறிவும்) as the two things that extend a family. 618 uses the same pairing when it assigns blame: lacking fortune is no disgrace, but lacking effort after knowing what should be known (அறிவறிந்து ஆள்வினை இன்மை) is. In both verses knowledge and effort are named together as what a person can be held to, as against fortune.
links.reason: 1022 ஆள்வினையும் ஆன்ற அறிவும் and 618 அறிவறிந்து ஆள்வினை pair the same two things as what a person answers for; only 618 actually sets them against fortune (பொறியின்மை), a small overstatement in the note.

links.note: 1023 has தெய்வம் tying up its garment (மடிதற்று) to go before the family-builder. 617 says the dark goddess lives in sloth (மடி) and the lotus goddess in the effort of the one without sloth (மடியிலான் தாள்). Both put divine favour on the side of the one who works; 1023's மடி (cloth) also echoes the மடி (sloth) that 617 and the chapter on sloth condemn.
links.reason: 'தெய்வம் மடிதற்றுத் தான்முந்துறும்' for the one who resolves to raise his family and 'மடியிலான் தாளுளாள் தாமரையினாள்' both place divine favour with the one who exerts himself; the மடி echo is offered only as an echo.

links.note: 773 says fierceness is called great manliness (பேராண்மை), and that helping a foe in distress (ஊராண்மை) is its edge. 1026 says good manliness (நல்லாண்மை) is making oneself the one who manages the house one was born in (இல்லாண்மை). Each verse takes ஆண்மை and coins a second compound that turns it toward care for others; Parimelazhagar notes that 'நல்' in 1026 is there to set it apart from the manliness of war.
links.reason: Both redefine ஆண்மை with a second coined compound: 773 'பேராண்மை... ஊராண்மை மற்றதன் எஃகு', 1026 'நல்லாண்மை... இல்லாண்மை'; Parimelazhagar's 'போர்த்தொழிலின் நீக்குதற்கு நல்லாண்மை என விசேடித்தார்' is cited correctly.

links.note: 1027 says that as in battle the load falls on the stout-hearted (வன்கண்ணர்), so among kin the burden (பொறை) falls on those able to carry it. 770 says an army has no existence without leaders, however many steady men it has (தலைமக்கள் இல்வழி இல்). 770 is the military fact that 1027 uses as its simile: numbers do not carry a force or a family, a few capable people do.
links.reason: Both say a few carry the many, but 1027's simile is about 'வன்கண்ணர்' (the stout-hearted fighters) bearing the battle, while 770 contrasts ample 'நிலைமக்கள்' with missing 'தலைமக்கள்' (leaders); saying 770 is the military fact behind 1027's simile overstates the match.

links.note: 615 describes one who does not want pleasure but wants the work (இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான்) as the pillar who wipes away his kin's sorrows. 1029 looks at that same person from the inside: his body seems to hold nothing but suffering. 1029 states the cost of the role that 615 praises; Parimelazhagar takes the question as noting that pleasure never reaches him.
links.reason: 615's 'இன்பம் விழையான்... துன்பம் துடைத்தூன்றும் தூண்' and 1029's 'இடும்பைக்கே கொள்கலம்... குடும்பத்தைக் குற்றம் மறைப்பான் உடம்பு' describe the same family-bearer, with 1029 voicing the cost; Parimelazhagar's 'இன்பத்திற்கு ஆதல் இல்லையோ' is cited correctly.

links.note: 42 says the householder is the support (துணை) of renouncers, the destitute and the dead. 1032 says the ploughmen bear (பொறுத்து) everyone who does not plough. Both verses identify one group whose ordinary work holds up all the others: the householder in the Book of Virtue, the farmer in the Book of Wealth.
links.reason: 'எழுவாரை எல்லாம் பொறுத்து' and 'இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் துணை' both name one group that carries the rest, in two books.

links.note: 1033 describes everyone but the farmer as those who bow, eat and walk behind others (தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல்பவர்). 967 says it is better to be called ruined than to live by going behind those who do not accept one (ஒட்டார் பின்சென்று வாழ்தல்). Both treat 'going behind' another for a living as a lesser life; 967 judges it by honour, and 1033 names farming as the livelihood that avoids it.
links.reason: தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல்பவர் and ஒட்டார் பின்சென்று வாழ்தல் both make 'going behind' another for a living the lesser life.

links.note: 389 says the world rests under the umbrella (கவிகை) of a king who can bear bitter words. 1034 says those who have the shade of grain will see the shade of many umbrellas come under their own umbrella (தங்குடைக்கீழ்), which Parimelazhagar takes as their own king's. Both use the royal umbrella's shade for dominion, but 389 credits the king's character and 1034 credits the farmers' harvest.
links.reason: கவிகைக்கீழ்த் தங்கும் உலகு (389) and பலகுடை நீழலும் தங்குடைக்கீழ் (1034) share the umbrella-shade figure for dominion, and Parimelazhagar does read தங்குடை as their king's. The contrast of sources is real.

links.note: 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules justly (பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு). 1034 says those who hold the grain bring many kings' umbrellas under their own. The dependence runs in both directions: in 545 good rule yields harvest, and in 1034 harvest yields the king's wider rule.
links.reason: 545 பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு follows just rule; 1034 அலகுடை நீழலவர் bring பலகுடை நீழல் under தங்குடை (their king's, per both commentators): the two directions of dependence are really there.

links.note: 1061 says that not begging (இரவாமை), even from those who give gladly without concealing (கரவாது), is worth ten million times more. 1035 says those whose way is to eat what their own hands produce do not beg (இரவார்) and give to askers without concealing (கரவாது ஈவர்). 1035 names the livelihood that makes the ideal of 1061 possible, and puts the farmer on the giving side of the same exchange.
links.reason: இரவார் ... ஈவர் கரவாது in 1035 reuses the terms of கரவாது உவந்தீயும் ... இரவாமை in 1061 and names the livelihood (கைசெய்தூண்) that makes not begging possible.

links.note: 1037 says that if ploughed soil is dried until a measure of dust (தொடிப்புழுதி) falls to a quarter (கஃசு), the crop thrives without even a handful of manure. 1038 says manuring is better than ploughing (ஏரினும் நன்றால் எருவிடுதல்). The two set tillage and manure against each other from opposite sides: thorough working of the soil can replace manure, yet as a rule manure counts for more than ploughing.
links.reason: 1037 பிடித்தெருவும் வேண்டாது makes thorough drying replace manure and 1038 ஏரினும் நன்றால் எருவிடுதல் ranks manure above ploughing; each limits the other, as the note says.

links.note: 1038 treats manure (எரு) and water (நீர்) as what makes a crop grow. In 1147 the woman says her love-sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water (கெளவை எருவாக அன்னைசொல் நீராக). The Book of Love takes the two inputs that 1038 gives as farming advice and uses them as a figure for what feeds her passion.
links.reason: 1038's farming pair எரு and நீர் returns as figure in 1147, 'கெளவை எருவாக அன்னைசொல் நீராக நீளும் இந்நோய்'; a distinctive and meaningful shared image.

links.note: 1039 says that if the owner (கிழவன்) stays away and does not go to it, the land turns against him and sulks like a wife. 553 says the king who does not look into things and do justice every day loses his land day by day (நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்). In both, land is lost through the owner's or ruler's lack of personal attention; Parimelazhagar reads 1039 too as requiring a daily visit.
links.reason: செல்லான் கிழவன் இருப்பின் நிலம் புலந்து ... and நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன் நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்: neglect by the owner loses the land. Parimelazhagar's நாள்தோறும் சென்று பார்த்து on 1039 is as cited.

links.note: 1039 compares the land to a wife (இல்லாள்) who sulks when her owner stays away. 1040 calls the land a good woman (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள்) who laughs at those who sit idle pleading poverty. The chapter closes with two verses that make the land a woman who responds to how a man treats her, by sulking in one and by laughing in the other.
links.reason: நிலம் ... இல்லாளின் ஊடி விடும் and நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும் both personify the land as a woman reacting to the man's neglect, in adjacent verses.

links.note: 1039 describes neglected land with the Book of Love's words for a lovers' sulk: it resents and sulks like a wife (புலந்து ... ஊடி விடும்). 1304, in the chapter on sulking, says that not appeasing one who has sulked (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a withered creeper at the root. The figures run in opposite directions: the land is compared to a sulking woman in 1039, and the neglected sulking woman to a plant in 1304.
links.reason: நிலம் புலந்து இல்லாளின் ஊடி விடும் and ஊடியவரை உணராமை ... வள்ளி முதலரிந்தற்று share ஊடல் and cross the land-woman and woman-plant figures as the note says.

links.note: 616 says effort creates prosperity and lack of effort brings in want (முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்திவிடும்). 1040 pictures the Land laughing at people who claim poverty while sitting idle (அசைஇ இருப்பார்). Both hold that such poverty comes from not working; 1040 states it as mockery from the land that would have paid them.
links.reason: 616 முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்திவிடும் and 1040 இலமென்று அசைஇ இருப்பாரை ... நகும் both trace want to idleness; the farming chapter restates the effort chapter's claim as the Land's mockery.

links.note: 171 says that coveting another's goods without fairness ruins the family (வெஃகின் குடிபொன்றி). 1043 names poverty itself a craving (நல்குரவு என்னும் நசை) and gives it the same effect on ancient descent. Read together, 1043 treats poverty as harmful to a lineage through the desire it breeds, the mechanism 171 states for covetousness.
links.reason: நல்குரவு என்னும் நசை destroying தொல்வரவு sits beside வெஃகின் குடிபொன்றி; Manakkudavar's gloss that poverty produces desire supports the shared mechanism, though 'develops' is slightly generous.

links.note: 1045 says many sufferings arrive within the one affliction called poverty (நல்குரவு என்னும் இடும்பையுள் பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள்). 1056 says that on seeing those free of the affliction of concealing, all the afflictions of poverty perish together (நிரப்பிடும்பை எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்). The next chapter answers this verse in its own terms: the sufferings that come as a group also leave as a group.
links.reason: நல்குரவு என்னும் இடும்பையுள் பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும் is answered by நிரப்பிடும்பை எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்; the group that arrives leaves together.

links.note: 1047 says the person in poverty unconnected with virtue (அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு) is looked on as a stranger even by his own mother. 117 says the world does not count as ruin the low state of one who stays in virtue (நன்றிக்கண் தங்கியான் தாழ்வு). The qualifier அறஞ்சாரா in 1047 marks the boundary 117 draws: estrangement follows poverty without virtue, while poverty with virtue is not held against a person.
links.reason: அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு in 1047 carries a condition, and 117's கெடுவாக வையாது உலகம் ... நன்றிக்கண் தங்கியான் தாழ்வு covers the complementary case of low estate with virtue.

links.note: 1048 is a poor man's cry: will the want that as good as killed me yesterday come today too (நெருநலும் கொன்றது போலும் நிரப்பு)? 532 uses the same noun and verb in a simile, constant poverty killing understanding (நிச்ச நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு). Both treat நிரப்பு as something that kills and that returns daily; Parimelazhagar glosses both with a man who fills his stomach each day only with great pain.
links.reason: நெருநலும் கொன்றது போலும் நிரப்பு and நிச்ச நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு give நிரப்பு the same verb கொல்; Parimelazhagar's glosses on both do speak of painfully filling the stomach day by day.

links.note: 1049 says one can even sleep in the midst of fire, but in want there is no closing the eyes (நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும்). 896 says one burned by fire may yet survive, but those who go on offending the great will not (எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம்). Both measure a non-physical danger by granting that fire can be endured and denying the same of the thing compared.
links.reason: நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும் and எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம் both concede fire as bearable in order to rank poverty and offending the great above it.

links.note: 1049 says that in poverty the eyes cannot close by any means (யாதொன்றும் கண்பாடு அரிது). In 1136 the man says his eyes will not close because of the girl, even at midnight (படல் ஒல்லா ... என் கண்). The same sign, eyes that cannot close, marks want in the Book of Wealth and longing in the Book of Love; 1136 is a lover's speech, so this is a shared figure and not a shared teaching.
links.reason: கண்பாடு அரிது and படல்ஒல்லா ... என் கண் share the sleepless-eye idiom, but sleeplessness is a stock sign in the love book and, as the note itself admits, only a figure is shared; thin, and closer to a shared image than a transferred pattern.

links.note: 1051 says ask when you find those fit to be asked (இரத்தக்கார்க் காணின்), and if they withhold, the blame is theirs. 1067, in the chapter on the dread of begging, says: if you must beg, do not beg from those who conceal (கரப்பார் இரவன்மின்). The two chapters take opposite attitudes to begging but give the same rule about whom to ask.
links.reason: இரத்தக்கார்க் காணின் இரக்க and கரப்பார் இரவன்மின் give the same rule about whom to ask, from chapters with opposite stances; கரப்பு appears in both.

links.note: 224 speaks from the giver's side: being asked is painful (இன்னாது இரக்கப்படுதல்) until one sees the asker's glad face. 1052 speaks from the asker's side: asking is a pleasure if what is asked comes without suffering (துன்பம் உறாஅ வரின்). Each verse makes the pain or pleasure of one party depend on how the exchange goes for the other.
links.reason: Giver's side and asker's side do complement each other, but the note's symmetry fails for 1052: on Parimelazhagar's reading துன்பம் உறாஅ வரின் is the asker's own trouble (தான் துன்புறாமல்), not how the exchange goes for the giver.

links.note: 1052 says even asking is pleasure to a person (இன்பம் ஒருவற்கு இரத்தல்) when the thing comes without pain. 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking, even asking water for a cow (நாவிற்கு இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்). They conflict if 1052 is read as commending asking under good conditions; 1052 speaks of pleasure and 1066 of disgrace, so the conflict depends on taking a disgraceful act as unable to be a pleasant one.
links.reason: இன்பம் ஒருவற்கு இரத்தல் under good conditions meets 1066's unconditional நாவிற்கு இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்; the note is candid about what the conflict depends on.

links.note: 218 says those whose sight knows what is due (கடனறி காட்சியவர்) do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even when they lack means. 1053 uses the same description, கடனறிவார், for the people before whom asking has a beauty; Manakkudavar glosses them as those who know ஒப்புரவு. The pairing identifies the fit giver of the begging chapter with the person 218 describes.
links.reason: கடனறிவார் (1053) and கடனறி காட்சியவர் (218) are the same people; Manakkudavar does gloss 1053's term as ஒப்புரவறிவார், tying the fit giver to 218.

links.note: 1053 says there is a beauty even in asking while standing before those of unconcealing heart who know what is due (கடனறிவார் முன்நின்று இரப்பும்). 708 says that if one has people who look within and understand, it is enough to stand looking at their face (முகம்நோக்கி நிற்க அமையும்). Parimelazhagar reads 1053 the same way: standing before such people is enough and nothing need be said, which is why the asking keeps some grace.
links.reason: முன்நின்று இரப்பும் and முகம்நோக்கி நிற்க அமையும் share standing before one who understands; Parimelazhagar on 1053 does say முன்நிற்றல் மாத்திரமே அமைதலின், as the note reports.

links.note: 1054 says asking from those who do not know concealing even in a dream is like giving (இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும்). 1061 takes the same givers, who give gladly without concealing and are dear as one's eyes (கரவாது உவந்தீயும் கண்ணன்னார்), and says not asking even of them is worth ten million times more (இரவாமை கோடி உறும்). 1061 limits the praise in 1054: the best case of asking still ranks below not asking.
links.reason: 1054 praises asking of கரத்தல் கனவிலும் தேற்றாதார்; 1061 takes the same கரவாது உவந்தீயும் givers and says இரவாமை கோடி உறும், limiting the earlier praise.

links.note: 571 says the world exists because the beauty called kindly regard exists (கண்ணோட்டம் ... உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு). 1055 uses the same word and construction: asking goes on because the unconcealing exist (உண்மையால்). In both, a practice or the world itself is said to rest on the existence of a disposition in some people.
links.reason: 1055 கரப்பிலார் வையகத்து உண்மையால் and 571 கண்ணோட்டம் ... உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு use the same உண்மையான் construction to rest a practice or the world on a disposition some people have.

links.note: 1055 says askers take up standing before others because people who do not conceal exist in the world (கரப்பிலார் வையகத்து உண்மையால்). 1059 says givers would have no renown if there were none who wished to ask and receive (இரந்துகோள் மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை). The two verses state the dependence in both directions: asking exists because of givers, and givers' standing exists because of askers.
links.reason: கரப்பிலார் வையகத்து உண்மையால் makes asking depend on givers, and இரந்துகோள் மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை makes givers' தோற்றம் depend on askers.

links.note: 1056 says that on seeing those free of the affliction of concealing, all the affliction of poverty perishes at once (நிரப்பிடும்பை எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்). 1063 says nothing is harder than the hardness of thinking 'we will end the affliction of want by begging' (இன்மை இடும்பை இரந்து தீர்வாம்). They conflict on whether asking can end poverty's distress, if 1056 is read as a general claim; Parimelazhagar removes the conflict by reading 1063 as blaming the choice of begging over effort.
links.reason: நிரப்பிடும்பை எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும் on meeting a giver conflicts with 1063's censure of இன்மை இடும்பை இரந்து தீர்வாம் if 1056 is general; the note names that reading.

links.note: 1056 gives the good outcome of asking: meeting those without concealment ends the afflictions of want. 1068 gives the other outcome: the unsafe boat called asking splits when it strikes the rock called concealment (கரவென்னும் பார்தாக்க). Both make the result of asking turn on கரவு in the person asked, so 1068 states the risk that 1056 leaves out.
links.reason: கரப்பிடும்பை யில்லாரைக் காணின் gives asking's success where there is no கரவு; கரவென்னும் பார்தாக்கப் பக்கு விடும் gives its wreck where there is, so the outcome turns on the same term.

links.note: 228 speaks of the giver's joy, the pleasure of giving and being glad (ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம்), which hoarders do not know. 1057 speaks of the asker's joy, the heart glad within (உள்ளுள் உவப்பது), when the giving is free of scorn. The same verb உவ marks gladness on both sides of one act of giving.
links.reason: 228 ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம் and 1057 உள்ளுள் உவப்பது use உவ for gladness at one act of giving seen from the giver's and the asker's side; the note is accurate.

links.note: 1058 says that without askers the world would be puppets coming and going, which makes askers part of a living world; Manakkudavar draws the conclusion that asking is therefore not to be held low. 1062 says that if one must live even by begging, let the maker of the world wander and perish (பரந்து கெடுக உலகியற்றியான்). They conflict on whether a world that contains begging is as it should be; the conflict depends on reading 1058 as approval and not only as a remark about what givers need.
links.reason: இரப்பாரை இல்லாயின் ... மரப்பாவை சென்றுவந்தற்று gives askers a place in a living world, while இரந்தும் உயிர்வாழ்தல் வேண்டின் பரந்து கெடுக உலகியற்றியான் curses such a world; the note states the reading the conflict needs.

links.note: 1060 tells the asker not to be angry at a refusal, since the affliction of his own want is witness enough (நிரப்பிடும்பை தானேயும் சாலும் கரி); Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take it as witness that means are hard to come by for anyone. 250 says that when going against someone weaker, think of yourself before those stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). Both restrain a person by turning him to his own experience as evidence of the other's position.
links.reason: 1060's 'நிரப்பிடும்பை தானேயும் சாலும் கரி' (his own want as witness, per Parimelazhagar, that means fail when needed) and 250's 'வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க' both restrain by pointing a person to his own experience; note reports the commentary correctly.

links.note: 616 says effort makes fortune and lack of effort brings want in (முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்); Parimelazhagar applies it to kings. 1063 calls it hardness (வன்மை) to think poverty's affliction can be ended by begging, and Parimelazhagar explains that the proper path, effort, is being set aside. 1063 applies 616's rule to the poor man and names begging as the wrong substitute for effort.
links.reason: முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும் gives the rule, and இன்மை இடும்பை இரந்து தீர்வாமென்னும் வன்மை, glossed by Parimelazhagar as setting முயற்சி aside, applies it to the poor man.

links.note: 1063 calls hard the thought that poverty can be ended by begging (இரந்து தீர்வாம்). 1068 gives a picture of why: begging is a boat without safety (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that splits when it strikes the rock of concealment (கரவென்னும் பார்). Manakkudavar says 1068 states the cause of poverty not ending, which makes it the reason behind 1063's claim.
links.reason: இரந்து தீர்வாம் in 1063 is the plan that 1068 pictures failing as ஏமாப்பில் தோணி striking கரவென்னும் பார்; Manakkudavar's remark that 1068 gives the cause of poverty not ending is quoted correctly.

links.note: 218 says those who see their duty do not slacken in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும்). 1064 says worth does not consent to asking even at a time without means (இடமில்லாக் காலும்). The same test, what a person does when resources are gone, is applied to giving in 218 and to asking in 1064: the good neither stop giving nor start begging.
links.reason: 'இடமில்லாக் காலும் இரவொல்லாச் சால்பு' and 'இடனில் பருவத்தும் ஒப்புரவிற்கு ஒல்கார்' apply the same test of destitution to begging and to giving, in nearly the same words.

links.note: 222 says taking is bad even if it is called a good path (நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல் தீது). 1066 says that even if one asks for water for a cow (ஆவிற்கு நீரென்று இரப்பினும்), nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both take the cow as a case of asking for the sake of virtue. Both verses deny that a good purpose removes what is wrong with asking or receiving.
links.reason: ஆவிற்கு நீரென்று இரப்பினும் and நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல் தீது both use a concessive to deny that a good end redeems asking or taking; Parimelazhagar (அறம் நோக்கி) and Manakkudavar (அறத்திற்காக இரத்தலும் ஆகாது) are cited correctly.

links.note: 656 says that even if one must see one's own mother hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்), one should not do what the worthy condemn. 1066 says that even asking water for a cow is degrading to the tongue (நாவிற்கு இளிவந்தது). Each picks the most sympathetic motive available, a hungry mother or a thirsty cow, and holds that it does not excuse the act.
links.reason: Both use a concessive with the most excusable motive ('ஆவிற்கு நீரென்று இரப்பினும்', 'ஈன்றாள் பசிகாண்பான் ஆயினும்') and still refuse the act; the shared argumentative form across begging and conduct is real.

links.note: 1053 says that even asking, standing before those of unconcealing heart who know their duty, has a certain beauty (இரப்பும் ஓர் ஏஎர் உடைத்து). 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking (இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்), even for a cow's water. They conflict if 1066 is read as covering every act of asking; on a narrower reading 1053 speaks only of asking from the right giver, which 1066 does not mention.
links.reason: இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல் is unconditional, while இரப்பும் ஓர் ஏஎர் உடைத்து grants beauty to asking from கடனறிவார்; the note states the reading the conflict depends on.

links.note: 1067 asks beggars not to beg of those who conceal (கரப்பார்). 1077 describes such people from the other side: the base will not even shake a wet hand (ஈர்ங்கை விதிரார்) for anyone but those whose fist would break their jaw. 1077 shows what asking a concealer comes to, and why 1067 pleads against it.
links.reason: கரப்பார் இரவன்மின் warns against asking those who withhold, and ஈர்ங்கை விதிரார் கயவர் shows that withholding in action; Manakkudavar's இரப்பார்க்குக் கொடாரென்றது ties 1077 to beggars.

links.note: 306 says anger burns even the safe raft called one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணை). 1068 calls asking a boat without safety (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that breaks on concealment. The same word for safety (ஏமம், ஏமாப்பு) marks the vessel in both: one's people are the safe one in 306, and asking is named the unsafe one in 1068.
links.reason: ஏமப் புணை and ஏமாப்பில் தோணி are the same distinctive figure of a safe or unsafe vessel, used in opposite senses, and the contrast is instructive.

links.note: 1068 calls asking a boat without safety (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that splits on the rock of concealment; the commentators supply poverty as the sea it was meant to cross. In 1164 the woman says the sea of love exists but the safe raft to swim it (ஏமப் புணை) does not. Both use the figure of a sea that must be crossed and a vessel that fails, 1068 as a teaching about begging and 1164 as a lover's complaint.
links.reason: ஏமாப்பில் தோணி and ஏமப் புணை ... இல் share the figure of a missing safe vessel, with the same ஏமம் word, in begging and in love.

links.note: 224 says being asked is unpleasant (இன்னாது இரக்கப் படுதல்) until one sees the asker's glad face. 1069 says the heart melts at the thought of asking. Taken together they say asking is painful on both sides, for the one asked in 224 and for the one who asks or contemplates it in 1069, and that only the gift ends the pain.
links.reason: Both concern the pain around asking (இன்னாது இரக்கப்படுதல் / இரவுள்ள உள்ளம் உருகும்), but they are not the same claim, and 1069's second half about கரவு is left out; 'only the gift ends the pain' comes from 224 alone.

links.note: 1057 says that on seeing those who give without scorn, the heart rejoices deep within (உள்ளம் உள்ளுள் உவப்பது உடைத்து). 1069 says that at the thought of asking the heart melts (உள்ளம் உருகும்), and at the thought of concealment even what remains is gone (உள்ளதூஉம் இன்றிக் கெடும்). Both follow the heart (உள்ளம்) through the act of asking; 1057 gives its state before a good giver and 1069 its state before a refusal. Parimelazhagar takes the heart in 1069 as the speaker's, while he reports others take it as the asker's.
links.reason: உள்ளம் is the subject in both: உள்ளுள் உவப்பது before one who gives without scorn (1057), உருகும் and உள்ளதூஉம் இன்றிக் கெடும் at இரவு and கரவு (1069). The report of Parimelazhagar ('எம் உள்ளம்', others 'இரக்கின்றவர் உள்ளம்') is correct.

links.note: 223 says not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing' (இலனென்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை), and giving, are found in one of good family; Pope takes the words as the giver's excuse, while Parimelazhagar first takes them as the asker's plea. 1070 says the asker's life leaves when the word is spoken (சொல்லாட); Parimelazhagar takes this as the concealer saying 'no'. On Pope's reading of 223 both verses are about the word of refusal, which the well-born never say and which 1070 says kills the hearer.
links.reason: The note correctly separates readings of இலனென்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை (Manakkudavar and Pope: the giver's refusal; Parimelazhagar first: the asker's plea) and ties the refusal reading to 1070's சொல்லாடப் போஒம் உயிர்.

links.note: 230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even dying is sweet when giving is not possible (ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை). 1070 says the asker's life goes at the word of refusal (சொல்லாடப் போஒம் உயிர்) and asks where the concealer's life hides (யாங்கொளிக்கும் கொல்லோ). 230 gives the giver's view that life without giving is not worth keeping; 1070 puts that standard to the one who can give and refuses, and wonders that his life stays.
links.reason: 230 சாதலின் ... இனிததூஉம் ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை and 1070 கரப்பவர்க்கு யாங்கொளிக்கும் கொல்லோ ... உயிர் both weigh life against not giving; the note keeps the difference between cannot give and will not give.

links.note: 600 says those without inner drive are trees, and their being human in form is the only difference (மரம் மக்களாதலே வேறு). 1071 says the base resemble people exactly (மக்களே போல்வர்). Both treat the human shape as something that can be present without what makes a person, lacking drive in 600 and lacking character in 1071.
links.reason: மரம் மக்களாதலே வேறு (600) and மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர் (1071) both treat the human form as present without what makes a person.

links.note: 201 says those given to evil deeds do not fear, and the excellent do fear, the intoxication called evil deed (தீவினையார் அஞ்சார் விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்). 1072 says the base are more fortunate than those who know what is good, because they have no distress in the heart (நெஞ்சத்து அவலம் இலர்). 1072 puts 201's fact in mock praise: Parimelazhagar says the verse scorns by implication, and that the point is their not fearing blame.
links.reason: நெஞ்சத்து அவலம் இலர் is the ironic form of தீவினையார் அஞ்சார்; Parimelazhagar on 1072 does say குறிப்பால் இகழ்ந்தவாறு and பழி முதலியவற்றிற்கு அஞ்சார், as the note reports.

links.note: 839 says the friendship of fools is very sweet (பெரிதினிது), because parting from it gives no pain. 1072 says the base are fortunate (திருவுடையர்), because their hearts have no distress. Both verses praise a bad thing for the absence of a pain that only something of value would cause.
links.reason: திருவுடையர் ... நெஞ்சத்து அவலம் இலர் and பெரிதினிது ... பீழை தருவதொன்றில் both praise ironically, by the absence of a pain that only something of value would cause.

links.note: 1072 calls the base fortunate (திருவுடையர்) for having no distress of heart, and 1073 calls them like the gods (தேவர் அனையர்) for doing as they please. Both give praise that is meant as blame; Parimelazhagar says so of each. The two together describe one condition, no inner check in 1072 and no outer one in 1073.
links.reason: திருவுடையர் ... நெஞ்சத்து அவலம் இலர் (1072) and தேவர் அனையர் ... மேவன செய்தொழுகலான் (1073) are both ironic praise of the கயவர்; the inner/outer split matches the Tamil and Parimelazhagar's தம்மை நியமிப்பாரின்றி.

links.note: 1073 says the base are like the gods because they too act as they please (மேவன செய்தொழுகலான்). 1075 says that where the base show proper conduct (ஆசாரம்) it is fear, and beyond that a little if there is something they desire. 1075 marks the limit on 1073's freedom: their doing as they please stops only at fear or gain; Parimelazhagar says doing what they like is their nature and conduct is not.
links.reason: 1073's மேவன செய்தொழுகலான் is limited by 1075's அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம் ... அவாவுண்டேல்; Parimelazhagar on 1075 does say doing as they like is their nature and ஆசாரம் is not.

links.note: 978 says greatness always bows and smallness adorns itself in admiration of itself (சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). 1074 says the base man, on seeing those worse than himself, outdoes them and swaggers (மிகப்பட்டுச் செம்மாக்கும்); this follows Parimelazhagar's reading of அகப்பட்டி as those of looser conduct, while Manakkudavar reads the word quite differently. On Parimelazhagar's reading 1074 shows where the self-admiration of 978 finds its material: in comparison with someone lower.
links.reason: அவரின் மிகப்பட்டுச் செம்மாக்கும் கீழ் matches சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து; the note correctly flags that this rests on Parimelazhagar's reading of அகப்பட்டி.

links.note: 1016 says the high do not care for the wide world unless they have shame as their fence (நாண்வேலி). 1075 says the conduct of the base is fear (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம்), which Parimelazhagar takes as fear of harm from the king. Each verse names what keeps a kind of person within bounds: shame from inside for the high, fear from outside for the base.
links.reason: அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம் (fear of the king, per Parimelazhagar) against நாண்வேலி for மேலாயவர்: outer fear and inner shame as the restraint of each kind. The paraphrase of 1016 follows the alternative reading Parimelazhagar records, which is defensible.

links.note: 1075 says the base behave properly out of fear. 1078 says the base, like sugar-cane, are of use only when crushed (கொல்லப் பயன்படும் கீழ்). 1078 applies the rule of 1075 to giving: what fear does for their conduct, force does for their generosity.
links.reason: அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம் and கொல்லப் பயன்படும் கீழ் both say the base respond only to compulsion; taking பயன்படும் as giving follows the commentators.

links.note: 221 says giving to those who have nothing is what giving is (வறியார்க்கொன்று ஈவதே ஈகை), and all other giving has the nature of a loan to be returned. 1077 says the base will not even shake a wet hand (ஈர்ங்கை விதிரார்) except for those whose bent fist would break their jaw; Parimelazhagar sums up that they give nothing to the weak and everything to those who hurt them. The base man's giving in 1077 is the reverse of 221's definition: it goes only to the strong.
links.reason: 221 defines ஈகை as giving to வறியார் and calls the rest குறியெதிர்ப்பை; 1077's கயவர் won't even ஈர்ங்கை விதிரார் except for கூன்கையர், so their giving is exactly the non-ஈகை kind, as the note says.

links.note: 1077 says the base give only to those who would break their jaw. 1078 states the same with a contrast and a figure: the worthy are of use at a word (சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர்), and the base, like sugar-cane, when crushed (கொல்லப் பயன்படும்). Parimelazhagar treats the two verses as a pair on how the base give.
links.reason: கொடிறுடைக்கும் கூன்கையர் அல்லாதவர்க்கு (1077) is restated with contrast and the sugar-cane figure, கொல்லப் பயன்படும் கீழ் (1078). Parimelazhagar's 'இவை இரண்டு பாட்டானும்' confirms the pairing; adjacent verses, so the gain is modest.

links.note: 216 says wealth with a person of நயன் is like a fruit-bearing tree ripening in the middle of the town (பயன்மரம் உள்ளூர்ப் பழுத்தற்று). 1078 says the base are like sugar-cane (கரும்புபோல்), of use only when crushed. Both use a plant's yield (பயன்) as the figure for how a person's wealth reaches others: the tree offers its fruit in the open, and the cane gives nothing until it is pressed.
links.reason: Both verses figure usefulness to others as a plant's yield: பயன்மரம் உள்ளூர்ப் பழுத்தற்று (open fruit) against கரும்புபோல் கொல்லப் பயன்படும் (yield only under crushing); the note describes both accurately.

links.note: 1078 says the worthy are of use as soon as they are told (சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர் சான்றோர்). 223 says not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing', and giving, belong to one of good family; Parimelazhagar records a second reading on which the giver gives before the asker has to say it. On that reading 223 goes one step beyond 1078: the worthy of 1078 give at a word, and the well-born of 223 give before the word.
links.reason: சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர் சான்றோர் gives at a word; Parimelazhagar does record a reading of இலனென்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை ஈதல் as giving before the asker has to speak, and the note ties the step beyond to that reading explicitly.

links.note: In 1081 the man cannot decide whether she is an அணங்கு, a choice peahen or a woman, and his heart reels (மாலும் என் நெஞ்சு). 918 says the embrace of deceiving women (மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு) is called an அணங்கு for those without discerning sense. The same word names a spirit that overpowers a man in both books: here it is a lover's wonder, there a warning, and Parimelazhagar glosses it in 918 as a divine woman who takes life through desire.
links.reason: அணங்கு is the operative word in both, as wonder in அணங்குகொல் and as danger in அணங்கென்ப மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு.

links.note: 1081 only asks whether she is an அணங்கு. In 1082, once she returns his look (நோக்கெதிர் நோக்குதல்), he says it is like an attacking அணங்கு (தாக்கணங்கு) who has also brought an army. The doubt of the first verse becomes a felt assault in the second, and Parimelazhagar reads 1082 as spoken after he has settled that she is human.
links.reason: அணங்குகொல் in 1081 becomes தாக்கணங்கு தானைக்கொண்டன்னது in 1082 once she returns the look, and Parimelazhagar does introduce 1082 with மானுட மாதராதல் தெளிந்த தலைமகன்.

links.note: In 1081 his heart reels (மாலும் நெஞ்சு) because it cannot place her among goddess, peahen and woman. In 1112 he scolds the same heart for being confused at flowers (மலர்காணின் மையாத்தி நெஞ்சே), as if her eyes were like what many can see. The confusion moves from what she is to what could be compared with her, and by 1112 he treats it as the heart's error.
links.reason: 1081 மாலும் என் நெஞ்சு and 1112 மையாத்தி நெஞ்சே show the same heart confused first about what she is and then about what resembles her கண்; the note reads both correctly.

links.note: In 775 a warrior whose glaring eye (விழித்த கண்) blinks when a spear is thrown counts that as running away. In 1082 the man looks, and her look answering his (நோக்கெதிர் நோக்குதல்) is like an army brought against him. Both treat meeting another's gaze as combat, one on the battlefield and one at first sight in love.
links.reason: Both join eyes and warfare (விழித்தகண் ... இமைப்பின் ஒட்டு; நோக்கெதிர் நோக்குதல் ... தானைக்கொண்டன்ன), but in 775 the eye flinches at a thrown spear, not at another's gaze, so 'meeting another's gaze as combat' overstates what 775 says.

links.note: 1082 says her returning look is like an attacking spirit come with an army (தாக்கணங்கு தானைக்கொண் டன்னது): the look only wounds. 1091 finds two looks in her eyes (இருநோக்கு), one that gives the sickness and one that is its medicine (நோய்நோக்கு ... அந்நோய் மருந்து). The next chapter adds the healing side that 1082 leaves out.
links.reason: 1082's returning look is purely an assault ('தாக்கணங்கு தானைக்கொண்டன்னது'); 1091 finds 'இருநோக்கு', 'நோய்நோக்கு' and 'அந்நோய் மருந்து', adding the healing look.

links.note: 1082 makes her answering glance an armed host (தானை). 1113, listing her beauties, calls her kohl-lined eyes spears (வேலுண்கண்). The eye as weapon is a fixed figure of the man's praise, used first as his alarm and later as a plain item of description.
links.reason: 1082 makes her returning look a தானை and 1113 has வேலுண்கண்; the eye-as-weapon figure is shared, though வேலுண்கண் is a stock epithet, and the note describes both uses accurately.

links.note: 765 defines an army as the force that can stand together even if Death comes raging at it (கூற்றுடன்று மேல்வரினும்). In 1083 the man says he now knows what is called Death (கூற்று): it has womanly grace and large warring eyes (பேரமர்க் கட்டு). Both set கூற்று in a battle; the Book of Wealth imagines standing against it, and the lover says he has met it in her eyes.
links.reason: கூற்று appears in both, with பேரமர்க் கட்டு giving 1083 a martial colour, but Death personified is a stock figure across the Kural and the two uses (a force an army withstands, a conceit for a woman's eyes) share little beyond the word.

links.note: 1083: 'I did not know before (பண்டறியேன்) what Death is; now I know'. 1226: the woman did not know (அறிந்ததிலேன்), while her husband had not left, that evening brings sickness. In both a lover says love has taught what was only a word before, the man at first sight and the woman in separation.
links.reason: பண்டறியேன் ... இனியறிந்தேன் and அகலாத காலை அறிந்ததிலேன் both have a lover say that love taught what was not known before; 'only a word before' fits 1083 better than 1226.

links.note: 279: the arrow is straight but cruel, the lute bent but sweet, so judge by what a thing does (வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்). 1084 sets a girl of womanly gentleness (பெண்டகைப் பேதை) against eyes that look as if they eat lives; Parimelazhagar takes அமர்த்தன as 'were at odds' with her nature. Both verses turn on a form that does not match its effect, one as a rule for judging ascetics and one as a lover's surprise.
links.reason: On Parimelazhagar's gloss அமர்த்தல்: மாறுபடுதல், the life-eating eyes are at odds with பெண்டகைப் பேதை, which matches 279's கணை கொடிது யாழ்கோடு செவ்விது (form against effect). The note flags that it rests on that gloss; Manakkudavar takes அமர்த்தன as 'suited'.

links.note: 326 says Death that eats life (உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று) does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing. 1084 says the eyes of this womanly, artless girl have a look that eats the life of those who see them (கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றம்). The lover gives her eyes the standing epithet of Death, which the previous verse (1083) has just named.
links.reason: The identical epithet 'உயிருண்ணும்' is Death's in 326 ('உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று') and the eyes' in 1084 ('கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றம்'), right after 1083 names கூற்று.

links.note: 1084: her eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see them (உயிருண்ணும்). 1221: the woman tells evening it is not evening but a time that eats the life of those once wed (மணந்தார் உயிருண்ணும் வேலை). The same phrase marks what kills each lover: for the man her eyes at first sight, for the woman the evening hour in his absence.
links.reason: கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் (1084) and மணந்தார் உயிருண்ணும் (1221) use the same life-eating phrase for her eyes and for the evening.

links.note: In 1085 the doe (பிணை) is one of three things her look might be, beside Death. In 1089 her doe-like artless look (பிணையேர் மடநோக்கு) and her modesty are ornament enough, so added jewels are pointless. The same doe glance is first one part of a threat and then her natural adornment.
links.reason: பிணையோ (1085) and பிணையேர் மடநோக்கு (1089) use the doe for her look within one chapter, first beside கூற்றம் and then as her natural ornament.

links.note: 1085 asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe, and says it has all three (இம்மூன்றும் உடைத்து); Parimelazhagar comments that it gives pleasure and pain together. 1091 states that plainly as two looks, one the sickness and one its cure. The puzzled question of 1085 is resolved into a doubleness he can name.
links.reason: நோக்கமிம் மூன்றும் உடைத்து and இருநோக்கு ... நோய்நோக்கொன் றந்நோய் மருந்து both find her look to be more than one thing at once; Parimelazhagar on 1085 says இன்பமும் துன்பமும் ஒருங்கு செய்யாநின்றது, as the note reports.

links.note: 1086 wishes her brows would screen her eyes (மறைப்பின்), for then the eyes would not cause him trembling pain. 1087 says the cloth over her breasts is like the face-cloth over a rutting elephant's eyes (கட்படாம்). Both are about a covering over something that harms him: one he wishes for and one he sees, and Parimelazhagar says of the second that the cloth keeps them from killing.
links.reason: Adjacent verses on a cover over what harms him: 1086 'புருவம் ... மறைப்பின் நடுங்கஞர் செய்யல', 1087 'கட்படாம் ... முலைமேல் துகில்'; Parimelazhagar's 'கொல்லாமல் காத்தலின்' is quoted correctly.

links.note: In 1086 the man says her eyes cause him trembling pain (நடுங்கஞர்) and wishes them screened. In 1171 the woman asks why her own eyes weep, since they showed him to her and so gave her this unending sickness (தண்டாநோய் தாம்காட்ட). Each lover names eyes as the cause of the pain; for him it is hers, for her it is her own.
links.reason: Eyes as the source of love's pain (நடுங்கஞர் செய்யல மன் இவள் கண்; தண்டாநோய் தாம்காட்ட) is a real shared motif and the note is accurate, but it is a commonplace across the love chapters and the pairing teaches little beyond the shared topic.

links.note: 1087: the cloth over her firm breasts is the face-cloth on a rutting bull elephant (கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேற் கட்படாம்). 24: the renouncer guards the five senses with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான்), a goad being the elephant-driver's tool. Both draw on the dangerous elephant held in check; the ascetic chapter makes the senses the elephant, and the lover makes her covered breasts the elephant.
links.reason: 1087 names the கடாஅக் களிறு under its கட்படாம்; 24's தோட்டி implies the elephant, and Parimelazhagar spells out பொறிகளாகிய யானை ஐந்து and says the cloth keeps the breasts from killing, so the restrained elephant is in both.

links.note: 1088 reports the first loss: his battlefield strength breaks at the sight of her forehead. 1134 says the fierce flood of love carries off the raft of shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை). The later verse generalises what 1088 exclaims, with manliness now lost along with shame.
links.reason: உடைந்ததே ... என் பீடு at one forehead (1088) becomes காமக் கடும்புனல் carrying off நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை (1134).

links.note: 1088: his might (பீடு), feared even by enemies in battle, has broken (உடைந்ததே) before her bright forehead alone. 1258: the woman says the soft words of that deceiving thief are the weapon that breaks her womanly firmness (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை). Each lover uses the language of war and breaking for the loss of the quality they prized in themselves, his strength and her restraint.
links.reason: உடைந்ததே ... என் பீடு and பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை use the same war-and-breaking language for each lover's lost strength.

links.note: 95: humility and sweet speech are a person's ornament and nothing else is (அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற). 1089: what use are foreign ornaments (ஏதில தந்து அணி) to one who has a doe's artless look and modesty? Both deny that added adornment counts beside an inborn quality, 95 as a rule of conduct and 1089 as a lover's praise.
links.reason: அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற and அணியெவனோ ஏதில தந்து both deny added ornaments beside a quality of the person; 'inborn' is a little loose for பணிவு and இன்சொல்.

links.note: 1090 uses liquor as the lesser pleasure that love outdoes. 1288 uses it as an exact likeness: 'your chest is to us as liquor is to those who are drunk on it (களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே), though it does shaming harm (இளித்தக்க இன்னா)'. The later verse grants what 1090 leaves unsaid, that the pull likened to drink goes on despite disgrace.
links.reason: Both use liquor for love (அடுநறா; களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே) but 1288 does not limit or condition 1090's claim that love outdoes drink; this is a shared figure used two ways, not a qualification.

links.note: 948 tells the healer to examine the disease, then its root (நோய்முதல்), then the means that subdue it (அது தணிக்கும் வாய்), as three separate things. 1102 first grants the ordinary rule, that the medicine is other than the disease, and then says love is the exception, where cause and remedy are the same person. The lover's verse marks love's sickness as a case the method of 948 does not cover.
links.reason: 948 separates நோய், நோய்முதல் and அது தணிக்கும் வாய், and 1102 itself states that ordinary rule (பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிற) before making her தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து, an explicit exception.

links.note: 213 says that in the world of the gods or here (புத்தேளுலகத்தும் ஈண்டும்) it is hard to find another good like ஒப்புரவு, doing one's part for others. 1103 asks whether the lotus-eyed one's world is as sweet as sleeping on the beloved's shoulders. Both measure an earthly thing against heaven and prefer it; in the Book of Virtue it is a duty, and here it is a lover's own claim about his pleasure.
links.reason: 213 புத்தேளுலகத்தும் ஈண்டும் ... ஒப்புரவின் நல்ல பிற பெறலரிது and 1103 இனிதுகொல் தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு both hold a thing of this life up against the heavenly world and find heaven no better.

links.note: 265: austerity is practised here because whatever is wanted is obtained as it is wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்). 1105: her shoulders are like each desired thing at the moment of desiring it (வேட்ட பொழுதின் அவையவை போலுமே). Both describe desire met exactly as it arises, promised to the ascetic through தவம் and claimed by the lover in her embrace.
links.reason: வேட்ட பொழுதின் அவையவை போலுமே mirrors வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்: desire met as it arises, in love and in தவம்.

links.note: 1101 says the objects of all five senses are found in her alone. 1105 says her shoulders are like whatever one craves, at the time one craves it. The first claim is about range, that she holds every kind of pleasure; the second adds timing, that she answers each wish as it comes.
links.reason: 1101's ஐம்புலனும் ஒண்தொடி கண்ணே உள gives range; 1105's வேட்ட பொழுதின் அவையவை போலுமே adds that she answers each desire as it arises.

links.note: 64: gruel stirred by the small hands of one's own children is far sweeter than ambrosia (அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிதே). 1106: her shoulders are made of ambrosia (அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன) because their touch revives his life. Parent and lover both reach for அமிழ்து to measure the nearness of someone of their own; the parent ranks the child's gruel above it and the lover equates her with it.
links.reason: அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன தோள் and அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிதே share only அமிழ்து as a stock standard of excellence, used for different things (reviving touch, taste); 'nearness of someone of their own' is the note's gloss.

links.note: 1106: his life sprouts afresh whenever he touches her. 1124: she is to his life what living is when they are together, and what dying is when she leaves (வாழ்தல் உயிர்க்கன்னள் ... சாதல் அதற்கன்னள்). Both tie his உயிர் to her presence; 1124 states the other half, which 1106's 'each time' (உறுதோறு) implies.
links.reason: உறுதோறு உயிர்தளிர்ப்ப (1106) and வாழ்தல் உயிர்க்கன்னள் ... சாதல் அதற்கன்னள் நீங்கும் இடத்து (1124) both tie his உயிர் to her presence, and 1124 supplies the absence half.

links.note: 229: eating alone to fill one's own store (தாமே தமியர் உணல்) is more bitter than begging. 1107: eating one's own after sharing it, in one's own house, is the model of sweetness, and the embrace is like it. Read together they give both halves of one judgement on eating: bitter when hoarded, sweet when shared.
links.reason: 229 தாமே தமியர் உணல் is இன்னாது and 1107 தமதுபாத்து உண்டற்று is the standard of sweetness; solitary and shared eating are judged oppositely, in the first and third books.

links.note: 1108 praises the embrace with no gap. In 1187 the woman says she lay embracing, shifted a little (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன்), and at once pallor was on her thick enough to scoop up. The woman's verse gives a reason from her side why the unbroken embrace is the sweet one: the least separation brings the pallor of parting.
links.reason: 1108 'வளியிடை போழப்படாஅ முயக்கு' and 1187 'புல்லிக் கிடந்தேன் புடைபெயர்ந்தேன் அவ்வளவில்... பசப்பு' both turn on the smallest gap in an embrace; 1187 as the woman's side of the same idea is a fair development.

links.note: 1108 specifies 'two who desire' (வீழும் இருவர்க்கு இனிதே): the close embrace is sweet to both. 1196: love on one side only is painful, and like a carrying pole it is sweet on both ends (இருதலையானும் இனிது). Both make sweetness depend on the love being mutual, 1108 in fulfilment and 1196 from the woman who lacks it.
links.reason: 1108 வீழும் இருவர்க்கு இனிதே and 1196 இருதலையானும் இனிது both make sweetness depend on mutual love.

links.note: 1109 counts sulking (ஊடல்) among the fruits of love. 1302 says sulking is like salt in the right amount, and letting it run a little long is like a little too much salt (சிறிது மிக்கற்றால் நீள விடல்). The later verse sets a limit on the first item of 1109's list: it is a gain only in measure.
links.reason: 1109 lists ஊடல் as பயன், and 1302 says புலவி is உப்பமைந்தற்று and spoiled by நீள விடல். 1302 limits the first item of 1109's list.

links.note: 1109 names quarrel, making up and union together as rewards without ranking them. 1326 ranks them: as digesting is sweeter than eating, sulking is sweeter than union (புணர்தலின் ஊடல் இனிது). The later verse takes one item from 1109's list and gives it first place.
links.reason: 1109 lists 'ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல்' together as love's gains without ranking; 1326 ranks 'புணர்தலின் ஊடல் இனிது'. Accurate and instructive.

links.note: 940: as a gambler loves the game more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம்), life loves itself more with each suffering (உழத்தொறூஉம்). 1110: each closeness shows love to be more than he knew, as each learning shows ignorance. Both describe an attachment that grows through its own repetition; the gambling chapter gives it as a warning and the lover as a delight.
links.reason: இழத்தொறூஉம் / உழத்தொறூஉம் and அறிதோறு / செறிதோறும் use the same -தொறும் simile for an attachment that grows with each repetition, as loss-deepened craving and as ever-renewed love.

links.note: 1145: as drinking is wanted more each time one gets drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்று), love is sweeter each time it is exposed. 1110: love is like finding one's ignorance each time one learns, each time he is close to her. Both say love grows by repetition and does not wear out; 1110 takes its likeness from knowledge and 1145 from drink, and they differ in what is repeated, union or exposure by gossip.
links.reason: Both use the தொறும் ... அற்றால் காமம் construction to say love increases with repetition (செறிதோறும்; வெளிப்படுந்தோறும்), and the note states that what is repeated differs.

links.note: 1111 says she is more delicate than the anicham (நின்னினும் மென்னீரள்); 1289 says love itself is more delicate than a flower (மலரினும் மெல்லிது காமம்) and few catch its right moment. The same comparative, softer than a flower, is applied first to the beloved's body and later to the experience of love.
links.reason: நின்னினும் மென்னீரள் and மலரினும் மெல்லிது காமம் apply the same comparative, softer than a flower, to her and then to love itself; could also be filed as same_image.

links.note: 1113 praises her as bamboo-shouldered (வேய்த்தோளவட்கு). 906, in the chapter on men ruled by their wives, says those who fear the wife's bamboo-like shoulders (அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சுபவர்) have no standing even if they live like the gods. The same stock epithet of beauty is admired in the Book of Love and named in the Book of Wealth as the thing an unmanned husband fears.
links.reason: வேய்த்தோளவட்கு and இல்லாள் அமையார்தோள் are the same bamboo-shoulder epithet, admired in one and the object of an unmanly fear in the other.

links.note: 1113 lists her features as metaphors: body a tender shoot (முறி), teeth pearls, and kohl-lined eyes that are spears (வேலுண்கண்). 1084 had already noticed the mismatch this list contains: her eyes, with a look that eats the life of those who see them, are at war (அமர்த்தன) with her gentle womanly nature. Read together, the spear in the inventory of soft things is the same contradiction 1084 names outright.
links.reason: The reading of 1084 அமர்த்தன as 'at war' is Parimelazhagar's (மாறுபடுதல்); Manakkudavar reads ஒத்தன, 'suit'. Finding the same contradiction in 1113's stock epithet வேலுண்கண் is the note's construction and depends on that one reading, which it does not flag.

links.note: 475 warns that even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle if the load is piled too high (அச்சிறும்). 1115 says she has worn anicham flowers without removing the stalks (கால்களையாள்), so no good drums will sound for her waist; Parimelazhagar explains that the waist will break under the weight and get the funeral drum. Both make the lightest possible load the breaking one, as counsel on overreach in 475 and as playful hyperbole about her slenderness in 1115.
links.reason: பீலிபெய் சாகாடும் அச்சிறும் and அனிச்சப்பூக் கால்களையாள் பெய்தாள் both turn the lightest load into the breaking one (same verb பெய்), and Parimelazhagar does supply the broken waist and funeral drum.
links.text_issue: 1115 reads நுகப்பிற்கு; should be நுசுப்பிற்கு (waist), as the commentary has it.

links.note: 1111 says she is more delicate than the anicham. 1115 pushes the claim to a comic limit: the unremoved stalks of that same flower (அனிச்சப்பூக் கால்களையாள்) are too heavy for her waist. The flower that was the standard of softness becomes a burden.
links.reason: 1111's நின்னினும் மென்னீரள் makes the anicham the standard of softness, and 1115's அனிச்சப்பூக் கால்களையாள் pushes it to hyperbole, the flower's stalks being too heavy for her waist.
links.text_issue: 1115 reads நுகப்பிற்கு; should be நுசுப்பிற்கு.

links.note: In 1081 the man, at first sight, cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels (மாலும் என் நெஞ்சு). In 1116 the confusion is moved to the sky: the stars cannot tell the moon from her face (அறியா) and wander from their places (பதியின் கலங்கிய). The lover's own bewilderment about what she is becomes, in the praise chapter, a bewilderment he attributes to the stars.
links.reason: மாலும் என் நெஞ்சு over what she is (1081) reappears as the stars' அறியா ... கலங்கிய over moon and face (1116); the note reads both verses accurately.

links.note: 1116 says the stars cannot distinguish the moon from her face. 1117 immediately denies that the two are alike: the moon fills out from loss and has a spot, and her face has none (மறுவுண்டோ). Parimelazhagar reads 1117 as mocking the stars for missing an obvious difference, so the second verse withdraws the equality the first seemed to grant.
links.reason: 1116 has the stars unable to tell மதியும் மடந்தை முகனும்; 1117 asks மறுவுண்டோ மாதர் முகத்து, and Parimelazhagar reads it as mocking the stars for missing the difference. The second verse takes back the likeness.

links.note: 782 uses the moon's phases for friendship: with the wise it fills like the crescent, with fools it shrinks like the moon after full. 1117 mentions the same cycle, a moon that shines only after filling its lost parts (அறுவாய் நிறைந்த), as a defect that her face does not share. The waxing that is a hopeful figure in 782 counts in 1117 as evidence of the moon's inconstancy.
links.reason: அறுவாய் நிறைந்த அவிர்மதி and நிறைநீர ... பிறைமதிப் பின்னீர both use the moon's filling and waning; Parimelazhagar's gloss of 1117 (முன் குறைந்த இடம் வந்து நிரம்பியே விளங்கும்) supports the note, though the verse's stated defect is the மறு.

links.note: Both verses address the moon with வாழி மதி. In 1118 the man tells it that it could have his love if it could shine like her face; Parimelazhagar hears the blessing as mockery. In 1210 the woman, left behind, asks it not to set so that her eyes may find the man who has gone without leaving her heart. The moon is a rival to be dismissed in the time of union and a helper to be begged in separation.
links.reason: Both close with the address வாழி மதி, in the man's praise in 1118 and the woman's plea படாஅதி in 1210; the contrast of roles the note draws is accurate.

links.note: In 1119 the man tells the moon that to resemble her face it must not appear for many to see (பலர்காணத் தோன்றல்). In 1311 the woman refuses the man's chest because all women feast on him in common with their eyes (கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்). Each lover applies the same standard from the other side: what is shared with every onlooker is no longer one's own.
links.reason: பலர்காணத் தோன்றல் (do not appear for many to see) and பெண்ணியலார் எல்லாரும் கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர் both treat being common to every onlooker's eyes as disqualifying, from the man's side and the woman's.
