links.note: 1111 opens the chapter by ranking her above the anicham in softness. 1120 closes it by making the anicham and swan's down hurt her feet like the nerunji fruit, a thorn (மாதர் அடிக்கு நெருஞ்சிப் பழம்). The flower moves from being less soft than she is to being painful to her. Parimelazhagar sets the verse in a refusal to take her on a desert elopement.
links.reason: 1111 நின்னினும் மென்னீரள் ranks her above the anicham; 1120 அனிச்சமும் ... மாதர் அடிக்கு நெருஞ்சிப் பழம் makes the flower hurt her. Parimelazhagar's elopement setting is reported correctly.

links.note: 64 says the gruel one's children have stirred with their small hands is far sweeter than amrita (அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிது). 1121 says the moisture at her white teeth is like milk mixed with honey (பாலொடு தேன்கலந் தற்று). In both, affection makes something bodily and ordinary taste better than the finest food, for a parent in one verse and a lover in the other.
links.reason: Both praise the taste of something bodily made sweet by affection (சிறுகை அளாவிய கூழ்; வாலெயிறு ஊறிய நீர்); note that 1121 says it is like பாலொடு தேன், not better than it as 64's அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிது says.

links.note: 1121 calls her பணிமொழி, the woman of soft, low speech, in a verse about the sweetness of her kiss. In 1258 the woman uses the same word for his speech: the soft words (பணிமொழி) of that thief of many deceits are the weapon that breaks her womanly reserve. The quality he savours in her is the one she names in him as a weapon.
links.reason: பணிமொழி stands for the woman herself in 1121 and for his speech as படை in 1258; the reversal is real. The note slightly overstates in saying he savours her speech, since the verse praises வாலெயிறு ஊறிய நீர்.

links.note: In 1123 the man orders the image in the pupil of his eye (கருமணியிற் பாவாய்) to leave, since otherwise there is no room for the woman he loves. In 1126 the woman says her lover never leaves her eyes (கண்ணுள்ளின் போகார்) and is too subtle to be hurt when she blinks. Both lovers place the other inside the eye; he has to make room for her, and she has him there already.
links.reason: Both verses of one chapter lodge the beloved in the eye (கருமணியிற் பாவாய்; கண்ணுள்ளின் போகார்) and the note is accurate, but his voice and hers are not different domains: this is a shared image.
links.text_issue: 1126 பருகுவரா looks like a misprint for பருவரார்.

links.note: 1122 says their bond is like that of body and life. 1124 draws the consequence: together she is to his life what living is (வாழ்தல்), and when she leaves she is what dying is (சாதல்). The comparison in 1122 becomes a statement of what separation will mean.
links.reason: உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை என்ன (1122) is turned in 1124 into வாழ்தல் உயிர்க்கு when together and சாதல் ... நீங்கும் இடத்து, the consequence of the same body-life comparison.

links.note: In 1124 the man says her leaving is death to his life (சாதல் அதற்கன்னள் நீங்கும் இடத்து). In 1151 the reply to his announced journey is that news of his quick return should be told to those who will be alive then (வாழ்வார்க் குரை); Parimelazhagar gives the line to her friend, Manakkudavar to the woman. Each side says that separation is not survivable, he at a brief parting after a meeting and her side when he leaves on a long journey.
links.reason: சாதல் அதற்கன்னள் நீங்கும் இடத்து and வல்வரவு வாழ்வார்க்கு உரை both say parting is not survivable, from the two sides; the speaker note on 1151 is accurate.

links.note: In 1126 she says her lover does not leave her eyes and is not hurt even if she blinks (இமைப்பின் பருவரார்), because he is so subtle. In 1129 she will not blink, knowing he would be hidden (இமைப்பின் கரப்பாக்கு அறிவல்). The same conceit is used both ways within one chapter: blinking is harmless in the first verse and a risk in the second, which shows these are playful defences of him and not one consistent picture.
links.reason: இமைப்பின் is used both ways (harmless in 1126, hiding him in 1129), which is a real and interesting shared conceit, but neither verse limits the other, and the conclusion that they are 'playful defences' and not one picture is the note's inference.
links.text_issue: 1126 reads பருகுவரா where the standard text has பருவரார்.

links.note: 1126 says he never leaves her eyes though the town thinks him gone. 1218 says that when she sleeps he is on her shoulder and when she wakes he hurries into her heart (நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர் விரைந்து). Parimelazhagar frames both as her defence of him against the charge of absence: she answers by locating him somewhere inside herself at every moment.
links.reason: கண்ணுள்ளின் போகார் and தோள்மேலர் ... நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர் both lodge him within her body, and Parimelazhagar frames both as answers to இயற்பழித்தல். The town thinking him gone is commentary context, not in 1126's Tamil.

links.note: In 1128 his presence in her heart is something she protects, to the point of avoiding hot food. In 1205 the same presence is a complaint: he keeps her out of his own heart and yet is not ashamed to come into hers without pause (எம்நெஞ்சத்து ஓவா வரல்). The later verse adds what 1128 leaves out, the question whether the dwelling is mutual.
links.reason: நெஞ்சத்தார் காதலவராக in 1128 is cherished; in 1205 எம்நெஞ்சத்து ஓவா வரல் is a reproach because தம்நெஞ்சத்து எம்மைக் கடிகொண்டார், which adds the condition of mutuality.

links.note: 1128 says that since her lover is in her heart (நெஞ்சத்தார் காதலவராக) she fears eating anything hot, knowing it would burn him. 1249 uses almost the same opening, உள்ளத்தார் காதலவராக, to ask her heart whom it goes out looking for when he is within it. The playful premise of 1128, said to defend him, is used in 1249 to rebuke her own restless heart.
links.reason: The shared opening நெஞ்சத்தார்/உள்ளத்தார் காதலவராக is real, but the verses do not make the same claim: 1128 defends him (வெய்துண்டல் அஞ்சுதும்), 1249 rebukes her heart (யாருழைச் சேறி). The note itself describes a reused phrase, not agreement.
links.text_issue: 1249 reads காத லவரால்; the commentary and the standard text have காதலவராக.

links.note: 1129 and 1130 end with the same line, ஏதிலர் என்னும் இவ் வூர். 1129 gives the town's ground for blame, her sleeplessness, which she explains as refusing to blink. 1130 states her answer directly: he lives gladly in her heart always (உவந்துறைவர் உள்ளத்துள் என்றும்), while the town says he lives apart.
links.reason: Adjacent verses sharing the line 'ஏதிலர் என்னும் இவ் வூர்'; 1129 'இமைப்பின் கரப்பாக்கு அறிவல்' gives the ground, 1130 'உவந்துறைவர் உள்ளத்துள் என்றும்' the direct answer.

links.note: In 1129 she does not blink for fear of losing sight of him, and for this the town calls him a stranger without love (ஏதிலர் என்னும் இவ் வூர்). In 1220 the people of the town say he has left her in waking life, and she asks whether they do not see him in dreams (கனவினால் காணார்கொல்). In both she sets the town's outward evidence against her inner experience of his presence, first in the eye and then in the dream.
links.reason: ஏதிலர் என்னும் இவ்வூர் and நம்நீத்தார் என்பர் ... இவ்வூரவர் both set the town's verdict against her experience of his presence, in the unblinking eye and in the dream.

links.note: In 1130 she is sure that he lives in her heart, and gladly (உவந்துறைவர்), against the town's talk. In 1204 she affirms the same thing, that he is always in her heart (எந்நெஞ்சத்து ஓஒ உளரே அவர்), and then asks whether she too has a place in his (யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர்நெஞ்சத்து). The confidence she shows the town in 1130 does not answer the doubt she admits in 1204: his presence in her heart says nothing about her place in his.
links.reason: உவந்துறைவர் உள்ளத்துள் என்றும் is restated in எந்நெஞ்சத்து ஓஒ உளரே அவர், and 1204 adds the doubt யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர்நெஞ்சத்து that 1130's confidence does not cover.

links.note: 1131 calls the palmyra horse the only safeguard for those who suffer in love. 1137 praises womanhood that suffers a sea of desire (கடலன்ன காமம் உழந்தும்) and still does not mount it (மடலேறா). The same verb உழந்து marks the same suffering, so 1137 limits 1131: the remedy is one a woman forgoes, and forgoing it is counted as worth.
links.reason: காமம் உழந்து ... மடலல்லது இல்லை is limited by காமம் உழந்தும் மடலேறாப் பெண்: same verb, same chapter, and the 'only refuge' is one a woman declines to her credit.

links.note: 1131 has the man say that for those worn down by love there is no strength that is a safeguard (ஏமம்) except the palmyra horse (மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி). In 1164 the woman says the sea of love exists but the safe raft to swim it does not (ஏமப் புணைமன்னும் இல்). The one ஏமம் he names is a man's recourse; her verse shows a sufferer for whom even that is missing.
links.reason: Both turn on ஏமம்: he has மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி as his one safeguard, and she says ஏமப் புணைமன்னும் இல்; the contrast of a man's recourse with her lack of any is fair.

links.note: In 1247 the woman tells her heart to give up either desire or shame, since she cannot bear the two together (காமம் விடு ஒன்றோ நாண்விடு). 1132 is that choice made: the man keeps desire and puts shame aside (நாணினை நீக்கி) to ride the palmyra horse. Read together, 1247 states the dilemma and 1132 shows one way out of it.
links.reason: காமம் விடு ஒன்றோ நாண்விடு states the choice, and நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து ... மடலேறும் makes it by dropping நாண். The speakers differ, and the note says so.

links.note: 1026 defines நல்லாண்மை as making oneself fit to manage the house one was born into (இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்). 1133 uses the same word for what the lover had before (நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன்) and has now exchanged for the palmyra horse. Set beside 1026's definition, the lover's loss is of the capacity that makes a man of use to his family, not only of pride.
links.reason: நல்லாண்மை is shared, but 1133 pairs it with நாண் as what the மடல்-rider has lost, in the ordinary sense of manly firmness; reading 1026's definition (இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்) into the lover's loss is the note's own addition.

links.note: In 1088 the man, on first seeing her, says his might (பீடு), which enemies dreaded in battle, has broken before her bright forehead. In 1133 he says the shame and good manliness he once had are replaced by the palmyra horse. The later verse carries the first collapse through to its end: what broke at first sight is now given up publicly.
links.reason: 1088 has பீடு உடைந்ததே before her forehead; 1133 has நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன் replaced by மடல். The later verse does carry the same loss of manly standing to a public end.

links.note: In 1133 the man says he once had shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன்) and today has the palmyra horse. In 1254 the woman says she used to say she had restraint (நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்மன்), yet her desire passes concealment and comes out in public. Each speaker sets a former self-possession against its loss to love; his loss is நாண் and ஆண்மை, hers is நிறை.
links.reason: நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன் and நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்மன் each set a former self-possession against its loss to love (மடல் / மன்று படும்), from the man's and the woman's side.

links.note: 306 says anger burns the safe raft that is one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணையைச் சுடும்). 1134 says the flood of love sweeps off the raft that is shame and good manliness (என்னும் புணை). In both a passion destroys the thing figured as the raft that keeps a person afloat: anger in the chapter on not being angry, desire here.
links.reason: Both end on புணை destroyed by a passion: காமக் கடும்புனல் உய்க்கும் ... என்னும் புணை and இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணையைச் சுடும்; the note describes each raft correctly.

links.note: 1134 has the flood of love carry away the raft called shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை). 1251 has the axe of desire break the door called restraint, bolted with the bar of shame (நிறையென்னும் நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). Both make shame a built defence that love's force destroys, one in the man's voice and one in the woman's.
links.reason: காமக் கடும்புனல் sweeps off the புணை of நாண் and நல்லாண்மை; காமக் கணிச்சி breaks the கதவு of நிறை bolted with நாணுத்தாழ்: the same claim that love's force destroys a built defence of shame, in his voice and hers.

links.note: In 1135 the man says the girl with small bangles gave him (தந்தாள்) the palmyra horse and the grief that evening brings. In 1183 the woman says he took her grace and shame and gave in return (கைம்மாறா ... தந்து) sickness and pallor. Each lover describes the affliction as a gift from the other, and in both verses shame is part of what is lost.
links.reason: தந்தாள் மடலொடு மாலை உழக்கும் துயர் and கைம்மாறா நோயும் பசலையும் தந்து both cast the affliction as the other's gift; shame is explicit in 1183 (நாணும் அவர்கொண்டார்) and implied in 1135 only through மடல்.
links.text_issue: The Parimelazhagar entry for 1135 in the packet is truncated at its start.

links.note: In 1136 the man's eyes will not close (படல் ஒல்லா) for the girl, so even at midnight (யாமத்தும்) he thinks of riding the palmyra horse. In 1252 the woman says desire, having no pity, rules her heart at its work even at midnight (யாமத்தும் ஆளும் தொழில்). Both use midnight, when all else rests, as the proof that love allows no rest.
links.reason: யாமத்தும் carries the point in both: படல்ஒல்லா ... என் கண் and நெஞ்சத்தை யாமத்தும் ஆளும் தொழில்; midnight as proof that love gives no rest, from the man and from the woman.

links.note: 71 asks whether there is a bolt that can shut love in (அன்பிற்கும் உண்டோ அடைக்குந்தாழ்), since the small tears of the loving make it known. 1138 says காமம் breaks through secrecy and appears in public. The Book of Virtue says of அன்பு what the Book of Love says of காமம்: neither can be kept hidden, and each publishes itself.
links.reason: அன்பிற்கும் உண்டோ அடைக்குந்தாழ் ... பூசல் தரும் and காமம் மறையிறந்து மன்று படும் say the same of அன்பு and காமம்: neither stays hidden.

links.note: In 1139 the woman's love, thinking 'not everyone knows' (அறிகிலார் எல்லாரும் என்றே), goes reeling through the street (மறுகின் மறுகும்). In 1180 she says the town easily learns the secret of those whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). In both the secret is given away by the lover herself and not by the town: by her love going about in 1139, by her eyes in 1180.
links.reason: In 1139 her காமம் itself மறுகின் மறுகும்; in 1180 her அறைபறை கண் give the மறை to the ஊரார்: in both she, not the town, is the source of the disclosure.

links.note: 877 advises not telling one's pain to those who do not know it (நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு). 1140 shows the reason from inside: those who have not suffered what the speaker suffered (யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா) laugh at her in plain sight. The statecraft maxim and the lover's complaint agree that pain gets no hearing from those who have not felt it.
links.reason: நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு நோவற்க (877) is about those who do not know of one's hurt, in a counsel against showing weakness; யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா ஆறு (1140) is about those who have not suffered the same. The note merges 'do not know' with 'have not felt', so the agreement is looser than stated.

links.note: In 1140 the woman says the unknowing laugh where she can see, because they have not undergone what she has (யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா ஆறு). In 1219 she says those who blame him for not being gracious in waking life are those who have not seen a lover in dreams (காதலர்க் காணாதவர்). Both explain the town's judgement by its lack of the lover's experience.
links.reason: 1140 யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா ஆறு and 1219 கனவினால் காதலர்க் காணாதவர் both explain others' mockery or blame by their not having had the experience; 'the town' is loose since commentators name the friend or other women.

links.note: 1141 says that because gossip has risen the precious life holds on (அலரெழ ஆருயிர் நிற்கும்). 1213 says the woman's life exists because she sees in dreams the one who gives nothing in waking life (காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர்). In each a lover's life is kept going by something that only stands in for the beloved: the town's talk in one, a dream in the other.
links.reason: அலரெழ ஆருயிர் நிற்கும் and கனவினால் காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர்: in each the life is held up by a stand-in for the beloved, gossip or dream.

links.note: 1141 says life stays because the gossip has risen. 1263 says the woman still exists by longing for his return (வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்). Both verses name the one thing that keeps life from leaving; in 1141 it comes from outside, from the town, and in 1263 from her own hope.
links.reason: அலரெழ ஆருயிர் நிற்கும் and வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன் each name the one thing that keeps life from leaving.

links.note: In 1142 the man says the town, not knowing how hard the flower-eyed woman is to reach (அருமை அறியாது), has given him gossip (அலரெமக்கு ஈந்தது). In 1150 the speaker says the town is raising the very talk 'we want' (யாம்வேண்டும் கெளவை எடுக்கும் இவ்வூர்). Both treat the town's gossip as an unintended service; Parimelazhagar reads ஈந்தது as help given, and reads 1150 as the friend counting on it.
links.reason: அலரெமக்கு ஈந்தது in 1142 and யாம்வேண்டும் கெளவை எடுக்கும் இவ்வூர் in 1150 both treat the town's gossip as something given to or wanted by the lovers, within the same chapter.

links.note: In 1143 the man says the gossip the town knows is like having obtained what he has not obtained (பெறாஅது பெற்றன்ன நீர்த்து). In 1213 the woman sees in dreams the man who gives nothing in waking life, and lives by it. Both take a substitute for union as if it were union: public talk for him, a dream for her.
links.reason: பெறாஅது பெற்றன்ன நீர்த்து (gossip) and கனவினால் காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர் (dream) both take a stand-in for union as sustaining.

links.note: In 1144 the man says his love thrives through gossip (கவ்வையால் கவ்விது காமம்) and without it would lose its nature and go slack. In 1147 the woman says the town's gossip is manure and her mother's words water to 'this sickness' (நீளும் இந்நோய்). Both say gossip feeds love; he calls what grows காமம் and welcomes it, she calls it நோய்.
links.reason: கவ்வையால் கவ்விது காமம் and ஊரவர் கௌவை எருவாக ... நீளும் இந்நோய் both say gossip feeds love, he naming it காமம் and she நோய்.

links.note: 1145 takes drinking as the model for love: each exposure makes love sweeter as each bout makes drink wanted. 1281 says being intoxicated at a thought and glad at a sight belong to love and not to liquor (கள்ளுக்கில் காமத்திற்கு உண்டு). So the likeness in 1145 has a limit the book itself states: liquor works only when drunk, love without contact.
links.reason: 1145 models love on drink (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால்); 1281 marks where the likeness ends (உள்ளக் களித்தலும் காண மகிழ்தலும் கள்ளுக்கில் காமத்திற்குண்டு).

links.note: In 1146 the woman saw him one day only, and the gossip has spread like the serpent seizing the moon (திங்களைப் பாம்புகொண்டற்று), which Parimelazhagar glosses as spreading everywhere. 957 says a fault in the well-born shows high, like the spot on the moon in the sky (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல்). Both use the moon as the thing whose blemish everyone sees: a brief event or a small fault becomes public because of where it sits.
links.reason: 'திங்களைப் பாம்புகொண்டற்று' and 'மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து' both use the moon's blemish as what everyone sees; Parimelazhagar's 'உலகமெங்கும் பரந்தது' supports the note.

links.note: 1147 makes the sickness of love a crop, manured by gossip and watered by a mother's words, that grows long (நீளும் இந்நோய்). 1227 makes the same இந்நோய் a flower that buds in the morning and opens in the evening. In both the woman describes her lovesickness as a plant with its own growth, fed in 1147 and timed in 1227.
links.reason: எருவாக ... நீராக நீளும் இந்நோய் (1147) and காலை அரும்பி ... மாலை மலரும் இந்நோய் (1227) both figure இந்நோய் as a growing plant, crop and flower.

links.note: 1144 says love thrives by gossip and would droop without it. 1148 puts the same point as a rebuttal of those who expect gossip to end the affair: it is ghee on fire. 1148 gives the image and the opposing view that 1144's plain statement lacks.
links.reason: கவ்வையால் கவ்விது காமம் is restated as நெய்யால் எரிநுதுப்பேம் ... கெளவையால் காமம் நுதுப்பேம். 1148 adds the image and the opposing view.

links.note: 1148 says that to think of putting out love with gossip is like thinking to put out fire with ghee (நெய்யால் எரி நுதுப்பேம்). 1260 asks whether those whose hearts are like fat put in fire (நிணம் தீயில் இட்டன்ன) can say they will hold out in a sulk. Both use fat meeting fire for love: in 1148 the fat feeds the fire, in 1260 the heart is the fat that melts.
links.reason: நெய்யால் எரி நுதுப்பேம் (1148) and நிணந்தீயில் இட்டன்ன நெஞ்சு (1260) both use fat meeting fire for காமம், with the difference the note states: fuel in one, the melting heart in the other.

links.note: In 1149 the woman asks whether she can be ashamed at gossip (அலர்நாண ஒல்வதோ) now that he has left her. In 1297 she says she has forgotten even shame (நாணும் மறந்தேன்), caught in a heart that cannot forget him. In both her shame gives way, in 1149 because his leaving has made it pointless and in 1297 because her own heart overrides it.
links.reason: அலர் நாண ஒல்வதோ and நாணும் மறந்தேன்: in both her நாண் gives way, with the different causes the note states (நீத்தக்கடை / மடநெஞ்சிற் பட்டு).

links.note: 1150 says the town is raising the gossip 'we want' (யாம்வேண்டும் கெளவை), and the lover will grant what is asked if he wishes. In 1143 the man asks whether the gossip the town knows is not his to have, since it is like gaining what he has not gained. Both sides welcome the talk: for him it stands in for union, and in 1150, on Parimelazhagar's reading, it is the ground for asking him to take her away.
links.reason: யாம்வேண்டும் கெளவை and உறாஅதோ ஊரறிந்த கெளவை both welcome the town's talk, for different reasons that the note states correctly, including Parimelazhagar's elopement reading of 1150.

links.note: Both open with the same words, மறைப்பேன்மன் ('I would hide it'), and both say the attempt fails: in 1161 the pain rises like spring water under baling, in 1253 desire shows itself without her intending it, like a sneeze (குறிப்பின்றித் தும்மல்போல்). Read together, one figure says concealment makes it grow and the other that it escapes her will altogether.
links.reason: Both open மறைப்பேன்மன் and both say concealment fails (ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்; தும்மல்போல் தோன்றி விடும்).

links.note: 1162: she cannot hide the sickness, and telling it to the one who caused it brings shame (உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்). 1200: she tells her heart that it means to tell its pain to one who is not close (உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய்) and might as well fill up the sea. Parimelazhagar reads both as about sending him word; 1200 adds futility to the shame that 1162 gives as the obstacle.
links.reason: 1162 நோய் செய்தார்க்கு உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும் and 1200 உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய் கடலைச் செறாஅஅய் both concern telling him the pain; 1200 adds futility, and Parimelazhagar does frame both around sending word.

links.note: 1017: those ruled by shame give up life for shame and do not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்). 1163 shows that ranking from inside: she drops neither love nor shame, and it is her life, the pole (உயிர் காவா), that takes the strain; Parimelazhagar adds that the life will snap.
links.reason: 1163 keeps both காமம் and நாண் hanging on உயிர் as the காவு, so life bears the strain rather than shame being dropped, which is 1017's நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் seen from within.

links.note: 10: the great sea of birth is swum by those who reach the Lord's feet and not by others (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்); Parimelazhagar supplies the feet as the raft. 1164: the sea of love exists and the raft to swim it does not (அது நீந்தும் ஏமப்புணை). The same structure of a sea crossed only with a support appears in the first chapter and in a separated woman's complaint.
links.reason: பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர் and காமக் கடல் ... அது நீந்தும் ஏமப் புணை இல் share the sea-that-must-be-swum figure with a needed support; the note correctly marks the raft in 10 as Parimelazhagar's supply.

links.note: 1165: she asks what those who bring grief in friendship would do as enemies; Parimelazhagar says this is aimed, in a sulk, at the friend who has not sent a message. 805 advises that when friends do something hurtful (நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின்) it should be understood as folly or as great intimacy. 805 offers the charitable reading that her question refuses.
links.reason: நட்பினுள் துயர்வரவு ஆற்றுபவர் and நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின் do meet on hurt from a friend, but a lover's sulking complaint is not limited or conditioned by 805's maxim, so qualifies does not fit and the tie is thin.

links.note: 629: one who does not crave the pleasure within pleasure does not come to pain within pain (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்). 1166: the pleasure of love is a sea and its pain when it afflicts is larger still (துன்பம் அதனிற் பெரிது). The woman's experience fits the link between relishing pleasure and suffering pain that 629 states as a rule in the Book of Wealth.
links.reason: 629 ties suffering to craving (இன்பம் விழையாதான்); 1166 only compares sizes (இன்பம் கடல் ... துன்பம் அதனிற் பெரிது) and does not link her pain to having relished. The fit is suggestive, not stated.

links.note: 1137 speaks of suffering a love like the sea (கடலன்ன காமம் உழந்தும்) and praises womanhood that still does not mount the palmyra horse. 1166 uses the sea twice over: love's pleasure is a sea, and when it afflicts (அடுங்கால்) the pain is greater than that. The sea is the book's measure for love, and 1166 says the measure is exceeded.
links.reason: கடலன்ன காமம் (1137) and இன்பம் கடல் ... துன்பம் அதனிற் பெரிது (1166) both measure love by the sea, and 1166 says the pain exceeds that measure. The note describes both verses accurately.

links.note: Both lovers are awake at midnight, with the same word யாமத்தும். The man in 1136 says his eyes will not close and even at midnight he thinks of mounting the palmyra horse; the woman in 1167 says that even at midnight she alone is there (யானே உளேன்), swimming without sight of shore. Sleeplessness in the dead of night is given to both sides.
links.reason: The shared யாமத்தும் and the sleeplessness are real, but neither verse makes a claim the other repeats: 1136 is about resolving on மடலூர்தல் and 1167 about being alone in a shoreless flood, so this is a shared motif and not agreement.

links.note: 1164 says the sea of love exists and there is no raft to swim it. 1167 continues the figure: she has swum the fierce flood (காமக் கடும்புனல் நீந்தி) and sees no shore (கரை காணேன்), and at midnight there is only herself. The second verse turns the missing raft into an actual, endless swim.
links.reason: 1164: காமக் கடல் exists and there is no ஏமப் புணை to swim it; 1167: காமக் கடும்புனல் நீந்திக் கரைகாணேன். The same figure continues in the same chapter from the missing raft to the shoreless swim.

links.note: 1168: the night has put all living beings to sleep and, she says with pity (அளித்து), has no companion but her. 1222: she tells the evening it looks sad-eyed (புன்கண்ணை) and asks whether its partner is as hard as hers. In both she treats a time of day as a fellow sufferer and puts her own state onto it; Parimelazhagar says as much of 1222.
links.reason: Real shared figure: the night pitied as having no துணை but her (அளித்திரா) and the evening addressed as புன்கண்ணை with a வன்கண் துணை. But both are the same speaker in the same domain of separation, so it is a shared personification, not a pattern carried to another domain.

links.note: Both use the phrase கொடியார் கொடுமை, 'the cruelty of the cruel one', for the absent man. In 1235 her shoulders, their old beauty faded, declare it; in 1169 she uses it as the measure the long nights exceed (கொடுமையின் தாம் கொடிய). 1169 moves the charge of cruelty from the man to the time itself.
links.reason: The exact phrase 'கொடியார் கொடுமை' opens both; 1235 has the shoulders declare it (உரைக்கும்) and 1169 uses it as the comparative base ('கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய... இரா'), as the note says.

links.note: 1169: the nights that pass so long these days (நெடிய கழியும் இரா) are crueller than the cruel one's cruelty. 1269: for those who pine with a set day of return in mind, one day passes like seven (ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல்). Both say that time stretches for the one who waits.
links.reason: நெடிய கழியும் இரா and ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல் செல்லும் both say time lengthens for the one waiting in separation.

links.note: In 1167 she herself swims the fierce flood of love and sees no shore; in 1170 it is her eyes that swim in flood water (வெள்ளநீர் நீந்தல), which is her tears. The chapter's water figure for love ends as literal water in the eyes.
links.reason: காமக் கடும்புனல் நீந்தி and வெள்ளநீர் நீந்தல ... என் கண் reuse the swimming figure within one chapter, first for love and then for her tear-flooded eyes.

links.note: 1170: if her eyes could go where he is as her heart does (உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின்), they would not be swimming in a flood of tears. 1244 turns the wish into a request: heart, take the eyes along when you go (கண்ணும் கொளச்சேறி), for they consume her in wanting to see him. Both rest on the idea that the heart can travel to him and the eyes cannot.
links.reason: 1170 'உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின் ... என் கண்' and 1244 'கண்ணும் கொளச்சேறி நெஞ்சே' share the conceit that the heart can go to him and the eyes cannot; the second makes it a request.

links.note: 1091 (the man): her kohl-lined eyes hold two looks, one that gives the sickness and one that is its cure (நோய்நோக்கு ... மருந்து). 1171 (the woman): her own eyes showed him to her and so she came to know an unabating sickness (தண்டாநோய்), and she asks why they weep. Eyes are the source of love's sickness in both, the other's eyes for the man and her own for the woman, and only his verse has a cure.
links.reason: தண்டாநோய் தாம்காட்ட (her own eyes) and நோய்நோக்கு ... மருந்து (her eyes on him) both make eyes the source of love's நோய்; the note's contrast is accurate.

links.note: 1171: she asks why her eyes weep, since they showed him to her (தாம் காட்ட யாம் கண்டது). 1244: the eyes consume her in their wish to see him (அவர்க்காணல் உற்று). In both she speaks of her eyes as agents apart from herself, with wants of their own that she pays for.
links.reason: தாம் காட்ட யாம் கண்டது (1171) and இவை என்னைத் தின்னும் அவர்க்காணல் உற்று (1244) both set the eyes (தாம்/இவை) apart from the speaker (யாம்/என்னை) as agents whose wants she suffers for.

links.note: 535: one who slipped by not guarding beforehand will grieve afterwards over his own error (முன்னுறக் காவாது ... பின்னூறு இரங்கிவிடும்). 1172: the eyes that looked without foresight now toil in misery (பைதல் உழப்பது). Parimelazhagar's comment on 1172 uses the same terms, that those who do not guard against what is coming can only bear it when it arrives.
links.reason: முன்னுறக் காவாது ... பின்னூறு இரங்கிவிடும் and தெரிந்துணரா நோக்கிய ... பைதல் உழப்பது share the pattern of no foresight then grief. Parimelazhagar on 1172 does use முன்னே வருவதறிந்து அது காவாதார்க்கு.

links.note: 792: the friendship of one who does not take it after examining again and again ends in grief that kills him (ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான் கேண்மை). 1172, on Parimelazhagar's reading: the eyes looked that day without examining and understanding what would follow (தெரிந்துணரா நோக்கிய) and now suffer. The rule about forming ties without scrutiny is applied to a look. Manakkudavar reads the first phrase differently, as having looked with knowledge.
links.reason: On Parimelazhagar's reading தெரிந்துணரா நோக்கிய is looking without examining, which matches ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான் கேண்மை; the note states the dependence and reports Manakkudavar's opposite reading (தெரிந்து உணர்ந்து நோக்கிய) correctly.

links.note: 1173: the eyes looked hastily of themselves (கதுமெனத் தாம் நோக்கி) and now weep of themselves, which is laughable. 435: the life of one who does not guard before a fault comes is destroyed like straw before fire (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்). Parimelazhagar explains the laughter in 1173 with that same phrase: it is laughable to those who guard before it comes.
links.reason: 1173 'கதுமெனத் தாநோக்கித் தாமே கலுழும்' is acting without forethought and then suffering, the pattern of 435 'வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்'; Parimelazhagar's gloss on 1173 does use 'வருமுன்னர்க் காப்பார்க்கு நகை விளைவிக்கும்'.

links.note: 1140: the ignorant laugh where she can see it (நகுப அறிவில்லார்), because they have not suffered what she has. 1173: she finds her own eyes' plight fit to be laughed at (நகத்தக்கது உடைத்து). Laughter at a lover's suffering comes from outsiders in one verse and from the sufferer herself in the other.
links.reason: நகுப அறிவில்லார் in 1140 and இது நகத்தக்கது உடைத்து in 1173 both make her suffering a matter for laughter, from outsiders and from herself; a real if light link.

links.note: 320: all pain falls on those who caused pain (நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம்). 1174: the eyes that fixed an inescapable sickness in her (உய்வில்நோய் என்கண் நிறுத்து) have themselves dried up and cannot weep. Parimelazhagar reads 1174 in these terms: having done her harm first, harm came to them of itself.
links.reason: நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம் is acted out in 1174, where the eyes that fixed உய்வில்நோய் in her are themselves நீருலந்த; Parimelazhagar's comment supports this.

links.note: 1166 says love's pain, when it afflicts, is greater than the sea (அதனிற் பெரிது). 1175 repeats the measure as an epithet, a love-sickness the sea cannot hold (கடலாற்றாக் காமநோய்), and goes on to assign blame for it to her eyes.
links.reason: துன்பம் அதனிற் (கடலின்) பெரிது becomes the epithet கடலாற்றாக் காமநோய், and 1175 then blames என் கண்.

links.note: 1173 finds it laughable that the eyes looked of themselves and weep of themselves. 1176 goes a step further: it is sweet (ஓஒ இனிதே) that the eyes which gave her this sickness have fallen into it too (தாஅம் இதற்பட்டது). The sequence moves from mockery of her eyes to satisfaction at their suffering.
links.reason: Within one chapter, இதுநகத் தக்கதுடைத்து about the eyes escalates to ஓஒ இனிதே ... கண் தாஅம் இதற்பட்டது; the mockery-to-satisfaction sequence is in the Tamil.

links.note: 1174 reports that the eyes have dried up and cannot weep (நீருலந்த). 1177 wishes exactly that on them: may the eyes that longed and melted to see him suffer on until their inner water is gone (உள்நீர் அறுக). What one verse states as their condition the other pronounces as a curse.
links.reason: நீருலந்த உண்கண் (1174) states what உள்நீர் அறுக (1177) wishes on the same eyes, within one chapter.

links.note: 1179: when he does not come the eyes do not sleep, and when he comes they do not sleep (வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின் துஞ்சா). 1295: the heart fears not having him and, having him, fears parting (பெறாஅமை அஞ்சும் பெறின் பிரிவு அஞ்சும்). The same two-sided bind is said of the eyes and of the heart, and Parimelazhagar explains 1179 by the fear of parting that 1295 names.
links.reason: வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின்துஞ்சா and பெறாஅமை அஞ்சும் பெறின்பிரிவு அஞ்சும் have the same two-sided bind, and Parimelazhagar glosses 1179's second half with பிரிவஞ்சி.

links.note: 1180 (the woman): the town can easily learn the secret of those whose eyes are beaten drums. 1271 (the man): though she hides it, her kohl-lined eyes go beyond her control (கரப்பினும் கையிகந்து) and have something to tell. Both lovers say her eyes disclose what she means to conceal.
links.reason: அறைபறை கண்ணார் அகத்து மறை and கரப்பினும் கையிகந்து ... உண்கண் உரைக்கல் உறுவது: in both her eyes tell what she hides, once in her voice and once in his.

links.note: 1160 speaks, with irony, of the many who agree to the hard thing, endure the parting and live on afterwards (அரிதாற்றி ... பிரிவாற்றிப் பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்); Parimelazhagar glosses அரிது ஆற்றி as consenting to the parting. 1181 is the woman who did consent (நல்காமை நேர்ந்தேன்) and now cannot bear the result. Read together, 1181 shows the cost of the consent that 1160 doubted anyone could really give.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar glosses அரிதாற்றி as consenting to the parting, and 1181's நல்காமை நேர்ந்தேன் is a woman who consented and now shows the cost in her பசப்பு.

links.note: In 1162 she cannot hide the sickness, and telling the one who caused it brings shame (உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்). In 1181 the question widens to யார்க்கு உரைக்கோ, to whom can I tell it at all, because she herself agreed to his going; Parimelazhagar adds that telling a self-made sorrow would itself be blame. The pair traces how the possible hearers for her complaint run out.
links.reason: 1162 உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும் (telling him shames) and 1181 யார்க்கு உரைக்கோ after நல்காமை நேர்ந்தேன்; the narrowing of possible hearers is in the Tamil.

links.note: 1182 has the pallor ride over her body with the pride of saying 'he gave me' (அவர்தந்தார் என்னும் தகையால்). 1183 uses the same verb of giving for an exchange: he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor (நோயும் பசலையும் தந்து). The pallor that boasts of being his gift in one verse is entered as his payment in the next.
links.reason: அவர்தந்தார் என்னும் தகையால் (1182) and நோயும் பசலையும் தந்து (1183) both make the பசப்பு his gift, as a boast and then as கைம்மாறு in an exchange.

links.note: 211 says obligation wants no return, கைம்மாறு வேண்டா கடப்பாடு, and points to the rain, which the world cannot repay. 1183 uses the same word bitterly: as கைம்மாறு for the grace and modesty he took, he gave sickness and pallor. The word that names the return a good giver does not ask for is here the name of a bad bargain.
links.reason: கைம்மாறு வேண்டா கடப்பாடு and கைம்மாறா நோயும் பசலையும் தந்து use the same word, once for the return a giver does not ask and once ironically for a bad exchange.

links.note: 1125 and 1184 open with the same words, உள்ளுவன் மன்யான். The man in 1125 says he would remember her qualities if he ever forgot them, and he does not know forgetting; the woman in 1184 says she thinks of him and yet turns pale. The same claim of constant thought is his proof of love and her complaint that such thought gives no protection.
links.reason: Identical opening உள்ளுவன் மன்யான் in both; his மறப்பறியேன் is a proof of love, her கள்ளம் பிறவோ பசப்பு a complaint that thinking of him does not stop the pallor.

links.note: In 1184 she thinks of him and speaks only of his merits (உள்ளுவன் ... உரைப்பது அவர்திறம்), and calls it deceit (கள்ளம்) that the pallor comes all the same. In 1250 she tells her heart that by keeping in it the man who left, she will lose still more beauty (இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின்). 1250 states as cause and effect what 1184 finds baffling: the faithful thinking does not hold the pallor off.
links.reason: 1184 உள்ளுவன் ... கள்ளம் பிறவோ பசப்பு finds the pallor's arrival a trick despite her faithful thinking; 1250 நெஞ்சத்து உடையேமா இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின் names keeping him in the heart as the cause of the loss.

links.note: In 1277 her bangles understood before she did that the lord of the shore had parted from her (நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). In 1185 the pallor spreads while he is still in sight. Both make the body register the parting faster than the mind or the facts do; 1277 pushes it to before the event.
links.reason: உவக்காண் செல்வார், இவக்காண் பசப்பூர்வது and நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை both have the body register the parting ahead of the mind, with 1277 going further.

links.note: 1185 points there to the lover going and here to the pallor spreading (உவக்காண் ... இவக்காண்); Parimelazhagar takes it as an earlier occasion when he had gone only a short way. 1278 says he left only yesterday and her body has been pale seven days (நெருநற்றுச் சென்றார் ... எழுநாளேம் மேனி பசந்து). One verse measures the pallor's speed in space and the other in time.
links.reason: உவக்காண் ... இவக்காண் பசப்பூர்வது and நெருநற்றுச் சென்றார் ... எழுநாளேம் பசந்து both say the pallor outruns the parting, one by distance and one by days; Parimelazhagar's 'earlier occasion' (பண்டும்) is reported correctly.

links.note: 285 describes those who, with goods in view, watch for another's lapse (பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார்), and denies them a loving nature. 1186 gives pallor the same posture: it watches for the weak moment (அற்றம் பார்க்கும்), which Parimelazhagar notes is a figurative use of 'watch'. The book's picture of the thief waiting for inattention is the picture the woman uses for what takes her colour.
links.reason: முயக்கற்றம் பார்க்கும் பசப்பு and பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார் share the posture of watching for a lapse; Parimelazhagar does call பார்க்கும் an இலக்கணைச் சொல் at 1186.

links.note: 1186 is the woman's account: pallor watches for a gap in her husband's embrace (முயக்கற்றம் பார்க்கும்) as darkness watches for a lamp to fail. 1238 is the man's memory of the same thing: he loosened the arms that held her and her forehead turned pale (முயங்கிய கைகளை ஊக்கப் பசந்தது). The two speakers confirm each other from either side of the embrace.
links.reason: முயக்கற்றம் பார்க்கும் பசப்பு and முயங்கிய கைகளை ஊக்கப் பசந்தது state the same fact, pallor at the first slackening of the embrace, from the woman's and the man's side.

links.note: In 1187 she lay embracing him, shifted a little (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன்), and at once the pallor was thick enough to scoop up. In 1239 the man recalls that a cool breeze cutting between them in the embrace (முயக்கிடைத் தண்வளி போழ) was enough to pale her eyes. Both verses, from the two partners, set the threshold of separation at the smallest physical gap.
links.reason: புடைபெயர்ந்தேன் அவ்வளவில் ... பசப்பு and முயக்கிடைத் தண்வளி போழப் பசப்புற்ற both make the smallest gap in an embrace enough for pallor.

links.note: 1188 complains that the talk fixes on her pallor and not on his leaving. 1190 says it is good to get the name of pallor, provided they do not spread talk of his unkindness (நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்); Parimelazhagar sets it as her reply when the friend has blamed him. The complaint of 1188 should therefore not be read as a wish to have him blamed: in 1190 she accepts the very imbalance she resents.
links.reason: 1188 complains that none say துறந்தார் அவர்; 1190 calls பசப்பெனப் பேர்பெறுதல் good provided நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின், and Parimelazhagar's setting (her reply after the friend blamed him) is as the note reports. 1190 does limit how 1188 should be read.

links.note: 1188 says people say only 'she has grown pale' and no one says 'he left her' (துறந்தார் அவர் என்பார் இல்). In 1220 the townspeople do say he has left her in waking life (நனவினால் நம்நீத்தார் என்பர்), and she answers that they must not see him in dreams. These are speeches at different moments, but together they show her objecting both when the town blames only her and when it blames him.
links.reason: The contrast is real (துறந்தார் அவர் என்பார் இல் against நம்நீத்தார் என்பர்), but neither verse limits the other; they are separate complaints at different moments, as the note admits, so 'qualifies' does not fit.

links.note: 1181 puts the consent on herself: நல்காமை நேர்ந்தேன், I agreed to his absence. 1189 names him as the one who brought her to agree (நயப்பித்தார்) and says let her body pale as it will if he stands well; Parimelazhagar reads நன்னிலையர் as free of fault, while Manakkudavar reads the condition as his suffering too. On Parimelazhagar's reading the two verses share out the responsibility and she keeps the cost.
links.reason: நல்காமை நேர்ந்தேன் (I agreed) against நயப்பித்தார் (he made me agree), with பசக்க/பசந்த in both; the two commentators' readings of நன்னிலையர் are reported correctly.

links.note: In 1189, on Parimelazhagar's reading, she accepts the pallor so long as the man who persuaded her is held blameless. In 1236 her arms thin and her bangles slip, and what pains her is hearing him called cruel (அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). In both she ranks his good name above her own wasting.
links.reason: 1189: பசக்கமன் பட்டாங்கென் மேனி if நயப்பித்தார் நன்னிலையர் ஆவர், which Parimelazhagar takes as his being held good; 1236: what hurts is கொடியர் எனக்கூறல். The note marks the dependence on Parimelazhagar for 1189 correctly.

links.note: 1190 hopes that her pallor can be talked of without his நல்காமை being talked of. In 1232 the friend says her pale, weeping eyes themselves seem to tell of the unkindness of the one she desired (நயந்தவர் நல்காமை சொல்லுவ போலும்). The same word நல்காமை shows the limit of her wish: the pallor is itself the report against him.
links.reason: 1190 accepts பசப்பு if they do not broadcast his நல்காமை; in 1232 the பசந்து பனிவாரும் கண் themselves நல்காமை சொல்லுவ போலும், so the pallor defeats the condition.

links.note: 1190 says being named for her pallor is good if people do not broadcast his unkindness (நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்). 1236 says the hurt is in hearing him called cruel (கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து), more than in the slipping bangles. Both verses make the talk against him, and not her own disfigurement, the thing she cannot bear.
links.reason: 1190 accepts the name பசப்பு if நல்காமை தூற்றார்; 1236 says the pain is அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து as bangles slip. In both the talk against him weighs more than her own wasting.

links.note: 1108, spoken in union, says the close embrace is sweet to two who desire each other (வீழும் இருவர்க்கு இனிதே). 1191, spoken in separation, says those loved by the ones they love (தாம்வீழ்வார் தம்வீழப் பெற்றவர்) have the stoneless fruit. Both place love's sweetness in the desire being mutual, using the same verb வீழ்; one says it from inside and the other from outside.
links.reason: Both rest sweetness on mutual desire with the same verb: தாம்வீழ்வார் தம்வீழப் பெற்றவர் and வீழும் இருவர்க்கு இனிதே.

links.note: 598 says those without drive never reach the pride of saying 'we are generous' (வள்ளியம் என்னும் செருக்கு). 1193 says the pride of saying 'we shall live' (வாழுநம் என்னும் செருக்கு) suits only those loved by the ones they love. The same construction makes a justified pride depend on a prior condition: inner drive in the one case, being loved in return in the other.
links.reason: வாழுநம் என்னும் செருக்கு and வள்ளியம் என்னும் செருக்கு share a distinctive quoted-pride construction, each tied to a prior condition (வீழப்படுவார்; உள்ளம்).

links.note: 1191 says those loved by the ones they love have 'obtained' (பெற்றவர் பெற்றாரே) love's stoneless fruit; Parimelazhagar ties the word to earlier good deeds. 1194 gives the negative: even those who are esteemed are கெழீஇயிலர் if the one they love does not love them, which Parimelazhagar glosses as lacking good deeds and Manakkudavar as being without what they desire. The pair states the same condition from both sides, and shows the commentators reading it as fortune and not merit.
links.reason: The positive and negative statement of the same condition (தாம்வீழ்வார் தம்வீழப் பெற்றவர் / வீழப்படாஅர் எனின்) is real, but the closing claim overreaches: only Parimelazhagar brings in நல்வினை, which is karmic merit, while Manakkudavar just glosses கெழீஇயிலர் as விருப்பமில்லாராவர், so 'the commentators' reading it as 'fortune and not merit' is not accurate.

links.note: 1195 asks what the one she loves can do for her when he has no love for her (தாம்காதல் கொள்ளாக் கடை). 1245 asks her heart whether a man who does not respond when she draws near (உற்றால் உறாஅதவர்) can be dropped as one who hates her (செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ). The second speech limits the first: finding no benefit in an unreturned love does not make her able to give it up.
links.reason: 1195's நமக்கெவன் செய்பவோ ... தாம்காதல் கொள்ளாக் கடை finds no benefit, and 1245's செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ denies that this lets her give him up.

links.note: 118 praises being level like the scale-beam and not leaning to one side (ஒருபால் கோடாமை) as the ornament of the worthy. 1196 applies the same test to love: borne on one end (ஒருதலையான்) it hurts, and on both it is sweet. Evenness between two sides is a mark of justice in the Book of Virtue and a condition of happiness here.
links.reason: ஒருதலையான் இன்னாது ... காப்போல இருதலையானும் and சீர்தூக்குங் கோல்போல் ... ஒருபால் கோடாமை both use an evenly loaded beam as the test, of mutual love in one and of impartiality in the other.

links.note: 1252 says the thing called desire has no eye, that is no pity (கண்ணின்று), since it works her heart even at midnight. 1197 asks whether Kaman, who stays and acts on one person only, does not see her pain and misery (காணான்கொல்). The complaint moves from the feeling to the god, and both use sight as the test of his mercy.
links.reason: கண்ணின்று (no eye/pity) of காமம் in 1252 and காணான்கொல் காமன் in 1197 both frame pitilessness as not seeing; a real development from feeling to god.

links.note: In 1308 the man asks what use suffering is when there is no lover who knows 'this one is suffering' (அஃதறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி). In 1197 the woman asks whether Kaman fails to see her suffering. Both speakers treat pain as needing a witness, and each finds the one who ought to notice absent.
links.reason: காணான்கொல் காமன் and அஃதறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி do share unnoticed suffering, but in 1197 Kaman is the one-sided afflicter (ஒருவர்கண் நின்றொழுகுவான்) who would stop if he saw, not a witness whose absence makes pain pointless as in 1308; 'pain needs a witness' fits only 1308.

links.note: 1198 calls hard those who live without receiving a sweet word from the beloved (இன்சொல் பெறாஅது). 1199 defines how little would count: though he gives no grace, any report of him is sweet to her ears (அவர்மாட்டு இசையும் இனிய செவிக்கு). Parimelazhagar reads இசை as any word at all, even that he is not coming, and links the two verses on that basis; Kalaignar takes இசை as his praise.
links.reason: இன்சொல் பெறாஅது (1198) and அவர்மாட்டு இசையும் இனிய செவிக்கு (1199): Parimelazhagar does read இசை as யாதானும் ஓர் சொல், even that he will not come, and Kalaignar as புகழ் உரை.

links.note: In 1213 her life continues because in dreams she sees the man who gives no grace in waking life (நனவினால் நல்காதவரை). In 1199 the man who gives no grace (நல்கார் எனினும்) still sweetens her ears by any word of him. In both she is sustained by a substitute for his presence, a dream or a report, while saying outright that he withholds himself.
links.reason: நல்கார் எனினும் and நல்காதவரை name the same withholding, and in each she lives on a substitute: இசை to the ear in 1199, கனவினால் காண்டல் in 1213.

links.note: 1164 says the sea of love exists and the raft to cross it does not (காமக் கடல் ... ஏமப் புணை இல்). 1200 tells the heart to fill up the sea (கடலைச் செறாஅஅய்) instead of telling its pain to the unloving; Pope takes this sea as her own sorrow, while Parimelazhagar takes it as the sea that torments her. On Pope's reading the two verses share the sea as the measure of her grief, with crossing it and filling it both out of reach.
links.reason: Both have கடல், but in 1200 கடலைச் செறாஅய் is filling the sea as an impossible task (the sea that torments her, in both commentators), not a sea of sorrow; the link holds only on Pope's added 'own sea (of sorrow)', which the Tamil does not contain.

links.note: Both verses turn on the word உள்ளினும். In 1201 the man says remembering gives unending joy (தீராப் பெருமகிழ்); in 1207 the woman says that even while she remembers, her heart burns (உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்), which Parimelazhagar explains as the separation burning her despite the memory. These are two speakers in two moods, so it is a limit on the first claim and not a contradiction in the book's teaching.
links.reason: உள்ளினும் carries opposite results: தீராப் பெருமகிழ் in 1201 and உள்ளம் சுடும் in 1207; the note rightly frames it as two speakers and a limit, not a contradiction.

links.note: 1201 (the man, for Parimelazhagar) says love is sweeter than toddy because it gives great joy that does not end even when only thought of (உள்ளினும் தீராப் பெருமகிழ்). 1281, spoken by the woman, makes the same comparison: elation at a thought and delight at a sight belong to love and not to toddy (கள்ளுக்கு இல் காமத்திற்கு உண்டு). The pairing shows the same judgment given from both sides of the couple, built on the same verb உள்ளுதல்.
links.reason: உள்ளினும் தீராப் பெருமகிழ் ... கள்ளினும் காமம் இனிது (1201) and உள்ளக் களித்தலும் ... கள்ளுக்கில் காமத்திற்குண்டு (1281) make the same toddy/love comparison on the same verb உள்ளுதல், from the two speakers.

links.note: 1202 says love is sweet in every way since no pain comes from thinking of the one you love (நினைப்ப வருவதொன்று இல், as the commentators read this edition's garbled line). In 1209 the woman's dear life is wasting because she thinks hard on his lack of tenderness (அளியின்மை ஆற்ற நினைந்து). The pairing shows that the sweetness of 1202 depends on what is remembered: the shared days, not the present neglect. Manakkudavar in fact reads 1202 as conditional, 'if no pain comes'.
links.reason: நினைப்ப வருவதொன்று இல் is limited by அளியின்மை ஆற்ற நினைந்து விளியுமென் இன்னுயிர்: what is remembered decides whether memory is sweet; the note flags the garbled line and Manakkudavar's conditional reading correctly.
links.text_issue: 1202 is garbled: எனைத்தொனறு ஏனிதேகாண் for எனைத்தொன்று இனிதேகாண், and the ending is printed ஏல் where Parimelazhagar reads இல்.

links.note: 1202 claims that thinking of the beloved brings no pain. In 1296 the woman says that when she sat alone and thought (தனியே இருந்து நினைத்தக்கால்), her heart stayed only to eat her (என்னைத் தினிய); Parimelazhagar specifies that what she thought of was his cruelties. The two speeches mark out the cases in which remembering comforts and in which it wounds.
links.reason: நினைப்ப வருவதொன்று இல் (no pain from remembering) is limited by தனியே இருந்து நினைத்தக்கால் என்னைத் தினிய இருந்ததென் நெஞ்சு; Parimelazhagar's அவர் கொடுமைகளை supports the note's distinction between the two cases.
links.text_issue: 1202 is garbled: எனைத்தொனறு ஏனிதேகாண் for எனைத்தொன்று இனிதேகாண், and the ending is printed ஏல் where Parimelazhagar reads இல்.

links.note: 1204 asks whether she too is in his heart, since he is always in hers (யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர்நெஞ்சத்து). 1205 gives the answer as an accusation: he has put a guard on his heart against her (தம்நெஞ்சத்து எம்மைக் கடிகொண்டார்) and yet comes unceasingly into hers. Manakkudavar reads 1205 as the woman, having doubted, now deciding that he does not think of her.
links.reason: யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர்நெஞ்சத்து (1204) is answered by தம்நெஞ்சத்து எம்மைக் கடிகொண்டார் (1205); Manakkudavar does say she doubted and then concluded he does not think of her.

links.note: 1205 complains that he keeps her out of his heart while entering hers without pause (எம்நெஞ்சத்து ஓவா வரல்). 1291 states the same imbalance to her own heart: his heart stays his (அவர்நெஞ்சு அவர்க்காதல்), so why is hers not hers? In 1205 she blames him for the unequal exchange, and in 1291 she blames her own heart.
links.reason: தம்நெஞ்சத்து எம்மைக் கடிகொண்டார் ... எம்நெஞ்சத்து ஓவா வரல் and அவர்நெஞ்சு அவர்க்காதல் ... நீ எமக்கு ஆகாதது state the same one-sided traffic between two hearts, blamed first on him and then on her own heart.

links.note: 1206: she exists only by remembering the days she had with him (உற்றநாள் உள்ள உளேன்), and asks what else she could live by. 1213: her life exists because she sees in dreams the man who gives nothing in waking (கனவினால் காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர்). Both make survival in separation depend on a mental substitute for his presence, memory by day and dream by night.
links.reason: உற்றநாள் உள்ள உளேன் (1206) and கனவினால் காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர் (1213) both make her survival depend on a mental stand-in for him.

links.note: 1206 says she lives by looking back at the days of union (உள்ள உளேன்). 1263 says she still lives by longing for his return (வரல் நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்). The same verb உளேன் is supported in one verse by the past and in the other by the expected future; Parimelazhagar on 1206 notes that the other supports, such as a messenger from him, are missing.
links.reason: உற்றநாள் உள்ள உளேன் and வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன் rest the same உளேன் on memory and on hope; Parimelazhagar on 1206 does say other supports are lacking.
links.text_issue: 1206 reads அவரொடி யான்; should be அவரொடு யான்.

links.note: 1207 says that even as she remembers, her heart is burned (உள்ளம் சுடும்). 1159 describes the same burning as a property of love's sickness: fire burns only when touched, and cannot burn when one moves away as love does (விடிற்சுடல் ஆற்றுமோ தீ). 1159 gives the general paradox of a fire that burns at a distance, and 1207 shows it at work inside memory.
links.reason: 1159's விடிற்சுடல் ஆற்றுமோ தீ gives the general figure of love burning at a distance where fire cannot, and 1207's உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும் is that burning at work in memory during separation.

links.note: In both verses the woman rejects the idea of forgetting him, which Parimelazhagar says the friend had advised in each case. 1207 asks what she would become if she forgot (மறப்பின் எவனாவன்); 1262 answers concretely that if she forgot today (இன்று மறப்பின்) her beauty would go and the bangles slip from her arms. Remembering hurts, but both verses hold that forgetting would be worse.
links.reason: மறப்பின் எவனாவன் in 1207 and இன்று மறப்பின் ... கலங்கழியும் காரிகை நீத்து in 1262 both refuse forgetting; Parimelazhagar's framing of 1262 as a reply to the friend's advice is in the packet.

links.note: 1199 says that though the one she longs for gives nothing (நல்கார் எனினும்), even a word about him is sweet to her ear. 1208 measures what an ungiving lover leaves her more sharply: his whole gift (சிறப்பு) is that he does not object to being thought of. Parimelazhagar takes 1208 as scorn of the friend's promise that he will come and be kind, whereas Manakkudavar takes the not-being-angry as real grace.
links.reason: நல்கார் எனினும் ... இசையும் இனிய and எனைத்து நினைப்பினும் காயார் அனைத்தன்றோ ... சிறப்பு both count the least thing from an ungiving lover as his gift, and 1208 is the sharper. The commentators' split (இகழ்வது vs அருள்) is reported correctly.

links.note: The verses share the words நினை and காய். In 1208 the woman says that however much she thinks of him he is not angry (எனைத்து நினைப்பினும் காயார்), and that this is all the honour he does her. In 1320 the man reports that when he merely sits thinking and looks at her she is angry (நினைத்திருந்து நோக்கினும் காயும்) and asks whom he is thinking of. The absent lover tolerates everything because he is not there to care, while the present one is questioned about every thought.
links.reason: எனைத்து நினைப்பினும் காயார் and நினைத்திருந்து நோக்கினும் காயும் share நினை and காய் in mirrored constructions (also அனைத்து); the contrast between the absent man's indifference and the present woman's jealousy is fairly drawn.

links.note: 1170 says that if her eyes could go where he is, as her mind does (உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின்), they would not be swimming in tears. 1210 looks for a way round that limit: on Parimelazhagar's reading, since both of them look at the moon, her eyes meet his there (கண்ணினால் காண). Manakkudavar reads it differently, as a complaint that the moon will not set and let her sleep and see him in a dream.
links.reason: 1170 regrets that her eyes cannot go உள்வழி as her உள்ளம் does, and Parimelazhagar's note on 1210 (the two pairs of eyes meeting on the moon, கண்ணினால் காண) is as the note reports, with Manakkudavar's alternative given.

links.note: In 1211 the dream arrives as the carrier of his message (காதலர் தூதொடு வந்த கனவு). In 1212 she wants to use the dream in the other direction: if her eyes would sleep, she would herself declare to him that she survives (உயலுண்மை சாற்றுவேன்). Parimelazhagar says this is spoken when she was thinking of sending a messenger, and that she would tell him in full what she would hold back from one.
links.reason: தூதொடு வந்த கனவு and துஞ்சின் கலந்தார்க்கு உயலுண்மை சாற்றுவேன் make the dream a channel in each direction; Parimelazhagar's தூது விடக் கருதி and தூதர்க்குச் சொல்லாது அடக்குவன are reported correctly.

links.note: Both verses end on the word விருந்து, a feast. In 1211 the woman (for Parimelazhagar) asks what feast she can make for the dream that came bringing her lover's messenger (யாதுசெய் வேன்கொல் விருந்து). In 1268 the man, away on the king's work, looks forward to the evening feast at home once the king has won (மாலை அயர்கம் விருந்து). The real feast waits on his return, and meanwhile she can offer hospitality only to a dream.
links.reason: Both close on 'விருந்து': 'கனவினுக்கு யாதுசெய் வேன்கொல் விருந்து' and 'மாலை அயர்கம் விருந்து'; the feast-for-a-dream against the feast-on-return is a meaningful shared figure (the note follows Parimelazhagar's speaker for 1268; Manakkudavar gives it to the woman).

links.note: 1212 makes everything depend on a condition: if her eyes would sleep when she begs them (யானிரப்பத் துஞ்சின்). 1179 says why the condition fails: her eyes do not sleep when he does not come and do not sleep when he does (வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின்துஞ்சா). Set beside chapter 122, this shows that the dream which consoles her in the following verses is not available to her at will.
links.reason: 1212 is a conditional wish (யானிரப்பத் துஞ்சின்) and 1179 a complaint that the eyes never sleep (வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின்துஞ்சா); they are not the same claim, and 1179 supplies why 1212's condition fails, which is a develops relation.

links.note: 1198 says no one in the world is harder than those who go on living without getting even a kind word from the one they love (வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்). 1213 has the woman living on though he gives her nothing in waking life (நனவினால் நல்காதவரை), and explains it: her life exists because she sees him in dreams (கனவினால் காண்டலின்). The second verse answers the first's charge of hardness by naming what keeps her alive.
links.reason: 1198 calls those who வாழ்வார் without an இன்சொல் the hardest; 1213 says உண்டென் உயிர் only because கனவினால் காண்டலின், which accounts for her surviving his நல்காமை.

links.note: 1170 regrets that her eyes cannot travel to where he is as her mind can. In 1214 the dream does the travelling: it seeks out the man who gives nothing in waking life and brings him (நல்காரை நாடித் தரற்கு), and so there is pleasure in the dream. Parimelazhagar spells it out: the dream goes to the country he went to, finds him and delivers him.
links.reason: 1170 laments that her eyes cannot go உள்வழி as the mind does; in 1214 the dream நாடித் தரற்கு, and Parimelazhagar says it goes to the land he went to and brings him. A real answer to the earlier wish.
links.text_issue: The Parimelazhagar entry for 1170 in the packet is truncated at its start.

links.note: 1201 says love gives a joy that does not end even in recollection (உள்ளினும் தீரா). 1215 says that what she saw in waking was sweet then, and the dream too is sweet just while it is seen (கண்ட பொழுதே இனிது). Manakkudavar glosses both pleasures as lasting for that moment; Parimelazhagar takes her point to be that dream and waking are therefore equal for her. On either reading the woman's sweetness is tied to the moment of seeing, where the man's persists in thought.
links.reason: உள்ளினும் தீராப் பெருமகிழ் (joy persisting in thought) is set against கண்ட பொழுதே இனிது (sweet only while seen); the note reports both commentators' glosses of 1215 fairly.

links.note: 1169 calls the long nights of separation crueller than the cruel man himself (கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய). 1216 wants the night's state never to end, with waking itself abolished (நனவென ஒன்றில்லை ஆயின்). The difference is sleep: the night is an enemy when she lies awake and a refuge when it brings the dream, and Parimelazhagar accordingly has her call waking a villain (பாவி).
links.reason: 1216 opposes நனவு to கனவு and does not mention night, so 'wants the night's state never to end' is the note's inference; the contrast with 1169's கொடிய ... நெடிய கழியும் இரா is real but looser than a qualification.
links.text_issue: 1169 begins with a stray '>' character.

links.note: In 1216 the woman says that if there were no such thing as waking, her lover would not leave her in the dream (கனவினால் காதலர் நீங்கலர் மன்). In 1329 the man, in the middle of a lovers' quarrel, wishes the night would lengthen so that he can go on pleading (நீடுக மன்னோ இரா). Both wish away the end of the night and both close on the wistful particle மன்; hers is said of a dream meeting and his of a real one.
links.reason: 1216 wishes away waking (நனவென ஒன்றில்லை ஆயின்), not the night's end, and 1329 ends on இரா, not மன்; the shared மன் and a loosely similar wish are thin, and both verses are in the same domain.

links.note: 819, on bad friendship, says the tie with those whose deeds are one thing and words another is bitter even in a dream (கனவினும் இன்னாது). In 1217 the lover who gives nothing in waking life hurts her in her dreams as well (கனவினால் ... பீழிப்பது). Both take the dream as the last place a person's unreliability should reach, and both find that it reaches there: one verse in the book of polity, the other in a lover's complaint.
links.reason: கனவினும் இன்னாது is an 'even in a dream' intensifier, while 1217's dream is an actual visitation set against நனவு; the shared கனவு is real but the note's common theme of unreliability reaching into dreams is overstated.

links.note: The two verses open with nearly the same words, நனவினால் நல்காதவரை and நனவினால் நல்காக் கொடியார், and reach opposite verdicts on the dream. In 1213 seeing him in dreams keeps her alive; in 1217 she asks why the cruel one torments her in dreams (எம்மைப் பீழிப்பது). Parimelazhagar places 1217 after she has woken and found him gone, so the dream comforts while it lasts and wounds once it has ended.
links.reason: Near-identical openings (நனவினால் நல்காதவரை / நனவினால் நல்காக் கொடியார்) with opposite verdicts on the dream: காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர் versus என்எம்மைப் பீழிப்பது; Parimelazhagar's setting for 1217 (விழித்துழிக் காணாளாயினாள்) is reported correctly.
links.text_issue: 1217 கனவனால் is a misprint for கனவினால்.

links.note: Both verses describe the same event: he is with her in sleep and gone on waking. In 1217 this is his cruelty; Parimelazhagar explains the torment as his being on her shoulder in the dream and vanishing when she wakes. In 1218 she tells it in his favour: asleep he is on her shoulder (தோள்மேலர்), and awake he hurries into her heart (நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர் விரைந்து), so he never leaves her at all. Parimelazhagar says 1218 is her defence of him after the friend had spoken against him.
links.reason: Same dream event valued oppositely: 1217 கனவினால் என்எம்மைப் பீழிப்பது versus 1218 துஞ்சுங்கால் தோள்மேலர் ... விழிக்குங்கால் நெஞ்சத்தர்; Parimelazhagar's settings are reported correctly.
links.text_issue: 1217: 'கனவனால்' is a typo for கனவினால்.

links.note: 1218 says that on waking he quickly becomes one who is in her heart (நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர்). 1249 tells her own heart that the lover is inside it (உள்ளத்தார் காதலவர்), so there is no one to go out looking for. Both use his dwelling in her heart to deny that he is absent; 1218 adds the dream so that both night and day are covered.
links.reason: 1218 விழிக்குங்கால் நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர் and 1249 உள்ளத்தார் காதலவர் both use his dwelling in her heart to deny his absence, matching Parimelazhagar's reading of 1218.

links.note: The two verses have the same construction: an opinion is held only by those who lack an experience. In 66, 'the flute is sweet, the lute is sweet' is said by those who have not heard their own children's prattle (மழலைச்சொல் கேளாதவர்). In 1219 those who blame the man for giving nothing in waking life are those who have not seen a lover in dreams (கனவினால் காதலர்க் காணாதவர்). Parental love in the first book and a lover's dream in the third both discredit a judgment by pointing to what its holders have not known.
links.reason: Both end on a negative participial noun naming those who lack the experience (கேளாதவர், காணாதவர்) and attribute a mistaken judgment to them; the construction is the same across two books.

links.note: 1236: with bangles and arms slackening, what pains her is hearing him called cruel (அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). 1219 goes from that pain to a rebuttal: those who blame him (நோவர்) are people who have not seen a lover in their dreams. Parimelazhagar gives both verses the same occasion, the friend speaking ill of the man, and says she puts her reply in 1219 on strangers out of displeasure with the friend.
links.reason: Both answer the friend's blame of the man: 1236 'அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து', 1219 'நல்காரை நோவர் ... காணாதவர்'; Parimelazhagar gives both the same occasion, as the note says.

links.note: 326 calls Death 'the life-eating' (உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று) and says it does not advance on the days of one who does not kill. 1221 gives the same epithet, உயிருண்ணும், to the evening that comes on women parted from their husbands. The pairing shows the woman addressing evening in the book's own language for Death; Parimelazhagar's note on 1229 says she thinks of evening as கூற்றம்.
links.reason: உயிருண்ணும் qualifies கூற்று in 326 and the evening hour in 1221, and Parimelazhagar on 1229 does say she speaks of evening 'கூற்றமாகக் கருதி'.

links.note: 334 says what shows itself as a 'day' (நாளென ஒன்றுபோற் காட்டி) is a blade that saws through life (உயிர் ஈரும் வாள்), for those who perceive it. 1221 has the parted woman tell the hour it is not evening (மாலையோ அல்லை) but a thing that eats the life of those once wed (உயிருண்ணும் வேலை; Parimelazhagar takes வேலை as a final hour, Manakkudavar and Kalaignar as a spear). Both unmask a unit of time as something that consumes life, one as a general truth of impermanence, the other as one lover's experience of separation.
links.reason: நாளென ஒன்றுபோற் காட்டி உயிர் ஈரும் வாள் (334) and மாலையோ அல்லை ... உயிருண்ணும் வேலை (1221) both unmask a unit of time as a consumer of உயிர்; the note reports the வேலை readings correctly.

links.note: 1223 says the evening that used to come budding with chill and looking wan (பனி அரும்பிப் பைதல்கொள் மாலை) now comes with revulsion budding and sorrow growing (துனி அரும்பித் துன்பம் வளர). 1227 says her sickness buds in the morning (காலை அரும்பி), swells through the day and opens in the evening. Both use அரும்பு, budding, for her pain, and together they give evening as both what brings the bud and when it opens.
links.reason: துனி அரும்பி (1223) and காலை அரும்பி ... மாலை மலரும் (1227) share the budding figure for her pain within the evening chapter.

links.note: 1169 says the long nights now passing are crueller than the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய). 1224 says that where her lover is absent (காதலர் இல்வழி) evening comes like ஏதிலர், pitiless strangers or foes, on a killing ground (கொலைக்களத்து). Both make a stretch of time into a cruel agent set beside human cruelty, and 1224 names the condition: it is so only in his absence.
links.reason: Both make a stretch of time a cruel agent (மாலை கொலைக்களத்து ஏதிலர் போல வரும்; இரா ... கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய), but 1169's இந்நாள் already carries the absence condition the note says 1224 adds, so nothing is developed.
links.text_issue: 1169: stray '>' at the start of the Tamil line.

links.note: 319 states a rule: hurt done to others in the forenoon (முற்பகல்) comes back to oneself in the afternoon (பிற்பகல்), of itself. In 1225 the woman asks what good she did to morning (காலைக்குச் செய்த நன்று) and what enmity she did to evening (மாலைக்குச் செய்த பகை). Her question assumes the same logic of return, that suffering answers something one did, and finds no deed of hers to explain evening's hostility.
links.reason: காலைக்குச் செய்த நன்று / மாலைக்குச் செய்த பகை does presuppose requital, but 319's முற்பகல்/பிற்பகல் are times of return while in 1225 morning and evening are the parties; the link rests on a general idea of desert plus a time-of-day echo.

links.note: In 1258 the woman says the soft speech (பணிமொழி) of her deceiving lover is the weapon that breaks her womanly reserve (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை). In 1228 the herdsman's flute is a weapon that kills (கொல்லும் படை). Both call a gentle sound a படை, one because it draws her to him and the other because it announces the evening without him.
links.reason: ஆயன் குழல் ... கொல்லும் படை and பணிமொழி ... பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை: a gentle sound called a படை in both. Accurate note; the shared figure makes same_image the closer type.

links.note: In 1168 the night has put all living beings to sleep (மன்னுயிர் எல்லாம் துயிற்றி) and she alone is its companion, so her suffering is solitary. In 1229 she says that when evening spreads, bewildering the mind (மதிமருண்டு; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take this as her own mind), the whole town is bewildered and suffers (பதிமருண்டு பைதல் உழக்கும்). The two speeches picture the world around her in opposite ways, asleep and untouched in one and sharing her distress in the other.
links.reason: The contrast is real (மன்னுயிர் எல்லாம் துயிற்றி vs பதிமருண்டு பைதல் உழக்கும்) but one is night and the other evening, so neither limits the other; it is a contrast of moods, not a qualification. The note's claim about Parimelazhagar's reading of மதிமருண்டு cannot be checked: his gloss here is cut off and what survives gives 'என் மதி' as others' reading.
links.text_issue: 1229: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is truncated in this edition (only 'மாலை படர்தரும் போழ்து' and the விளக்கம் remain).

links.note: In 1209 the woman says her dear life is perishing (விளியும் என் இன்னுயிர்) as she thinks much on the lack of kindness of one who said they were not separate. In 1230 her life, which had not died till now (மாயா உயிர்), is dying in the dim evening as she thinks of the man whose nature is wealth (பொருள்மாலையாளரை உள்ளி). Both say that thinking of him is what wears her life away, and each names him by a reproach: his broken word in one, his preference for wealth in the other.
links.reason: உள்ளி ... மாயும் என் மாயா உயிர் and விளியும் என் இன்னுயிர் ... ஆற்ற நினைந்து: in both, thinking of him wears her life away, and பொருள்மாலையாளர் / வேறல்லம் என்பார் are both reproachful namings.

links.note: In 1263 she says he left desiring victory with his own resolve as companion (உரன் நசைஇ உள்ளம் துணையாகச் சென்றார்), and that she still lives by desiring his return (வரல் நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்). In 1230 thinking of the man given to wealth makes her life die. Both name him by the aim he left for, but in one speech the thought of him keeps her alive and in the other it kills; these are two moments of the same speaker, not a doctrine.
links.reason: He is named by his aim in both (பொருள்மாலையாளர்; உரன் நசைஇ ... சென்றார்), and உள்ளி ... மாயும் உயிர் stands against வரல் நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்; the note rightly limits this to two moments of one speaker. 'Victory' for உரன் is Parimelazhagar's gloss, which is acceptable.

links.note: 71 says love cannot be bolted in, because the small tears of the loving make it public (புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்). 1232 says her eyes, pale and running with tears (பசந்து பனிவாரும் கண்), seem to tell of the unkindness of the one she desired (நல்காமை சொல்லுவ போலும்). The same mechanism, tears that disclose, works in both; in 71 they reveal the weeper's love, in 1232 they also accuse the absent lover.
links.reason: புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும் and நல்காமை சொல்லுவ போலும் ... பனிவாரும் கண் both make tears a disclosure; the note marks the difference in what is disclosed.

links.note: In 1180 the woman says the town easily learns the secret of those like her whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). In 1232 the friend says her pale, weeping eyes seem to be telling of his unkindness. Both treat the eyes as announcing what she would keep hidden; the woman says it of herself and the friend says it to urge her to bear up, as Parimelazhagar frames it.
links.reason: அறைபறை கண்ணார் in 1180 and சொல்லுவ போலும் ... கண் in 1232 both make the eyes broadcast what she would hide.

links.note: In 1157 the woman asks whether the bangles slipping past her wrist do not proclaim (தூற்றாகொல்) that the lord of the shore has left her. In 1233 the shoulders that swelled on the day of union (மணந்தநாள் வீங்கிய தோள்) seem to announce fully that he has parted (தணந்தமை சால அறிவிப்ப போலும்). In both her body makes the separation public without her speaking; 1233 adds the contrast with how the same shoulders looked at union.
links.reason: 1157 'துறந்தமை தூற்றாகொல்... வளை' and 1233 'தணந்தமை சால அறிவிப்ப போலும்... தோள்' both have her body announce his departure; 'மணந்தநாள் வீங்கிய' adds the contrast noted.

links.note: In 1277 her bangles understood before she did that the lord of the cool shore had parted (தணந்தமை ... முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). In 1233 her shoulders announce that he has parted, with the same word தணந்தமை. In 1277 the body is first to know of the parting, and in 1233 it is the one that tells others.
links.reason: தணந்தமை is in both, known first by the வளை in 1277 (முன்னம் உணர்ந்த) and announced by the தோள் in 1233 (சால அறிவிப்ப போலும்).

links.note: 1234 and 1235 share the line தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள், shoulders whose old beauty has faded. 1234 describes the loss: with her partner gone (துணை நீங்கி) they have lost their fullness and the bangles slip. 1235 turns the same shoulders into testimony that declares the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும்), so the repeated line moves from description to accusation.
links.reason: Both end தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள்; 1234 describes (பணைநீங்கிப் பைந்தொடி சோரும்), 1235 makes the shoulders testify (கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும்).

links.note: In 1262 the woman tells her friend that if she forgets him today (இன்று மறப்பின்), her beauty will leave her shoulders and her ornaments will slip off (கலங்கழியும் காரிகை நீத்து). In 1234 the beauty has faded and the bangles are slipping because her partner is gone (துணை நீங்கி). Read together, the bodily loss follows his absence whether she remembers or forgets, though in 1262 she holds that remembering is what prevents it.
links.reason: Both have the shoulders losing beauty and the bangles slipping (பைந்தொடி சோரும் ... கவின் வாடிய தோள்; கலங்கழியும் காரிகை நீத்து), but 1234 says nothing about remembering, so 'whether she remembers or forgets' is the note's inference and no qualification is made.

links.note: In 1188 the woman complains that people say only 'she has grown pale' and no one says 'he has left her' (துறந்தார் அவர் என்பார் இல்). In 1235 the wasted shoulders themselves declare his cruelty. One speech says the visible change brings talk about her alone, and the other says the same kind of change speaks against him; the difference is in who is reading the body, the town or the friend.
links.reason: 1188 says none will say துறந்தார் அவர்; 1235 says the wasted shoulders themselves கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும், and Parimelazhagar adds that outsiders will then say it too. The note's contrast holds.

links.note: In 1235 the friend, in Parimelazhagar's reading, says the shoulders with bangles lost and old beauty faded declare the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும்). In 1236 the woman answers that with bangles and shoulders slackening, what pains her is the saying that he is cruel (அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). The second verse limits the first: the body's evidence stands, but she refuses the charge drawn from it.
links.reason: 1236 takes up 1235's own words (தொடியொடு தோள், கொடியார்/கொடியர்) and objects to கொடியர் எனக்கூறல்; Parimelazhagar frames it as her reply to the friend's reproach.

links.note: In 1169 the woman herself speaks of the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமை) when she says the long nights are crueller still. In 1236 she is pained when he is called cruel (கொடியர்).
