The pair shows that she uses the word in her own lament and does not accept it from another's mouth; these are different moments of a dramatised speaker, not a contradiction in teaching.
links.reason: கொடியார் கொடுமை in her own mouth in 1169, and அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து in 1236 (Parimelazhagar: the friend's words). The note describes both correctly and does not overclaim a contradiction.

links.note: In 1162 she says she cannot hide this sickness, and that telling it to the one who caused it brings shame (உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்). In 1237 she asks her heart whether it can gain honour by telling him of her wasting shoulders. The two give opposite values to the same act of telling him, shame in one and possible honour (பாடு) in the other; in 1237 it is the heart and not she herself who would carry the word.
links.reason: 1162 says உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும் of telling the one who caused the pain, while 1237 asks the heart whether it can பாடு பெறுதி by உரைத்து the same thing to him; the note reads both correctly and the shame/honour contrast over one act is real.

links.note: In 1182 the woman says pallor spreads and rides over her body with the pride (தகையால்) that he was the one who gave it. In 1240 the man says the pallor of her eyes felt distress (பருவரல்) on seeing what her forehead had done. Both give the pallor feelings of its own, pride in one and distress in the other, so that பசப்பு is spoken of as a party to the love and not only its symptom.
links.reason: Both personify பசப்பு: in 1182 it rides her body with pride ('தகையால்... மேனிமேல் ஊரும்'), in 1240 it feels distress ('பருவரல் எய்தின்றே'); note accurate.

links.note: 1238 says that when he loosened the embracing arms her forehead turned pale. 1240 says the pallor of her eyes itself came to distress (கண்ணின் பசப்போ பருவரல் எய்தின்றே) on seeing what the bright forehead had done (ஒண்ணுதல் செய்தது கண்டு). 1240 depends on 1238 for what the forehead did; Parimelazhagar explains that the eyes' pallor was abashed that the forehead had paled sooner than they did, at a smaller cause.
links.reason: ஒண்ணுதல் செய்தது கண்டு in 1240 points back to பசந்தது ... நுதல் in 1238, and Parimelazhagar's வெள்கிற்று explanation is as the note reports.

links.note: In 1102 the man says that medicines for other ailments are things other than the ailment (பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிற), but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து). In 1241 the woman, apart from him, asks her heart to think of any medicine at all (எனைத்தொன்றும் ... மருந்து) for her sickness. Read together, 1102 explains why her heart has nothing to offer: the only cure is the absent person who caused the illness.
links.reason: 1102: பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிற, but she is தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து; 1241 asks the heart for any மருந்து for the எவ்வநோய். The mirrored use of நோய்/மருந்து across the two speakers supports the note's reading.

links.note: 1195 asks what those we love can do for us if they do not love in return (தாம் காதல் கொள்ளாக் கடை). 1242 draws the conclusion and turns it on her own heart: since he has no love (காதல் அவரிலர் ஆக), its suffering is folly (நோவது பேதைமை). The first states the uselessness of one-sided love, the second names persisting in it as foolishness.
links.reason: தாம் காதல் கொள்ளாக் கடை ... எவன் செய்பவோ and காதல் அவரிலர் ஆக நீ நோவது பேதைமை state the same point about one-sided love, the second turned on her own heart.

links.note: 1308, which Parimelazhagar gives to the man during a sulk, asks what use suffering is where there is no lover who recognises that one suffers (நோதல் எவன் ... அஃதறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி). 1242 has the woman tell her heart that suffering is folly when he has no love (நோவது பேதைமை). Both speakers, from either side of the relationship, make pain depend for its point on the other's loving awareness of it.
links.reason: காதல் அவரிலராக நீ நோவது பேதைமை and நோதல் எவன் ... அஃதறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி both make suffering pointless without the other's love.

links.note: 1204 asks whether she too is in his heart, since he is always in hers (யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர் நெஞ்சத்து). 1243 gives her own bleak answer: a compassionate thought of her does not exist in the one who caused the sickness (பரிந்துள்ளல் பைதல்நோய் செய்தார்கண் இல்). The question of 1204 has by chapter 125 become a settled premise for scolding her heart.
links.reason: யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர்நெஞ்சத்து is the open question that பரிந்துள்ளல் ... செய்தார்கண் இல் answers in the negative.

links.note: 1243 asks the heart why it sits and suffers in thought (இருந்துள்ளி என் பரிதல்) when he has no pitying thought. 1296 says that when she sits alone and thinks (தனியே இருந்து நினைத்தக்கால்) her heart is there only to eat her (என்னைத் தினிய). Both describe sitting and remembering as self-inflicted harm, and each blames the heart for it.
links.reason: இருந்துள்ளி என்பரிதல் நெஞ்சே and தனியே இருந்து நினைத்தக்கால் என்னைத் தினிய இருந்ததென் நெஞ்சு share sitting-and-thinking as harm centred on the heart.

links.note: 1283 says that though he disregards her and does only as he pleases, her eyes will not rest without seeing him (கொண்கனைக் காணாது அமையல கண்). 1244 says the eyes, wanting to see him (அவர்க் காணல் உற்று), eat her. Both make the eyes an appetite of their own that her judgment of him does not govern.
links.reason: இவை என்னைத் தின்னும் அவர்க்காணல் உற்று and கொண்கனைக் காணாது அமையல கண் both give the eyes a craving of their own to see him; 'her judgment of him' applies only to 1283's பேணாது பெட்பவே செய்யினும்.

links.note: 807, on old friendship, says that those whose bond came by the way of love do not cut off love even when ruinous things are done to them (அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார்). 1245 asks whether she can let him go as an enemy merely because he does not return her closeness. The logic of long friendship in the Book of Wealth, that injury does not license abandonment, reappears as a lover's rhetorical question.
links.reason: அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார் and செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ both refuse to cut a bond of love because of the other's ill treatment; Manakkudavar's கைவிடுதல் இயல்போ supports the note, though Parimelazhagar reads 1245 as lack of strength to leave.

links.note: 1245 asks the heart whether one can abandon as an enemy (செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ) the man who does not respond when she draws close (யாம் உற்றால் உறாஅதவர்). 1292 complains that the heart, even having seen that he is not close (உறாஅதவர்க் கண்ட கண்ணும்), goes to him on the thought that he will not be hostile (செறாஅர் என). The two share the pair உறாதவர் / செறு, and show the same refusal to treat coldness as enmity, once owned by her and once blamed on the heart.
links.reason: The pair உறாஅதவர் with செற்றார்/செறாஅர் recurs in both verses, and in both his not responding is refused the status of hostility, once as her own question and once as a charge against the heart.

links.note: 1286 says that when she sees him she sees no faults, and when she does not see him she sees nothing but faults (காணுங்கால் காணேன் தவறாய காணாக்கால் காணேன் தவறல்லவை). 1246 calls the heart's anger in his absence false because it never survives the sight of him (காதலர்க் கண்டால் புலந்துணராய்). 1286 states the pattern plainly; 1246 uses it to discredit the anger felt while apart.
links.reason: 1286's காணுங்கால் காணேன் தவறாய is the general pattern, and 1246's காதலர்க் கண்டாற் புலந்துணராய் ... பொய்க்காய்வு uses it to call the present anger false.

links.note: 1246 tells the heart that when it sees the lover it cannot even sulk and then be reconciled (புலந்துணராய்), so its present anger is a false heat (பொய்க்காய்வு காய்தி). 1294 makes the same charge: the heart will not first raise a quarrel and then enjoy (துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்), so no one will plan with it. In both the heart is accused of being incapable of the sulk it pretends to.
links.reason: 1246 புலந்துணராய் ... பொய்க்காய்வு காய்தி and 1294 துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய் both charge the heart with being unable to sulk first when it sees him.

links.note: 1247 leaves open which of desire and shame is to go (காமம் விடு ஒன்றோ நாண் விடு). 1251, opening the next chapter, reports the outcome: the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint that shame had bolted (காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் ... நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). The choice she offers her heart in 1247 is settled in 1251 by force, not by decision.
links.reason: 1247 offers the heart a choice (காமம் விடு ஒன்றோ நாண் விடு); 1251 has காமக் கணிச்சி break the நிறை door bolted with நாணுத்தாழ். The same காமம்/நாண் contest is settled by force in the next chapter's opening verse.

links.note: 967, on honour, says that being called ruined is better than living by going behind those who do not accept one (ஒட்டார் பின் சென்று ஒருவன் வாழ்தலின்); Parimelazhagar takes this of following scorners for gain. 1248 calls her heart a fool for going behind the one who left without grace (பிரிந்தவர் பின்செல்வாய் பேதை). The standard of honour from the Book of Wealth is the one she applies to her own heart, though in love she cannot enforce it.
links.reason: பிரிந்தவர் பின்செல்வாய் பேதை mirrors ஒட்டார் பின் சென்று வாழ்தல் in 967; the honour rule about following those who reject you recurs in love. 'She cannot enforce it' is a small addition not in the verse.

links.note: 1248 calls the heart a fool for going after the man who left (பிரிந்தவர் பின்செல்வாய்) while grieving that he gives no grace. 1293 asks the heart whether it follows him as it likes (பெட்டாங்கு அவர் பின் செலல்) because the ruined have no friends. Both speak of the heart 'going behind him' as a desertion of her that she can see but not stop.
links.reason: பிரிந்தவர் பின்செல்வாய் பேதைஎன் நெஞ்சு and நெஞ்சே நீ பெட்டாங்கு அவர்பின் செலல் both reproach the heart for going after him and leaving her, in the two chapters addressed to the heart.

links.note: 1207 says she does not know how to forget, and that even remembering burns her heart (உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்). 1250 says that holding him in her heart will cost her yet more beauty. Both count remembering him as a harm to herself, while 1207 adds that forgetting is not available to her.
links.reason: 1207 does say உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும், but its thrust is மறப்பின் எவனாவன், that forgetting would be worse; 1250 argues the other way, toward not holding him in the heart, so 'same claim' holds only for one clause.

links.note: In 1250 she says that if she keeps in her heart the man who left without coming close (துறந்தாரை நெஞ்சத்து உடையேமா), she will lose still more beauty (இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின்); Parimelazhagar frames this as a case for forgetting him. In 1262 she tells her friend that if she forgets him today, beauty will leave her and the bangles slip from her arms (இன்று மறப்பின் ... கலங்கழியும் காரிகை நீத்து). The two speeches give opposite accounts of whether remembering or forgetting costs her beauty; both are a speaker's words in the moment, and the conflict holds on Parimelazhagar's reading of the settings.
links.reason: 1250 நெஞ்சத்து உடையேமா இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின் makes remembering cost beauty; 1262 இன்று மறப்பின் ... காரிகை நீத்து makes forgetting cost it. The claims are opposed and the note says it depends on the commentator's settings.

links.note: 1167 says she swims the flood of desire and sees no shore, and even at midnight only she is awake (யாமத்தும் யானே உளேன்). 1252 says desire has no pity (கண் இன்று), for it sets her heart to work even at midnight (யாமத்தும் ஆளும் தொழில்). Both mark midnight, when Parimelazhagar notes all others rest, as the hour that shows desire does not release her.
links.reason: யாமத்தும் stands in both (யாமத்தும் ஆளும் தொழில்; யாமத்தும் யானே உளேன்) and Parimelazhagar glosses the hour in each as when everyone else rests (எல்லாரும் தொழிலொழியும் / எல்லோரும் துயிலும்), as the note says.

links.note: 1253 likens desire to a sneeze that appears without one's intending it; Parimelazhagar glosses that it cannot be held in. In 1318 the man does stifle a sneeze (தும்முச் செறுப்ப), and she weeps that he is hiding from her that his people are thinking of him. The sneeze is in both an involuntary sign of what is within, and 1318 shows that even suppressing it is read as a disclosure.
links.reason: Both use the sneeze (தும்மல்போல் தோன்றிவிடும் / தும்முச் செறுப்ப) as something that betrays what one would hide; in 1318 the sign is of others' உள்ளல் rather than of one's own feeling, a small looseness in the note.

links.note: 1180 says it is not hard for the town to get the secret of those like her, whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). 1254 says her desire goes past concealment into the public place (மன்று படும்). 1180 supplies a means by which the exposure described in 1254 happens: her own eyes announce it.
links.reason: 1254: என் காமம் மறையிறந்து மன்றுபடும்; 1180: மறைபெறல் ஊரார்க்கு அரிதன்று for those with அறைபறை கண். Both turn on மறை being lost to the town, and 1180 names the eyes as the means.

links.note: 1245 asks whether she can abandon as hostile (செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ) the man who does not answer her love. 1255 turns that private question into a general statement: not following the hostile (செற்றார் பின் செல்லா) is a dignity unknown to those with love's sickness (காமநோய் உற்றார் அறிவதொன்று அன்று). The word செற்றார் links them, and the second explains why the first could only be a rhetorical question.
links.reason: செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ is answered in general form by செற்றார்பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை காமநோய் உற்றார் அறிவதொன்று அன்று; the shared செற்றார் and the same speaker make the development real.

links.note: In 1168 she calls the night அளித்து, pitiable or kindly, because having put every living thing to sleep it has no companion but her. In 1256 she uses the same word of her grief (அளித்தரோ ... துயர்), which Parimelazhagar takes as scorn. In both she speaks to her tormentor in the language of grace and pity, which is how these monologues voice bitterness.
links.reason: அளித்தரோ (1256) and அளித்திரா (1168) use the same word of grace ironically for what torments her; Parimelazhagar's சால நன்று confirms the scorn in 1256.

links.note: 1255 states in general terms that the lovesick do not know the dignity of not going after one who is hostile. 1256 applies it to herself with irony: how gracious (அளித்தரோ) is this grief, which wants her to go after the one who is hostile (செற்றவர் பின் சேறல் வேண்டி). The pair moves from a maxim about lovers to her own case, and Parimelazhagar reads அளித்து as mockery.
links.reason: செற்றவர் பின் சேறல் வேண்டி repeats செற்றார்பின் செல்லா from the previous verse and turns the maxim on herself; Parimelazhagar's 'சால நன்று' for அளித்து is the mockery the note reports.

links.note: In 1247 she cannot bear desire and shame together and asks her heart to give up one (காமம் விடு ஒன்றோ நாண் விடு). In 1257 the matter is settled in his presence: when he does what she longs for, shame is simply not known to her. The conflict that is unbearable in his absence does not arise once he is there.
links.reason: 1247 cannot bear காமம் and நாண் together; 1257 says நாணென ஒன்றோ அறியலம் when the beloved does what she longs for, so the conflict lapses in his presence.

links.note: 1297 says that, caught up with a foolish heart that cannot forget him, she has forgotten even shame (நாணும் மறந்தேன்). 1257 says she knows nothing of a thing called shame (நாண் என ஒன்றோ அறியலம்) when the one she cherishes does out of desire what she longs for. The two verses give the same loss of shame from two moments, separation in 1297 and reunion in 1257.
links.reason: நாணென ஒன்றோ அறியலம் (1257) and நாணும் மறந்தேன் (1297) give the same loss of நாண் under love; the situations the note assigns follow Parimelazhagar's settings.

links.note: 555 asks whether the tears of those who suffer under a ruler are not the weapon that wears away his wealth (கண்ணீர் அன்றே செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை). 1258 has the same form of question: are his humble words not the weapon that breaks our womanhood (பணிமொழி அன்றோ ... உடைக்கும் படை). In both a soft thing, tears or gentle speech, is named as the real weapon against something that looks strong.
links.reason: Both use the same rhetorical question naming a soft thing as படை: பணிமொழி அன்றோ ... உடைக்கும் படை and கண்ணீரன்றே ... தேய்க்கும் படை.

links.note: 985 says that bowing is the strength of those who accomplish things and the weapon by which the worthy turn their opponents (பணிதல் ... மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). 1258 calls her lover's lowly speech (பணிமொழி) the weapon that breaks her firmness. Humility as a படை is praised in the ethics of the worthy, and in the love poems the woman sees the same device used on her and calls its user a thief.
links.reason: 985 பணிதல் ... மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை and 1258 பணிமொழி ... பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை both call lowliness a படை, in ethics and in the woman's complaint.

links.note: 1259 narrates one occasion: she went away to sulk and embraced him when she saw her heart joining him. 1260 turns it into a general question about people whose hearts melt like fat in fire, and whether 'we will stand in a sulk' (ஊடி நிற்பேம் எனல்) is even open to them. The second verse gives the reason for the first.
links.reason: Adjacent verses: 1259 'புலப்பல் எனச்சென்றேன் புல்லினேன்' is the instance, 1260 'நிணந்தீயில் இட்டன்ன நெஞ்சினார்க்கு உண்டோ ... ஊடி நிற்பேம் எனல்' the general reason.

links.note: 1287 asks what use it is to sulk when one knows the sulk will prove false (பொய்த்தல் அறிந்து என் புலந்து), like those who jump into a stream knowing it will carry them off. 1260 asks whether those with hearts like fat put in fire (நிணம் தீயில் இட்டன்ன நெஞ்சினார்) can ever say they will hold out in a sulk. One image is of being swept away and the other of melting, and both conclude that the sulk cannot be sustained.
links.reason: நிணந்தீயில் இட்டன்ன நெஞ்சினார்க்கு உண்டோ ... ஊடி நிற்பேம் எனல் and பொய்த்தல் அறிந்தென் புலந்து both say a sulk cannot be kept up, through different images.

links.note: In 776 the warrior takes up his days (தன் நாளை எடுத்து) and files every day without a wound as wasted; in 1261 the wife marks off the days of his absence (நாளொற்றி) until her finger wears down. Both keep a ledger of days, the soldier's reckoned by wounds received and the waiting wife's by absence endured.
links.reason: Both reckon days: 776 தன் நாளை எடுத்து (Parimelazhagar: எடுத்து எண்ணி) sorts them by விழுப்புண், and 1261 அவர்சென்ற நாளொற்றி marks them off until the finger wears down.

links.note: 1261 shows the woman's finger worn (தேய்ந்த விரல்) from marking the days since he left (அவர்சென்ற நாளொற்றி); 1269 says that for those pining with the return day in mind (வருநாள்வைத்து ஏங்குபவர்க்கு) one day passes like seven. 1269 gives the felt arithmetic behind 1261's tally: the days she counts are each lived as many.
links.reason: நாளொற்றித் தேய்ந்த விரல் counts the days, and ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல் செல்லும் says how each counted day feels to the one waiting.

links.note: 615 praises the man who wants the work and not pleasure (இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான்) as a pillar to his kin; in 1263 the wife describes her husband as gone desiring victory with his own resolve for company (உரன்நசைஇ உள்ளம் துணையாக), which Parimelazhagar glosses as not desiring enjoyment. 1263 shows the same man from inside the house: she stays alive only by desiring his return (வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்), the same verb நசைஇ set against his.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar glosses உரன்நசைஇ as 'இன்பம் நுகர்தலை நச்சாது வேறலை நச்சி', which matches இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான், and நசைஇ recurs in வரல்நசைஇ as the note says.

links.note: In 1263 she waits for the man who left wanting victory; in 1268, which Parimelazhagar assigns to the man away on the king's service, he wishes the king would engage and win (வினைகலந்து வென்றீக வேந்தன்) so that he can join his wife for the evening. On that reading the pair gives both ends of one separation: her longing for his return and his impatience for the work to finish.
links.reason: உரன்நசைஇ ... சென்றார் வரல்நசைஇ and வினைகலந்து வென்றீக வேந்தன் மனைகலந்து give the two ends of one separation on Parimelazhagar's speaker assignment, which the note states as a condition.

links.note: 476 warns that one who has climbed to the tip of a branch (நுனிக்கொம்பர் ஏறினார்) and pushes further loses his life; in 1264 her heart, thinking of his return, கோடுகொடு ஏறும், which Manakkudavar and Kalaignar read as climbing a tree's branches to look for him (Parimelazhagar reads it as swelling up like a tree putting out branches). On the climbing reading the same image marks reckless overreach in the book on statecraft and eager hope here.
links.reason: The shared tree-climbing image exists only on Manakkudavar's and Kalaignar's reading of கோடுகொடேறும், as the note says; even then 476's point is going past the நுனிக்கொம்பர், and the two uses have little to say to each other.

links.note: In 1170 her heart goes to where he is, and she wishes her eyes could follow (உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின்); in 1264 her heart rises thinking of his return (வரவுள்ளி). Both make the heart the part of her that moves toward him while she stays put; on Manakkudavar's reading of 1264 it even climbs to do the seeing her eyes cannot.
links.reason: 1170 உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின் has the heart go to him; 1264 கோடுகொடேறும் என் நெஞ்சு is a heart moving toward him only on Manakkudavar's tree-climbing reading. On Parimelazhagar's it swells with joy, so 'both' overstates.
links.text_issue: 1264: 'கோடுகொ டேறும்' looks like a contraction or slip for கோடுகொடு ஏறும்.

links.note: In 1187 pallor seizes her the moment she shifts a little in his embrace (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன் அவ்வளவில்); in 1265 she says the pallor on her shoulders will leave once she has seen him to her eyes' fill (கண்ணாரக் கண்டபின் நீங்கும்). Together they give pallor's rule in the Book of Love: it comes with the slightest distance and goes only with his presence, which Parimelazhagar underlines by noting that merely hearing of his return will not do.
links.reason: பசப்பு arrives at புடைபெயர்ந்தேன் அவ்வளவில் (1187) and leaves only கண்ணாரக் கண்டபின் (1265): onset at the least distance, cure only by his presence.

links.note: 1283 says her eyes will not rest without seeing her husband (கொண்கனைக் காணாது அமையல கண்) even though he does as he pleases; 1265 prays to see the same கொண்கன் until her eyes are full. Both make the eyes' need to see him the thing that must be satisfied before anything else can mend.
links.reason: காண்கமன் கொண்கனைக் கண்ணார and கொண்கனைக் காணாது அமையல கண் share the eyes' need to see the கொண்கன் across two chapters; 'before anything else can mend' fits 1265 better than 1283.

links.note: 1101 says all five senses find their objects in her; in 1266 she will 'drink' him (பருகுவன்), which Parimelazhagar explains as drinking that nectar through all five gateways of sense. On his reading 1266 is the woman's version of 1101, with the five-sense enjoyment compressed into a single verb.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar glosses பருகுவன் in 1266 as drinking 'வாயில்கள் ஐந்தானும்', which is exactly the ஐம்புலனும் of 1101, so the note's claim checks out.

links.note: In 1102 the man says that medicine for a disease is normally something else, but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து); in 1266 the woman says that if he comes for one day she will drink him in so that all her sickness is destroyed (பைதல்நோய் எல்லாம் கெட). Each lover names the other as both the cause and the only cure.
links.reason: தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து (1102) and பருகுவன் பைதல்நோய் எல்லாம் கெட (1266): each lover is the other's cure; in 1266 that he is also the cause is implied by the separation, not stated.

links.note: 1109 lists sulking, reconciling and uniting (ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல்) as the rewards of those joined in love; 1267 shows the woman, before he has even returned, unable to choose between sulking and embracing and wondering whether to combine them. What 1109 states as a sequence of pleasures, 1267 shows as one impatient wish for all of them at once, which is how Parimelazhagar explains its place in this chapter.
links.reason: 1109's ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல் becomes 1267's புலப்பேன்கொல் புல்லுவேன் கொல்லோ கலப்பேன்கொல்; Parimelazhagar does explain the விதுப்பு as wanting to do all of them.
links.text_issue: 1267: விரன் is a typo for வரின்.

links.note: 1269 says one day passes like seven (ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல்) for those awaiting the return day; in 1278 she says he left only yesterday (நெருநற்று) and she has been pale for seven days (எழுநாளேம்). Both use seven days to measure how separation distorts time, stretching a day of waiting in 1269 and running ahead of the departure itself in 1278.
links.reason: ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல் and நெருநற்றுச் சென்றார் ... எழுநாளேம் both use seven days for time distorted by separation. The contrast drawn is accurate.

links.note: 71 asks if there is any bolt to shut love in, since the small tears of the loving announce it (புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்); 1271 says her eyes tell something despite her concealment. The claim that affection cannot be locked away and that the eyes give it out appears in the book on virtue as a general truth about அன்பு and in the Book of Love as a scene.
links.reason: The pattern is shared (கரப்பினும் ... உண்கண் உரைக்கல் உறுவது; புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்), but 1271 does not claim that affection cannot be hidden: on Parimelazhagar's setting her eyes give away an unspoken fear, so it is not the same claim.

links.note: 709 says the eye itself tells enmity and friendship (கண்ணுரைக்கும்) to those who know its kinds; in 1271 the man tells her that though she hides it, her eyes have slipped her control and have something to say (உண்கண் உரைக்கல் உறுவது). The minister's skill of reading the eye in the book on statecraft is the lover's skill here, with the same verb உரை for what the eye does.
links.reason: The eye speaks in both with the same verb: 709 கண்ணுரைக்கும், 1271 உண்கண் உரைக்கல் உறுவது; reading the eye moves from statecraft to love.

links.note: 1272 says this girl has a great measure of womanly nature (பெண்நிறைந்த நீர்மை பெரிது), which Parimelazhagar takes as artlessness beyond the usual; 1280 says that telling love's sickness with the eyes and pleading is womanhood added to womanhood (பெண்ணினால் பெண்மை உடைத்து). The chapter's first observation about her is given its content at the end: her womanliness is her saying it with the eyes and not in words.
links.reason: The shared term is real (பெண்நிறைந்த நீர்மை / பெண்ணினால் பெண்மை உடைத்து), but Parimelazhagar takes 1272's நீர்மை as excessive மடமை, a different quality from 1280's speaking with the eyes, and 1272 is the chapter's second verse, not its first; 'given its content' overstates.

links.note: 1273 compares her unspoken meaning to a thread that shows through the gems (திகழ்தரு); 1274 compares it to the scent inside a closed bud (முகைமொக்குள் உள்ளது நாற்றம்). Parimelazhagar distinguishes them: the first lies within yet is visible outside, the second is not visible outside at all, so the pair moves from a sign that can be seen to one that can only be inferred.
links.reason: Adjacent similes: Parimelazhagar marks 1273's thread as 'புறத்துப் புலனாம்' and 1274's scent as 'புறத்துப் புலனாகாத', the distinction the note reports.

links.note: 1227 describes love's sickness as budding in the morning (காலை அரும்பி), swelling through the day and flowering at evening; 1274 places an unspoken meaning inside the bud of her smile (நகைமொக்குள்). Both use the bud for a feeling that is already there and has not yet opened, pain in the one and a hidden intention in the other.
links.reason: Both use a bud (முகைமொக்குள்; காலை அரும்பி), but 1274 uses it for something concealed inside while 1227 uses it as the first stage of a day-long opening (போதாகி ... மலரும்); the note's 'not yet opened' reading fits 1274 and only loosely fits 1227.

links.note: 1091 finds two looks in her eyes, one that gives the sickness and one that is its medicine (அந்நோய் மருந்து); 1275 finds in her covert behaviour a medicine that ends great sorrow (உறுதுயர் தீர்க்கும் மருந்து). In both the remedy is not anything she says but something to be read in a sign she gives.
links.reason: மருந்து appears in both, located in a sign and not in speech: her நோக்கு in 1091, her கள்ளம் (concealed hint) in 1275.

links.note: 1092 values the small look her eyes steal (கண்களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம்) at more than half of love; 1275 says her கள்ளம், her stealth, contains a medicine. Theft is the figure for her indirect signalling in both, at first meeting in 1092 and after reunion in 1275.
links.reason: கண்களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம் (1092) and செய்திறந்த கள்ளம் (1275) both use stealth (களவு/கள்ளம்) for her covert signal that he prizes; the shared figure is meaningful.

links.note: 1275 says the stealth with which she acted and withdrew (செய்திறந்த கள்ளம்) holds a medicine for great sorrow; 1279 states what she did (அஃதாண்டவள் செய்தது): she looked at her bangles, her shoulders and her feet. Parimelazhagar ties the two explicitly, taking 1279's அஃது to point back to 1275, so that the silent gesture is the 'stealth' and its meaning, going with him, is the cure.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar on 1279 explicitly refers அஃது back to செறிதொடி செய்திறந்த கள்ளம் (1275), so the tie is textual and not the proposer's invention.

links.note: 827 warns not to take an enemy's bowing words at face value, because a bow's bending signals harm (வில்வணக்கம் தீங்கு குறித்தமையான்); in 1276 the woman reads his unusually great tenderness (பெரிதாற்றிப் பெட்பக் கலத்தல்) as a sign of coming absence. The same inference, that excess of kindness points to its opposite, is advice about false friends in one book and a wife's reading of her husband in the other, though she alleges no enmity.
links.reason: A real likeness in reading a kind gesture as a sign of harm, but 827 argues from known enmity (ஒன்னார்கண் சொல்வணக்கம்), not from excess, and in 1276 the tenderness (பெரிதாற்றிப் பெட்பக் கலத்தல்) is sincere. 'Excess of kindness points to its opposite' fits only 1276.

links.note: 1277 says her bangles knew of his parting before she did; 1278 says her body has been pale for seven days though he left only yesterday. The two adjacent speeches make the same point with different signs: her body responds to his intention to leave before the leaving is an acknowledged fact.
links.reason: நெருநற்றுச் சென்றார் ... எழுநாளேம் மேனி பசந்து and முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை both show her body responding before the parting is a fact; Parimelazhagar reads both this way.

links.note: 1093 reports a wordless act and reads it: she looked, and having looked bowed her head (நோக்கினாள் நோக்கி இறைஞ்சினாள்), and that (அஃது) was water poured on their bond; 1279 reports that she looked at her bangles, her shoulders and her feet, and that (அஃது) is what she did there. Both verses consist of a sequence of looks followed by அஃது, leaving the meaning to be drawn from the gesture, at courtship in 1093 and at the threat of parting in 1279.
links.reason: நோக்கினாள் நோக்கி இறைஞ்சினாள் அஃது and தொடிநோக்கி ... அடிநோக்கி அஃது share the sequence of looks summed up by அஃது; both are in the love book, so same_image fits better than parallel_domain.

links.note: 1234 describes separation's effect: the shoulders lose their fullness and old beauty and the bangles slip (பைந்தொடி சோரும்… தோள்); in 1279 she looks at bangles and soft shoulders (தொடிநோக்கி மென்தோளும் நோக்கி) and then at her feet. Read with 1234, her first two glances name what will happen if she is left, and the third, as Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take it, names her alternative of walking with him.
links.reason: தொடிநோக்கி மென்தோளும் நோக்கி in 1279 names exactly what 1234 says separation does (பைந்தொடி சோரும் ... வாடிய தோள்), and the commentators read அடிநோக்கி as her intent to go along.

links.note: 1053 says that even asking has a beauty of its own (இரப்புமோர் ஏஎர் உடைத்து) when done before those who know their duty and do not withhold; 1280 says her asking (இரவு), done with the eyes, has a womanliness of its own (பெண்மை உடைத்து). The word for begging is the same, and both grant it a grace under conditions, though the chapter on begging means alms and 1280 means a lover's plea.
links.reason: இரப்பும் ஓர் ஏஎர் உடைத்து and கண்ணினால் ... இரவு பெண்மை உடைத்து share the word and the 'asking has a grace' construction, and the note states the difference in sense.

links.note: 1137 says nothing has greater worth than womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and still does not mount the palmyra horse (மடலேறாப் பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்கது இல்); 1280 says that telling love's sickness with the eyes and pleading (கண்ணினால் காமநோய் சொல்லி இரவு) is womanhood upon womanhood. Both praise as specifically womanly the refusal to declare desire openly, 1137 by what she will not do and 1280 by the silent means she uses instead.
links.reason: மடலேறாப் பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்கது இல் (1137) and கண்ணினால் காமநோய் சொல்லி ... பெண்மை உடைத்து (1280) both praise as womanly the refusal to declare desire openly.

links.note: In 1281 love is set above liquor: it delights at a thought and a look, which liquor cannot do. In 1288, in the same chapter, his chest is itself like liquor to those who have got drunk on it (களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே), wanted though it does shameful harm (இளித்தக்க இன்னா செயினும்). The chapter uses the one image both ways, first to say love exceeds drink and then to say it compels like drink.
links.reason: Within one chapter கள்ளுக்கில் காமத்திற்குண்டு ranks love above liquor and களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே then likens his chest to it despite இளித்தக்க இன்னா: one image used both ways, as stated.

links.note: 433 says those ashamed of blame treat a fault as small as a millet as if it were a palmyra (தினைத்துணையாங் குற்றம்... பனைத்துணையாக் கொள்வர்). 1282 uses the same two measures in the other direction: with love as large as a palmyra, even a millet of sulking over his fault is to be avoided. In 433 the small fault is magnified; in 1282 the small grievance is to be dropped.
links.reason: Both pair தினைத்துணை with பனைத்துணை: 433 magnifies a millet-sized குற்றம் to a palmyra, 1282 forbids even a millet of ஊடல் when காமம் is palmyra-sized. The shared measure is distinctive and used in opposite directions.

links.note: 1302 says sulking is like salt in the right amount and is spoiled only by being prolonged a little (உப்பமைந் தற்றால் புலவி). 1282 says that when love is full to a palmyra's measure, not even a millet of sulking is wanted (தினைத்துணையும் ஊடாமை வேண்டும்). Read together, 1282 states a condition, காமம் நிறைய வரின், under which the measured sulk that 1302 recommends falls to nothing; Parimelazhagar takes 1282 as the woman voicing her own haste in the form of general advice.
links.reason: 1302 allows புலவி in the measure of salt, and 1282's தினைத்துணையும் ஊடாமை வேண்டும் under காமம் நிறைய வரின் states a condition where even that measure goes; Parimelazhagar's remark on her haste (தன் விதுப்பு) is reported correctly.

links.note: 1257 says she knows nothing of shame when the one she cherishes does, in desire, what she wants (பேணியார் பெட்ப செயின்). 1283 reuses the two words with the sense turned round: even if he does only what he himself wants, without cherishing her (பேணாது பெட்பவே செய்யினும்), her eyes will not rest without seeing him. The second verse removes the condition of the first: her yielding does not depend on his doing what pleases her.
links.reason: பேணியார் பெட்ப செயின் (1257) and பேணாது பெட்பவே செய்யினும் (1283) reuse the same two words with the condition reversed, and her eyes still காணாது அமையல.

links.note: 1246 tells the heart that when it sees the lover it cannot stay in a sulk, so its present anger is false (பொய்க்காய்வு). 1284 is that prediction coming true: she set out to sulk and the heart forgot it and went to unite (அதுமறந்து கூடற்கண் சென்றது).
links.reason: காதலர்க் கண்டால் புலந்துணராய் in 1246 predicts what 1284 reports: ஊடற்கண் சென்றேன் ... அதுமறந்து கூடற்கண் சென்றது என் நெஞ்சு.

links.note: 1284 reports to her friend that her heart forgot the sulk and went to unite. 1294 gives the consequence: since the heart will not first sulk and then enjoy (துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்), who will consult with it about such things again (நின்னொடு சூழ்வார் யார்). The report of the heart's desertion in one chapter becomes the quarrel with the heart in the next.
links.reason: 1284 ஊடற்கண் சென்றேன்...கூடற்கண் சென்றது என் நெஞ்சு and 1294 துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய் describe the same failure of the heart to sulk first; Parimelazhagar on 1294 ties it to புணர்ச்சி விதும்பல், so the consequence reading holds.

links.note: 190 asks what harm could come if people saw their own faults as they see strangers' faults (ஏதிலார் குற்றம்போல் தங்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்). 1285 says she cannot see her husband's fault when he is before her, as the eye cannot see the kohl-stick touching it. In both, what is nearest is what goes unseen; 190 treats this as a failing to correct, and 1285 as a fact about love.
links.reason: கோல்காணாக் கண் is about nearness blinding; 190's ஏதிலார் குற்றம்போல் தங்குற்றம் காண்கிற்பின் is about self versus stranger and says nothing of nearness, so 'what is nearest goes unseen' is the note's abstraction over a thin tie of not seeing a fault.

links.note: 1285 gives the image: the eye does not see the stick that is lining it, and she does not see his blame when she sees him (பழிகாணேன் கண்ட இடத்து). 1286 states the other half that the image implies: when she does not see him she sees nothing but his faults (காணாக்கால் காணேன் தவறல்லவை). Parimelazhagar's gloss on 1285 already supplies this, saying the eye has seen the stick at every other time.
links.reason: 1286's காணாக்கால் காணேன் தவறல்லவை states the converse that 1285's பழிகாணேன் கண்ட இடத்து implies; Parimelazhagar's முன்னெல்லாங் கண்டிருந்தும் on 1285 supports the note.

links.note: 1286: seeing him, she sees no faults; not seeing him, she sees nothing else. In 1297 she calls her heart மடநெஞ்சு, and Parimelazhagar defines that மடமை as exactly this reversal: remembering when he is absent, and forgetting when he is present, faults that ought to be remembered at sight and forgotten in absence. On his reading 1297 names and blames what 1286 only describes.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar's gloss of மடமை in 1297 (remembering faults when unseen, forgetting them when seen) is exactly the reversal 1286 describes in காணுங்கால் காணேன் தவறாய; the note cites it accurately and marks it as his reading.

links.note: 1134: the fierce flood of love carries off the raft of shame and manliness (காமக் கடும்புனல் உய்க்கும்). 1287: why sulk knowing it will prove false, like those who leap into a stream knowing it will carry them off (உய்த்தல் அறிந்து புனல்பாய்பவர்). The same water and the same verb, உய்த்தல், are used by the man of his restraint in 1134 and by the woman of her sulk here.
links.reason: Both have புனல் with the verb உய்த்தல் (உய்க்கும் / உய்த்தல் அறிந்து புனல்பாய்பவர்) for being swept away by love, once of the man's நாண் and நல்லாண்மை and once of the woman's sulk.

links.note: 940: as the gambler loves the game more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல்), the living being loves life more with each suffering. 1288: liquor is wanted by the drunk even as it does them shameful harm, and so is his chest. Both explain an attachment that grows through injury by a vice from the same group of chapters (dice in 940, liquor in 1288).
links.reason: இன்னா செயினும் களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே and இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல் both explain attachment persisting through harm by a vice simile; 'grows' fits 940 literally and 1288 via Parimelazhagar's மேன்மேல் விரும்பப்படுவதாய.

links.note: 1145: as drinking is wanted more each time one gets drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால்), love is sweeter each time it is exposed. 1288: his chest is as liquor is to those who have got drunk on it (களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே), though it does shameful harm. Both take the drinker's returning appetite as the likeness for love; 1288 adds the harm and the shame that 1145 leaves out.
links.reason: களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே and களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால் both use the drinker's returning appetite for love, and 1288 adds இளித்தக்க இன்னா.

links.note: 1289 says few attain love's செவ்வி, its right moment or condition. 1306 gives a figure for missing it on either side: without துனி and புலவி love is like fruit over-ripe or unripe (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று). Parimelazhagar places 1289 in a sulk that will not yield to appeasement, so the fineness it speaks of is the same fineness of timing that 1306 puts in terms of ripeness.
links.reason: சிலர் அதன் செவ்வி தலைப்படுவார் and கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று both concern love's right ripeness; Parimelazhagar sets 1289 in உணர்ப்புவயின் வாரா ஊடல் and uses செவ்வி in glossing 1306.

links.note: 1290 remembers her sulk ending because her eagerness to embrace was greater than his. 1327 states the rule the man later draws: in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses has won, as is seen in the union (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்). Her giving way in 1290 is a case of the defeat that 1327 counts as victory.
links.reason: In 1290 she கண்ணின் துனித்தே and then gave way, புல்லுதல் என்னினும் தான் விதுப்புற்று, which is an instance of 1327's ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார் ... கூடலிற் காணப்படும்.

links.note: 72: the loveless belong wholly to themselves, and the loving belong to others even in their bones (அன்பிலார் எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர்). 1291: his heart is for him (அவர்நெஞ்சு அவர்க்காதல்), so why, heart, are you not for me (நீ எமக்கு ஆகாதது). The woman's complaint is 72's distinction seen from the inside: the one who loves no longer owns her own heart, and the one who does not love keeps his.
links.reason: 72 அன்பிலார் எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர் ... அன்புடையார் ... உரியர் பிறர்க்கு matches 1291 அவர்நெஞ்சு அவர்க்காதல் ... நீ எமக்கு ஆகாதது: the unloving keeps his heart, the loving one has lost hers.

links.note: 1255 says the dignity of not going after one who has turned away (செற்றார்பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை) is something the lovesick cannot know. 1292 shows it: her heart goes to him (சேறி) though it has seen that he is not attached to her. 1255 gives the general statement and 1292 the instance, addressed to the heart that does the going.
links.reason: செறாஅரெனச் சேறி என் நெஞ்சு in 1292 is an instance of what 1255 states generally, the heart going after one who is உறாஅதவர்/செற்றார்; the verbal echo செல்லா/சேறி supports it.

links.note: 752 says everyone scorns those who have nothing and everyone honours the rich (இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்). 1293 has the woman quote the same worldly observation as a saying, கெட்டார்க்கு நட்டார் இல், and ask her heart whether that is why it leaves her and follows him. The pairing shows a hard fact from the chapter on wealth being used in the Book of Love as a taunt, with the woman as the ruined one and her heart as the fair-weather friend.
links.reason: கெட்டார்க்கு நட்டார் இல் is cited as a saying (என்பதோ) and is close kin to இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்; the reuse as a taunt to the heart is real. 'The same observation' is slightly generous (friendless vs scorned).

links.note: 787 defines friendship as turning a friend from ruin and, when ruin comes, sharing the suffering (அழிவின்கண் அல்லல் உழப்பதாம் நட்பு). The saying in 1293, that the ruined have no friends, describes how the world behaves and not what friendship is; by the standard of 787 her heart, which goes after him as it pleases (பெட்டாங்கு அவர்பின் செலல்), has failed as a friend. The woman's question, என்பதோ, shows she is quoting the saying to reproach, not endorsing it.
links.reason: கெட்டார்க்கு நட்டார் இல் என்பதோ (1293) is a quoted saying put as a reproachful question; அழிவின்கண் அல்லல் உழப்பதாம் நட்பு (787) defines friendship by the opposite standard. The note reads both accurately.

links.note: 798 warns against taking the friendship of those who cut away in distress (அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார் நட்பு). In 1293 the one who deserts in distress is her own heart, which cannot be declined as a friend. The verse turns the advice of the friendship chapters into a predicament with no remedy.
links.reason: அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார் நட்பு is exactly what her heart does in கெட்டார்க்கு நட்டார் இல் என்பதோ ... அவர்பின் செலல்; the friendship vocabulary (நட்டார்) is in the verse itself.

links.note: 1260 asks whether those with hearts like fat in fire can say they will hold out in a sulk (புணர்ந்தூடி நிற்பேம் எனல்). 1294 tells the heart that it will not sulk first and enjoy afterwards, so no one will plan such things with it. Both say the intention to sulk cannot survive her own heart; 1294 adds that she will stop consulting it.
links.reason: 1260's உண்டோ புணர்ந்தூடி நிற்பேம் எனல் and 1294's துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய் both say her melting heart defeats any plan to sulk; 1294's இனி ... சூழ்வார்யார் adds the refusal to consult it.

links.note: 1330 says sulking is the pleasure of love, and the pleasure of sulking is to come together and embrace (ஊடுதல் காமத்திற்கு இன்பம்). 1294 has the woman want exactly that order, first make a quarrel and then enjoy (துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்), and complain that her heart will not do it. The book's closing statement of how a sulk should work is, in 1294, a plan she cannot carry out.
links.reason: துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய் is the heart refusing the sequence that 1330 praises (ஊடுதல் ... கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்); the note reads both correctly.

links.note: 293: do not lie about what your heart knows, for after the lie your own heart will burn you (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). 1296: thinking alone, she finds her own heart is there to eat her. In both the tormentor is one's own heart and the setting is solitude with what one knows; 293 makes this the working of conscience, and 1296 gives it as the experience of the abandoned lover, with no fault of hers involved.
links.reason: 293 தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும் and 1296 என்னைத் தினிய இருந்ததென் நெஞ்சு both make one's own heart the tormentor, and the note marks the difference (conscience versus a faultless lover's solitude).

links.note: 1207 says she does not know forgetting, and even remembering burns her heart (உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்). 1296 says that when she sits alone and thinks (நினைத்தக்கால்), her heart consumes her. Both make thinking of him in his absence the source of the pain; in 1207 the heart is what is burned, in 1296 it is what does the harm.
links.reason: நினைத்தக்கால் என்னைத் தினிய இருந்ததென் நெஞ்சு and உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும் both make remembering in his absence the cause of pain, with the heart as victim in one and agent in the other.

links.note: 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame's sake and do not give up shame for life's sake (நாண்துறவார்). In 1297 the woman has forgotten shame because her heart cannot forget him, and Parimelazhagar glosses the shame as dearer to her than life, the valuation of 1017. The pairing sets the rule from the chapter on shame beside a speaker in the Book of Love who holds that rule and reports failing it; it is her confession, not a contrary teaching.
links.reason: நாணும் மறந்தேன் is a lapse from உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால் நாண்துறவார்; Parimelazhagar's என் உயிரினும் சிறந்த நாண் is quoted correctly and the note rightly calls it a confession, not a counter-teaching.

links.note: In 1132 the man says his body and life, unable to bear it, will mount the palmyra horse, with shame set aside (நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து). In 1297 the woman says she has forgotten shame through her heart's inability to forget him. Each sex is shown losing நாண் to love; the man sets it aside to act in public, and the woman finds it gone.
links.reason: 1297 நாணும் மறந்தேன் and 1132 நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து show the woman and the man each losing நாண் to love; the note states both correctly.

links.note: 967 says it is better to be called ruined where one stands than to live by following those who do not accept one (ஒட்டார்பின் சென்றொருவன் வாழ்தலின்). In 1298 the heart, described as loving life (உயிர்க்காதல் நெஞ்சு), counts scorning him as the disgrace and goes on dwelling on him. The chapter on honour ranks honour above life; the heart in 1298 keeps the vocabulary of disgrace (இளிவு) but, out of attachment to life, applies it so as to stay with the one who slighted her. This is the heart's reasoning as she reports it, not a rival doctrine.
links.reason: 967's ஒட்டார்பின் சென்று வாழ்தலின் ... கெட்டான் எனப்படுதல் நன்று is inverted by the உயிர்க்காதல் நெஞ்சு that fears இளிவு yet keeps after one who scorned her; Parimelazhagar's 'இறந்துபட மாட்டாமையானும்' backs the note, which is careful not to call it doctrine.

links.note: 1184: she thinks of him and what she speaks of is his merit (உரைப்பது அவர்திறம்), and still the pallor comes. 1298: her heart thinks of what pertains to him (அவர்திறம் உள்ளும்), judging that to scorn him would be a disgrace. The phrase அவர் திறம் with உள்ளுதல் appears in both; in 1184 it is her own loyal practice that goes unrewarded, and in 1298 it is something her heart does that she stands apart from.
links.reason: The shared அவர்திறம் with உள்ளு- is real but is an ordinary phrase, and it means his merits in 1184 (உரைப்பது அவர்திறம்) and his side in 1298; the contrast the note builds on it is thin.

links.note: 1255 says the dignity of not going after one who has turned away is unknown to the lovesick (செற்றார்பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை). In 1298 her heart reasons the opposite way about where disgrace lies: it thinks that to scorn him would be a disgrace (எள்ளின் இளிவாம் என்று எண்ணி) and so keeps thinking of his side. 1298 shows the lovesick heart not merely ignorant of that dignity, as 1255 has it, but supplied with its own argument from honour for doing without it.
links.reason: 1255 says செற்றார்பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை is unknown to the lovesick; 1298's heart reasons எள்ளின் இளிவாம் என்று எண்ணி and so அவர்திறம் உள்ளும், giving the lovesick heart its own honour-argument; note matches both texts.

links.note: 36 says virtue, done without delay, is the companion that does not die when one dies (பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை). 1299 says that in grief there is no companion if one's own heart is not one. Both verses ask what stays with a person when other support is gone; Book One answers virtue, and the lover's verse names the heart and finds it missing.
links.reason: The link is carried by the word துணை (பொன்றாத் துணை; நெஞ்சந் துணையல் வழி); 36 is about what goes with one at death and 1299 about a lover whose heart will not cooperate in a quarrel, so 'what stays when other support is gone' is a thin common frame.

links.note: 1263 describes the man as having left with his own heart or resolve for companion (உள்ளம் துணையாகச் சென்றார்). 1299 asks who can be a companion in grief when one's own heart is no companion (நெஞ்சந் துணையல் வழி). The heart as துணை is what he had on setting out and, on Parimelazhagar's assignment of 1299 to the man, what he lacks when she will not be reconciled; Manakkudavar gives 1299 to the woman.
links.reason: துணை is shared, but 1263's உள்ளம் is his resolve (ஊக்கம்) on setting out while 1299's நெஞ்சம் is the heart that will not side with its owner; joining them into one story of what he had and then lost is the note's construction, and it holds only on Parimelazhagar's speaker for 1299.

links.note: 1299 asks who will be a companion in grief when one's own heart is not (தாமுடைய நெஞ்சந் துணையல் வழி). 1300 repeats the frame, தாமுடைய நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி, and draws the further step: then it is a small matter that strangers are not one's own. The pair moves from the loss of the nearest help to an inference about everyone else, and Parimelazhagar gives both to the man, where the first eight verses of the chapter are the woman's.
links.reason: 1300 repeats 1299's frame (தாமுடைய நெஞ்சம் துணையல் வழி / தமரல் வழி) and extends it to ஏதிலார்; Parimelazhagar assigns both to the தலைமகன் (இதுவும் அது).

links.note: 188 asks what those who spread even the faults of their closest (துன்னியார்) will do to strangers (ஏதிலார் மாட்டு). 1300 argues that when one's own heart is not one's own, strangers (ஏதிலார்) not being one's own is a slight thing. Both reason from the nearest relation to ஏதிலார்: if the bond fails at the closest point, nothing can be expected further out.
links.reason: Both argue a fortiori from the nearest tie to ஏதிலார்: துன்னியார் குற்றமும் ... என்னைகொல் ஏதிலார் மாட்டு and நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி ... தமரல்லர் ஏதிலார். Same word and same logic in ethics and love.

links.note: 882 says do not fear enemies who are like swords, but fear the tie with enemies who are like kin (கேள்போல் பகைவர்). 1300 finds the same reversal inside one person: the heart that should be தமர், one's own people, is not, and beside that the distance of outsiders hardly counts. The lesson of the chapter on enmity within, that the danger is in what is closest, is applied in 1300 to the heart.
links.reason: Both use kin-terms (கேள்போல் பகைவர்; நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி), but 882 warns of an enemy disguised as kin while 1300 argues a fortiori that strangers' distance is nothing when one's own heart is not தமர்; no danger-from-the-closest is asserted in 1300, so 'the same reversal' overstates a loose likeness.

links.note: 1291 opens the chapter with the woman asking her heart why it is not hers when his heart is his own (நீ எமக்கு ஆகாதது). 1300 closes it with the general form: when one's own heart is not one's kin (நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி), it is nothing that strangers are not. Parimelazhagar gives the first to the woman and the last to the man, so the chapter begins and ends with the same complaint from each side.
links.reason: நீ எமக்கு ஆகாதது (1291) and தாமுடைய நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி (1300) are the same complaint that one's own heart is not one's own; Parimelazhagar does give 1291 to the woman and 1299-1300 to the man, as the note says.

links.note: 1301 has the friend urge the woman to hold back her embrace and sulk (புல்லாது இராப் புலத்தை) so they can watch his pain 'a little' (சிறிது). 1302 states the limit that word implies: sulking is like salt in right measure, and letting it run on (நீள விடல்) is like salt in excess. Parimelazhagar reads the சிறிது of 1301 as already pointing to this rule.
links.reason: 1301's சிறிது is given its measure by 1302's உப்பமைந்தற்றால் புலவி ... நீள விடல், and Parimelazhagar does say சிறிது is used because sulking must not be prolonged.

links.note: 1301 proposes not embracing (புல்லாது) in order to see his அல்லல்நோய். 1303 uses the same two words from the other side: leaving the one who sulks unembraced (புல்லா விடல்) is like giving அல்லல்நோய் to those already in distress (அலந்தாரை). Read together, the pain that 1301 treats as a brief test is the pain 1303 says must not be left standing.
links.reason: புல்லாது / புல்லா விடல் and அல்லல்நோய் are shared, but the sufferers differ: in 1301 the man suffers when the sulker withholds, in 1303 the sulker (புலந்தாரை) suffers when not embraced. The note's 'the pain of 1301 is the pain of 1303' blurs this.

links.note: In 1301 the friend wants the sulk kept up so that his suffering can be seen for a while. In 1329 the man himself wishes she would go on sulking (ஊடுக மன்னோ) and the night grow long so that he may keep pleading (யாம் இரப்ப). Both sides treat the sulk as something to prolong on purpose, hers to watch and his to beg.
links.reason: புல்லாது இராஅப் புலத்தை ... காண்கம் சிறிது and ஊடுக மன்னோ ... நீடுக மன்னோ இரா both want the sulk prolonged on purpose, from her side and from his.

links.note: 1302 gives the measure: a little sulking seasons, a little too long spoils. 1306 gives the two failures by name: without துனி and புலவி, love is like கனி and கருக்காய், which Manakkudavar reads as overripe fruit and unripe fruit. Together they make sulking a matter of degree, judged by taste, in both verses through a food image.
links.reason: உப்பமைந்தற்றால் புலவி ... சிறிது மிக்கற்றால் நீள விடல் and துனியும் புலவியும் இல்லாயின் காமம் கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று both gauge quarrelling by taste in a food figure; Manakkudavar does gloss rotten fruit and unripe fruit.

links.note: 1303 says that leaving unembraced those who have sulked (புலந்தாரைப் புல்லா விடல்) is like giving sharp pain to those already suffering (அலந்தாரை அல்லல்நோய் செய்தற்று). 1304 says that not appeasing those who sulk (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a withered creeper at the root (வாடிய வள்ளி முதல் அரிந்தற்று). The pair states one claim twice, once as added hurt and once as a finishing cut. Parimelazhagar takes both as the wife's taunt sending the man back to his other women.
links.reason: புலந்தாரைப் புல்லா விடல் = அலந்தாரை அல்லல்நோய் செய்தற்று and ஊடியவரை உணராமை = வாடிய வள்ளி முதலரிந்தற்று state one claim with two similes; Parimelazhagar's framing is reported correctly.

links.note: 1304 compares leaving a sulking lover unappeased to cutting an already withered creeper at its root (வாடிய வள்ளி முதல் அரிந்தற்று). 1030 says a family with no good man to prop it falls when trouble cuts it at the foot (இடுக்கண் கால் கொன்றிட வீழும்); Parimelazhagar takes this as an axe at the tree's base. Both picture a weakened plant that needed support and got the cut instead, once in love and once in the household.
links.reason: 1304 வாடிய வள்ளி முதலரிந் தற்று and 1030 இடுக்கண்கால் கொன்றிட வீழும் both cut a weakened plant at the base; Parimelazhagar's axe and family-as-tree reading of 1030 is reported correctly.

links.note: 1305, on Parimelazhagar's reading, has the man find beauty in her sulk even though he is good and blameless. 1321 gives her side: he has no fault (இல்லை தவறு அவர்க்கு), yet the way he shows tenderness (அவர் அளிக்குமாறு) is what makes sulking possible. Both verses detach the sulk from any real offence.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar on 1305 says sulking is sweet even to the blameless (தவறில்லார்க்கும்), and 1321 says இல்லை தவறவர்க்கு ஆயினும் ஊடுதல்; both separate the sulk from a real offence. The note marks its dependence on Parimelazhagar for 1305.

links.note: 1305 says that for men good in their qualities (நலத்தகை நல்லவர்க்கு) the beauty (ஏர்) is the sulking in flower-eyed women; Parimelazhagar reads this as 'even for the faultless, sulking is sweet'. 1325 says the same in plainer terms: though without fault (தவறிலர் ஆயினும்), being kept from the soft shoulders of the one they love has something in it (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). Manakkudavar reads 1305 differently, taking நல்லவர் as the other women.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does gloss 1305 as 'தவறில்லார்க்கும் புலவி இனிது', which matches 1325's தவறிலர் ஆயினும் ... ஆங்கொன் றுடைத்து; the note reports Manakkudavar's different reading.

links.note: 1306 puts it negatively: without quarrels, serious and light, love is fruit at the wrong stage. 1330 puts it positively: sulking is the pleasure of love (ஊடுதல் காமத்திற்கு இன்பம்), and the pleasure of sulking is the embrace that follows. The chapter 133 verse states as a conclusion what 1306 argues by image.
links.reason: துனியும் புலவியும் இல்லாயின் காமம் கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று (1306) and ஊடுதல் காமத்திற்கு இன்பம் (1330) make the same claim, by image and by direct statement.

links.note: 1307 finds a pain inside sulking (ஊடலின் உண்டு ஆங்கு ஓர் துன்பம்): the thought of whether union will be delayed or not. In 1152 the woman says union itself holds the misery of fearing separation (பிரிவு அஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு). In both, a state counted as pleasant carries worry about what comes next.
links.reason: ஊடலின் உண்டாங்கோர் துன்பம் (1307) and பிரிவஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு (1152) both find anticipatory worry inside a pleasurable state.

links.note: 1330 calls sulking the pleasure of love, provided the embrace follows (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). 1307 fastens on that proviso: because one cannot be sure the union will not be long delayed (புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல்), the sulk has its own pain. 1307 is the reservation built into 1330's praise.
links.reason: கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின் is the proviso in 1330 and புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல் in 1307 is the doubt about exactly that proviso.

links.note: 1308 asks what use it is to suffer where there is no lover who knows 'this one is hurt' (நொந்தார் என்று அஃது அறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி). 877, in the chapter on enemies, advises: do not voice your hurt to those who do not know you are hurt (நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு). The same roots நோ and அறி carry one rule in love and in statecraft: displayed pain is wasted on someone who does not perceive it.
links.reason: நோதல் எவன் ... அஃதறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி and நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு use the same roots நோ and அறி for the same point about pain shown to one who does not perceive it.

links.note: In 1308 suffering is pointless when the other does not know or care that one suffers. In 1200 the woman tells her heart that reporting its great pain to one who is not close (உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய்) is like trying to fill in the sea. Man and woman reach the same judgment from opposite sides of the couple.
links.reason: நோதல் எவன் ... அஃதறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி and உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய் கடலைச் செறாஅஅய் both judge pain spent on an unresponsive beloved to be futile, from the man's and the woman's side.

links.note: 1308 says the man's hurt is useless without a lover who recognises it. 1309 gives the general form: as water is sweet in shade, sulking is sweet only with those who love (வீழுநர் கண்ணே இனிது). Parimelazhagar assigns both to the man, in a sulk that she is not answering.
links.reason: Adjacent verses: நோதல் is pointless without காதலர் who அறியும் it, and புலவி is இனிது only வீழுநர் கண்ணே; 1309 generalises 1308 and Parimelazhagar's இதுவும் அது confirms one speaker.

links.note: 1309 limits the sweetness of sulking to those who love (வீழுநர் கண்ணே). 1323 asks whether any heaven matches sulking with those joined like water with earth (நிலத்தொடு நீர் இயைந்தன்னார் அகத்து). Both say the value of the sulk depends on the closeness of the two, and both use water to say it.
links.reason: புலவியும் வீழுநர் கண்ணே இனிது and புலத்தலின் புத்தேள்நாடு உண்டோ ... நீரியைந் தன்னார் அகத்து both tie the sweetness of sulking to the closeness of the pair, each with a water figure.

links.note: 1310 calls the heart's wish to join with one who neglects it mere craving. In 1255 the woman says the dignity of not going after those who have turned away (செற்றார் பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை) is something the love-sick do not know. Both admit that desire overrides self-respect toward an indifferent partner.
links.reason: 1310's கூடுவேம் என்பது அவா toward one who lets the sulk wither and 1255's செற்றார்பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை ... அறிவதொன்று அன்று both concede that desire defeats self-respect before a neglectful partner.

links.note: In 1310 the man, on Parimelazhagar's reading, says that his heart's intent to join with one who leaves him to wither in the sulk (ஊடல் உணங்க விடுவாரோடு) is just craving (அவா). In 1292 the woman scolds her heart for going to him even after seeing that he is not close to her (உறாஅதவர்க் கண்ட கண்ணும்). Each blames the heart for running to someone who has shown no care.
links.reason: என் நெஞ்சம் கூடுவேம் என்பது அவா and உறாஅதவர்க் கண்ட கண்ணும் ... சேறி என் நெஞ்சு both blame the heart for going toward one who withholds care; Parimelazhagar's என்றான் confirms the male speaker in 1310.

links.note: 1304 compares the unappeased sulker to a withered creeper (வாடிய வள்ளி) cut at the root. 1310 speaks of being left to dry up in the sulk (ஊடல் உணங்க விடுவார்). The wife's warning and the man's complaint use the same picture of a plant left without water; Parimelazhagar places 1310 in a sulk she does not answer.
links.reason: உணங்க (to languish, dry up) and வாடிய வள்ளி do share a sense of withering within the same chapter, but 1310 has no plant, and 1304's figure is cutting a creeper at the root (முதல் அரிந்தற்று), not leaving it without water. 'The same picture of a plant left without water' overstates a one-word echo.

links.note: In 1312 the woman says he sneezed while she was sulking, knowing (அறிந்து) she would have to say 'live long' and so speak to him. In 1253 the sneeze is the example of what happens without intention: desire comes out குறிப்பின்றித் தும்மல்போல். Parimelazhagar notes that 1312 treats a natural sneeze as a deliberate one, which is the subtlety the chapter title names.
links.reason: தும்மினார் ... அறிந்து (a sneeze read as deliberate) against குறிப்பின்றித் தும்மல்போல் (the sneeze as the type of the involuntary). Parimelazhagar's இயல்பான் நிகழ்ந்த தும்மலைக் குறிப்பான் நிகழ்ந்ததாகக் கோடலின் is as cited.

links.note: 1311 gives her stated ground: every woman takes him in with her eyes (கண்ணின் பொது உண்பர்). 1313 shows the same worry applied to a trifle: a wreath must have been put on to be shown to another woman (ஒருத்தியைக் காட்டிய சூடினீர்). Her jealousy in both is about who sees him.
links.reason: 1311's கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர் and 1313's ஒருத்தியைக் காட்டிய சூடினீர் both turn on other women seeing him, a general charge and then a trifling instance in the same chapter.

links.note: In 1313 the man reports that even wearing a wreath makes her angry (காயும்): 'you wore it to show some woman'. In 1321 the woman says he has no fault (இல்லை தவறு அவர்க்கு), yet his way of showing tenderness can bring on a sulk. 1321 supplies from her mouth what the man's complaints in chapter 132 imply: the grounds are invented.
links.reason: 1313 shows an accusation with no basis (ஒருத்தியைக் காட்டிய சூடினீர் என்று காயும்); 1321 has her say இல்லை தவறவர்க்கு yet his அளி can bring on ஊடுதல். Her admission supplies what his complaint implies.

links.note: In 1314 he says 'we love more than anyone' (யாரினும் காதலம்) and she turns it on him: 'than whom, than whom?' (யாரினும் யாரினும்). 645 advises speaking a word only after knowing there is no other word that can defeat it (வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து). The love scene shows that rule failing in a comic way: his own word, repeated back, is the one that beats him.
links.reason: யாரினும் யாரினும் (1314) is a jealous quibble in a lovers' sulk, not a counter-argument of the kind 645's வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து has in view; the note's 'rule failing' is an ingenious overlay with only a loose shared pattern.

links.note: In 1315 a promise limited to this birth (இம்மை) makes her weep. 107 says the good remember through all seven births (எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும் உள்ளுவர்) the friendship of those who removed their distress. Her complaint measures his promise against the span the book itself uses for lasting bonds.
links.reason: இம்மைப் பிறப்பில் against எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும்: her tears make sense against the book's own multi-birth span for a lasting bond, and the note claims no more than that.

links.note: In 1314 'more than anyone' is heard as implying other loves; in 1315 'we will not part in this birth' (இம்மைப் பிறப்பில் பிரியலம்) fills her eyes with tears, because she hears a parting in the next. Parimelazhagar describes the move in 1315: she takes a plain statement as a hinting one. Both verses turn a strong assurance into an offence by what it leaves unsaid.
links.reason: யாரினும் யாரினும் என்று ஊடினாள் and இம்மைப் பிறப்பில் பிரியலம் ... கண்நிறை நீர்கொண்டனள்: each assurance is heard for what it leaves unsaid, as Parimelazhagar's வெளிப்படு சொல்/குறிப்புச் சொல் remark confirms.

links.note: 1316 has her treat remembering as proof of forgetting. In 1207 the woman, alone, says she does not know forgetting (மறப்பறியேன்) and that even remembering burns. The standard she holds him to in 1316, never having forgotten at all, is the one she claims for herself in separation.
links.reason: உள்ளினேன் என்றேன் ... என்மறந்தீர் treats remembering as implying forgetting, and மறப்பறியேன் in 1207 is that same standard claimed by the woman for herself.

links.note: In 1312 she suspects his sneeze was a trick to get the customary 'live long' out of her. In 1317 she gives that blessing (வழுத்தினாள்) and at once takes it back (அழித்து அழுதாள்) with a new suspicion. One sneeze is read two ways in the chapter, as a stratagem and as proof of another woman.
links.reason: Same chapter, same sneeze motif: தும்மினார் ... நீடுவாழ்கென்பாக்கு அறிந்து in 1312, வழுத்தினாள் ... அழித்தழுதாள் in 1317; calling it 'one sneeze' is slightly loose but the reading holds.

links.note: In 1317 sneezing brings the charge that some woman is thinking of him. In 1318 he holds the sneeze back (தும்முச் செறுப்ப) and she weeps anyway: 'are you hiding from me that your people think of you?' (நுமர் உள்ளல் எம்மை மறைத்திரோ). The two verses close both exits: sneezing and not sneezing are both faults.
links.reason: தும்மினேனாக ... யாருள்ளித் தும்மினீர் (1317) and தும்முச் செறுப்ப அழுதாள் நுமர் உள்ளல் எம்மை மறைத்திரோ (1318) are consecutive and the second closes the remaining exit, as the note says.

links.note: In 1319 even his effort to appease her makes her angry (உணர்த்தினும் காயும்): 'you must be like this with others too'. 693 warns those who serve kings that once suspicion has arisen, clearing it is hard for anyone (கடுத்தபின் தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது). The court maxim and the bedroom scene describe the same trap: reassurance offered to a suspicious mind is taken as more evidence.
links.reason: உணர்த்தினும் காயும் and கடுத்தபின் தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது both say suspicion resists reassurance; 'taken as more evidence' is explicit only in 1319, a mild overstatement for 693.

links.note: 1304 says not appeasing one who sulks (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a withered creeper at the root. In 1319 he does appease her (தன்னை உணர்த்தினும்) and that too is a fault. Taken together, the man is blamed in chapter 131 for not doing what chapter 132 shows cannot be done to her satisfaction.
links.reason: 1304's ஊடியவரை உணராமை blames not appeasing and 1319's தன்னை உணர்த்தினும் காயும் shows appeasing also angering her, but 1319 is a comic complaint that does not limit 1304's claim, and Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take 1304's ஊடியவர் as other women, which the note ignores when it says the man is blamed for not appeasing her.

links.note: In 1311 her objection is to other women's eyes on him (கண்ணின் பொது உண்பர்). In 1320 it is to his eyes on her, which she thinks are really on another woman; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both explain that she supposes he is matching her limbs against someone else's. The chapter opens and closes on the look as the place where she locates unfaithfulness.
links.reason: கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர் (1311) and யாருள்ளி நோக்கினீர் (1320) both locate her grievance in a look, at the start and end of the chapter.

links.note: 1313, 1319 and 1320 share the frame '…even if I do X, she is angry (…இனும் காயும்), saying …'. In 1313 the act is wearing a wreath; in 1320 it is only sitting and looking at her (நினைத்திருந்து நோக்கினும்), which she takes as comparing her with someone (யார் உள்ளி நோக்கினீர்). The series runs from adornment down to a silent look, so that no act of his is left free of suspicion.
links.reason: சூடினும் காயும் (1313) and நோக்கினும் காயும் (1320) share the frame, each followed by her suspicious quotation ending என்று; the note describes both accurately.

links.note: In 1311 the woman refuses his chest because all women 'feast on it in common with their eyes' (கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்), a sulk with a stated ground. In 1321 she grants there is no fault at all and says his tenderness itself brings the sulk on; Parimelazhagar explains this as her thought that others too might receive that same tenderness. On his reading the jealousy of 1311 survives in 1321 with its ground removed.
links.reason: இல்லை தவறவர்க்கு ஆயினும் ஊடுதல் வல்லது அவர் அளிக்குமாறு; Parimelazhagar does explain it as the thought that others too would get this தலையளி, which ties it to கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர் in 1311, and the note attributes that to him.

links.note: In 1321 the woman says he has no fault (இல்லை தவறவர்க்கு), yet the way he shows tenderness (அவர் அளிக்குமாறு) is able to produce a sulk. In 1325 the man says that even when men are faultless (தவறிலர் ஆயினும்), being kept from the soft arms of the one they love 'has a certain something' (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). The chapter opens each speaker's side with the same concession: the sulk it praises needs no offence.
links.reason: 'இல்லை தவறவர்க்கு ஆயினும் ஊடுதல்' and 'தவறிலர் ஆயினும் ... அகறலின் ஆங்கொன் றுடைத்து' make the same concession from the woman's and the man's side.

links.note: Both verses use the rare word சிறுதுனி for a brief bad spell in something good. In 1010 the short want of the renowned rich is like the rain-cloud going dry (மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தனையது); in 1322 the small pain that sulking brings may make his good tenderness droop (நல்லளி வாடினும்), yet it gains worth (பாடு பெறும்). In each the dryness is temporary and belongs to a giver whose giving is not in doubt.
links.reason: சிறுதுனி occurs in both for a brief bad spell in something good: மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தனையது and நல்லளி வாடினும் பாடு பெறும். The shared sense is accurate.

links.note: 1322 says tenderness may wilt (வாடினும்) under the small pain of a sulk and still come to greatness. 1304 uses the same verb for the limit: not reconciling one who has sulked is like cutting an already wilted creeper at the root (வாடிய வள்ளி முதலரிந்தற்று). The wilting is harmless only if the sulk is ended; Parimelazhagar reads 1304 as the woman speaking of his other women.
links.reason: The shared verb is real (வாடினும்; வாடிய வள்ளி) but what wilts differs: his நல்லளி in 1322, the sulking woman figured as a creeper in 1304. The note's 'the wilting is harmless only if the sulk is ended' merges the two, and Manakkudavar construes 1322 differently.

links.note: 1306 says love without துனி and புலவி is like fruit over-ripe or unripe (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று), so some quarrel is needed. 1322 names the amount: only the 'small துனி' that arises in a sulk (ஊடலின் தோன்றும் சிறுதுனி), which leaves his tenderness greater even if it droops for a while. Parimelazhagar on 1306 takes துனி as the full-grown quarrel and புலவி as the young one, so 1322's சிறு marks the tolerable dose.
links.reason: 1306 requires both துனி and புலவி (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று) and 1322 specifies ஊடலின் தோன்றும் சிறுதுனி as the kind that leaves நல்லளி greater; Parimelazhagar's ripe/young quarrel gloss on 1306 is correctly reported.

links.note: 828 warns that a weapon lies hidden inside an enemy's hands folded in worship (தொழுதகையுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்), and his tears are the same. 1324 finds a weapon (படை) inside the lovers' sulk, which Parimelazhagar explains as the other's bowing and humble words. Submission as a concealed weapon is a danger to be detected in false friendship and, in love, the means by which the sulk is ended.
links.reason: படை in both; Parimelazhagar does gloss 1324's உள்ளம் உடைக்கும் படை as வணக்கமும் பணிமொழியும், matching 828's தொழுதகையுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும். The note states the dependence on the commentator.

links.note: 1251 says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted with shame (காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் நிறையென்னும் ... கதவு). 1324 uses the same verb for the resolve to keep sulking: a weapon arises that breaks the heart (உள்ளம் உடைக்கும் படை). What was a breach forced during separation in 1251 becomes, inside the sulk, a breaking that leads to the embrace that does not let go (புல்லி விடா).
links.reason: காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் ... கதவு (1251) and உள்ளம் உடைக்கும் படை (1324) share உடைக்கும் and an implement that breaks her resistance; the note reads both correctly, though same_image would fit as well.

links.note: Both verses turn on the same phrase, 'the soft arms of the one they love' (தாம்வீழ்வார் மென்றோள்). In 1103 sleeping on them is set against the world of the lotus-eyed one; in 1325 being kept away from them (அகறலின்), though one is faultless, 'has a certain something' (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). The repeated phrase shows the book's last chapter finding a pleasure in the very absence of what the first union praised.
links.reason: Both verses carry the identical phrase தாம்வீழ்வார் மென்றோள்; 1103 praises துயில் on them, 1325 finds ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து in அகறல் from them, as the note says.

links.note: 1325 says that being kept from her arms by a sulk has a pleasure of its own (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). 1307 says sulking also holds one pain: the thought of whether union will be delayed or not (புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல் என்று). Parimelazhagar gives both to the man, 1325 after the making up and 1307 during the sulk, so the pleasure of 1325 is one judged in hindsight.
links.reason: The qualification is real: 1325 'அகறலின் ஆங்கொன் றுடைத்து' against 1307 'ஊடலின் உண்டாங்கோர் துன்பம்'. But Parimelazhagar marks 1307 'இதுவும் அது', continuing 1305's occasion of the man speaking after the sulk is over, not during it, so the note's during/after contrast is not his.

links.note: In 1319 the man reports that even when he tries to appease her she is angry (உணர்த்தினும் காயும்), saying he is like this with others too: a complaint that he is blamed without cause. In 1325 he grants the same situation, a man without fault (தவறிலர் ஆயினும்) kept from her arms, and finds something to enjoy in it. The groundless sulks listed in chapter 132 are re-read as a pleasure in chapter 133.
links.reason: 1319 உணர்த்தினும் காயும் shows him blamed without cause, and 1325 தவறிலர் ஆயினும் ... அகறலின் ஆங்கொன்றுடைத்து finds a pleasure in exactly that situation.

links.note: 944 instructs: know that the earlier meal is digested (அற்றது அறிந்து) and eat only when thoroughly hungry (துவரப் பசித்து). 1326 says the digesting of what was eaten is sweeter than eating (உணலினும் உண்டது அறல் இனிது), and so sulking is sweeter than union. The chapter on medicine states as a rule of health what the man uses as his simile; Parimelazhagar on 1326 draws the same line, that one who eats when hungry eats more and with more relish.
links.reason: உண்டது அறல் இனிது (1326) uses as a simile what 944 gives as a rule (அற்றது அறிந்து ... துவரப் பசித்து). Parimelazhagar on 1326 does say பசித்துண்ணும்வழி மிக உண்ணலுமாய் இன்சுவைத்துமாம்.

links.note: 1326 ranks sulking above union: ஊடல் is sweeter than புணர்தல் for love. 1330 calls sulking love's pleasure but adds that the pleasure of the sulk itself lies in being able to come together and embrace (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). The closing verse makes the sulk's sweetness depend on the union that 1326 placed below it, as digestion has value for the next meal.
links.reason: 1326's புணர்தலின் ஊடல் இனிது is conditioned by 1330's அதற்கின்பம் கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்: the sulk's pleasure depends on the union it was ranked above.

links.note: 931 says not to want gambling even if you win, since what is won (வென்றதூஉம்) is like the hook a fish has swallowed. 1327 says that in a sulk the loser is the winner (தோற்றவர் வென்றார்). The two verses reverse the apparent result of a contest in opposite directions: the gambler's win is a loss that shows later, and the lover's loss is a win that shows later in union (கூடலிற் காணப்படும்).
links.reason: ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார் and வென்றதூஉம் தூண்டிற்பொன் மீன்விழுங்கி அற்று both invert a contest's apparent result, but in opposite directions and for unrelated reasons; the shared pattern is a clever abstraction more than a common logic.

links.note: 802 says intimate liberty is a limb of friendship and that 'being உப்பு to it' (அதற்கு உப்பாதல்) is the duty of the worthy; Parimelazhagar reads this as being pleasant toward that liberty. 1328 uses உப்பு for the savour of union after a sulk, which Parimelazhagar again glosses as sweetness. In both, salt stands for the relish that makes something a close companion does, a liberty or a sulk, enjoyable and not an offence.
links.reason: உப்பு is used for relish in both (அதற்கு உப்பாதல்; கூடலில் தோன்றிய உப்பு), a distinctive figure, and Parimelazhagar glosses both as sweetness.

links.note: In 1238 the man recalls that when he loosened the arms that embraced her, her forehead turned pale (பசந்தது ... பேதை நுதல்). In 1328 he recalls union so intense that her forehead sweated (நுதல் வெயர்ப்ப). Her forehead is the place where he reads both the first sign of separation and the fullness of union.
links.reason: நுதல் வெயர்ப்ப in union and பசந்தது ... பேதை நுதல் when the embrace loosens: the same man reads her forehead at both extremes. The note is accurate, though the forehead is a common site in these chapters.

links.note: 1052 says even begging is a pleasure to a person if what is begged for comes without pain (இன்பம் ஒருவற்கு இரத்தல்). In 1329 the man wants the sulk and the night prolonged so that he may beg (யாம் இரப்ப), treating the pleading itself as something to enjoy. Begging, which chapter 107 calls degrading, is here a pleasure because the giver is not in doubt, which is the condition 1052 sets.
links.reason: யாமிரப்ப நீடுக மன்னோ இரா treats pleading as enjoyable, and 1052 says இன்பம் ஒருவற்கு இரத்தல் when what is asked comes without pain; that the giver in 1329 'is not in doubt' is the note's inference, not in the verse.

links.note: 1307 names the one pain within sulking: the thought of whether union will be delayed or not (புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல்). 1329 wishes for that delay, asking that she keep sulking and the night grow long (ஊடுக ... நீடுக). Parimelazhagar gives both to the man, 1307 during a sulk and 1329 after one has ended well, so the delay feared in the moment is desired in retrospect.
links.reason: 1307's pain is புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல், and 1329 wishes ஊடுக ... நீடுக மன்னோ இரா; the same prolonging is feared in one and wished in the other, and the note's wording matches both.

links.note: 1302 says a sulk is like salt in the right amount, and letting it run long (நீள விடல்) is like a little too much. 1330 makes the sulk love's pleasure only if embrace follows (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). Parimelazhagar reads 1330's condition through this measure: the sulk must be ended at the right point, between a quarrel too ripe and one too young, and that is hard to judge.
links.reason: 1302 sets a measure for புலவி (உப்பமைந்தற்று; நீள விடல் is excess) and 1330 makes ஊடல்'s pleasure conditional on கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின். Parimelazhagar's gloss on 1330 (அளவறிந்து நீங்குதல் அரிது, between முதிர்ந்த துனி and முதிராத புலவி) is reported accurately.

links.note: 1330 says the sulk's own pleasure comes if the lovers get to unite and embrace (பெறின்). 1304 states the other case: not reconciling one who has sulked (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a wilted creeper at the root. The conditional in 1330 is a real one, and 1304 shows what a sulk is when the condition fails.
links.reason: 1330's condition கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின் is the case 1304 shows failing: ஊடியவரை உணராமை is வாடிய வள்ளி முதலரிந்தற்று. A real condition on the pleasure of sulking.

summary_full_run.run: Full run of docs/link-pass-plan.md over the 123 chapters outside the pilot, 2026-11-15 to 2026-11-16
summary_full_run.method: 62 Claude agents each took two chapters, read an index of all 1,330 readings, and proposed up to 3 links per verse after reading the Tamil, the commentaries, Pope and Subramuniyaswami's translation for both verses. Existing links were hidden from them. 34 other agents graded every pair not already in the graph, blind, with 5 unmarked known-grade links in each packet.
summary_full_run.limits: All proposers and graders are Claude without a Tamil lexicon. On the known-grade links the graders were mildly lenient, and they passed a larger share of the new proposals as sound than of links already known to be sound. A new link is unlikely to be better than a confirmed one, so the proposals' longer, more careful notes are probably raising grades. Treat a sound grade from this pass as weaker evidence than one from the earlier audits. No Tamil scholar has reviewed any of this.
